en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Single-Recitation Chapter of the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

The Introduction to the Work I pay homage to the Sugata, who is free from the cycle of rebirths, revered by the world of humans and gods, whose heart is cooled by compassion, and whose darkness of delusion has been dispelled by the lamp of wisdom.
“I revere that unsurpassed Dhamma which the Buddha— having developed and realized the state of Buddhahood— has attained, being free from all taints.
I revere the legitimate sons of the Sugata, those who crush the army of Māra.”
I pay homage with my head to the Noble Saṅgha, the assembly of all eight [types of noble ones].
Thus, by the power of this merit consisting of the worship of the Triple Gem performed by me with a clear mind— may my obstacles be thoroughly dispelled.
“For the sake of elucidating the meaning of the excellent Aṅguttara Nikāya— which is adorned with the Ekaka,
Duka, and so forth, and which generates diverse eloquence in the preeminent preachers of the Dhamma—
the commentary was composed from the beginning by the Vāsīṭṭhas.”
That which was chanted five times, and subsequently chanted again:
"It was brought to the island of Siṃhala by the great Mahinda, who was masterful;
it was established in the Sinhalese language for the benefit of the island-dwellers."
“Then, having set aside the delightful Sinhalese language, I composed [this work] in a faultless manner,
conforming to the principles of the *Tanti* (the canonical scriptures).
Without violating the tradition of the Elders who are the lamps of the lineage of the Theras, I have maintained the *Samaya* (the established doctrine).”
For those who dwell in the Mahāvihāra and possess subtle discernment:
“Having abandoned the matter that has been repeatedly approached,
I shall elucidate the meaning for the sake of the satisfaction of virtuous people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma.”
“The description of Sāvatthī and other cities has already been given below by me while explaining the meaning of the Long and the Middle [Nikāyas].
Indeed, the specific accounts that were told there have been related in detail.”
There is nothing further here concerning them, though I shall provide a detailed exposition.
However, as for those meanings of the suttas which are not revealed without their underlying narratives (vatthu),
I shall also present those narratives in order to clarify them.
“The discourse on virtue, the ascetic qualities, and all the meditation subjects;
the detailed exposition of the jhānas and attainments together with the methods for conduct;
all the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and the compendium of the calculation of wisdom.”
The aggregates, elements, bases, and faculties, as well as the four noble truths;
the teaching on the mode of conditions, which is perfectly pure and subtle in its method;
the lineages of liberation and the paths, as well as the cultivation of insight.
“Since all this has been very thoroughly explained by me in the *Visuddhimagga*,
I shall not discuss it further here. Indeed,
this *Visuddhimagga* stands in the midst of the four Āgamas.”
"Having established it, he will clarify the meaning as it was spoken therein.
Therefore, having taken both this [text] together with that commentary,
you should understand the meaning based on the *Aṅguttara*."
Summary Discourse 1.
Explanation of the Chapter on Form and so forth (Rūpādivagga).
Therein, the Aṅguttara Āgama consists of the Ekaka-nipāta, Duka-nipāta, Tika-nipāta, Catukka-nipāta, and Pañcaka-nipāta.

There are eleven nipātas: the Chakkanipāta (Sixfold Chapter), Sattakanipāta (Sevenfold Chapter), Aṭṭhakanipāta (Eightfold Chapter), Navakanipāta (Ninefold Chapter), Dasakanipāta (Tenfold Chapter), and Ekādasakanipāta (Elevenfold Chapter).
As for the number of suttas: "Nine thousand suttas, and five hundred suttas..."
“There are fifty-seven suttas in the Aṅguttara Āgama.
Among its sections (nipātas), the Ekaka-nipāta is the first; among the suttas, the Cittapariyādāna-sutta is the first.

Furthermore, the introduction beginning with “Thus have I heard” (evam me sutaṃ), spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the first. Now, as for that First Great Council:
This has been explained in detail at the beginning of the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*; therefore, it should be understood according to the method set forth therein.
Regarding the introduction (*nidāna*) beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*): herein, *evaṃ* is a particle (*nipāta*), while *me* and so forth—
These are the names and phrases. Regarding the expression "dwells at Sāvatthī": here, *vi* is a prepositional phrase (*upasaggapada*), and *harati* is a verbal phrase (*ākhyātapada*);
in this manner, first of all, the analysis of the phrases is to be understood.
As for the meaning, the word *evaṃ* (thus) has many distinct senses, such as comparison, indication, encouragement, reproach, acceptance, manner, illustration, and restriction.
For instance, this [term *evaṃ*] occurs as a simile in such passages as: “Thus, by a mortal who has been born, much wholesome [deed] must be done.
It occurs as an instruction in such passages as: “In this way you should advance; in this way you should retreat. It occurs as encouragement in such passages as:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. And it occurs in such passages as: “In this very way, O outcaste, whether in this or that [place]...”
In such passages as, “He speaks in praise of that shaveling ascetic,” it is used in the sense of censure.
In such passages as, “‘Yes, venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One,” it is used in the sense of assent.

In such passages as, “‘It is in this way, venerable sir, that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,’” it is used in the sense of manner. [And in such passages as,] “Come, young man, go to where the ascetic...”

“Ānanda, go to him; having approached, in my name ask the ascetic Ānanda whether he is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort—‘The young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, asks whether the venerable Ānanda is free from illness...
[and so on] ...dwelling in comfort. And say this: ‘It would be well indeed if the venerable Ānanda...”
In such passages as, "Let him approach the residence of the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, out of compassion," it is used as an illustration.
"What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these states wholesome or unwholesome?
"Unwholesome, venerable sir. "Are they blameworthy or blameless? "Blameworthy, venerable sir. "Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise?"
“Does it blow? “It does, venerable sir. “When fully undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering or not?
What is your view in this matter? “When fully undertaken and practiced, venerable sir, they lead to harm and suffering;

such is our view in this matter,” and so on—in these cases, it is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). And here, it should be understood as being used in the senses of manner, indication, and emphasis.
Therein, by means of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) in the sense of manner, he illuminates this meaning: the speech of that Blessed One— in its every aspect—

is skillful in various methods, originated from manifold inclinations, endowed with both meaning and phrasing, possessed of diverse wonders, profound in its penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, and the teaching,
and reaching the range of hearing for all beings according to each one's own language.
Who is capable of knowing [this]? Nevertheless, having generated a desire to hear with all one's might, one says, "Thus have I heard; it was heard by me too in this manner.

By way of illustration, saying "I am not self-become, nor has this been realized by me," he liberates himself and indicates the entire discourse that is now to be spoken with the words, "Thus have I heard; it was heard by me too in this manner."
In the sense of definitive determination, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are learned:
namely, Ānanda; among those who possess mindfulness, those who possess intelligence, those who possess fortitude, and among attendants, namely, Ānanda.
Thus [he spoke]. Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda was skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in the phrasing, and skilled in etymological interpretation.

By thus demonstrating his own power of retention in accordance with the state of being praised by the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) as one "skilled in what precedes and what follows," he generates in beings a desire to hear:
"Thus have I heard; and that indeed, whether in meaning or in phrasing, is neither deficient nor redundant—it is exactly so and must not be viewed otherwise."
The particle *me* is seen in three senses. For instance, in such passages as “*Gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyan*,” its meaning is “by me.
In such passages as “*Sādhu me, bhante, Bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū*,” its meaning is “to me.
In such passages as “*Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavathā*,” its meaning is “my. But here, however, [it means] “by me.”
The word *suta* is applicable to two meanings: "heard" and "my own.

This term *suta*, whether with a prefix (*sa-upasagga*) or without a prefix (*an-upasagga*), is divided into many distinct meanings, such as: going, renowned, moistened, accumulated, application, cognizable by the ear, and that which is known by following the door of the ear.

For instance, in phrases such as *senāya pasuto* ("gone forth with the army"), the meaning is "going. In phrases such as *sutadhammassa passato* ("of one who sees the Dhamma heard"), [the meaning is "heard"].
The meaning is "of one who is well-known for the Dhamma. In such phrases as "the lustful toward the lustful," the meaning is "the defiled toward the defiled.
In such phrases as "by you, abundant merit has been accumulated," the meaning is "accumulated. In such phrases as "those wise ones intent on jhāna," the meaning is "devoted to jhāna.
In such phrases as "seen, heard, and sensed," the meaning is "to be cognized by the ear. "One who retains what is heard..."
In such passages as “one who has accumulated what was heard,” the meaning is “one who has cognized [the teaching] following the ear-door.

Here, however, the meaning is either “that which has been apprehended by means of the ear-door” or “the act of apprehending. For when the word *me* (by me) has the sense of *mayā* (by me), it is appropriate to say:
“Thus have I heard—that is, it has been apprehended by me by means of the ear-door. When it has the sense of *mama* (my), it is [appropriate to say]: “Thus my...”
"It is heard" (*sutaṃ*) is appropriate as "retention following the ear-door.
Thus, among these three terms, *evaṃ* indicates the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness; *me* indicates the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness;
and *sutaṃ* indicates a grasping that is neither deficient nor excessive and is non-perverted, by way of negating the state of not having heard. Likewise, *evaṃ*.
This is the explanation of how the stream of consciousness, proceeding through the door of the ear, engages with its object in various ways.
“By me” (*meti*) is an expression of the self. “Heard” (*sutanti*) is an expression of the Dhamma. Herein, this is the summary:
“Nothing else was done by me regarding the stream of consciousness proceeding in various ways toward its object; rather, this was done: ‘this Dhamma was heard.’”

"Tathā" (thus) is the manifestation of that which is to be demonstrated. "Evaṃ" (so) is the manifestation of the person. "Sutaṃ" (heard) is the manifestation of the person's function. This is what is meant: "That discourse which I shall demonstrate, that was heard by me thus.
Likewise, "tathā evaṃ" is the demonstration of the various modes of that mental continuum through which there occurs the grasping of diverse meanings and phrasing;
for "evaṃ" is a designation of mode. "Me" is the designation of the agent. "Sutaṃ" is the designation of the object.
To this extent, by means of the mental continuum proceeding in various modes, the determination of grasping the object is accomplished for the agent who possesses that [continuum].

Alternatively, "thus" (*evaṃ*) is a designation for the function of the person (*puggala*); "heard" (*sutaṃ*) is a designation for the function of consciousness (*viññāṇa*); and "by me" (*me*) is a designation for the person endowed with both functions.
Herein, the summary is as follows: by me, a person possessing the consciousness whose function is hearing, by way of consciousness...
The word *suta* (heard) is used here by way of conventional designation for the function of hearing.
In that context, both *evaṃ* (thus) and *me* (to me) are designations of what does not exist from the standpoint of the true and ultimate sense (*saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*).
For what is there here, in the ultimate sense, that could receive the designation "thus" or "to me"? The word *suta*, however, is a designation of what does exist.

For that which is apprehended here by the ear exists in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*). It is a designation by way of clinging (*upādāpaññatti*), because it must be spoken of in dependence upon this or that [object], such as "thus" and "mine.
It is a designation by way of comparison (*upanidhāpaññatti*), because it is spoken of in comparison with what has been seen and so forth, such as "heard.
And here, by the word "thus," he illustrates non-delusion; for one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating things in their various aspects.
"Has been heard. By the word "heard," he demonstrates the non-forgetfulness of what has been heard.
For one whose learning has been forgotten does not, after some time, claim, "I have heard this. Thus, through non-delusion, wisdom (*paññā*) is established;

through non-forgetfulness, however, mindfulness (*sati*) is established. In that regard, there is the capacity for grasping the phrasing through mindfulness preceded by wisdom; [and] through mindfulness preceded by...

It is the capacity for penetrating the meaning by means of wisdom. Through the conjunction of the capacity for both [meaning and phrasing], there is the accomplishment of being a "steward of the Dhamma," because of the capacity to preserve the treasury of the Dhamma which is endowed with both meaning and phrasing.
According to another method: by the word "thus" (evam), he illuminates wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), for one who attends unwise to things lacks the penetration of various aspects.
By the word "heard" (suta), he demonstrates non-distraction, because one whose mind is distracted lacks the capacity for hearing.
For indeed, even when a person with a distracted mind is told of every kind of excellence, he says, "I have not heard it; say it again.
And herein, through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), he accomplishes his own right aspiration as well as his prior performance of merit, provided that his mind is rightly directed.

Or because of the absence of that [merit] in one who has not previously performed merit. Likewise, through non-distraction, one accomplishes the hearing of the True Dhamma and reliance upon a true person.
For one whose mind is distracted is unable to hear, and there is no hearing for one who does not rely upon a true person.
Another method: because "thus" refers to the grasping of various meanings and phrasing through the occurrence of diverse modes within the continuum of consciousness.

It is said: “There is [this], and this is the description of its various aspects. Furthermore, such a noble aspect does not belong to one who has not previously performed merit for the sake of making oneself free from desire (*appaṇihita*).

Therefore, by the word “thus” (*evaṃ*), he illustrates his own attainment of the latter two wheels through this noble aspect. By the word “heard” (*suta*), he illustrates the attainment of the former two wheels through the application of hearing;
for it is not possible for one living in an unsuitable place [to attain them].

Nor can there be hearing for one who lacks reliance upon true persons (*sappurisa*). Thus, through the accomplishment of the latter two wheels, the purity of disposition (*āsaya-suddhi*) is established;

and through the accomplishment of the former two wheels, the purity of application (*payoga-suddhi*) is established. By that purity of disposition, the excellence of realization (*adhigama-vyatti*) is accomplished;

by the purity of application, the excellence of scripture (*āgama-vyatti*) is accomplished. Thus, for one whose application and disposition are pure, and who is endowed with both scripture and realization—

Just as the dawn precedes the rising of the sun, and just as wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) precedes wholesome action (*kusalakamma*), the introductory setting (*nidāna*) is placed so that it may serve as a precursor to the Blessed One’s words; thus he said, "Thus have I heard," and so forth.

According to another method: by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which indicates various modes of penetration, [the author] demonstrates the existence within himself of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) regarding meaning (*attha*) and eloquence (*paṭibhāna*).

He illuminates. By the word "heard" (*suta*), which indicates the penetration of the various things to be heard, he demonstrates the possession of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) regarding the Dhamma and its terminology.
And by speaking this word "thus" (*evaṃ*), which indicates wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), he demonstrates:
"These teachings have been examined by me with the mind and well-penetrated through right view. By speaking this word "heard," which indicates application to listening...
He declares: “Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and mastered by word.
By both of these [statements], he demonstrates the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing, thereby generating respect for listening.

For one who does not listen with respect to a teaching that is perfect in meaning and phrasing is excluded from great benefit; thus, having generated respect, the Dhamma should be heard with careful attention.
By this entire phrase, "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda, by not attributing the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata to himself, transcends the plane of the unworthy person;
and by professing his status as a disciple, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he withdraws the mind from what is not the true Dhamma and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma. "Only..."
By declaring, "This has indeed been heard by me, and it is the word of that very Blessed One," he liberates himself,
refers to the Teacher, applies himself to the word of the Victor, and establishes the guide of the Dhamma. Furthermore,
by saying "Thus have I heard," he does not claim the state of having produced [the teaching] himself, but rather elucidates the prior discourse.
“This was received by me directly from that Blessed One— the one confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, the possessor of the ten powers, the one who stands in the place of the bull,
the roarer of the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma,
the Wheel-Turner of the sublime True Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
“Regarding this speech, no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained concerning its meaning, its doctrine, its words, or its phrasing.
Thus, it destroys lack of faith in this Dhamma among all gods and humans and generates the perfection of faith. Therefore, this is said:
“It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching;”
"Thus have I heard"—thus speaks this disciple of Gotama.
"Ekaṃ" (one) is a designation for a numerical limit. "Samayaṃ" (at one time) is a designation for a delimited occasion. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time) is an indication of an unspecified [occasion].
In this context, the word *samaya*—in the sense of assembly, moment, time, collection, cause, and view; [is used]."
"It is seen in the sense of acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as "Perhaps tomorrow we might approach him, taking into account the time and the occasion," the meaning is *samavāya* (conjunction).
However, in such passages as "There is, monks, only one moment and one occasion for the living of the holy life (*brahmacariya*)," [the meaning is different].
*Moment*: In such passages as “the time of heat,” “the time of feverish distress,” and so forth, it means *time*. In such passages as “The great assembly in the forest,” it means *multitude*.
[In the passage: “Indeed, Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate this point: ‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī;
the Blessed One will know me as the bhikkhu named Bhaddāli who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation’—this too... [it means time].
In such passages as, "Now, Bhaddāli, that time had not yet been penetrated by you," it refers to the cause (*hetu*). In such passages as, "Now at that time,
the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta was staying in Mallikā’s Park, in the single-hall Tindukācīra grove,
where they discuss various doctrines," it refers to a view (*diṭṭhi*).

In such passages as, “The goal that is in this very life, and the goal pertaining to the future life—the wise person who realizes these goals is called ‘learned,’” it refers to acquisition (*paṭilābha*).

In such passages as, “Through the realization of conceit, he brought an end to suffering,” it refers to abandonment (*pahāna*). [And] in the case of “of suffering... [it refers to full understanding].
In such passages as “the sense of oppression, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of change, the sense of convergence,” it means penetration.

Here, however, its meaning is time (*kāla*). By this, he indicates one particular occasion (*samaya*) among the various divisions of time, such as years, seasons, months, half-months, nights, days, forenoon, midday, afternoon, the first watch, middle watch, last watch, and moments.

In this regard, although among these years and so forth, whatever discourse was spoken in whichever year, season, month, fortnight, portion of the night, or portion of the day—all that was well-known and well-determined by the Elder through his wisdom. For he [knew]:
"Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight..."
When it is stated thus, "on such a portion of a night or on such a portion of a day," it is not possible to easily memorize,
recite, or cause others to recite it, and much would have to be said; therefore, condensing that meaning into a single phrase,
he said, "at one time."

Furthermore, there are these various occasions of the Blessed One among gods and humans— such as the occasion of his descent into the womb, the occasion of his birth, the occasion of his spiritual urgency,

the occasion of his great renunciation, the occasion of his practice of austerities, the occasion of his victory over Māra, the occasion of his full enlightenment, the occasion of his dwelling in happiness in this very life, the occasion of his teaching, and the occasion of his final Nibbāna—
which are exceedingly well-known and distinguished by many different times.

Among those times, he illuminates one specific time known as the "time of teaching. Furthermore, among the times for the functions of wisdom and compassion, it is the time for the function of compassion;

among the times for practicing for one's own welfare and the welfare of others, it is the time for practicing for the welfare of others; among the times for the two duties of those who have assembled, it is the time for a discourse on the Dhamma;
and among the times for the practice of teaching, it is the time of teaching. Among these as well—
Referring to one among the various occasions, he said, "at one time. But why, in this case,
is there not an indication using the locative case— as in the Abhidhamma expression, "at whatever time [a state] belonging to the sense-sphere," and in other Sutta passages such as,
"Bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures"?
In the Vinaya, the description was made using the instrumental case, as in the expression, “At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One...”;

yet here, instead of doing so, the description is made using the accusative case, as in “at one time. This is because the meaning is possible both there [in the Abhidhamma] and here, though in different ways.

For in that context—the Abhidhamma—and in other Sutta passages besides this one, the sense is locative (the sense of a location), whereas here the sense is that of a characteristic of existence through existence (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇattha).
And it is possible [to explain it thus]: for "occasion" (*adhikaraṇa*) has the sense of time and the sense of a collection (*samūha*).

By means of the existence of those phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) mentioned therein, and by means of the existence of the "occasion" (*samaya*)—which is reckoned as the momentary conjunction of causes—their own existence is characterized.
Therefore, in order to indicate that meaning, the locative case is employed in the description.
In the Vinaya, both the sense of cause (*hetu*) and the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) are possible.

For that time at which the training rules were laid down was difficult to discern even for Sāriputta and others; thus, by means of that time as a cause and as an instrument, the Blessed One, while laying down the training rules and having regard for the reason for laying down those training rules, dwelt here and there.
Therefore, it is for the purpose of illustrating that meaning [that this is stated].
In that case, the designation was made using the instrumental case.
However, here and in other similar instances, the sense of absolute conjunction (*accantasaṃyoga*) is possible.
For at whatever time the Blessed One taught this or another discourse, he dwelt at that very time in an abiding of compassion. Therefore...
The use of the accusative case here is made for the purpose of illustrating that meaning. Therefore, it is said:
"Depending on various meanings, [the grammatical relation] is expressed by the locative and the instrumental;
elsewhere it is called 'time' (samaya), but here it is expressed by the accusative."
The Ancients, however, explain: “At that time,” “by that time,” or “at one time”—these are merely differences in expression;
in all cases, the meaning is simply the locative case. Therefore, even when “at one time” is said, it should be understood to mean “at one [particular] time.”

"Bhagavā" means venerable (*garu*). For in the world they call one who is venerable "Bhagavā. And since he is venerable to all beings because of his preeminence in all virtues, he should be understood as "Bhagavā.
It has also been said by the ancients: "Bhagavā" is the best word; "Bhagavā" is the supreme word.
He is venerable and worthy of reverence; therefore he is called "Bhagavā."
Furthermore:
"He is fortunate, he has overcome [defilements], he is endowed with [glories], he possesses the [eight] fortunes;
he is one who has enjoyed [the world], who has vomited out [craving], and who has gone beyond all states of existence—therefore he is the Blessed One (Bhagavā)."

The detailed meaning of this term should be understood according to this verse as well; it has already been explained in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati-niddesa*).
To this extent, by stating "Thus have I heard" (*evam me sutaṃ*), he demonstrates the Dhamma exactly as it was heard and makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One manifest. By this, [he shows]:
"This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this is your Teacher."
He consoles the people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher.
By the phrase "at one time the Blessed One," he demonstrates the Blessed One's absence at that time, thereby establishing the parinibbāna of the physical body (rūpakāya). By this, [he shows]:
"Even such a teacher of the noble Dhamma, the possessor of the ten powers, whose body was like a mass of thunderbolts—he too..."
"The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna; by what other means could hope for life be generated?"—thus he inspires those intoxicated with the pride of life and rouses them toward the True Dhamma.
By saying "Thus," he points out the excellence of the teaching (*desanā-sampatti*); by "heard by me" (*me sutaṃ*), the excellence of the disciple (*sāvaka-sampatti*);
by "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*), the excellence of the time (*kāla-sampatti*); and by "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*), the excellence of the teacher (*desaka-sampatti*).

"At Sāvatthī" means in the city of that name. This locative case is used here in the sense of proximity. "Dwells" (*viharati*) is a general indication of one who possesses any particular dwelling among the postures, the divine dwellings, the brahma-dwellings, or the noble dwellings.
Here, however, it indicates association with one of the postures distinguished as standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One dwells even when standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
For he maintains and carries his personal existence (attabhāva) without it falling, having interrupted the obstruction of one posture with another;
thus, he is said to "dwell" (viharati).
"At Jeta’s Grove" means in the grove of Prince Jeta. For that [grove] was planted, nurtured, and protected by him, and he was its owner;
therefore, it became known as "Jeta’s Grove," and it was in that Jeta’s Grove.

"In Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery" means in the monastery belonging to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, which [he acquired] by the relinquishment of fifty-four crores of gold for the sake of the Buddha and his retinue.
"In the monastery belonging to Anāthapiṇḍika, which had been dedicated to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, is stated in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*, in the explanation of the *Sabbāsava Sutta*.
Therein it might be asked: "If the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, then it should not be said 'in Jeta’s Grove'."
If he were dwelling there [in Sāvatthī], it could not be said that he was "in Sāvatthī," for it is impossible to dwell in two places at one time.
However, this should not be viewed in such a way. Have we not already stated that "the locative case is used in the sense of proximity"?
Therefore, just as when herds of cattle are grazing near the Ganges or the Yamunā, they are said to be "grazing on the Ganges" or "on the Yamunā,"...
Just as those who move about are called "wandering," so too here, when he dwells at Jetavana near Sāvatthī,
he is said to "dwell at Sāvatthī in Jetavana. For the mention of Sāvatthī is for the purpose of indicating the village of his alms-round,
while the remaining words are for the purpose of indicating a place of residence suitable for one who has gone forth.

In this context, by the mention of Sāvatthī, the Venerable Ānanda demonstrates the Blessed One’s support for householders; by the praise of Jetavana and so forth, he demonstrates his support for those who have gone forth.
Likewise, by the former [mention], there is the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification through the acceptance of the four requisites;
by the latter, there is the demonstration of the means for avoiding devotion to sensual pleasure through the abandoning of sense-objects. By the former...
And by the former [verse], the application to the teaching of the Dhamma; by the latter, the inclination toward seclusion.
By the former, the approach through compassion; by the latter, the withdrawal through wisdom. By the former, the inclination toward accomplishing the welfare and happiness of beings;
by the latter, the state of being untainted while effecting the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, the comfortable dwelling characterized by not abandoning righteous happiness.

The former [is] the sign of application to superhuman states; the latter, the sign of application to states beyond those of ordinary men. By the former, there is the great benefit to human beings; by the latter, to deities.
By the former, the state of being born in the world and having grown up in the world;
by the latter, the state of being unsullied by the world. By the former: "Monks, one person, arising in the world, arises for the welfare of many people..."
"for the welfare of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
From this statement, [the first verse] refers to the accomplishment of that purpose for which the Blessed One appeared;
the latter [verse] refers to the dwelling appropriate to the place where he appeared. For the Blessed One, first in the Lumbinī grove, and secondly...
Regarding "the seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*): it arose in the forest itself because of its arising as both mundane and supramundane.
Therefore, by such a method as this, the application of the meaning here should be understood as showing that his dwelling was indeed in the forest.
In that context, "there" (*tatra*) is an indication of place and time; for it means "at whatever time he dwells," and "in whichever monastery."
He dwells there; thus he indicates the monastery. Or rather, he indicates it as being appropriate to the place and time for what is to be spoken.
For the Blessed One does not speak the Dhamma at an inappropriate place or time. In this regard, the passage beginning with "It is not the right time, Bāhiya," serves as proof.

The particle *kho* is a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*), a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*), or to indicate the beginning of a time (*ādikāla*). The term *Bhagavā* is an indication of one who is revered by the world.

"Bhikkhus" is a term for persons engaged in listening to discourse. Furthermore, the meaning of the word here should be understood according to such methods as: "A bhikkhu is so called because he is a beggar (bhikkhaka); he is a bhikkhu because he has entered upon the practice of begging.

"Addressed" means he spoke to them, he talked to them, he called out to them; this is the meaning here. Elsewhere, however, it also occurs in the sense of making known. As it is said: "I address you..."

“Monks, I declare this to you, monks. Also regarding the calling [of someone]: as it is said, “Come, monk, address Sāriputta in my name. The word “monks” (*bhikkhave*) is an illustration of the manner of addressing;
and that is stated because of his accomplishment through the possession of qualities such as the habit of begging (*bhikkhana-sīla*).

For those skilled in grammar consider that a *bhikkhu* is one endowed with the quality of the habit of begging, a *bhikkhu* is one endowed with the quality of the nature of begging, and a *bhikkhu* is one endowed with the quality of performing begging well.

And by means of that expression established through the conjunction of qualities such as the habit of begging, he reveals the mode of livelihood practiced by people both low and high, thereby effecting a restraint against the states of arrogance and dejection. Thus: "O monks."
With these words, preceded by the casting of glances from eyes that are gentle and expansive with the outpouring of compassion, he brings them face-to-face with his own countenance.
And by those very words, which signal his desire to speak, he generates in them a desire to hear.
Furthermore, by means of that very form of address, he enjoins them to listen and attend with great care; for the success of the Dispensation depends upon listening and attending with care.
If it is asked: "Since other gods and humans were also present, why did he address only the bhikkhus?"—it is because they were the eldest, the most excellent, and those who were constantly near him.

For the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to the entire assembly; and among that assembly, the bhikkhus are the eldest because they were the first to arise [in the dispensation], and they are the most excellent because, beginning from their state as homeless renunciants, they followed the Teacher’s conduct and received the entirety of the Dispensation.
Furthermore, they were near him while sitting there because of their proximity to the Teacher; they were always in his presence because of their constant attendance upon the Teacher.
Moreover, he addressed them specifically as those who are fit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, owing to the existence of the practice exactly as instructed.
But for what purpose did the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, first address the bhikkhus rather than teaching the Dhamma directly?

It is for the purpose of generating mindfulness. For monks may be sitting there thinking of something else, with distracted minds, reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to their meditation subject; if the Dhamma were taught without addressing them, they would be unable to observe:
"What is the source of this teaching? What is its condition? On account of what occasion (aṭṭhuppatti) has it been taught?"
They might grasp it wrongly, or they might not grasp it at all. Therefore, for the purpose of arousing mindfulness in them, the Blessed One first addresses them and subsequently teaches the Dhamma.
"Venerable Sir" (Bhadante) is a term of respect, or it is the giving of a reply to the Teacher. Moreover, here [the word] "monks" (bhikkhave)—
The Blessed One, speaking, addressed those bhikkhus. Saying “Venerable sirs,” they replied to the Blessed One.
Thus the Blessed One spoke first, saying “Bhikkhus,” and they replied, saying “Venerable sirs.
He caused them to give the response “Bhikkhus,” and they gave the response “Venerable sirs. “Those bhikkhus” refers to those whom the Blessed One addressed.
*Te Bhagavato paccassosuṃ*: they replied to the Blessed One; that is to say, having turned toward him, they listened, accepted, and received the Blessed One’s address.
*Bhagavā etadavoca*: the Blessed One spoke this entire discourse which was now to be spoken.
And up to this point, that which was [requested] by the Venerable Ānanda for the sake of easy comprehension of this sutta...
The introduction (*nidāna*), adorned by the factors of time, place, teacher, assembly, and location, has been spoken; the commentary on its meaning is now complete.
Now follows the commentary on form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates, beginning with the passage: "Monks, I do not perceive even a single form... as set forth by the Blessed One.

The opportunity for the commentary on the Sutta has now arrived. Since this commentary on the Sutta becomes clear only when spoken after investigating the occasion for the Sutta's delivery (*suttanikkhepa*), the investigation into that occasion must first be understood. For there are four occasions for the delivery of a Sutta:

one arising from the Teacher’s own inclination (*attajjhāsaya*), one arising from another’s inclination (*parajjhāsaya*), one prompted by a question (*pucchāvasika*), and one arising from a specific circumstance (*aṭṭhuppattika*). Among these, those Suttas which the Blessed One—
Without being requested by others, he spoke solely out of his own inclination, such as the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, the *Vattha Sutta*, and so forth;
these are examples of "deposition through one's own inclination. However, those [teachings] such as, "Rāhula’s qualities conducive to the ripening of liberation have indeed matured;
what if I were now to train Rāhula further for the destruction of the taints?"—these are "depositions through another's inclination."

Thus, having observed the inclinations, patience, intentions, aspirations, and capacity for understanding of others, [the teachings] were spoken according to the inclinations of others—such as the *Rāhulovāda Sutta*, the *Dhammacakkappavattana*, and so forth; the "deposition" (*nikkhepa*) of these is according to the inclinations of others.
However, when various gods and humans approached the Blessed One, they [requested them] in such and such ways...

They ask questions. Regarding those discourses spoken by the Blessed One when thus questioned—such as those connected with deities (*devatāsaṃyutta*) or those connected with the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta*)—their placement is "occasioned by a question" (*pucchāvasika*).

However, regarding those spoken in dependence on a specific circumstance that has arisen—such as the *Dhammadāyāda-sutta* or the simile of the son’s flesh (*puttamaṃsūpama*)—their placement is "occasioned by a particular incident" (*aṭṭhuppattika*).
Thus, among these four modes of placement (*nikkhepa*), this sutta belongs to the category of being "inclined toward another" (*parajjhāsaya*).
This is a formal placement (nikkhepa). For this has been placed by way of the underlying intention (adhiḷāsaya) of others. Of whom’s intention? That of men who are heavy with regard to forms.
Therein, in the phrases beginning with “I say not, O bhikkhus,” the negative particle (*na*) has the sense of negation.
“I” refers to himself. “O bhikkhus” is an address to the bhikkhus. “Another” means other than the female form that is about to be described. “Even a single form” means even one form.
"Contemplates" (*samanupassāmīti*) refers to two kinds of contemplation: contemplation by means of knowledge (*ñāṇa-samanupassanā*) and contemplation by means of view (*diṭṭhi-samanupassanā*).

Among these, "he contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent" is called contemplation by means of knowledge. However, "he contemplates form as self," and so forth, is called contemplation by means of view.
Of these two, it is contemplation by means of knowledge that is intended here.
[This is] what is intended. Furthermore, the connection with the letter *na* of this word should be understood. For this is what is meant:
"Bhikkhus, even when looking with the knowledge of omniscience, I do not perceive even a single form (*rūpa*) other than this.
[The phrase] "which thus remains, having taken possession of a man's mind" refers to that form which, for a man who values form, remains obsessing his mind.
It remains having encompassed, grasped, and exhausted the wholesome consciousness of the four planes.

For in such passages as, “having encompassed the entire herd of elephants,” the term *pariyādāna* means grasping; whereas in such passages as, “Bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, encompasses all sensual lust,” it means exhausting. In this context, both meanings are applicable.
In this context, when this [material] form grasps the wholesome consciousness of the four planes,
it does not grasp it with the hand like a person seizing a cluster of blue lotuses, nor does it consume it by heating it up like fire consuming water on a hearth.
Rather, while simultaneously obstructing its arising, it both grasps and consumes the wholesome consciousness of the four planes.
This should be understood. Therefore it was said: “It persists, having seized hold of a man’s mind. “Yathayidaṃ” means “just as this.
“Itthirūpaṃ” means the form of a woman. In that regard: “And what, bhikkhus, do you call ‘form’ (rūpa)?
It is called ‘form,’ bhikkhus, because it is afflicted (ruppati). By what is it afflicted? By cold, too...”
The etymological meaning and the general characteristic of *rūpa* (matter) should be understood according to the Sutta passage: "It is broken (*ruppati*), it is even broken by heat.

However, this word *rūpa* is employed in many senses, such as aggregate (*khandha*), existence (*bhava*), sign (*nimitta*), condition (*paccaya*), body (*sarīra*), color (*vaṇṇa*), and shape (*saṇṭhāna*). Indeed, in the passage, "Whatever matter there is, whether past, future, or present," [it refers to the aggregate].
It occurs in the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*). In the phrase “he develops the path for rebirth in the form realm,” it refers to existence in the form realm (*rūpabhava*).
In the phrase “perceiving no forms internally, he sees forms externally,” it refers to the kasiṇa sign.
In the phrase “Bhikkhus, unwholesome, unskillful states arise together with form, not without form,” it refers to the condition (*paccaya*). [And] “space enclosed is merely reckoned as form.”
In the phrase "it goes," it refers to the body. In the phrase "dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," it refers to color (vaṇṇa).

In the phrase "one who is measured by form, one who is delighted by form," it refers to shape (saṇṭhāna). By the word "etc.," such instances as "the form that is dear, the form that is pleasant, the form that is unattractive" should also be included.
However, here it refers to the female form, which is comprised of the fourfold origination and is designated as the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana).

It pertains to color. Furthermore, whatever color belonging to a woman—whether it be her inner or outer garment, an ornament, perfumes, cosmetics, and so forth, or jewelry, garlands, and so forth—that is attached to her body and serves as an object for a man’s eye-consciousness, all of this should be understood as "woman-form" (*itthirūpa*) alone. Monks, woman-form [is the object] for a man.
"It persists by seizing the mind": this is stated for the purpose of strengthening what was said previously.

Alternatively, the previous statement—beginning with "Monks, just as this female form"—was spoken by way of a simile, whereas this [present statement] is spoken by way of demonstrating the power of that seizure.
Herein, this is the story regarding the power of the seizure of the female form: it is said that the Great-Tusked Naga King [dwelt] at Cetiyagiri.

Having had the Mahāthūpa constructed at Ambatthala and performed the offering known as the Giribhaṇḍapūjā, he would go from time to time to Cetiyagiri surrounded by his harem and give a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
In a place where many people gather, mindfulness does not remain well-established in everyone; and the king’s chief queen, named Damilādevī, was in the prime of her youth.
She was beautiful and inspiring. Then, a certain elder monk named Cittatthera, who had gone forth in old age, looked at her according to his unrestrained habit;

having grasped the sign in the object of her form, he wandered about like one possessed, saying at every place where she stood or sat, "O Tamil queen! O Tamil queen! From that time on, even the young novices...
They gave him the name Thera Ummattaka-citta and so addressed him. Then, before long, that queen passed away.
When the young novices had returned from visiting the cemetery with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, they went to his presence and said:
"Venerable Citta-thera, for whose sake you lament, we have seen the cemetery of that queen."
"Having gone, we have returned. Even when this was said, not believing him, he spoke words like those of a madman:
"To whichever cemetery you went for the sake of seeing [the body], your faces are smoky!
Thus, this female form remained obsessing the mind of the Elder Umattakacitta.
There is another story: It is said that one day King Saddhātissa, surrounded by his harem, came to the monastery.
A certain youth, standing at the gate-tower of the Lohapāsāda, remained unrestrained and gazed at a woman.
She too, halting her movement, gazed back at him. Both of them were consumed by the fire of lust that had arisen within them.
They died. Thus, the form of a woman obsesses the mind of a youth.
There is another account: it is said that a certain young monk from the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra went to the monastery at the gate of the village of Kāḷadīghavāpi for the purpose of receiving a lesson.
Having finished his duty of receiving the lesson, he did not heed the advice of those who wished him well, but [went] to a place where there were young novices...
Thinking, "If I am questioned, I shall be able to describe the layout of the village," he went for alms in the village;
there, having perceived a sign in an unwholesome object and returning to his own dwelling place, he recognized the cloth she was wearing.
When she asked, "Venerable sir, where did you obtain this? and he learned that she was dead, [he thought], "A woman such as this has [passed away] because of me."
Thinking, "She died depending on me," he was consumed by the fire of lust that had arisen within him and met his end.
In this way, too, it should be understood that this female form remains obsessing the mind of a man.

2. The second and subsequent cases are stated according to the inclinations of those who value sound and so forth. Among them, "the sound of a woman" refers to that which is produced from the mind of a woman.

The sound of speech, song, and instrumental music; furthermore, even the sound produced by a woman’s dress and ornaments, or by her bodily movements, as well as the sounds of the lute, conch, drum, and so forth, should be understood as "the sound of women.
For all of these remain, having completely captivated the mind of a man.
In this regard, the cases of the golden crab, the golden peacock, the novice monk, and others should be understood.
It is said that a great family of elephant-nagas dwelt depending on a certain mountain range.
Not far from there was a large lake used for their enjoyment, and in that lake lived a golden crab born of the animal realm. Whenever anyone entered that lake, he would seize them with his pincers.
Seizing him by the feet with his tusks as if with claws, he brought him under his control and killed him.
Seeking an opportunity, the elephant-chiefs roamed about, having appointed one great elephant as their leader. One day, he seized that elephant-chief.
Endowed with strength and mindfulness, the elephant-chief thought: "If I let out a cry of fear, they will all flee at once instead of sporting as they please."
He stood perfectly still. Then, knowing that everyone had crossed over, he cried out to let his wife know that he had been captured by him, saying:
"The deer with the horn, whose eyes are long and wide..."
"Only bones and skin, water-dwelling and hairless;
overcome by this, I weep piteously:
'May you not indeed abandon me, who am as dear to you as life itself.'"
Having heard him and realized that her husband had been captured, she spoke thus to the elephant and the crocodile in order to free him from that danger:
"Noble sir, I will not abandon you, O sixty-year-old elephant;
you are as dear to me as the earth bounded by its four oceans."
“Of all the crabs in the ocean, in the Ganges, and in the Yamunā, you are the best of those born in water; release the husband of her who weeps!
Upon hearing the sound of the woman’s voice, the crab loosened his grip. Then the elephant said, “This very one is his—”

Saying, "There is room," he placed one leg in the manner of having already grasped it, lifted the second, stepped upon its back with that foot, crushed it to powder, dragged it a short distance, and flung it onto the shore.
Then all the elephants gathered together and, thinking, "This is our enemy," crushed it to pieces.
Thus, for the time being, the sound of women remained obsessing the mind of the golden crab.
The golden peacock, having entered the Himalayas and dwelling in a great mountain thicket, constantly observed the solar disk at the time of sunrise and, providing protection for himself, spoke thus:
“This one with eyes, the sole king, rises;
he is the color of a firebrand, the illuminator of the earth.”
I pay homage to him, who has the color of a lotus, who illuminates the earth;
through him, may we dwell guarded today throughout the day.
Those brahmins who have mastered the Vedas in all things...
Homage to them, and may they protect me!
Homage to the Buddhas, homage to Awakening!
Homage to those who are liberated, homage to liberation!
“Having made this his protection,
the peacock wanders in search of food.
Having gathered his fodder for the day, as he enters his dwelling place in the evening, even after looking at the sun’s orb as it has set, he speaks this verse:
“The one-eyed king, golden-hued,
the radiance of the earth— him, the golden-hued radiance of the earth, I revere.
“Let us dwell tonight restrained by that [vow].
To those brahmins who have mastered all things through the Vedas, I pay homage; may they protect me.”
Homage to the Buddhas, homage to Awakening;
homage to those who are liberated, homage to liberation.
Having made this protection, he—
"I made my dwelling.
Having passed seven hundred years in this manner, one day,
hearing the cry of a peahen hen even before the protective ritual was completed, he failed to perform the ritual and fell under the power of the hunter sent by the king.
[The golden peacock] approached. Thus, the sound of a woman’s voice remains having completely captivated the mind of the golden peacock.
However, the young man dwelling on Mount Chāta and the young man dwelling at Sudhāmuṇḍaka met with ruin and calamity upon hearing the sound of a woman’s voice.
3. Thirdly, regarding "the scent of a woman": this refers to the sense-sphere of odor (gandhāyatana) produced by a woman through the four modes of origination. This is the bodily scent of a woman.
It has a foul odor; however, what is intended here is the scent of external ointments and the like applied to the body.
For some women have the smell of a horse, some the smell of a ram, some the smell of sweat, and some the smell of blood. Yet a certain blind fool might even become infatuated with such a woman.
But as for the Woman-Treasure of a Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti):
The scent of sandalwood wafts from her body and the scent of lotus from her mouth. This [natural fragrance] does not belong to all women;
rather, it is only the scent of external applications such as ointments that is intended here.

However, animals such as elephants, horses, and oxen go one, two, three, or even four *yojanas* away following the seasonal scent of females of their own species. Whether it be the scent of a woman’s body,
Whether it be the scent of a woman’s clothing, undergarments, ointments, unguents, jewelry, garlands, or other perfumes—all such things are to be understood simply as "the scent of a woman.
4. Regarding the fourth [object], "the taste of a woman" (*itthirasa*): this refers to the sense-sphere of taste (*rasāyatana*) produced by the four causes in a woman.

However, the Venerable Cūḷanāga and Cūḷābhaya of the Tipiṭaka maintain: "This [taste] consists both of the 'taste of hearing'—by way of her compliance with one's requests—and the 'taste of enjoyment'."

"This is the essence of a woman," they say. But what of that? Even the taste of the saliva used for smearing the lips of a woman, as well as the taste of the rice gruel, food, and so forth given by her to her husband—all this should be understood as the "essence of a woman.
For many beings have met with ruin and disaster by grasping at whatever was given directly by their own wives as being "sweet."

5. In the fifth [case], "the touch of a woman" (*itthiphoṭṭhabba*) refers to the physical contact with a woman’s body; the touch of even the garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth that have come into contact with a woman’s body should likewise be understood as the "touch of a woman.
All of this obsesses the mind of a man, just like the touch of an unwholesome object for a young bhikkhu reciting the scriptures in a group on the courtyard of the Great Cetiya.

Thus the Teacher, taking each one from among form and the rest according to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) and latent dispositions (*āsaya*) of beings, said: "I do not see another such as this.

For just as the female form of a man who prizes form causes the arising of consciousness, binds it, fetters it, ties it, deludes it, and utterly confuses it, so it is not with the remaining [objects] such as sound and the rest. And just as for those who prize sound and the rest...
Sounds and so forth are not like the objects such as visible forms. For some, the mind is occupied by only one object among visible forms and the rest;

for others, it may be occupied by two, three, four, or even all five. Thus, these five discourses were spoken by way of the "five heavy ones" (*pañcagaruka*), and not by way of the *Pañcagaruka-jātaka*.
However, the *Pañcagaruka-jātaka* is cited here for the purpose of providing corroboration.

It should be told. For in that regard, when a market town and so forth were established by non-human beings in the middle of a wilderness, among the Great Man’s five companions, one who was heavy with respect to form became entangled in the object of form and met with ruin and disaster;

those heavy with respect to sound and so forth likewise became entangled in the objects of sound and so forth. Thus, it should be brought forward and told for the purpose of providing a witness. Now, these five—
The discourses were spoken solely by way of the five things held in high esteem.
And since it is not only men who hold these five things in high esteem, but women do so as well, he spoke five further discourses by way of them too.
Their meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. Regarding the illustrative stories (*vatthu*) as well—
In the first sutta, the background story concerning the deceased royal concubine should be understood as that of a young man standing at the door of the Lohapāsāda palace;
this has already been explained in detail above. 7.
In the second sutta, the background story concerning a woman who subsisted on her beauty in Bārāṇasī should be understood; [the story of] Guttila the lute-player...
He sent a thousand [pieces of gold] for a certain woman, but she, having mocked him, did not wish to accept it.
Thinking, "I shall do what must be done in this matter," immediately after the evening meal, he prepared himself in full attire and sat at another house door facing her house;
having tuned the strings of his lute so that they were even and balanced, he [matched] the sound of the song to the pitch of the strings.

He sang without overstepping [the boundaries]. That woman, hearing the sound of his song and thinking it was the sound of the door opening, thought, "I will go to him through the open window," and she met her death right there in mid-air. 8.
In the Third Sutta, sandalwood fragrance wafts from the body of the Wheel-turning Monarch, and lotus fragrance from his mouth.
This is what should be brought forth. And here, this background story should be understood:

It is said that in Sāvatthī, the husband of a certain householder’s daughter, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, thought, “It is not possible for me to fulfill this Dhamma while remaining a householder,” and he went forth into homelessness in the presence of a certain alms-collecting elder. Then, [thinking] of his wife, “She is now without a husband,”...
Having learned this, King Pasenadi of Kosala had her brought into the inner palace.
One day, taking a bunch of blue lotuses, he entered the palace and gave one blue lotus to each woman.
As the flowers were being distributed, two fell into that woman's hands. Displaying a joyful expression, she sniffed them and wept. The king—
Seeing her in both these conditions, he had her summoned and questioned her. She explained the reason for her joy and the reason for her weeping.

Although she spoke thus up to three times, the king did not believe her; therefore, on the following day, he had all fragrant scents such as garlands and ointments removed from the entire royal residence, and having prepared seats for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, [he invited] the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha...
Having given a great almsgiving to the community of monks, at the conclusion of the meal, he asked that woman, "Which elder is yours?
When she replied, "This one," and the Teacher recognized her, the householder paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, let the community of monks go together with you;
our Elder So-and-so will deliver the blessing. The Teacher set aside that monk.
He went to the monastery. As soon as he began to speak words of appreciation there, the entire royal palace became as if filled with fragrance.
The king, becoming confident that "this is indeed true," asked the Teacher about the reason on the following day.
The Teacher said, "In the past, while listening to a discourse on the Dhamma, she respectfully uttered the word of praise, 'Excellent! Excellent!'"
He heard it, O Great King, and by that root this benefit was obtained,” he explained.
“When one says ‘Excellent, excellent!
at the time of a teaching on the True Dhamma, a fragrance is born from the mouth, just like a lotus in water.”
The remainder is clear in all respects. In this chapter, only the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) has been discussed. This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on Form and so forth.
2. Commentary on the Chapter on the Abandoning of the Hindrances (*Nīvaraṇappahānavagga*).

11. Regarding the phrase "even a single phenomenon (ekadhammaṃ) in the first [case] of the second [set]," here "phenomenon" (dhamma) should be understood in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being (nissattaṭṭhena), as in such passages as "at that time, there are phenomena" (tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā honti).
Therefore, "even a single phenomenon" means even a single nature devoid of a sentient being;
this is the meaning here. However, regarding the term "unarisen" (anuppanno), it refers to [the state] for the maintenance of beings already born, or for the arising of those seeking existence...

In such passages as, “Or, monks, for the purpose of assisting... as many beings as there are, whether footless or two-footed,” the particle *vā* should be understood in the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*), not in the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). This is the meaning here:
by whatever factor unarisen sensual desire arises, and arisen sensual desire leads to further increase and expansion.
"I do not see any other sign like that beautiful sign. In this context, "unarisen" means unborn, unproduced, unmanifested, and unevolved.

"Sensual desire" refers to the hindrance of sensual desire, which has been explained in detail according to the method beginning with: "whatever sensual desire, sensual passion, sensual delight, and sensual craving there is regarding sense pleasures.
"Arises" means it is produced and becomes manifest. Furthermore, this...
It should be understood that [a defilement] arises either by way of non-manifestation or by way of not having experienced its object;
for otherwise, in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there is nothing that has not already arisen.

In this regard, for some, a defilement does not manifest due to the practice of the round of duties (*vatta*); for others, it does not manifest due to the bonds (*gantha*), the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), or concentration (*samādhi*).
By means of one or another of the ninefold tasks of insight (vipassanānavakamma) and so forth. How so? For a certain person is endowed with the observance of duties (vattasampanna);

as he performs the eighty-two minor duties, the fourteen major duties, and the duties concerning the shrine courtyard, the Bodhi-tree courtyard, the water pavilion, the Uposatha hall, and the duties for visitors and those departing, his defilement finds no opportunity.
Later, however, having abandoned the duties, for that person whose duties have been broken...
It arises by way of improper attention and the lapse of mindfulness while one is practicing. In this way, too, that which has not yet arisen is said to "arise" by way of non-occurrence.
A certain person is devoted to the texts; he takes up one Nikāya, or two, or three, or four, or even five. For him...
For one who grasps, recites, causes others to recite, teaches, or explains the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas—
according to its meaning, its text, its sequence, and its internal consistency— defilement finds no opportunity. However, later on,
when he has abandoned his literary work and wanders about indolently, through the arrival of improper attention and the neglect of mindfulness, [defilement arises].
It arises. In this way too, that which has not arisen arises by way of non-occurrence.
Furthermore, there is a certain person who is a bearer of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*); having undertaken the thirteen qualities of the ascetic practices, he conducts himself accordingly.
While he maintains those qualities of the ascetic practices, the defilement finds no opportunity. Later on, however, his ascetic practices...
For one who has abandoned [the training] and turned back toward abundance, it arises by way of improper attention and the loss of mindfulness.
In this way, even though it has not arisen, it is said to "arise" by virtue of its non-occurrence.
A certain person has mastery over the eight attainments; for him, regarding the first jhāna and so forth, there is mastery in adverting and so on.
For one dwelling in this way, defilement finds no opportunity.

However, at a later time, for one whose jhāna has declined or has been neglected, and who dwells devoted to idle chatter and the like, it arises due to improper attention and the abandonment of mindfulness.
Thus, even in this sense, that which was previously unarisen is said to "arise" by way of its manifestation.
But another is a practitioner of insight (vipassaka); he dwells performing the work of either the seven contemplations or the eighteen great insights.

As he dwells in this way, the defilement finds no opportunity. Later on, however, when he abandons the work of insight and dwells with excessive physical rigidity, there arise unwise attention and the neglect of mindfulness.
It arises by coming upon [an object]. In this way too, even though it has not yet arisen by way of non-occurrence, it is said to "arise.
A certain person becomes a supervisor of new construction; he has a Uposatha hall, a dining hall, and so forth built.
While he is thinking about the requisites for those buildings, the defilement finds no opportunity. But later, when his new construction is finished or abandoned...

Or it arises by way of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the abandonment of mindfulness (*sati-ossagga*). In this way, too, that which has not yet arisen is said to arise by virtue of its non-occurrence.
Furthermore, there is one who has come from the Brahma-world as a pure being (*suddhasatta*); because he has not practiced [defilements], the defilement finds no opportunity.
However, at a later time, when he has acquired the habit of practice, [the defilement arises] by way of improper attention and the abandonment of mindfulness.
It arises. Thus, even by way of non-occurrence, that which has not arisen is said to "arise. In this way, first, the arising of what has not arisen should be understood by way of non-occurrence.
How [is it understood] by way of an object not previously experienced?
Here, someone [encounters] a pleasing object such as a form (*rūpa*) or the like, which has never been experienced before.

He obtains it; then, due to improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and the abandonment of mindfulness (*sativossagga*) regarding that object, lust arises. Thus, in the case of an object not previously experienced, what was unarisen is said to "arise.
"Arisen" means born, fully born, produced, fully produced, and manifested. "For the sake of further increase" means for the sake of repeated occurrence.

"Vepullāya" means for the state of expansion, for the state of becoming a mass. In this regard, it is impossible that sensual desire which has arisen once will not cease, or that what has once ceased will arise again.
However, when one [instance] has ceased, its arising again and again—either upon that same object or another object—is said to lead to further increase and to expansion.
“Subhanimitta” (the sign of the beautiful) refers to an object that is a basis for lust.
In the passage, “Bhikkhus, evil unwholesome states arise with a sign, not without a sign,” *nimitta* is a name for a condition.
In the passage, “Bhikkhus, by a bhikkhu devoted to higher consciousness, five signs should be attended to from time to time,” it refers to a cause.

Regarding the phrase “he pursues and develops that sign,” this refers to concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the phrase “by resorting to which sign, for one who attends to that sign, the immediate destruction of the taints (*āsava*) occurs,” this refers to insight (*vipassanā*).

However, here the term “sign of beauty” (*subhanimitta*) is intended to mean a desirable object-dhamma that serves as a basis for lust. “Attending to it improperly” means: “In this regard, what is... [the rest of the sentence follows].
What is improper attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*)? It is the attention that regards the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful;
it is attention that is off the path, the mind’s turning toward, repeated turning toward, mental engagement, focused application, and attention in a manner contrary to the truths.
This is called improper attention. Of this attention...
"By way of attending [to the object] through an improper method. 12.
In the second [hindrance], "ill-will" (*vyāpāda*) is the state of the mind's corruption, a departure from its natural state, like a failure in digestion.
Regarding this, it has been explained in detail: "What is the hindrance of ill-will? Hostility arises thus: 'He has done me harm. etc.
This is a designation for the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*). "The sign of resentment" (*paṭighanimitta*) refers to an undesirable sign;
it is a designation for both resentment itself and that which has resentment as its object. This is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"Resentment is the sign of resentment, and any state that has resentment as its object is also the sign of resentment. The rest here is the same as in the case of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).

It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. And just as it is here, so it is in the subsequent sections as well; for in each respective place, I shall mention only the specific distinction. 13.
Regarding the third [hindrance], *thīnamiddha* means both *thīna* (sloth) and *middha* (torpor). Among these, *thīna* is the unwieldiness of the mind; this is a designation for the state of laziness.
*Middha* is the unwieldiness of the three aggregates; it is [the result of] the torpor of a monkey.

This is a designation for the state of being drowsy. For both [of these], the detailed exposition should be understood according to the method beginning: "In this context, what is *thina* (sloth)? It is the unwieldiness, the unfitness for work, the sinking, the sluggishness of the mind.
In this context, what is *middha* (torpor)? It is the unwieldiness, the unfitness for work, the shrouding, the enveloping of the body.
The terms beginning with "discontent" (*arati*) are [explained] in the *Vibhaṅga*.
They should be understood according to the method already analyzed. For this has been said:
"In that regard, what is discontent (*arati*)? Discontent with secluded lodgings or with various other superior wholesome states;
a lack of delight, a lack of enjoyment, longing, and agitation—this is called discontent."

In this context, what is lethargy (*tandī*)? That which is lethargy, the state of being lethargic, the tendency toward lethargy, indolence, the state of being indolent, the condition of indolence—this is called lethargy.

In this context, what is yawning (*vijambhitā*)? That which is the stretching of the body, yawning, bending forward, bending backward, stooping, bowing, or a physical ailment—this is called yawning. In this context, what is drowsiness after eating (*bhattasammada*)?
That which is the intoxication with food, the fatigue from food, the feverish distress of food, and the bodily sluggishness of one who has eaten—this is called "intoxication by food.
In this context, what is mental sluggishness (*cetaso līnatta*)?

That which is the mind’s lack of health, lack of wieldiness, sinking, deep sinking, sluggishness, the state of sinking, the fact of having sunk, torpor, the state of torpor, and the fact of having become torpid in the mind—this is [mental sluggishness].
"And it is called 'mental sluggishness.
Herein, the first four states are conditions for the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor both by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support;
however, mental sluggishness itself is not co-nascent with itself, though it is so by way of the category of decisive support.
14. In the fourth [jhāna], "restlessness-and-worry" (*uddhacca-kukkucca*) refers to both restlessness and worry. Therein, "restlessness" (*uddhacca*) is the state of agitation of the mind.
"Worry" (*kukkucca*) is the remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) arising from not having done what is wholesome and having done what is evil.

"Lack of mental tranquility" (*cetaso avūpasamo*) is another name for this very restlessness-and-worry. "Of one whose mind is untranquil" (*avūpasantacittassa*) means by means of [the absence of] meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

Or [it is the condition] for one whose mind has not been calmed by insight (vipassanā). Furthermore, this lack of calm is a condition for restlessness-and-worry (uddhacca-kukkucca) by way of its decisive support (upanissaya-koṭi).

15. In the fifth [section], "doubt" refers to the hindrance of doubt (vicikicchā-nīvaraṇa), which has been explained in detail according to the method beginning with "he is uncertain regarding the Teacher. "Improper attention" (ayoniso-manasikāra) has the very same characteristic as previously stated. 16.
In the sixth [section], "unarisen sensual desire does not arise" means either by way of its non-occurrence or by way of the object not having been experienced.
Just as with a two-day-old fever, it does not arise because of two causes; likewise, it remains suppressed and does not obtain a further cause or condition.
Here too, the non-manifestation [of defilements] should be understood by way of the duties (*vatta*) and so forth.

For in some cases, when one is engaged in the duties according to the method already described, the defilement finds no opportunity even while one is performing those duties, by virtue of the duties themselves.
It is suppressed. Having thus suppressed it and turned away from it, he attains Arahantship, like the Elder Milakkhatissa.
It is said that this venerable one was born into a hunter's family while wandering for alms at the Gāmeṇḍavāla Mahāvihāra in the Rohaṇa country.

Having come here and established a household, thinking, "I shall support my wife and children," I set up a hundred mortar-pestles, laid out a hundred snares, and erected a hundred stakes, accumulating much evil. One day, taking fire and salt from my home, I went into the forest.
Having killed a deer caught in a snare and eaten the meat roasted on coals, I became thirsty.
Having offered the oblation, he entered the Gāmeṇḍavāla Mahāvihāra. At the water-shed, finding not even enough water to quench his thirst in ten water-jars, he began to complain:
"How is it that in this dwelling place for so many monks, there is not even enough water to satisfy the thirst of those who have come here parched? Then the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissa—
Having heard his words, as he was going toward him, he saw ten water-jars full of water in the water-shed and thought, "This must be a being who is a living peta.
Saying, "Lay follower, if you are thirsty, drink the water," he lifted up a jar and poured it into his hands. This was due to his past karma.
The yellowish water vanished as soon as it was drunk, like a drop cast into a hot skull; even as he drank from the entire jar, his thirst was not quenched.
Then the Elder said to him, "Upāsaka, such a terrible deed you have committed that you have become a peta this very moment;
what will your future retribution be like?"
Having heard his words, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency. He paid homage to the Elder, dismantled those threshing-machines and other implements, and went home in haste.
Looking upon his wife and children, he broke his weapons and released the island deer and birds into the forest.
Then, returning to the Elder, he requested the going-forth. "Friend, the going-forth is difficult; how [can you do it]? he asked.
“Will you go forth? “Venerable sir, having seen such a direct cause as this, how could I not go forth?
The Elder gave him the meditation subject of the fivefold skin and ordained him.

Having become diligent in his duties and learning the word of the Buddha, one day, while [studying] the *Devadūta Sutta*, he heard: “Then, monks, the wardens of hell throw him back again into the Great Hell...”
Having heard this passage, [the monk] said, “They cast back into the Great Hell a being who has already experienced such a mass of suffering;
oh, Venerable Sir, how terrible is the Great Hell! “Yes, friend, it is terrible. “Is it possible, Venerable Sir, to see it?
“It is not possible to see it, but I shall show you one illustration that will give you an idea of what it is like,” he said, and then [addressed] the novice...
"Having had him instructed, have a pile of wet wood prepared on a stone slab. He did so.

While remaining seated as he was, the Elder, having performed a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi*), drew out from the Great Hell a spark of fire the size of a glowworm and, while the man was looking on, cast it into the Elder's pile of wood.
Its falling upon that spot and the subsequent burning of the wood-pile until it turned to ashes—[all occurred] right before his eyes.
It was neither later nor earlier; it had come to pass.
Having seen him, he asked, "Venerable sir, how many burdens (dhura) are there in this teaching? "Friend, there is the burden of insight (vipassanādhura) and the burden of study (ganthadhura).
"Venerable sir, while the burden of study is indeed the responsibility of one who is capable, for me, however, it is a source of suffering."
“With faith, I shall fulfill the duty of insight; give me a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna),” he said, and after paying homage, he sat down.
The Elder, recognizing him as “a monk perfected in his duties,” placed him at the head of those responsible for the duties and taught him a meditation subject.
Having received the meditation subject, he applied himself to the work of insight and fulfilled his duties. One day, at the Cittala-pabbata Mahāvihāra...
He performed his duties: one day at the Gāmeṇḍavāla Mahāvihāra, and one day at the Gocaragāma Mahāvihāra.
As soon as sloth and torpor descended upon him, out of fear of neglecting his duties, he would soak a bundle of straw, place it on his head, and sit with his feet immersed in water.
One day, he performed his duties for two watches at the Cittalapabbata Mahāvihāra.
Having done so, at the time of the powerful dawn, when she had begun to fall asleep, he sat placing fresh straw upon his head.
On the slope of the eastern mountain, while a novice monk was reciting the Aruṇavatiya Sutta—“Exert yourselves, strive, apply yourselves to the Buddha’s teaching; —he heard it.
