Shake off the army of Death, as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut.
"Whoever shall dwell heedfully in this Dhamma and Discipline,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering."

Upon hearing this account, he thought, "The Fully Enlightened One must have spoken this to a bhikkhu of such energy as myself," and having thus given rise to joy, he attained meditative absorption (jhāna).

Taking that very state as his foundation, he established himself in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and, striving again and again, reached Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). At the time of his final passing away (parinibbāna),...
And showing that very reason, he spoke thus:
“Carrying a whole bundle of straw upon my head, I walked about;
I have reached the third stage—of this there is no doubt for me.”
In one such person, the defilement that has been suppressed by means of the practice remains suppressed in that way.

In another person, by the same method as described—while engaged with the scriptures, learning them, reciting them, teaching them, or explaining them—the defilement finds no opportunity; it remains suppressed by means of the scriptures.
It occurs. Having thus suppressed it and turned away from it, he attains Arahatship, like the Elder Maliyadeva.

It is said that when that venerable one had been a bhikkhu for three years, he was receiving his lessons and practicing insight meditation at the Maṇḍalārāma Mahāvihāra in the village of Kallaka. One day, while he was walking for alms in Kallaka village—

A certain female lay devotee, having offered a bowl of rice gruel and conceived a motherly affection for him, had the Elder sit within her residence, fed him choice food, and asked, "Venerable sir, in which village do you live? He replied, "I am a lay devotee who performs the work of copying manuscripts at the Great Monastery of Maṇḍalārāma.
She said, "In that case, dear one, stay right here permanently until you have finished your work of copying manuscripts."
"Please accept alms. Having consented, he accepted alms there regularly;
at the conclusion of his meal, while offering a blessing, he would depart after speaking only these two words: "May there be happiness; may she be freed from suffering.
For three months during the rainy season, providing for her alone and honoring her with alms-food, [he remained] until the Great Pavāraṇā.
Through the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he attained Arahantship. The resident Elder said, "Friend Mahādeva, today a great multitude will assemble at the monastery;
you should give a gift of Dhamma to them. The Elder consented.
The young novices gave notice to the laywoman: "Today your son will preach the Dhamma; [go to] the monastery..."
“Having gone, you shall hear it. “Dear ones, not everyone understands the Dhamma discourse.
For all this time my son has been speaking to me, he has spoken only these two phrases: ‘May there be happiness; may he be freed from suffering. Do not joke.
“Do not concern yourself with whether he knew or did not know, laywoman. Go to the monastery and listen to the Dhamma itself.”
"Listen," he said. The female lay devotee (upāsikā), taking perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, went there, paid her respects, and sat down to hear the Dhamma at the conclusion of the assembly.
Both the preacher of the day’s discourse and the reciter of the morning recitation, having recognized their own limitations, rose from their seats.
Then the Elder Maliyadeva sat upon the Dhamma throne, took up his fan, and delivered a gradual discourse (anupubbikathā).
“I have offered words of appreciation to the Great Laywoman using only two phrases for three months and two days;

today, having contemplated those same two phrases throughout the entire night by means of the Three Piṭakas, I shall explain their meaning. Having thus begun the teaching of the Dhamma, he spoke throughout the whole night.
At the conclusion of the discourse with the rising of the dawn, the Great Laywoman was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Furthermore, in that very same Mahāvihāra, an elder named Tissabhūti, while studying the Vinaya, entered a village at the time for almsround and looked upon an object of sensual distraction. Greed arose within him;
without moving his planted foot, he poured the rice-gruel from his own bowl into the bowl of the young attendant and said, "If this thought continues to increase..."

"He will cause me to sink into the four states of misery. Having turned back from there, he went into the presence of his teacher, paid homage, and standing to one side, said: "A certain ailment has arisen in me;
I shall return if I am able to cure it, otherwise I shall not return. You should review the recitation with me during the day and again in the evening."
"Set aside [the recitation], but do not set aside the recitation at dawn.

Having said this, he went into the presence of the Elder Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita, who dwelt in the Malaya region. While the Elder was arranging the surroundings of his own leaf-hut, he did not even look at him and said, "Friend, put away your bowl and robes.
"Venerable sir, I have a certain ailment; if you would treat it..."
“Can you? I shall return it. “Friend, you have come to one capable of treating a disease that has arisen;
return it. Thinking, “Our teacher would not speak thus without knowing,” the monk Subbaco set aside his bowl and robes, performed the duties for the elder, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
The Elder, knowing, "This one is of a lustful temperament," taught him the meditation subject of the foul (asubha).
He rose, slung his bowl and robes over his shoulder, and paid homage to the Elder again and again. "Friend Mahābhūti, why do you show such excessive reverence?
[He replied: "Venerable sir, if I am able to perform my own duty, that is well; if not..."
"This is my last sight of him! "Go, friend Mahābhūti;
for such a son of good family who is devoted to the proper practice, neither jhāna, nor insight, nor the path, nor the fruit is difficult to obtain.
Having heard the elder’s words and having shown him his profound respect, he went to the root of the *sepaṇṇi* bush that he had previously identified on his way there.
Sitting cross-legged and taking the meditation subject of foulness as his foundation, he established insight and,
having become established in Arahantship, attained the recitation at dawn. For those such as these, the defilements suppressed by means of the texts remain suppressed in that very way.
But for another who maintains the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) in the manner already described, the defilement finds no opportunity; it is suppressed by means of the ascetic practices themselves.
Having thus suppressed it and turned away from it, he attains *arahantship*, just like the Elder Mahāsīva, who dwelt in a mountain cave near a village.
It is said that while the Elder was living at the Tissamahāvihāra in Mahāgāma...
He taught the Tipiṭaka, both by way of its meaning and its text, to eighteen great assemblies.
Standing under the Elder’s instruction, sixty thousand bhikkhus attained arahantship.
Among them, one bhikkhu, filled with joy regarding the Dhamma he had realized, thought: "Does this happiness exist for our teacher as well?"
Thus, while reflecting, he realized the elder’s status as an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and thought, "By some means I shall arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in the elder.
He went from his own dwelling to the elder’s presence, paid homage, performed the customary duties, and sat down.
Then the elder said to him, "Why have you come, friend? Are you a forest-dweller? "If you will grant me the opportunity, one..."
“I have come, venerable sir, thinking, ‘I shall take up the Dhammapada. “Many, friend, are taking it up; there will be no opportunity for you.

Finding no opportunity at any time during the day or night, he said, “Venerable sir, since there is no opportunity like this, how will you find the opportunity for death? Then the Elder thought: “This man has not come for the sake of the recitation.”
“He has come, but he has come for the purpose of inspiring spiritual urgency in me.
That elder, saying, “Venerable sir, a monk must indeed be like me,” paid homage to the elder and, rising into the sky which was the color of a gem, departed.
From the moment he had gone, the elder, having been stirred by spiritual urgency, taught the recitation during the day and the recitation in the evening.
Having placed his bowl and robes within arm’s reach, and having received the recitation at dawn, he descended together with the bhikkhu who had brought the bowl and robes.
Having resolved upon the thirteen ascetic qualities in their entirety, he went to a lodging in a mountain cave on the outskirts of a village.
After tending to the cave and setting up his bed and chair, he thought: “Until I have attained Arahantship, I shall not lean my back against the bed.”
Thinking, "I will not open [my eyes]," he bound his mind and descended to the walking path. As he was striving with the thought, "Today I shall attain Arahatship;
today I shall attain Arahatship," the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) arrived.
As the invitation ceremony drew near, he became exceedingly exhausted as he reflected, "Having abandoned the state of an ordinary person (puthujjana), I shall perform the invitation of purification."

Being unable to produce either the path or the fruit through that invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he said, "Even one like me, who has applied himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), does not attain it;
how difficult to obtain indeed is this state of Arahatship!

Having spoken thus, he remained devoted to standing and walking meditation according to that very method, and after practicing the duties of a recluse for thirty years, [he beheld] the full moon standing in the midst of the Great Invitation Ceremony (*mahāpavāraṇā*).
Seeing this, he thought, "Is it the lunar disk that is pure, or is it my own virtue? Reflecting thus, he perceived: "In the lunar disk, its dark spots are visible;
but for me, from the day of my full ordination until this very day, there has been no black spot or blemish in my virtue.
Having reflected in this way, his heart was filled with joy and gladness, and because his knowledge was fully matured, he experienced rapture.

Having suppressed [the defilements], he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). In such a person, the defilement suppressed by means of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) remains suppressed in that very way.
For another, however, because of the frequent attainment of the first jhāna and so forth in the manner already described, the defilement finds no opportunity to arise.
It is suppressed by means of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). Having thus suppressed it and turned away from it, he attains *arahantship*, just like the Elder Mahātissa.
It is said that from the time he reached the age of twenty, the Elder was a master of the eight attainments.
Through the non-occurrence of defilements suppressed by those attainments, and by means of study and inquiry, he [reached] the vicinity of the Noble Path.
He preached, yet even at the age of sixty, he did not realize his own status as a worldling (*puthujjana*).
Then one day, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus from the Mahāvihāra at Tissamahārāma sent a message to the Elder Dhammadinna, who resided at Talaṅgara, saying:
"May the Elder come and preach the Dhamma to us. The Elder consented and said: "There is one older than myself..."
"There is no other bhikkhu; however, the Elder Mahātissa is my teacher of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).

I shall go, making him the senior of the Saṅgha," he thought. Surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, he went to the Elder’s dwelling, performed the duties for the Elder at the day-quarters, and sat down to one side.
The Elder said, “Dhammadinna, why have you come so late? “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied.
“The Saṅgha of bhikkhus sent a message to me from the Tissamahāvihāra. I am not going alone; rather, desiring to go together with you, I have come.
While thus engaging in friendly conversation, he added by way of elaboration, “Venerable sir, when did you [send this]?”
“Has the Dhamma been realized? he asked. “Friend Dhammadinna, it has been sixty years,” he replied.
“But can you, venerable sir, enter into meditative attainment? “Yes, friend. “Then could you, venerable sir, create a lotus pond?
“It is not difficult for me, friend,” he said, and right there in front of him, he created a lotus pond. “Here—”
When he was told, "Venerable sir, please create a single lotus grove," the Elder created that as well. [The king said: "Now, show me a large flower here.
The Elder showed him that too. [The king said: "Show me the form of a woman about sixteen years of age here.
The Elder showed him the form of a woman about sixteen years of age. Then he said to him: "Venerable sir, this—again and again—"
“Regard it as beautiful. The elder, looking at the female form he himself had created, gave rise to lust.
Then, realizing his own state as a worldling (*puthujjana*), he thought, “Good man, be my support,” and sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture before his pupil.
“It was for this very purpose, venerable sir, that I came,” [the pupil said]. Then, by means of the meditation on the foul (*asubha*), the elder [reduced the lust] to a slight degree.
Having prepared the meditation subject and explained it to the elder, Dhammadinna Thera went outside to give him privacy.
As soon as that elder, who had thoroughly mastered his mental formations, stepped out from his daytime resting place, he attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Then, having appointed him as the senior monk (*saṅghatthera*), Dhammadinna Thera went to the Tissa Mahāvihāra and [addressed] the Saṅgha...
He gave a discourse on the Dhamma. In such a case, the defilement suppressed by means of meditative attainment remains suppressed in that very way.
However, for another who performs the work of insight (*vipassanā*) according to the method already described, the defilement finds no opportunity;
it is suppressed by means of insight itself. Having thus suppressed it and turned away from it, he—
One attains arahantship, like the approximately sixty bhikkhus who had begun insight meditation during the time of the Buddha.
It is said that they received a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered a secluded forest, and while practicing insight,
because the defilements did not manifest, they formed the perception, "We have realized the path and the fruit," and for the sake of the path and fruit—
Without making an effort, they came into the presence of the Teacher, thinking, "We shall report the Dhamma we have penetrated to the One of Ten Powers.
Even before they arrived, the Teacher said to the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, today monks who have performed the work of striving will come to see me.
Do not grant them an opportunity to see me; rather, go to the fresh cemetery."
“...you should practice the meditation on the foul while it is still moist,” he sent word to them. When they arrived, the Elder delivered the message spoken by the Teacher.
They thought, “The Tathāgata would not have spoken without knowing; surely there must be a reason for this.
They went to a fresh cemetery and, looking at the moist corpses, they conceived a sense of greed and said, “Surely this is what was meant by the Perfectly Enlightened One...”
"It will be seen," they thought, and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), they began the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) they had obtained from the very beginning.
The Teacher, knowing that they had commenced insight (*vipassanā*), while seated in the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭi*), spoke this verse of illumination:
"These gourds which have not yet reached [maturity], like those in the autumn wind..."
"The bones are pigeon-colored; having seen them, what pleasure is there?
At the conclusion of these verses, they were established in the fruit of Arahantship. For those such as these, the defilements suppressed by means of insight remain suppressed in that very way.
In the case of another, while performing new work (navakamma) according to the method already described, the defilement finds no opportunity due to the influence of that new work.
It is indeed suppressed. Having thus suppressed it and turned away from it, he attains Arahantship, just like the Elder Tissa at Cittalapabbata.
It is said that when he was eight years old, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arose within him;
being unable to dispel it, he washed his robe, dyed it, baked his alms-bowl, and shaved his hair.
Having paid homage to his preceptor, he stood there. Then the Elder said to him, "Friend Mahātissa, why do you appear as if dissatisfied?
"Yes, venerable sir, dissatisfaction has arisen in me; I am unable to dispel it.
The Elder, observing his disposition and seeing that he possessed the necessary support for attaining Arahantship, spoke out of compassion: "Friend..."
“Tissa, we are old; build us one place to live in. The monk, who had never before been asked for a second time, consented, saying, “Very well, venerable sir.
Then the elder said to him, “Friend, while doing this building work, do not neglect your recitation of the scriptures nor your meditation subject.”
“Pay attention, and from time to time perform the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*. “I shall do so, venerable sir,” he replied.
Having paid homage to the elder, he looked about for a suitable location and thought, “It can be built here.

He filled it with timber, burned it down, cleared it, surrounded it with bricks, and fitted it with doors, windows, and so forth, together with the preparation of the walking-paths, walls, and other structures.
Having completed the construction of the cave and prepared the bed and chair, he went into the presence of the Elder, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, the work on the cave is finished;
please dwell here. [The Elder replied,] "Friend, you have performed this task with great hardship;
today, you alone shall dwell here for one day. He said, "Very well, venerable sir," and having paid homage and washed his feet, [he entered].
Having entered his cell and sat down cross-legged, he reflected upon the deed he had performed.
As he thought, "I have performed agreeable bodily service for my preceptor," joy arose within him.
Suppressing that joy, he established insight and attained the supreme fruit of Arhatship. For one such as this—
Defilement suppressed by means of new work (navakamma) remains suppressed in that very way.

However, some beings who have come from the Brahma-world are pure; because they do not habituate themselves [to defilements], the defilement does not manifest, being suppressed by the force of existence (bhava).
Having rendered that [defilement] thus suppressed and having turned away from the round of rebirth, he attains Arahantship.

He takes it up, just like the Venerable Mahākassapa. For that Venerable One, even while still in the midst of the household life, without enjoying sensual pleasures and having renounced great prosperity, went forth into homelessness.

On the way, seeing the Teacher coming to meet him, he paid homage to Him, received full ordination through the three exhortations, and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) at dawn on the eighth day.
[He] attained [it]. For one such as this, the defilement suppressed by means of existence (*bhava*) remains suppressed in that very way.

However, for one who, having encountered an object such as a form never experienced before, establishes insight right there, turns away from it, and attains Arahantship—for such a person, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), by virtue of encountering an object never before experienced, is said not to arise even when it has not yet arisen.
Regarding the phrase "arisen sensual desire is abandoned": here, "arisen" means born, become, and fully developed. "Is abandoned" means it is abandoned by these five types of abandonment:

abandonment by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*), abandonment by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*), abandonment by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*), abandonment by tranquilization (*paṭipassaddhippahāna*), and abandonment by escape (*nissaraṇappahāna*).
The meaning is that it is abandoned by these five abandonments and does not arise again. In this regard:
It should be understood that insight is "abandonment by way of substitution of opposites" (tadaṅgappahāna) because defilements are abandoned by means of it;
attainment is "abandonment by suppression" (vikkhambhanappahāna) because it suppresses defilements;
the path arises cutting off [defilements], fruition is the subsiding [of them], and Nibbāna is the escape from all defilements—these are [the types of abandonment].
Three types of abandoning are spoken of: abandoning by cutting off (*samuccheda*), abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*), and abandoning by escape (*nissaraṇa*).
The meaning is that [the defilements] are abandoned by these five types of abandoning, both mundane and supramundane.
"The sign of foulness" refers to the first jhāna with an object that has arisen among the ten kinds of foulness. Thus said the ancients.
—“The foul is the sign of the foul; states with the foul as their object are also the sign of the foul. Thus he attends wisely.
“In this context, what is wise attention? It is attending by way of the skillful means of attention as described in the method beginning with “the impermanent as impermanent,” and so forth.
“And sensual desire that has not yet arisen does not arise” means that what has not yet come into manifestation does not come into manifestation.
"And arisen sensual desire is abandoned": once arisen sensual desire is abandoned by means of the fivefold abandonment.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: apprehending the sign of the foul, devotion to the development of foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having good friends, and talk that is suitable. For [sensual desire] is tenfold...

Sensual desire is abandoned by one who grasps the sign of foulness, by one who develops it, by one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, and also by one who is moderate in eating—having the habit of drinking water and sustaining himself when there is space for four or five morsels of food. Therefore this was said:
“Without having eaten four or five morsels, one should drink water;”
“It is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
Thus, by associating with virtuous friends such as the Elder Tissa the worker on the foul, who delight in the meditation on foulness, sensual desire is abandoned;
it is also abandoned through appropriate talk based on the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it was said:
—“Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire.
17. Seventh: “Loving-kindness as liberation of mind” means loving-kindness that pervades the welfare of all beings.
Because the consciousness associated with it is liberated from obstructive states such as the hindrances, it is therefore called “liberation of mind. Specifically,
Or rather, it should be understood as "liberation of mind" because it is liberated from the obsession of all ill-will.

In this context, while the term "loving-kindness" (*mettā*) applies to the preliminary stage as well, because it is described here as "liberation of mind," only absorption (*appanā*) by way of the threefold or fourfold jhāna is intended.
"Attending wisely" means attending to that liberation of mind through loving-kindness according to the characteristics already stated.
For one who attends with the attention of skillful means.

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill will: grasping the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reflection on one’s own karma as one’s own property, abundance of circumspection, having virtuous friends, and talk that is conducive [to the goal].

For even in one who learns loving-kindness (*mettā*) by means of any one of the methods—whether directed toward specific persons, non-specific persons, or the pervasion of the directions—even ill-will (*byāpāda*) is abandoned; and also for one who develops loving-kindness by way of the directional pervasions, whether specifically or non-specifically. [One should reflect: "What will you achieve by being angry with this person?
Will you be able to destroy his virtue (*sīla*) and so forth? Have you not yourself come here by means of your own karma?"

Will you go by your own karma alone? To be angry with another is like taking glowing embers, red-hot iron rods, excrement, and so forth, with the desire to strike someone else. What will this person do to you when they are angry?
Will they be able to destroy your virtue (*sīla*) and other qualities? This person has come here by their own karma and will depart by their own karma alone.
"Like a gift that has not been accepted, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger of his will fall back upon his own head"— thus,
for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma by oneself and by another, and for one who stands in reflective discernment after having reflected on the ownership of kamma by both,
as well as for a virtuous friend such as the Elder Assagutta who delights in the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Ill will is abandoned even while one is practicing [the meditation]; it is also abandoned through talk based on loving-kindness and conducive to it while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of ill will.
The rest here and in what follows should be understood according to the method already stated; I shall, however, mention only the specific differences.
18. In the eighth [section], regarding the elements of exertion (*ārambha-dhātu*) and so forth: the element of exertion is the initial exertion of energy (*vīriya*).
The element of departure (*nikkama-dhātu*) is stronger than that, because it has departed from indolence (*kosajja*).

The element of striving (*parakkama-dhātu*) is even stronger than that, because it advances toward ever-higher stages. However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), it says: "Exertion of the mind for the dispelling of sensual desires..."
"Exertion of the mind for the removal of obstacles, and striving of the mind for the cutting of bonds"—having said this, it is stated that "by these three verses, supreme energy alone is described.
"Of one who has initiated energy" means of one whose energy is both perfected and exerted. Therein, [energy] free from the four faults...
It should be understood that "energy has been aroused. It is neither too slack nor too tense;
it is neither inwardly constricted nor outwardly distracted. This energy is twofold: bodily and mental. In this regard:
"Here, a bhikkhu purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting during the day."
Thus, for one who exerts himself and strives with the body by dividing the day and night into five parts, bodily energy is to be understood.

This may be through the delimitation of time, such as: "I will not emerge from this shelter until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging," or: "I will not break this cross-legged posture."
In this way, the mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*) should be understood as belonging to one who binds the mind by means of the divisions such as sitting, or who is fitting it together and striving.

Both of these types of energy are appropriate here. For by both kinds of this energy, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) that have not yet arisen do not arise in one who has initiated energy, and sloth and torpor that have already arisen are abandoned, as in the case of the Elder Milakkhatissa.
...like the Elder Mahāsīva who dwelt in a mountain cave near a village, like the Elder Pītimallaka, and like the Elder Tissa, son of a householder.
Among these, the first three and others like them were those who had initiated vigor through physical energy;
the Elder Tissa, son of a householder, and others like him were those who had initiated vigor through mental energy; while the Elder Mahānāga, who dwelt at Uccāvālu, however—

He was indeed one who had initiated energy through both types of effort. It is said that for seven days the Elder walked back and forth, for seven days he stood, for seven days he sat, and for seven days he lay down.
For the Great Elder, there was not even a single posture that was unsuitable;
having developed insight during the fourth week, he established himself in Arahatship.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor:
taking note of the fault in overeating, changing one’s posture, attending to the perception of light, living in the open air, having virtuous friends, and engaging in suitable conversation.

For when one who has eaten his meal—like the Brahmins Āharahatthaka, Bhuttavamitaka, Tatravaṭṭaka, Alaṃsāṭaka, Kākamāsaka, and others—is sitting in his night-quarters or day-quarters practicing the duty of a recluse, [these things are necessary].
Drowsiness and lethargy come creeping over one like a great elephant;

however, for a bhikkhu who drinks water after setting aside space for four or five mouthfuls and maintains the habit of subsisting on that much, it does not occur. Thus, by taking this as the sign regarding overeating, drowsiness and lethargy are abandoned.
Furthermore, they are abandoned by changing from whichever posture drowsiness and lethargy have overcome one to another.

Dullness and drowsiness are abandoned by one who attends to the light of the moon, the light of a lamp, or the light of a torch at night, or to the light of the sun during the day; by one who lives in the open air;
and by one who serves a spiritual friend like the Elder Mahākassapa, who has himself abandoned dullness and drowsiness.
They are also abandoned by talk concerning the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that are conducive to practice while standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it was said:
—“Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor.
In the ninth [section], “of one whose mind is stilled” means of one whose mind has been stilled by either jhāna or insight.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: being well-versed in the teachings, asking many questions, ...
In the Vinaya, these are: knowledge of what has been laid down, association with the elders, friendship with the virtuous, and appropriate discourse.
For even by means of great learning—when one masters one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas according to both the text and the meaning—even agitation and remorse are abandoned;
and for one who frequently inquires into what is allowable and what is unallowable regarding the formulations of the Vinaya.

Restlessness and remorse are abandoned by one who has attained mastery, by one who recognizes what has been done, by approaching elder monks who are advanced in years, by attending upon spiritual friends such as the Elder Upāli who are experts in the Vinaya, and by appropriate talk concerning what is allowable and what is not allowable during standing, sitting, and other activities.
Therefore it is said: "Six things [lead to the abandoning] of restlessness and remorse..."
“...they lead to its abandoning.
20. “By attending wisely, bhikkhus,” as it was said according to the method already stated, refers to one who attends by way of the means.
Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt: being well-versed in the teachings, being a thorough questioner, ...
In the Vinaya, there are: knowledge of what has been laid down, abundance of resolute confidence, friendship with the virtuous, and appropriate discourse.
For even by means of much learning—whether one is mastering one or, *pe*, five Nikāyas according to the text and according to the meaning—doubt is abandoned;
as is the case for one who is frequently engaged in inquiry concerning the Three Jewels, or for one who has attained mastery in the Vinaya.

Doubt is abandoned both by one who possesses abundant resolve known as faith that is settled upon the Three Jewels, and by one who serves a spiritual friend such as the Elder Vakkali, who is resolved through faith;
it is also abandoned by appropriate talk concerning the qualities of the Three Jewels during standing, sitting, and other activities.
Therefore it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt."
“They lead [to rebirth],” he said. In this Chapter on the Abandoning of the Hindrances, the process of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Abandoning of the Hindrances. 3.
Commentary on the Chapter on Unworkability.
21–22. In the first [case] of the third [tetrad], "undeveloped" means not increased by way of cultivation, not set in motion through the process of development.
"Unworkable" means it is not capable of work (*kammakkhama*) nor fit for work (*kammayogga*). In the second [case], the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was stated.

Furthermore, here in the first [case], "mind" refers to a mind arisen by way of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); in the second, it refers to a mind arisen by way of the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭa*).

In this regard, the distinction should be understood as follows: the round (vaṭṭa) and the basis of the round (vaṭṭapāda), the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭa) and the basis for the turning away from the round (vivaṭṭapāda).

"The round" refers to the round of the three planes; "the basis of the round" refers to the karma that leads to the acquisition of the round; "the turning away from the round" refers to the nine supramundane states;

and "the basis for the turning away from the round" refers to the karma that leads to the acquisition of the turning away from the round. Thus, in these suttas, it is precisely the round and the turning away from the round that are discussed.
23–24. In the third [section], the mind that has arisen should be understood by way of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) alone. It leads to great harm:

even while bestowing the excellences of gods and humans, as well as the lordships of Māra and Brahmā, it gives only a mass of suffering, repeatedly providing birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as well as the cycles of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and dependent origination.

"It leads to great harm" means that it results in great disadvantage. In the fourth [sutta], "consciousness" refers specifically to consciousness arisen by way of turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
In the fifth and sixth [suttas], the distinction is that it is "undeveloped" and "unmanifest. Herein, the intended meaning is as follows:

consciousness arisen by way of the round of existence, even though it has arisen, is indeed undeveloped and unmanifest. Why? Because among the supramundane foundations—namely, jhāna, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna—it does not exist.
Because it is unable to leap forward [into those states]. However, that which has arisen by way of turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is said to be "developed" and "manifest.
Why? Because it is able to leap forward into those states. But the Elder Phussamitta, resident of Kurundaka, said:
"Friend, only the path-consciousness itself is called 'developed' and 'manifest.'"

27–28. "Not practiced frequently" (*abahulīkata*) means not performed repeatedly. These two [types of consciousness] should also be understood as states of consciousness arisen by way of both the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and the unrolling of the round (*vivaṭṭa*). 29.
In the ninth [consciousness], it "brings about" (*adhivahati*) or "conveys" (*āharati*) the suffering described in the manner beginning with "Birth, too, is suffering";
thus, it is "conveying suffering" (*dukkhādhivaha*). *Dukkhādhivāha* is also a reading. Its meaning is: directed toward the noble dhammas, such as the supramundane jhāna that serves as a basis.
It is called *dukkhādhivāhaṃ* because it carries (*adhivāhīyati*) suffering and drives one along (*pesīyati*). This too is simply a consciousness arisen by way of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

For even though it bestows the aforementioned prosperities of gods, humans, and so forth, it is called *dukkhādhivahaṃ* because it carries one toward birth and the rest, and it is called *dukkhādhivāhaṃ* because it is difficult to direct toward the attainment of the noble Dhamma.
30. In the tenth [classification], "mind that brings happiness" (*sukhādhivaha*) refers specifically to the mind arisen by way of turning away from the cycle of existence (*vivaṭṭa*).

For it carries forth and brings about divine happiness over human happiness; meditative happiness over divine happiness; the happiness of insight (*vipassanā*) over meditative happiness; the happiness of the path (*magga*) over the happiness of insight; the happiness of the fruit (*phala*) over the happiness of the path;
and the happiness of Nibbāna over the happiness of the fruit. Thus, it is called "that which brings happiness."
It is called "conducive to happiness" because it is directed toward noble states such as the supramundane jhānas that serve as a basis;

it is exceedingly tranquil and resembles a well-discharged thunderbolt, and thus it is also said to be "conducive to happiness. In this chapter as well, only the cycle of existence and its cessation have been discussed.
This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on the Unworkable.

4. Commentary on the Chapter on the Untamed (Adantavagga) 31. Regarding the first [sutta]: "Untamed" (*adanta*) means like an untamed elephant, horse, or similar beast, characterized by its wildness. "Mind" (*citta*) refers specifically to the mind arisen within the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*). 32. Regarding the second:

"Tamed" (*danta*) means like a tamed elephant, horse, or similar beast, characterized by its lack of wildness. In these two suttas as well, it is precisely the mind arisen within the cycle of existence that is spoken of according to the modes of the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*) and the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*). And just as it is here, so it is in those that follow.
33. In the third [verse], "unguarded" (*agutta*) means not protected, lacking the restraint of mindfulness, similar to an unguarded elephant or horse.
34. In the fourth, "guarded" (*gutta*) means protected, possessing unremitting restraint of mindfulness, similar to a guarded elephant or horse. 35–36.

The fifth and sixth [verses] are spoken according to the inclination of those who understand by way of the terms "unprotected" (*arakkhita*) and "protected" (*rakkhita*); however, the meaning here is exactly the same as before.
37–38. This same method applies to the seventh and eighth verses as well. Here, however, the simile should be understood by way of an unsecured house door and so forth.
39–40. The ninth and tenth verses are stated by connecting them with all four lines. In this chapter as well, only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its reversal (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained.
Explanation of the *Adanta-vagga*.
5. Explanation of the Chapter on the Well-Directed Mind (Paṇihitacittavagga) 41.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter]: *seyyathāpi* is a particle used in the sense of a simile.
In this regard, the Blessed One sometimes presents a simile surrounding a particular meaning, as in the *Vattha-sutta*, or in suttas such as the *Pāricchattaka-upama* and the *Aggikkhandha-upama*.
And in some instances, it shows the meaning by surrounding it with a simile, as in the *Loṇambilasutta*, and as in the *Suvaṇṇakārasutta*, the *Sūriyopama-sutta*, and others.
But here, in this *Sālisūkopama*, while showing the meaning by surrounding it with a simile, he said: "Just as, monks," and so forth.
Therein, *sālisūka* means the awn of the rice grain; the same method applies to the awn of barley as well.
The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). "Misdirected" (*micchāpaṇihita*) means wrongly placed.

The meaning is that it was not placed with the tip pointing upwards in such a way that it would be able to pierce. "It will split" (*bhecchati*) means it will break; the meaning is that it will cut the skin.
"By a mind misdirected" (*micchāpaṇihitena cittena*) means by a mind wrongly placed. This refers to a mind arisen in accordance with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
This was said with this underlying intention (*sandhāya*). "Ignorance" (*avijjā*) refers to the great ignorance that is dense, thick, and consisting of non-knowing regarding eight points.

"He will produce clear knowledge" (*vijjā*): here, "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) means the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. "Nibbāna": it is called thus because it has emerged from the possession of craving; it is the Deathless (*amata*).
"He will realize" (*sacchikarissati*) means he will make it directly manifest (*paccakkhaṃ karissati*).
42. In the second [verse], "well-directed" (*sammāpaṇihita*) means placed properly by being held upright so that it can be broken.
"Tread upon" (*akkanta*): here, it is indeed "tread upon" by the foot, while "pressed down" (*uppīḷita*) is by the hand;

however, it is expressed as "tread upon" (*akkanta*) according to conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*). This, indeed, is the noble convention (*ariyavohāra*). But why [are these] others, such as the *sepaṇṇika* thorn and the *madanaka* thorn?
Did he not take large ones, but instead take only the fine and weak rice-husks or barley-husks?
This was for the purpose of showing that even a very small wholesome deed is capable of leading to the turning away from saṃsāra (vivaṭṭa).
For whether it be a fine and weak rice-husk or a barley-husk, or even the largest of the *sepaṇṇika* thorns, *madanaka* thorns, and so forth—among these, whichever it may be...
Just as one cannot break a hand or foot, or draw blood from them, when they are placed correctly,
but can do so when they are placed incorrectly; even so, whether it be a small act of merit such as giving a handful of grass,

or a great act of merit such as giving a meal at the proper time— if one performs it while aspiring for the success of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*) and thus depending on that round— then [it does not lead to liberation].
If it is established wrongly, one is able to bring about only the round of existence (*saṃsāra*), not its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*).

However, for one who aspires toward cessation by thinking, "May this gift of mine lead to the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)," and thus establishes it correctly according to the principle of cessation, it is indeed capable of bestowing even Arahantship, the knowledge of Paccekabodhi, or omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). For this has been said:
“The analytical knowledges and the liberations, as well as the perfections of a disciple;
the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha and the stage of a Buddha—all this is obtained by means of this.
In these two suttas, the cycle of existence and its cessation are explained.
43. "With a corrupted mind" means with a mind corrupted by hatred. "Having encompassed his mind with one's own mind" means having delimited his mind by means of one's own mind.
"As it was brought and placed" means just as it was brought and set down;
thus he should be said to be "standing in hell. "The states of deprivation," and so forth, are all merely synonyms for hell.
For *niraya* (hell) is called an *apāya* (state of loss) because it is devoid of what is reckoned as pleasure; it is a *duggati* (bad destination) because it is a resort for suffering;
it is a *vinipāta* (falling away) because those who have committed evil deeds fall into it helplessly; and it is a *niraya* in the sense of being without sustenance.

In the fourth [verse], *pasannaṃ* means clarified by the clarity of faith (*saddhāpasāda*). *Sugatiṃ* means a destination of happiness. *Saggaṃ lokaṃ* means the world that is truly supreme (*suṭṭhu agga*) due to its excellence in form and other qualities.
45. In the fifth [simile], "a pool of water" (*udakarahada*) means a body of water.
"Turbid" (*āvila*) means not clear. "Agitated" (*luḷita*) means not settled. "Muddy" (*kalalībhūta*) means turned into mud. Regarding "oysters and shells" (*sippisambuka*) and so forth:
oysters and shells together are "oyster-shells. Pebbles and gravel together are "pebbles-and-gravel. A mass or collection of fish is "a school of fish" (*macchagumba*).
Regarding the phrase "whether walking or standing": here, the pebbles and gravel remain standing;

the others, however, both walk and stand. Just as, even when some cows are standing, sitting, or lying down between times, one says "these cows are grazing" by referring to those that are grazing, so too the others are called "grazing" because of the pebbles and gravel that are indeed standing. Thus, [it is said] even while the pebbles and gravel are standing.
With reference to the other two who are "standing," it is said [they are] "moving"; with reference to the other two who are "moving," even a pebble or a stone is said to be "moving.

"Turbid" means enveloped by the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). In the phrases "for one's own sake," etc., "one's own" refers to [the benefit] pertaining to this very life (*diṭṭhadhammika*) for oneself.

The aim that is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane for oneself is called "one's own welfare" (*attattha*). The aim that is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane for one's own future life is called "the welfare of others" (*parattha*);
for it is the aim for another that is "the welfare of others. Both of these together are called "the welfare of both" (*ubhayattha*).
Furthermore, even the mundane and supramundane aim pertaining to both one's present life and one's future life for oneself is called "one's own welfare."
The welfare of another that is of such a kind is called "the welfare of others" (*parattha*); both of these together are called "the welfare of both" (*ubhayattha*).
Or, "beyond human states" (*uttariṃ vā manussadhammā*) means beyond those human states comprised by the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

For this tenfold Dhamma was undertaken spontaneously by humans who experienced a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) at the end of an intermediate eon (*kappa*), even without another teacher to encourage them to undertake it.
It is called "human dhamma. Beyond that, however, the meditative absorptions (jhāna), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and the fruit (phala) are to be understood.

"The distinction of noble knowledge and vision" refers to the distinction known as knowledge and vision which is appropriate for the noble ones (ariya), or capable of producing the state of a noble one.

For it should be understood that knowledge itself is "knowledge" in the sense of knowing, and "vision" in the sense of seeing; this is a designation for the divine eye-knowledge, insight-knowledge, path-knowledge, fruition-knowledge, and reviewing-knowledge.
46. In the sixth [sutta], *accha* means not turbid; it is also appropriate as "clear" (*pasanna*). *Vippasanna* means perfectly clear. *Anāvila* means not turbid;
the meaning is "completely pure," which is to say it is free from froth, bubbles, scum, seaweed, and moss. *Anāvilena* means by one who is liberated from the five hindrances.
The rest is exactly according to the method explained in the fourth [sutta]. In these two suttas as well...
Only the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*) have been explained.
47. Regarding the phrase "of the various kinds of trees" (*rukkhajātānaṃ*): this is the genitive case used in the sense of the nominative;
the meaning is "the various kinds of trees. This is a designation for trees. *Yadidaṃ* is merely a particle. *Mudutāya* means by way of softness. For some tree, by its color...

One tree is foremost for its fragrance, another for its flavor, and another for its firmness; however, it shows that the *phandana* tree is foremost and best because of its softness and its workability.

In the passage, "Bhikkhus, the mind when developed and cultivated," it is the mind that has been developed by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), as well as that which has been practiced repeatedly, which is intended. (From the *Kurundaka-vāsī*)

But the Elder Phussamitta said: "Friend, that which is called 'mind' that is exclusively soft and wieldy is precisely the mind of the fourth jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).
48. "Thus easily turning" means thus arising quickly and ceasing quickly.
"Yāvañca" is a particle used in the sense of an excessive measure; the meaning is "it is exceedingly difficult. "Idaṃ" is a mere particle. "Cittaṃ" means...
Some teachers indeed say it is "life-continuum consciousness" (*bhavaṅgacitta*), but having rejected that, it is stated:
"In this context, 'consciousness' is intended to mean anything whatsoever, even down to eye-consciousness.
Regarding this matter, King Milinda questioned the Dhamma-preacher, the Venerable Nāgasena: "Venerable Nāgasena, the mental formations that arise in a single moment of a finger-snap..."
“If they were material, what size heap would they be?

“Great King, a hundred cartloads of rice, and three and a half cartloads, and seven *sattambaṇa* measures, and two *tumba* measures—these do not approach even a fraction, do not approach a part, do not approach a portion of a single moment of consciousness that occurs in the blink of an eye. Then why was it [said] by the Perfectly Enlightened One?
Was it not said that "even a simile is not easy to provide"?

For just as a simile for the long duration of an eon was given by means of a mountain a league high filled with mustard seeds, a simile for the suffering of hell by means of being struck by a hundred spears, and a simile for the happiness of heaven by means of the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch—even so should it be done here. In that regard, it is possible...
"However, venerable sir, [you] have made a simile by way of a question," [it is said]. In this sutta, because there is no question, no simile is made.
For this sutta was spoken at the conclusion of a teaching on the Dhamma. Thus, in this sutta, that which is called the "heap of mind" (cittarāsi) has been explained.
49. In the ninth [verse], "radiant" (*pabhassara*) means white and pure. "Mind" (*citta*) refers to the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅga-citta*).

But does the mind have a color? It does not. Whether it has one of the colors such as blue and so forth, or whether it is colorless, it is called "radiant" because of its purity. This too is pure due to the absence of defilements.

"Luminous" (*pabhassaraṃ*). "And that" (*tañca kho*) refers to that life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*). "By adventitious" (*āgantukehi*) means by those not co-nascent, which arise later at the moment of impulsion (*javana*).
"By defilements" (*upakkilesehi*): because it is defiled by lust and so forth, it is called "defiled. How so?
Just as parents who are virtuous and endowed with good conduct, or teachers and preceptors, [are affected] by those who are immoral...
This should be understood as follows: by reason of their sons and their pupils and co-residents who are ill-behaved and lacking in virtue, they receive disrepute and ill-fame, [the criticism being]:
"They do not reprove, train, exhort, or instruct their own sons, nor their pupils and co-residents.
They are like parents endowed with good conduct.

The life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta) should be regarded as being like the teacher or the preceptor; and just as those [teachers] suffer a loss of reputation through their sons and so forth,

so too the naturally pure life-continuum consciousness becomes called "defiled" by adventitious secondary defilements (upakkilesa) arising through the influence of states of consciousness such as those accompanied by greed, which possess the inherent nature of lust, hatred, and delusion at the moment of impulsion (javana).

50. In the tenth [moment] as well, the consciousness is simply the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness. It is called "completely free" because at the moment of impulsion (javana), it does not become lustful, does not become hateful, and does not become deluded;
rather, by way of wholesome states such as those associated with triple-rooted knowledge, it arises as being completely free from adventitious defilements.
Here too, it is just as in the case of children and others who possess virtue and are endowed with good conduct.
Mothers and others receive praise for their reputation, thinking, "These very beautiful ones are training, exhorting, and instructing their own children. Likewise,
by virtue of the wholesome consciousness that has arisen at the moment of impulsion (javana), this life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness is said to be free from adventitious defilements.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Well-Directed Mind (Paṇihitacittavagga). 6. Commentary on the Chapter on the Snap of the Fingers (Accharāsaṅghātavagga). 51.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the sixth [chapter]: "That uninstructed worldling" refers to that life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta) belonging to one devoid of learning.
The worldling (*puthujjana*). In this context, one should be known as "one who has not heard" (*assutavā*) because of the absence of both scriptural tradition (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).

For one who examines this discourse from the beginning according to its meaning does not [know]—either by way of scriptural tradition or [realization]—"This is called the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*);
though naturally pure, it is defiled by the adventitious defilements (*upakkilesa*) such as greed that arise at the moment of impulsion (*javana*). Nor...

One knows by way of realization (*adhigama*). However, one who lacks the study, inquiry, and discernment regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, the nature of conditions (*paccayākāra*), the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), and so forth, possesses neither the scripture (*āgama*) that accomplishes the penetration of knowledge as it truly is, nor the realization (*adhigama*) because of not having attained what is to be attained through practice.
Due to this absence of both scripture and realization, he is to be known as "one who has not heard" (*assutavā*). And this person—
“A worldling (puthujjana) is so called because of the causes such as the generation of many (puthu) defilements, and because this person is included among the many (puthu).
For he is a worldling because of the causes such as the generation of the various kinds of defilements and so forth. As it has been said:
“They generate various defilements, thus they are *puthujjana*s; they have not abandoned the various views of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), thus they are *puthujjana*s;
they look toward the faces of various teachers, thus they are *puthujjana*s; they have not emerged from the various realms of existence, thus they are *puthujjana*s;
they perform various volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), thus they are *puthujjana*s; they are swept away by various floods (*ogha*), thus they are *puthujjana*s.”
They are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various individual fevers; they are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various individual anxieties;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually attached, greedy, infatuated, deluded, obsessed, stuck, clinging, and entangled in the five strands of sensual pleasure;
they are called *puthujjana* because they are individually obstructed, covered, enveloped, and shut in by the five hindrances.
"Ordinary persons (puthujjana) are those who are covered and concealed.

Or, he is called an *puthujjana* because he is included among the multitude (*puthu*)—those who have passed beyond the path of counting, who are turned away from the noble Dhamma, and whose conduct consists of base qualities.

Alternatively, he is called an *puthujjana* because he has gone into a separate reckoning as one distinct from those endowed with virtues such as moral discipline and learning, being unassociated with them.
The "person" referred to by the noble ones is the worldling (*puthujjana*). Thus, by these two phrases—"the uninstructed worldling"—those [two types] are indicated:
"Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun:
one is the blind worldling, and the other is the virtuous worldling."
Two types of worldlings (*puthujjana*) have been mentioned; it should be understood that among them, the "blind worldling" is the one being referred to here.

"He does not understand things as they really are" means he does not know according to their true nature that "this life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) is thus defiled by adventitious corruptions, and thus it is free from them. "Therefore" means because he does not know.
Therefore, by saying "there is no development of the mind," he shows that there is neither stability of mind nor mastery of mind; I say "it does not exist" precisely because of its non-existence. 52.
In the second [sutta], "one who has heard" means one endowed with what has been heard. Furthermore, the meaning of the term "one who has not heard" here should be understood by way of its opposite.
"Noble disciple": there is one who is noble but not a disciple, such as the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas.

And: there is one who is a disciple but not noble, such as a householder who has not yet attained the fruit; there is one who is neither noble nor a disciple, such as those belonging to various other sects;
there is one who is both noble and a disciple, such as the ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan son, who have attained the fruit and understood the teaching.
In this context, however, whether one is a householder or one who has gone forth, anyone who is "learned" (sutavā) [is intended].

By virtue of the meaning of what has been said, one who is endowed with what has been heard should be understood as "this noble disciple. "He understands it as it really is" means he knows according to its true nature:
"In this way, this life-continuum consciousness is free from adventitious defilements; in this way, it is defiled.
"There is the cultivation of the mind" refers to the stability of the mind and the mastery of the mind.
He shows that he says "it exists" precisely because of its state of existing. In this sutta, powerful insight (balava-vipassanā) is discussed;
some say it is nascent insight (taruṇa-vipassanā).
This third [sutta] was spoken on account of a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). But by what occasion was it spoken? It was spoken on the occasion of the Fire-Mass Simile Sutta.
It is said that on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Great Monastery of Jetavana.
For Buddhas, wherever they may dwell, five kinds of duties are never abandoned. Indeed, there are five duties of a Buddha:
the duty before the meal, the duty after the meal, the duty during the first watch of the night, the duty during the middle watch of the night, and the duty during the last watch of the night.
In this regard, this is the duty before the meal: having risen early in the morning, the Blessed One—

having performed his bodily care such as washing the face for the sake of favoring his attendants and for the sake of physical comfort, and having spent the time until the hour for the alms-round in a secluded seat—
puts on his lower robe at the time for the alms-round, fastens his waistband, dons his upper robe, and takes up his bowl.
Sometimes he enters a village or a town for alms alone, and sometimes surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
sometimes in his ordinary manner, and sometimes while many miracles are taking place.
For instance, as the Lord of the World enters for alms, winds of gentle speed go before him and clear the earth, and clouds release droplets of water.
Some winds, laying down dust upon the path, stand above as a canopy;
others gather flowers and scatter them upon the path. Elevated portions of the ground sink down, and depressed portions rise up;
at the moment of setting foot down, the ground becomes level, or lotus flowers with pleasant touch receive the feet. [This is] of the Indakhīla.
As soon as his right foot was set down, six-colored rays of light issued from his body;
adorning the palaces, gabled houses, and other structures—which appeared as if draped in variegated cloths or suffused with the golden hue of molten gold—they flashed hither and thither.
Even elephants, horses, birds, and other creatures, though remaining in their respective places, let out sounds in a sweet manner.
Likewise, they play drums, lutes, and other musical instruments, as well as the bodily ornaments of humans.

By that sign, people know: "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms. Dressed well and properly robed, taking perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, they depart from their homes, enter the middle of the street, and respectfully honor the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having honored and paid homage [to the Blessed One], they requested, "Venerable sir, please give ten bhikkhus for us, twenty for us, fifty... [and so on]... a hundred for us.
Then, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and preparing a seat, they respectfully served him with almsfood.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he surveyed their underlying mental continuums and, accordingly—

He teaches the Dhamma so that some are established in the refuges, some in the five precepts, some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning, and some, having gone forth, attain the supreme fruit of arahantship.
Having thus assisted the great multitude, he rises from his seat and goes to the monastery. Having arrived there, in the fragrant pavilion...
He sits upon the excellent Buddha-seat that has been prepared, awaiting the conclusion of the monks' meal.
Then, at the conclusion of the monks' meal, the attendant informs the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One enters the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*).
This, first of all, is the duty before the meal.

Then the Blessed One, having thus finished his meal, sat in the vicinity of the Fragrant Cottage, washed his feet, and standing upon the footstool, exhorted the community of monks: "Monks, strive with diligence!
Rare is the arising of a Buddha in the world; rare is the attainment of human birth; rare is the perfection of the opportune moment; rare is..."
“Going forth is rare; hearing the true Dhamma is rare. Thereupon, some asked the Blessed One for a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
The Blessed One gave them a meditation subject suited to their individual temperaments.
Then, having paid homage to the Blessed One, they all went to their respective night-quarters and day-quarters—some to the forest, some to the foot of a tree.
Some [beings] saw one or another of the mountains, some the abode of the Four Great Kings... and so on... and some the abode of Vasavatti.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the Fragrant Chamber, if he so desired, would for a moment lie down in the lion’s posture on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Then, having refreshed his body, he would rise and survey the world during the second watch.
During the third watch, in whatever village or town he dwells depending upon, the great multitude there, having given alms before the meal,
afterwards— well-robed and well-dressed— and taking perfumes, flowers, and so forth, assembles at the monastery. Then the Blessed One,
having approached with a miracle suited to the assembly that has gathered, proceeds to the Dhamma Hall and ascends the excellent Buddha-seat prepared there.

Seated, he teaches the Dhamma at the appropriate time and on the appropriate occasion; then, having discerned the right time, he dismisses the assembly, and the people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, depart. This is the duty after the meal.
Having thus completed his duties after the meal, if he wishes to bathe his limbs, he rises from the Buddha’s seat.
Having entered the bath-house, he warms his limbs with water prepared by his attendant.
The attendant, having brought the Buddha’s seat, arranges it in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber.
The Blessed One, having put on his well-dyed inner robe, fastened his waist-band, and draped his upper robe over one shoulder, enters there alone and sits down.
Having remained in seclusion for a short while, the bhikkhus then come from here and there to attend upon the Blessed One.
There, some ask questions, some seek a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and some request a teaching on the Dhamma.
The Blessed One spends the first watch of the night fulfilling their intentions. This is the duty of the first watch.
But at the conclusion of the duties of the first watch, when the monks had paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities of the entire ten-thousandfold world system,
seeking an opportunity, approached the Blessed One and asked questions, even about matters as small as four syllables that had been previously prepared.
The Blessed One spent the middle watch answering the questions of those deities.
This is the duty of the middle watch.

As for the last watch, however, having divided it into three sections, he spends one section in walking meditation in order to relieve the physical fatigue of his body, which has been oppressed by sitting since before the meal; in the second section, [he enters] the fragrant chamber.
Having entered, mindful and clearly comprehending, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture.

Rising in the third watch of the night and sitting up, he surveys the world with his Buddha-eye for the purpose of seeing those individuals who have performed meritorious deeds—such as generosity and virtue—in the presence of previous Buddhas. This is the duty of the final watch of the night.
On that very day, while remaining intent upon this same matter, the Blessed One surveyed the world and saw this:
"While I am wandering on tour through the kingdom of Kosala, when I have taught a discourse using the simile of the mass of fire, sixty bhikkhus will attain arahantship;
the warm blood of about sixty will gush from their mouths, and about sixty householders will [return to] the state of lay life."
They will go there. Among them, those who have reached Arahantship will surely attain it upon hearing any teaching of the Dhamma.
However, desiring to wander on tour for the sake of gathering the other bhikkhus, he said, "Ānanda, inform the bhikkhus.
The Elder went from cell to cell and said, "Friends, the Teacher desires to wander on tour for the sake of gathering the great multitude."
"Come, those who wish to go," he said. The bhikkhus, their minds filled with joy as if they had received a great gain, thought:
"We shall indeed have the opportunity to behold the golden-hued body of the Blessed One as he teaches the Dhamma to the great multitude, and to hear his sweet discourse on the Dhamma.
Thus, though their hair was grown long, they shaved it off; though their bowls were soiled with grime, they polished them; and though their robes were stained, [they prepared themselves].
Having washed their robes, they became ready to depart. The Teacher, surrounded by an unbounded Saṅgha of bhikkhus, set out on a walking tour through the kingdom of Kosala.

Traveling by way of villages and market towns, and proceeding no more than one gāvuta, half a yojana, three gāvutas, or a full yojana at a time, he one day saw in a certain place a large hollow tree engulfed in flames.

Thinking, "Having taken this very matter as the basis, I shall deliver a teaching on the Dhamma adorned with seven factors," the Teacher halted his journey, approached the foot of a certain tree, and assumed a seated posture.
The Elder Ānanda, understanding the Teacher’s intention, thought, "Surely there must be a reason; Tathāgatas do not undertake a journey without a reason."
Having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, he sat down. The Teacher, having sat down, addressed the monks:
"Do you see, monks, that great mass of fire? And so he taught the *Aggikkhandhopama Sutta* (The Simile of the Mass of Fire).
While this exposition was being delivered, warm blood issued from the mouths of about sixty monks.
It was revealed; about sixty monks abandoned the training and returned to the lower life, while the minds of about sixty monks were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

For upon hearing that exposition, the mental body of about sixty monks became feverish; when the mental body became feverish, the physical body made of kamma became feverish; and when the physical body made of kamma became feverish...
Hot blood, which had been stored within, gushed from his mouth.

About sixty monks, thinking, "It is indeed difficult to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) completely and purely for as long as life lasts under the Buddha's teaching," renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
About sixty other monks, directing their knowledge toward the Teacher’s teaching, attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
In that regard, those whose warm blood gushed from their mouths incurred a *pārājika* offense.

Those who returned to the state of householders wandered about violating the minor and lesser training rules (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*). Those who had attained *arahantship* remained pure in virtue (*parisuddhasīla*) as before.
Thus, the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma became fruitful for all three of these groups.
"Let it be fruitful for those who have attained Arahantship; but how has it become fruitful for others?
For even they, had they not heard this teaching of the Dhamma, would have remained heedless and would not have been able to leave their positions.
Consequently, their growing evil would have caused them to sink into the states of misery. But having heard this teaching, they became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
Having left their positions and established themselves on the level of a novice, they fulfilled the ten precepts and applied themselves with wise attention;
some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners, while others were reborn in the world of the devas.
Thus, even for those who had committed a *pārājika* offense, it was fruitful. As for the others, however, had they not heard this teaching of the Dhamma—

As time passes, they will gradually incur offenses entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*) and even those involving defeat (*pārājika*), and having been reborn only in the woeful states, they will experience great suffering.
However, upon hearing this teaching, [they will think]: "Oh, how well-restrained is the Buddha’s dispensation!
It is not possible for us to fulfill this practice for as long as we live; therefore, having renounced the training, we shall adopt the status of lay followers (*upāsaka*)."
“Having fulfilled [our duties], we shall be freed from suffering,” they said, and returned to the state of householders.

Having established themselves in the three refuges, observed the five precepts, and fulfilled the duty of lay followers (*upāsaka*), some became stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), some once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), and some non-returners (*anāgāmin*);
others were reborn in the world of the gods. Thus, for them too, it was indeed fruitful.
Having heard this Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, the hosts of devas—both those who had heard it before and those who had not—wandered about proclaiming it to everyone.

Having heard it again and again, the bhikkhus exclaimed, "It is difficult, sirs, to practice the holy life (brahmacariya) in its fullness and purity for as long as life lasts under the dispensation of the Buddhas! And at that very moment, ten bhikkhus, twenty...
Sixty, a hundred, or even a thousand monks became householders.
After wandering on tour as he pleased, the Teacher returned once more to Jetavana and addressed the monks:
"Monks, while wandering on tour, the Tathāgata has for a long time lived in a crowded state. Monks, I wish to dwell in seclusion for half a month; let no one [approach me]."

“He should be approached, except by one person carrying almsfood. Having spent half a month in solitude, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and, while walking on a tour of the monastery together with the Elder Ānanda, saw that the community of monks had become sparse in every place he looked.
Knowing full well [the reason], he asked the Elder: “Ānanda, at other times...”
"When the Tathāgata had gone on his alms-round and returned to Jetavana, the entire monastery was ablaze with the color of saffron robes and stirred by the breeze of the seers;
but now the community of monks appears diminished, and for the most part the monks are pale and wan—what could this be?
[The Buddha replied: "At present, the Blessed One has given you a teaching on the Dhamma using the simile of a mass of fire."
From the time this was said, the bhikkhus became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and,

thinking, "We shall not be able to fulfill this Dhamma in every respect, and it is improper for us who do not conduct ourselves rightly to enjoy what has been given in faith by the people," they returned to the state of householders.
At that moment, a sense of spiritual urgency regarding the Dhamma arose in the Blessed One. He then said to the Elder:
"While I was spending my time in seclusion, no one told me of even a single point of consolation for my sons.

Indeed, there are many grounds for consolation in this Dispensation, like the numerous landing places for entering the ocean. Go, Ānanda, and prepare the Buddha’s seat in the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber."
“Having prepared the way, assemble the community of monks. The Elder did so. The Teacher, having ascended the excellent Buddha-throne and addressed the monks, said:
“Monks, that which is called the ‘preliminary stage’ of loving-kindness (*mettā*) is neither absorption (*appanā*) nor access (*upacāra*);
it is merely the suffusion of benevolence toward beings. Having spoken thus, on this occasion, he taught this *Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta Sutta*.
In this context, "for the mere duration of a finger-snap" means for the mere duration of a finger-clap; the meaning is: for the mere duration of making a sound by clapping two fingers together.
"A mind of loving-kindness" means a mind that radiates welfare toward all beings. "He cultivates": how does he cultivate it?
He cultivates it by attending to it, he cultivates it by knowing it, he cultivates it by seeing it, he cultivates it by reviewing it, and he cultivates it by resolving the mind upon it.
He cultivates it; resolving with faith, he cultivates it; exerting energy, he cultivates it; establishing mindfulness, he cultivates it;
concentrating the mind, he cultivates it; understanding with wisdom, he cultivates it; directly knowing what is to be directly known, he cultivates it;
fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he cultivates it; abandoning what is to be abandoned, he cultivates it; developing what is to be developed...
"Developing, he cultivates; realizing what is to be realized, he cultivates.
Here, however, it should be understood that he "cultivates" merely by means of the occurrence of the spreading of welfare preceded by loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Possessing jhāna" (*arittajjhāno*) means having non-empty jhāna, or having not abandoned jhāna. "Dwells" (*viharati*) means moves about, proceeds, or protects.
He acts, he causes to act, he moves, he dwells; therefore it is said, "he dwells. By this phrase, the dwelling in the postures of a bhikkhu who cultivates loving-kindness is described.
"One who carries out the Teacher’s instruction" means one who acts according to the Teacher’s teaching. "One who acts upon the exhortation" means one who performs what has been exhorted.
Here, a single utterance is an "exhortation" (*ovāda*), while a repeated utterance is an "instruction" (*anusāsanī*). A face-to-face utterance is also [included].
Exhortation (*ovāda*), sending [a message], and instruction (*anusāsanī*). Exhortation is speech regarding a matter that has already arisen;
instruction is speech—whether regarding a matter that has arisen or one that has not—by way of establishing a rule (*tantiṭhapanavasena*). Thus should the distinction be understood.
But in the ultimate sense, "exhortation" and "instruction" are these two terms synonymous, identical, equal, equivalent, and of the same nature.

"Taṃ ñeva" (that very thing). Herein, "Monks, if a bhikkhu cultivates a mind of loving-kindness for even the duration of a finger-snap"—this alone is both the Teacher’s instruction and his exhortation.
Because he carries this out, he should be understood as one who acts according to the instruction and follows the exhortation. "Amoghaṃ" means not empty.
"Raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ" refers to the alms-food of the country received by one who has gone forth, having abandoned the circle of kinsmen and depending upon the country.
Almsfood obtained from the houses of others is called "the country’s alms" (*raṭṭhapiṇḍa*).
Regarding the phrase "he consumes": there are four ways of consuming—consumption by theft, consumption as a debt, consumption as an inheritance, and consumption as an owner.
Among these, the consumption of one who is immoral is called "consumption by theft. The unreflective consumption of one who possesses virtue is called "consumption as a debt."
The use [of requisites] by the seven types of trainees (sekkha) is called "use as an inheritance. The use by one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is called "use as an owner.
In this regard, for this bhikkhu, this use of the alms-food of the kingdom becomes fruitful for two reasons.
By cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (mettā) for even the duration of a finger-snap, the bhikkhu becomes the master of the alms-food of the kingdom.
"By being free from debt and as an heir, he enjoys [the gift]—thus his enjoyment of the alms of the kingdom is not in vain.

Even for a monk who cultivates loving-kindness for as little as the snap of a finger, the gift given to him becomes of great significance, of great fruit, of great benefit, of great radiance, and of great expansion;
thus his enjoyment of the alms of the kingdom is not in vain. What need is there to speak of those who..."

Regarding the phrase "cultivating it extensively": as for those who frequently practice, develop, and repeatedly perform this mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*), what more need be said here that they consume the alms-food of the kingdom fruitfully?
For such monks, being the rightful owners of the kingdom's alms-food, consume it as debt-free heirs.
54–55. "In the fourth [treatise], 'he develops' means he causes to arise and increases. In the fifth, 'he attends to' means he applies the mind.

The remainder in these two [treatises] should be understood according to the same method as stated in the third. For he who cultivates (āsevati) is the very one who develops (bhāveti), and he is the one who attends to (manasi karoti).
