By whichever mind one cultivates, by that very same [mind] one develops, and by that very same [mind] one attends to. [Thus spoke] the Fully Enlightened One."
However, because he has thoroughly penetrated that element of phenomena (dhammadhātu) through which one is said to have attained mastery in teaching,
by relying on his own mastery in teaching, his sovereignty over the Dhamma, his skill in the various analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and his unimpeded omniscient knowledge, he displayed—
within a single moment and within a single state of consciousness itself— divided into three distinct parts.
56. In the sixth [section], "whatever" (*ye keci*) is an indefinite expression. "Unwholesome" (*akusalā*) is a definite expression specifying them.

To this extent, all unwholesome states are exhausted without remainder. "Associated with the unwholesome" (*akusalabhāgiyā*) and "belonging to the side of the unwholesome" (*akusalapakkhikā*) are names for the unwholesome themselves.
For some unwholesome states indeed associate with the unwholesome by way of co-arising (*sahajāta*), while others do so by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
And because they belong to their side, they are called "conducive to the unwholesome" and "belonging to the faction of the unwholesome.
All these are "preceded by mind": mind goes before them, that is, first, thus they are "preceded by mind.
For although these [mental factors] arise together with the mind, have the same basis, cease simultaneously, and share the same object, [they are so called] because—
However, since the mind is their arouser, maker, progenitor, originator, and producer, they are said to be "preceded by the mind.

Regarding the phrase "it arises first": just as when it is said, "The king has gone out," there is no need to ask whether "only the king has gone out, while the rest of the royal army has gone out or not," for it is understood that everyone has gone out; so too here.

In the same way, from the moment it is said that "the mind has arisen," there is no reason to ask whether the remaining co-nascent, conjoined, and associated states have arisen or not; all of them are known simply as "arisen.
It is for this reason that the mind—though sharing with those states the same arising and the same cessation—is [distinguished] from those phenomena.
It is said that [the mind] arises first. The word *anvadeva* means *anudeva*, which signifies "together with" or "at one and the same time.

One should not, however, grasp the mere shadow of the literal expression and conclude that "first the mind arises, and afterwards the mental factors," for it is the meaning (*attha*) that is the refuge, not the letter (*byañjana*).
This same principle applies to the verse: "Phenomena are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are made of the mind."

57. Regarding "wholesome" (*kusala*) in the seventh [section], wholesome states belonging to all four planes are spoken of. The remainder should be understood in the same manner as explained in the sixth [section].

58. Regarding the eighth [section]: "In this way, monks, negligence (*pamāda*)," here "monks" (*bhikkhave*) is an address; the meaning is "in this way, this negligence. "Negligence" is the mode of being negligent.
For it has been said: "In that regard, what is negligence? It is [the failure to guard] regarding bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct, or the five..."
Or the relinquishing of the mind toward the strands of sensual pleasure, the failure to provide further support for that relinquishing; or, regarding the cultivation of wholesome states,
lack of diligence, lack of constancy, lack of steadfastness in practice, a state of sluggishness, the casting aside of desire,
the casting aside of the burden, lack of resolve, lack of application, lack of repetition, lack of development, and lack of frequent practice— whatever is of such a nature.
“Negligence, neglecting, and the state of being negligent—this is called negligence.

As for the statement “wholesome states that have arisen decline,” this is said with reference to *jhāna* and insight (*vipassanā*). However, once the paths and fruits have arisen, there is no further falling away from them.
In the ninth [section], diligence (*appamāda*) is to be understood in detail by way of its being the opposite of negligence.
60. Regarding "indolence" (*kosajja*) in the tenth [chapter], it is the state of being indolent (*kusīta*). The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Accharāsaṅghāta-vagga*. 7.
Commentary on the *Vīriyārambha-ādi-vagga*.

61. In the first [section] of the seventh [chapter], "the undertaking of energy" (*vīriyārambha*) means the undertaking of the energy of right effort (*sammappadhāna*), which possesses four functions; the meaning is the state of having undertaken, exerted, and perfected that energy.

62. In the second [section], "great desire" (*mahicchatā*) means great greed. With reference to this it is said: "In that regard, what is great desire? It is [the lack of contentment with] robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
Or, for one who is not content with the five strands of sensual pleasure, there is the desire for more;
such a longing, a state of longing, great desire, lust, intense lust, and the intense lust of the mind—this is called "great desire" (mahicchatā). 63.
In the third [case], "fewness of desires" (appicchatā) is non-greed (alobha). "Of one who has few desires" means of one who is without desire. Here, the phrasing is elliptical.
The meaning, however, is exhaustive. For he is not called "one of few wishes" (appiccha) merely because of the presence of a small amount of wishing;
rather, he is called "one of few wishes" because of the very presence of non-greed (alobha), which has been repeatedly cultivated through the absence of wishing.

Furthermore, in this context, the distinction between excessive wishing (atricchatā), evil wishing (pāpicchatā), great wishing (mahicchatā), and fewness of wishes (appicchatā) should be understood. Therein:
"Insatiability" (atricchā) is the longing for the gains of others when one is not satisfied with one's own complete gains.
One endowed with this [insatiability] perceives even a cake cooked in a single vessel as if it were poorly baked and small when it falls into his own bowl;
yet, that very same cake, when placed in another's bowl, appears as if well-baked and large. This is the "exaggeration of non-existent qualities."
Furthermore, lack of moderation in receiving gifts and having evil desires is what is called *pāpicchatā*. This is indeed mentioned in the Abhidhamma in such passages as:
"Here, someone being faithless thinks, 'May people know me to be faithful,'" and so forth. A person endowed with that [desire] establishes himself in hypocrisy (*kohañña*).
However, the desire for the recognition of one's existing virtues, as well as lack of moderation in receiving gifts, is what is called *mahicchatā*.
She too has been included by way of this principle: "Here, someone who is faithful desires, 'May people know me as faithful'; one who is virtuous desires, 'May people know me as virtuous.
A person endowed with such qualities is difficult to satisfy;
even his own mother, once she has given birth to him, is unable to win over his mind. Therefore, this is said:
“The mass of fire, the ocean, and the person of great desire—let these three be satisfied by providing requisites with a cart.
Furthermore, having hidden one’s own virtues, and knowing the proper measure in receiving, is what is called fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*); one who is endowed with that [is so described].
A person, though possessing faith, out of a desire to conceal the virtues existing within himself,
does not wish for it to be known by people that "I am faithful. Likewise, though being virtuous, secluded, learned, energetic,
endowed with concentration, wise, and one whose taints are destroyed, he does not wish for it to be known by people that "I am one whose taints are destroyed," just like the Elder Majjhantika.
It is said that this Elder was one whose taints were utterly destroyed, yet his bowl and robe were worth only a mere penny.
On the day of the great festival for the monastery of King Asoka, he served as the senior monk of the Saṅgha.

Seeing his extreme frugality, people said to him, "Venerable sir, please stay a little away from here. The Elder replied, "If they do not show hospitality toward an arahant like me who has destroyed the taints..."
“Who else will do it? Having said this, he submerged himself in the earth and emerged while still taking the alms-food that had been set aside for the senior elder of the Saṅgha.
Even though he was one whose taints were destroyed, he did not wish for people to know him as “one whose taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, such a bhikkhu of few desires brings about unarisen gain and makes what has arisen stable, [and he does so] with regard to the minds of the donors.
He fulfills [the requirements]. For in whatever measure he takes little for himself due to his own fewness of desires, in that same measure people, being confident in his conduct, give much to him.

Furthermore, there is another fourfold fewness of desires: fewness of desire regarding requisites, fewness of desire regarding ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and fewness of desire regarding the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
"Having few desires regarding attainment. In this context, one who has few desires regarding the four requisites is called "one with few desires regarding requisites.
He knows the donor's capacity, he knows the nature of the gift, and he knows his own strength.
For if the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a small amount, he takes only a little according to the donor's capacity. Regarding the gift...
When there is little [to give] but the donor wishes to give much, he takes only a small amount on account of the gift to be given.
When the gift to be given is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he takes only a moderate amount, knowing his own capacity.

One who does not wish to make known the presence within himself of the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) is called "one who is few in regard to ascetic practices" (dhutaṅga-appiccha). Of him—

These are the instances for the purpose of contemplation: it is said that the Elder Mahākumāra, who lived in a charnel ground for sixty years, was not recognized by even a single other bhikkhu. For this very reason he said:
“For sixty years in the charnel ground, I have dwelt without interruption.”
"May my second brother not recognize me;
oh, what a supreme dweller in the charnel ground! On Cetiya Mountain there lived two elder brothers who were *theras*.
The younger one, having taken a piece of sugarcane sent by his attendant, went to the presence of the elder and said, "Venerable sir, please partake of this. And as for the elder's meal duty...
It was time for him to rinse his mouth. He said, "Enough, friend. "Venerable sir, do you observe the practice of eating at a single sitting?
"Bring some sugar-cane pieces, friend. Although he had been one who eats at a single sitting for fifty years, he used the food while concealing his ascetic practice (dhutaṅga);
having rinsed his mouth, he then resolved upon the ascetic practice again and departed.
However, one who, like the Elder Sāketatissa, does not wish to make known his state of great learning is called "one who is few in regard to the scriptures" (pariyatti-appiccha).
It is said that the Elder, not finding the opportunity for recitation and interrogation because he did not make time for them, thinking, "When, venerable sir, will you find the moment of death?
was exhorted by this question; he then dismissed his following and went to the Kaṇikāravālikasamudda Monastery.
There, having been of assistance to the senior, junior, and middle-ranking monks during the rainy season,
he departed after shaking the countryside with a discourse on the Dhamma on the Uposatha day of the Great Pavāraṇā.
However, as for one who, being among those such as stream-enterers and so forth, does not wish to make known his status as a stream-enterer or the like— this...
One who desires little in terms of attainment (*adhigamappiccha*) is like the three sons of noble family and like Ghaṭīkāra the potter.

However, in this context, it should be understood that even a trainee (*sekha*) or an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) who possesses powerful non-greed through long-standing practice is one who desires little. 64.

In the fourth [case], "non-contentment" (*asantuṭṭhi*) refers to the greed characterized as dissatisfaction that arises in one who serves, associates with, and attends upon persons who are themselves discontented.
65. "Contentment" (santuṭṭhitā) refers to the contentment characterized by non-greed that arises in one who serves, associates with, and attends upon persons who are content.
"Of one who is content" means of one endowed with contentment regarding various requisites.
Furthermore, this contentment is of twelve kinds, namely: contentment with whatever robe one obtains, and contentment according to one's capacity; [and so forth].
Contentment according to suitability is threefold. It is the same with alms-food and so forth.
This is its detailed explanation: here, a bhikkhu receives a robe, whether beautiful or ugly;
he maintains himself with that alone and does not long for another, nor does he accept it even if he receives one. This is his contentment with whatever robe is obtained (*yathālābhasantosa*).
Furthermore, if one is naturally weak or overcome by illness and old age, he becomes exhausted when putting on heavy robes.
Even though he exchanges those with a fellow monk of similar standing and makes do with lighter ones, he remains content.
This is his contentment regarding robes according to his strength. Another person obtains excellent requisites; he [obtains] robes of fine cloth and so forth.
Having obtained either a single robe of great value or many robes, and having given them [thinking], "This is for the elders who have long been ordained;
this is suitable for those of great learning; this is for the sick;
this is for those of little gain," he might even take their old robes or scraps of cloth gathered from rubbish heaps, sew them together into a *saṅghāṭī*, and wear it.
He is indeed content. This is his contentment with robes as they happen to be suitable.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined;
he sustains himself with that alone, does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not accept it. This is his contentment with almsfood as it happens to be obtained. But whoever...

If he receives almsfood that is contrary to his natural constitution or contrary to his illness—such that by consuming it he becomes unwell—he gives it to a fellow monk of similar temperament, and having eaten suitable food from that person's hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse.
This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another...

He receives abundant and excellent almsfood. Yet, having given that robe-like food to elders, those long-ordained, the learned, those who receive little, or the sick—or else, having shared what remains with them or having gone for alms himself, he eats a mixed meal; even so, he remains contented.
This is his contentment with almsfood as it is appropriate.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives a lodging that is either pleasing or unpleasing;
he gives rise to neither joy nor dejection on account of it, but is content with whatever he has received, even if it is merely a spread of grass.
This is his contentment with whatever lodging is obtained. However, as for that which is contrary to his own nature or contrary to his illness...

If he obtains a lodging where, while living there, he finds it uncomfortable, he gives that to a fellow monk of like standing and remains content even while living in whatever suitable lodging belongs to that monk.
This is his contentment with respect to lodgings according to his strength.
Furthermore, another person of great merit obtains many excellent lodgings, such as caves, pavilions, gabled houses, and so forth. He—

Just as with robes and other requisites, he remains content even while living anywhere, having given [his own] to elders, those long-ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick. This is his contentment with a dwelling-place that is appropriate to his status.
Furthermore, [he reflects]: "A superior dwelling-place is a ground for negligence; for one sitting there, sloth and torpor descend, and for one overcome by sleep..."
Reflecting thus, "Evil thoughts manifest as I am waking up," he does not accept even when such a lodging is offered.
Having declined it, he remains content even while dwelling in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or elsewhere.
This is his contentment with a lodging as it suits him.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives medicine, whether coarse or refined;

he is content with whatever he receives and does not long for anything else, and even if he finds more, he does not take it. This is his contentment with what is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine.
But one who needs oil and receives molasses gives that to a fellow bhikkhu of similar status and [takes what he needs].
Even when making medicine by taking oil from someone’s hand or seeking out something else entirely, he remains content.
This is his contentment with whatever strength he has regarding the requisite of medicine.
Another person of great merit receives abundant, high-quality medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses; he treats that [medicine] just like a robe.
Having given to elders, those long-ordained, the learned, those who receive little, and the sick, he remains content even while subsisting on whatever is brought back by them.
But when one person, having placed *muttaharītaka* in one bowl and the four sweets (*catumadhura*) in another,
is told, "Venerable sir, take whichever you wish," and he says, "If his illness is cured by either of these..."
Then, thinking, "The so-called *muttaharītaka* (urine-medicine) has been praised by the Buddha and others," he rejects the four sweets and prepares his medicine with *muttaharītaka*;
even so, he remains supremely content. This is his "contentment with what is appropriate" (*yathāsāruppa-santosa*) regarding the requisite of medicine.
Among these three types of contentment for each of the requisites, however, contentment with what is appropriate is the foremost.
66–67. In the sixth and seventh [factors], lack of reasoned attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) and reasoned attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) have the characteristics already explained above.

The rest here is of obvious meaning. 68. In the eighth, "lack of clear comprehension" (*asampajañña*) is the state of not being clearly comprehending; this is a designation for delusion (*moha*). "Of one who is not clearly comprehending" (*asampajānassa*) means of one who does not know, who is confused.

69. In the ninth, "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*) is the state of being clearly comprehending; this is a name for wisdom (*paññā*). "Of one who is clearly comprehending" (*sampajānassa*) means of one who knows clearly.

70. Tenth, regarding "evil friendship" (*pāpamittatā*): one who has evil, base friends is an "evil friend. The state of being an evil friend is "evil friendship"; this is the name for the four aggregates (*khandha*) that function in that manner.
And it is said: "In this context, what is evil friendship? Those persons who are faithless, immoral, unlearned, stingy, and lacking wisdom.
Whatever association, close association, constant association, following, thorough following, devotion, devotedness, and intimacy there is with them—that is [evil friendship]."
“This is called having evil friends.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Arousing of Energy, etc. 8.
Commentary on the Chapter on Having Virtuous Friends, etc.

71. Regarding the first [factors] of the eighth [tetrad]: "good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) means one who has good friends is a "good friend"; the state of being such is "good friendship. The remainder should be understood according to the method of opposites already stated.

72–73. Regarding the second [tetrad]: "application" (*anuyoga*) means *yoga* (exertion) or *payoga* (practice). "Non-application" (*ananuyoga*) means lack of *yoga* or lack of *payoga*. "By application" (*anuyogā*) means by means of application. "By non-application" (*ananuyogā*) means by means of non-application.
"Of wholesome states" (*kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*) refers to wholesome states belonging to the four planes. The third [tetrad] is of plain meaning.
74. *Catutthe bojjhaṅgā*: the seven states that constitute the factors (*aṅga*) of a being who is awakening.
Alternatively, they are called "factors of awakening" because through that harmony of states one awakens, emerges from the sleep of delusion, or realizes the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths.

They are also called "factors of awakening" because they are the constituent parts of that awakening (*bodhi*). "In what sense are they 'factors of awakening'? They are factors of awakening in the sense that 'they awaken' (*bujjhanti*)."

“They are called *bojjhaṅga*s because they awaken (*anubujjhanti*); they are called *bojjhaṅga*s because they wake up (*paṭibujjhanti*); they are called *bojjhaṅga*s because they fully awaken (*sambujjhanti*);
they are called *bojjhaṅga*s because they lead to awakening (*bodhāya saṃvattanti*). Thus, this term has been analyzed.
In the fifth [section], by the phrase “they reach the fulfillment of development,” the stage of the factors of awakening as they truly are is indicated.
Thus they have been named. Furthermore, this [enlightenment] is fourfold: insight (vipassanā), jhāna that serves as the basis for insight, the path (magga), and the fruit (phala).

Among these, at the time of arising in insight, the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅgā) are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara); at the time of arising in jhāna that serves as the basis for insight, they are of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara);
and at the time of arising in the paths and fruits, they are supramundane (lokuttara). Thus, in this [context]...
In the Sutta, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are explained as belonging to four planes.
76. This is the introduction (nikkhepa) based on a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppattika). For this was introduced on that occasion:
it is said that a large number of bhikkhus were seated together in the Hall of Dharma (dhammasabhā). Among them, concerning the general Bandhula Mallaseṇāpati—
This discussion arose: "Friends, such-and-such a family was formerly one with many relatives and many supporters, but now it has become one with few relatives and few supporters.

Then the Blessed One, knowing their mental disposition and perceiving that "a great teaching will take place once I have gone there," emerged from the Gandhakuṭī and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma Hall.
Having sat down, he asked, “Monks, about what topic are you gathered here now? They replied, “Lord, there is no other talk concerning villages, market towns, and so forth;

we are sitting here saying that such-and-such a family was formerly well-connected with many relatives and had many supporters, but now it has become one with few relatives and few supporters. On account of this occasion, the Teacher—
He began this discourse with the words: "Monks, this is a minor loss.
In this context, "minor" means small or limited in measure. For by this loss, there is no falling away from heaven or from the Path;
he said this because it is merely a loss pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). This is the lowest [form of loss].

"This is the last of it, this is the wretched: namely, the decline of wisdom. This means that whatever decline there is in my teaching regarding the wisdom of the ownership of one's actions, the wisdom of meditative absorption, the wisdom of insight, the wisdom of the path, and the wisdom of the fruit—this is the final one, this is the wretched one;
the meaning is that this is to be discarded.
77. This seventh [case] is also told by way of an occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). It is said that while the bhikkhus were seated in the Hall of Truth, some of them spoke thus:
"That family named so-and-so was formerly one with few relatives and few supporters;
now it has become one with many relatives and many supporters. With reference to whom did they speak thus? With reference to the laywoman Visākhā.
And the Licchavis of Vesālī. The Teacher, having understood their mental disposition, arrived in the same manner as before and, seated upon the Dharma-seat, asked:
"Bhikkhus, about what talk are you gathered here now? They explained it exactly as it was.
On this occasion, the Teacher began this Sutta. In that context, the word *appamattikā* means...
It is "limited" because there is an absence of those who, by depending on that prosperity, have attained heaven or the path.
"The increase of wisdom" refers to the growth of wisdom such as the understanding of one's own karma (*kammassakata*). "Therefore" means:

since what is called the increase of relatives is merely pertaining to this present life, it is small and limited, and thus incapable of leading to heaven or the path; therefore. "By the increase of wisdom" means by the growth of wisdom regarding one's own karma and so forth.

78. This eighth case was also told by way of an occasion. It seems that a number of bhikkhus, having sat down together in the Hall of Truth, were speaking concerning the son of a very wealthy merchant:

"Such-and-such a family was formerly possessed of great wealth and vast gold and bullion, but now it has become one of little means. The Teacher, arriving in the same manner as before, [addressed] them...
Having heard these words, he began this sutta.

79. This ninth [sutta] was also spoken on account of a specific occasion. It is said that while the monks were seated together in the Hall of Truth, they spoke concerning the merchant Kākavaliya and the merchant Puṇṇa:
"Such-and-such a family was formerly of little wealth, but now it is of great wealth."
“It has been born,” they said. The Teacher, having arrived in the same manner as before and having heard their words, began this Sutta.
The remainder of both these [discourses] should be understood according to the method already stated below.
The tenth [discourse] was also spoken on account of a specific occasion. It is said that in the Hall of Truth, the monks were discussing the Great King of Kosala.
Regarding this, they said, "Such-and-such a family was formerly of great renown and had a large retinue; now it has become of little renown and has a small retinue.
The Blessed One, having arrived in the same manner as before and heard their words, began this teaching on the Dhamma.
The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.
Commentary on the Chapter on Good Friends and Others. 9. Commentary on the Chapter on Heedlessness and Others. 81.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the ninth chapter as well, it was spoken by way of an introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*). It is said that a number of bhikkhus were in the Hall of Dhamma.
Seated together, they spoke concerning Kumbhaghosaka, saying, "Such-and-such a family was formerly of little wealth and small retinue, but now it has become of great renown and large retinue.
The Teacher, having arrived in the same manner as before and heard their words, began this Sutta. Its meaning is to be understood in the same way as explained below.
82. Regarding the second [sutta] and those that follow, "for great harm" (*mahato anatthāya*) means for the sake of great harm. The rest here is self-evident.
This concludes the commentary on the *Pamādādivagga*. 10. Commentary on the *Dutiyapamādādivagga*.
98. In the tenth [verse], "internal" (*ajjhattika*) means internal by way of being one's own internal [domain]. "Factor" (*aṅga*) means a cause.

"Having made it thus" (*iti karitvā*) means having done so. This is what is meant: "O monks, having made it a cause that has arisen within oneself, in one's own personal continuum, I do not see any other single cause."

110–114. *Bāhiraṃ* means existence outside of one’s own internal continuum. *Saddhammassa* means of the true Dhamma; the meaning is "of the teaching. *Sammosāya* means for the sake of confusion or destruction. *Antarahānāya* means for the sake of disappearance or non-recognition. 115. *Ṭhitiyā* means for the sake of long endurance.

*Asammosāya* and *anantarāhānāya* should be understood by way of the opposites of what was stated [above]. The rest here follows the same method as explained in the fourfold permutation (*catukkoṭika*). 130.

Regarding the subsequent passages beginning with "teaching what is not Dhamma as Dhamma," first, according to the method of the Suttanta, there are the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

Dhamma is [the wholesome], while the ten unwholesome courses of action are adhamma. Likewise, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path—are called Dhamma.
[Conversely,] the three foundations of mindfulness and the three right efforts...
The three bases of psychic power, the six faculties, the six powers, the eight factors of enlightenment, and the ninefold path;
as well as the four types of clinging, the five hindrances, the seven underlying tendencies, and the eight wrongnesses—this is what is non-Dhamma.
In this regard, if one takes any portion of what is non-Dhamma and thinks, "We shall make this non-Dhamma into Dhamma," [it is not so].
Thinking, "In this way our teacher’s lineage will lead to liberation, and we shall become famous in the world," they speak of that which is non-Dhamma as "this is Dhamma";

thus they are said to illuminate non-Dhamma as Dhamma. Likewise, by taking one portion of what constitutes Dhamma and saying, "This is non-Dhamma," they are said to illuminate Dhamma as non-Dhamma. According to the method of the Vinaya:
But a legal procedure that is carried out after having accused and reminded one of a factual basis that is true, and according to what has been admitted, is called "Dhamma.
A legal procedure that is carried out without having accused or reminded one of a factual basis that is untrue, and without what has been admitted, is called "adhamma.
According to the method of the Suttantas, it is the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, the removal of delusion, restraint, abandonment, and reflective discernment.
This is called *vinaya*: the non-discipline, the lack of restraint, the non-abandonment, and the lack of reflective discernment regarding lust and the other [defilements]—this is called *avinaya*.

By way of the method of *vinaya*, the perfection of the subject matter (*vatthu*), the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*), the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*), the perfection of the boundary (*sīmā*), and the perfection of the assembly (*parisa*)—this is called *vinaya*.
The failure of the subject matter, the failure of the motion, the failure of the proclamation, [the failure of the boundary, and the failure of the assembly...]
"Failure regarding the boundary and failure regarding the assembly—this is called non-discipline (avinaya).

According to the method of the Suttantas, that which was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata—the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts... [and so on] ...the noble eightfold path; as well as the three foundations of mindfulness, the three right efforts, the three..."
"The four bases of psychic power, the six faculties, the six strengths, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path"—this was not spoken, nor uttered by the Tathāgata.

"According to the method of the Vinaya, there are four *pārājika* offenses, thirteen *saṅghādisesa*, two *aniyata*, thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya*, and [thirty-nine] *pācittiya* offenses"—this was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata. There are three *pārājika* [offenses], fourteen...
That "there are three *saṅghādisesas*, the two *aniyatās*, thirty-one *nissaggiya-pācittiyas*, and [the rest] *pācittiyas*"— this was neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata.
According to the method of the Suttantas, there is the daily attainment of the fruition (*phala-samāpatti*),

the attainment of the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*), the surveying of the world with the Buddha-eye, the teaching of the Suttantas based on specific occasions (*aṭṭhuppatti*), and the narration of Jātaka stories— this is [the true teaching].

It was customary [for them] not to enter into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) daily... nor to tell birth stories (*jātakakathā*); this was not customary. According to the method of the Vinaya:
for one who has been invited, it is customary to depart on a journey after spending the rains retreat and obtaining leave; to depart on a journey after the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*);
and to exchange greetings first with visiting monks (*āgantuka*). This was customary.
The non-performance of that which has been practiced is called "unpracticed.
According to the method of the Suttanta, the four foundations of mindfulness... [etc] ...the eightfold path—this is called "proclaimed";
the three foundations of mindfulness... [etc] ...the ninefold path—this is called "unproclaimed. According to the method of the Vinaya, the four...
"The three *pārājika*s... [and so on] ...the thirty-one *nissaggiya-pācittiya*s"—this is what is called "laid down" (*paññatta*). "The three *pārājika*s...
[and so on] ...the thirty-one *nissaggiya-pācittiya*s"—this is what is called "not laid down" (*apaññatta*).
Furthermore, as for that which is stated at the conclusion of all the Suttas: "These three [factors] cause the true Dhamma to disappear."

In this context, there are five kinds of disappearance: the disappearance of realization (*adhigama-antaradhāna*), the disappearance of practice (*paṭipatti-antaradhāna*), the disappearance of the scriptures (*pariyatti-antaradhāna*), the disappearance of the marks (*liṅga-antaradhāna*), and the disappearance of the relics (*dhātu-antaradhāna*).

Therein, "realization" refers to the four paths, the four fruits, the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), the three types of higher knowledge (*vijjā*), and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). When that [realization] declines, it begins with the analytical knowledges.
From that point on, [the attainment] declines. For indeed, for only a thousand years after the Parinibbāna of the Buddhas are they able to produce the *paṭisambhidā*;
beyond that, the six *abhiññās*; and when they are no longer able to produce even those, they produce the three *vijjās*.
As time goes by, being unable to produce even those, they become *sukkha-vipassaka* (dry-insight practitioners). By this very [process]...
By means of skillful methods, there are non-returners, once-returners, and stream-enterers. While these individuals remain, the attainment [of the Dhamma] is said not to have disappeared.
However, with the passing away of the very last stream-enterer, the attainment is said to have disappeared.
This is what is called the disappearance of attainment.

The disappearance of practice means that, being unable to produce the jhānas, insight, the path, and the fruit, they maintain only the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla). As time passes, they think:
"We have maintained our virtue in its fullness and applied ourselves to striving, yet we are not able to realize either the path or the fruit; there is no penetration of the Noble Dhamma at present."
Having reached a state of finality, being full of indolence, they do not exhort one another nor remind one another;

lacking a sense of urgency, from that point on they trample upon minor and lesser rules. As time passes, they incur offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*) and serious offenses (*thullaccaya*), and thereafter a grave offense (*garukāpatti*).
Only the offense of defeat (*pārājika*) remains standing. This is for those who guard against the four offenses of defeat.
Even while hundreds or thousands of bhikkhus are living, the practice is not said to have disappeared;

however, when the last bhikkhu [passes away] either through a breach of virtue or through the end of his life, it has disappeared—this is what is called the disappearance of the practice (*paṭipattiantaradhāna*).

As for the "scripture" (*pariyatti*), it refers to the word of the Buddha in the Three Piṭakas together with the commentaries and the canonical text (*pāḷi*). As long as that remains, so long does the scripture remain.
It is called "complete. As time passes, the kings and crown princes become unrighteous;
when they are unrighteous, the royal ministers and others become unrighteous; then so do the inhabitants of the kingdom and the countryside.
Because of their unrighteousness, the rain god does not rain properly, and consequently, the crops do not flourish. When those [crops] fail, the providers of requisites...
They were unable to provide the requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; consequently, the bhikkhus, being distressed by a lack of requisites, were unable to support their pupils.

As time passed, the scriptures (pariyatti) declined; they were no longer able to preserve them according to their meaning (atthavasena), but preserved them only according to the text (pāḷivasena). Then, as time passed further, even the text...
They were unable to preserve it in its entirety; first, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka was lost.
As it was being lost, it was lost starting from the very top. For the *Paṭṭhāna-mahāpakaraṇa* was lost first;
when that was lost, the *Yamaka*, *Kathāvatthu*, *Puggalapaññatti*, *Dhātukathā*, *Vibhaṅga*, and *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* followed.
Thus, when the Abhidhamma Piṭaka has declined from its summit, the Sutta Piṭaka declines.
First, the Aṅguttara Nikāya declines; within that, first the Ekādasaka Nipāta, then the Dasaka Nipāta...
[and so on] ...until finally the Ekaka Nipāta. When the Aṅguttara has thus declined from its summit, the Saṃyutta Nikāya declines.
First, the Mahāvagga perishes; then the Saḷāyatanavagga, the Khandhavagga, the Nidānavagga, and the Sagāthāvagga.
Thus, when the Saṃyutta Nikāya has perished, the Majjhima Nikāya perishes starting from its summit.
First, the Upari-pannāsaka perishes; then the Majjhima-pannāsaka, and then the Mūla-pannāsaka.
Thus, when the *Majjhima Nikāya* has been lost, the *Dīgha Nikāya* begins to decline from its very beginning.
First the *Pāṭhika-vagga* is lost, then the *Mahā-vagga*, and then the *Sīlakkhandha-vagga*.
When the *Dīgha Nikāya* has thus been lost, the *Sutta Piṭaka* is said to be lost; they preserve only the *Jātaka* together with the *Vinaya Piṭaka*.

Only those possessed of a sense of shame preserve the Vinaya Piṭaka; however, those desiring gain, thinking "there is nothing to be observed even when the Suttanta is recited," preserve only the Jātakas.
As time passes, they become unable to preserve even the Jātakas.
Then, first the Vessantara Jātaka is lost to them, and after that, in reverse order, the Puṇṇaka Jātaka.
At the conclusion of the Mahānāradajātakaya, the Apaṇṇakajātaka was lost. Thus, when the Jātakas were lost, they preserved only the Vinayapiṭaka.
As time passed on and on, even the Vinayapiṭaka began to decline from its very summit.
First the Parivāra was lost, then the Khandhaka, then the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, and finally the Mahāvibhaṅga, in that successive order.
They preserve only the Uposatha Khandhaka. Even then, the scripture has not disappeared.
As long as even a four-line stanza remains current among human beings, the scripture remains undestroyed.
At that time, a king who was faithful and devoted had a purse containing a thousand coins placed upon a golden casket on the back of an elephant.
“Let whoever understands this four-line verse spoken by the Buddhas take this thousand pieces,” he proclaimed by having a drum beaten throughout the city.
When no one came forward to take it, [the king thought], “Even when the drum is beaten but once, there are those who hear and those who do not hear.
Having had it beaten up to three times and still receiving no taker, the king’s men returned that purse of a thousand pieces to the royal palace.
When they enter [the city], at that time the scriptures (*pariyatti*) are said to have disappeared. This is what is called the disappearance of the scriptures.
As time passes further and further, the wearing of robes, the holding of bowls, the contracting and extending of limbs, and the looking forward and looking aside are no longer graceful.
Like the ascetics of the Nigaṇṭha sect, the monks place their bowls upon the tips of their forearms, like a gourd vessel.
They wander about carrying it; even to this extent, the outward sign remains unremoved.
But as time passes, they lower it from their upper arms and wander about either holding it by hand or suspended from a string.
Furthermore, they do not dye their robes in a manner suitable for dying, but wander about with them the color of elephant lips or teeth. As time passes further still, even the dye no longer exists.
Even when cutting off the fringes or piercing the waistband, they use it for only a single *kappa*. Then, having pierced the waistband again, they do not make a *kappa* for it.
Thereafter, making neither of these two, they cut off the fringes and wander about like wandering mendicants (*paribbājaka*).
As time passes, thinking, "What use have we for this?", they hold a small fragment of saffron cloth in their hand.
Or they bind them by the neck, or cause them to be attached by the hair, or, while maintaining their wives, they wander about making their living by plowing and sowing.
At that time, those giving offerings give to these people for the sake of the Saṅgha.
It was with reference to this that the Blessed One said: "Ananda, in the future there will indeed be those who belong to the lineage (gotrabhū)."

“Those who wear the saffron robe around their necks but are immoral and of evil character—when people give a gift dedicated to the Saṅgha for the sake of those immoral ones, even then, Ānanda, I declare that the offering made to the Saṅgha is incalculable and immeasurable.
Then, as time passed, while performing various kinds of work, [some] thought, “This is a mere distraction; what use have we for this? and they cut off a piece of the saffron robe.
They cast them away in the forest. At that time, it is said that the "disappearance of the signs" occurs.

From the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa onwards, it is said that the Yonakas took up the practice of wandering about clothed in white garments. This is what is called the disappearance of the signs.
As for the disappearance of the relics, it should be understood as follows: there are three types of parinibbāna—the parinibbāna of the defilements—...
The parinibbāna of the aggregates, and the parinibbāna of the relics. Therein, the parinibbāna of the defilements occurred at the seat of enlightenment;
the parinibbāna of the aggregates occurred at Kusinārā; the parinibbāna of the relics will occur in the future.
How so? Because, failing to receive honor and respect here and there, the relics [will remain] through the power of the Buddhas' resolve.

They go to places where they may receive honor and respect. As time passes, however, honor and respect will cease to exist in all places. For at the time of the decline of the Dispensation, all the relics in this island of Tambapaṇṇi will assemble at the Mahācetiya;
from there, they will go to the Rājāyatana Cetiya on Nāgadīpa, and from there, to the Bodhipallaṅka.
Relics from the abode of the Nāgas, from the world of the devas, and even from the Brahma-world shall proceed to the very seat of the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhipallaṅka).
Not even a relic the size of a mustard seed shall perish along the way.

All the relics, having assembled at the terrace of the Great Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa), shall assume the form of a Buddha and display the splendor of the Buddha’s body seated cross-legged upon the terrace of enlightenment. [The thirty-two marks...]
The eighty marks of a Great Man, the secondary characteristics, and the fathom-wide radiance—all were perfectly complete.
Then, as on the day of the Twin Miracle, they performed a miracle and displayed it.
At that time, there was no being existing as a human who had gone there; rather, all the deities throughout the ten thousand world-systems gathered together and said, "Today..."
"The Ten-Powered One is passing away; from this moment on, there will be darkness," they lamented.
Then, heat issued forth from the body of relics and caused that body to reach the state of non-manifestation (*apaṇṇattika*).
A flame arising from the body of relics would have risen as far as the Brahma-world, even if only a portion of the relics the size of a mustard seed had remained.
It will become like a single net. When the elements have reached their exhaustion, it will be severed. Having displayed such great majesty, the relics vanish.

Then the assembled hosts of devas, having paid honor with celestial perfumes, garlands, music, and so forth—just as on the day of the Buddhas’ final passing away—circumambulate them three times, pay homage, and [depart].
Having said, "Blessed One, may we be able to see a Buddha who will arise in the future," they each go back to their own respective places.
This is what is called the disappearance of the relics (*dhātu-antaradhāna*).
Of these five kinds of disappearances, the disappearance of the scriptures (*pariyatti-antaradhāna*) alone is the root. For, through the scriptures...
When the practice disappears, the study of the scriptures disappears; when the study of the scriptures remains, the practice is established.
For this very reason, during the great terror of Caṇḍālatissa on this island, Sakka, the king of the gods, fashioned a great raft and announced to the bhikkhus:
"A great danger shall arise; the rain-god will not send rain properly; the bhikkhus [will be deprived] of the requisites."
“Exhausted as they are, they will not be able to preserve the scriptures;
it is fitting that you, noble sirs, go to the other shore and protect your lives. Ascend this great raft and go, venerable ones.
Those for whom there is no room to sit here may go by placing their chests against pieces of wood; there shall be no fear for anyone.”
Then, having reached the shore of the ocean, sixty bhikkhus made a pact, saying, "We have no need to go further;

remaining right here, we shall preserve the Tipiṭaka. Turning back from there, they went to the Dakkhiṇa-Malaya country and lived subsisting on roots, tubers, and leaves. While their bodies were still strong, they would sit and engage in recitation.
They did so; having drawn up sand in pits, surrounded it, and gathered their heads together in one place, they rehearsed the scriptures.
In this manner, for twelve years, they preserved the complete Tipiṭaka along with its commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*).
When the danger had subsided, the seven hundred bhikkhus, in the places where they had been, [recited] even a single syllable of the Tipiṭaka along with its commentaries.
Without leaving behind even a single consonant or vowel, they arrived at this very island and entered the Maṇḍalārāma monastery in the district of Kallagāma.
Hearing news of the elders' arrival, sixty monks who had been remaining on this island went forth, thinking,
"We shall see the elders," and while purifying the Tipiṭaka together with the elders, [they found] not even a single syllable or a single consonant...
They did not see anyone named Asamaṇḍa. At that place, this discussion arose among the elders:

"Is the study of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) the root of the Dispensation, or is it practice (*paṭipatti*)? The Paṃsukūlika elders said, "Practice is the root," while the Dhamma-preachers said, "The scriptures.
Then the elders [addressed] them both: "By the mere words of you two..."
“We will not do so; bring us a discourse spoken by the Victor,” they said. To show that bringing forth a discourse was no burden, he recited this sutta:
“Subhadda, if these monks were to dwell rightly, the world would not be empty of Arahants.
Great King, the Teacher’s instruction has practice as its root and practice as its essence. As long as practice endures, it remains. Thus he spoke the sutta.
They cited it. Having heard this sutta, the Dhamma-preachers cited this sutta for the purpose of establishing their own position:
"As long as the Suttantas endure, and as long as the Vinaya shines, so long will they see the light, just as when the sun has risen."
“When the Suttantas have disappeared and the Vinaya has been forgotten,
there will be darkness in the world, like when the sun has set.
When the Suttantas are preserved and remain intact, the practice is preserved.”
“The wise one established in practice does not fall away from security from bondage.
When this sutta was brought forward, the Paṃsukūlika Theras remained silent; the words of the Dhammakathika Theras alone prevailed.
For just as, among a hundred or a thousand cows, there is the cow that preserves the lineage...

When that lineage does not exist, that tradition is not maintained; even so, although there may be hundreds or thousands of monks who have undertaken insight (vipassanā), if the scripture (pariyatti) is absent, there is no penetration of the Noble Path (ariyamagga).
And just as when marks are set upon a stone slab for the purpose of identifying a treasure-pot, [the treasure can be found] as long as those marks endure.

As long as that jar of treasure has not been lost, it is said that it does not exist [as lost]. In the same way, as long as the *pariyatti* (the scriptures) remains, it is said that the Dispensation (*sāsana*) has not disappeared.
Commentary on the Second Chapter on Negligence, etc. 11. Commentary on the Chapter on What is Not Dhamma (*Adhammavagga*).
140. In the eleventh chapter, the passages beginning with "What is non-Dhamma is non-Dhamma" should be understood according to the method already stated. The rest here is self-evident.
This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on Non-Dhamma (Adhammavagga). 12. Commentary on the Chapter on Non-Offenses (Anāpattivagga).

150. Furthermore, regarding the twelfth [section], in the passages beginning with "no offense" and "an offense," that which is stated in various places as "there is no offense for one who does not know, for one whose mind is not intent on theft, for one not intending death, and for one not intending to proclaim [the fault] or to release [the burden]"—this is called "no offense.
That which is stated by way of the method beginning with "for one who knows, for one whose mind is intent on theft," and so forth, is called "an offense."
Namely, five classes of offenses are called light offenses; two classes of offenses are called heavy offenses. Two classes of offenses are called grave offenses;
five classes of offenses are called non-grave offenses. Six classes of offenses are called curable offenses;
one class of offenses, the *pārājika* class, is called incurable offenses.
An offense with remedy (*sappaṭikammāpatti*) is indeed an offense that has a remainder; an offense without remedy (*appaṭikammāpatti*) is indeed an offense without a remainder.
The rest is clear everywhere.
This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on Non-offenses (*Anāpattivagga*).
13. Commentary on the Chapter on the Single Person (Ekapuggalavagga) 170.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the Chapter on the Single Person: "A single person" (*ekapuggala*) means one person. Here, "one" (*eka*) has the sense of excluding a second or more; it is a numerical limitation.
"Person" (*puggala*) is a conventional expression (*sammutikathā*), not an expression concerning ultimate reality (*paramatthakathā*). For [the term refers to] the Blessed Buddha...
Teaching is twofold: conventional teaching (*sammutidesanā*) and ultimate teaching (*paramatthadesanā*).
Among these, such as "person, being, woman, man, kshatriya, brahmin, deva, Māra," is conventional teaching;
such as "impermanent, suffering, non-self, aggregates, elements, sense-bases, foundations of mindfulness," is ultimate teaching. In this regard, the Blessed One...
To those who, having heard the teaching by way of conventional designation (*sammuti*), are capable of penetrating its meaning, abandoning delusion, and attaining distinction,
he teaches the teaching of conventional designation. But to those who, having heard the teaching by way of the ultimate sense (*paramattha*),
are capable of penetrating its meaning, abandoning delusion, and attaining distinction, he teaches the teaching of the ultimate sense.

In this regard, there is this simile: Just as a teacher who is skilled in local dialects and capable of explaining the meaning of the three Vedas explains the meaning in the Tamil language to those who understand the Tamil language, and in whichever other language—such as Andhra or others—it is appropriate for them, he explains it in that very language;
even so, those young students, having come to a teacher who is clever and proficient...
They master their craft very quickly. In this context, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is like the teacher;
the three Piṭakas, which stand as the objects to be expounded, are like the three Vedas; skill in conventional and ultimate truth is like proficiency in the local dialects;
and the beings to be trained, who are capable of penetrating [the truth] by way of both the conventional and the ultimate, are like the young students from various regions.

The teaching of the Blessed One should be understood as being given by way of both conventional and ultimate truth, just as the teacher’s explanation of the Tamil language and so forth [is given by way of both its conventional usage and its ultimate phonetic analysis].
And it has been said in this regard:
“The Fully Enlightened One, the best among speakers, Proclaimed two truths:”
There is the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.
The conventional expression is true by reason of worldly convention;
the ultimate expression is true by reason of the actual nature of phenomena.
“Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in conventional usage, no false speech arises when he employs conventional designations.

Furthermore, the Blessed One speaks on the discourse of the person for eight reasons: for the purpose of illustrating moral shame and dread of blame, for the purpose of illustrating that one is the owner of one’s own kamma, and so forth.

It is for the purpose of illustrating individual personal effort, for the purpose of illustrating the immediate (ānantariya) kamma, for the purpose of illustrating the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), for the purpose of illustrating past lives, for the purpose of illustrating the purification of offerings (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi), and for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention.
For if it were said, "The aggregates, elements, and sense-bases feel shame and dread," the great mass of people would not understand; they would fall into confusion and become resistant.
One might ask: "What is this that is called 'the aggregates, elements, and sense bases being ashamed and afraid'? However, when it is said, "A woman is ashamed and afraid;
a man, a kshatriya, a brahmin, a deva, or Māra [is ashamed and afraid]," one understands, does not fall into confusion, and does not become an adversary.
Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating shame and fear of wrongdoing.

The same principle applies even when it is said: “The aggregates (khandhā) have karma as their owner; the elements (dhātuyo) and the bases (āyatanāni) [are likewise]. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating that one is the owner of one’s own karma.

The same principle applies even when it is said: “The great monasteries such as Veḷuvana were caused to be built by means of the aggregates, the elements, and the bases. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating individual human agency (paccatta-purisakāra).
“The aggregates deprive a mother of life, a father, an arahant, commit the offense of shedding blood, and commit the offense of causing a schism in the Saṅgha...”

The same principle applies even when it is said, "The elements and the sense-bases act. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating the immediate (ānantariya) kamma.

The same principle applies even when it is said, "The aggregates feel loving-kindness; the elements and the sense-bases [do so]. Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person for the purpose of illustrating the divine abodes (brahmavihāra).

The same principle applies even when it is said: “The aggregates (khandhā) recollect past lives; the elements (dhātuyo) and the bases (āyatanāni) [recollect them]. Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating past lives, the Blessed One speaks in terms of a person (puggala).

Even when it is said: “The aggregates receive the gift; the elements and the bases [receive it],” the great multitude does not understand, falls into confusion, and becomes an opponent, asking: “What is this that you call ‘the aggregates, elements, and bases receiving [the gift]’? “Persons [receive it]…”
When it is said, "The virtuous ones of beautiful character accept [it]," one knows this; one does not fall into confusion, nor does one become an adversary.
Therefore, the Blessed One speaks of the person (puggala) for the purpose of illustrating the purification of offerings (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi).

Furthermore, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention (lokasammuti); they teach the Dhamma while remaining established in worldly designations (lokasamaññā), worldly terminology (lokanirutti), and worldly expression (lokābhilāpa). Therefore, the Blessed One also speaks of the person for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention.

Thus, because he is one and a person, he is called "the Single Person" (*ekapuggala*). In what sense is he the Single Person? In the sense of being peerless, in the sense of being distinguished by his qualities, and in the sense of being unequaled.

For he is the Single Person in the sense of being peerless, since—beginning with the mental advertence to the ten perfections in their proper sequence—he is peerless among the rest of the world both in terms of the qualities that are the requisites for enlightenment and in terms of the Buddha-qualities themselves. And those who...
Those qualities are superior to the qualities of all other beings; thus, he is a single person in the sense of being distinguished by his qualities.
The previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones were unequal to all beings, yet this one alone is equal to them in both the qualities of the form-body and the qualities of the name-body;
thus, he is a single person in the sense of being equal to the unequaled.

"World" refers to three worlds: the world of beings (*sattaloka*), the world of space (*okāsaloka*), and the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*). A detailed explanation of these is given in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Among these, it is the world of beings that is intended here. Even when arising in the world of beings, he does not arise in the world of the devas nor in the world of the Brahmas, but arises only in the human world.
And even within the human world, he does not arise in another world-system, but in this very one.
He arises within a world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). Even there, not in all places.
To the east is the town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that is Mahāsālā;
beyond that are the bordering districts, while on this side lies the Middle Country. To the southeast is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that—
The bordering districts are from within the center. To the southern direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika;
beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the center. To the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūṇa;
beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the center. To the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja.
"Beyond that are the bordering countries; on this side is the Middle Country.
Thus defined, the Buddha arises in the Middle Country, which is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference.
Not only the Tathāgata, but also the Paccekabuddhas, the Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Elders, the Mother of the Buddha, and the Father of the Buddha [arise there].
It is precisely here that universal monarchs (cakkavatti-rāja) and other brahmins and householders who have attained the essence arise.
As for the statement "when arising, he arises," both of these are merely incomplete expressions.
However, the meaning here should be understood as follows: when arising, he arises for the welfare of many people, and not for any other reason. And such is the characteristic in this context.
This cannot be refuted by any other definition of sound (*saddalakkhaṇa*).
Furthermore, the distinction here should be understood as follows: "arising," "in the process of arising," and "having arisen.
For he, having received the prophecy from the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, was searching for the qualities that constitute a Buddha.
Having seen the ten perfections (pāramīs), one who has made the resolution, “These qualities must be fulfilled by me,” is called "one who is arising" even while fulfilling the perfection of giving.

Likewise, while fulfilling these ten perfections—the perfection of virtue... [and so on] ...up to the perfection of equanimity—or while fulfilling the ten secondary perfections (upapāramīs)—he is called "one who is arising.
He is also called "one who is arising" even while fulfilling the ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs).
He is called "arising" even while relinquishing the five great renunciations. He is called "arising" even while fulfilling his own welfare, the welfare of his kinsmen, and the welfare of the world.

He is called "arising" even while bringing to their ultimate perfection the qualities that produce a Buddha over four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons. Having abandoned the Vessantara existence...
Even while remaining in the Tuṣita heaven for seventy-five million and six hundred thousand years after taking rebirth there, he is said to be "arising.
Likewise, when requested by the deities, he gazes upon the five great observations (*pañcamahāvilokita*) and takes rebirth in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā;
even while dwelling in the womb for exactly ten months, he is said to be "arising."
[He is] called "one who is arising" even while remaining in the midst of the household for twenty-nine years.

Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, even on the day Rāhula Bhadda was born, when he went forth together with Channa, mounting Kaṇḍaka, his excellent steed, he is called "one who is arising.
Even as he crossed over the three kingdoms, on the bank of the Anomā River—
Even while going forth, he is said to be "arising. Even while performing the Great Exertion for six years, he is said to be "arising.
Even while consuming coarse food once his knowledge had reached maturity, he is still said to be "arising.
At evening time, on the full moon of Visākha, having ascended the Great Seat of Enlightenment and scattered the hosts of Māra, he recollects his past lives during the first watch of the night.
Having purified the divine eye during the middle watch, and having comprehended the twelvefold dependent origination in both forward and reverse order immediately following the last watch,
even while penetrating the path of stream-entry, he is said to be "arising. This applies likewise at the moment of the fruit of stream-entry,
at the moment of the path of once-returning, at the moment of the fruit of once-returning, and at the moment of the path of non-returning.
At the moment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), it is said to be "arising"; at the moment of the path of arahantship (arahattamagga), it is said to be "arising";

and at the moment of the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala), it is said to be "arisen. For in the case of Buddhas, the various supernormal powers such as the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (iddhividhañāṇa) do not arise sequentially as they do for disciples;
rather, together with the path of arahantship, the entire mass of qualities, including omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), arrives all at once.
It is so called. Therefore, because all their tasks have been accomplished, they are said to have "arisen" at the moment of the fruit of arahantship.
In this sutta as well, it should be understood that the phrase "it arises" refers precisely to the moment of the fruit of arahantship;
for here, "it has arisen" is the intended meaning.
"For the welfare of many" means he arises for the sake of the benefit of the great multitude. "For the happiness of many" means he arises for the sake of the happiness of the great multitude.
"Out of compassion for the world" means he arises out of compassion for the world of sentient beings.
Which world of sentient beings? That which, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma and having drunk the drink of the Deathless, [embraces] the Dhamma...
He penetrated [the truth]. For after the Blessed One had spent seven weeks at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa) and arrived at Isipatana from the Seat of Enlightenment,
when he taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta— beginning with, "Bhikkhus, these two extremes are not to be pursued by one who has gone forth"—
eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, together with the Venerable Aññā Koṇḍañña Thera, drank the drink of the Deathless (amatapāna).
[The Buddha] drank; [this radiance] arose out of compassion for this world of beings.

On the fifth day, at the conclusion of the *Anattalakkhaṇa-sutta*, the five bhikkhus of the group were established in *arahatta*; this [radiance] also arose out of compassion for this world of beings.
Thereafter, he established fifty-five men, headed by the youth Yasa, in *arahatta*; then, in the Kappāsika forest grove...
He brought thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group to the three paths and the three fruits;
he arose out of compassion for this world of beings. At the conclusion of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta at Gayāsīsa, he established a thousand matted-hair ascetics in Arahatship.
In the Tālaṭṭhivana grove, eleven million brahmins and householders, headed by Bimbisāra, [attained the fruits] of the Teacher.
Having heard the teaching on the Dhamma, they were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and ninety-one million beings were established in the refuges.

At the conclusion of the *Tirokuṭṭa-anumodanā*, eighty-four thousand living beings drank the drink of the Deathless (*amata-pāna*). At the assembly of the garland-maker Sumanas, [it was drunk] by eighty-four [thousand];
at the assembly of Dhanapālaka, by ten thousand beings; and at the assembly of the *Khadiranga-jātaka*.
In the assembly of the jackal-Ājīvaka, eighty-four thousand beings drank the drink of the Deathless;

in the assembly of the merchant Ānanda, eighty-four thousand beings drank the drink of the Deathless. On the day of the discourse on the *Pārāyana Sutta* at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, fourteen koṭis drank the drink of the Deathless.
On the day of the Twin Miracle, twenty koṭis of beings [drank it] in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
While sitting upon the Paṇḍukambala stone, having made his mother a bodily witness, he taught the Abhidhamma consisting of the seven treatises;
at that time, eighty koṭis of beings drank the drink of the Deathless. During the Descent of the Gods, thirty koṭis of beings did so.
In the Sakkapañha Sutta, eighty thousand deities drank the drink of the Deathless. And in the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the Maṅgala Sutta, and the Cūḷarāhulovāda...
Regarding "the practice of equanimity of mind": there is no limit to the number of beings who have attained realization (*abhisamaya*) in these four states.

This [teaching] has arisen out of compassion for this world of beings. Furthermore, this meaning should be understood by way of those who, from this day forward and in the future, will establish themselves on the path to heaven and liberation by relying upon this Dispensation (*sāsana*).
"Of gods and humans" means that he has arisen not only for the sake of gods and humans, but also for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the rest—the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth.

However, this was said specifically to show those persons who possess the causal conditions for rebirth and are capable of realizing the paths and fruits. Therefore, it should be understood that he has arisen for their welfare, benefit, and happiness as well.

"What is the one person?"—this is the question. Now, this question is fivefold: a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen, a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen, a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt, a question for the purpose of assent, and a question out of a desire to speak.

This is their distinction: What is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen? It is when a characteristic is by nature unknown, unseen, unmeasured, unexamined, unmanifested, and undeveloped. For the sake of knowing it, for the sake of seeing it, for the sake of measuring it, and for the sake of examining it...
When one asks a question for the sake of making manifest and for the sake of discerning, this is a question for the illumination of what has not yet been seen (*adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*).
What is a question for the corroboration of what has been seen (*diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā*)? One already knows, has seen, weighed, judged, made manifest, and discerned the characteristic by nature;
he then asks a question together with other wise persons for the sake of corroborating it.
This is the question concerning the correlation of what has been seen.
What is the question for cutting through doubt? One who by nature leans toward uncertainty, leans toward perplexity, and is of a dualistic mind, thinking:
"Is it thus? Is it not thus? What indeed? How indeed? asks a question for the purpose of cutting through that doubt.
He asks; this is a question for the purpose of cutting off doubt.
What is a question for the sake of obtaining consent? The Blessed One asks a question with the consent of the bhikkhus:
“What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But that which is impermanent—”
“Is that suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But as for what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “Certainly not, venerable sir. This is a question seeking agreement.

What is the inquiry out of a desire to speak? The Blessed One asks a question of the bhikkhus out of a desire to speak: “Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four? This is the inquiry out of a desire to speak.
In this regard, the Buddhas do not have the first three types of inquiry. Why?

Because for the Buddhas, throughout the three times, there is nothing—whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether pertaining to time or timeless—that is unseen, unknown, unmeasured, uninvestigated, or not fully realized.
There is nothing that has not been manifested; therefore, for them there is no inquiry regarding the illumination of what was previously unseen.
Furthermore, as for that which has been penetrated by the Blessed One through his own knowledge, there is no need to reconcile it with any other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
Therefore, for him there is no inquiry regarding the reconciliation of what was seen.
Since, however, he is free from doubt, has crossed over uncertainty, and has dispelled all hesitation regarding all phenomena, he has no question for the purpose of cutting through perplexity.
The other two questions, moreover, exist for the Blessed One; among these, this should be understood as the question arising from a desire to speak.
Now, elucidating the "One Person" who was questioned by means of that question, [the text says]: "The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
He said: "In that regard, the Blessed One is called 'Tathāgata' for eight reasons: he is a Tathāgata because he has come (āgata) thus; he is a Tathāgata because he has gone (gata) thus;
he is a Tathāgata because he has come to the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa); he is a Tathāgata because he has perfectly awakened to the true dhammas as they really are;
he is a Tathāgata by virtue of seeing things as they truly are; he is a Tathāgata by virtue of speaking things as they truly are; he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting as he speaks."
"In the sense of overcoming, he is the Tathāgata.

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata because he has come thus? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones came having exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world, just as the Blessed One Vipassī came, just as the Blessed One Sikhī, and just as the Blessed One Vessabhū...
“The Blessed One has come, just as the Blessed One Kakusandha came, just as the Blessed One Koṇāgamana came, and just as the Blessed One Kassapa came.
What is meant by this? By that same resolve through which these Blessed Ones came, by that very same resolve our Blessed One has also come.
Or alternatively: “Just as the Blessed One Vipassī… [and so on] …just as the Blessed One Kassapa [fulfilled] the perfection of giving…”
Having fulfilled [the perfections], having fulfilled the perfections of virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity—
having thus fulfilled these thirty perfections (pāramīs), namely ten basic perfections, ten intermediate perfections,
and ten ultimate perfections— and having fulfilled the five great sacrifices, which are the sacrifice of limbs, the sacrifice of eyes, wealth, kingdom, sons, and wife;

Having renounced everything, fulfilled his preliminary practices, former conduct, preaching of the Dhamma, conduct for the sake of others' knowledge, and so forth, and having reached the pinnacle of the practice of wisdom, he has come;
in that same way our Blessed One has come.
And just as the Blessed Vipassī …pe… the Blessed Kassapa [perfected] the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, and the five faculties—
He has come having developed and cultivated the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;
likewise, our Blessed One has come in that same way, thus he is the Tathāgata.
"Just as Vipassī and the others in the world..."
"The sages have attained omniscience here;
likewise this Sakyan sage has also arrived,
and for that reason he is called the Tathāgata, the one with vision."
Thus, he is a Tathāgata because he has come in such a way.
How has he gone in such a way that he is a Tathāgata? Just as the Blessed One Vipassī went [after birth]...
up to ... the Blessed One Kassapa went. And how did he go? For immediately upon being born, he stood firm on the earth with level feet.

Facing north, he took seven steps with a stride. As it is said: “Immediately after his birth, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta, having established himself on the earth with level feet, walked seven steps facing north while a white parasol was held over him;
he surveyed all directions and uttered a lion’s roar.”
‘I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world;
this is my final birth, there is now no further becoming. And that going of his was true, not false, serving as a precursor to many distinguished attainments.
For the fact that he stood with level feet immediately upon being born was the sign of his acquisition of the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).

The facing toward the north is the omen of the state of transcendence over the entire world; the taking of seven steps is the omen for the acquisition of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*);
the waving of the yak-tail whisks mentioned here in the verse, "The yak-tail whisks with golden handles wave about," is the omen for the crushing of all rival teachers;
and the holding of the white parasol is the omen for the acquisition of the supreme, stainless white parasol of liberation, which is the fruit of Arhatship.
The preliminary sign of surveying all directions is the omen for the attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience;
the utterance of the voice of a bull is the omen for the irreversible turning of the supreme wheel of Dhamma.
In the same way, this Blessed One has also gone. And how was that going of his truly in accordance with those very specific attainments?
By way of being a prior sign. Therefore the ancients said:
"Just as soon as he was born, like the Lord of Elephants, he touched the earth with his even feet."
Thus Gotama strode seven steps,
while the Maruts held up a white parasol for him.
Having gone those seven steps, Gotama—
He surveyed the directions all around with equanimity;
he uttered speech endowed with the eight factors,
like a lion standing upon a mountain peak.
Thus he has gone thus, therefore he is the Tathāgata.
Or alternatively, just as the Blessed One Vipassī … [and so on] … just as the Blessed One Kassapa, this Blessed One likewise has gone by means of renunciation, having abandoned sensual desire;
by means of non-ill will, having abandoned ill will; by means of the perception of light, having abandoned sloth and torpor; by means of non-distraction … [and so on].
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse through the discernment of phenomena (*dhammavavatthāna*), he has gone; having shattered ignorance (*avijjā*) with knowledge (*ñāṇa*), he has gone;

having dispelled discontent with gladness (*pāmojja*), and having thrown open the door-panel of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) with the first jhāna, having stilled applied and sustained thought (*vitakkavicāra*) with the second jhāna, having faded away from rapture (*pīti*) with the third jhāna, and [having abandoned] pleasure and pain with the fourth jhāna...
Having abandoned [them], having transcended the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity by means of the attainment of the base of infinite space;

having transcended the perception of the base of infinite space by means of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness; having transcended the perception of the base of infinite consciousness by means of the attainment of the base of nothingness;
and having transcended the perception of the base of nothingness by means of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—he has gone.
By means of the contemplation of impermanence, one abandons the perception of permanence; by the contemplation of suffering, the perception of pleasure;
