by the contemplation of non-self, the perception of self; by the contemplation of disenchantment, delight; by the contemplation of dispassion, lust; by the contemplation of cessation, arising;
by the contemplation of relinquishment, grasping; by the contemplation of destruction, the perception of solidity; and by the contemplation of vanishing...
Accumulation; the perception of permanence through the contemplation of change; the perception of signs through the contemplation of the signless;
longing through the contemplation of the desireless; misapprehension through the contemplation of emptiness; misapprehension by grasping at a core through higher wisdom and insight into phenomena;

misapprehension by delusion through knowledge and vision of things as they truly are; misapprehension by clinging through the contemplation of danger; and misapprehension by non-reflection through the contemplation of reflective discernment.
Having broken the defilements associated with views by means of the stream-entry path,
having abandoned the gross defilements by means of the once-return path, having eradicated the subtle defilements by means of the non-return path,
and having completely severed all defilements by means of the arahant path— he has gone thus; for this reason also he is called the Tathāgata.
How is he a Tathāgata because he has come to the characteristic of suchness (*tathalakkhaṇa*)? The characteristic of hardness in the earth element is suchness, it is not otherwise;

the characteristic of cohesion in the water element, the characteristic of heat in the fire element, the characteristic of distension in the air element, the characteristic of non-obstruction in the space element, and the characteristic of cognizing in the consciousness element are suchness, they are not otherwise.

The characteristic of matter is being afflicted; the characteristic of feeling is experiencing; the characteristic of perception is perceiving; the characteristic of volitional formations is forming; the characteristic of consciousness is cognizing.

The characteristic of applied thought is directing onto; the characteristic of sustained thought is examining; the characteristic of rapture is pervading; the characteristic of pleasure is gratification; the characteristic of one-pointedness of mind is non-distraction; the characteristic of contact is touching.

The faculty of faith has the characteristic of resolution; the faculty of energy, the characteristic of exertion; the faculty of mindfulness, the characteristic of establishing; the faculty of concentration, the characteristic of non-distraction; the faculty of wisdom, the characteristic of discernment.

The power of faith has the characteristic of being unshakable by lack of faith; the power of energy, by indolence; the power of mindfulness, by forgetfulness; the power of concentration, by agitation; the power of wisdom, by ignorance.
The characteristic of the mindfulness enlightenment factor is establishment; the characteristic of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor is investigation;

the characteristic of the energy enlightenment factor is exertion; the characteristic of the rapture enlightenment factor is pervasion; the characteristic of the tranquility enlightenment factor is pacification;
the characteristic of the concentration enlightenment factor is non-distraction; [and the characteristic] of the equanimity enlightenment factor...
The characteristic of right view is reflection; the characteristic of right intention is directing toward; the characteristic of right speech is encompassing;
the characteristic of right action is originating; the characteristic of right livelihood is purification.
Right effort has the characteristic of exertion; right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing; right concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction.
Ignorance has the characteristic of unknowing; volitional formations have the characteristic of intending; consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing;
mentality has the characteristic of bending toward an object; form has the characteristic of being affected; the six sense bases have the characteristic of being a base.
Contact has the characteristic of touching; feeling has the characteristic of being felt; craving has the characteristic of being a cause; clinging has the characteristic of grasping;
becoming has the characteristic of accumulation; birth has the characteristic of arising; aging has the characteristic of decaying;
and death has the characteristic of passing away.
The characteristic of the elements is emptiness; the characteristic of the sense-bases is being a base; the characteristic of the foundations of mindfulness is establishing;

the characteristic of the right efforts is exertion; the characteristic of the bases of power is succeeding; the characteristic of the faculties is predominance; the characteristic of the powers is unshakability;
the characteristic of the factors of enlightenment is leading out; the characteristic of the path is being a cause.

The characteristic of the truths is suchness; the characteristic of serenity is non-distraction; the characteristic of insight is contemplation; the characteristic of serenity and insight is their single flavor;

the characteristic of the pair is their non-transgression [of each other]. The characteristic of purification of virtue is restraint; the characteristic of purification of mind is non-distraction; the characteristic of purification of view is seeing.
The characteristic of the knowledge of destruction is eradication; the characteristic of the knowledge of non-arising is tranquility.
The characteristic of zeal is its root; the characteristic of attention is its origination; the characteristic of contact is its convergence; the characteristic of feeling is its meeting point;
the characteristic of concentration is its predominance; the characteristic of mindfulness is its sovereignty;
the characteristic of wisdom is its transcendence; the characteristic of liberation is its essence; and the characteristic of Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, is its consummation.

It is thus, it is not otherwise. Thus, because he has arrived at the characteristic of "thus" (tathalakkhaṇa) by way of the course of knowledge, having reached it without deviating and having attained it, he is the Tathāgata.
Because he has come to the characteristic of "thus," he is the Tathāgata.
How is he the Tathāgata because he has fully awakened to the phenomena that are thus (tathadhamma) as they really are? The "phenomena that are thus" are the four [noble truths].
The Noble Truths. As it is said: “These four, monks, are real, not unreal, not otherwise.
Which four? ‘This is suffering,’ monks—this is real, this is not unreal, this is not otherwise,” and so on in detail.
And the Blessed One has fully awakened to these; therefore, because he has fully awakened to what is real (*tatha*), he is the Tathāgata.
It is so called because the word "gone" (*gata*) here has the sense of "perfectly awakened.
Furthermore, the sense of being produced and brought about through the condition of birth for aging-and-death is real, not unreal, not otherwise...
[and so on] ...the sense of being produced and brought about through the condition of ignorance for volitional formations is real, not unreal, not otherwise. Thus, regarding ignorance—

The conditionality of volitional formations, the conditionality of consciousness for volitional formations... [and so on] ...the conditionality of aging-and-death for birth is such, not otherwise, and not different.

The Blessed One has fully awakened to all that. Therefore, because he has fully awakened to such things (tathā-dhamma), he is called the Tathāgata. Thus, because he has fully awakened to such things as they really are, he is the Tathāgata.

How is the Tathāgata “one who sees things as they truly are”? In the world with its devas... [and so on]... including gods and humans, whatever form-object there is that comes within the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems, the Blessed One knows and sees it in all its aspects.
By knowing and seeing it thus, he [understands it] by way of being desirable, undesirable, and so forth.
Or, by way of the terms available among the seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, or by way of the analysis according to numerous names— such as "What is that form which is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*)?
It is that form derived from the four great elements which is visible and impinging,
blue, yellow," and so forth— in thirteen sections and fifty-two methods.
It is exactly so; it is not otherwise. This same principle applies to sounds and other objects that come within the range of the ear-door and the rest.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas...
including gods and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, or investigated by the mind—that I know."
“I have directly known that; it is known by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata does not stand [in need of] that. Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of seeing things as they truly are (*tathadassitā*).

In this context, the derivation of the term *Tathāgata* should be understood in the sense of one who sees thus (*tathadassī*). How is he the Tathāgata because of speaking what is true (*tathavāditā*)?
On the night when the Blessed One, seated on the invincible throne at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), [attained enlightenment...]
Having crushed the heads of the three Māras, he attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;
and from the night he attained that enlightenment until the night he passed away into the Nibbāna-element without residue between the twin Sāl trees—
in this interval of time measuring forty-five years, whatever was spoken by the Blessed One during the first, middle, and final enlightenments—

The Sutta, Geyya... [and so on] ...the Vedalla—all that is blameless in both meaning and phrasing, neither deficient nor redundant, complete in every aspect, crushing the intoxication of lust and crushing the intoxication of hatred and delusion;
therein there is not even a hair’s breadth of error; all of it is as if stamped with a single seal, as if from a single mold.
It is as if measured, as if weighed on a single balance; it is exactly so, not otherwise. Therefore he said:

"Cunda, whatever the Tathāgata speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between the night he awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night he passes away into the Nibbāna-element without residue—all that [is exactly so]."
“That remains exactly so and not otherwise; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. Here, the word *gata* has the sense of “speaking.
Thus, he is the Tathāgata because of his speaking of what is thus.

Furthermore, *āgada* means speaking; the meaning is “speech. Since his speech (*āgada*) is thus (*tatho*), that is, unerring, by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, it is “Tathāgata. In this way, the derivation of the term should be understood in this sense.
In what sense is the Tathāgata so called because of his acting accordingly (*tathākāritā*)? For the Blessed One’s body conforms to his speech, and his speech conforms to his body;
therefore, he is one who acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts.
And for one who has become such, his body has gone (*gata*) in the same way as his speech—this is the meaning—or his speech has gone in the same way as his body; thus he is the Tathāgata.
For this very reason it was said: “Bhikkhus, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, as he speaks, so he acts;
as he acts, so he speaks. Therefore he is called the ‘Tathāgata. In this way, he is a Tathāgata by virtue of acting in accordance with his word.
How is he a Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming? Having made the peak of existence above and the Avīci hell below his limits—
Horizontally, throughout immeasurable world-systems, he surpasses all beings by virtue of his moral conduct, concentration, wisdom, and liberation;
there is no equal or measure for him. He is incomparable, immeasurable, unsurpassed—the king of kings, the god of gods, the supreme among Sakka-s, the supreme among Brahma-s.
Therefore it was said: "In the world with its devas, bhikkhus... [etc.]..."
“Among gods and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, unconquered; he is all-seeing and possesses mastery. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.
In this regard, the derivation of the word should be understood as follows: it is like a medicine (*agada*). What, then, is this? It is both the splendor of his teaching and the power of his merit.
For by means of that great majesty, this physician, like a snake charmer with a divine antidote, [overcomes] all rival teachers and the world with its gods.

He overcomes the world. Thus, because his excellence in teaching and his accumulation of merit—which are true and unerring in overcoming the entire world—should be understood as an "antidote" (*agada*), the letter *da* is changed to *ta*, and he is to be known as the *Tathāgata*. In this way, he is the *Tathāgata* in the sense of overcoming.

Furthermore, he is the *Tathāgata* because he has gone (*gata*) to suchness (*tathā*); he is the *Tathāgata* because he has gone to what is real (*tathaṃ gata*); and "gone" means understood or transcended.

"Attained and practiced"—this is the meaning. In this context, he is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to, or understood, the "thusness" (*tathā*) of the entire world through the full understanding of its nature as it is (*tīraṇapariññā*).
He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone beyond, or transcended, the "thusness" of the origin of the world through the full understanding of its abandonment (*pahānapariññā*).

He is a *tathāgata* because he has gone to, or reached, the "thusness" of the cessation of the world through its realization (*sacchikiriyā*). [He is a *tathāgata*] regarding the path leading to the cessation of the world through its "thusness"...
One who has gone and entered [the path] is a *tathāgata*. Therefore, as it was said by the Blessed One:
"The world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the *tathāgata*; the *tathāgata* is detached from the world.
The origin of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the *tathāgata*; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the *tathāgata*. The cessation of the world..."
Monks, the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata.
The practice leading to the cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata;

the practice leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Whatever, monks, in this world with its devas... [and so on] ...all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
"Therefore he is called 'Tathāgata'.

Its meaning should be understood in this way. And this is merely a brief introduction for illustrating the state of being a Tathāgata; only a Tathāgata himself could describe the state of being a Tathāgata in its entirety.

However, regarding the two terms "Arahant" and "Sammāsambuddho," [the meaning is as follows]: because of being far removed (ārakatta), because of having slain enemies (arīnaṃ) and spokes (arānaṃ), and because of [having abandoned] conditions and so forth...
They should be understood as "arahants" for these reasons: because they are worthy (araha) of the highest offerings, because they have removed (rahābhāva) evil deeds, and so forth.
Furthermore, he is the "Sammāsambuddha" because he has perfectly and individually awakened to all phenomena; this is the brief explanation here.
However, these two terms are explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* within the commentary on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
171. "Manifestation in the second [life]" means arising or accomplishment. "Rare in the world" means rare, very rare, and extremely rare in this world of sentient beings.
Why is it rare? Because it is not possible for one to become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of giving only once;
nor by doing so twice, ten times, twenty times, fifty times, or even a hundred times.
It is not possible for one to become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of giving for a thousand years, a hundred thousand years, or even a hundred thousand koṭis of years; likewise,
it is not possible by doing so for one day, two days, ten days, twenty days, fifty days,
a hundred days, a thousand days, a hundred thousand days, a hundred thousand koṭis of days, or for one month.
Two months... [and so on] ...one hundred thousand million months. One year, two years... [and so on] ...one hundred thousand million years.
One aeon, two aeons... [and so on] ...one hundred thousand million aeons.

It is not possible to become a Buddha by fulfilling the perfection of giving for even one incalculable aeon, or two incalculable aeons, or three incalculable aeons. [The same applies to] the perfection of virtue, the perfection of renunciation... [and so on].
The same principle applies to the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*). However, it is rare because of this reason:

that it is possible for one to become a Buddha only after fulfilling the ten perfections (*dasapāramī*) for four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand eons at the very limit of time.
172. Regarding the third [epithet], *acchariyamanusso*: he is a wonderful human being (*acchariya-manussa*). "Wonderful" (*acchariya*) refers, for example, to a blind man climbing a mountain.
The meaning is that it is not permanent like [something] solid. This, first, is the method of etymology (*saddanaya*). This, however, is the method of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathānaya*):
it is "marvelous" (*acchariya*) because it is worthy of a finger-snap; the meaning is that it is to be seen by snapping one's fingers. Furthermore:
"Monks, with the appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, four marvelous and wonderful qualities appear."
He is called a "wonderful person" (*acchariyamanussa*) because he is endowed with many such marvelous and extraordinary qualities.

He is also called a "wonderful person" because it is his habitual practice (*āciṇṇa*). Indeed, for no one else is it a habitual practice to sit having bound the mind at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (*mahābodhimaṇḍa*) in the presence of a single Buddha, after having brought together the eight factors that accomplish the resolution (*abhinīhāra*); this is the practice of the Omniscient Bodhisatta alone.
This was his custom. Likewise, having received a prophecy in the presence of the Buddhas and becoming one who does not turn back, he resolved upon the foundation of energy;
even the fulfillment of the qualities that make a Buddha was the custom of no one else, but was the custom of the Omniscient Bodhisatta alone.
Likewise, having caused the perfections to take root and remaining in an existence such as that of the Vessantara incarnation—
Having given a great gift of seven hundred elephants adorned with every ornament and seven hundred horses,
and having dedicated as objects of his generosity a son like Jāli Kumāra, a daughter like Kaṇhājinā, and a wife like Queen Maddī,
he remained for the duration of his lifespan; and in his second existence, he took rebirth in the Tusita heaven.
This is not the practice of anyone else; it is the practice of the Omniscient Bodhisattva alone.
Having remained in the Tusita heaven for the full span of his lifespan and having accepted the entreaty of the deities, he performed the five great observations.
Then, mindful and clearly comprehending, passing away from the Tusita heaven, even his taking of rebirth in a family of great wealth is not the practice of anyone else.
All these were the habitual practices of the Omniscient Bodhisatta: likewise, on the day of taking rebirth, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system;
dwelling in the mother’s womb with mindfulness and clear comprehension;

on the day of emerging from the mother’s womb with mindfulness and clear comprehension, the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system; immediately upon birth, taking seven steps; and the divine white parasol.
It includes his retention [of the teachings], the tossing up of the divine hair-whisk, and his surveying of all directions with the gaze of a lion;
having seen no being equal to himself, his roaring of the lion’s roar, “I am the foremost in the world”;
his Great Renunciation after abandoning great prosperity once his knowledge had reached maturity; and [his sitting cross-legged] upon the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa).
Beginning with the victory over Māra, and having accomplished the purification of the recollection of past lives and the divine eye,

at the moment he penetrated the mass of qualities of omniscient knowledge during the dawn, there occurred the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system and the unsurpassed setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma through the three revolutions of the first teaching of the Dhamma—
all such things as these belong to no one else.
It was practiced; it was practiced by the Omniscient Buddha himself. One who has practiced in this way is called a "person of the stream" (*anusota*) and a "wonderful person" (*acchariya-manussa*).
173. Regarding the fourth [term], *kālakiriyā*: it is called *kālakiriyā* because it is an act that becomes manifest at a particular time (*kāle*).
For the Tathāgata, having remained for forty-five years, [taught] the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, and the ninefold teaching of the Teacher (*satthusāsana*), numbering eighty-four thousand...
Having proclaimed thousands of aggregates of Dhamma and having made the great multitude incline toward and lean toward Nibbāna, he lay down between the twin Sāl trees;
then, addressing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and exhorting them with diligence, mindful and clearly comprehending, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
This activity of his was manifest until the present day; thus, it was manifest at that one time.
“Death” means passing away. “It is regrettable” means it causes remorse.

In that regard, the death of a wheel-turning monarch causes remorse for gods and humans within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). The death of Buddhas causes remorse for gods and humans throughout ten thousand world-systems.
Therefore it is said: “It is regrettable to many people.”
174. In the fifth [verse], "without a second" (*adutiya*) means being without a second because of the absence of a second Buddha. For there are four types of Buddhas:

the Buddha of learning (*sutabuddha*), the Buddha of the Four Truths (*catusaccabuddha*), the Pacceka Buddha, and the Omniscient Buddha (*sabbaññubuddha*). Among these, a monk who is very learned is called a Buddha of learning.
One whose taints are destroyed is called a Buddha of the Four Truths. [The Omniscient Buddha is one who has fulfilled] the perfections for two incalculable eons and a hundred thousand aeons...
One who, having fulfilled [the perfections], has personally realized the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) is called a Paccekabuddha.

One who, having fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable eons (asaṅkhyeyya) plus a hundred thousand kappas, has crushed the heads of the three Māras and realized the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), is called a Samma-sambuddha. Among these four types of Buddhas, it is only the Samma-sambuddha who...
"Without a second" means that no other person called an omniscient Buddha arises together with him.
"Without a companion" means that he has no companion equal to him either in his physical form or in the Dhammas he has penetrated; thus he is "without a companion.
However, by this alternative method: "The Blessed One indeed has companions, namely the practices of those in training (sekkhā)."
Those in training and those beyond training are called the "companions" of the Buddhas. Regarding the term *appaṭima*: a *paṭimā* is said to mean a physical form (*attabhāva*);
since there is no other form equal to that physical form, he is *appaṭima*.

Furthermore, even among those images made of gold, silver, and so forth that people fashion, there is not even a space the size of a hair’s tip capable of being made similar to the physical form of the Tathāgata.
"Nameless" means that he is peerless in every respect.
"Matchless" means that there is no one at all who can be his equal even in terms of his physical person; thus he is matchless.

"Peerless" means that among those teachings taught by the Tathāgata in such ways as "the four foundations of mindfulness," there is nothing—such as the four [foundations of mindfulness]—that is his equal.

There is no one capable of producing a counterpart [to him] in the manner described by the phrases "the foundations of mindfulness" or "the three or five [aggregates]," and thus he is *appaṭibhāga* (without counterpart).
He is *appaṭipuggala* (without a rival) because there is no other person capable of making such a claim as "I am a Buddha.
He is *asama* (unequaled) precisely because he has no rival among all sentient beings. He is *asamasama* (unequaled among the unequaled).
The "unequaled ones" (asamā) are said to be the omniscient Buddhas of the past and future; he who is equal to those unequaled ones is "equal to the unequaled" (asamasama).

"The foremost among bipeds" means that the Perfectly Enlightened One is the very pinnacle among beings—whether they be footless, bipeds, quadrupeds, many-footed, possessed of form, formless, percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient. Why, then, is he specified here as "among bipeds"?

When it is said "the foremost," it is by way of being the most excellent. For in this world, when one who is called "foremost" arises, he does not arise among those without feet, four-footed beings, or many-footed creatures;
he arises only among two-footed beings. Among which two-footed beings? Among humans and among devas.
When arising among humans, he is a Buddha capable of governing the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
Having sacrificed, he is reborn. When being reborn among the devas, he arises as Mahābrahmā, the wielder of power over ten thousand world-systems.
He becomes either his attendant (kappiyakāraka) or his monastery attendant (ārāmika). Thus, by way of this even more excellent status, he is called the foremost of bipeds.
175–186. "With the manifestation of one person, monks, there is the manifestation of the great eye.

Monks, with the manifestation of this one person—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—there is the manifestation of the great eye. When that person has manifested, it is indeed manifested.
It does not appear without its manifestation. "Manifestation" means arising or accomplishment.
Of what eye? Of the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). Of what kind? Like the insight-wisdom of the Elder Sāriputta, and like the concentration-wisdom of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
The same method applies to light and the other [factors]. It is indeed like the light of wisdom of both Chief Disciples.
For here, "light" (*āloka*) is intended as a radiance similar to the illumination of wisdom (*paññā-obhāsa*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that these three—"of great vision," "of great light," and "of great radiance"—are spoken of as a mixture of mundane and supramundane qualities.

Regarding the "six unsurpassables" (*cha anuttariyāni*): they are the six supreme states (*uttama-dhamma*) devoid of anything superior to them. Therein, the unsurpassable in seeing (*dassanānuttariya*)...

The unsurpassedness of hearing, the unsurpassedness of gain, the unsurpassedness of training, the unsurpassedness of service, and the unsurpassedness of recollection—these are the six unsurpassed things.

The meaning is that the manifestation of these occurs. For the Venerable Elder Ānanda receives the opportunity to see the Tathāgata with his eye-consciousness morning and evening; this is the unsurpassedness of seeing. Another who is a stream-enterer...
Whether one is a once-returner or a non-returner, if they obtain a vision of the Tathāgata just as the Elder Ānanda did, this too is unsurpassed vision (*dassanānuttariya*).

Furthermore, another person who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), having obtained a vision of the One Possessing Ten Powers just as the Elder Ānanda did, increases that vision and attains the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*). This is indeed called "vision" itself; it is the vision of the root.
Furthermore, there is the unsurpassed sight.
And the fact that the Elder Ānanda alone constantly receives the words of the One of Ten Powers with his auditory consciousness—this is the unsurpassed hearing.
Other stream-enterers and so forth, like the Elder Ānanda, [also hear] the word of the Tathāgata...
They obtain [the opportunity] for hearing; this too is a supreme excellence of hearing (*savanānuttariya*).

Furthermore, another virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), like the Venerable Ānanda, having obtained the opportunity to hear the word of the Tathāgata, increases that hearing and brings one to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
This is merely "hearing," whereas the original hearing is called the supreme excellence of hearing.

When the Elder Ānanda alone attains faith in the One of Ten Powers, this is the unsurpassed attainment. When others as well—such as stream-enterers and the like—attain the acquisition of faith in the One of Ten Powers just as the Elder Ānanda did, this too is the unsurpassed attainment.
Furthermore, when another virtuous worldling, having attained the acquisition of faith in the One of Ten Powers just as the Elder Ānanda did, [proceeds] with that...
Having increased his gains, he brings others to the path of stream-entry; this is merely called "gain. However, the gain of the root [of the Dhamma] is called the "supremacy of gain.
And it is the Elder Ānanda alone who trains in the three trainings within the dispensation of the One of Ten Powers; this is the "supremacy of training.
Other stream-enterers and so forth also train in the three trainings within the dispensation of the One of Ten Powers, just like the Elder Ānanda.

This too is the unsurpassed training. Furthermore, another type of virtuous worldling, like the Elder Ānanda, having trained in the three trainings within the teaching of the One of Ten Powers and having increased those trainings, reaches the path of stream-entry.
This is simply called "training," whereas the fundamental training is called the "unsurpassed training."
Furthermore, it is the Elder Ānanda himself who constantly attends upon the One of Ten Powers; this is the unsurpassed service.
Others as well—such as stream-enterers and so forth—also attend upon the One of Ten Powers frequently, just like the Elder Ānanda; this too is unsurpassed service.
Moreover, another person, a virtuous worldling, having attended upon the One of Ten Powers just like the Elder Ānanda, that service...

Having increased [that mindfulness], one brings about the path of stream-entry; this is indeed called "service" (*pāricariyā*). However, the "fundamental service" (*mūlapāricariyā*) is called the "supreme service" (*pāricariyānuttariya*).
And it is the Elder Ānanda alone who recollects the mundane and supramundane qualities of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (*dasabala*); this is the "supreme recollection" (*anussatānuttariya*).
Other stream-enterers and so forth also recollect the mundane and supramundane qualities of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, just like the Elder Ānanda.

This too is the unsurpassedness of recollection (*anussatānuttariya*). Furthermore, an ordinary person who is a "good-farer" (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*), like the Venerable Ānanda, attains the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) by recollecting the mundane and supramundane qualities of the One Possessing Ten Powers (*dasabala*) and increasing that recollection;
this is simply called "recollection. However, the root-recollection (*mūlānussati*) is what is called the "unsurpassedness of recollection. These are the six unsurpassed things.
The manifestation of these occurs. Furthermore, it should be understood that these six unsurpassed qualities (*anuttariya*) are taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
Regarding the phrase "there is the realization of the four analytical knowledges" (*catunnaṃ paṭisambhidānaṃ sacchikiriyā*):

there are indeed four analytical knowledges—analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). Among these, regarding meanings...
Knowledge of meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*);

knowledge regarding the expression of the language of meaning and phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*); and knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition of these, however, is found in the Abhidhamma. Regarding these four analytical knowledges, when a Buddha has arisen—

There is the realization (paccakkhakiriyā), which does not occur without the arising of a Buddha; the meaning is "the direct verification of these. It should be understood that these too are described as both mundane and supramundane.
"Penetration of the manifold elements" refers to the eighteen elements, such as the eye-element and the form-element, [which are realized] only when a Buddha has arisen.
There is penetration; the meaning is that it does not occur without the arising of a Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "penetration of the various elements" (*nānādhātupaṭivedha*), here these eighteen elements themselves should be understood as "various elements" (*nānādhātu*) because they possess diverse intrinsic natures.

Furthermore, the penetration that occurs by way of discerning their diversity—namely, "these have diverse intrinsic natures"—is what is called "penetration of the various elements. "The realization of the fruit of clear knowledge and liberation" (*vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyā*).
Here, "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge regarding the fruit; "liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the remaining states associated with that fruit.
"The realization of the fruit of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyā*): "stream" (*sota*) is the first path; the fruit to be attained by means of that stream is the "fruit of stream-entry.

The fruits of once-returning and so forth are well known. (187) "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) means having no superior. "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) means the supreme wheel. For this word "wheel" (*cakkā*)—
“From four he attained eight, and from eight, sixteen;
from sixteen, thirty-two. The wheel of one who desires too much rolls upon his head;
for the person overcome by desire, the wheel revolves upon his crown.”

In this context, it refers to the wheel of the chest. In the passage, “The people of the countryside, mounted on wheels, were traveling about,” it refers to the wheel of postures (*iriyāpatha-cakka*).
In the passage, “Then, monks, that wheelwright set in motion the wheel which had been completed in six months,” it refers to a wooden wheel (*dāru-cakka*).
And in the passage, “The brahmin Doṇa saw on the Blessed One’s feet wheels with a thousand spokes,” [it refers to the wheel-mark].

Here [it refers] to the wheel of characteristics (*lakkhaṇacakra*). In the passage, “Monks, there are these four wheels; for gods and humans endowed with them, the fourfold wheel turns,” it refers to the wheel of prosperity (*sampatticakra*).
In the passage, “The divine wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) appears,” it refers to the wheel of jewels (*ratanacakra*).
But here, it occurs as the wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakra*).

Regarding the phrase "set in motion": here, one should understand this classification as follows—namely, that the Wheel of Dhamma is "being brought forth," "brought forth," "arisen," "arisen," "set in motion," and "set in motion. From what point is it said that the Wheel of Dhamma is "being brought forth"?
It is when, having been a brahmin named Sumedha, [he saw] the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation...

Having seen the benefit and given the great gift of seven hundred [items], he went forth into the ascetic life and developed the five supernormal powers (*pañca abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha samāpatti*).
From that point on, it is said that he "set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakkaṃ abhinīharati*).
From what point is it said to have been set in motion? It was when, having brought together the eight qualities at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha...
Having bound his mind to the seat of Great Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa) and established a resolution of energy, thinking, "I shall not rise until I have received the prophecy," he lay down.
From the moment he received the prophecy from the One Possessing the Ten Powers (dasabala), it is said that the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) was brought forth.
From what point does one say it is "aroused"? From that point onward, even while fulfilling the perfection of giving (dānapāramī), one arouses the Wheel of Dhamma.

...is called "arousing the Wheel of Dhamma. Even while fulfilling the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*)... [and so on] ...even while fulfilling the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramī*), one is said to arouse the Wheel of Dhamma.

Even while fulfilling the ten perfections (*pāramī*), the ten secondary perfections (*upapāramī*), and the ten ultimate perfections (*paramatthapāramī*); even while making the five great renunciations (*mahāpariccāga*);
and even while fulfilling the conduct for the benefit of kinsmen (*ñātatthacariyā*), one is said to arouse the Wheel of Dhamma. This was in the state of existence as Vessantara.

Having stood [in the Tusita heaven], having given the great gift of seven hundredfold offerings, having placed his wife and children at the head of the distribution of alms, and having reached the pinnacle of the perfections (*pāramī*), he was reborn in the Tusita city.
Having remained there for the full span of his lifespan and being entreated by the deities, he gave his promise;
even while performing the five great observations (*pañcamahāvilokana*), he is indeed said to have set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. [He then took] rebirth in a mother’s womb.
Even while taking hold [of the earth], even at the moment of rebirth-linking when he caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to tremble,
even on the day of his emergence from his mother’s womb when he likewise made the world tremble, even as a newborn infant when he took seven steps and uttered the lion’s roar,
“I am the foremost in the world,” even while dwelling in the midst of the household for twenty-nine years, and even when making the Great Renunciation;
While going forth on the bank of the Anomā River, while exerting heroic effort for six years at the Great Struggle,
and after eating the honey-rice porridge given by Sujātā and casting the golden bowl into the river, he arrived at the sublime seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in the evening;
there, sitting and surveying the eastern world-system, he shattered the host of Māra even while the sun was still shining.
In the first watch of the night, while recollecting his former births; in the middle watch, while purifying his divine eye;

and at the time immediately following the dawn, while comprehending the nature of conditions and penetrating the path of stream-entry, realizing the fruit of stream-entry, realizing the path of once-returning and its fruit, the path of non-returning and its fruit, and the path of arahantship...
Even while penetrating [the truth], one is indeed said to "set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
However, it is at the moment of the fruit of Arahantship that the Wheel of Dhamma is truly said to have been set in motion by him.

For in the case of the Buddhas, the entire mass of mundane and supramundane qualities is accomplished together with the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, at that moment, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been set in motion by him.

When, indeed, is it said that he "sets in motion"? After spending seven weeks at the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), having made the Elder Aññākoṇḍañña a bodily witness at Isipatana in the Deer Park, while teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he is said to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.
But when the Elder Aññākoṇḍañña, having received the hearing produced by the power of the Ten-Powered One’s knowledge of teaching—
It should be understood that the Wheel of the Dhamma (dhammacakka) is said to have been set in motion from the very moment the Dhamma was first realized;
from that point onward, it is so designated. This term "Wheel of the Dhamma" is a name for both the knowledge of teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa).

Of these two, the knowledge of teaching is mundane (lokiya), while the knowledge of penetration is supramundane (lokuttara). To whom do this knowledge of teaching and knowledge of penetration belong? They belong to no one else.
It should be understood that this refers to both the knowledge of teaching and the knowledge of penetration belonging to the Fully Enlightened One alone.
"In a perfectly correct manner" means by way of cause, method, and reason.
"He sets it in motion again" means that just as one walking behind follows one who is walking ahead, so too does the Elder set in motion again what was previously set in motion by the Teacher.
How so? For when the Teacher says, "Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness.

Which four?", he is indeed setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion; and when the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, says, "Friends, there are these four foundations of mindfulness," he is indeed causing the Wheel of Dhamma to follow after it. The same applies to the right efforts and the other [foundations].

This is the method. And this method is to be applied not only to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), but also to such passages as: "Monks, there are these four noble truths," and "Monks, there are these four noble lineages.
In this way, it is said that the Fully Enlightened One sets the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and the Elder sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
Furthermore, when the Elder who has thus set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion teaches or proclaims the Dhamma,
it is as if the Teacher himself has taught and proclaimed it. For whether it be any monk, nun, layman, laywoman, deva, Sakka, Māra,
or Brahmā who teaches or proclaims the Dhamma, all that is indeed taught and proclaimed by the Teacher.
He alone is called "the one who acts"; however, the rest of the people are merely those standing on the side of the letter-carriers. How so?

Just as whatever action people perform after reading a royal decree—whether that action is done by someone personally or caused to be done by someone else—it is said to have been "caused to be done by the king.
For the Perfectly Enlightened One is like the great king, and the royal decree is like the Dhamma.
The word of the Buddha in its three baskets (Tipiṭaka) is like the letter itself.

Just as one reads the letter of the leaf-gift and then performs various tasks, so too is the teaching and exposition for others after having mastered the word of the Buddha by one's own strength for the four assemblies.
In that regard, just as [the task] is performed or caused to be performed by anyone after reading the letter...

Just as that work was indeed caused to be done by the king, even so it should be understood that whatever Dhamma is taught or proclaimed by anyone else is nonetheless said to have been taught and proclaimed by the Teacher himself. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on the Single Individual.
14. Etadaggavagga (14) 1.
Paṭhamaetadaggavagga: Commentary on the Words "Foremost" (Etadagga)

188. Regarding "Etadaggesu" (among these foremost), in the first section of the first chapter, *etadagga* means "this is the foremost. Furthermore, this word *agga* is seen in the senses of beginning, peak, portion, and best.
For instance, in such passages as, "From this day forward (*ajjatagge*), friend gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭhas and Nigaṇṭhīs," it is seen in the sense of a beginning.
[And] in the passage, "With that very fingertip (*aṅgulaggena*), one might touch that fingertip (*taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ*)," [it is seen in the sense of a portion].
In such passages as "the tip of a bamboo" (*ucchaggaṃ veḷaggaṃ*), it means the end.

In such passages as "I allow you, monks, to divide [it] by the portion of the monastery or the portion of the courtyard—whether it be sour-tipped, sweet-tipped, or bitter-tipped" (*ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā... vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetun*ṭi), it means a part or portion.

In such passages as "To whatever extent, monks, there are beings, whether footless... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them" (*yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā... tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī*ṭi), it means the best or preeminent.
"Koṭi" (the limit) applies here both to the "limit" and to the "best. For those elders are the "limits" in their respective positions; they are thus the foremost and the best.
Therefore, "this is the foremost" means "this is the limit" and "this is the best"—this is the meaning here. This same method applies to all suttas.
Furthermore, this designation as "foremost" is obtained through four causes: from the occasion of the arising [of the discourse], from the source, from the person, and from the subject matter.

"Because of the excellence of his qualities and because he has fulfilled his duties. In this regard, one elder may receive this foremost position for one reason, another for two, another for three, and another for all four, like the Venerable Elder Sāriputta.

For he received this foremost position both on account of the origin of the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*) due to his great wisdom, and also on account of his arrival and other such factors. How so? At one time...
At that time, while residing at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher, having displayed the Twin Miracle—the crushing of the heretics—at the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree, reflected:
"Where indeed did the previous Buddhas enter the rains retreat after performing the Twin Miracle?
Perceiving that it was "in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven," he displayed two steps and [then] with the third...

At that very spot, he stood waiting in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. When Sakka, the king of the gods, saw the Blessed One, he rose from his seat upon the Paṇḍukambala stone and went out to meet him together with the host of devas. The devas thought:
"Sakka, the king of the gods, surrounded by his host of devas, sits upon the Paṇḍukambala stone sixty yojanas in length and enjoys his prosperity."
"From the moment the Buddhas sit down, it is not possible for anyone else to even place a hand here.

The Teacher, sitting there, knowing their state of mind, sat down covering the entire yellow-sandalwood stone slab with his shaven seat as if he were a great wearer of rag-robes. While sitting thus, he [covered] his own body...
One should not assume that he made [the seat] large and thus made the Paṇḍukambala stone small;

for the domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable. Seated thus, having made his mother a bodily witness, he taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—beginning with "wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states"—to the deities of the ten thousand world-systems.
At the place of the miracle as well, the entire assembly of twelve leagues approached the Elder Anuruddha and asked, "Venerable sir, where has the One of Ten Powers gone?

He replied, "He has gone to the realm of the Thirty-three, to the Paṇḍukambala stone, having entered the rains retreat to teach the Abhidhamma. They said, "Venerable sir, we will not depart without seeing the Teacher."
"Do you know when the Teacher will arrive? Find out the time of the Teacher's arrival. "Place the burden upon the Elder Mahāmoggallāna;
he will go into the presence of the Buddhas and bring back the message. "But does the Elder not have the power to go there?
"He certainly has it, but he spoke thus so that those possessing special qualities might see their own distinction. Thus said the great multitude.
Having approached the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and received the Teacher’s instruction, he requested him to come.
Even as the great multitude looked on, the Elder sank into the earth, went inside Sineru, paid homage to the Teacher, and said:
"Venerable Sir, the great multitude desires to see you; they wish to know the day of your arrival."
"In that case, tell him: 'In three months from now, you shall see us at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa.
The Elder, having delivered the Blessed One’s message, spoke it to the great multitude. The great multitude remained right there for those three months, encamping their army.
Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika provided rice porridge and meals for a retinue of twelve leagues for the duration of those three months.
The Teacher, having taught the seven treatises, made a gesture indicating his intention to descend to the world of men.
Sakka, the king of the gods, addressed Vissakamma and commanded him to construct a staircase for the Tathāgata’s descent.
He fashioned a staircase with golden steps on one side, silver steps on the other, and jeweled steps in the middle.
Standing upon the jeweled staircase, the Teacher resolved, "Let the great multitude see me.

By his own supernatural power, he also resolved, "Let the great multitude see the Great Niraya Hell. Knowing that a sense of spiritual urgency had arisen in them from seeing the hell, he showed them the world of the devas.
Then, as he was descending, Mahābrahmā held a parasol over him, and Sakka, King of the Devas, [held another].
Pāṭala took up the fan; Suyāma, the king of the gods, fanned him with a divine yak-tail whisk;
and Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba gods, descended before him playing his yellow-bellied lute, which was strung with fifty strings.
As the Buddhas were being established upon the earth, [the beings thought], "I shall be the first to pay homage! I shall be the first to pay homage!"
The great multitude stood still. However, with the Blessed One’s first lifting of his great foot, neither the great multitude nor the eighty great disciples reached the first prostration;
only the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, reached it.
Then, amidst the assembly extending for twelve yojanas, the Teacher [set aside] the group of five ordinary worldlings, thinking, "Let them know the power of the Elder’s wisdom."
He began a series of questions. Thinking, "First, the ordinary people of the world will observe," he asked a question concerning the level of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
Those who were capable of observing each answered. Second, having transcended the domain of the ordinary person, he asked a question regarding the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
The ordinary persons became silent; only those who had attained stream-entry spoke. Then, [he asked] of the stream-enterers...
Having transcended their domain, he asked a question regarding the path of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmi*). The stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) remained silent, while only the once-returners answered.
Having transcended even their domain, he asked a question regarding the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmi*).
The once-returners remained silent, while only the non-returners answered. Having transcended even their domain, he asked a question regarding the path of arhatship (*arahatta*).
He questioned them. Those who were non-returners remained silent; only the arahants spoke.
Then he questioned the well-known disciples starting from the lowest rank, and they each spoke, remaining within the scope of their own analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*).
Then he questioned Mahāmoggallāna; the other disciples remained silent, and the Elder alone spoke. [The Buddha then asked] regarding his scope as well...
Having passed beyond that, he asked a question within the domain of the Elder Sāriputta. Mahāmoggallāna remained silent, and the Elder Sāriputta alone answered.
Having passed beyond even the Elder’s domain, he asked a question within the domain of the Buddha.
Even though the General of the Dhamma directed his attention, he was unable to see [the answer], for it extended to the four directions—east, west, north, and south.
Looking here and there toward the four cardinal and intermediate directions, he was unable to discern the source from which the question had arisen.
The Teacher, perceiving the elder’s exhaustion, thought, "Sāriputta is weary; I shall show him the method.
Saying, "Wait a moment, Sāriputta," he added, "This question is not within your domain; it is the domain of the Buddhas."
Having thus declared the domain of the Buddhas, saying, "Of those who are all-knowing and glorious," he said, "Sāriputta, do you regard this as 'it has come to be'?

The Elder, understanding, "The Blessed One is teaching me the comprehension of the body composed of the four great elements," replied, "It is understood, Blessed One; it is understood, Sugata. At this point, the following discussion arose:
"O friends, the Elder Sāriputta is indeed possessed of great wisdom! For he has explained a question entirely unknown to all others;
and standing upon the method bestowed by the Buddhas, he has explained a question within the domain of the Buddhas.
Thus, the power of the Elder’s wisdom has surpassed everything that was covered by the fame and renown of the Buddhas. Thus it was said.

Thus, by way of this occasion for discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the Elder received the foremost position due to his great wisdom. How so by way of his lineage? For regarding this very same occasion for discourse, the Teacher said: "Sāriputta was not wise only now; even in the past, having gone forth as a seer (*isi*) for five hundred births, he was possessed of great wisdom—'He who went forth for five hundred births...'"* *The verse continues:* yo pabbajī jātisatāni pañca, sāriputto vaṇṇavā yasassī; tassa sutvāna dhammaṃ, sotāpattiphalaṃ apāpuṇi. "He who went forth for five hundred births, Sāriputta, the handsome and renowned; having heard his Dhamma, [the king] attained the fruit of stream-entry."* *The verse continues:* yo pabbajī jātisatāni pañca, sāriputto vaṇṇavā yasassī; tassa sutvāna dhammaṃ, sakadāgāmiphalaṃ apāpuṇi. "Having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures,
pay homage to Sāriputta, who is free from passion, whose faculties are well-composed, and who has attained final Nibbāna."
Thus, while cultivating the life of renunciation, at one time he was reborn in a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī.
Having mastered the three Vedas and seeing no essence therein, he conceived the thought: "It is fitting to go forth and seek the single Dhamma of liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisatta too was reborn in a prominent brahmin mahāsāla family in the kingdom of Kāsī.
Having grown up and mastered his craft, he saw the peril in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation.

Abandoning the household life, he entered the Himalayas, performed the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, and having realized the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he dwelt in a region of the Himalayas, subsisting on roots and fruits from the forest. That young man also went forth and followed him.
He went forth in the presence [of the Teacher]. His retinue was great, consisting of about five hundred seers.
Then his senior disciple, taking a portion of the assembly, went to the path frequented by humans in order to partake of salt and sour gruel.
At that time, the Bodhisatta passed away in that very region of the Himalayas. At the very moment of his passing away—
His pupils gathered together and asked him, "Has anyone among you attained any distinction?
The Bodhisatta replied, "There is nothing. Having spoken thus, he was reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma-world without falling away from his jhāna.
Although he was an attainer of the base of nothingness, there is no rebirth-linking for Bodhisattas in the formless realm. Why? Because it is an unsuitable place.
Thus, although he was one who had attained the formless absorptions, he was reborn in the realm of form.
His pupils did not offer him any honor or respect, thinking, "The teacher said, 'There is nothing,' so his passing away was in vain.
Then, after the rains retreat had passed, that senior pupil returned and asked, "Where is the teacher? [They replied: "He has passed away."
“‘Who? ‘Did you ask about the qualities attained by the teacher? ‘Yes, we asked. ‘What did he say? ‘He said, “There is nothing.
‘We too thought, “The teacher has no qualities whatsoever,” and so we did not offer him honor or respect.
‘You did not understand the meaning of what was said; the teacher is an attainer of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana).’”
Then they did not believe the words of his senior disciple. Although he spoke again and again, he was unable to make them believe.
Then the Bodhisatta, reflecting, thought: "This foolish multitude does not accept the words of my senior disciple;
I shall make this matter manifest. Having descended from the Brahma-world, he stood at the edge of the hermitage.
Standing there as if suspended in the air, he praised the power of wisdom of his senior disciple and spoke this verse:
“Even if more than a thousand who lack wisdom were to gather together and cry out for a hundred years, [they would not equal one person of wisdom].”
"A single wise man alone is better, who understands the meaning of what is spoken.

Having thus instructed the company of seers, the Bodhisatta departed for the Brahma-world. The rest of the company of seers, too, remained without falling away from their meditative absorption (jhāna).
Having offered the sacrifice and passed away, he was reborn with the Brahma-world as his destination. There, the Bodhisatta attained omniscience;
the senior pupil became the Elder Sāriputta, and the remaining seers became the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples.
Thus, it should be understood that even in the past, Sāriputta possessed great wisdom and was capable of understanding in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief.
And taking this very group of five ordinary persons as the occasion for the discourse,
he said: "Even if more than a hundred who lack wisdom were to come together and meditate for a hundred years..."
"Better than a hundred fools is a single wise man;
he understands the meaning of what is spoken.
He also related this Jātaka. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous Jātaka.
Furthermore, taking this same group of five worldlings as the occasion for the teaching, it was said:
“Those who possess perception are miserable, and those who are without perception are also miserable;
avoiding both of these, that bliss of attainment is free from blemish.”

He related this Anaṅgaṇa Jātaka. And here, when the Teacher was about to pass away, being questioned by his disciples, he said: "Neither percipient nor non-percipient. The rest should be understood in the manner already stated.
Furthermore, taking this very group of five ordinary persons as the occasion, he said:
"He who, by means of wisdom, gains a foothold upon the radiance of the moon and the radiance of the sun..."
“By means of jhāna without applied thought, one becomes a dweller in the Ābhassara realm.”—This is the Candābhajātaka he related.
Here too, when the Teacher was passing away, being questioned by his pupils, he said:
“The white kasiṇa is called the Moonlight; the yellow kasiṇa is called the Sunlight. Whoever, through wisdom, [perceives] both of these...”
"He gains confidence, enters, and leaps forward; by means of the second jhāna, which is without applied thought, he goes to the Ābhassara realm.
Thinking, 'I am such as this,' he said: 'The radiance of the moon, the radiance of the sun. The rest should be understood in the same manner as before.
And it was precisely this group of five worldlings (*puthujjana*) who provided the occasion for this discourse."
“A wise person should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent.
I see myself now as I have come to be, just as I had wished.
A wise person should indeed aspire; he should not become despondent.”
“I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
A wise person should indeed strive and not despair;
I see myself as one who has become exactly as I wished.”
“A wise person should indeed exert effort and not become despondent;
for I see myself as one who has been pulled from the water onto dry land.
Even when brought to suffering, a man of wisdom...”
One should not cut off hope for the arrival of happiness;
for many contacts, both harmful and beneficial,
approach a mortal even when they are not anticipated.
“Even that which was unthought of comes to pass, and even that which was thought of perishes;
for riches, whether for a woman or a man, do not arise from mere thinking.
Sarabha, that which you formerly pursued in the mountain fastness—”
"You live off the prowess of one whose heart is undaunted.
He who rescued you from the difficult-to-cross hells,
having fashioned for you a raft of stone, was Sarabha."
“You spoke to that deer of undaunted spirit who had been brought to suffering and released from the jaws of death:
‘Were you not there yourself at that time?’”
Or did someone tell this to you?
Are you one whose veil is removed, a seer of all?
Or is your knowledge, O Brahmin, of such a terrifying nature?
“I was not there at that time,
nor did anyone explain this to me;
[I know it] from the well-spoken verses and phrases.”
“O Lord of Men, the wise bring about the goal.”—At that time, he related the Sarabha Jātaka from the Thirteen-Nipāta.
Furthermore, these five Jātakas were told by the Teacher to the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, with the words:
“In the past as well, my son knows the detailed meaning of what was spoken in brief.”

These [qualities] were spoken of solely for the purpose of manifesting the power of his wisdom; thus, by way of his lineage, the Elder attained this foremost rank due to his great wisdom. How was he "one who had mastered his practice"?

It is said that when the Elder preached the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he did so without ever omitting the Four Truths; thus, by virtue of having mastered his practice, the Elder attained this foremost rank due to his great wisdom. How was it "by excellence of qualities"?
For, setting aside the One Possessing Ten Powers (the Buddha), not even a single disciple could equal him in great wisdom.
"There is no one equal to the General of the Dhamma"—thus, on account of his preeminent qualities, the Elder received this foremost position due to his great wisdom (*mahāpaññatā*).
And just as the Elder Sāriputta did, so too the Elder Mahāmoggallāna received this foremost position for all four of these reasons. How so?
For the Elder was possessed of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*); even one like Nandopananda...
“He tames the Naga kings”—thus it was first obtained from the occasion of its arising. But he has not only now been of great psychic power and great majesty;
even in the past, during five hundred births when he had gone forth as an ascetic, he was of great psychic power and great majesty.
“He who went forth for five hundred births...”
“Having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures—
pay homage, Moggallāna, to him who is free from passion, whose faculties are perfectly composed, and who has attained final Nibbāna.”

Thus it is obtained even from the perspective of his arrival. It was the Elder’s habit to go to hell and, for the sake of inspiring confidence in the beings there, resolve upon coolness by his own power of psychic potency (*iddhi*), create a lotus the size of a wheel, sit upon the pericarp of that lotus, and deliver a discourse on the Dhamma;
likewise, he would go to the world of the gods, inform the assembly of devas of their karmic destiny, and proclaim the Truth.

He received [this designation] because he spoke thus: "I have fulfilled my duties. And he received it because of his preeminence in virtue, for apart from the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was no other disciple possessed of such great psychic power and majesty as Mahāmoggallāna.
Just as he did, the Elder Mahākassapa also received this foremost position for all these same reasons.
How so? For the Sammasambuddha went out to meet the Elder for a distance of three gavutas, ordained him with the three exhortations, and after exchanging robes, gave them to him.
At that moment, the great earth, bounded by the waters, shook;
and the fame of the Elder spread, overwhelming the hearts of the great multitude. Thus...
He obtained it from the occasion of the arising of the matter (*aṭṭhuppatti*). And he was not only a possessor of the ascetic practices (*dhutadharo*) now;
even in the past, throughout five hundred births, though he had gone forth as an ascetic seer (*isi*), he remained a possessor of the ascetic practices. "He who went forth for five hundred births..."
"Having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures,
pay homage to Mahākassapa, who is free from passion, whose faculties are well-composed, and who has attained final Nibbāna."
Thus it was obtained by way of his arrival. It was also obtained because of the Elder’s established practice (*ciṇṇavasita*):

when he preached the Dhamma while seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he did so without ever abandoning the ten bases of discourse (*dasakathāvatthu*). Furthermore, it was obtained because of his preeminence in virtue:
with the exception of the Fully Enlightened One, there was no other disciple equal to Mahākassapa in the thirteen ascetic qualities (*dhutaguṇa*).
In this same manner, it is appropriate to praise the virtues of those various elders according to their respective attainments.

For it was solely by virtue of his own qualities that the Perfectly Enlightened One—just as a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti-rāja), having attained the glory of sovereignty within the world-system through the power of the Wheel-treasure, thinks:
"I have attained what was to be attained; what need have I now for the gaze of the multitude?"—remained free from concern.
Having sacrificed [all else], he enjoys the glory of sovereignty itself; yet from time to time, sitting in the place of judgment,
he restrains those who deserve restraint and supports those who deserve support, and he appoints to various offices those who are fit for such positions—
just so does one who has attained the sovereignty of Dhamma through the power of the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) realized at the Great Seat of Enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa).
The Dhamma King, thinking, "What is the use of my looking at the world now? I shall experience the unsurpassed bliss of the attainment of fruition," did not fall into indolence;

rather, seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he uttered the Brahma-voice endowed with eight factors and, while teaching the Dhamma, [addressed] those individuals characterized by dark qualities who were to be restrained.
Just as one who casts [a person] into the base of Mount Sineru restrains them by terrifying them with the fear of the states of woe,
and just as one who lifts up a person suitable for upliftment places them at the very peak of existence, so too, the Buddha—

having restrained those such as the Elder Aññākoṇḍañña and other disciples who were suitable to be established in specific ranks by means of the very qualities of their actual nature— established them in those respective ranks according to their true characteristics; this is the "foremost" (etadagga).
“Monks, among my disciples who are bhikkhus of long standing, this one is the foremost, namely Aññā-Koṇḍañña,” and so forth.
This is the story of the Elder Aññā-Koṇḍañña.
In that context, the phrase “foremost” has already been explained. “Of those of long standing” means of those who know the nights. Having set [him] aside...
Indeed, since there is no other disciple who went forth earlier than the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña after the Fully Enlightened One,
the Elder is known as *rattaññū* (one who knows the nights) because, from the time of his going forth, he has known the nights for a long time.
Because he was the very first to penetrate the Dhamma, from the moment that Dhamma was penetrated by him, it has been that night for a long time.

He is called *rattaññū* (one who knows the nights) because he knows [the time]. Furthermore, the demarcation of days and nights is evident to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), and since he was the first among them to have destroyed the taints, he is thus the foremost, the very first, and the best among the disciples who know the nights.
Therefore it is said: "Among those who know the nights, this is Aññā-Koṇḍañña."
And here, *yadidaṃ* is a particle; with reference to the Elder, its meaning is "who this [is]," and with reference to the word *agga* (foremost), it means "which this [is].
"Aññāsikoṇḍañña" means Koṇḍañña by name and Koṇḍañña who has realized [the truth]. For this very reason it was said:
"Koṇḍañña has indeed understood, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood! Thus, this [was the name] of the Venerable Koṇḍañña.

“His name was indeed Aññāsikoṇḍañña. Now, according to this method, one should consider for all [the elders]: during the time of which Buddha did this elder make his original aspiration and formal resolve; when did he go forth into homelessness; when did he first realize the Dhamma; and when was he appointed to a specific position? Thus it is said: “At that time, Ānanda, Koṇḍañña the brahmin was my chief attendant. At that time too, Ānanda, I was a wheel-turning monarch named Mahāpanāda. And at that time, Ānanda, the Tathāgata Kassapa was my preceptor. At that time too, Ānanda, I made a vow, saying: ‘Just as this Venerable Koṇḍañña is the chief attendant of the Tathāgata Kassapa, so may I also become the chief attendant of the Tathāgata.

It was on account of that vow, Ānanda, that I have become the chief attendant of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, regarding the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña: during the time of which Buddha did he make his original aspiration and formal resolve? When did he go forth? When did he first attain the Dhamma? When was he established in a specific position? In this manner, one should investigate for all [of them].
The performance of questions among these foremost disciples is to be understood.
Regarding this, first, this is the sequential account concerning the question of this Elder:
One hundred thousand aeons ago, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world; when he had realized all-knowing wisdom, from the great seat of enlightenment...
As he was rising, a great lotus flower sprang up from the great earth to receive his foot as soon as it was lifted, for the purpose of supporting it;
its central petals were ninety cubits long, its filaments thirty cubits, its pericarp twelve cubits, and the spot where his foot rested was eleven cubits. Of that Blessed One...

His body was fifty-eight cubits in height. When his right foot was placed upon the pericarp of the lotus, dust the size of large water-jars rose up and descended, sprinkling his body; when he set down his left foot, a similar lotus likewise arose and received his foot.
Rising from that as well, dust of the same aforementioned measure rose up and sprinkled his body.
Overpowering that dust, the radiance issuing from the body of that Blessed One made the area for twelve yojanas all around a single expanse of light,
like a stream of molten gold poured from a mechanical tube. At the time of lifting the third step,
the lotus that had first emerged vanished, and another new lotus sprang up to receive his foot.
By this very same principle, wherever he desired to go, there too a great lotus would emerge.
For that reason, his name became "Padumuttara Sammāsambuddha.
Thus, having arisen in the world with a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, that Blessed One, for the sake of gathering the great multitude...
While wandering for alms through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, he arrived at the city of Haṃsavatī.
Upon hearing that he had arrived, his father, the Great King, went out to meet him. The Teacher delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to him.
At the conclusion of the teaching, some attained the stage of stream-entry, some once-returning, some non-returning, and some reached arahantship. The king [invited him] for the following day...

Having invited the One Possessing the Ten Powers and having had the time announced for the following day, he gave a great almsgiving at his own residence to the Blessed One, who was accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
After the Teacher had delivered a discourse of thanksgiving, he returned to the monastery.
Following that very same procedure, the citizens gave alms on the next day, and the king gave alms on the day after that; in this manner, they continued giving for a long period of time.
At that time, this elder was reborn in a family of great householders in the city of Haṃsavatī.

One day, at the time when the Buddhas were teaching the Dhamma, the inhabitants of the city of Haṃsavatī were seen going toward the Buddha, toward the Dhamma, and toward the Saṅgha, with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, inclining, leaning, and tending in those directions; and by that great multitude...

He went together to the place where the Dhamma was being taught. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara established a certain bhikkhu—who had been the first to realize the Dhamma in his own dispensation—in the position of the foremost.
Having heard of this matter, that clansman thought, "This bhikkhu is indeed great; for it is said that, setting aside the Buddha, no other has realized the Dhamma before him."
"There is no one who has already penetrated the Dhamma. Oh, would that I too might become capable of penetrating the Dhamma for the first time within the teaching of a future Buddha!
Having thought thus, at the conclusion of the discourse, he approached the Blessed One and invited him, saying, "Please accept my almsfood tomorrow. The Teacher consented.
Having thus paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he went to his own residence.

Throughout the entire night, he adorned the place where Buddhas sit with fragrant garlands, flower wreaths, and so forth; then, having prepared exquisite hard and soft foods, at the end of that night, [he approached] the Blessed One, who was in his own residence surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.

Having given fragrant rice porridge accompanied by various kinds of fine flour preparations, side dishes, soups, and condiments, at the conclusion of the meal he placed a piece of cloth sufficient for the three robes at the feet of the Tathāgata and thought: "I do not wander for the sake of a meager station;
I wander aspiring for a great station. Yet it is not possible [to attain it] by means of this alone."

“Having given alms for one day, I shall make a resolution for that particular state. Thinking, “I will give a great almsgiving for seven days in succession and then make my resolution,” he gave a great almsgiving for seven days according to that very same routine.
At the conclusion of his meal, he had the storehouse of cloth opened, placed the finest, most delicate garments at the feet of the Buddhas, and [presented them] to the hundred thousand monks.
Having clothed himself in the three robes and approached the Tathāgata, he said, "Venerable Sir,

may I also, like that bhikkhu whom you designated seven days ago as foremost among those who are capable of realizing the first Dhamma after going forth in the dispensation of a Buddha yet to arise in the future," and [he stood] at the feet of the Teacher.
He lay down placing his head [on the ground].
Having heard his words, the Teacher thought, "This son of good family has performed a great service;
will this aspiration of his be fulfilled or not? Sending forth his knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*), he reflected and perceived, "It shall be fulfilled."
...you see. For indeed, when Buddhas advert their minds toward the past, the future, or the present, there is no obstruction whatsoever.

Even across hundreds of thousands of millions of eons in the past or future, or even across thousands of world-systems in the present, [their knowledge] is entirely dependent upon adverting the mind and dependent upon attention. Thus, by means of that which is unimpeded—
By means of his knowledge, the Blessed One saw this: "At the end of one hundred thousand future eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world;
at that time, this aspiration of his will be fulfilled. Then he said to him:
"O son of good family, at the end of one hundred thousand future eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world."
“At the conclusion of his first discourse on the Dhamma, the Sutta on the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma in its three rounds,
you shall, together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, be established in the fruit of stream-entry,
endowed with the thousandfold method. Having thus prophesied for that clansman, the Teacher taught the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma and [passed away] into the Nibbāna without residue.
He attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna. When he had passed away, his body became a single solid mass like a block of gold;

they constructed a shrine for his body seven yojanas in height. The bricks were made of gold, yellow orpiment and realgar served as the mortar, and oil performed the function of water. This was during the time when the Buddhas were still living.
The radiance of their bodies pervaded twelve *yojanas*, but when they had attained final nibbāna, rays of light issued forth and spread for a hundred *yojanas* in every direction.
This merchant, having surrounded the bodily relic-stūpas of the Buddhas, had them adorned with a thousand jewels worth many millions. On the day the stūpas were consecrated—

He had a jewel-house built within the inner shrine. Having performed great meritorious deeds consisting of giving and other virtues for one hundred thousand years, he passed away from there and was reborn in the city of the gods.
While transmigrating among gods and humans, ninety-nine thousand kappas, nine hundred kappas, and nine kappas elapsed. After the passing of such a length of time—
Ninety-one aeons ago, this son of good family was reborn in a householder’s home in a village near the gate of the city of Bandhumatī.
His name was Mahākāla, and his younger brother was named Cūḷakāla.
At that time, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, having descended from the Tusita heaven, [was born] in the city of Bandhumatī to King Bandhuma...
