He was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen. Gradually attaining omniscience, when requested by Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
and considered his younger half-brother, Prince Khaṇḍa, and Tissa, the son of the royal chaplain, as those who would first penetrate the Dhamma.
Seeing that they were capable, [the Blessed One thought], "I shall teach them the Dhamma and also provide for my father.
Returning through the air from the Seat of Enlightenment, he descended at Khema Migadāya, summoned those two, and taught them the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, both of them, together with eighty-four thousand living beings, were established in the fruit of Arahantship.
Then, eighty-four thousand other sons of noble family who had not gone forth during the time of the Bodhisatta, having heard this news, came into the presence of the Teacher;
after hearing the teaching of the Dhamma, they were established in the fruit of Arahantship.
Right there, the Teacher appointed Khaṇḍa Thera to the position of chief disciple and Tissa Thera to the position of second disciple.
The king, having heard that news and thinking, "I shall see my son," went to the park.

Having heard the teaching of the Dhamma, he established himself in the three refuges. He invited the Teacher for the following day's meal, and after paying homage and circumambulating him, he departed.
Having entered his excellent palace and seated himself, he reflected: "My eldest son has gone forth and become a Buddha."
“My second son is my chief disciple; the son of the family priest is the second disciple.
These remaining monks also, even during their time as householders, used to wander about surrounding my sons alone. They were my burden before, and they are my burden now;
I myself shall attend to them with the four requisites, and I will give no opportunity to others. [He spoke thus] from the gateway of the monastery.
Starting from [the palace] as far as the gate of the royal residence, he had a fence of acacia wood constructed on both sides and had it covered with cloths;
above, he had a canopy made, adorned with golden stars and various flower garlands hanging down as thick as palm trunks,
and the floor below was spread with variegated carpets, while inside, on both sides, were flowering creepers.
Having placed flowers among the various perfumes and perfumes among the various flowers for the purpose of perfuming the entire path with the full water-pot, he announced the time to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to the royal palace through the inner curtain itself;
having performed the meal-duty, he returned to the monastery. No one else even saw him.
[He] receives [nothing]; how then could he obtain alms or perform an act of worship?

The city-dwellers thought: "Today it has been seven years and seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world, yet we do not even get to see him, much less give him alms, perform worship, or hear the Dhamma."
To hear it. The king, thinking "The Buddha is mine, the Dhamma is mine, the Saṅgha is mine," cherishes them as his own and attends upon them personally.
Yet, when the Teacher appears, he does so for the welfare of the world including its devas, not for the sake of the king alone.
For hell is not hot for the king alone; for others, it is like a grove of blue lotuses. Therefore, [the Teacher attends] the king...
"We shall say this: 'If he gives us our teacher, that is well.
If he does not give him, we will fight with the king, seize the Saṅgha, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving. But it is not possible for us to do this with only the ordinary citizens;
let us take at least one leading man. Having approached the general, they explained this matter to him.
Having reported this, they said, "Master, will you take our side or that of the king?
He replied, "I shall take your side; however, the first day must be given to me. They agreed.
He approached the king and said, "Sire, the citizens are angry with you. "For what reason, dear one? he asked.
"Your Majesty, it seems you alone attend upon the Teacher, while we receive nothing. "If they receive even now, they do not become angry.
But since they receive nothing, they wish to fight with you, O King. "I shall fight, my son; I will not give the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus [to them].
"Your Majesty, your own slaves say, 'We shall fight with you. Whom will you take [as allies]?"
"Will you fight? "Am I not the commander-in-chief? "I am unable to do so without the citizens, Your Majesty.

Then the king, realizing that "the citizens are powerful and the commander-in-chief is on their very side," said, "Let them give me my Saṅgha of monks for another seven years and seven months. The citizens did not accept.
The king, having thus reduced [the period] from six years or five years, requested another seven days.
The citizens, thinking, "It is no longer right to act with such extreme harshness toward the king," gave their consent.
The king then prepared the almsgiving arrangements that had been set for seven years and seven months, but prepared them for only seven days; for six days, he [gave] to some...
Having given the gift while they were still unaware, on the seventh day he summoned the citizens and asked, "Dear ones, will you be able to give such a gift?
They replied, "Surely this has arisen for Your Majesty because of us alone," and said, "We shall be able.
The King, wiping away his tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One.
“Venerable sir, I thought, ‘I shall serve six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus for as long as I live with the four requisites, without making anyone else a burden.
Now, however, the citizens have given their permission;
for they would become resentful toward the Blessed One, thinking, ‘We are not allowed to give alms. Therefore, from this day forward, please show them favor. Thus he spoke.
Then, on the second day, the general gave a great almsgiving. Thereafter, the citizens, having performed honors and hospitality even more excellent than those shown by the king, gave their own alms.
In this very same manner, as the procession passed through the entire city in order, the inhabitants of the gateway village prepared honors and hospitality.
The householder Mahākāla said to Cūḷakāla: "To the One Endowed with the Ten Powers..."
"Honors and respect will come to us alone; what honor shall we perform? "Brother, you yourself must decide.
"If you would do it according to my wish, in our sixteen karīsa fields there is rice that has already set grain.
Having split open the rice sheaves and taken them, have them cooked in a manner suitable for the Buddhas. Thus...
"If this is done, it will be of no benefit to anyone; therefore, I do not approve of this.

"If you do not do it, I shall be allowed to treat my own property as my own," he said, and having divided the field measuring sixteen *karīsas* down the middle and established a boundary at the eight-*karīsa* point, he split open a rice pod and took [the grain] while the field was still undivided.
Having had milk-rice cooked and having added the four sweet substances, he gave it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
Whenever the householder’s womb was opened, the place from which [the rice] was taken would fill up again. At the time of threshing, he gave the best of the threshed grain;
together with the village dwellers, he gave the first-fruits of the crop; at the time of reaping, the best of the reaped; at the time of binding into bundles, the best of the bound.
Among the sheaves and so forth, he gave the best sheaf, the best from the threshing floor, the best from the grain heap, and the best from the granary.
In this way, he gave the first-fruits offering nine times for that single crop. Yet even that crop was abundant and yielded a surplus.
Having performed such meritorious deeds according to this very method, as long as the Buddha endures and as long as the Saṅgha endures—
Passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the devas, and wandering through successive births among both devas and humans, he experienced prosperity for ninety-one aeons.
Then, at the time when our Teacher appeared in the world, he was born into a family of great brahmin householders in the brahmin village of Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu.
On the day of his naming ceremony, he was given the name Koṇḍañña the youth.
They gave him a name. As he grew up, he mastered the three Vedas and reached the further shore of the science of omens and mantras.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having descended from the Tusita heaven, was reborn in the city of Kapilavatthu.
On the day of his naming ceremony, one hundred and eight brahmins were clothed in new garments and served a meal of milk-rice with little water and honey.
Having had them fed, they selected eight men from among them, seated them upon a high platform, and having laid the Bodhisatta—
adorned and arrayed in his finery— upon a pillow of fine linen, they brought him into their presence for the purpose of examining his marks.
The brahmin seated on the seat of honor, having observed the excellence of the Great Man’s physical form, [raised] two fingers...
He raised one finger. In this manner, seven people raised their fingers in succession. Among them, however, the youngest was the young brahmin Koṇḍañña;
having observed the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s marks, he thought, "There is no reason for him to remain in the midst of a household;
he will certainly be one whose veil is rent asunder and become a Buddha," and thus he raised only a single finger. As for the others, however—
The seven persons, seeing two possible destinies—that "if he dwells at home, he will become a universal monarch (cakkavatti) king; if he goes forth, he will become a Buddha"—raised two fingers.
But this Koṇḍañña, a being in his final existence who had performed his duties and surpassed the other seven in wisdom, [considered] these marks...
"For one endowed with such qualities, there is no remaining in the midst of a household; he will undoubtedly become a Buddha.
Thus he saw only one possible destiny, and therefore he raised a single finger. Then the brahmins, having gone to their own homes, addressed their sons:
"Dear ones, we are old; [we shall go to see] the son of King Suddhodana who has attained omniscience."
“Whether we believe it or not, when that prince has attained omniscience, you should go forth into his dispensation.
And Great King Suddhodana, beginning with the Bodhisatta’s nurses, provided him with all necessary care and caused the Bodhisatta to grow.
When the Great Being had reached maturity and, like a god, experienced the fullness of prosperity, [his faculties] became fully ripened.

Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation through his knowledge, on the very day Prince Rāhula was born, accompanied by Channa, he mounted Kaṇḍaka and, with the gates opened by deities, made the Great Renunciation.
During that same night, having crossed three kingdoms, he went forth on the bank of the Anomā River; there, the great brahmin Ghaṭīkāra brought him the banner of an arahant.
As soon as he had set out, like an elder of sixty years, he reached Rājagaha with a graceful deportment;

there, having walked for alms and eaten his meal in the shade of Paṇḍava Mountain, he declined the invitation of the Magadhan king to share the glory of sovereignty, and eventually proceeded to Uruvelā, [thinking]: "It is delightful..."
"Ah, this spot of earth is indeed fit for a son of noble family who seeks to strive in spiritual exertion!
Having thus resolved his mind toward striving, he took up residence there.
At that time, the other seven brahmins had departed according to their karma; however, the youngest of all was the one who had examined the marks.
The young brahmin Koṇḍañña was healthy. Having heard that "the Great Man has gone forth," he approached the sons of those brahmins and said this:
"It is said that Prince Siddhattha has gone forth. For he will undoubtedly become a Buddha.
If your fathers were healthy, they would have gone forth today after departing from home. If you also desire it—"
"Come, let us go forth following that Great Being. However, they were not all able to become of one mind.
Three persons did not go forth; with the brahmin Koṇḍañña as their leader, the other four went forth.
Having gone forth, these five, wandering for alms among villages, market towns, and royal capitals, came into the presence of the Bodhisatta.
They arrived. For six years, while the Bodhisatta was exerting himself in the Great Struggle, they attended upon the Mahāsatta, thinking, "Now he will become a Buddha;
now he will become a Buddha," and remained in his immediate presence.

But when the Bodhisatta, even though spending his time on only a single sesame seed, grain of rice, and so forth, failed to achieve penetration into the Noble Dhamma through his practice of austerities—
Having understood that [the food] was non-existent, he took coarse food; at that time, they departed and went to Isipatana.

Then the Bodhisatta, having restored his skin, flesh, and blood through the consumption of coarse food, ate the excellent meal given by Sujātā on the day of the full moon of Visākha, and having cast the golden bowl against the current of the river, [thought]: "Today..."
Having made the firm resolve, "I shall become a Buddha," at the time of evening, while being praised with hundreds of eulogies by the Naga king Kāla,
he ascended the Great Seat of Enlightenment (Mahābodhimaṇḍa). Seated cross-legged in an immovable position, facing the eastern direction of the world-system,
and having resolved upon energy endowed with four factors, even while the sun was still shining, he [confronted] the army of Māra.
Having dispelled [obscurations] during the first watch of the night by recollecting his former births, and having purified his divine eye during the middle watch,
he applied his knowledge to dependent origination at the time of dawn. While contemplating the cycle of the modes of conditions in forward and reverse order,
he penetrated the uncommon omniscient knowledge realized by all Buddhas, and [directed it] toward Nibbāna as its object.
He spent seven days right there in the attainment of the fruit.
By this same method, having dwelt at the seat of enlightenment for seven times seven days, he partook of the honey-morsel meal at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree;
then, returning again to the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree and sitting there, he [reflected upon] the profundity of the Dhamma.

Having reflected thus, his mind inclined toward indolence; being then entreated by Mahābrahmā, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings distinguished by sharp faculties and other qualities.
Having given his promise to Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma, he considered, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma? and, knowing that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away, [he proceeded further].
Again, reflecting thus: "The group-of-five monks have been very helpful to me, for they attended upon me when I was intent on striving.
What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the group-of-five monks?"—he gave rise to this thought.
However, all of this was merely a reflection of the Buddhas; setting that aside, however...
There was no one else capable of penetrating the Dhamma before Koṇḍañña the brahmin.

He too had performed meritorious service for this very purpose during a hundred thousand eons, having offered the first-fruits of his harvest nine times to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Then the Teacher, taking his bowl and robe, traveled by stages to Isipatana and approached where the group of five monks was.
Upon seeing the Tathāgata approaching, they were unable to maintain their agreement.
One received his bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing his feet.
One was washing his feet, while the other stood fanning him with a palm-leaf fan.

Having thus shown them their proper duties as they sat nearby, the Teacher, making the Elder Koṇḍañña his personal witness, began the Discourse on Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dhamma, the unsurpassed three-turning cycle.
There were only five persons in the assembly of humans; as for the assembly of devas—
It was boundless. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Koṇḍañña, together with eighteen koṭis of great Brahmās, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then the Teacher, addressing the Elder while saying, "He has understood the Dhamma that I have brought through hundreds of hardships;
therefore, he is named Aññā-Koṇḍañña (Koṇḍañña who has understood)," said: "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!"
"Koṇḍañña has indeed understood! he said. That very name was given to him. Therefore it is said:
"Thus, this was the name of the Venerable Koṇḍañña—Aññātakondañña (Koṇḍañña who has understood).
Thus the Elder was established in the fruit of stream-entry on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight, Bhaddiya Thera [was established].
On the second day of the fortnight, Elder Vappa; on the third day of the fortnight, Elder Mahānāma;

and on the fourth day of the fortnight, Elder Assaji were established in the fruit of stream-entry. But on the fifth day of the fortnight, at the conclusion of the teaching of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, all of them were established in Arhatship.
Now at that time, there were six Arhats in the world. From then on, the Teacher— having established the great multitude of people,
including fifty-five men headed by the youth Yasa, about thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group in the Kappāsika forest grove,
and one thousand former matted-hair ascetics on the Piṭṭhipāsāṇa rock at Gayāsīsa— on the path of the Noble Ones, [led] those headed by Bimbisāra...
Having established eleven nahutas of beings in the fruit of stream-entry and one nahuta in the three refuges,
and having caused the teaching to flourish and bear fruit upon the surface of Jambudīpa, making the entire circle of Jambudīpa radiant with the saffron robes and fragrant with the scent of the seers,
he at one time arrived at the great monastery of Jetavana; dwelling there in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
Seated upon the excellent Buddha-throne that had been prepared, while teaching the Dhamma, he placed Koṇḍañña in the foremost position among those monks who had first realized the Dhamma,
in order to show that "among my sons, Koṇḍañña is the most eminent. The Elder,
seeing the two chief disciples performing such acts of veneration toward him, did not wish to depart from the presence of the Buddhas.
Having made the offering and seeing that "the young man Puṇṇa, having gone forth, will become the foremost preacher of the Dhamma in the Dispensation," he went to the brahmin village of Doṇavatthu.
There, he ordained his own nephew, the young man Puṇṇa, and thinking, "This one shall dwell in the presence of the Buddhas," he established him as a resident disciple of the Buddhas.
Then, he himself approached the One of Ten Powers and said, "Blessed One, for me..."
“The village dwelling is unsuitable; I am unable to live amidst such crowds. I shall go to the Chaddanta Lake and dwell there.
Having thus obtained the Blessed One’s permission, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Teacher, and went to the Chaddanta Lake.
There, living in dependence upon the Chaddanta elephant herd, he spent twelve years and attained final Nibbāna right there in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The Story of the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna (189–190).

Regarding the second and third [verses], "of those possessed of great wisdom" means of those endowed with vast insight (*mahāpaññā*). "Of those possessing psychic power" means of those perfected in supernormal powers (*iddhi*). Sāriputta and Moggallāna are the names of those two elders.

As for the sequence of events concerning their answering of questions, this is the traditional account: more than a hundred thousand aeons ago, at the end of an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*)—
Sāriputta was reborn in a family of great brahmin landowners; by name he was known as the young brahmin Sarada.
Moggallāna was reborn in a family of great householders; by name he was known as Sirivaḍḍhana the householder.
Both of them were childhood friends, having played together in the dust. After his father passed away, the young brahmin Sarada [inherited] the great wealth belonging to the family.
Having practiced [the household life], one day, having gone into seclusion, he thought:
"I know only the existence of this world, but not the existence of the world beyond; and for beings who are born, death is indeed certain.
It is fitting that I go forth into homelessness and seek the Dhamma of liberation. He approached his friend and said: "Friend Sirivaḍḍhana..."
“Having gone forth, I shall seek the Dhamma of liberation; will you be able to go forth with me?
“I will not be able, my friend; you alone go forth. He reflected: “There are no such things as companions or kinsmen who go along when one departs for the next world;
what one has done belongs to oneself alone. Then [he went to] the storehouse of treasures...

Having caused [the city] to be cleared out and having given a great alms-giving to the poor, the destitute, the travelers, and the beggars, he entered the foothills of the mountain and went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Following him, one, two, then three, and so on, seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*) went forth in succession.
Having realized the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), he [taught them] to those matted-hair ascetics as well.
He explained the preliminary practice of the *kasiṇa* spheres. They all likewise developed the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*).
At that time, a Buddha named Anomadassī appeared in the world. His city was named Candavatī;
his father was the kshatriya Yasavanta, his mother was Queen Yasodharā, his Bodhi tree was the *ajjuna* tree, and his chief elder was Nisabha.
There were two chief disciples, namely the Elder Anoma and the Elder [Anuruddha]; the attendant was the Elder named Varuṇa;
there were two chief female disciples, Sundarī and Sumanā; his lifespan was one hundred thousand years; his body was fifty-eight cubits in height;
the radiance of his body pervaded twelve yojanas; and he had a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
Then one day, at the time of dawn, having emerged from the attainment of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-samāpatti*) and surveying the world, he saw the ascetic Sarada and thought:
"Today, by reason of my going into the presence of the ascetic Sarada, there will be a great teaching of the Dhamma;
he will aspire to the position of chief disciple, and his companion, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana..."
"Since this is the occasion for the second disciple, and at the conclusion of the teaching his retinue of seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics will attain arahantship,
it is fitting for me to go there. Taking his own bowl and robe, and without informing anyone else,
he went alone like a lion to where the disciples of the ascetic Sarada were gathering fruits.
At the gates, while the ascetic Sarada was looking on, [the Bodhisatta] descended from the sky and stood upon the earth, saying, "May he know my state as a Buddha.
Seeing both the majesty of a Buddha and the perfection of his physical form, the ascetic Sarada contemplated the manual of marks and thought:
"One endowed with these marks, if living in the midst of a household, would be a king..."
"Either he will become a Wheel-turning Monarch, or, going forth from the world, he will become an omniscient Buddha who has removed the veil [of ignorance].
This man is undoubtedly a Buddha. Having realized this, he went out to meet him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, prepared a seat, and offered it to him.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. The ascetic Sarada also [prepared] what was suitable for himself...
Having taken a seat, he sat down to one side.
At that time, seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics, having taken very choice and nutritious fruits, arrived in the presence of their teacher;
they looked at the seats where both the Buddhas and their teacher were sitting and said:
“Teacher, we used to wander about thinking, ‘There is no one in this world greater than you,’ yet this man seems to us to be greater than you.
“My dear ones, what are you saying? Do you wish to make Mount Sineru, which rises six million eight hundred thousand yojanas high, equal in height to a mustard seed?
Do not attempt to draw a comparison between me and an omniscient Buddha.”
"Little sons. Then those ascetics said, "If this were a lowly being, our teacher would not have brought such a simile;
how great indeed is this man! And they all fell at his feet and paid homage with their heads.
Then the teacher said to them, "Dear ones, we have no gift worthy of the Buddhas; the Teacher..."
"And when you have come here at the time for alms-round, we shall give you whatever gifts we can afford.
Bring whatever choice fruits there are. Having had them brought, he washed his hands and personally placed them in the Tathāgata’s bowl.
As soon as the Teacher had accepted the fruits, the deities added divine essence to them.
The ascetic even strained the water himself before giving it to him.
Then, when the Teacher had finished his meal, washed his hands, and was seated, he summoned all his resident pupils and sat down near the Teacher, engaging in a friendly conversation.
The Teacher thought, "Let the two chief disciples come with the community of monks."
Having understood the Teacher’s intention, those [devas] accompanied by a retinue of one hundred thousand who had destroyed the taints arrived, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood to one side.
Then the ascetic Sarada addressed his pupils: “Sirs, even the seats for the Buddhas are low; there is not even a seat for the hundred thousand recluses.
It is fitting that you perform a magnificent honor to the Buddha today. From the foot of the mountain, [bring] flowers endowed with color and fragrance...”
"Bring flowers! Although the time for conversation seemed like a protracted delay, the domain of those possessing psychic power is inconceivable;

thus, in just a moment, those ascetics brought back flowers endowed with exquisite color and fragrance and prepared a flower-seat one *yojana* in extent for the Buddhas, three-quarters of a *yojana* for the two Chief Disciples, and various sizes such as half a *yojana* for the rest of the monks.
For the newest member of the Saṅgha, it was sufficient for an ox. When the seats had been thus prepared,
the ascetic Sarada stood before the Tathāgata with his hands joined in reverential salutation and said, "Venerable Sir, for the sake of my long-term welfare and happiness,
please ascend this flower-seat."
“Having gathered various flowers and perfumes together,
and having prepared a seat of flowers, I spoke these words:
‘O Hero, here is a seat prepared for you, worthy of you.’”
“Seating yourself upon the flower-throne, please gladden my heart.
“For seven days and nights the Buddha sat upon the flower-throne,
gladdening my heart and bringing joy to the world with its devas.”
When the Teacher had thus seated himself, the two chief disciples and the remaining bhikkhus sat down each on his own assigned seat.
The ascetic Sarada stood holding a large flower-parasol over the head of the Tathāgata.
The Teacher, thinking, "May this honor shown to the matted-hair ascetics bear great fruit," entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Knowing that the Teacher had entered into meditative attainment, the two chief disciples and the rest of the monks also entered into attainment.
While the Tathāgata remained seated for seven days in the attainment of cessation, when the time for alms-round arrived, the resident monks partook of forest roots and fruits;
at all other times, they stood with palms joined in reverence toward the Buddhas.
But the ascetic Sarada, without even going out for alms, spent seven days in joy and happiness, following the very manner of one who holds a flower-parasol.
The Teacher, emerging from cessation, addressed the Elder Nisabha, his chief disciple, who was seated on his right side.
“Nisabha, offer words of appreciation for the flower-seats provided by the ascetics who show such honor.

The Elder, his mind filled with joy like a great warrior who has received a magnificent reward from a wheel-turning monarch, stood upon the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple and began the expression of appreciation for the flower-seats.
At the conclusion of his discourse, he addressed the second disciple: “You too, teach the Dhamma. Thus spoke the Elder Anoma.
Having reflected upon the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Piṭakas, he preached the Dhamma. Yet, despite the teaching given to the two disciples, not even one of them attained realization.
Then the Teacher, standing upon the immeasurable domain of a Buddha, began his discourse on the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, with the exception of the ascetic Sarada, all seventy-four thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahatship.
They arrived. The Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks.
At that very moment, their hair and beards vanished, and the eight requisites appeared already fastened upon their bodies.
Why did the ascetic Sarada not attain Arahatship? Because his mind was distracted. It is said that, regarding the Buddhas...

Having sat on the second seat and stood upon the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*), from the moment he began to listen to the teaching of the Chief Disciple as the latter was preaching the Dhamma, the thought arose in him:
"Oh, may I too, in the dispensation of the Buddha who will arise in the future, obtain the very same office of a disciple that this one has obtained! With that reflection, he...
He was unable to attain penetration of the path and its fruits. However, having paid homage to the Tathāgata and standing before him, he asked:
"Venerable Sir, who is that bhikkhu sitting on the seat immediately behind you; what is his name in your dispensation? [The Buddha replied:
"He is one who has set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma following my own turning of it, and who has reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple. Sixteen...
“Having penetrated through with wisdom and standing firm in my teaching, this one named the Elder Nisabha is my chief disciple.
“Venerable Sir, as for the honor I performed by holding a flower-parasol for seven days, I do not, by the fruit of this, aspire to any other sovereignty or the state of a Brahmā;
rather, in the future, may I be like this Elder Nisabha.”
He made this aspiration: "May I become the chief disciple of a single Buddha.
The Teacher, wondering, "Will this man's aspiration be fulfilled?
sent forth his knowledge of the future and, looking into it, saw that it would be fulfilled after the passing of an incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand aeons.
Having seen the ascetic Sarada, he said: "This aspiration of yours shall not be in vain.
However, after the passing of an incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand kalpas, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world.
His mother will be the queen named Mahāmāyā, his father King Suddhodana, his son Rāhula, and his attendant Ānanda."
“...named Moggallāna will be his second disciple; you, however, shall be his chief disciple, the General of the Dhamma named Sāriputta.
Having thus prophesied for the ascetic and delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, he leaped into the air, surrounded by the community of monks.
The ascetic Sarada also went into the presence of the elder disciples and [informed] his friend, the householder Sirivaḍḍhana.
He sent a message: "Venerable sirs, tell my friend:
'Your friend, the ascetic Sarada, has made a wish at the feet of the Buddha Anomadassi for the position of chief disciple in the dispensation of the future Buddha Gotama;
you, therefore, should aspire to the position of second disciple. Having spoken thus, even before the elders had departed, he—
Having gone along one side, he stood at the door of Sirivaḍḍha’s residence.
Sirivaḍḍha, thinking, "Ah, it has been a long time since my noble master arrived," had him seated on a seat and sat down himself on a lower seat.
He then asked, "Venerable sir, your assembly of disciples is not to be seen. "Yes, friend, our hermitage—"
"A Buddha named Anomadassī came; we paid him honor according to our own means.
The Teacher taught the Dhamma to all of us, and at the conclusion of that teaching, with the exception of myself, the rest attained arahantship and went forth.
Why did you not go forth? [He replied: "When I saw the Teacher’s chief disciple, the Elder Nisabha, in the future..."
"I aspired to the position of chief disciple in the teaching of the Buddha named Gotama who is about to arise;
you too should aspire to the position of second disciple in his teaching. "Venerable sir, I have no acquaintance with the Buddhas.
"Let the conversation with the Buddhas be my responsibility; you prepare for the great office."
Having heard the words of the ascetic Sarada, Sirivaḍḍhana had a space measuring eight *karīsa* in extent made level at the gate of his residence according to royal measurement;
he had it strewn with sand, scattered flowers with parched grain as the fifth element, and erected a pavilion with a canopy of blue lotuses.
He then prepared a seat for the Buddha and had seats arranged for the remaining bhikkhus, and [prepared] a great...
Having prepared honors and hospitality, he gave notice to the ascetic Sarada for the purpose of inviting the Buddhas.
Upon hearing his words, the ascetic took the community of monks headed by the Buddha and went to his residence.
Sirivaḍḍhana went out to meet him, took the bowl from the hands of the Tathāgata, and [led him] to the pavilion.

Having had [the hall] entered and having given the water of hospitality (*dakṣiṇodaka*) to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha as they sat upon the prepared seats, he served them with exquisite food;

at the conclusion of the meal, he clothed the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha in costly robes and said, "Venerable Sir, this undertaking is not for the sake of a minor matter; by this very [act]..."
“Please show compassion for seven days according to this fixed schedule,” he said. The Teacher consented.
Having offered a great almsgiving for seven days according to that very schedule, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood with palms joined, saying:
“Venerable Sir, my friend, the ascetic Sarada, aspired to become the foremost disciple of whichever Teacher I might serve; I too—”
“I shall become his very second disciple.
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied:
“After passing beyond an incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand kalpas, you will become the second disciple of Gotama Buddha.”
“You shall become [a Buddha],” he said. Having heard the Buddhas’ prophecy, Sirivaḍḍhana was overjoyed.
The Teacher, having delivered his expression of gratitude after the meal, returned to the monastery together with his retinue.

From that time forth, Sirivaḍḍhana performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life and was reborn in the world of the sense-sphere devas during the second aeon. As for the ascetic Sarada, he—four...
Having cultivated the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
From that point onward, no account of any intervening events for either of these two is told.
However, even before our Buddha was born, the ascetic Sarada, in the village of Upatissa not far from the city of Rājagaha, [was born] to the Brahmin woman Sārī.
He took rebirth in a womb. On that very same day, his friend also took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin woman Moggallī in the village of Kolita, not far from Rājagaha.
It is said that those two families had been close and inseparable friends for seven successive generations. For both of them, on one and the same day—
They provided protection for their pregnancy. When ten months had passed, sixty-six nurses attended to them once they were born.
On the day of the naming ceremony, because the son of the Brahmin woman Sārī was the son of the eldest family in Upatissa Village, they gave him the name Upatissa;
because the other was the son of the eldest family in Kolita Village, they gave him the name Kolita. They...
Both of them, having attained maturity, reached the further shore of all arts.
Whenever the young man Upatissa went to the river, the park, or the mountain for the sake of recreation, he was accompanied by five hundred golden palanquins;
the young man Kolita had five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses. Both men were attended by retinues of five hundred young men each.
In Rājagaha, there was an annual festival called the Giraggasamajja; for both of them, they prepared a single couch in one and the same place.
Both men sat together on that very spot, watching the festival:

they laughed at places where laughter was appropriate, were moved by emotion at places where emotion was appropriate, and gave gifts at places where it was fitting to give gifts. For them, by this very means—

Because their knowledge had reached maturity, on that one day when they were watching the festival according to custom, there was no laughter where they would have laughed as on previous days, nor any agitation where they would have been agitated, nor any giving of gifts where it would have been appropriate to give gifts.
However, both men thought thus: "What is there here to look at? All these people..."
“Before even a hundred years have passed, they will fall into a state of non-existence. Therefore, it is fitting for us to seek the Dhamma of liberation.
Having taken this as their objective, they sat down.
Then Kolita said to Upatissa: “Friend Upatissa, you are not as joyful and exultant as on other days.”
“Kolita, you are displeased; what have you observed? “Venerable Sir, I am sitting here thinking:
‘In looking at these things there is no essence; this is useless. It is fitting to seek the Dhamma of liberation for oneself.
But why are you displeased? He replied in the same manner. Then [the Buddha], seeing that he shared the same aspiration as himself—
Having understood this, Upatissa said to him: "The thought of both of us is the same;
however, as we seek the Dhamma of liberation, it is fitting that we both go forth into homelessness. In whose presence shall we go forth?
Now at that time, the wanderer Sañjaya was residing at Rājagaha with a large assembly of wanderers.
Together. Thinking, "We shall go forth in his presence," they went forth in the presence of Sañcaya along with five hundred young brahmins.
From the time they had gone forth, Sañcaya attained an abundance of extra gains and the highest excellence.
Within just a few days, they mastered the entire system of Sañcaya and said, "Teacher, yours..."
They asked, "Is the time for knowing only this much, or is there something further? Sañjaya replied, "It is only this much; you have understood everything. Having heard his words, they reflected:
"If this is so, living the holy life (brahmacariya) in his presence is useless. We went forth seeking the Dhamma of liberation, yet he [possesses] only this."
"It is impossible to produce [such a person]. But Jambudīpa is vast;
as we travel through its villages, market towns, and royal capitals, we will certainly find a single teacher who teaches the Dhamma of liberation.
From then on, wherever they heard that there were wise recluses or brahmins, they went there and engaged them in discussion on questions.
They did so. When they were questioned, there was no one else capable of answering those questions, yet they themselves provided the answers.
Having thus traversed the whole of Jambudīpa and returned to their own place, they made an agreement, saying:
"Friend Kolita, whoever first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other."
At that time, our Teacher, having attained his first full enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma,
eventually arrived at Rājagaha. Then, at the time when it was said, "Sixty-one Arahants have appeared in the world," he dispatched them—
saying, "Go forth, monks, on tour for the welfare of many people"— for the purpose of proclaiming the virtues of the Triple Gem.
Among the monks, the Elder Assaji, who was one of the group of five, turned back and returned to Rājagaha itself.
On the following day at dawn, taking his bowl and robe, he entered Rājagaha for alms.
At that time, the wanderer Upatissa, having finished his morning meal, was on his way to the wanderers’ park.
Seeing the elder, he thought: "I have never before seen such a renunciant.
Surely this is one of those monks in the world who are either Arahants or have entered the path to Arahantship;
what if I were to approach this monk and ask him a question: 'Friend, on whose account have you gone forth?'"
“Who is your teacher, or whose Dhamma do you approve of? Then it occurred to him:
“It is not the right time to ask this bhikkhu about his question; he has entered among the houses and is walking for alms.
Suppose I were to follow closely behind this bhikkhu along the path frequented by those seeking [alms]. He followed the elder...
Seeing him going toward a certain place after receiving alms-food, and perceiving his desire to sit down, he prepared and gave him his own recluse’s seat.
At the conclusion of the elder’s meal, he also gave him water from his own water-pot.
Having thus performed the duties of a pupil, and having exchanged pleasant greetings with the elder who had finished his meal, he said:
“Friend, your faculties are serene, your complexion is pure and bright.
Under whom, friend, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess? Thus he asked. The Elder replied:
“Friend, there is a Great Ascetic, a son of the Sakyans who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan; it is under that Blessed One that I have gone forth.”
“I have gone forth, and that Blessed One is my Teacher; it is the Dhamma of that very Blessed One that I find pleasing,” he said.
Then [the wanderer] asked him, “But what does your venerable teacher profess? What does he declare?
The Elder thought, “These wanderers are indeed opponents of the Teaching; I shall demonstrate the profundity of this Teaching. Regarding himself—
Showing his state as a novice, he said: "Friends, I am new, having recently gone forth;
I have only just come to this Dhamma and Vinaya, so I am not yet able to teach the Dhamma in detail.
The wanderer replied: "I am named Upatissa. Speak as much or as little as you are able; by means of a hundred or a thousand methods..."
Thinking, "It is my burden to penetrate this," he said:
"Whether you speak little or much, tell me only the meaning;
I have need only of the meaning—what will you do with many words?"
When this was said, the Elder recited the verse: "Of those phenomena that arise from a cause...

Having heard only the first two lines, the wanderer was established in the path of stream-entry, which possesses a thousandfold method; the remaining two lines were completed at the moment he became a stream-enterer.
Having become a stream-enterer, and observing that no further higher distinctions were arising, he reflected: "There must be a reason for this."
He said to the Elder, "Venerable sir, do not increase the teaching of the Dhamma further; let it remain just this much. Where does our Teacher dwell?
"In the Veḷuvana grove, O wanderers. "Venerable sir, you go on ahead. I have a companion.
We have made a mutual agreement: 'Whichever of us first attains the Deathless..."
“Let him announce it. Having released that promise, I will take my companion and return to the presence of the Teacher by the very path you have taken.

Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself at the elder’s feet with the fivefold salutation, circumambulated the elder three times, and after dismissing the elder, set out toward the park of the wanderers.
When the wanderer Koliya saw him approaching from afar, he thought, "Today my friend's facial expression is not like it was on other days;
surely he must have attained the Deathless. He therefore asked about his attainment of the Deathless.
The other acknowledged to him, "Yes, friend, I have attained the Deathless," and recited that very same verse.
At the conclusion of the verses, Kolita established himself in the fruit of stream-entry and asked, "Friend, where does the Teacher dwell?
"Friend, it is said he dwells in the Veḷuvana," replied his teacher, the Elder Assaji.
"In that case, friend, let us go; we shall see the Teacher. Indeed, this Elder Sāriputta was always devoted to honoring his teacher.
Therefore, he said this to his companion, the young man Kolita: "Friend, we shall tell our teacher, the wanderer Sañjaya, of the Deathless we have attained.

If he understands, he will penetrate it; if he does not penetrate it, he will believe us and go into the presence of the Teacher. Having heard the teaching of the Buddhas, he will achieve penetration of the path and its fruits."
Then the two men went to Sañcaya and said, "Teacher, what are you doing?
A Buddha has appeared in the world; the Dhamma is well-proclaimed; the Saṅgha is practicing the good path. Come, let us go see the One of Ten Powers.
He replied, "What are you saying, dear ones? and having restrained them, he extolled to them only the attainment of the highest gain and the highest fame. They said, "For us..."
"May such a life as a resident pupil be yours forever; however, you must decide for yourselves whether to go or not," they said.
Sañcaya, realizing that "these men, knowing so much, will not do as I say," replied, "Go, dear ones;
in my old age, I am no longer able to live the life of a resident pupil. They, by many...
Being unable to awaken him by means of various reasons, they took with them those people who were following their own advice and went to Veḷuvana.
Then, of their five hundred pupils, two hundred and fifty turned back, while two hundred and fifty went along with them.
As the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly, he saw them from afar and addressed the bhikkhus: "These..."
“Monks, two companions are coming—Kolita and Upatissa. They shall become my foremost pair of disciples, a blessed pair.
Then he expanded his teaching of the Dhamma according to the temperaments of that assembly.
With the exception of the two chief disciples, all those two hundred and fifty wanderers attained arahantship. The Teacher—
“Come, monks,” he said, and extended his hand. The hair and beards of them all vanished, and miraculous bowls and robes appeared, fastened to their bodies.
Even for the two chief disciples, miraculous bowls and robes appeared; however, the task of the three higher paths was not yet completed.
Why? Because of the greatness of the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple.

Then, on the seventh day after his ordination, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was practicing the duties of a recluse near the village of Kallavāla in the kingdom of Magadha, he was overcome by sloth and torpor. Being stirred by the Teacher, he dispelled that sloth and torpor;
and while listening to the meditation subject on the elements bestowed by the Tathāgata, he brought the task of the three higher paths to completion.

He reached the pinnacle of the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections. The Elder Sāriputta, too, having passed half a month from the day of his own going forth, was dwelling together with the Teacher near that same Rājagaha in the Sūkarakhata Cave;
while the Discourse on the Comprehension of Feelings was being taught to his own nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha—
By directing his knowledge according to the Suttas, he reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection of knowledge (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*), like one eating a meal prepared by another.
At the conclusion of the teaching, his nephew was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Thus, while the Tathāgata was dwelling in Rājagaha, both great disciples brought their task regarding the disciple’s perfection of knowledge to its ultimate consummation.
The Bowl. Later on, however, while residing at Jetavana, the Teacher established both great disciples in their respective positions, saying: "Among those of great wisdom, this is Sāriputta;
among those possessed of supernormal powers, this is Mahāmoggallāna. Thus ends the story of the Elder Mahākassapa.
191. Regarding the phrase "of those who speak on the ascetic practices" (*dhutavādānaṃ*) in the fourth [section]:

here, one should understand the ascetic (dhuta), one should understand the speaker of the ascetic (dhutavāda), one should understand the ascetic qualities (dhutadhamma), and one should understand the ascetic factors (dhutaṅga). In this context, "ascetic" (*dhuta*) refers either to a person whose defilements have been shaken off, or to the Dhamma that shakes off defilements.
As for the "speaker of the ascetic" (*dhutavāda*), there is one who is ascetic but not a speaker of the ascetic; there is one who is not ascetic but a speaker of the ascetic; there is...
There is one who is neither *dhuta* nor a proponent of the *dhuta* qualities; and there is one who is both *dhuta* and a proponent of the *dhuta* qualities.

In this regard, he who has shaken off his own defilements by means of the *dhuta* qualities, yet does not exhort or instruct others in the *dhuta* qualities—like the Elder Bākula—is *dhuta* but not a proponent of the *dhuta* qualities.
As it is said: "Thus, the venerable Bākula was *dhuta* but not a proponent of the *dhuta* qualities. But he who...

One who does not shake off his own defilements by means of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), but merely advises and instructs others in them—like the Elder Upananda—is "not ascetic, though a proclaimer of asceticism.
As it is said: "Thus this venerable Upananda was not ascetic, though a proclaimer of asceticism.
But one who has failed in both [the practice and the proclamation], like Lāḷudāyī, is "neither ascetic nor a proclaimer of asceticism. As it is said: "Thus this..."

“Venerable Lāḷudāyī is neither ascetic nor one who speaks in praise of asceticism. But he who is accomplished in both, such as the Elder Mahākassapa, is both an ascetic and one who speaks in praise of asceticism.
As it is said: “In this regard, the Venerable Mahākassapa is both an ascetic and one who speaks in praise of asceticism.
The ascetic qualities (dhutadhammā) should be understood as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, and the state of being free from worldly affairs.

These five qualities, which are the attendants of the volition for the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), are called "ascetic qualities" (*dhutadhamma*) because of such statements as, "relying on fewness of wishes alone.
Among them, fewness of wishes and contentment fall under non-greed (*alobha*); while effacement and seclusion fall under two qualities, namely non-greed and non-delusion (*amoha*).
Here, steadfastness is simply knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Therein, by means of non-greed, regarding the things to be rejected...

Through non-delusion, one shakes off greed and the delusion that conceals the dangers inherent in those very things. Through non-greed, one shakes off devotion to the pleasure of sense desires, which occurs by way of indulging in permitted things;
and through non-delusion, one shakes off devotion to self-mortification, which occurs by way of excessive austerity in the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas).
Therefore, these states should be understood as "ascetic qualities" (dhutadhammas).

"The ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) should be understood" means that the thirteen ascetic practices should be understood, beginning with the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice (*paṃsukūlikaṅga*) and ending with the sitter’s practice (*nesajjikaṅga*).

Regarding "of those who speak of the ascetic life, this one is Mahākassapa," he placed the Elder Mahākassapa in the foremost position, meaning that among all those who profess the ascetic life, this Elder Mahākassapa is the chief. As for "Mahākassapa," there are Uruvelakassapa and Nadīkassapa.
Gayākassapa and Kumārakassapa—compared to these minor elders, this one was great; therefore, he is called Mahākassapa.
Regarding his life story, this is the sequential account: it is said that in the past, at the end of a hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
While he was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park near the city of Haṃsavatī...

There was a householder named Vedeha, possessing a wealth of eight hundred million, who, having eaten a fine meal early in the morning, resolved upon the precepts of the Uposatha, took perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, went to the monastery, honored and paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.
At that moment, the Teacher [addressed] the third disciple, the Elder Mahānisabha: "Bhikkhus, this is the foremost..."
“Among my disciples, the bhikkhus who advocate the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), this one, namely Nisabha, is the foremost,” thus the Teacher placed him at the head of that list.

Having heard this, the lay follower was filled with faith; when the great assembly had risen and departed at the conclusion of the Dhamma talk, he paid homage to the Teacher and said, “Venerable sir, please accept my almsfood tomorrow. “The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is large, lay follower. “How large?”
"Lord, there are six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus. "Venerable sir, please accept the almsfood without leaving even a single novice behind in the monastery.

The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Knowing that the Teacher had consented, the lay follower went home, prepared a great offering, and on the following day, announced the time for the Teacher's arrival. The Teacher—
Taking his bowl and robe and surrounded by the community of monks, he went to the house of the lay follower and sat on the prepared seat.
At the conclusion of the water for the guest-offering, while receiving the rice-gruel and other foods, he performed the distribution of the meal. The lay follower also sat down near the Teacher.
In the meantime, the Elder Mahānisabha, wandering for alms, entered that very same street. Upon seeing him, the lay follower—
Having risen and gone to him, he paid homage to the Elder and said, "Venerable sir, please give me your bowl.
The Elder gave him his bowl. "Venerable sir, please enter right here; the Teacher is sitting at home as well. "It will not be appropriate, lay follower," [the Elder replied].
The lay follower took the Elder's bowl, filled it with almsfood, brought it out, and gave it to him. Then, having followed after the Elder—

Having returned and sat down in the presence of the Teacher, he said: “Venerable Sir, when it was said that the Teacher was sitting in the house, the Elder Mahānisabha did not wish to enter even then; is there perhaps some quality in him that surpasses your own qualities?
Now, Buddhas have no such thing as stinginess regarding their own virtues. Then the Teacher spoke thus: “Upāsaka,…”
"We sit at home waiting for alms, but that bhikkhu does not sit thus waiting for alms.
We dwell in lodgings within the village, but he dwells only in the forest. We dwell under cover, but he dwells only in the open air.
Thus he spoke, as if filling the great ocean, "Such are his virtues and such are his qualities," said the lay follower.
By his very nature, like a lamp already burning that is drenched with oil, he became even more serene and thought:

"What is the use of other attainments for me? In the future, in the presence of a certain Buddha, I shall make a resolution to become the foremost among those who preach the ascetic practices (dhuta)."

Then, having again invited the Teacher and given a great almsgiving for seven days according to that same method, on the seventh day he presented the three robes to the Great Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Prostrating himself at the feet of the Teacher, he spoke thus:

"Venerable Sir, whatever bodily action of loving-kindness, whatever verbal action of loving-kindness, and whatever mental action of loving-kindness I have performed while giving alms for these seven days—"
“May my verbal action and mental action be established in loving-kindness; by this, I do not aspire to any other heavenly success, whether as a Sakka, a Māra, or a Brahmā.

Rather, may this action of mine be a solemn declaration for the sake of attaining, in the future, the position reached by the Elder Mahānisaṃbha in the presence of a certain Buddha, and for the sake of being foremost among those who maintain the thirteen ascetic practices.”
The Teacher, observing, "A great position has been aspired to by this man; will it be fulfilled or not?
and seeing that it would indeed be fulfilled, said: "A pleasing position you have aspired to.
In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand kappas, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; you shall become his third disciple, the Elder Mahākassapa."
Having heard this, the lay follower thought, "There are no such things as two kinds of speech from the Buddhas," and he regarded that prosperity as something already attained on the following day.
Having given various kinds of gifts, guarded his virtue, and performed various kinds of wholesome deeds for the duration of his life,
he passed away there and was reborn in heaven.
From that time forth, experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, he passed away from the world of the gods and was reborn in a certain aged brahmin family during the ninety-first aeon ago,
while the Blessed One Vipassī was dwelling in the Khema Deer Park near Bandhumatī.
And at that time, the Blessed One Vipassī [appeared] every seventh year.
He delivered a discourse on the Dhamma, and a great clamor arose. Deities throughout the entire Jambudīpa proclaimed, "The Teacher will preach the Dhamma!
The brahmin heard that message. He possessed only a single set of undergarments and upper cloth, and likewise his wife had only one;
they shared a single outer robe between them. Thus, he was known throughout the entire city as "the single-clothed brahmin."

It was observed as follows: whenever there was an assembly of brahmins for some business, the brahmin would leave his wife at home and go himself. But when there was an assembly of brahmin women, he would stay at home while the brahmin woman, having put on that garment, would go.
On that particular day, however, the brahmin said to the brahmin woman: "Madam, what [is this] during the night?"
“You will hear the Dhamma by day,” he said. “We are women by birth and cannot hear it at night; we shall hear it by day.

Having thus addressed the brahmin, she put on that garment, went out with the female lay disciples during the day, paid homage to the Teacher, and sitting to one side, listened to the Dhamma. Afterward, she returned together with those same lay disciples.
Then the brahmin, having left his wife at home, put on that cloth and went to the monastery.
At that time, the Teacher was seated upon a decorated Dharma-throne in the midst of the assembly;
holding a fan of peacock feathers, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, making Mount Sineru his pinnacle, and churning the ocean.
He preached the Dhamma. As the brahmin sat in the assembly listening to the Dhamma, in the very first watch of the night, five-colored rapture arose, filling his entire body.
He gathered up the cloth he was wearing and thought, "I shall give it to the One of Ten Powers.
However, as he contemplated the thousandfold disadvantages of that [gift], avarice arose within him. He [thought], "To the brahmin wife..."
"I have only this one garment; I have no other covering, and it is impossible to go outside without wearing something," he thought, and in every way he was unwilling to give it up.
When the first watch of the night had passed, the same joy arose in him during the middle watch as well.
Thinking exactly as before, he remained unwilling to give it up. Then, during the middle watch...
When he had departed, even during the final watch of the night, joy arose in him just as before.
Thinking, "Whether it be crossing over or death, I shall know later," he folded his garment and placed it at the feet of the Teacher.
Then, folding his left hand and striking it three times with his right hand, he cried out three times, "Victory is mine! Victory is mine!"
And at that time, King Bandhumā was sitting behind the Dhamma throne within the curtain, listening to the Dhamma.
To the king, the sound of the words "I have conquered" was unpleasant. He sent a man, saying, "Go and ask him what he is saying.
Having been sent by him and questioned, the man said: "The rest [of the assembly] have mounted elephant-vehicles and so forth, and are equipped with swords, shields, and other weapons..."
"Capturing the enemy army and conquering them is not a marvelous victory;
however, as if crushing the mind of stinginess with a mallet and driving it away, I gave the cloth I was wearing to the One of Ten Powers.
That stinginess of mine has been conquered," he said. Then that man approached.
He reported that occurrence to the king. The king said, "Alas, we did not know what was appropriate for the One of Ten Powers;
the brahmin knew. Having spoken thus, he sent a pair of garments. Seeing this, the brahmin thought:
"While I was sitting in silence, this man gave nothing to me first, yet he gave it to me while I was speaking of the Teacher's virtues. It was because of the Teacher's virtues [that he acted]."
“What use have I for what has been obtained? he thought, and gave even that pair of garments to the One of Ten Powers.

The king, having asked, “What was done by the brahmin? and hearing that “even that pair of garments was given by him to the Tathāgata alone,” sent two other pairs of garments. He gave those as well. The king sent four more, and so on until—
He sent thirty-two pairs of garments. Then the brahmin thought, "If I were to increase this amount, it would be as if I were taking back what was given.
So, taking two pairs of garments for himself—one for his own sake and one for his wife—he gave the remaining thirty pairs to the Tathāgata alone.
From that time forth, he became a trusted confidant of the Teacher.

Then one day, the king, seeing him listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher during the cold season, gave him his own red woolen cloak worth a hundred thousand pieces and said, "From now on, listen to the Dhamma wearing this.
He thought, "What use have I for this woolen cloak being placed upon this putrid body? and [he remained] within the fragrant chamber.

Having spread a canopy over the Tathāgata’s couch, he departed. Then one day, the king went to the monastery early in the morning and sat down in the presence of the Teacher inside the fragrant chamber.
At that moment, the six-colored rays of the Buddha struck the woolen blanket, and the blanket shone with extraordinary brilliance. Looking at it and recognizing it, the king said: “Venerable Sir, …”
“This blanket is ours; it was given by us to a single-robed brahmin. “Great King, you have honored the brahmin, and the brahmin has honored us.

The king, becoming confident that “the brahmin understood what was appropriate, but we did not,” made everything that was beneficial to people into groups of eight, and thus established the gift known as the “All-Eight” (Sabba-aṭṭhaka).
Having given [these], he appointed him to the position of family priest. He too, thinking, "Sixty-four is what is called 'eight times eight,'" had sixty-four meals on tally-sticks prepared;
having given alms for as long as he lived and guarded his virtue, when he passed away from there, he was reborn in heaven.
Passing away again from there, in this present kappa, he was born during the time of two [Buddhas]: the Blessed One Koṇāgamana and the Blessed One Kassapa.
Between two Buddhas, he was reborn in Bārāṇasī in the household of a householder.
Having grown up and living the life of a householder, one day he went for a walk in the forest. At that time, a Paccekabuddha was making robes on the bank of a river;
as the wind did not blow, he began to fold them up and set them aside. Seeing this, [the householder asked], "Why?"
“Venerable sir, please collect it and set it aside,” he said. [The Elder replied,] “There is not enough wind.
“Venerable sir, use this one,” he said, giving him a garment (*sāṭaka*), and made this aspiration: “May there never be any deficiency for me in whatever place I am reborn.
Then, while his wife was quarreling with his sister-in-law at home, the Paccekabuddha entered for alms.
He entered. Then his sister, having given alms-food to the Paccekabuddha, made a wish concerning his wife:
"May one avoid such a fool for a hundred leagues.
Standing at the door of the house, she heard this and thought, "Let him not eat the meal given by this woman! She took the bowl, discarded the alms-food, and [departed].
Having filled it with gruel, she gave it to him. The other woman, seeing this, said: "Foolish woman!
You may revile me or strike me, but it is not fitting to throw away food from the bowl of one who has fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable eons and give him gruel instead.
Then, reflection arose in her husband's wife. She said, "Wait, venerable sir!"
Having discarded the *kalala* (fetal waste), washed the bowl, rubbed it with fragrant powder, and filled it with the four sweets, he placed it—
shining with ghee of the color of a lotus calyx poured over the top— into the hand of the Paccekabuddha and made this aspiration:
"Just as this alms-food has become luminous, may my body likewise become luminous."
The Paccekabuddha, having expressed his appreciation, sprang into the air. Those two, husband and wife, performed wholesome deeds for the duration of their lives and were reborn in heaven;

subsequently, passing away from there, the layman was reborn in Bārāṇasī during the time of the Samma-sambuddha Kassapa as the son of a merchant possessing eighty crores of wealth, while the other was reborn as the daughter of a merchant of similar means.
When he had reached maturity, they brought that very same merchant’s daughter to him.

Due to the power of that past karma whose fruit had not yet been experienced, as soon as she entered the chamber, her entire body became foul-smelling, like an opened latrine. The merchant’s son asked, “Whose scent is this?”
Having heard, "The merchant’s daughter," he sent her to her family home by the very method of being brought out, saying, "Bring her forth.
By that same method of being brought out, she was turned back at seven places.
At that time, the Fully Enlightened One Kassapa attained final nibbāna; [he was honored] with solid-walled [stūpas] worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
They began constructing a stupa one yojana in height with bricks of red gold. While that stupa was being built, the merchant’s daughter thought:
"I have been turned back from seven places; what is the use of my life?
She had the jewelry and ornaments from her own body broken up and had a golden brick made, one cubit long and one span wide.
It was four finger-breadths in height. Then, taking a lump of yellow orpiment and realgar, and bringing eight handfuls of blue lotuses, she went to the site where the stupa was to be built.
At that moment, a row of bricks being laid around the perimeter was short by one brick from the corner-stone.
The merchant’s daughter said to the mason, "Place this brick here."
“Mother, you have come at an auspicious time; set it yourself. She climbed up, mixed yellow orpiment and red arsenic with oil, and using that as a binding agent, she laid down the brick.
Having made an offering of eight handfuls of blue lotuses upon it and paid homage, she made this aspiration:
“In every place where I am reborn, may the fragrance of sandalwood issue from my body and the fragrance of the blue lotus from my mouth.”
Having made his aspiration, he paid homage at the cetiya, circumambulated it, and departed.
At that very moment, mindfulness arose in the merchant’s son to whom she had first been led, concerning her;
for a festival had also been proclaimed throughout the city. He said to his attendants: "At that time, here..."
“The merchant’s daughter has been brought here; where is she? “She is in her family home, Master. “Bring her here; we shall celebrate the festival,” he said.
They went, paid their respects to her, and stood there. When she asked them, “What brings you here, dear ones? they explained what had happened.
She replied, “Dear ones, I have already worshipped the Cetiya with my own jewelry; I have no more ornaments left. They went and told the merchant’s son.
They reported this. [The treasurer thought,] "Bring her; we shall obtain her ornaments. They brought her.
As soon as she entered the house, the entire dwelling was filled with the fragrance of sandalwood and the scent of blue lotuses.
The merchant’s son asked her, "Previously, a foul odor issued from your body, but now from your body..."
"The scent of sandalwood emanates from her body, and the fragrance of blue lotuses wafts from her mouth; what is this?

She then related the deeds she had performed from the very beginning. The merchant’s son, gaining confidence in the thought, "How truly liberating is the teaching of the Buddha," wrapped a golden stupa one *yojana* in height with a fine woolen cloak and adorned it here and there with golden lotuses as large as chariot wheels.
He adorned it. Their pendants were twelve cubits long. Having remained there for the duration of his lifespan, he was reborn in heaven;
passing away from there, he was reborn in a certain minister’s family at a place one *yojana* from Bārāṇasī.
The merchant’s daughter, too, having descended from the world of the gods, was reborn as the eldest daughter in the royal family.
When they had reached maturity, a festival was proclaimed in the village where the prince lived. He said to his mother, "Mother, give me a garment; I shall play at the festival.
She brought out a washed cloth and gave it to him. "Mother, this is too coarse; give me another," he said.
She brought out another and gave it to him, but he rejected that as well. She brought out yet another and gave it to him.
He refused that as well. Then his mother said to him, "Dear son, in a household such as ours, we have no merit for obtaining anything more delicate than this.
"In that case, mother, I shall go to a place where it can be obtained," he replied.
"Son, I desire for you the acquisition of the kingdom in the city of Bārāṇasī this very day. Having paid homage to his mother, he departed.
He said, "I am going, mother. "Go then, dear son," she replied. It was thought by her: "Where will he go?

Will he sit here or there in the house? But he, departing according to the course of his merit, went to Bārāṇasī and lay down in the park upon a lucky stone slab, covering himself with his upper robe even to his head. And it so happened that the King of Bārāṇasī had passed away.
The seventh day arrived.
Having performed the funeral rites for the king, the ministers sat in the royal courtyard and deliberated: "The king has only one daughter and no son;
a kingdom without a king is not fitting. Who shall be king? Having thus deliberated, they said, "You be [the king]."
"You must come," they said. The chaplain replied, "It is not right to look about too much;

let us release the Phussa-chariot. Having yoked four horses the color of white water-lilies, and having placed the fivefold royal insignia and the white parasol upon the chariot itself, they released the chariot and had musical instruments played behind it. The chariot—
Having exited through the eastern gate, he set out toward the park. Some said, "He is going toward the park out of habit;
let us turn him back. The chaplain said, "Do not turn him back. The chariot, having circumambulated the prince, stood ready for him to mount.
The chaplain drew back the corner of his upper garment and looked at the soles of the prince's feet.
“Let this island be; he is fit to rule over the four continents surrounded by two thousand islands,” he said.
Then, saying, “Strike the musical instruments again! Strike the musical instruments again! he had them struck three times.
Thereupon the prince opened his mouth, looked out, and asked, “For what purpose have you come? “O King, for you.”
"He has attained the kingship. "How do they call him? "He is the Lord who has passed away to the state of the gods. "How many days have elapsed? "Today is the seventh day.
"Does he have a son or a daughter? "He has a daughter, Your Majesty, but no son. "I shall make her queen.
Thereupon, they immediately had a consecration pavilion constructed and adorned the princess with all kinds of ornaments.
Having brought him to the park, they performed the prince’s consecration ceremony.
Then, once he had been consecrated, they presented him with a garment worth a thousand pieces of gold. He asked, "What is this, dear sirs? "It is a lower garment, Your Majesty.
"Is it not coarse, dear sirs? Is there nothing finer than this? [They replied,] "There is for humans..."
"O King, there is nothing finer than these garments for use;
such is what your king wears. "Yes, Your Majesty," they replied. "I do not think your king is a man of merit. Bring a golden pitcher; we shall obtain the garments.
They brought the golden pitcher. He rose, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, and—
Taking water in his hand, he sprinkled it toward the eastern direction; immediately, having split the solid earth, eight wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) arose.
Again, taking water, he sprinkled it toward the south, the west, and the north—thus he sprinkled all four directions.
Having done so eight times in each direction, thirty-two wish-fulfilling trees arose.
Thus, having dressed in one divine cloth and draped another over his shoulders, he said, "Have the drums beaten throughout King Nanda’s realm,
proclaiming that no women shall spin thread. Having spoken thus, he raised the royal parasol,
adorned and prepared for state, mounted upon the back of a noble elephant, entered the city, ascended the palace, and enjoyed great prosperity.
As time passed in this way, one day the queen, seeing the king’s great prosperity, showed an expression of compassion, saying, "Oh, what asceticism!
When asked, "What is this, O Queen? she replied, "Your Majesty, your prosperity is exceedingly great. In the past, you performed good deeds out of faith in the Buddhas;
now, however, you do not perform the wholesome merit that serves as a requisite for the future."
“To whom shall I give? There are none who possess virtue. He replied, “Your Majesty, Jambudīpa is not empty of Arahants;
you should simply prepare the gift, and I shall find the Arahants. On the following day, the king had alms prepared at the eastern gate.
Early in the morning, the queen, having resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha, lay down on her chest upon the upper terrace of the palace, facing the east.
"If there are Arahants in this direction, let them come tomorrow and receive alms from us," he said.
There were no Arahants in that direction, so they gave that honor to poor beggars.
On the following day, having prepared alms-giving at the southern gate, he acted in the same way; on the next day, at the western gate.

On the day of the virtuous (Sajjana) at the northern gate, however, when the queen had likewise invited them, the eldest of the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were dwelling in the Himalayas—the sons of Padumavatī—addressed his younger brothers:
"Friends, King Nanda invites you; please accept his invitation. Having accepted, on the following day...
Having washed their faces at the Anotatta Lake and come through the air, they descended at the northern gate.
People went and reported to the king, "Your Majesty, five hundred paccekabuddhas have arrived.
The king, together with the queen, went forth, paid homage, and taking their bowls, he escorted the paccekabuddhas up to the palace; there he gave them alms, and at the conclusion of their meal—
The king prostrated at the feet of the senior elder of the Saṅgha, and the queen prostrated at the feet of the junior member of the Saṅgha, saying:
"Venerable sirs, may you not be distressed for lack of requisites; may we not diminish in merit. Grant us your promise to reside here for as long as we live.
Having obtained this promise, he constructed five hundred leaf-huts and five hundred walking-paths in the park in every respect.
Having prepared a dwelling place, they had him reside there.
As time passed in this manner, the king’s frontier region rose in rebellion.
He instructed the queen, saying, “I am going to pacify the frontier; do not neglect the Paccekabuddhas,” and then departed. Even before he had returned, the Paccekabuddhas—

The life-formations were exhausted. Having sported in the play of jhāna throughout the three watches of the night, the Paccekabuddha Mahāpaduma, at the rising of the dawn, grasped his support-board and, while still standing, attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa). By this same method, the others did so as well;
thus, they all attained final nibbāna. On the following day, the queen smeared the place where the Paccekabuddhas had sat with green cow dung.
Having had flowers strewn and incense offered, she sat waiting for their arrival;
seeing no sign of them coming, she sent a man, saying, "Go, dear son, find out whether the noble ladies are unwell in any way.
He went, opened the door of Mahāpaduma’s leaf-hut, and not finding them there, proceeded to the walking-path.
Seeing him standing leaning against the backrest of his seat, he paid homage and said, "It is time, venerable sir.

[The other] replied, "What shall a body that has attained final Nibbāna say? He is likely sleeping. Thinking thus, he went over, touched the feet with his hand, and knowing from their coolness and stiffness that they had attained final Nibbāna, he went to the presence of the second one.
Having thus learned that all three had attained final Nibbāna, he went to the royal palace. When asked, "Where are the Paccekabuddhas, dear father?
he replied, "They have attained final Nibbāna, Your Majesty. The Queen, weeping and wailing, came out and went there with the citizens;
she had the funeral rites performed, and having completed the services for the Paccekabuddhas' bodies, she took their relics.
He established a cetiya.
When the king returned after having pacified the border regions, he went out to meet the queen who had come to welcome him and asked:
"My lady, have you not been negligent regarding the Paccekabuddhas? Are the noble ones free from illness? "The queens have passed away," she replied. The king thought: "Even for such as these..."
“The death of wise men has occurred; where can there be escape for us?
Without going to the city, he entered the park itself, summoned his eldest son, prepared him for the kingship, and himself went forth into the wandering life of a recluse.
