The queen, thinking, “Now that he has gone forth, what shall I do? likewise went forth right there in the park.
Having developed the two jhānas, they passed away from there and were reborn in the Brahmā world.
While they were dwelling right there, our Teacher appeared in the world, set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, and eventually entered Rājagaha.
While the Teacher was residing there, this young brahmin Pippali lived in the brahmin village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha.

He was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of the brahmin Kapila; this Bhaddā Kāpilānī was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of a brahmin of the Kosiya clan in the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom.
As they grew up in due course, when Pippali the youth reached his twentieth year and Bhaddā reached her sixteenth year, their parents—
Having looked at their son, they pressed him very hard, saying, "Dear one, you have reached the age of maturity;
you must establish the family lineage. The young man said, "Do not speak such words within my hearing.
I will look after you as long as you live; after your passing, I shall go forth and enter the religious life."
After a few days had passed, they spoke to him again, but he likewise refused. They spoke yet again, and he refused once more.
From that point on, his mother spoke to him incessantly.
Thinking, "I shall persuade my mother," the young man gave a thousand *nikkhas* of red gold to the goldsmiths.

Having had a female form fashioned, and after the completion of its bathing, rubbing, and other preparations, he had her dressed in red garments, adorned with beautiful flowers and various ornaments, and then summoned his mother, saying:
"Mother, if I can obtain such an object as this, I shall remain at home; if not, I will not."
“I shall dwell [here]. The wise Brahmin lady thought: “My son is meritorious, a giver of gifts who has made a firm resolve;
while performing merit, he did not do so alone. Surely those who have performed merit together with him must be like golden figures.
Having summoned eight Brahmins and satisfied them with all their desires, she [prepared] a golden figure.
Having placed him on the chariot, he dispatched them, saying, “Go, dear sons;
wherever you see a girl of a family equal to ours in birth, lineage, and wealth, give her this very golden image as a gift.
Thinking, “This is indeed our business,” they set out and considered, “Where shall we go? and decided upon the Madda country.
“Let us go to the Madda kingdom,” they said, and so they went to the city of Sāgala in the Madda kingdom.
There, having placed that golden image at a bathing ford, they sat down to one side.
Then Bhaddā’s nurse, having bathed and adorned Bhaddā and seated her in the bedchamber, was coming to bathe herself when she saw that image.
Thinking, "My noble daughter has come here," he threatened her;

then, shouting, "You ill-behaved woman, why have you come here?", he raised his palm and struck her on the side of the cheek, saying, "Go quickly! Her hand trembled as if it had struck against a rock.
She stepped back and thought, "Having seen such a stiff and thick-necked man, I nevertheless gave rise to the perception that 'he is my noble daughter'."
"For it is not even fitting for my noble daughter to accept a lower garment," he said. Then those men surrounded him and asked, "What kind of woman is this sister of yours?
He replied, "Who is she? My noble daughter is a hundredfold and a thousandfold more beautiful than her;
when she sits within a chamber twelve cubits high, there is no need for a lamp, for by the radiance of her own body—"
“Dispelling darkness. Saying, “In that case, come,” they took Khujjā, placed her upon a golden chariot, and standing at the door of the brahmin of the Kosiya clan, announced their arrival.
The brahmin, having offered them hospitality, asked, “Where have you come from? “From the village of Mahātittha in the kingdom of Magadha.”
"From the house of the brahmin Kapila. "For what reason have you come? "For this very reason. "Excellent, dear ones!
Our brahmin is of equal birth, clan, and wealth; I shall give him my daughter," she said, and took the gift.
They sent a message to the brahmin Kapila: "The girl has been found; do what must be done. That...
Having heard the news, they informed the young Brahmin Pippali, saying, "It seems the girl has been found.
The young man thought, "I thought she would not be obtained; yet they say she has been found. Since I have no desire for her, I shall send a letter.
Having gone into private, he wrote a letter: "Let Bhaddā obtain a household life befitting her own birth, lineage, and wealth; as for me..."
“Having gone forth, I shall go into homelessness; do not later feel regret.

Bhaddā too, having heard that he intended to give her to such-and-such a man, went into seclusion and wrote a letter: “May my noble son obtain a household life befitting his own birth, lineage, and wealth;
I, however, shall go forth and enter homelessness—do not later feel regret.”
Two leaves met on the way. "Whose leaf is this? "It was sent by the young brahmin Pippali to Bhaddā.

"And whose is this? "It was sent by Bhaddā to the young brahmin Pippali. When this was said, he read both of them and, saying, "Behold the work of children," he tore them up, threw them away in the forest, and wrote a leaf with identical wording. From there—
And they sent for one another from there as well. Thus, even though they were unwilling, their meeting took place.
On that very day, the young man took a single flower garland and set it aside. Bhaddā also placed those [garlands] in the middle of the bed.
Having both finished their evening meal, they came together, thinking, "We shall ascend the bed," and the young man [stood] on the right side.
“Climb onto the couch. Having climbed onto the left side, Bhaddā said, “We shall know that passion has arisen in whichever side the flowers wither;
this flower-garland must not be touched. Yet, out of fear of physical contact with one another’s bodies, they spent the entire three watches of the night without descending into sleep.
But by day, there was not even a mere smile. Unmixed with worldly pleasures, they did not manage the household while their parents were still living;
however, when they had passed away, they did so. The young man’s great fortune consisted of seven hundred and eighty million pieces of wealth;
yet on a single day, his body must be turned over and discarded as nothing more than gold dust.
It was appropriate to receive exactly twelve *nāḷi* measures by Magadha measure. There were sixty great reservoirs equipped with water-lifting machines,
a royal workshop extending twelve *yojana*, fourteen villages equal in size to Anurādhapura, fourteen elephant divisions, fourteen cavalry divisions,
and fourteen chariot divisions.
Thus, one day, having mounted his decorated horse and being surrounded by a great multitude of people, he went to his estate and stood at the edge of a field.
Seeing crows and other birds picking up and eating earthworms and other small creatures from the place torn open by the ploughs, he asked, "Sirs, what are these eating?
"Earthworms, noble sir. "To whom does the evil committed by these belong?"
“Is it so? “It is so, noble sir. He thought: “If the evil committed by these people falls upon me, what will my wealth of seven hundred and eighty million be to me?
What will my twelve-league plantation be? What will my sixty irrigation ponds bound by embankments be?
What will my fourteen villages be? Having handed all this over to Bhaddā Kāpilānī, I shall go forth into homelessness.”

At that moment, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, having had three jars of sesame seeds spread out in the inner courtyard and sitting surrounded by her nurses, saw crows eating the sesame seeds and asked, "Nurses, what are these eating?
"Seeds, noble lady. "Who would incur demerit for this? "We would, noble lady. She thought: "My four-cubit cloth..."

"It is enough for me to receive only a measure of rice from a stalk; if, however, this unwholesome deed committed by so many people were to fall upon me, then certainly, even in a thousand existences, I would not be able to lift my head from the cycle of rebirth.
As soon as the noble sons arrive, I shall hand over everything to them, depart, and go forth into homelessness."
The young man arrived, bathed, ascended the palace, and sat upon a costly couch.
Then they prepared food suitable for a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) for him. After both had eaten and the attendants had departed, they sat down in a secluded and comfortable place.
Then the young man said to Bhaddā: "Bhaddā, how much wealth did you bring with you when you came to this house?"
“Shall I bring it? “Fifty-five thousand carts, noble sir.
“I shall deliver all of this—whatever eighty-seven crores of wealth there are in this house, consisting of mechanical devices, sixty ponds, and so forth—all of it to you alone.
“But where are you going, noble sir? “I shall go forth into the homeless life. “Noble sir, I too—”
"We have been sitting here waiting for your very arrival, thinking, 'I too shall go forth.
To them, the three realms of existence appeared like a leaf-hut on fire.

Having had garments dyed with the juice of *kasāva* and earthen bowls brought from the market, they had their hair shaved off by one another and declared: 'Our going forth is for the sake of those who are Arhats in the world.'"
Having spoken thus, they placed their bowls in their bags, slung them over their shoulders, and descended from the palace. No one among the slaves or laborers in the house recognized them.
Then, as they were departing from the brahmin village and traveling through the gate of the slave village, the inhabitants of the slave village recognized them by their deportment and gestures.
Weeping, they fell at their feet and said, "Noble sirs, why do you leave us behind as if we were helpless?"
“Friends, we have gone forth because these three states of existence are like a thatched hut on fire;
if we were to set even one among you free, it would not suffice for even a hundred years. You yourselves should wash your heads, live as free men, and sustain your lives.
Having said this, they departed while those [slaves] were still weeping. As the Elder walked ahead, he turned back and looked upon them.
She thought: "This Bhaddā Kāpilānī, the most precious woman in all Jambudīpa, is following behind me.
It is indeed possible that someone might think: 'Even though they have gone forth, these women cannot exist without [men];
they are doing what is unbecoming. Or perhaps someone, having become malicious toward us, might fill the states of misery."
[He thought,] “It would be better for me to go after abandoning this [woman. Thus he conceived this thought.
As he was walking ahead, seeing a forked path, he stood at its head. Bhaddā also came up, paid homage, and stood there.
Then he said to her: “Bhaddā, seeing such a woman coming behind me, [I thought: ‘These...’”
"Thinking, 'Even after going forth, they cannot exist without [men],' the great multitude with defiled minds toward us would fill the realms of misery.
At this crossroads, you take one path; I shall go by the other.
"Yes, noble sir, women are indeed a stain upon those who have gone forth. Thinking, 'Even after going forth, they cannot exist without [men],' the great multitude..."
“They will see our fault; you take one path, and I, having taken another, shall go on alone.
Having circumambulated him three times to the right and prostrated with the fivefold reverence at four places, he raised his hands in a brilliant añjali with the ten fingers joined together and said:
“The friendship cultivated over the course of a hundred thousand aeons is broken this very day.”
Having said, "You are of the right-hand caste; the right-hand path is suitable for you.
We are women, of the left-hand caste; the left-hand path is suitable for us," they paid homage and set out on their respective paths.
At the moment they had split apart, this great earth thought: "Although I am able to support the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Sineru, I cannot bear your virtues."
As if crying out, "I cannot bear it," she trembled; a sound like a thunderclap resounded in the sky, and the Cakkavāḷa mountain rang out.
Sitting in his Fragrant Chamber within the Great Monastery at Veḷuvana, the Perfectly Enlightened One heard the sound of the earth’s trembling.

Reflecting, "For whom indeed does the earth tremble? he perceived: "The young brahmin Pippali and Bhaddā Kāpilānī have gone forth, renouncing immeasurable prosperity for my sake; this earthquake has occurred at the place of their separation due to the power of both their virtues.
It is fitting that I too should provide them with support. Having thus reflected, he emerged from the fragrant chamber.
Taking his own bowl and robe, and without taking leave of any of the eighty great elders, he traveled thirty gāvutas to meet him halfway.
Between Rājagaha and Nālandā, at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree, he sat down cross-legged.
As he sat, however, he did not do so like some other refuse-rag wearer, but rather in the full attire of a Buddha.

Having grasped them, he sat down emitting thick Buddha-rays eighty cubits long. Thus, at that moment, Buddha-rays—measuring the size of leaf-canopies, cart-wheels, and gabled houses—flickering and streaming hither and thither, produced the appearance of the simultaneous rising of a thousand moons and a thousand suns, and made that forest region one mass of light.
With the glory of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, it was like a cluster of stars brilliantly shining.
The forest shone forth like the sky, like water filled with blossoming lotuses and water-lilies;
for while the trunk of a banyan tree is white, its leaves are green, and its fruits are red,
on that day the hundred-branched banyan tree was entirely golden in color.

The Elder Mahākassapa, thinking, "This one will be my Teacher; it was for his sake that I went forth," walked with bowed head from the moment he first saw him, and after paying homage at three places, he said, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple.
Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am a disciple. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Kassapa,..."
“If you were to perform this act of homage upon the great earth, even she would not be able to sustain it.
But the homage performed by you, who know such greatness of virtue in the Tathāgata, cannot move even a single hair on my body.
Sit down, Kassapa; I shall give you your inheritance. Then the Blessed One [instructed him] with three exhortations.

He granted him full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having granted it, he departed from the foot of the Bahuputtaka *nigrodha* tree and set out on the road with the Elder as his attendant monk (*pacchāsamaṇa*).

The Teacher’s body was variegated with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*), while Mahākassapa was adorned with seven of the marks of a Great Man. He was like a great golden ship following behind the Teacher.
He followed him step by step. Having traveled a short distance along the road, the Teacher stepped off the path and made a gesture of sitting down at the foot of a certain tree.
Knowing that the Teacher wished to sit, the Elder folded his own patched outer robe (saṅghāṭī) into four layers and spread it out for him.
The Teacher sat down there, touched the robe with his hand, and said, "Kassapa, this rag-robe (pilotikasaṅghāṭī) of yours is indeed soft.
The Elder, perceiving that "the Teacher speaks of the softness of my robe;
he must wish to put it on," said, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One put on the robe. "What will you wear? [he asked].
“Kassapa? “I shall wear it, Bhante, if I may receive your undergarment.
“But Kassapa, will you be able to wear this rag-robe worn out by use?
For on the day I took up this rag-robe, the great earth shook down to its watery boundaries; this is a rag-robe worn out by the use of the Buddhas.”

"A robe cannot be worn by one of meager virtue; it is fitting that this be taken only by one who is capable, able to fulfill the practice, and a wearer of rag-robes from birth," he said, and then exchanged robes with the Elder.
Having thus performed the exchange of robes, the Blessed One put on the robe worn by the Elder, and [the Elder put on] the Teacher's robe.
The Elder put on his robe. At that moment, even this great earth, though insentient, shook as far as the edge of the ocean, as if saying: "Venerable sir, you have performed a difficult feat;
there has never before been one who gave a robe he himself was wearing to a disciple;
I am unable to bear your virtue. The Elder thought: "Now I have gained [the victory]."
Thinking, "This is the robe used by the Buddhas; what further remains for me to do now? he refrained from pride.
Having undertaken the thirteen ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) right in the presence of the Buddhas, he remained an ordinary person (puthujjana) for only seven days;
on the eighth dawn, together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he attained Arhatship. The Teacher also said: "Bhikkhus, Kassapa..."
Having praised the Elder with such suttas as, "He approaches families like the moon, withdrawing both body and mind, ever-new among families,
free from arrogance," [the Buddha] later, taking this very episode from the *Kassapa-saṃyutta* as the occasion,
declared of the Elder: "In my teaching, Mahākassapa is the foremost of those monks who advocate the ascetic practices (*dhuta-vāda*)."
"He established him in a position.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Anuruddha (192).
Regarding the fifth [category], "of those with the divine eye, namely Anuruddha": among the bhikkhus possessing the divine eye, it was the Elder Anuruddha.
"He says, 'The foremost. His preeminence is to be understood through his mastery of practice.
It is said that the Elder, having set aside the mere elaboration of eating, spent all other time increasing his light and dwelling while surveying beings with the divine eye.
Thus, through his mastery of practice day and night, he became known as the foremost among those possessing the divine eye. Moreover, for a hundred thousand aeons..."
By virtue of his aspiration, he became the foremost among those possessing the divine eye.

Regarding his inquiry, this is the sequential account: this clansman also went with the great multitude to the monastery after the meal for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

At that time, there was a certain householder of noble family whose name was not well known. Having paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, he stood at the edge of the assembly and listened to the discourse on the Dhamma.
The Teacher, having connected the teaching according to its proper sequence, designated a certain monk endowed with the divine eye as pre-eminent in that position.
Then it occurred to the householder: "Great indeed is this bhikkhu, since the Teacher himself has placed him in the foremost position among those with the divine eye.
Oh, may I too become the foremost among those with the divine eye in the dispensation of the Buddha who will arise in the future!
Having formed this thought, he went through the midst of the assembly and invited the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for the following day's meal.
Having invited them together and given a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha on the following day,
thinking, "I have aspired to a great station," he invited them again for the next day with the same formula, saying,
"For today and tomorrow," and after providing a great alms-offering for seven days, he presented the finest garments to the Blessed One and his retinue.
“Blessed One, I do not perform this act of honor for the sake of divine attainment or human attainment. However,
since you placed that bhikkhu in the foremost position among those with the divine eye seven days ago,
may I too, in the future, become the foremost among those with the divine eye in the dispensation of a certain Buddha, just like that bhikkhu.”
Having made this aspiration, he lay down at the Teacher’s feet. The Teacher, looking into the future and knowing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, said:
“O man, at the conclusion of one hundred thousand future eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise;
in his dispensation, you shall become Anuruddha, the foremost among those possessed of the divine eye.”
Having spoken thus and offered words of thanksgiving for the meal, he returned to the monastery.
The householder, too, performed virtuous deeds without ceasing as long as the Buddha remained in the world.
When the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the seven-league golden stupa that had been completed and approached the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, saying, “Venerable sirs, ...”
"What is the preliminary practice for the divine eye? he asked. "It is fitting, lay follower, to give gifts of lamps," [the teacher] replied.
"Very well, venerable sir; I shall do so," he said, and first had a thousand lamp-trees made for a thousand lamps.
After that, he had more than that, and after that, even more than those—many thousands of lamp-trees.
He had [them] made. As for the remaining lamps, they were immeasurable.

Having thus performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, and wandering through the realms of devas and humans, after the passing of one hundred thousand aeons, during the time of the Sammasambuddha Kassapa, he was reborn in a householder’s home in Bārāṇasī; and when [the Buddha] had attained final Nibbāna...
When the Teacher had passed away, [he] had many bronze bowls made for the Yojanika Cetiya, filled them with the cream of ghee,
and placed a single lump of sugar in the middle of each; having set them on fire and caused them to be arranged around the Cetiya so that the rim of one touched the rim of another,
he had his own largest bronze bowl made, filled it with the cream of ghee, and [placed it] upon that.
Having caused a thousand rings to be fashioned all around the rim of a bronze vessel, and having wrapped a pinnacle in the middle with cloth and caused it to be lacquered,
he took the bronze vessel upon his head and circumambulated the *cetiya* for an entire night,
traveling a *yojana*. Thus, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life even in that very existence, he was reborn in the world of the gods.
Furthermore, when no Buddha had yet arisen, he took rebirth in the house of a poor family in that very city and lived there supported by a merchant named Sumanaseṭṭhi; his name was Annabhāra.
Now, that merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi gave a great daily alms-giving at the door of his house to the poor, the destitute, the needy, and beggars. Then, one day—
The Paccekabuddha named Upāriṭṭha had entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana.
Emerging from that state, he reflected, "Whom should I assist today? For Paccekabuddhas are indeed compassionate toward those who are miserable.
He thought, "Today it is fitting for me to assist Annabhāra," and [he saw that] now Annabhāra—
Knowing that he would return from the forest to his own home, [the Paccekabuddha] took his bowl and robe,
rose up into the air from Mount Gandhamādana, and stood before Annabhāra at the village gate.
Seeing the Paccekabuddha with his bowl empty in his hand, Annabhāra paid homage to the Paccekabuddha and said, "Is it not..."
“Venerable sir, have you received alms? he asked. “We shall receive them, O one of great merit,” they replied.
“Venerable sir, please stay right here for a moment,” he said, and hurrying back to his own home, he asked his wife, “My dear, is there the portion of rice set aside for me, or not?
“There is, husband,” she replied. He went from there and took the bowl from the hands of the Paccekabuddha.
Having arrived, she said: "Bhadde, because we failed to perform wholesome deeds in a previous existence, we live here hoping for food.
When there is a desire to give among us, there is no object to be given; when there is an object to be given, we find no recipient.
Today I saw the Paccekabuddha Upaṭṭhāka, and I have a portion of food. This portion of food is for me..."
"Place this in this bowl.
The clever woman thought, "Since my husband gives me a share of his meal, I too ought to have a share in this act of giving.
Thus, she placed her own portion of the meal into the bowl of Upaṭṭha, the Paccekabuddha.

He gave it. Annabhāra brought forth a bowl, placed it in the hand of the Paccekabuddha, and said, "Venerable sir, may we be released from such a miserable life. "So be it, you of great merit," he replied.
He spread his own upper robe in one place and said, "Venerable sir, sit here and partake. The Paccekabuddha sat there.
Having sat down, he partook of the meal while reflecting upon the ninefold repulsiveness.
After he had finished eating, Annabhāra offered him water for washing the bowl. Having completed his meal, the Paccekabuddha said:
"May all that you desire and pray for be fulfilled."
“May all his aspirations be fulfilled, just like the moon on the fifteenth day.

Having offered this expression of appreciation, he set out upon the road. The deity residing in the umbrella of the merchant Sumana exclaimed three times, “Oh, what a gift! A supreme gift! Well-established upon Upaṭṭha! and gave her approval.
The merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi said, "Do you not see me giving alms for all this time?

[The other replied,] "I do not give my approval for your giving; rather, having gained confidence through the alms-food given by you to the Paccekabuddha Upaṭṭha, it is for that reason that I give my approval.
The merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi thought: "How wonderful! While I have been giving alms for so long, I have never seen a deity..."

“I was unable to cause him to give his approval (*sādhukāra*). This Annabhāra, living in dependence upon me, has caused me to give my approval by the mere gift of a single portion of almsfood, because he has obtained a suitable recipient.
It is fitting that, having given what is appropriate for him, I should make this almsfood my own. Having thus summoned Annabhāra, [he said]: “Today, by you—of anyone...”
“Have you given any gift? he asked. “Yes, noble sir; I gave my own portion of alms-food to the Paccekabuddha Upāriṭṭha.
“Well then, good man, take this coin and give this alms-food to me. “I will not give it to you, noble sir.
He increased the amount until it reached a thousand coins, but Annabhāra said, “Even for a thousand, I will not give it. “Very well, good man, if—”
“If you do not give almsfood, take the thousand [pieces of gold] and give me the *patti*.
“I do not know whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to give even this; however, having asked the noble Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha, if it should be appropriate to give, I will give it.
Having gone and reached the Paccekabuddha, she said, “Venerable sir, the merchant Sumanas has given me a thousand...”
"Having given, he asks for the merit in the alms-food given to you, saying: 'Did I give it, or did I not give it? Wise man, I shall give you a simile.
Suppose there were a village of a hundred households, and a lamp were lit in only one house;
then the others, each having soaked their own wick with oil and lit it, would take [their lamps]. Is there light from the first lamp, or is there not?"

“Venerable sir, the radiance is even greater. “In the same way, whether it be a ladleful of gruel or a spoonful of alms-food, when a wise person gives a share of their own alms-food to others—whether they give to a hundred or to a thousand—the merit increases for as many as they give to.
You gave only a single portion of alms-food to the merchant Sumanas.”
"But when the merit has been given, there are two portions of alms-food: one for you and one for him.
Having paid homage to the Paccekabuddha, he went to the presence of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi and said, "Sir, take the merit of the alms-food.
"Then, take a thousand kahāpaṇas. "I do not sell the alms-food; it was given out of faith."
"But I give you a gift," he said. "Dear father, you give me a gift out of faith toward me, but I give you a thousand out of honor for your virtue;
take it, dear father. He replied, "So be it," and took the thousand.
"Dear father, from the moment you have received this thousand, there is no need for you to perform manual labor with your own hands; [you shall walk] in the street..."
"Build a house and live there; whatever you require, have it brought to me and take it.
Alms given to a Paccekabuddha who has just emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) yield their fruit on that very day.
Therefore, although the merchant Sumanas did not go to the royal palace with his load of food on other days, he went having taken it on that particular day.
On account of Annabhāra’s merit, the king did not look toward the treasurer, but looked only at Annabhāra.
"Your Majesty, why do you look so intently at this man? "I am looking at him because he was never seen before on another day.
"Your Majesty, he is indeed worthy of being looked upon. "But what quality of his makes him worthy of being looked upon? "Today, instead of eating his own allotted portion of rice..."
“Because it was given to the Paccekabuddha Upāriṭṭha, the god received a thousand [pieces] from my hand. “What is his name?
“His name is Annabhāra, O god. “Since he has received [it] from your hand, he deserves to receive [it] from my hand as well;
I too shall pay him honor,” he said, and gave him a thousand. “Do you know where his dwelling place is, friend?”
"Excellent, Your Majesty! they said. While cleaning one section of the house, they struck spot after spot with a spade and saw treasure jars standing neck-to-neck;
they reported this to the king. The king said, "In that case, go and dig them up.
As they dug and dug, the jars went further down. They went back again and reported it to the king. The king—
“Dig at the command of Annabhāra,” he said. They went and dug, saying, “At the very word of Annabhāra.
Wherever they were struck with the spade, jars rose up like clusters of mushrooms from the ground.
Having brought forth the wealth, they made a heap in the presence of the king. The king, having assembled his ministers, [asked], “In this city, whose...”
“Does anyone else possess such wealth? he asked. “No one, O King,” they replied.
“In that case, let this Annabhāra be known as the foremost merchant in wealth in this city. On that very day, he received the insignia of a merchant-chief (*seṭṭhicchatta*).
From then on, having performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life, he passed away and was reborn in the world of the gods. For a long time...
Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in the city of Kapilavatthu in the home of the Sakyan Amitodana at the time of our Teacher’s appearance.
On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Anuruddha.

He was the younger brother of Mahānāma the Sakyan and the son of the Teacher’s younger paternal uncle; he was exceedingly delicate and possessed of great merit. Even when [food] was placed in a golden bowl for him...
Almsfood arose for him. Then one day his mother, thinking, "I shall make it known that my son has nothing," covered an empty golden bowl with another golden bowl and sent it off.
On the way, deities filled it with divine cakes. Thus he became one of great merit. [He lived] in three dwellings suited to the three seasons.
Surrounded by adorned dancing girls in palaces, he enjoyed prosperity like a god.
At that same time, our Bodhisatta, having descended from the Tusita heaven, took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of King Suddhodana;
and having gradually reached maturity, he lived for twenty-nine years within the household.
Having completed his great renunciation and departed, he gradually realized all-knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
After spending seven weeks at the Seat of Enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
While bestowing favor upon the world, he arrived at Rājagaha. Hearing that "my son has come to Rājagaha," [the King] said, "Go, my man, to my..."
When his father sent for him, saying, “Bring your son,” he ordained ten ministers, each accompanied by a retinue of a thousand, through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-pabbajjā*).
Then, at the request of the Elder Kāḷudāyī to go on a journey, he departed from Rājagaha with a retinue of twenty thousand monks and went to the city of Kapilavatthu.
There, in the assembly of his kinsmen, he performed many miracles of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) that were truly wondrous.
Having delivered a diverse teaching on the Dhamma and caused the great multitude to drink the draught of the Deathless, he took his bowl and robes on the following day and stood at the city gate.
Reflecting, "What indeed is the custom of all omniscient Buddhas who have come to a noble city?
and knowing that "walking for alms from house to house in regular order is the custom," he proceeded to walk for alms in regular order.
Having heard, "My son is wandering for alms," the king came;
[the Buddha] preached the Dhamma to him, led him into his own residence, and after receiving the honors and hospitality he had prepared, he bestowed favor upon his kinsmen there.
Then, having ordained Prince Rāhula, he set out on a wandering tour from Kapilavatthu through the kingdom of the Mallas, and before long arrived at the Mango Grove of Anupiya.
At that time, King Suddhodana, having assembled the Sākiya people, said:
"If my son had lived the life of a householder, he would have become a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) endowed with the seven treasures.
My grandson, Prince Rāhula, would also have walked about surrounded by a host of nobles; you too [should consider] this matter."
“Know this: now that my son has become a Buddha, let there be an entourage of kṣatriyas.
Each of you, from your respective families, give one boy. When this was said, a thousand kṣatriya youths went forth all at once.
At that time, Mahānāma was the head of a household; he approached Anuruddha and Sakka and said this:
“Dear Anuruddha, at present many well-known Sakyan youths are following the Blessed One who has gone forth and have themselves gone forth.
In our family, no one has yet gone forth from the home life into homelessness.
Therefore, either you go forth, or I shall go forth. Having heard his words, he lost interest in the household life.
He went forth from the home life into homelessness as the seventh among himself. The sequence of his renunciation is already recorded in the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
Thus, after they had gone to the Mango Grove at Anupiya and gone forth, during that very same rainy season, the Elder Bhaddiya attained Arahatship;
the Elder Anuruddha produced the divine eye, and Devadatta [attained] the eight meditative attainments.
Ānanda Thera was reborn [in the Brahma world] and established himself in the fruit of stream-entry;
Bhagu Thera and Kimila Thera later attained Arahantship. For all these elders, however, their respective past aspirations and resolutions will manifest at the place where they have come to be.
This Anuruddha Thera, meanwhile, [was in the presence] of the General of the Dhamma...

Having taken up his meditation subject, Anuruddha went to the Eastern Bamboo Deer Park in the Cetiya country and, while practicing the duties of a recluse, reflected upon the seven thoughts of a great man;

he grew weary at the eighth. The Teacher, knowing that "Anuruddha is wearying at the eighth thought of a great man," and thinking, "I shall fulfill his aspiration," went there and sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared.

Having sat down and fulfilled the eighth reflection of a Great Man, and having expounded the practice of the Great Noble Lineage adorned by contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation, he rose into the air and returned to the Bhesakaḷā Grove.
As soon as the Tathāgata had departed, the Elder became a possessor of the three knowledges and one whose taints were destroyed; [he thought], "The Teacher, knowing my mind..."
Having arrived and fulfilled the eighth thought of a Great Man, he bestowed it upon me. And my own heart’s desire has reached its fulfillment.
Concerning this Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas and the Dhamma he himself had penetrated, he spoke these verses:
“Having understood my intention, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, [bestowed it].”
With a mind-made body, he approached by means of psychic power.
"Just as my intention was, so he taught even further:
the Buddha, who delights in the non-proliferated, taught the non-proliferated."
“Having understood his Dhamma, I dwelt delighting in the Teacher’s dispensation;
having attained the threefold knowledge, I have fulfilled the Buddha’s instruction.
Later, while residing at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying: “Among those who possess the divine eye in my dispensation, Anuruddha is the chief.”
The Story of the Elder Bhaddiya (193).
In the sixth [verse], "of those born of high families" means those born into noble lineages.
Bhaddiya was the Sakyan prince who went forth together with the Elder Anuruddha. "Son of Kāḷigodhā": that queen was black-complexioned; her name, however, was Godhā.
Therefore, he is called “Kāḷigodhā”; the meaning is “the son of her. But why is he called the foremost of those from high-born families?
Is there no one of even higher birth than him? Yes, there is none.
For his mother was the eldest in age among the Sākiyan women, and he himself, having renounced the sovereignty attained within the Sākiyan clan, went forth into homelessness. Therefore—

He is called the foremost among those of noble birth. Moreover, by the power of his former aspiration, he was reborn in royal families for five hundred successive births in regular succession and indeed ruled as king. For this reason also, he is called the foremost among those of noble birth.
Now, this is the sequential account regarding his past deeds: in the past, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a family of great wealth.
Having been reborn, he went to hear the Dhamma in the manner already described.

On that day, seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among the bhikkhus from noble families, he thought, “In the future, it would be fitting for me also to become the foremost among the bhikkhus from noble families in the dispensation of a Buddha. Having thus invited the Tathāgata, he—
Having given a great alms-offering for seven days to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, he prostrated at his feet, making this aspiration:
"Venerable Sir, by the fruit of this gift, I do not desire any other success;
rather, in the future, under the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I become the foremost among the bhikkhus from noble families."
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his undertaking would succeed, prophesied: "This work of yours will be successful.
At the end of one hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; in his dispensation, you shall become the foremost of the monks from noble families.
Having thus given the prediction and delivered a discourse of thanksgiving for the meal, he went to the monastery. He too—
Having received that prophecy, he inquired about the karma conducive to birth in a high-born family;
he had Dharma-seats constructed, had coverings spread upon them, provided Dharma-fans, established a rotation for Dharma-preachers, and offered oil for lamps in the Uposatha hall.
Having thus performed many kinds of wholesome deeds throughout his life, when he passed away there, he was reborn among the devas.
And while wandering among humans, during the interval between the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Possessor of the Ten Powers, and our own Blessed One,
he was reborn in Bārāṇasī in the house of a householder.
At that time, many Paccekabuddhas, having come from Mount Gandhamādana, arrived at the Ganges in Bārāṇasī.
Sitting down in a comfortable spot on the bank, they partook of the alms-food.
That householder, having learned that they regularly took their meal-break at that very place, spread out eight stone slabs and served the Paccekabuddhas for as long as he lived.
Then, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans during the interval between Buddhas, in this present arising of a Buddha—
He was born into a kṣatriya family in the city of Kapilavatthu. On the day of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name Bhaddiya Kumāra.
Upon reaching maturity, in the manner described below in the *Anuruddha Sutta*, he became one of the six kṣatriyas;
and while the Teacher was dwelling in the Anupiya mango grove, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and attained arahantship.

He attained [the fruit]. Later, while residing at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher placed the Elder Bhaddiya—the son of Kāḷigodhā—into the foremost position, declaring: "In my dispensation, among those of noble birth, the Elder Bhaddiya is the foremost.
The Story of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka-Bhaddiya.
194. "Of those with sweet voices" (*mañjussarānaṃ*) means of those with melodious voices.
"Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya": he was short in stature and named Bhaddiya. Regarding his inquiry, this is the sequential narrative:

he too, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, was born into a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī, and in the manner already described, [he went] to the monastery for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
At that time, seeing the Teacher designate a certain monk of sweet voice as foremost among his disciples, he conceived the thought:
"O, may I too in the future become the foremost of monks with sweet voices within the dispensation of a Buddha, just like this monk!
Having thus resolved, he invited the Teacher and, for seven days, [honored] the community headed by the Buddha.
Having given a great alms-offering to the community of monks, he made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the fruit of this gift, I do not desire any other excellence;
rather, in the future, under the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I become the foremost among those monks with sweet voices.
Having thus prayed, he lay down at the feet of the Teacher. The Teacher, surveying the future, saw that his wish would be fulfilled.

“‘This deed of yours will succeed; at the end of one hundred thousand eons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and you will become the foremost among the monks with sweet voices in his dispensation. Having thus prophesied, he went to the monastery.
And he, having received that prophecy, performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life and, after passing away from there, was reborn among the devas.”
While wandering among humans during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Vipassī, he became a cuckoo named Cittapattaka.

Living in the Khema Deer Park, one day he went to the Himalayas; while returning after picking a sweet mango fruit with his beak, he saw the Teacher surrounded by the community of monks and thought: "On other days..."
“Empty indeed I have seen the Tathāgata; but today this mango fruit has come for the sake of my children.
I shall bring more for them, but it is fitting that I give this one to the One of Ten Powers. Having descended, he moved through the air.
The Teacher, knowing his mind, looked toward his attendant named the Elder Asoka. He [took] the bowl...
Having brought it out, he placed it in the Teacher’s hand. That cuckoo set the mango fruit into the bowl of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
The Teacher sat right there and consumed it. With a mind full of serene confidence, the cuckoo repeatedly reflected upon the virtues of the One Possessing Ten Powers;
having paid homage to the One Possessing Ten Powers, he went to his own nest and spent seven days in the bliss of rapture.
Such was the wholesome karma performed by him in that existence; by means of this karma, his voice became sweet.
However, during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, when the construction of a cetiya had begun, they asked, "What size shall we make it?
"Seven yojanas in size. "This is too large; let us make it six yojanas. "This too is too large; let us make it five yojanas, four yojanas..."
When it was said, "three yojanas, two yojanas," he, being the chief architect at that time, said, "Come, sirs,
it is right to prepare for its easy maintenance in the future. Taking a measuring line,
he stood at a distance of one *gāvuta* while marking out the perimeter, saying, "Let each opening be one *gāvuta*, and the Cetiya shall be one *yojana* in circumference and one *yojana* in height."
He said: "They stood by his word. Thus, he set a limit for the Buddha who is immeasurable.
Because of that kamma, in every place where he was reborn, he was of a smaller stature than others. During the time of our Teacher, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a family of great wealth;
they gave him the name Bhaddiya. When he reached maturity, while the Teacher was at the Great Monastery of Jetavana—
While residing there, he went to the monastery and, having heard a discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith.
He went forth, received a meditation subject from the Teacher, and by practicing insight (vipassanā), he attained Arahantship.
Later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among the bhikkhus of sweet voice.
The Story of the Elder Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja 195.
Regarding the eighth [verse], "of those who roar the lion’s roar": *sīhanādikānaṃ* means of those who are roaring the lion’s roar. As for *Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja*:
it is said that on the very day he attained *arahatta*, taking his bowl, he went from monastery to monastery and from cell to cell, [thinking]: "To whom..."
"Should there be any doubt regarding the path or the fruit, let him question me"—thus he roared his lion’s roar as he wandered.
Standing even before the Buddhas, he roared his lion’s roar, saying: "Venerable Sir, in this dispensation, the task that was to be done has reached its culmination for me.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who roar the lion’s roar.
Regarding his past deeds, this is the sequential account: it is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in the form of a lion at the foot of a mountain.
At dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world, perceived his perfection of causes;
having wandered for alms in Haṃsavatī and finished his meal, he went after the lion had departed for its prey to the cave where the lion dwelt.
Having entered, he sat cross-legged in mid-air and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Sīha, having returned from foraging and standing at the mouth of the cave, saw the One of Ten Powers seated within the cave and thought:
"There is no other being capable of entering my dwelling place and sitting there; truly great is this person, who [sits] within the cave."
He sat down with his legs crossed in the full lotus posture. The radiance of his body spread out and pervaded everything around him;
never before had I seen such a marvel. "This person must be the foremost among those worthy of worship in this world;
it is right for me to pay him honor according to my ability and strength. Thus he spoke, and [gathered] various flowers from both water and land.

Having gathered flowers from the ground as far as the place where he was seated on his couch, he spread out a seat of flowers and stood for the entire night facing the Tathāgata, paying homage to him. On the following day, having removed the old flowers, he spread out the seat with new flowers.
In this very manner, having prepared the flower-seat for seven days and generated powerful joy and gladness, he remained there.
He took up his guard at the entrance of the cave. On the seventh day, the Teacher emerged from cessation and stood at the entrance of the cave.
Sīha, the king of beasts, circumambulated the Tathāgata three times, paid homage at four places, and then withdrew to stand aside.
The Teacher, thinking, "This much will suffice as a supporting condition for him," rose into the air and returned to the monastery itself.
That lion, too, having passed away while suffering from the separation from the Buddha, took rebirth in a family of great *sāla* trees in the city of Haṃsavatī.

When he reached maturity, one day, while going to the monastery with the city-dwellers and listening to the preaching of the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who roar like lions; and [the youth], in the same manner as previously described, [made a vow].
Having performed a great almsgiving for seven days and aspired to that particular state, he was prophesied by the Teacher upon seeing that his wish would be fulfilled.

Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed away there and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a prominent brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha. By name, he was Bhāradvāja.
He was so named. When he reached maturity, having mastered the three Vedas, he wandered about teaching the mantras to five hundred young brahmins.
Because of his status as the eldest, he personally accepted alms from all those invited to feasts.
It is said that he was somewhat of a greedy nature; together with those young brahmins, he would ask, "Where is the rice-gruel? Where is the meal?"
He wandered about seeking only rice gruel, boiled rice, and snacks; because he wandered seeking alms-food wherever he went, he became known as Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja.
One day, when the Teacher had arrived at Rājagaha, he heard a discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth into homelessness.
While practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahatta*.

At the very moment he reached *arahatta*, taking his key, he went from monastery to monastery and from cell to cell, wandering about while uttering a lion’s roar: "Whoever has any doubt regarding the path or the fruit, let him question me. One day, by the merchant of Rājagaha...

Having caused it to be hoisted up by means of a succession of bamboo poles and suspended in the air, he took by supernormal power a bowl made of the heartwood of sandalwood, which was the color of jasmine flowers, and surrounded by the great multitude who were offering shouts of "Well done!", he returned to the monastery and placed it in the hand of the Tathāgata.
Although the Teacher already knew, he asked: "Bhāradvāja, from where did you obtain this bowl?"

He related the reason for what had occurred. The Teacher, having rebuked him in many ways, saying, "You have displayed such a superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) to the great multitude; you have done what ought not to be done," declared:
"Monks, a superhuman state or a miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya) must not be displayed to laypeople. Whoever should display it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
He laid down a training rule.
Then, in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, this discussion arose: “On the very day he attained arahantship, the Elder Sīhanādi spoke in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, saying:
‘Whoever has any doubt regarding the path or the fruit, let him ask me.’”
He declared his attainment of Arahantship even in the presence of the Buddhas, while the other disciples remained silent.
By means of that very lion’s roar, he inspired faith in the great multitude, ascended into the air, and took the sandalwood-essence leaf.
Those monks, combining these three qualities together, reported them to the Teacher. And the Buddhas indeed...
“They censure what is worthy of censure and praise what is worthy of praise”—in this context, having taken up only that quality of the Elder which is worthy of praise, [the Buddha said]:
“Monks, it is because of the development and cultivation of three faculties that the bhikkhu Bhāradvāja declared final knowledge: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived...’”
‘What was to be done has been done; I know there is nothing further for this state of being.
Of which three? Of the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
It is, monks, because these three faculties have been developed and cultivated that the bhikkhu Bhāradvāja declared final knowledge: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived...’”

Having praised the Elder with the words, “What was to be done has been done; I understand that there is no further state of being such as this,” he placed him in the foremost position among the monks who utter the lion’s roar.
This is the story of the Elder Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī.
196. On the ninth [day], Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta by name was born; he was called Puṇṇa because he was full [of merit], and "Mantāṇiputta" because he was the son of the brahmin woman Mantāṇī.

Regarding his interrogation, this is the sequential account: it is said that even before the appearance of the Blessed One Padumuttara, the One of Ten Powers, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great brahmin landowners. On the day of his naming ceremony...
They gave him the name Gotama. When he reached maturity, having mastered the three Vedas and become skilled in all arts, he wandered about accompanied by a retinue of five hundred young brahmins.
Upon examining even those three Vedas, and seeing no path to liberation, he thought:
"This so-called triad of Vedas is like the trunk of a plantain tree—smooth on the outside but devoid of essence within; what is the use of wandering about while holding onto this?"

"It is like a mere threshing-floor; what use have I for this? Having thus gone forth into the ascetic life (isipabbajjā) and developed the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), he thought, "May I, without falling away from jhāna, be reborn in the Brahma-world.
Then, together with five hundred young men, he went to the foot of a mountain and went forth into the ascetic life. His retinue consisted of eight thousand matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila).

They existed. Having realized the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*) and the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭha-samāpatti*), he instructed them in the preliminary practice of the meditation objects (*kasiṇa-parikamma*).
Abiding by his advice, they all likewise realized the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments.
When a long period had passed and that ascetic Gotama had reached old age, the Ten-Powered One Padumuttara attained his first full enlightenment.
Having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he dwelt near the city of Haṃsavatī surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
One day, at the time of dawn, while surveying the world, he perceived that the assembly of the ascetic Gotama possessed the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship,
and that the ascetic Gotama himself would, in a future age, become a monk who preaches the Dhamma in the dispensation of the Buddha then to arise.
Having seen that his aspiration was "May I become the foremost," he performed his bodily care early in the morning, took his own bowl and robes himself,
and when the disciples of the ascetic Gotama had gone out to gather roots, fruits, and forest produce in the guise of a stranger,
he went and stood at the door of Gotama’s leaf-hut. Although Gotama did not know that a Buddha had appeared in the world, [he saw him].
Seeing the One of Ten Powers from afar, he recognized: "This man appears as one liberated from the world;

by the perfection of his physical form and the marks with which he is endowed, it is known that if he remains in the midst of a household, he will become a wheel-turning monarch, but if he goes forth, he will become an omniscient Buddha who has rolled back the veil [of ignorance].
Having understood this, he paid homage to the One of Ten Powers at the very first sight.
Saying, “Come this way, Blessed One,” he prepared a Buddha-seat and offered it to him. The Tathāgata sat down, teaching the Dhamma to the ascetic.

At that moment, those matted-hair ascetics, thinking, “Having given the most excellent forest roots and fruits to our teacher, we shall eat what remains,” were approaching when they saw the One of Ten Powers seated on a high seat, while their teacher was seated on a low seat.
Seeing this, they said, "Look! We used to wander about thinking, 'In this world, there is no one superior to our teacher.
But now, we see someone sitting on a high seat while making our teacher sit on a low seat;
surely this must be a great man! And so, taking up their baskets, they approached. The ascetic Gotama [thought], "These people are coming to me because of the Ten-Powered One..."

Fearing that they might pay homage to him while he was nearby, he spoke from a distance: "Sirs, do not pay homage to me! This person seated here is the Supreme Being in the world with its devas, worthy of homage by all;
pay homage to him. Thinking, "The Teacher would not speak thus without knowing," the ascetics all paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata.
"Sirs, [pay homage] to another for us—the One of Ten Powers..."

“There is no food suitable to be given; we shall give this forest root and fruit,” he thought, and he placed the most excellent of delicacies into the bowls of the Buddhas. The Teacher partook of the forest roots and fruits.
Immediately thereafter, the ascetic also partook together with his disciples. Having finished his meal, the Teacher said, “The two Chief Disciples...”

He thought, "Let them come, bringing with them a hundred thousand bhikkhus. At that moment, the chief disciple, the Elder Mahādevala, reflecting, "Where has the Teacher gone? realized, "The Teacher is waiting for our arrival.
Taking a hundred thousand bhikkhus, he went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and stood there paying respect.
Gotama said to his pupils, “Sons, we have no other offerings; the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is in distress.
We shall prepare a flower seat for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Bring flowers from both water and land!
They immediately brought back, by means of their psychic power, flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain.

The seats were prepared in the very same manner as described in the account of the Elder Sāriputta. That he entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and that a sunshade was held over him—all this is to be understood according to the same method already stated.
On the seventh day, the Teacher emerged from cessation; seeing the ascetics standing around him, [he considered] their fitness for the role of Dhamma-preachers.
He addressed that foremost disciple: “Monk, great honor has been paid by this company of seers;
offer words of thanksgiving for their flower-seats. Having accepted the Teacher’s word, he mastered the Three Piṭakas and delivered the thanksgiving.
At the conclusion of his discourse, the Teacher himself let forth the Brahma-voice and taught the Dhamma.
He taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of that teaching, with the exception of the ascetic Gotama, the remaining eighteen thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahatship.
However, Gotama, being unable to achieve realization in that very existence, said to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the name of this monk by whom the Dhamma was first taught in your dispensation? This was Gotama.
“He shall be the foremost of those who preach the Dhamma in my teaching. Having made this aspiration, saying, “Venerable sir,
by the fruit of this service performed by me for seven days, may I too— in the future, in the teaching of a certain Buddha—
become the foremost of those who preach the Dhamma, just like this bhikkhu,” he prostrated himself at his feet.
The Teacher, looking into the future and knowing that the ascetic’s aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle, prophesied:
"In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand kappas, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; you shall become the foremost of the Dhamma-preachers in his dispensation.
Having thus prophesied, he said to those ascetics who had attained Arahatship, "Come, monks. All [became monks].
With their hair and beards vanished, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power, they became like elder monks of sixty years' standing.
The Teacher, taking the community of bhikkhus, went to the monastery.
Gotama also, having served the Tathāgata for as long as he lived and having performed meritorious deeds according to his strength, [remained] for a hundred thousand aeons.

Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was born during the time of our Blessed One into a prominent brahmin family in the brahmin village of Doṇavatthu, not far from the city of Kapilavatthu. On the day his name was given, they named him Puṇṇa Māṇava.
When the Teacher had attained full enlightenment and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, he eventually arrived [there] in due course.
While residing near Rājagaha, the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña went to Kapilavatthu,
ordained his own nephew Puṇṇa Māṇava, and on the following day, having returned to the presence of the One of Ten Powers, paid homage to the Blessed One and, taking leave of him,
went to the Chaddanta Lake to dwell there. Puṇṇa, the son of Mantāṇī, [was thus ordained] by his maternal uncle, the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña.

Without going into the presence of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, he thought, "I will go into the presence of the One Possessing the Ten Powers only after I have brought my duties as a renunciant to their ultimate fulfillment.

He remained right there in Kapilavatthu, applying himself to wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), and before long he attained *arahantship*. Five hundred sons of noble family who had gone forth under him likewise [attained the same].
They were [ordained]. The Elder himself, having attained the ten bases of discourse, exhorted them with those same ten bases of discourse.
Standing by his exhortation, they all attained arahantship.
Knowing that their duty as renunciants had reached its culmination, they approached their preceptor and said:
“Venerable sir, our task has reached its conclusion; we have obtained the ten bases of great discourse.
It is now time for us to see the One of Ten Powers. When the Elder heard their words, he thought:

“The Teacher knows that I have obtained the ten bases of great discourse. When I teach the Dhamma, I do so without ever departing from those ten bases of great discourse. If I were to go [to the Buddha]...”
"All these bhikkhus will go surrounding me; however, it is improper for me to go in such a crowd and see the One of Ten Powers. Let these [bhikkhus] go first and see him. He said to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, you go on ahead and see the Tathāgata; in my name, pay homage at the feet of the One of Ten Powers. I too—"
“We shall go by the path you have taken.

All those elders—residents of the kingdom that was the Blessed One’s birthplace, all of them whose taints were destroyed, and all of them who had attained the ten topics of discourse—did not disregard their preceptor’s instruction;
traveling by stages on their journey, they covered a road of sixty yojanas.
Having passed beyond Rājagaha and gone to the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana, they paid homage at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers and sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Blessed Buddhas to exchange greetings with visiting monks;
therefore, the Blessed One addressed them in this manner: "I hope, monks, that you are faring well," and so forth.
Having exchanged pleasant greetings, he asked, "Monks, where have you come from? When they replied,
"From our native land," he said, "Monks, who in the native land is so esteemed by his fellow celibate practitioners,
being himself moderate in desires and a speaker of moderation among the monks?"
He questioned a monk who had attained the ten bases of discourse. They replied, "Venerable sir, it is the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta.
Having heard that report, the Venerable Sāriputta desired to see the Elder.
Then the Teacher went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī. The Elder Puṇṇa learned of the arrival of the One Possessed of Ten Powers there.
Having heard this, he thought, "I shall see the Teacher," and having gone there, he reached the Tathāgata within the inner perfumed chamber itself.

The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma and paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, the Elder went to the Blind Men’s Grove for seclusion and sat at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest. Sāriputta the Elder also [went] to him...
Having heard of his arrival, he went along with his disciples; finding a suitable place, he approached the foot of that tree and exchanged greetings with the Elder.
He then asked about the sequence of the seven purifications. The Elder answered each of his questions as they were asked.
They both rejoiced in one another’s well-spoken words. Later, the Teacher, in the midst of the community of monks—
Seated, he established the Elder in the foremost position among those who preach the Dhamma.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Mahākaccāna.
Regarding the tenth [sutta], "of what was spoken in brief": this refers to the Dhamma spoken in brief; [the Buddha] [expounded] its meaning in detail.
"Of those who analyze" means of those who, having expanded that teaching, analyze its meaning.
It is said that while others are able to fulfill the Tathāgata’s concise statement either by way of the meaning or by way of the phrasing, this Elder is able to do so by way of both.
Therefore, he was called "the foremost. His previous aspiration was also of such a kind.
Now, this is the sequential account regarding his interrogation: It is said that during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a family of great householders.
Having grown up, one day he went to the monastery in the manner already described.
Standing at the edge of the assembly, as he listened to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher explaining in detail the meaning of what had been spoken by himself in brief to those who were analyzing it.
Seeing a certain bhikkhu being placed in the foremost position, he thought, "Great indeed is this bhikkhu, that the Teacher praises him in such a way;
it behooves me also, in the future, under the dispensation of a Buddha, to become like this.
Having invited the Teacher and given a great almsgiving for seven days in the manner already described, he said, "Venerable Sir, regarding this honor I have performed..."

“I do not pray for any other success through this fruit; rather, in the future, under the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I also obtain that very same position, just like the bhikkhu whom you have appointed to that position seven days from now,” he said, making this aspiration and prostrating at the Teacher’s feet.
The Teacher, looking into the future, saw: “This son of noble family’s wish will be fulfilled.”
Having seen this, he declared: "O son of good family, at the end of one hundred thousand future eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise;
you shall become the foremost among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief within his dispensation.
Having thus prophesied and offered words of appreciation, he departed.
That clansman, too, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, wandered among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons.
During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he took rebirth in a noble family in Bārāṇasī.

After the Teacher had attained Parinibbāna, he went to the site where the Golden Cetiya was being built and made an offering with a golden brick worth a hundred thousand [pieces]. He thought: "In whatever place the Blessed One is reborn, may I..."
He made this aspiration: "May my body be golden-colored.

Then, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*, he was reborn at the time of our appearance as the One of Ten Powers in the house of a chaplain in the city of Ujjain.
On the day of his naming ceremony, [the chaplain said]: "My son has a golden-colored body..."
“Since he has come taking his own name for himself,” they gave him the name Kañcanamāṇava.
As he grew up, he mastered the three Vedas and, upon his father’s passing, obtained the position of court chaplain. By virtue of his clan, he became known as Kaccāna.
King Caṇḍapajjota, having assembled his ministers, said: “A Buddha has appeared in the world; those capable of bringing him [here]—”
“Go and bring him back, dear ones. “Your Majesty, there is no one else capable of bringing the One of Ten Powers;
only the teacher, the Brahmin Kaccāna, is capable. Send for him. The king had him summoned and said, “Dear son, go into the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
[The Brahmin replied,] “Great King, I will go once I am permitted to go forth into the religious life. “Whatever you wish, dear son,” said the king.

“Father, having done so, bring the Tathāgata here. He thought, “There is no need for a large retinue when going into the presence of the Buddhas,” and he went along with him as the eighth person. Then the Teacher taught him the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, together with seven other people, he attained Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Teacher said, “Come, monks.”
He extended his hand. At that very moment, they all had their hair and beards vanish and, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power, became like elders of sixty years' standing.
When the Elder saw that his own task had reached its conclusion, instead of remaining silent, he [addressed] the Teacher, just as the Elder Kāḷudāyī had done.
He spoke in praise of going for the purpose of traveling to Ujjenī. When the Teacher heard his words, he understood:
"Kaccāna is hoping for my visit to his native land. Now, Buddhas do not go to an improper place for the sake of a single reason.
Therefore, he said to the Elder: "Bhikkhu, you yourself go; in you..."

"Even when he has gone, the King will be pleased. The Elder, thinking, "There are no two kinds of speech for the Buddhas," paid homage to the Tathāgata and, traveling toward Ujjenī with the seven monks who had come with him, entered for alms in a market town called Telapanāḷi along the way.
In that market town, there were two daughters of wealthy merchants.
Among them, one was born into a decayed family; she was poor and lived by relying on a nurse after her parents passed away.

Her physical form, however, was flourishing, and her hair was exceptionally long compared to others. In that same town, there was another girl who was the daughter of a wealthy merchant family, but she was destitute.
Previously, [the first girl] had sent her to the other’s presence, saying, "I will give you a hundred or a thousand [pieces of money]."
Even after saying this, she was unable to have her hair pulled out.
On that day, however, the merchant’s daughter saw the Elder Mahākaccāna approaching with seven monks, their bowls empty;
seeing him, she thought, "This one golden-hued monk, a kinsman of the Brahmā, [is as radiant] as if he had just been washed..."
"He comes on foot, and I have no other wealth. However, the daughter of such-and-such a merchant sent these hair-cuts for their sake.
Now, with the proceeds obtained from this, it will be possible to give a gift to the Elder.
Having said this, she sent the nurse, invited the Elders, and had them sit within her house. While the Elders were seated, she entered the inner chamber.
Having had her own hair dressed by the nurse, she said, “Mother, give these hairs to the daughter of such-and-such a merchant;
bring back whatever she gives, and we shall provide almsfood for the noble ones.
The nurse, wiping away her tears with the back of her hand while supporting her heart-flesh with one hand, hid herself near the elders.
Taking those hairs, they went into the presence of that merchant’s daughter.
For even merchandise that is of great value does not inspire respect unless it is presented by oneself; therefore, the merchant’s daughter thought:
"Previously, I was unable to have these hairs brought to me even for a vast amount of wealth, but now—"
“From the time they were cut, they will not grow back from their original roots,” she thought.
She said to the nursemaid, “Previously, I could not get your mistress to have her hair restored even for a great sum of money;
yet hair that has fallen off anywhere due to death is worth eight kahāpaṇas. She then gave her eight kahāpaṇas. The nursemaid—
Having brought it, he gave it to the merchant’s daughter. The merchant’s daughter, valuing each alms-offering at one kahāpaṇa, had them given to the elders.
The elder, having reflected and perceived the merchant’s daughter’s spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), asked, "Where is the merchant’s daughter?
"In the inner chamber, venerable sir," they replied. "Summon her," he said. Out of reverence for the elders, she came with a single word.
Having paid homage there, she conceived powerful faith, thinking: "Almsfood established in a fertile field yields its fruit even in this very life.
Thus, along with her salutation of the elders, her hair returned to its natural state.
The elders, taking that almsfood, rose up into the air right before the eyes of the merchant’s daughter and descended into the Golden Grove.
Seeing the Elder, the park-keeper went into the presence of the king and said, "Your Majesty, my noble master Kaccāna, the royal chaplain, has gone forth and come to the park.
King Caṇḍapajjota went to the park, and after the Elder had finished his meal, he paid homage to him with the fivefold prostration and sat down to one side.
He asked, "Venerable sir, where is the Blessed One? The Teacher, without coming himself, [sent word].
“I sent for you, Great King. “Where, venerable sir, did you receive almsfood today?
The Elder related everything that the merchant’s daughter had done so skillfully, corresponding to the king’s own inquiries.
The king prepared a dwelling place for the Elder, invited him there, and having gone to his residence, he commanded the merchant’s daughter and established her in the position of chief queen.
This woman obtained fame even in this very life.
From that time forth, the king paid great honor to the Elder. Having gained confidence through the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma, the great multitude went forth into homelessness in his presence.
From that time forth, the entire city was illuminated by the single color of the saffron robes.
There was a wind blowing both with and against the current. That queen, having conceived, gave birth to a son after the lapse of ten months.
On the day of the naming ceremony, they gave him the name Gopālaka Kumāra after his maternal grandfather, the merchant.
Because of her son’s name, the queen became known as Gopālamātā. Having placed great faith in the Elder, that queen informed the king.
He had a monastery built for the Elder in the Kañcanavana grove. After the Elder had brought prosperity to the city of Ujjenī, he returned once more to the presence of the Teacher.

Later, while staying at Jetavana, the Teacher—having established the occasion for these three discourses, namely the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta, the Kaccānapeyyāla, and the Pārāyana Sutta—spoke to the Elder in brief.
"He placed [them] in the foremost position among those who analyze the meaning in detail.
This concludes the commentary on the First Chapter. 14. The Chapter on the Foremost (Etadagga-vagga).
(14) 2. The Second Chapter on the Foremost:
The Story of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, 198–200.
In the first [sutta] of the second [chapter], "mind-made" (*manomaya*) means produced by the mind. "With a mind-made body, by means of psychic power..."
In the passage where it is said, “he approached,” the so-called mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) is that which is produced by the mind.
In the passage where it is said, “he arises with a certain mind-made body,” the so-called mind-made body is that which is generated by the mind.
It is this latter sense that is intended here. In that context, when other bhikkhus generate a mind-made body, they [generate] three...
They produce either four, but not many; and they produce them by making them exactly alike, performing only a single kind of kamma.
However, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka created a thousand ascetics with a single act of adverting consciousness.
He did not make even two people alike, nor were they performing a single kind of kamma. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who manifest mind-made bodies.

Among those skilled in the turning away of the mind (*cetovivaṭṭa-kusala*), Cūḷapanthaka alone was the foremost; however, among those skilled in the turning away of perception (*saññāvivaṭṭa-kusala*), the Elder Mahāpanthaka is said to be the foremost.

In this regard, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka is called "skilled in the turning away of the mind" because he had attained the four fine-material-sphere jhānas, while the Elder Mahāpanthaka is called "skilled in the turning away of perception" because he had attained the four immaterial-sphere jhānas.

Thus it was said. Cūḷapanthaka is called "skilled in the turning away of the mind" due to his proficiency in concentration (*samādhi*); Mahāpanthaka is called "skilled in the turning away of perception" (*saññā*) due to his proficiency in insight (*vipassanā*).
Furthermore, one of them is expert in the characteristics of concentration, while the other is expert in the characteristics of insight.

Likewise, one is immersed in concentration, while the other is immersed in insight. Moreover, one is expert in the compendium of factors (*aṅga*), while the other is expert in the compendium of objects (*ārammaṇa*).
Likewise, one is skilled in the determination of the factors (*aṅga*) and the other is skilled in the determination of the object (*ārammaṇa*); thus should the application be made here.
Furthermore, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka, having attained the fine-material-sphere jhānas, emerged from those jhāna-factors and reached Arahantship;
thus he was skilled in the turning away of the mind (*cetovivaṭṭa*). The Elder Mahāpanthaka, having attained the immaterial-sphere jhānas, emerged from those jhāna-factors...
One who has attained *arahantship* is skilled in the turning away from perceptions. Because both were born on a path (*pantha*), they were named Panthakas.
Of these two, the one born first was named Mahāpanthaka, and the one born later was named Cūḷapanthaka.
Now, regarding the life-stories of these two, this is the sequential narrative: it is said that in the past, during the time of Buddha Padumuttara—
Two brothers who were householders living in the city of Haṃsavatī were faithful and confident;
they went regularly into the presence of the Teacher to listen to the Dhamma. One day, the younger brother saw the Teacher praise a certain bhikkhu endowed with two qualities:
"Among those in my teaching who manifest a mind-made body and who are skilled in the turning of the mind..."
Seeing him being placed in the foremost position as "this bhikkhu is the best," he thought: "Great indeed is this bhikkhu;
being alone, he wanders having fulfilled two factors. It is fitting for me also, in the future, to wander as one who fulfills two factors in the dispensation of a Buddha.
