He invited the Teacher in the same manner as before and offered a great almsgiving for seven days.

Having given [the gift], he spoke thus: "Venerable sir, may I too, through the fruit of this meritorious deed, become a fulfiller of these two qualities—just like that bhikkhu whom you placed at the very head of the 'foremost' ranks seven days ago, saying, 'This one is the foremost in my teaching,' by virtue of his mind-made body and his skill in the turning away of the mind. Thus he made his aspiration.
The Teacher, looking into the future, saw that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstacle;

he prophesied, "In the future, at the end of one hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise, and he will establish you in these two positions," and having offered words of appreciation, he departed. One day, his brother also [approached] the Teacher.
Seeing the Buddha place a monk skilled in the turning away from perceptions in the foremost position, he performed service in that very same way and made a formal aspiration;
the Teacher also gave him a prediction.
Both of these individuals, having performed wholesome deeds while the Teacher was still living, [performed offerings] at the shrine of the physical relics at the time of the Teacher’s final passing.
Having performed an offering of gold, they passed away from there and were reborn in the world of the gods.

As they continued to wander through existences among gods and humans, one hundred thousand eons elapsed. In that regard, the meritorious deed performed by Mahāpanthaka in the interim is not mentioned here;
however, Cūḷapanthaka, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, [remained] for twenty thousand years.
Having performed the meditation on the white kasiṇa, he was reborn in the city of the gods.
Then, after our Teacher had attained full enlightenment and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he resided at the Great Monastery of Veḷuvana in dependence upon Rājagaha.
It is appropriate to relate the birth of these two while standing in this place. It is said that in Rājagaha, within a family of wealthy merchants...
The daughter, having formed an intimacy with her own slave and thinking, "Others too might find out about this deed of mine," spoke thus: "It is not possible for us to live in this place;
if my parents should discover this fault, they will cut us to pieces. Let us go and live in a foreign land," and she [gave him] the wealth she had in hand.
Taking her with him, he departed through the main gate and both went their way, thinking, "We shall dwell wherever we find a place unknown to others.
While they were living in one place, through their cohabitation, a fetus was conceived in her womb.
When her pregnancy had reached maturity, she consulted with her husband: "My pregnancy has come to term;
for both of us, giving birth in a place devoid of kinsmen and friends would surely be a source of suffering.
Let us go to our own family home. He delayed the days, saying, "Let us go today," or "Let us go tomorrow. She thought to herself:
“This fool, because of his own great faults, does not dare to go; moreover, parents are indeed those who seek only one’s welfare.

Whether he goes or not, it is fitting that I go. When he had departed from the house, she put away the household goods and, having informed the neighbors of her departure for her own family home, set out on the road.
Then that man, having returned home and not seeing her, questioned his neighbors;
hearing that she had gone to her family home, he pursued her with speed and caught up with her on the way. There, she too gave birth right then and there.
He asked, "What is this, my dear? She replied, "A son has been born, my lord. He asked, "What shall we do now?"
"The purpose for which we were going to our family home has already been accomplished on the way;
what shall we do by going there? Let us turn back. With one mind, the two of them turned back.
Because that child was born on the road (*pantha*), they gave him the name Panthaka. Not long after that, she became pregnant once more. All...
It should be expanded in the same manner as before. Because that child was also born on the road, they gave the first-born the name Mahāpanthaka and the one born later the name Cūḷapanthaka.
Taking both children with them, they went back to their own dwelling place. While they were living there, this...
When the boy Mahāpanthaka heard other children calling their parents "uncle" and "aunt," he questioned his mother:
"Mother, the other children speak of 'uncles' and 'aunts'; do we have no relatives?
"Yes, dear son, you have no relatives here; however, in the city of Rājagaha, you have a relative, the merchant Dhanaseṭṭhi."
“...there is a grandfather, and there you have many kinsmen. Why do you not go there, my dear?
Since she did not tell her son the reason for her own non-going, and as her sons continued to press her again and again, she said to her husband:
“These children distress me excessively; will our parents eat us raw upon seeing us?”
"Come, let us show the children their grandfather’s family. [The other replied: "I shall not be able to appear before them in person, but I will lead him there.
"Very well, master; by whatever means possible, it is right that the children see their grandfather’s family alone.
Thus, the two men took the children and, traveling by stages, eventually reached Rājagaha and stood at the city gate near a certain...
Having made her residence in the hall, the mother of the children informed her parents that she had arrived bringing the two children with her.
Upon hearing that message, they said, "For those wandering through the cycle of existence, there is no such thing as 'son' or 'daughter';
they have committed a great offense against us and cannot stand before our eyes. However, having taken this much wealth..."
"Let both people go to a comfortable place and live; however, let them send the children here.
The merchant’s daughter took the wealth sent by her parents, placed it directly into the hands of the messengers who had come for the children, and sent them off.
The children grew up in their maternal grandfather's family. Among them, Cūḷapanthaka was very young, while Mahāpanthaka lived with his grandfather.
He went to hear the Dhamma discourse of the One Possessing the Ten Powers. As he constantly listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, his mind inclined toward the going forth.
He said to his grandfather, “If you would grant me permission, I would go forth.
“What are you saying, dear? To me, your going forth is more auspicious than the going forth of the entire world. If...”
“Are you able, dear boy, to go forth? Having agreed, he went into the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher asked, “What is it, Great Merchant? Have you obtained a son? “Yes, Bhante; this boy is my grandson, and he says, ‘I wish to go forth in your presence,’” he said.
The Teacher commanded a certain alms-collecting elder, “Ordain this boy. The elder [instructed him] in the meditation subject of the fivefold skin (the *tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having instructed him, he ordained him. Having mastered much of the Buddha’s word, when he had completed his full year of training, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Having become fully ordained, by applying himself to wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), he became an attainer of the four formless-sphere jhānas;
emerging from those jhāna-factors, he reached Arahantship. Thus, he was the foremost among those skilled in the turning away from perception (*saññā-vivaṭṭa-kusala*).
Having been born, he spent his time in the bliss of meditation and the bliss of the fruit [of the path], and he thought:
"Is it possible to give this bliss to Cūḷapanthaka? Then, going to the presence of the Elder Merchant (Ayyakaseṭṭhi), he said:
"Great Merchant, if you consent, I shall ordain Cūḷapanthaka. "Please ordain him, venerable sir," [the merchant replied]. The Elder...
Having ordained the boy Cūḷapanthaka, he established him in the ten precepts. While the novice Cūḷapanthaka was in the presence of his brother, [the latter spoke this verse]:
"Just as a fragrant red lotus, blooming at dawn, remains full of its scent;”
“Behold Aṅgīrasa shining forth, blazing like the sun in the sky”—he recites this verse.
As he takes each successive line after the one already taken, the previous one is lost. To him...
Four months passed while he was striving to learn this single verse.
Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, “Cūḷapanthaka, you are incapable in this dispensation; you have not been able to learn even a single verse in four months.
How then will you bring your purpose as a renunciant to its fulfillment? Depart from here.”
Thus dismissed by the Elder, he stood weeping at the edge of the monastery.
At that time, the Teacher was dwelling near Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove.
On that occasion, Jīvaka sent a man with the instruction: “Invite the Teacher together with five hundred bhikkhus. Now, at that time...
At that time, Mahāpanthaka was the distributor of alms. When he was told, "Venerable sir, please accept alms for five hundred bhikkhus," he replied, "I accept for all except Cūḷapanthaka.
Upon hearing those words, Cūḷapanthaka became even more overcome with dejection. The Teacher [observed] Cūḷapanthaka’s distress.
Seeing this, [the Buddha] thought, "Cūḷapanthaka will attain awakening when I have gone," and so he went and showed himself in a place not far away, saying, "Why are you weeping, Panthaka?

"Venerable Sir, my brother is dismissing me. "Panthaka, your brother does not possess the knowledge of the underlying tendencies and latent dispositions of other persons; you, indeed, are a person to be converted by a Buddha."
Having fashioned it by means of supernormal power, he gave him a pure piece of cloth, saying, "Panthaka, take this and,
saying 'Dust-remover, dust-remover,' develop it. He,
taking the piece of cloth given by the Teacher, rubbed it with his hand, saying, "Dust-remover, dust-remover."
He sat down. As he rubbed it, the hairs became soiled with bodily elements. As he rubbed it further, it became like the residue wiped from a mortar.
Having reached the ripening of his knowledge, he established the contemplation of destruction and fall upon that [cloth] and thought:
"This piece of cloth was originally white and pure, yet by depending on this body subject to clinging..."

"It has become defiled; this mind, too, has such a destiny. Having developed concentration and made the four fine-material-sphere jhānas his foundation, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having become an attainer of the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya), he was capable of being one and becoming many, and of being many and becoming one. And by means of the path of Arahantship itself...
The Tipiṭaka and the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) had also arrived.
On the following day, the Teacher went with four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus and sat down in Jīvaka’s residence.
However, Cūḷapanthaka did not go because his alms-food had not been accepted. Jīvaka...
When he began to give the rice gruel, the Teacher covered the bowl with his hand. "Why, venerable sir, do you not take it?
[the man asked]. "There is a certain bhikkhu in the monastery named Jīvaka," he replied. He then sent a man, saying, "Go, my good man, and bring the noble one who is sitting in the monastery.
Even before that man had arrived, the Elder Cūḷapanthaka [had already gathered] a thousand bhikkhus.
Having created [the monks], he made even one of them unlike another, and he performed for each of them monastic duties—such as the distribution of robes—in a manner unlike that of the others.
That man, seeing the great number of monks in the monastery, went and told Jīvaka:
"Venerable sir, the Saṅgha of monks in this monastery is very large; therefore, it will not be possible to summon a venerable one from there."
“I know him. Jīvaka questioned the Teacher: “Venerable sir, what is the name of the monk sitting in the monastery?
“He is named Cūḷapanthaka, Jīvaka. “Go, sir, ask ‘Which one is named Cūḷapanthaka? and bring him here.
He went to the monastery and asked, “Venerable sir, which one is named Cūḷapanthaka? “I am Cūḷapanthaka.”
“I am Cūḷapanthaka,” he said, and even a thousand bhikkhus spoke thus. Returning again, he told Jīvaka, “About a thousand bhikkhus are all saying, ‘I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka’;
I do not know which one among them should be summoned. Because he had penetrated the Truths, Jīvaka understood by inference that these were bhikkhus possessed of supernormal power.
Knowing this, he said to the monk who had spoken first, "Tell them, 'The Teacher summons you,' and then say, 'Come, dear ones, take hold of the hem of my robe.
That monk went to the monastery and did as instructed; at that very moment, about a thousand monks vanished.
He then took the Elder and departed. At that instant, the Teacher received the rice-gruel.
When the One Possessing the Ten Powers had finished his meal and entered the monastery, a discussion arose in the Dhamma Hall:
“How great indeed are the Buddhas! They have endowed a monk who was unable to learn even a single verse for four months with such great supernormal power.
The Teacher, knowing the mental disposition of those monks, went there, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked: “What is it?”
“Speak, monks,” he asked. “We shall say nothing else, Blessed One;
we shall speak only of your own virtues, for Cūḷapanthaka has received a great gain from you.

“It is not surprising, monks, that now, having followed my instruction, he should receive the inheritance of the supramundane; this was also so in the past, even while he remained with immature knowledge.”
"By following my instruction, he obtained a worldly inheritance. The monks requested, "When was that, venerable sir?
The Teacher brought up the past for those monks and showed it to them:
"Monks, in the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, a king named Brahmadatta reigned. At that time..."
There was a wise and competent man named Cūḷakaseṭṭhi who understood all omens.
One day, while going to attend upon the king, he saw a dead mouse in the middle of the street; at that moment, having calculated the constellations, he said this:
"It is possible for a son of good family endowed with vision, having taken this mouse, to support a wife and carry out his work."

"And let him employ it. A certain son of a poor family, having heard those words of the merchant, thought, "This man will not speak without knowing [the facts]," so he caught a mouse and gave it to a cat in a certain shop for its sake, receiving a *kākaṇika* coin in return.
Having bought molasses with that *kākaṇika* and taken some water in a small pot, he met those returning from the forest.
Seeing the garland-makers, he gave them small pieces of molasses and offered them water from his bowl.
They each gave him a handful of flowers. With that flower-money, on the following day as well, he took molasses and a jar of water and went to the flower garden.
On that day, the garland-makers [offered] half-grown flower clusters to him.
Having given [the money], they departed. Before long, by this means, he obtained eight kahāpaṇas.

Again, on a day of wind and rain, having gone to a neglected garden and sitting there having made a heap of fallen timber, he obtained sixteen kahāpaṇas from a royal potter. When twenty-four kahāpaṇas had thus been acquired—
Thinking, "I have this means," he placed a water jar in a spot not far from the city gate and served five hundred grass-cutters with water.
They said to him, "Friend, you have been very helpful to us; what can we do for you?
He replied, "When a need arises for me, you will do it for me," and so saying, he wandered here and there.
He established a friendship with both a land-trader and a sea-trader.
The land-trader informed him, "Tomorrow a horse-dealer will come to this city bringing five hundred horses.
Having heard his words, he gave instructions to the grass-cutters, telling each of them to bring two bundles of grass instead of one.
Having done so, he had it brought. Then, at the time when the horses were entering the city, he sat down having made a heap of a thousand bundles of grass at the inner gate.
The horse-dealer, unable to find fodder for the horses anywhere in the entire city, paid him a thousand [pieces of money] and took that grass.
Then, after a few days had passed, a companion of his who was engaged in maritime trade informed him, "A great ship has arrived at the port.
Thinking, "This is the means," he took a chariot for a short time, fully equipped with all its trappings, for eight kahāpaṇas.
He went to the harbor, gave a signet ring as a pledge to the boatman, and [stood] not far away.
Having had a curtain enclose that spot, he sat there and commanded his men:
"When foreign merchants arrive, announce them with the third herald. Hearing that a ship had arrived, about a hundred merchants from Benares came, thinking, "We shall take the goods.
[He said: "You will not obtain the goods; at such-and-such a place, by a great merchant..."
"A solemn oath has been given. Having heard this from them, they went into his presence;
the footmen, by virtue of their previous understanding, announced the arrival of those merchants through the third miracle.
Those hundred merchants each gave a thousand pieces of gold, and having traveled together with him by boat, they again gave a thousand pieces each and dismissed the boat.

They made their own goods their own property. That man, having taken two hundred thousand [pieces of gold], came to Bārāṇasī and, thinking, "It is right to be grateful," took one hundred thousand and went into the presence of Cūḷaseṭṭhi.
Then Cūḷaseṭṭhi asked him, "My dear son, what have you done to obtain this wealth? He replied, "By you..."
He said, "Having stood by the method taught, [the goal] was attained within just four months.

When the merchant heard his words, he thought, "Now it is no longer fitting to treat such a boy as the property of another," and so he gave him his daughter who had reached marriageable age and made him the master of his entire household.
That noble youth, upon the death of the merchant, took up the position of merchant in that city.

Having taken it, he remained for the duration of his lifespan and then departed according to his karma. After the Teacher had related these two accounts and established the connection, he spoke this verse at the time of his full enlightenment:
"Even with a small load, the wise and discerning man..."
"He raises himself up, like a tiny spark kindling into a flame.
Thus the Teacher demonstrated this causal sequence to those assembled in the Dhamma Hall.
This is the progressive narrative beginning from the former aspirations of both these great disciples. Later, however, the Teacher, surrounded by a host of noble ones—
Seated upon the Dhamma-throne, he placed the Elder Cūḷapanthaka in the foremost position among those who manifest mind-made bodies and those skilled in the turning away of the mind,
and the Elder Mahāpanthaka among those skilled in the turning away of perception.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Subhūti.

201. Regarding the third [classification], "those who dwell in the state free from conflict" (*araṇavihārīnaṃ*): this refers to those who dwell free from defilements (*nikkilesavihārīnaṃ*). For "conflict" (*raṇa*) is said to be the defilements such as lust and the rest;

by their absence, dwelling free from defilements is called "dwelling in the state free from conflict. Those who possess this are "those who dwell in the state free from conflict. Among them, the Elder Subhūti is the foremost.
Although other *khīṇāsavas* (those whose cankers are destroyed) are also indeed dwellers in the state free from conflict, [Subhūti is preeminent].
However, this name was acquired by the Elder because of his teaching of the Dhamma.

For when other bhikkhus teach the Dhamma, they speak with partiality, either praising or disparaging; but the Elder, when teaching the Dhamma, teaches without deviating from the method taught by the Teacher.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who dwell in non-conflict (*araṇavihārin*).
202. Regarding the fourth [verse], "of those worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ*), this means those who are deserving of offerings (*dakkhiṇāraha*).

In that regard, although others who have destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*) are also supreme recipients of offerings, the Elder, while wandering for alms, would enter the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettājhāna*) in every house;

then, emerging from that attainment, he would accept alms-food, thinking, "In this way, it will be of great fruit for those who give the alms. Therefore, [he is described as] "of those worthy of offerings."
He was called "Aggā" (the Foremost). However, his personal existence (*attabhāva*) was perfectly accomplished;
it shone exceedingly, like a decorated gateway or a painted cloth. Therefore, he is called Subhūti.
Regarding his inquiry, this is the sequential narrative: it is said that even before the Blessed One Padumuttara had appeared...
He was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a great brahmin family; they gave him the name Nanda Māṇava.

When he reached maturity, having mastered the three Vedas and seeing no essence therein, he went forth as an ascetic on a mountain slope together with his retinue of forty-four thousand young men, and attained the five supernormal powers and the eight...
He attained the meditative absorptions (samāpatti) and caused his disciples as well to become attainers of jhāna.
At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having appeared in the world and dwelling in dependence on the city of Haṃsavatī,
one day at dawn, surveying the world, perceived the potential for the ascetic Nanda’s matted-hair disciples to attain arahantship.
Having seen that the ascetic Nanda, who was endowed with two factors, had made an aspiration for a higher status as his disciple,
[the Buddha] attended to his body early in the morning, took his bowl and robe during the forenoon,
and went to the hermitage of the ascetic Nanda in the same manner described in the account of the Elder Sāriputta. There, he accepted offerings of various fruits and had a seat prepared with flowers.
The attainment of the cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) should be understood in the manner already described.

However, having emerged from cessation, the Teacher commanded a certain disciple—who was endowed with two factors, namely the factor of dwelling in the state free from conflict (*araṇavihāra*) and the factor of being worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*)—saying, "Offer words of thanksgiving for the flower-seats to the company of seers. He [the disciple], of his own...
Standing in his place and reflecting upon the Tipiṭaka, he offered a blessing of appreciation. At the conclusion of his discourse, the Teacher himself taught the Dhamma.
At the end of that teaching, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained Arahatship.
However, the ascetic Nanda, having taken a mental sign from the monk who had offered the blessing, applied his knowledge according to the Teacher’s instruction.
He was unable to send them. The Teacher extended his hand toward the remaining bhikkhus, saying, "Come, bhikkhus.
All of them had their hair and beards vanish and were endowed with requisites created by supernormal power, appearing like elders of sixty years' standing.
The ascetic Nanda, having paid homage to the Tathāgata, stood before him and said: "Venerable Sir, as for the bhikkhu who [belonged to] the group of seers..."
“Who among you in the Dispensation is this person who has performed the rejoicing at the flower-seats? [The Buddha replied:

“He has attained the foremost rank by virtue of his practice of dwelling in non-affliction (*araṇavihāra*) and his quality of being worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). “Venerable Sir, through this meritorious deed performed during these seven days, I do not aspire for any other success;
rather, in the future, under the Dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I possess these two qualities just like this Elder.”
He made this aspiration: "May I come to possess [these qualities]. Seeing that there would be no obstacle, the Teacher gave his prediction and departed.
The ascetic Nanda, having heard the Dhamma from the One of Ten Powers from time to time, was reborn in the Brahma-world without falling away from his jhāna.
This was his wholesome deed; however, his intermediate deeds are not recounted here.
Thus, after the passing of one hundred thousand eons, he was reborn in Sāvatthī in the house of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi;
they gave him the name Subhūti. Later on, when our Teacher had appeared in the world, he was dwelling in dependence upon Rājagaha.
At that time, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika took merchandise for trade and set out from Sāvatthī toward his own friend...
Having gone to the house of the Rājagaha merchant and learned that the Teacher had arisen [there], he approached the Teacher while he was dwelling in the Sītavana forest;
at his very first sight of him, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

Having requested the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī, he established monasteries along the forty-five *yojanas* of the road, making a donation of one hundred thousand pieces of gold for every single *yojana*.

Having purchased the Prince Jeta’s park in Sāvatthī—an area measuring eight karīsas according to royal measure—for a price of one hundred million, he had a monastery for the Blessed One built there and presented it to him.
On the day of the monastery’s consecration, this householder Subhūti went with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika; while listening to the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth into homelessness.
Thus, having been fully ordained, he mastered the two matrices (mātikā) and requested instruction on a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Practicing the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) in the forest, he developed insight (vipassanā) and, taking the jhāna of loving-kindness (mettājhāna) as his foundation, attained Arahantship.
When teaching the Dhamma, he spoke the Dhamma according to the aforementioned method; when wandering for alms, he likewise [proceeded] from the jhāna of loving-kindness according to that same method.

Having risen, he went out to receive alms. Then, for these two reasons, the Teacher established him in the foremost position among those monks who dwell in peace and those who are worthy of offerings.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Forest.

203. Regarding the fifth [lesson], "of those dwelling in the forest" (*āraññakānaṃ*) means of those who live in the wilderness (*araññavāsīnaṃ*). Revata Khadiravaniya was the younger brother of the Elder Dhammasenāpati.

He did not dwell in the forest in the same way that other elders dwell there—having observed the suitability of the woods, the suitability of the water, and the suitability for alms-round—but rather, disregarding these suitable conditions, he dwelt in a desolate, stony, and rocky uneven place.
He dwelt in a Khadira forest; therefore, he is called the foremost of those who live in the wilderness.

Regarding his life story, this is the sequential account: it is said that in the past, during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he was born in the city of Haṃsavatī and lived there engaged in boat-work at the landing-place of the Mahāgaṅgā river where it meets the Payāga. In him—
At that time, the Teacher, wandering on tour with a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, arrived at the Payāgapatiṭṭhāna ford.
Upon seeing the One of Ten Powers, he thought: "From time to time, I have had no opportunity to see a Buddha;
this is my moment to accumulate wholesome kamma. He then had a fleet of boats moored together and a canopy of cloth spread over them.
Having had fragrant garlands and wreaths prepared and having had a fine cloth carpet spread beneath [the ship], he ferried the Teacher and his retinue to the opposite shore.
At that time, the Teacher designated a forest-dwelling bhikkhu as preeminent in this category. When the boatman saw him, he...
“Just as it was for him, it is fitting that I too, in the future, become the foremost among forest-dwellers in the dispensation of a certain Buddha.
Having thus invited the Teacher, given a great almsgiving for seven days, and prostrated at the feet of the Teacher, he said:
“Venerable Sir, just like that bhikkhu whom you have designated as the foremost, may I also [become so] in the future in the dispensation of a certain Buddha.”

He made an aspiration, saying, "May I become the foremost. Seeing that there would be no obstacle, the Teacher prophesied, "In the future, under the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you will be the foremost of those who dwell in the forest," and then he departed.
However, no other matter was discussed in the interim.

Thus, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering among gods and humans, he took rebirth in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance in the Magadha country, in the brahmin village of Nālaka, in the womb of the brahmin woman Sārī.
He was born as the youngest of three brothers and three sisters, and they gave him the name Revata. Then, for him—
The parents thought, “As soon as a child grows up, the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, take him away and ordain him.
We shall bind our son Revata with the bonds of the household while he is still young.
So they brought a girl from a family of equal status, had Revata pay homage to his grandmother, and said, “Dear child, you will become even older than your grandmother.”
Having heard their conversation, Revata thought: “This girl is young, standing in the first stage of life;
it is said that her beauty will be like the beauty of my own grandmother. I shall ask them what their intention is.
Having thought this, he said: “What are you saying? “Father, this girl is just like our grandmother...”
“I say that they shall reach old age. He asked, “Will her form become like this?
“Dear son, what are you saying? Only those of great merit become like this.
He thought: “Indeed, by this very process, this form will become wrinkled with skin, with grey hair, and with broken teeth.”
"What shall I do by being attached to such a form? I shall follow the very path my brothers have taken.
Speaking thus as if playing, he said to the young boys of his own age, "Come, sirs, let us play at running," and went out. [His father said:
"Dear one, do not go outside on an auspicious day. He, as if playing with the boys—
When his own turn to run arrived, he would go a short distance, delay, and then return. When the second turn arrived, he returned as if having gone more quickly than before.

When the third turn arrived, realizing, "This is my time," he fled from that very spot, went to the forest where the *paṃsukūlika* bhikkhus resided, paid homage to the elders, and requested the going-forth.
He begged them, saying, "Good sirs, we do not know whose son you are; moreover, you have come here in full regalia, so who would venture to ordain you?
Grasping both his arms, he cried out with a great wail, "They are robbing me! They are robbing me!
Then the monks gathered from here and there and said, "Good sir, in this place..."
“There is no one at all taking your robe or your jewelry, yet you say, ‘They are plundering me.
With what in mind do you say this? “Venerable sir, I am not speaking with reference to my robes or ornaments;
rather, it is the plundering of my three prosperities that is occurring, and it is with reference to that that I speak. Do not ordain me for now.”
"But you must know my brother. "What is your brother's name? "In his time as a householder he was named Upatissa, but now he has become known as Sāriputta," they replied.
"Friends, that being so, this noble son is indeed our younger brother;
yet our elder brother, the Dhammasenāpati, spoke to us previously, saying: 'All our kinsmen...'"
"Anyone who comes claiming to be our relative, even if they hold wrong views, you must ordain them by whatever means possible. "But this one is the elder’s own brother;
ordain him," they said, and having spoken thus, they instructed him in the meditation subject of the fivefold skin and ordained him.
Then, when he had completed his years of residence, they conferred full ordination upon him and engaged him in the practice of the meditation subject.
The Elder, having taken up his meditation subject, entered a khadira forest of the kind described in a place not far from his teachers and preceptors, and practiced the duties of a recluse.

While he was striving with the resolve, "I shall not see the One of Ten Powers or my brother the Elder until I have attained Arahantship," three months passed; for that youth of delicate upbringing, even coarse food was difficult to consume.
While he was eating, his mind became "wrinkled" (contracted); the meditation subject had not reached liberation.
After three months had passed, having performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) and completed the rains retreat, he practiced the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) in that very same place.
As he was practicing the duty of a recluse, his mind became one-pointed; increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he attained Arahatship.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, it is said that my younger brother Revata has gone forth;
whether he finds delight in it or not, I shall go and see him. The Blessed One, knowing that Revata had begun insight meditation, refused him twice;
but when requested for a third time, and knowing that he had attained Arahantship, he said: “Sāriputta,…”
“I too shall go; inform the bhikkhus. The Elder, having assembled the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, announced to everyone:
“Friends, the Teacher wishes to go on a journey; those who wish to go, let them come.
At the time of departing for the journey of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, those bhikkhus left behind are few, [thinking], “The Teacher’s body is golden-hued...”
“Perhaps we shall see him, or perhaps we shall hear his sweet discourse on the Dhamma. Thus, for the most part, many were indeed desirous of going.
So the Teacher, surrounded by a great community of monks, set out, thinking, “I shall see Revata.
Then, at a certain place, the Elder Ānanda, having come upon a forked path, asked the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, regarding this [path]...”
“There are two routes; by which route shall the Saṅgha go? “Which route, Ānanda, is the direct one?
“Venerable sir, the direct route is thirty yojanas long and is a path frequented by non-human beings; however, the circuitous route is sixty yojanas long, but it is safe and well-supplied with food.
“Ānanda, has Sīvali come along with us? “Yes, venerable sir, he has come. “In that case—”

"Let the Saṅgha take only the straight path; we shall test Sīvali’s merit. Accompanied by the community of monks, the Teacher ascended a forest path for the purpose of testing the merit of the Elder Sīvali.
From the point where they began ascending the path, the host of deities constructed cities at every *yojana* and provided for the community of monks headed by the Buddha.

He prepared a dwelling in the monastery for the purpose of providing him with robes. The sons of the gods, acting like laborers sent by the king, took rice gruel, solid food, and other provisions, and went about asking, "Where is the venerable Sīvali? Where is the venerable Sīvali?
Having caused the elder to accept that honor and hospitality, he went into the presence of the Teacher. The Teacher partook together with the community of monks.
In this very manner, the Teacher, receiving honor and respect, traveled at most one *yojana* per day;
having traversed a wilderness thirty *yojanas* in extent, he arrived at the dwelling place of the Elder Khadiravaniya.
The Elder, learning of the Teacher’s arrival, prepared a monastery in his own residence sufficient for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Having created by means of his psychic power a fragrant chamber for the One Possessed of Ten Powers, as well as night-quarters, day-quarters, and so forth, he went out to meet the Tathāgata.
The Teacher entered the monastery by way of a path adorned and prepared.
Then, once the Tathāgata had entered the fragrant chamber, the monks entered the lodgings they had received according to seniority. The deities [cried out]: "It is not the time!"
"For food," they brought eight kinds of drinks. The Teacher drank the drink together with the Saṅgha.
In this very manner, half a month passed while the Tathāgata was receiving such honor and respect.
Then, some discontented bhikkhus sat down in one place and started a conversation: "The Teacher, the One Endowed with Ten Powers..."
“Having said, ‘He is the younger brother of my chief disciple,’ he has come to see such a monk engaged in building work.
In the vicinity of this monastery, what will the Jetavana Mahāvihāra or the Veḷuvana Vihāra and others do for him?
This monk, too, is a performer of such building work; what indeed will he accomplish as the duty of a recluse?”
Then the Teacher thought: "If I dwell here for a long time, this place will become crowded;
forest-dwelling bhikkhus, by nature, seek solitude, and Revata’s dwelling will become uncomfortable. Thereupon, he went to Revata’s daytime resting place.
The Elder was alone at the end of the walking path, leaning against a support-board on a stone slab.
Seated there, Revata saw the Teacher approaching from afar; he went out to meet him and paid homage.
Then the Teacher asked him: “Revata, when you hear the sounds of wild beasts and fierce elephants, horses, and so forth in this place, what do you do?
“Venerable Sir, as I listen to their sounds, a delight in the forest arises within me.”
At that place, the Teacher spoke to the Elder Revata on the benefits of dwelling in the forest using five hundred stanzas;
then, on the following day, having walked for alms in a nearby location and sent the Elder Revata back,
he [observed] how those monks who had spoken ill of the Elder had forgotten their walking sticks, sandals, oil-flasks, and sunshades.
They returned for the sake of their own requisites; yet even as they went back by the same path they had come, they were unable to recognize that place.

For previously they had traveled by a well-adorned and prepared road, but on that day, traveling by an uneven path, they sat down squatting at various spots and moved along on their knees. And they [encountered] thickets...
Treading upon both the path and the thorns, they went to the place where their own belongings were kept;
there, they recognized their respective parasols, sandals, walking sticks, and oil flasks among each of those acacia stakes.
At that time, recognizing him as "this monk possessed of psychic power," they took up their own requisites [thinking], "This is the honor prepared for the One of Ten Powers."
“They have come saying, ‘His name is such-and-such.
The laywoman Visākhā asked the monks who had gone ahead while she was sitting in her own home:
“Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of the Elder Revata pleasant? “It is pleasant, laywoman; it resembles the Nandana Grove, the Citralatā grove, and so forth.”
"This is the lodging. Then she asked the bhikkhus who had arrived last of all: "Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of the Elder Revata pleasant?
"Do not ask, laywoman; it is improper to speak of this. It is a desolate wilderness, uneven with gravel and stones, a thornwood forest;
that is where the bhikkhu dwells. Visākhā [asked] both those who had come before and those who came after.
Having heard the talk of the bhikkhus, [the king] wondered, "Whose words are true?
After his meal, taking perfumes and garlands, he went to attend upon the One of Ten Powers. Having paid homage and sat down to one side, he asked the Teacher:
"Venerable Sir, some noble ones praise the dwelling place of the Elder Revata, while others criticize it; what does this mean?"
“Venerable sir,” [she asked]. Having said, “Visākhā, whether it be delightful or not, that place where the minds of the Noble Ones delight is alone called ‘delightful,’” he spoke this verse:
“In a village or in the forest, on low ground or on high ground;”
“Wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is delightful.
Later, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the great monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among the forest-dwelling bhikkhus.
This is the story of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata.
204. "Of those who meditate" (*jhāyinam*) means of those who have attained the jhānas and who delight in jhāna.
It is said that this elder, setting aside only a few, would enter into more jhāna-attainments than even the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) himself.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of meditators. He is called Kaṅkhārevata because of his state of being prone to doubt (*kaṅkhā*). Here, "doubt" (*kaṅkhā*) refers to remorse (*kukkucca*).
The meaning is "one who is scrupulous. But are there not others who are scrupulous? There are; however, this elder even gave rise to scruples regarding what was allowable (*kappiya*).
Because his scrupulousness became so well-known, he came to be known by the name Kaṅkhārevata. This is the sequential account regarding his answering of questions:
it is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, in the same manner as previously described...
Having gone to the monastery with a great multitude of people, he stood at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma.
Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost place among those who delight in meditation (*jhāna*), he thought, "In the future, it is fitting that I too become like this.
At the conclusion of the teaching, he invited the Teacher and, as before, provided great honor for seven days.
Having performed this act of merit, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, by means of this meritorious deed, I do not aspire for any other success;

rather, just as that bhikkhu was placed by you seven days ago in the foremost position among those who practice jhāna, may I too become the foremost among those who practice jhāna in the dispensation of a future Buddha. Thus he made his aspiration.
The Teacher, looking into the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied:

"At the end of one hundred thousand future eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; in his dispensation, you shall become the foremost of those who practice meditation. Having spoken thus, he departed.
He performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life, and after wandering through the realms of gods and humans for one hundred thousand eons, [he was reborn] in our...
At the time of the Blessed One, he was reborn in a family of great wealth in the city of Sāvatthī.
Later, having gone to the monastery with a great multitude of people to hear the Dhamma after the meal, he stood at the edge of the assembly;
hearing the discourse on the Dhamma from the One of Ten Powers, he acquired faith, went forth, received full ordination, and requested a meditation subject.
While performing the preliminary work for jhāna, he became an attainer of jhāna; taking jhāna itself as his foundation, he reached the fruit of arahantship.

Excepting those attainments that must be entered by the One of Ten Powers (the Buddha), he would enter many other attainments, and thus for day and night he became one who had mastered mastery over the jhānas. Later, the Teacher, taking note of this quality of his, said:
He placed him in the foremost position among those who meditate. However, because he gave rise to remorse regarding things that were actually permissible—thinking, "Friend, sugar is not allowable;
mung beans are not allowable"—he became known as Kaṅkhā-Revata (The One of Doubt) due to his state of doubt, which is synonymous with remorse.
This is the story of the Elder Soṇa Koḷivisa.
205. "In the seventh [verse], 'of those who have aroused energy' means of those who have exerted energy, who possess perfected energy.
'Soṇa Koḷivisa': 'Soṇa' is his name; 'Koḷivisa' is his clan (gotta). Alternatively, the meaning is 'Koṭivessa';
the intention is that he was the son of a Vessa family who had reached the pinnacle (koṭi) of prosperity. For while the energy of other monks must be increased..."
However, for the Elder, there was only a deficiency to be remedied. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who have aroused energy.
Regarding his history, this is the sequential account: it is said that in the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn into a family of wealthy merchants;
they gave him the name Sirivaḍḍha-kumāra. When he reached maturity, in the same manner as before, he went to the monastery.
Having gone and stood at the edge of the assembly, he listened to the Dhamma.
Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost place among those of ardent energy, he thought, "In the future, it is fitting that I too should become like this.
At the conclusion of the teaching, he invited the One of Ten Powers, gave a great almsgiving for seven days, and made his aspiration in the manner already described. The Teacher—
Seeing that his aspiration had been fulfilled, [the Elder] gave a prediction in the same manner as before and departed for his monastery.
That merchant Sirivaḍḍha, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons.
Then, after the Parinibbāna of Kassapa Buddha—the Great Sage of the Ten Powers—at the beginning of this present aeon, and before our own Blessed One had appeared...
He took rebirth in a noble family in Bārāṇasī. He used to play in the Ganges with his companions.

At that time, a certain Paccekabuddha wearing worn-out robes, thinking, "I shall enter the rains retreat having built a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges near Bārāṇasī," was gathering sticks and creepers that were submerged by the water.
The prince went with his companions, paid his respects, and stood there, asking, "Venerable sir, what are you doing?
[The monks replied,] "Prince, as the rainy season is approaching, it is necessary for those who have gone forth to find a place to dwell.
[The prince said,] "Venerable sir, may the noble one come this very day at whatever time; tomorrow I shall provide a dwelling place for the noble one."
“I shall do so,” he said. The Paccekabuddha, having come with the intention, “I shall show favor to this very boy,” consented.
Having understood his consent, the king departed;
on the following day, having prepared honors and hospitality, he stood waiting for the arrival of the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha, too, [thought], “Where indeed shall I go for alms today?”
Reflecting, "I shall obtain [him]," and knowing [the answer] through his supernormal knowledge, he went to the very door of that man's house.

Upon seeing the Paccekabuddha, the prince felt great affection; he took the bowl, gave him alms-food, and requested a promise, saying, "Venerable Sir, please come to the door of my house for this entire rainy season," and then attended to the Paccekabuddha’s meal duties.
When his companions had departed, he went with them and, in a single day,
had a leaf-hut, a walking path, and places for standing and sitting by night and day built for the Paccekabuddha, and gave them to him. At the moment of entering that very leaf-hut,
thinking "let not the mud stick to my feet," he [took off] his own robe worth a hundred thousand [pieces].
Having spread a red woolen blanket as a floor-covering,
and seeing that the radiance of the Paccekabuddha’s body was identical in color to the blanket, he became exceedingly joyful and said:
“Just as this blanket shines with such intense radiance from the moment you stepped upon it, so too shall it be for me in every place where I am reborn.”
“May the color of my hands and feet be like the color of a *bandhujīvaka* flower, and may my touch be like the touch of a layer of cotton that has been carded a hundred times.
Having attended upon the Paccekabuddha for three months, he offered him the three robes at the time of his departure.
With his bowl and robes complete, the Paccekabuddha departed for Mount Gandhamādana.
That noble son, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, took rebirth during the time of our Blessed One in the house of a chief merchant in the city of Kāḷacampā.
From the moment of his conception, thousands of gifts began to arrive at the merchant’s household.
And on the day of his birth, the entire city was filled with a single, universal honor and respect.
Then, on the day of his naming ceremony, his parents said, "Our son has come having taken his own name with him;
the skin of his body is as if sprinkled with liquid red gold," and they gave him the name Soṇa Kumāra.
Then, having brought sixty nurses to him, they raised him in comfort like a young god. Of such a nature was he...
The method of cultivation was as follows: having ploughed a plot of land measuring sixty karīsas, they nourished it with three kinds of water.
When the irrigation channels entered the fields, they poured many thousands of jars of milk-water and scented water.
At the time when the rice ears were being milked, [this was done] for the purpose of preventing birds such as crows from eating the leftovers.

For the sake of protecting the ears of grain within the sheaves from being scratched by fine insects, they drive stakes at intervals around the perimeter and across the interior, place cross-beams on top, cover them with palm-leaf mats, and encircle the whole area with a fence;
thus, they maintain a guard all around. When the crop has ripened, they prepare the granary by decorating its interior with the four kinds of fragrant incense, and then—
They perfumed them with the finest fragrances. Thousands of men entered the field, cut the rice heads from their stalks, formed them into handfuls, tied them with ropes, and dried them.
Then, having spread fragrances on the floor of the granary, they spread the rice heads on top. Thus, having arranged them in alternating layers...
Spreading [the grain] until they fill the granary, they close the door; when three years have passed, they open the granary.
When it is opened, the entire city becomes fragrant with sweet scents.
Once the rice has been harvested, rogues buy and take the husks, while the junior attendants receive the broken grains (*kuṇḍaka*). Having sifted the rice grains from those struck by the pestle—
They take it. Having placed it in a golden basket of diamonds, they strain it a hundred times;
then, having added it once to the boiled juice of the *jāti* flower that has been taken, they remove it. The surface of that food becomes like a *sumana* flower.
They place that food in a golden bowl and set it upon a silver platter filled with boiled honeyed milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) mixed with very little water.
Having prepared it and taken it, they go and place it before the merchant’s son.
He eats just enough for his own sustenance, rinses his mouth with scented water, and washes his hands and feet.
Then, once he has washed his hands and feet, they offer him various kinds of mouth-perfume. At the place where he steps...
They spread out carpets made of choice cloth as his bed-covering. The soles of his hands and feet are the color of the *bandhujīvaka* flower;
their touch is like that of finely carded cotton wool. On the soles of his feet, hairs grow in the pattern of jeweled earrings.
Whenever he becomes angry with someone, he says, "Prepare the ground, I shall tread upon it. When he has reached maturity...
Having had three palaces constructed suitable for the three seasons, they provided them with theatrical performances.
Experiencing such great prosperity, he lived there as if he were a god.
Then, when our Teacher had attained omniscience and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, [he resided] near Rājagaha.
While he was living there, the King of Māgadha summoned him for the purpose of seeing the hair on his feet;
having been sent into the presence of the Teacher along with eighty thousand village headmen, he heard the preaching of the Dhamma, gained faith, and requested the going-forth from the Teacher.
Then the Blessed One asked him, "Have you been permitted by your mother and father? and upon hearing that he had not been permitted, [the Blessed One said:]
“Sonā, the Tathāgatas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father,” he replied, declining.
Saying, “Very well, Blessed One,” he accepted the Tathāgata’s words with his head;
he went to his parents, obtained their permission, returned to the presence of the Teacher, and was ordained in the presence of a certain bhikkhu.
This is the summary here; however, the detailed procedure for his going forth is found in the Canon itself.

Having received both the going forth and the full ordination, as he was dwelling at Rājagaha, many kinsmen and blood relatives, as well as friends and associates, brought him honors and respect, and spoke in praise of his physical perfection.
Other people also came to see him. The Elder thought: "Many people are coming to me;
how shall I be able to perform work regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) or insight (*vipassanā*)?
What if I were to have the meditation subject explained by the Teacher, go to the Sītavana charnel ground, and practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) there? There...
"Indeed, many people will not come here out of disgust for this cemetery; such being the case, my task will reach its fulfillment," he thought.
Having requested a meditation subject from the Teacher, he went to the Sītavana and began to practice the duties of a recluse.
He reflected: "My body is extremely delicate; it is certainly not possible for me to proceed with ease."
“It is better to attain happiness by exerting oneself and performing the duties of a recluse even while the body is worn out.
Thereupon, he resolved upon standing and walking meditation alone and applied himself to striving. As he did so, blisters arose on the edges of his tender soles and burst open;
the entire walking path became nothing but blood. When his feet were worn away, he strove using his knees and his hands as well.
He walked back and forth. Even though he exerted such firm energy, being unable to produce even a mere radiance, he thought:
"If there were anyone else who had initiated such energy, they would be just like me.

Yet, despite striving in this way, I am unable to produce either the Path or the Fruit. Surely I am neither one who understands through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*), nor one who understands through an expanded teaching (*vipañcitaññū*)."
“I am not one to be led; I must not remain at the level of a mere student of the words. What is the use of my going forth?
Having returned to the lower life, I shall enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds.
At that moment, the Teacher, knowing the elder’s thought, [appeared] in the evening surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

Having gone there, he saw the walkway stained with blood; after exhorting the Elder with the parable of the lute, he taught him a meditation subject for the purpose of balancing energy and tranquility, and then returned to Gijjhakūṭa itself.
The Elder Soṇa, having received the exhortation in the presence of the One of Ten Powers, was established in Arahatship before long. Then, at a later time, the Teacher [was staying] in Jetavana.
Surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, while teaching the Dhamma, he placed the Elder [Soṇa] in the foremost position among those who have aroused energy.
This is the story of the Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.
Regarding the eighth category, "among those of beautiful speech": "speech" (vākkaraṇa) refers to the act of speaking; thus, it means "those of sweet speech."

This is the meaning. For this elder, together with the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to the Tathāgata within a single fragrant chamber in a sweet voice. Then the Teacher gave him his approval.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those of beautiful speech. His personal name was Soṇa, but he wore an earring worth ten million.
Therefore he is called Kuṭikaṇṇa; the meaning is "Point-Ear.

Regarding his past deeds, this is the sequential account: during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he likewise went to the monastery with the great multitude as before, stood at the edge of the assembly, and while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, [he saw] the Teacher...
Seeing a certain bhikkhu being placed in the foremost position among those of beautiful speech, he thought, "In the future,
it would be fitting for me also to become the foremost among those of beautiful speech in the dispensation of a Buddha.
Having invited the One Possessed of Ten Powers and given a great almsgiving for seven days, he said, "Venerable Sir, whichever bhikkhu you [choose] from here seven days hence..."
He established him in the foremost position among those of eloquent speech and made this aspiration:
"By the fruit of this meritorious deed, may I too become such a person in the dispensation of a future Buddha.

Seeing that there would be no obstacle for him, the Teacher prophesied: "In the future, in the dispensation of Gotama Buddha, you shall be the foremost of those with eloquent speech," and then he departed.
He too, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons.

Prior even to the appearance of our Ten-Powered One (the Buddha), he passed away from the world of the gods and took rebirth in the womb of a female lay follower named Kāḷī Kuraragharikā. When her pregnancy was mature, in the city of Rājagaha, she...
She had come to our family residence.
At that time, our Teacher, having attained omniscience, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma at Isipatana.
For the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, ten thousand deities from the world-systems gathered there. Among them was one [who was] twenty-eight...

Among the generals of the *yakkhas*, a *yakkha* named Sātāgira, having heard the Dhamma discourse of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*). He thought:
"Has this same sweet Dhamma discourse been heard by my companion Hemavata, or not? Looking among the assembly of gods, he did not see him.
“Surely my companion does not know that the Three Jewels have appeared; I shall go, praise the One of Ten Powers, and proclaim the Dhamma he has realized.
With these thoughts, he set out for his presence by way of Rājagaha together with his own retinue.
Hemavata, too, seeing the Himalayas in full bloom out of season over an extent of three thousand yojanas, thought,
"I shall sport in the Himalayan pastimes together with my companion Sātāgira," and set out toward Rājagaha at the very head of his own retinue.
At the house of the female lay follower Kāḷī, the wife of their noble family, the two vanguards of both armies met.
Having come together, they said, “Whose assembly are you? “Sātāgira’s. “Whose assembly are you?
“Hemavata’s. Delighted and joyful, they went and informed those two yakṣa generals.
At that very moment, they too arrived at the top of the laywoman’s residence. Sātāgira said to Hemavata, “Where, friend, ...”
“Are you going? “Yes, friend. “For what reason? “Having seen the Himalayas in bloom, I shall sport there with you.
“But where are you going, friend? “To your presence, friend. “For what reason?
“Because you know whether the Himalayas are in bloom or not? “I do not know, friend.”

"Prince Siddhattha, the son of the Great King Suddhodana, having caused the ten-thousandfold world system to tremble and having realized omniscient knowledge, set in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma in the midst of the devas of the ten-thousandfold universe. Do you not know that he has set it in motion?
"I do not know, venerable sir. "You thought that only this much place had blossomed; of him—"
"Indeed, today the entire ten-thousandfold world system has become like a single cluster of flowers for the sake of honoring this man.
"Let the flowers bloom first; you have seen that Teacher with your own eyes.
"Yes, friend, I have seen the Teacher, I have heard the Dhamma, and I have drunk the Deathless. "I [shall explain] this Dhamma of the Deathless..."
“I have come to you so that I may inform you of this as well. While they were thus conversing with one another, the laywoman rose from her state bed and sat down;
hearing that exchange of words, she took note of the sound. Having observed it, she reflected:
“This sound is above, not below; it is spoken by a non-human being, not by a human being.”
Having fixed his ear and steadied his mind, he sat down.
Then [the yakkha Sātāgira said]: "Today is the fifteenth day, the Uposatha;
the divine night has arrived."
"Come, let us see the Teacher Gotama, whose name is truly sublime"—
thus spoke Sātāgira.
“Is the mind well-directed (so asked the Yakkha Hemavata) toward all beings by you who are such-like?
Is it well-directed toward both the pleasant and the unpleasant?”
"Having brought intention under control.
Thus Hemavata asked about the Teacher’s bodily conduct, livelihood, and mental conduct. Sātāgira answered each question as it was asked.
Thus, in the *Hemavata Sutta*, by way of describing the beauty and qualities of the Teacher’s physical form, [the discourse proceeds].
When Hemavata’s discourse on the Dhamma was finished, he directed his knowledge accordingly and was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

Then the female lay follower Kāḷī, having never before seen the Tathāgata while another was teaching the Dhamma, developed faith through hearsay and became established in the fruit of stream-entry, as if she were eating food provided by another. She—
Among all women, she became the foremost as the first stream-enterer. On the very night she attained stream-entry, her delivery took place;
on the day the name was given to the child she had obtained, they named him Soṇa.
Having lived in her father-in-law’s house for as long as she desired, she returned to her own family home.
At that time, the Elder Mahākaccāna was residing on Mount Upavatta near that city.
A female lay devotee attended upon the Elder. The Elder went regularly to her residence.
The youth Soṇa, too, who frequented the Elder’s presence constantly, became a person of great trust. At a later time, he [approached] the Elder...
He went forth in the presence [of the Elder]. Desiring to ordain him, the Elder sought out a group for three years and then conferred full ordination upon him.
Having been ordained, he requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), developed insight (*vipassanā*), and attained *arahantship*.

Having mastered the *Sutta Nipāta* in the presence of that very Elder, and having completed the rains retreat and performed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he became desirous of seeing the Teacher.
He asked his preceptor for leave. The Elder said: "Soṇa, when you have gone, the Teacher will have you dwell in a single Perfumed Chamber and will request you to preach the Dhamma;
you shall preach the Dhamma. The Teacher, being pleased with your discourse on the Dhamma, will grant you a boon.
When you receive the boon, take this and this, and [say] in my name to the One of Ten Powers:"
“Pay homage at his feet. Having been permitted by his preceptor, he went to the house of his lay mother and informed her.

She said, “Very well, dear son; as you go to see the One of Ten Powers, take this woolen blanket, spread it upon the floor of the Teacher’s Fragrant Chamber, and cover it. Elder Soṇa took that blanket and [went to] the lodging.

Having settled his affairs, he gradually made his way to the Teacher’s dwelling place. At the very moment the One of Ten Powers was seated upon the Buddha’s throne, he approached, paid homage, and stood to one side.
The Teacher exchanged greetings with him and addressed the Elder Ānanda: “Ānanda, find lodgings for this bhikkhu. The Elder [responded to] the Teacher...
Having understood his intention, he spread it out as if raising a floor-covering right there inside the fragrant chamber.
Then the Blessed One, having spent much of the night in the open air, entered the monastery;
the Venerable Soṇa also, having spent much of the night in the open air, entered the monastery. During the last watch of the night, the Teacher lay down in the lion’s posture.

Having made his preparations, he rose at dawn and sat down. Knowing that by this time Soṇa’s physical fatigue would have subsided, he requested of the Venerable Soṇa, “May it please you, monk, to speak on the Dhamma.
The Elder Soṇa, with a sweet voice and without missing even a single syllable, recited the discourses of the Aṭṭhakavagga.
At the conclusion of the discourse, the Blessed One gave his approval, saying, "Well-grasped is the Dhamma by you, monk;
the teaching today is exactly the same as when it was taught by me, with nothing lacking and nothing added," thereby manifesting his state of serene confidence.
The Elder Soṇa, perceiving that "this is the opportunity," paid homage to the One of Ten Powers at the word of his preceptor.
Starting with the full ordination (*upasampadā*) performed by a community of five including one who holds the Vinaya, he requested all the boons, and the Teacher granted them.

Again, at the word of his mother, the female lay devotee (*upāsikā*), the Elder paid homage and presented a woolen blanket, saying, "Venerable Sir, this blanket has been sent by the female lay devotee to be used as a floor-covering for your Fragrant Chamber.
Having given the blanket, he rose from his seat and paid homage to the Teacher.
Having performed a circumambulation, he departed. This is the summary here; however, in detail, everything from the Elder’s going forth onwards is indeed recorded in the Sutta.
Thus, having received eight boons from the presence of the Teacher, the Elder went to his preceptor and [related] everything.
He reported that news to her. On the following day, he went to the gate of his mother, the laywoman (*upāsikā*), and stood there for alms.

Hearing that "my son has arrived at the gate," the laywoman came out in haste, paid him homage, took the bowl from his hand, seated him within the residence, and gave him food. Then, at the conclusion of his meal, she said to him:
“Did you see the One of Ten Powers, dear? “Yes, lay follower. “Was he paid homage by you in my name? “Yes, he was paid homage;
and I also spread that woolen blanket of mine out as a ground-covering where the Tathāgata was staying.
“What, dear? Did you give a Dhamma talk to the Teacher, and did the Teacher grant you his approval? “By you...”
"How was it known, O laywoman? "Father, on the day the One of Ten Powers gave his applause to you, the deity residing in my house said:
'The deities throughout the entire ten-thousandfold world-system have given their applause. She added:
'Father, I hope that you will explain the Dhamma discourse you have related to me according to the very method used by the Buddhas.'"

The Elder accepted his mother’s words. Having understood his consent, she had a pavilion erected at the gate and, following the very method of discourse used by the One of Ten Powers, she had him deliver a Dhamma talk herself. This is the story that arose here.
Later on, while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those of eloquent speech.
The Story of the Elder Sīvalī (207).

Regarding the ninth [category], by stating "among those who obtain gains, namely Sīvalī," it is shown that, with the exception of the Tathāgata, the Elder Sīvalī is the foremost among the monks who obtain gains.
This is the sequential account concerning his past deeds: he too, in the past, during the time of Buddha Padumuttara...
Having gone to the monastery in the same manner described above, he stood at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma.
Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost place among those who receive gains, he thought, "It is fitting that I too should become like this in the future.
He invited the One of Ten Powers and, as before, gave a great almsgiving for seven days, saying, "Bhagavā, may I also [become like him] through this..."

He made this aspiration: "I do not seek any other excellence through this formal act of authorization; rather, in the future, under the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I become the foremost among those who receive gains, just as that bhikkhu was established by you in that very same position.
The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacle, said: "This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled in the future, under the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama..."
Having replied, “It will succeed,” he departed.

That clansman also, having practiced wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, wandered through the realms of gods and humans until the time of Vipassī Buddha, when he took rebirth in a village not far from the city of Bandhumatī. At that time, the inhabitants of the city of Bandhumatī...
Having conversed repeatedly with the king, they gave alms to the One of Ten Powers.
One day, while all of them were giving alms together, they wondered, "What indeed is lacking in our offering?
and did not see honey or sugar-curd. Thinking, "We shall fetch it from somewhere," they stationed a man on the road leading into the city from the countryside.
They set them down. At that time, this clansman, having taken a jar of sugar and curds from his own village, was going to the city thinking, “I shall fetch something.
Having washed his face, and thinking, “I will enter with my hands and feet washed,” he looked for a convenient spot;
seeing a stalk of honey free of flies, about the size of a plowshare, he thought, “This has arisen for me through merit.”
Having taken it, he entered the city. A man stationed by the citizens saw him and asked, "Sir, for whom are you carrying this?
He replied, "For no one at all, my lord; rather, I have brought this to sell.
[The man said,] "In that case, sir, take this coin and give me this honey and sugar-curd."
He thought: "This is not of great value, yet he gives much all at once; it is right to test him.
Then he said to him, "I do not give for a single kahāpaṇa. "If that is so, take two and give them to me. "Even for two I do not give.
By this means, increasing and increasing, it reached a thousand. He thought: "It is too much to press him further..."
"It is not proper; let it be for now, I shall ask what must be done with this. Then he said to him:
"This is not of great value, yet you give much; for what purpose do you take this? [The man replied:
"Sir, the city-dwellers, having rebelled against the king, were giving gifts to the Six-Fold Being Vipassī, and they gave these two items as part of their offerings."
"Without seeing it, they search for it. If these two things are not obtained, the citizens will suffer defeat.
Therefore, I shall give a thousand pieces of gold and take it. "But is this permitted only for the citizens, and not for others to give?
"There is no prohibition against anyone giving it. "But is there anyone among the citizens who gives it?"
“Do you say that he gives a thousand [pieces] on a single day? “No, sir. “But do you know that these two are worth a thousand each?
“Yes, I know it. “In that case, go and inform the citizens: ‘A certain man will not give these two for their price;
he wishes to give them with his own hand. Therefore, you should remain unconcerned regarding these two.’”
"But you, be the bodily witness to my preeminence in this act of giving. Then that villager,
taking five pungent spices with a māsaka coin he had set aside for his travel expenses, ground them into powder, strained a sour gruel from curd,
pressed a honeycomb over it, mixed it with the powder of the five pungent spices, and placed it in a lotus leaf.
Having placed it inside and prepared it, he took it and sat down at a spot not far from the One of Ten Powers.
While observing his turn for the honors being presented by the great multitude, he saw an opportunity;
approaching the Teacher, he said, "Blessed One, this is my gift from a poor man; please accept it out of compassion for me. The Teacher—

Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One accepted it with a stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings and made a resolution so that it would not be exhausted even as it was served to the six million eight hundred thousand monks.
Then that clansman, having finished his meal duties, paid homage to the Blessed One and, standing to one side, said: “I have seen...”
“May the Blessed One accept today the hospitality being offered by the residents of the city of Bandhumatī for you;
may I too, through the result of this deed, attain the highest gain and the supreme state in every birth I take.
The Teacher said, “So be it, noble son,” and having delivered a discourse of thanksgiving for the meal to him and the city-dwellers, he departed.

That clansman also, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, during this current appearance of a Buddha, he took rebirth in the womb of Suppavāsā, the king’s daughter.
From the moment of his conception, hundreds of gifts arrived morning and evening, and Suppavāsā attained great prosperity. Then, in order to test her merit—
They cause the seed-trays to be touched with the hand; from each single seed, even a hundred or a thousand tally-sticks are obtained.
From a field of only one *karīsa*, fifty or sixty wagons of grain arise. Even when the time comes to fill the granaries, they cause the gate of the granary to be touched with the hand;
through the merit of the King’s daughter, the very spot where those who take grain receive it becomes filled once again.

Even when her food-pot was full, she would say, "This is for the merit of the princess," and as long as they did not draw it out while giving to anyone, the food would never run out. Seven years passed while the child was still in the womb.
When the fetus had matured, she experienced great suffering for seven days. She addressed her husband, saying, "Before my death..."
Thinking, "I will give a gift while she is still alive," she sent her to the presence of the Teacher, saying:
"Go, report this matter to the Teacher and invite him; whatever the Teacher says, take careful note of it and, having returned, tell it to me.
She went and reported her message to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "May she be well..."
“May Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter, being herself well and free from illness, give birth to a healthy son,” he said.
Having heard this, the king paid homage to the Blessed One and set out toward the interior of the village.
Even before his arrival, the fetus emerged from Suppavāsā’s womb like water from a water-pot; those sitting around her were all weeping with tearful faces.
He began to laugh. The great multitude, joyful and elated, went to announce the King’s message to his son.
The King, seeing their gestures, thought, "I suppose the discourse delivered by the One of Ten Powers has reached its conclusion.
He returned and delivered the Teacher’s message to the princess. The princess said, "The meal you invited me to eat is indeed my very life."
“There will be a festival of auspicious offerings; go and invite the One of Ten Powers for seven days. The king did accordingly.
For seven days they provided a great almsgiving for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Because the boy was born while cooling the agitated hearts of all his kinsmen, they gave him the name Sīvali. He... for seven days...
Because he had dwelt in the womb for many years, from the time of his birth he was capable of performing all tasks.
On the seventh day, the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, engaged in a conversation with him. The Teacher also spoke this verse in the *Dhammapada*:
“He who has transcended this quagmire, this difficult path, this cycle of existence, and delusion;”
“One who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, a meditator, unshaken, free from doubt, extinguished through non-clinging—him I call a brahmin.
Then the Elder said to him: “But why did you go forth after having experienced such a mass of suffering as this?”

“Is it not proper? “I would go forth, venerable sir, if I could obtain permission. When Suppavāsā saw the boy conversing with the Elder, she thought, “What is my son talking about with the General of the Dhamma?
She approached the Elder and asked, “Venerable sir, what is my son saying to you? [She told him] what she herself had experienced.
“Having spoken of the suffering of dwelling in the womb, he says, ‘With your permission, I shall go forth. ‘Very well, venerable sir, let him go forth,’ they said.
The Elder led him to the monastery, gave him the meditation subject of the five aggregates of clinging (*tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna*), and while ordaining him, said:
‘Sīvali, you have no need for any other instruction; the very suffering you experienced for seven years [in the womb] is sufficient.’”
“Reflect upon it. “Venerable sir, it is your responsibility to ordain me; as for what I am capable of doing, I shall know that myself.
At the very moment he removed the first tuft of hair, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry;
at the moment he removed the second, in the fruit of once-returning; and at the third, in the fruit of non-returning. But for all of them—
The shaving of his hair and the realization of Arahatship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after the other.
From the day he went forth, the four requisites for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus arose for him according to his wish. Thus the story originated here.
Later on, the Teacher went to Sāvatthī. The Elder paid homage to the Teacher and said, "Bhante, for me..."
“I shall test my merit; give me five hundred bhikkhus,” he said. “Take them, Sīvalī,” [the king replied].
Taking those five hundred bhikkhus, he set out toward the Himalayas, traveling along a forest path.
First, he saw a deity dwelling in a banyan tree, who gave alms for seven days. Thus he—
“First he saw Nigrodha, second Paṇḍava Mountain;
thirdly at the Aciravatī River, fourthly at the excellent ocean.
Fifth was Himavanta, and sixth he approached Chaddanta.”
"Seventh, Gandhamādana; eighth, then Revata.

At all these places, they gave alms for exactly seven days each. However, on Mount Gandhamādana, the divine king named Nāgadatta gave a gift of milk-rice on one day and a gift of ghee-rice on another day.
The Saṅgha of bhikkhus said, “Friend, neither milch cows being milked nor the churning of curds are seen belonging to this king of the devas;

from where, O king of the devas, does this arise for you? “Venerable sirs, this is the fruit of giving a meal with a ticket of milk during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa,” the king of the devas replied. Later, the Teacher [spoke] to Revata of the Khadiravana forest...

Having established the origin of the narrative through the act of going out to meet him, [the Buddha] placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who have attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of glory within his own dispensation.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Vakkali (208).
