Regarding the tenth section, "among those resolved through faith" (*saddhādhimuttānaṃ*): this means among those monks who are resolute in faith, those possessing powerful faith.
This shows that the Elder Vakkali was the foremost. For while faith must be increased in others, in this elder it had become something that needed to be diminished.
Therefore, he was called the foremost among those resolved through faith (*saddhādhimutta*). His personal name was Vakkali.
Regarding his past deeds, this is the sequential narrative: in the past, during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, according to the method already described...

Having gone to the monastery and standing at the edge of the assembly while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost place among those resolved through faith.

Thinking, “In the future, it is fitting that I too should become like this,” and in the same manner as previously described, he invited the Teacher, gave a great almsgiving for seven days, and after paying homage to the One of Ten Powers, said: “Venerable Sir, may I also—”

"By this act of merit, may you become the foremost among those resolved through faith in the teaching of a future Buddha, just as the bhikkhu who was placed at the head of those resolved through faith," he thus made his aspiration.
Seeing that there would be no obstacle for him, the Teacher gave a prediction and departed.

Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered among gods and humans until, at the time of our Teacher, he took rebirth in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī; they gave him the name Vakkalīti.
When he had grown up and mastered the three Vedas, he saw the Ten-Powered One wandering in Sāvatthī surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and [beheld] the excellence of the Teacher’s physical form.
Gazing [at him], never satiated by the sight of his physical perfection, he wandered about together with the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
When the Teacher went to the monastery, he would go with him and stand watching the excellence of his body.
When the Teacher sat in the Dhamma Hall and preached the Dhamma, he stood directly in front of him and listened to the Dhamma. Having thus acquired faith, he—
Thinking, "If I live in the midst of a household, I will not obtain a constant sight of the One of Ten Powers," he requested the going-forth and went forth in the presence of the Teacher.
From that time on, except for the time of taking food, at whatever place he stood during the remaining hours, he was able to see the One of Ten Powers.
While standing there, he abandoned wise attention and remained merely gazing at the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
The Teacher, waiting for his wisdom to reach maturity, said nothing even though the man continued wandering there for a long time looking only at the physical form.
Then, knowing that "his wisdom has now reached maturity and it is possible to awaken him," he spoke thus:
“What is the use to you, Vakkali, of seeing this putrid body? For whoever, Vakkali, sees the Dhamma, he sees me;
whoever sees me, he sees the Dhamma. For, Vakkali, seeing the Dhamma, one sees me; seeing me, one sees the Dhamma.”
Even though the Teacher was thus exhorting him, the Elder was unable to go elsewhere, for he could not bear to leave the sight of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.

Then the Teacher, thinking, "This bhikkhu will not attain awakening without experiencing a sense of spiritual urgency," went to Rājagaha as the time for the commencement of the rains retreat drew near.
On the day the rains retreat began, he dismissed the Elder, saying, "Begone, Vakkali! And the Buddhas...
Their words were not to be accepted; therefore, the Elder, unable to stand up against the Teacher and unable to endure coming before the One of Ten Powers for three months, thought:
"What can I do now? I have been dismissed by the Tathāgata;
I do not obtain his presence. What is the use of my life? Thus, on Mount Vulture Peak, he went to a place of precipice.

"Mount [the chariot]. The Teacher, perceiving his state of exhaustion, thought, "If this bhikkhu does not receive comfort from my presence, he will destroy the underlying potential for the paths and fruits. Thus, to reveal himself, he emitted a radiance.
From the very moment the bhikkhu saw the Teacher, the great dart of sorrow was cast out. The Teacher [stood] by a dried-up pond.
As if bringing across a flood, he spoke this verse from the *Dhammapada* in order to arouse powerful joy and gladness in the Elder Vakkali:
“The bhikkhu who is full of gladness, having faith in the Buddha’s teaching,
shall attain the peaceful state, the bliss that is the stilling of all formations.”
And to the Elder Vakkali, [the Buddha] extended his hand, saying, “Come, Vakkali. The Elder, having generated intense joy, thinking, “I have seen the Ten-Powered One;
I have even received his invitation to come,” did not realize his own state of departure, wondering, “Whither am I going?
and while still standing on the mountain, he leaped into the air directly before the Ten-Powered One with his first step.
While reflecting upon the verse spoken by the Teacher, he suppressed his rapture even in mid-air and, attaining Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā),
descended while paying homage to the Tathāgata. At a later time, as the Teacher sat in the midst of the assembly of noble ones,
he placed the Elder in the foremost position among those devoted to faith (saddhādhimutta).
Commentary on the Second Chapter. 14.
The Chapter on the Foremost (Etadagga-vagga) (14). 3.
The Third Chapter on the Foremost (Tatiya-etadagga-vagga).
209. In the first [sutta] of the third chapter, "of those desiring training" (*sikkhākāmānaṃ*) means: of those who, longing for the three trainings, train with affection.
By the name "Rāhula," he points to his own son, the Elder Rāhula.
It is said that from the day of his going forth, whenever the Elder rose early in the morning, he would take up a handful of sand and think: "O, that I might today [be like] the One of Ten Powers..."
"...and may I receive such instruction and exhortation from my teachers and preceptors"—thus he aspired.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who desire training. 210.
Regarding the second [epithet], "of those gone forth through faith": this refers to those who have gone forth out of faith. "Raṭṭhapāla" means one who protects the kingdom (*raṭṭhaṃ pāletuṃ*).
Because he was capable of restoring a divided kingdom and was born into a family capable of doing so, he became known as Raṭṭhapāla.
Indeed, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith;
after fasting for fourteen meals and obtaining his parents’ permission to go forth, he was ordained. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith.
The Story of the Elders Rāhula and Raṭṭhapāla Regarding the manner in which these two elders were questioned, this is the sequential narrative:
it is said that both of them were born in the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of wealthy householders. When they were young...

Neither their names nor their clans were mentioned. However, when they reached maturity and established themselves in the household life, both of them, upon the passing of their respective fathers, summoned their own treasurers;
and seeing immeasurable wealth, they thought: "Our grandfathers, fathers, and so forth took this vast heap of wealth along with themselves..."
“They were unable to go; now it is fitting for us to take this wealth by whatever means possible.
Thus, both men began to give great alms to the poor, the destitute, and others at four locations.
One of them, having asked each person who came to his almsgiving what they desired, gave rice gruel, solid food, and other provisions to each according to their preference.
Because he gave [food] in that manner, he became known by the name Āgatapāka (He Who Gives Upon Arrival).

The other, however, gave after filling his vessel again and again without even asking, and because of that reason he became known by the name Anaggapāka (He Who Does Not Give the Best); the meaning is "He Who Gives an Immeasurable Quantity.
One day, early in the morning, both of them went outside the village for the purpose of washing their faces. At that time, from the Himālaya...
Two ascetics of great psychic power, having come through the air for the purpose of seeking alms, descended not far from those companions and stood to one side, thinking, "Let them not see us.
Both of them, having prepared their equipment such as gourd vessels and other requisites, approached and paid homage to those who had gone into the village for alms. Then they...
The ascetics asked, "At what time did you arrive, O you of great merit? They replied, "Just now, venerable sirs.
Having taken the gourd vessels from their hands, they led them each to their own homes;
and at the conclusion of the meal, they obtained a promise from them to come regularly for alms.
Among them, one ascetic possessed a body-element that was burning with fever.
By his own supernatural power, he split the waters of the great ocean in two, went to the abode of the Nāga king Pathavindhara, and sat there for his midday rest.
Having returned after taking advantage of a favorable season, while giving a blessing after the meal at the house of his attendant, he said: "The abode of the Nāga king Pathavindhara..."

“May it be like this,” he said. Then one day his attendant asked him: “Venerable sir, when you offer the blessing of thanksgiving, you say, ‘May it be like the Naga palace of Pathavindhara. We do not know its meaning;
what does this mean, venerable sir? “Yes, householder, I say that your prosperity is like the prosperity of the Naga king Pathavindhara.”
"Let it be so," he said. From that time forth, the householder fixed his mind upon the abode of the Naga King Pathavindhara.
The other ascetic, having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, spent his daytime rest in the empty Serisaka Mansion.
As he was coming and going, he beheld the splendor of Sakka, the king of the gods, and [spoke] to his own attendant.
While making an act of appreciation, he said, "May it be like the Sakka-vimāna.
Then the other householder friend questioned that ascetic in the same manner as the first had. Having heard his words, he fixed his mind upon the realm of Sakka.
Both of them were reborn in the very places they had desired.
Having been reborn in the abode of the Earth-Sustainer, he became known as the Naga King Pathavindhara.
At the moment of his birth, seeing his own form, he felt remorse, thinking: "How unfortunate that this ascetic, who is my family preceptor, has praised a place so unpleasing to me!
This is merely a place for crawling about on one's chest; surely he knows no other place. Thus he was filled with regret.
It happened that at that very moment, the Naga dancers, adorned and prepared, raised their musical instruments in all directions.
At that same instant, he cast off that form and assumed the appearance of a young brahmin youth.
And every half-month, the Four Great Kings go into the presence of Sakka; therefore, he too was accompanied by Virūpakkha, the king of the Nagas.
He went together with Sakka to pay his respects. Seeing him approaching from afar, Sakka recognized him.
Then, when he had come near and stood before him, Sakka asked, "Where have you been reborn, my good man? He replied, "Do not speak thus, Great King;
I have been reborn in the place where one must crawl on the chest, but you, however, have obtained a virtuous friend. "My good man," [Sakka said].
"Do not think, 'I have been reborn in an improper place. The Ten-Powered One, Padumuttara, has appeared in the world;
having performed meritorious service for him, aspire to this very place, so that we both may dwell in happiness.
He replied, "So be it, Your Majesty," and having gone and invited the Ten-Powered One, Padumuttara, to his own Naga abode, he [addressed] the assembly of Nagas...
Together with him, he prepared honors and hospitality for the entire night.
On the following day, when the dawn had risen, the Teacher addressed his attendant, the Elder Sumanas:
"Sumanas, today the Tathāgata will go on a long alms-round; let no ordinary monks come, nor even those who have mastered the Tipiṭaka."

“Let only those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and possess the six super-knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) come. Having heard the Teacher’s words, the Elder announced them to everyone.
Together with the Teacher, one hundred thousand bhikkhus leaped into the sky.
Pathavindara, having come out to meet the One Possessing the Ten Powers along with his retinue of nāgas, stood surrounding the Teacher at the edge of the ocean.

The jewel-colored waves, having gazed upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus while crushing them, looked first at the Teacher and finally at the youngest member of the Saṅgha, the Tathāgata’s son named the novice Uparevata, and thought:
"Such power of psychic potency as this is not surprising for the other disciples; however, such power of psychic potency in this young child is truly most wonderful."
He gave rise to joy and gladness.

Then, while the One of Ten Powers was seated in his palace and the other monks were taking their seats starting from the end of the row, the seat of the novice Uparevata reached the very place in front of the Teacher.
Even as the Naga king was giving rice-gruel and solid food, [he continued...]
At times he would look at the One of Ten Powers, and at times at the novice Uparevata.
It was said that thirty-two marks of a Great Man were visible upon his body, just as they were on the body of the Teacher. Then the Nāga king thought, "This novice appears like the Buddhas;
what indeed could be the reason for this? and [he questioned] a certain bhikkhu sitting not far away.
He asked, "Venerable sir, what is this novice to the One of Ten Powers? "He is a son, Great King," he replied.
He thought, "This bhikkhu is truly great; he has obtained the status of a son to such a Tathāgata who has attained such supreme excellence.
Even his body appears in part like the bodies of the Buddhas. In the future, I too shall become such a one."
“It is fitting that this should come to pass. Having given a great almsgiving for seven days, he made an aspiration:
“Venerable Sir, by the power of this meritorious deed, may I become the son of a future Buddha, just like this Uparevata.
Seeing that there would be no obstacle, the Teacher prophesied: “In the future, you will become the son of Gotama Buddha,” and then departed.
When another half-month had arrived, Pathavindhara went again with Virūpakkha to attend upon Sakka.
Then, as he stood nearby, Sakka asked him: "Friend, do you desire this world of the gods?
"I do not desire it, Great King. "What fault did you see in it? "There is no fault, Great King; however, I [saw] the Ten-Powered One..."
I saw the novice Uparevata. From the moment I saw him, my mind did not turn elsewhere;
therefore, I made this aspiration: "In the future, may I have such a son as this for one Buddha.
You too, Great King, make an aspiration, and we shall never be apart from you in whatever place we are reborn.

Sakka, having accepted his words, saw a bhikkhu of great majesty and, reflecting, "From which family has this son of noble family gone forth after renouncing the world? he perceived: "This man is the son of a family capable of restoring a broken kingdom;
having undergone fourteen fasts and obtained his parents' permission for the going-forth..."
Having realized, "He has gone forth," and yet acting as if he did not know, he questioned the One of Ten Powers. Then, having performed great honors for seven days, he made this aspiration:
"Venerable Sir, by the result of this wholesome deed, may I, like this son of good family, become the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith in the dispensation of a future Buddha."

The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacles, prophesied: "Great King, in the future, in the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, you shall become the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith.
Having spoken thus, he departed. Sakka also returned to his own celestial city.
Both of them, passing away from the place where they were reborn and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, elapsed many thousands of aeons.
Now, at the end of ninety-two aeons ago, a Buddha named Phussa appeared in the world.
His father was King Mahinda, and he had three uterine younger brothers. Day after day, the king, cherishing the thought, "The Buddha is mine alone;
the Dhamma is mine; the Saṅgha is mine," personally provided the Ten-Powered One with a regular supply of food.
Then one day, the border region rose in revolt. He addressed his sons: "Sons, the border has risen;
either you or I must go. If I go, you must attend upon the One of Ten Powers according to this method.
All three of them replied at once: "Father, there is no need for you to go; we shall deal with the bandits."
Thinking, “We shall disperse them,” they paid homage to their father, went to the frontier, dispersed the bandits, and returned as victors in battle.
On the way back, they consulted with their footmen: “Sirs, at the very moment we departed, our father would grant a boon;
which boon shall we choose? “Noble sirs, after your father’s passing, [a boon] will be difficult to obtain.”
“There is no other boon; however, accept the boon of attending upon your eldest brother, the Buddha Phussa,” they said.
They replied, “It is excellent that you have spoken thus,” and with one mind, they all went and saw their father.
At that time, their father, being pleased with them, granted them a boon. They chose the boon: “We shall attend upon the Tathāgata for three months.”
They made their request. The king said, "This cannot be given; choose another boon.
"Father," they replied, "we have no need for any other boon. If you wish to grant us one, give us this very boon.
As they spoke thus again and again, the king, reflecting that he had already promised it and could not refuse, said: "Sons, I [grant it to you]..."
“I grant you this boon; however, those known as Buddhas are difficult to approach, like lions that wander alone.
Therefore, you must be diligent in attending upon the One Possessed of the Ten Powers.
They thought: “We must attend upon the Tathāgata in a manner that is truly fitting for us.”

"It is fitting," they said; and with one mind, they all undertook the ten precepts and, becoming free from the stench of raw flesh, appointed three men to attend upon the Teacher at the place of almsgiving.
Among them, one was the provider of wealth and grain, one was the builder, and one was the organizer of the offerings.
Of these, the provider of wealth and grain became King Bimbisāra in the present age, and the builder became the lay follower Visākha.
The Elder Raṭṭhapāla was the organizer of the almsgiving. Having performed wholesome deeds there throughout his life, he was reborn in the city of the gods.
This Elder Rāhula, however, was born during the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa as the eldest son of King Kiki of Kāsi;
they gave him the name Prince Pathavindhara. He had seven sisters.
They had seven monasteries built for the One of Ten Powers. Pathavindharo obtained the position of viceroy.
He said to those sisters, "Give me one [monastery] among those monasteries you have had built. They replied, "Brother, you are established in the position of viceroy;
it is you who ought to give to us. You should build another monastery yourself. He [acted] upon their word.
Having heard this, he had five hundred monasteries built; some say he also had five hundred meditation cells built.
Having performed wholesome deeds there throughout his life, he was reborn in the city of the gods.
Now, during this appearance of a Buddha, Prince Pathavindhara took conception in the womb of our Bodhisatta’s chief queen, while his friend [was born] in the kingdom of Kuru.
He was born in the merchant Raṭṭhapāla’s house in the town of Thullakoṭṭhita.
Then, after our Ten-Powered One had attained full enlightenment and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he eventually came to Kapilavatthu and ordained Prince Rāhula.
The procedure for his ordination is indeed recorded in the Pāḷi. Having thus been ordained—
The Teacher, out of a desire to constantly exhort him, spoke the *Rāhulovāda Sutta*.
Rāhula, too, rising early in the morning, would take sand in his hand and say, "May I receive this much instruction today from the One of Ten Powers, as well as from my teacher and preceptor.
A discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: "How indeed worthy of exhortation is the novice Rāhula!"

"A son who is worthy of his father. Knowing the disposition of the monks' minds, the Teacher thought, "If I go there, a discourse on the Dhamma will increase, and Rāhula’s virtue will become manifest.
He went and sat upon the Buddha’s seat in the Dhamma Hall and addressed the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?"
“Blessed One, let us speak of the novice Rāhula’s capacity for receiving instruction. Standing at this spot, the Teacher, for the purpose of illustrating Rāhula’s virtues, recounted the Migajātakaya:
“The deer who was well-versed in the three ways, possessed of many wiles...”
"At midnight I drank from the eight-horned [vessel];
breathing upon the ground through a single tube,
my nephew was struck by six arrows."
Then, when he was a seven-year-old novice, [the Buddha] taught him the Ambalaṭṭhikārāhulovāda Sutta, thinking:
"Lest Rāhula, on account of his youth, should speak a conscious lie even for the sake of play.
When he was an eighteen-year-old novice, as he entered the town for alms behind the Tathāgata, he beheld the physical beauty of both the Teacher and himself.

To him who was thinking thoughts connected with the household life, the Teacher preached the Mahā-Rāhulovāda Sutta according to the method beginning with, “Rāhula, whatever form there is,” and so forth.
Furthermore, both the Rāhulovāda in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* and the Rāhulovāda in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* constitute the Elder’s very practice of insight (*vipassanā*).
Then, knowing that his knowledge had reached maturity, while seated in the Andhavana grove during the period when he was still a novice bhikkhu, the Teacher delivered the Cūḷa-Rāhulovāda.
He preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Elder Rāhula, together with one hundred thousand times ten million deities, attained Arahantship;
as for the deities who had become stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners, they were beyond counting.
Later, while seated in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who desire training in this Dispensation.
But when the Teacher had set out on a journey through the kingdom of Kuru and arrived at Thullakoṭṭhita, the noble youth Raṭṭhapāla, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith.
Having obtained his parents’ permission, he approached the One of Ten Powers and, by the Teacher’s command, went forth in the presence of a certain elder. From the day of his going forth...

From that time on, whenever the merchant householder saw monks passing by the door of his residence, he would revile and abuse them, saying, "What business do you have in this house? You had an only son; you took him away and left. Now what will you do?
After the Teacher had stayed at Thullakoṭṭhita for half a month, he returned once more to Sāvatthī.
He arrived there. There, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, applying systematic attention and performing the necessary work, increased his insight and attained arahantship.
Having obtained the Teacher’s permission, he went to Thullakoṭṭhita to see his parents;
while wandering for alms there from house to house in regular order, he received at his father’s residence some stale sour gruel.
Enjoying that [alms-food] as if it were the Deathless, he accepted the invitation of his father;
on the following day, having partaken of alms at his father’s residence, he aroused the perception of foulness toward the women who stood there adorned and arrayed.
While still standing, he preached the Dhamma, and like an arrow released from a bowstring, he sprang into the air and went to King Koravya’s Migacīra park.
Seated upon the Maṅgala stone slab, he taught the Dhamma adorned with the four kinds of loss to the king who had come to see him;
then, wandering on his alms tour by stages, he returned once again to the presence of the Teacher. Thus this story originated.
Later, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, he [addressed] the Elder in this Dispensation...
"He placed [him] in the foremost position among the sons of good family who had gone forth out of faith.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna (211).
Regarding the phrase "of those taking the first voting-ticket in the third [category]," it refers to the monks who were the very first to take the voting-tickets.

This shows that the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna was the foremost. It is said that on the day he was invited by Mahāsubhaddā, while the Tathāgata was traveling toward Ugganagara, the Elder uttered the first lion’s roar, saying:
"Today the Teacher will go a long distance for alms; let not worldlings take voting tickets;
let only the five hundred whose taints are destroyed take them. Thus he roared the lion’s roar at the very outset.

He took a voting ticket (*salāka*). On the day he was invited by Cūḷasubhaddā, even as the Tathāgata was traveling toward Sāketa, he took the very first voting ticket among the five hundred bhikkhus; likewise when they were traveling toward the Sunāparanta country.
For these reasons, the Elder became known as the foremost among those who take the voting ticket first. His name, however, was Kuṇḍadhāna.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential narrative: It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Having gone to the monastery in the manner already described and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being foremost among those who take the first voting-ticket. He then performed an act of service for the Buddhas.
Having performed that service and aspired to that position, he was prophesied by the Teacher after the latter foresaw no obstacles.
Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans and was reborn during the time of Kassapa Buddha as a deity dwelling on the earth.
Furthermore, for Buddhas of long lifespan, there is no half-monthly Uposatha; such was the case for the Ten-Powered One, Vipassī.
Indeed, during the interval between the six-year periods, there was a Uposatha every six years; however, the Ten-Powered Kassapa recited the Pātimokkha every sixth month.

At the time of his recitation of the Pātimokkha, two monks who were friends living in different directions would go [to him], thinking, "We shall perform the Uposatha. This earth-deity thought: "Of these two monks..."
"Their friendship is exceedingly firm; even if there were someone to cause a rift, would it break, or would it not?
While observing their opportunity, she walked not far from them.
Then, one elder, having placed his bowl and robes in the hand of another, [went] to a convenient place with water for the purpose of washing his body.
Having gone there and washed his hands and feet, he emerged from the grove assembly hall.
A terrestrial deity followed behind that elder, appearing as a woman of exquisite form;
she seemed to be shaking out his hair and binding it, wiping away the dust from his back, and arranging and putting on his lower garment. Thus she attended the elder.
Following step by step, they emerged from the thicket. Standing to one side, the Elder Companion saw this situation and was overcome with grief, thinking:
"Now I have lost the long-standing affection I shared with this bhikkhu.
Had I known he would come to such a state, I would not have placed my trust in him for all this time."
As he was returning after having reflected thus, he said: "Come now, friend, here is your bowl and robe;

I will not travel along the same path with such a wicked companion. Upon hearing those words, the heart of that modest bhikkhu felt as if it were pierced by a sharp spear. Then he said to him: "Friend, what is this you say?"
“For all this time I have not known even a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*). Yet today you call me a ‘wicked man’;
what have you seen? “What need is there for anything else seen?
Have you not seen that you departed from this place together with a woman so beautifully adorned and prepared? “Friend, this is not so; I did not [do such a thing].”
"I see a woman. Although he spoke thus up to three times, the other elder, not believing his words, took only the matter of what he himself had seen as the truth;
instead of going by the same path as him, he went to the presence of the Teacher by another route.
The other also went to the presence of the Teacher by yet another route.

Then, at the time of entering the Uposatha hall, that monk recognized the other monk in the Uposatha assembly and thought, "There is such a wicked monk in this Uposatha assembly; I will not perform the Uposatha together with him.
He went out and stood outside. A terrestrial deity [thought], "I have committed a grave deed..."
Saying this, he approached him in the guise of an elderly lay follower and asked, "Venerable sir, why are you standing in this place?
He replied, "Lay follower, a wicked monk has entered this Uposatha hall;
I will not perform the Uposatha with him, so I have gone out and am standing outside. [The other said,] "Venerable sir, do not speak thus."
"Take it; this bhikkhu is pure in virtue. As for what you saw regarding a woman—it was I myself.
For the purpose of testing you, thinking, 'Is the affection of these elders firm or not firm?
I performed that deed while observing their sense of shame and lack of shame. But who are you, good man? "I am a certain earth-deity, venerable sir."
Even as he was speaking, the deva stood by means of his divine power, fell at the elder’s feet, and requested of him: “Venerable sir, forgive me;
the elder did not know this fault. Let us perform the Uposatha. Having thus entreated the elder, he led him into the Uposatha hall.
The elder then performed the Uposatha in that one place, but not again with him on account of their former friendship.
"He was in one place together with [him]" means that this elder’s deed is not told;
however, the elder who had been censured attained Arahantship while practicing insight meditation (vipassanā) again and again.
By the result of that deed, the earth-deity was not released from the states of misery for the duration of an interval between Buddhas. If...
However, from time to time he returns to the human state, and whatever offense was committed by anyone else falls upon him alone.
During the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in Sāvatthī into a brahmin family;
they gave him the name Dhāna-māṇava. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas, and in his old age, he [attended] the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.

Having heard this, he gained faith and went forth. From the day of his full ordination, a woman fully adorned and prepared would enter the village together with him whenever he entered, and leave whenever he left;
she would also enter the monastery when he entered and stand there while he stood—thus she was seen to follow him constantly.
The Elder did not see her, yet by the result of that previous karma, she appeared before others.
When women in the village were giving alms of rice-gruel, they would joke, saying, "Venerable Sir, this one ladle of gruel is for you, and this one is for our friend here.
This caused the Elder great distress. Even when he had gone to the monastery...
The novices and young bhikkhus surrounded him and mocked him, saying, "A *koṇḍa* has been born!
For that reason, he came to be known by the name Thera Kuṇḍadhāna.
Rising up again and again, unable to endure the jesting they were making toward him, he fell into a state of madness and cried out, "You *koṇḍas*! Your preceptor..."
“Koṇḍā! Teachers Koṇḍā! he said. Then they reported this to the Teacher:
“Kuṇḍadhāna speaks such harsh words together with the young novices. The Teacher summoned him and, having asked, “Is it true, monk?
and being told, “It is true, Blessed One,” He said, “Why do you speak thus? [He replied: “Venerable Sir, unable to endure constant harassment...”
"How can this be? [he asked]. Having said, "You are unable to exhaust the karma you committed in the past until this very day;
do not speak such harsh words to the bhikkhus again," he spoke thus:
"Do not speak harshly to anyone; when spoken to, they may retort to you."
"Hostile speech is indeed painful; counter-blows may strike you back.
But if you restrain yourself like a cracked gong, you have reached Nibbāna; no hostility exists within you."
Furthermore, they reported to the King of Kosala the Elder’s conduct in wandering about with a woman.

The King said, "Go, my men, and investigate," and having sent them, he himself went to the Elder’s dwelling place with a small retinue and stood to one side, observing. At that moment, the Elder was engaged in needlework.
While he was sitting there performing his duties, that woman appeared as if standing nearby.
Seeing her, the king thought, "There must be a reason for this," and went to the place where she stood.
As he approached, she acted as if she had entered the Elder’s leaf-hut. The king likewise entered the leaf-hut together with her.

Having entered and looked everywhere, not seeing [anyone], he formed the perception: "This is no woman; it is a single result of the Elder’s kamma. Although he first went near the Elder, he did not pay him homage.
Then, realizing that the reason for his initial thought was untrue, he returned, paid homage to the Elder, and sat down to one side. He asked: "Venerable sir, I hope you have obtained almsfood?"
“Are you not weary? he asked. The Elder replied, “It is well, Great King. “I understand, venerable sir, how it is for you, noble one;
who indeed would have faith in those who live amidst such defilement?
From now on, you have no need to go anywhere; I shall attend to you with the four requisites.”
"Do not neglect proper attention," he said, and established a regular supply of almsfood for him.
Having obtained this support from the king, the Elder, with his mind made one-pointed through suitable food, developed insight and attained Arahantship.
From that time on, that woman vanished.
While living in the city of Ugganagara in a family of wrong views, Mahāsubhaddā resolved upon the Uposatha, thinking, "May the Teacher have compassion for me.
Having become free from the scent of raw flesh (pure), she stood on the upper terrace of the palace and said:
"May these flowers, without falling in between, remain as a canopy over the head of the One of Ten Powers; by this sign, tomorrow the One of Ten Powers [will come]."
"May he accept alms from me together with a hundred bhikkhus," she said, and having made this declaration of truth, she scattered eight handfuls of *sumana* flowers.
The flowers went forth and, at the time of the Teacher’s preaching of the Dhamma, they remained suspended as a canopy over the Teacher's head.
Seeing that *sumana* flower canopy, the Teacher mentally accepted Subhaddā’s alms offering, and on the following day—
When dawn had broken, he said to the Elder Ānanda: "Ānanda, today we shall go on alms-round to a distant place;
do not give voting tickets to worldlings, but give them only to the Noble Ones. The Elder announced this to the monks:
"Friends, the Teacher will go on alms-round to a distant place today; let not worldlings take tickets, but only the Noble Ones."
"Let them take [the voting tickets]. Elder Kuṇḍadhāna said, "Bring one, friend," and extended his hand first.
Ānanda, having formed the thought, "The Teacher does not cause such monks as these to receive a voting ticket;
he causes only the Noble Ones to receive them," went and reported this to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Give a voting ticket to him who asks for one. The Elder—
He thought: "If it were not proper to give a voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna, then the Teacher would have prevented me;
there must be a reason for this. Thinking, "I shall give a voting ticket to Kuṇḍadhāna," he set out on his journey.
Before he had even arrived, the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna had already attained the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā).

Standing in the air by means of supernormal power (iddhi), he stretched out his hand and took the voting ticket (salāka), saying: "Bring it, friend Ānanda! The Teacher knows me; the Teacher does not forbid a monk such as I from taking the first voting ticket.
The Teacher, making this the occasion for instruction, established the Elder in the foremost position among those who take the first voting ticket in this Dispensation.
The Story of the Elder Vaṅgīsa (212).
In the fourth [verse], the phrase "of those possessed of ready wit" indicates that the Elder Vaṅgīsa is the foremost among those endowed with ready wit.
It is said that as this elder was approaching the presence of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, from the very moment he came within the range of his vision, by means of the moon...
Having compared [the Teacher] with the sun, the sky, the great ocean, the elephant king, and the lion, the king of beasts—
even while speaking the praises of the Teacher through many hundreds and thousands of verses— he approaches him. Therefore,
he became known as the foremost of those possessed of ready wit (*paṭibhānavantānaṃ*).

Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential narrative: It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he took rebirth in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Proceeding to the monastery in the same manner as before and listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those possessed of ready wit (*paṭibhānavantānaṃ*), and [the man] performed an act of service for the Teacher.
Having made the aspiration, "May I too become the foremost among those possessed of eloquence in the future," he was prophesied by the Teacher.

Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed away and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
They gave him the name Vaṅgīsa-māṇava. When he reached maturity, he mastered the three Vedas.
Having pleased his teacher and mastered the science called *chavasīsamanta*, he would strike a corpse’s head with his fingernail and know,
"This being has been reborn in such-and-such a womb. Knowing,
"This is our means of livelihood," the brahmins had the young man Vaṅgīsa seated in a covered carriage.
While wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, they would station themselves at city gates or market-town gates;
perceiving that the great crowds had gathered there in heaps, they would say, "Whoever sees Vaṅgīsa will obtain wealth, or obtain fame, or go to heaven.
Having heard their words, many people, desiring to see him, offered bribes.
[They] are [there]. The kings and high ministers go to them and ask, "What is the teacher's special knowledge?
[The teacher replies: "You do not know. In the whole of Jambudīpa, there is no other scholar equal to our teacher.
At the end of three years, having had the heads of those who have died brought, and having struck them with his fingernail, he knows: 'This being was in such-and-such a womb...'"
...he knows, "I have been reborn. Vaṅgīsa, for the purpose of cutting through the doubts of the great multitude, would bring various people forward and have each of them speak of their own destiny.
Relying on him, the multitude would receive a hundred or even a thousand [pieces of money] from their hands.
Having taken the young brahmin Vaṅgīsa and wandered about as they pleased, the brahmins returned again to Sāvatthī. Vaṅgīsa—
Standing not far from the Jetavana Mahāvihāra, he thought: "They say the ascetic Gotama is wise;
however, it is not right for me to always act solely according to their word;
it is also right to go into the presence of other wise men. He said to the brahmins: "You go; I will not [go] with many."
“Let us go together and see the ascetic Gotama. They said to him, “Vaṅgīsa, do not find it pleasing to see the ascetic Gotama;
for whoever sees him, he ensnares them with his magic power.
Disregarding their words, Vaṅgīsa went into the presence of the Teacher, exchanged pleasant greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
Then the Teacher asked him: "Vaṅgīsa, do you know any craft? "Yes, Master Gotama, I know one called the 'Cemetery-Head Spell' (chavasīsamanta).
"What does that spell do? "By reciting that spell over the head of someone who has died even three years ago, and striking it with my fingernail, I can know the place where they have been reborn.
The Teacher [then spoke] of one who had arisen in hell...
He showed him three heads: one of a being reborn among humans, one of a being reborn among the devas, and one of a being who had attained final nibbāna.
Having struck the first head, he said, "Master Gotama, this being has gone to hell.
"Excellent, excellent, Vaṅgīsa! You have seen clearly. Where has this being gone? "To the human world."
“O Gotama,” he said. “Where has this being gone? “To the world of the devas, O Gotama. Thus he spoke of the destination reached by all three.
But when the Teacher had attained final nibbāna, Vaṅgīsa struck the head with his fingernail and could see neither the end nor the limit.
Then the Teacher asked him, “Are you unable to do so, Vaṅgīsa? “I am able to see it, O Gotama; let me investigate.”
He turned those words over and over again: "So much... so much... How could he know the destination of one whose taints were exhausted by means of an outsider's mantra?
Then sweat broke out from the top of his head. Feeling ashamed, he stood silent. Then the Teacher said to him, "Are you weary, Vaṅgīsa?
"Yes, Master Gotama, I am unable to know the place to which this being has gone."
“If you know, then speak. Having said, “Vaṅgīsa, I know this, and even more than this,” he recited these two verses from the Dhammapada:
“He who fully understands the passing away of beings and their rebirth everywhere;”
“One who is unattached, well-gone, awakened— him I call a brahmin.
One whose destination neither gods, nor gandhabbas, nor humans know—
the one with taints destroyed, an arahant— him I call a brahmin.”
Then Vaṅgīsa said: "Master Gotama, there is no loss whatsoever in giving knowledge for the sake of knowledge;
I will give you the mantra that I myself know, so you must give this mantra to me. "Vaṅgīsa, we do not give a mantra for a mantra;
it is not in this way that we give," he replied. "Very well, Master Gotama, give me the mantra."
Having shown him honor and making a gesture of reverence with his hands, he sat down.
"Vaṅgīsa, in your tradition, is there no probation for those who receive a costly mantra or anything else? "There is, Master Gotama.
"But you consider our mantra to be without probation? "Brahmins, indeed, are never satisfied with mantras; therefore, that..."
He said to the Blessed One, “Sir Gotama, I shall perform the ritual of *niyāma* as taught by you.
The Blessed One said, “Vaṅgīsa, when we give this spell, we give it to one who shares our same religious mark (*liṅga*).
Vaṅgīsa said to the brahmins, “Whatever must be done, it is fitting that I go after receiving this spell. [The brahmins replied,] “If you go forth into homelessness, we [shall do so].”
"Do not worry; having mastered this mantra, I shall become the foremost in all of Jambudīpa.
This being so, it will also be auspicious for you. For the sake of the mantra, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "First, observe the period of probation for the mantra," and then explained the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra). The wise being [mastered] the thirty-two aspects...
While reciting his lessons there, he established the contemplation of rise and fall, developed insight, and attained arahantship.
When he had attained arahantship, the brahmins thought, "What is Vaṅgīsa’s current state?
We shall go and see him. They went to him and asked, "Master Vaṅgīsa, did you learn this craft in the presence of the ascetic Gotama?"
They asked. "Yes, we have trained. "Then come, let us go. "Go yourselves; my business with you is finished.
"We told you right from the start, 'The ascetic Gotama ensnares those who come to see him with his magic. "Indeed, you are now under the power of the ascetic Gotama."
"Having fallen into such a state, what can we do in your presence? they said, and departed by the very path by which they had come.
As for the Elder Vaṅgīsa, whenever he went to see the One of Ten Powers, he would go while composing a single verse of praise.
Therefore, while seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those possessed of ready wit.
The Story of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta (213).
Regarding the phrase "of those who are beautiful on all sides" (*samantapāsādikānaṃ*), it means "of those who are pleasing in every way. *Upasena* is the name of that elder.
Furthermore, because he was the son of the brahmin Vaṅganta, he is called "Vaṅgantaputta" (the son of Vaṅganta). This, then, is the elder.

He was not only personally handsome, but his assembly was also handsome; thus, by virtue of the name he acquired based on that assembly, he became known as the foremost of those who are "all-around handsome" (*samantapāsādikānam aggo*).
As for his history regarding the answering of questions, this is the sequential account: during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he lived in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Having been reborn in a noble family, he reached maturity and, proceeding in the same manner as before, went into the presence of the Teacher while listening to the Dhamma.
Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who are "all-encompassing and serene" (*samantapāsādika*),
he performed a service for the Teacher, aspired to that very station, and having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During this appearance of a Buddha, he took rebirth in the womb of the brahmin woman Sāri at the brahmin village of Nālaka;
they gave him the name Upasena.
When he had reached maturity, having mastered the three Vedas and heard the Dhamma in the presence of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, he acquired faith.
He went forth. Having been ordained for one year, thinking, "I shall increase the noble lineage," he caused a certain son of good family to go forth and receive full ordination in his presence.

After the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā), while his student had been ordained for one year and he himself was two years ordained, he thought, "The One of Ten Powers will be pleased upon seeing me," and taking his student with him, he approached the One of Ten Powers.
He had come to see [the Teacher]. After the Teacher had paid him homage, he asked him as he was sitting to one side:
"How many years have you been ordained, bhikkhu? "I am two years ordained, Blessed One. "But how many years has this bhikkhu been ordained? "He is one year ordained, Blessed One.
"What is this bhikkhu to you? "He is my co-resident, Blessed One. Then the Teacher said to him: "Very quickly indeed..."
“You, foolish man, have turned toward abundance,” he said, and rebuked him in many ways.

Having received this rebuke from the Teacher, the Elder paid homage to the Blessed One and thought, “With this very face, as beautiful as the full moon, I shall cause the Teacher to give his approval (sādhukāra) based on the assembly itself. On that very day, he went to a certain place.
Having practiced the work of insight (vipassanā), he attained arahantship before long.
Since the Elder had gone forth after leaving a great family and was indeed a preacher of the Dhamma whose voice resounded throughout the earth,
many people— having gained confidence through his preaching of the Dhamma and having gone forth from their families of friends, ministers, and kinsmen— [followed him].

The sons of noble families went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder. The Elder explained the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), saying, "I am a forest-dweller; you too may go forth if you are able to become forest-dwellers. When they replied, "We shall be able, venerable sir," he granted them the going-forth.
By their own strength, they resolved upon each respective ascetic practice. At the time when the Elder himself was ten years old...
Having made the Vinaya proficient, he ordained them all. Thus, there were about five hundred monks who became his retinue.
At that time, while residing at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, the Teacher said: "Monks, I desire to spend half a month..."
Having announced to the community of monks, "I shall dwell in seclusion," he became a solitary dweller.
The community of monks also made a formal agreement, saying, "Whoever approaches to see the Blessed One must be made to confess a *pācittiya* offense.
At that time, the Elder Upasena, thinking, "I shall see the Blessed One," went to Jetavana with his own retinue and approached the Teacher.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. For the purpose of initiating a conversation, the Teacher addressed a certain co-resident pupil of the elder:
“Bhikkhu, are those rag-robes pleasing to you? “Venerable sir, those rag-robes are not pleasing to me,” he said;
yet, out of reverence for his preceptor, he explained his state as a wearer of rag-robes. At this point, the Teacher said: “Excellent, excellent!”
“Upasena,” he said, giving his approval to the elder and speaking in many ways of his virtues.
This is the summary here; however, this story is recorded in detail in the Pāḷi itself.
Later, when the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, he placed the elder in the foremost position among those who are "all-appealing" (samantapāsādika) in this Dispensation.
The Story of the Elder Dabba (214). Regarding the sixth [case], "of those who assign lodgings": this refers to those assigning lodgings (*senāsana*).

It is said that at the time when the Elder was assigning lodgings, among the eighteen great monasteries, there was no cell (*pariveṇa*) left uncleaned, nor any lodging (*senāsana*) left unattended or unswept.
There were no beds or stools, nor was there any drinking water or water for washing. Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who prepare lodgings.
His name was Dabba Tissa; however, because he was born into the royal family of the Mallas, he was called Mallaputta.
Regarding his career in answering questions, this is the sequential account: during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, in the city of Haṃsavatī...
Having been reborn in a noble family and reached maturity, he went to the monastery in the manner previously described.
While listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among those who assign lodgings.

Having performed an act of service and aspired to that very position, he was prophesied by the Teacher. Thereafter, having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, [he was reborn] among gods and humans.
Having wandered through saṃsāra, he went forth at a time when the teaching of the Seer Kassapa was declining.
At that time, seven bhikkhus—including himself and six others—became single-minded; seeing others showing disrespect toward the Teaching, they thought, "What shall we do here?
Let us perform the duty of a recluse in seclusion and bring an end to suffering," and so they constructed a ladder.
Having ascended the peak of the high mountain, he said, "Those who know the strength of their own minds, let them descend by means of a ladder;
those who are attached to life, let them come down; do not be full of regret later. Then, with all of them becoming single-minded, they set up the ladder.
Having exhorted one another, saying, "Be heedful, friends," they sat down in places according to their own inclinations.
They began to practice the duties of a recluse (*śramaṇadharma*).
There, one elder, having attained *arhatship* on the fifth day, thought, "My task is accomplished;
what shall I do remaining in this place? By means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said, "Friends, take this almsfood."
"Enjoy [the alms-food]; let the duty of wandering for alms be my responsibility; you perform your own work," he said.
"Friend, did we say this while setting up the ladder: 'Whosoever first realizes the Dhamma, let him bring back alms;
having eaten what he has brought, the rest shall practice the ascetic's duty'?"
“...will they do? “No, friends. “You have obtained [this] through your own past causes; we too, being able, will bring an end to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Go, then! The elder, unable to convince them, ate his alms-food in a comfortable place and departed.
Another elder, having attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) on the seventh day, from there—
Having passed away, he was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa Brahmā-world.

The other elders also, having passed away from there, wandered among gods and humans for the duration of one Buddha-interval, and were then reborn in various families during this current appearance of a Buddha.
One was reborn in the royal palace in the city of Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
One was reborn in the kingdom of Pabbateyya in the womb of a female wanderer; one was reborn in the kingdom of Bāhiya in the house of a householder;

and one was reborn in Rājagaha in the house of a householder. This Venerable Dabba, however, took conception in the house of a Mallan king in the city of Anupiya in the kingdom of the Mallas. When his mother was in the throes of childbirth...
She passed away. Having taken her dead body to the cemetery, they placed it upon a wooden pyre and set fire to it.
By the force of the fire, her abdominal membrane became heated and split in two. By the power of his own merit, the boy leapt up and landed upon a wooden pillar.
They took the boy and gave him to his grandmother. As she was giving him a name, [she looked at] the wooden pillar...
Because he had fallen [into the water] and regained his life, they gave him the name Dabba.

When he was seven years old, the Teacher, accompanied by the community of monks, while wandering on tour through the Mallan country, arrived at the town of Anupiya and stayed in the Ambavana grove at Anupiya. Upon seeing the Teacher, Prince Dabba, by that very sight...
Having gained confidence and desiring to go forth, he asked his grandmother, “I wish to go forth in the presence of the One of Ten Powers.
She replied, “Very well, dear child,” and taking Dabba Kumāra with her, she went into the presence of the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, please grant this boy the going-forth.
The Teacher gave a sign to a certain bhikkhu, saying, “Bhikkhu, [give this boy the going-forth].”
“Please ordain him. Having heard the Teacher’s words, that elder ordained Dabbakumāra and taught him the meditation subject of the five aggregates (the *tacapañcaka*).

Being a being endowed with past roots of merit who had made the necessary resolve, as the first circle of hair was being shaved away, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*);
as the second circle of hair was being shaved away, he established himself in the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-phala*); and at the third...

Regarding the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*): however, the shaving of all his hair and the realization of the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphalasacchikiriyā*) occurred neither later nor earlier [than that].
Having dwelt in the Mallaraṭṭha country for as long as he desired, the Teacher went to Rājagaha and took up residence in the Veḷuvana.
There, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta, having gone into seclusion and reflected upon the completion of his own task, [set his mind] upon performing services for the Saṅgha.
Desiring to apply himself to the body, he thought: "What if I were to arrange lodgings for the Saṅgha and assign meals?

He went into the presence of the Teacher and reported his reflection. The Teacher gave him his approval and accepted his appointment as the arranger of lodgings and the assigner of meals. Then [the Teacher] said to him:
Thinking, "This Dabba, though still young, stands in a great position," they ordained him at the age of only seven years.

From the very moment of his full ordination, the Elder began arranging the lodgings for all the monks residing in the vicinity of Rājagaha, and after receiving alms-food, he would assign it to them. His role as the arranger of lodgings—
He became well-known in all directions: “It is said that Dabba Mallaputta assigns lodgings in one place for monks who are companions;
he assigns lodgings even in distant places. For those unable to go there, he leads them by means of psychic power.
Then, at all times—whether it was the right time or not—the monks would say to him, “Friend, please assign us lodgings in Jīvakambavana.”
“...in our Migadāya deer park at Maddakucchi. Having thus directed them to their lodgings, they proceeded while watching for his supernatural power (*iddhi*).
He too, having fashioned a mind-made body through his *iddhi*, created for each elder a monk identical to himself;
then, walking before them with a finger emitting light, he said, “This is the couch,” and so forth.
Having said, "This is the seat," and so forth, and having prepared the lodging, he would return once more to his own dwelling place.
This is the summary here; however, this story is recorded in detail in the Pāḷi itself.
Later on, the Teacher, taking this very incident as the occasion for a discourse, while sitting in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, [praised] the Elder among those who prepare lodgings.
"He placed him in the foremost position.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Pilindavaccha (215).
Regarding the phrase "dear and pleasing to the deities" in the seventh [section]: the Elder Pilindavaccha was both dear to and pleasing to the deities.

He shows that he was the foremost. It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, he became a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī rājā*) and established the great multitude in the five precepts, making them destined for heaven.
It is further said that most of the deities reborn in the six heavenly realms of sensual pleasure did so because they received his instruction;
and in each place where they were reborn, upon observing their own prosperity, they wondered, "Who indeed..."

Reflecting, "It was by depending on him that we obtained this attainment of heaven," and seeing this elder, they thought, "It is by depending on the elder that we have now obtained [this]," and so they paid homage to the elder morning and evening.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who are dear and pleasing to the deities. His clan name was Pilinda and his personal name was Vaccha; both of these—
Having been thus associated with him, he is called Pilindavaccha.
This is the sequential account regarding his past deeds: it is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great wealth;
hearing the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma in the manner previously described, he [honored] the Teacher...
Seeing a bhikkhu being established in a position dear and pleasing to the deities, he aspired to that very status;
having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered among gods and humans until, during this present dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
They gave him the name Pilindavaccha. At a later time, [he heard] the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma...
Having heard this, he gained faith, went forth, and received full ordination. Developing insight, he attained arahantship.
Yet, when conversing with both laypeople and monks, he continued to address them using only the term "outcaste," saying, "Come, outcaste! Go, outcaste! Bring it, outcaste!
Take it, outcaste! When they reported this matter to the Tathāgata, they questioned him about it.
“The Blessed One said, ‘The noble ones (ariya) do not use harsh speech. Venerable sir, for the noble ones there is no such thing as harsh speech by way of disparaging others;

however, it might occur due to habits cultivated in previous lives. “Venerable sir, the Elder Pilindavaccha, rising up again and again, while conversing with both householders and monks, would say, ‘Outcaste!’”
“...calls him a ‘vasala’; what is the reason for this, Blessed One? “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this habit belongs to my son;
in the past, for five hundred births, he was reborn in brahmin families as one who spoke of ‘vasalas.
Thus he speaks by virtue of his habitual practice, not out of harshness. For even if the speech of the Noble Ones is harsh, it is so by way of intention.”
Having stated, "Because of its non-harsh nature it is indeed pure; not even the slightest evil is found herein," he spoke this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
"One should utter speech that is not harsh, informative, and true;
that by which one does not revile anyone—that, I say, is a brahmin."

Then one day, as the Elder was entering Rājagaha for alms, he saw a man entering the city carrying a vessel filled with long peppers. Seeing him, the Elder said, "What is in your vessel, outcaste? The man thought:
"This ascetic has been speaking harsh words to me since early morning; this is indeed appropriate for him."
“It is proper to speak,” he said. “Venerable sir, there is mouse-dung in my bowl. “It shall be so, you outcaste!
As that elder was looking at it, everything became nothing but mouse-dung.
He thought, “These long peppers appear like mouse-dung; is this their true nature or not? While investigating, he took one with his hand.
He squeezed it. Then, realizing it was mouse-dung, a powerful dejection arose within him.
Thinking, "Is it only these that are like this, or are all the peppers so? he went and looked;
seeing that all the peppers were exactly like that, he pressed his hand against his heart and said, "This is not the work of another; this is the work of the monk I saw early this morning."
“Surely there must be some means; by searching for the place where he has gone, we shall discover the reason.
Having thus asked the way the Elder had taken, he set out.
Then a certain man, seeing him walking with such extreme ferocity, said, “O man, you are walking with extreme—”
“You go as if you were frantic; for what purpose are you going? he asked. He reported the matter to him.
Having heard his words, he said: “Sir, do not worry; my noble master Pilindavaccha will be there.
Fill this very vessel, take it, go, and stand before the Elder. When he asks, ‘What is this?’”
"When he says, 'Outcaste!', you should say, 'Peppercorns, venerable sir. The Elder will say, 'So shall it be; outcaste!
Then all the peppercorns will return to their original state. He did exactly so, and all the peppercorns became as they were before.
This is the extent of that story. Later on, however, the Teacher [spoke] precisely for the sake of being pleasing and dear to the deities.
Having made him the subject [of this account], he placed the Elder among the foremost of those dear and pleasing to the deities.
This is the story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya (216).
Regarding the eighth category, "those of quick direct knowledge," the Elder Dārucīriya is the foremost among those who have quickly attained direct knowledge.
[The Blessed One] shows this. For this elder attained Arahatship at the conclusion of a brief teaching on the Dhamma; there was no need for preliminary practice regarding the paths and fruits.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those of quick higher knowledge (*khippābhiññā*). However, because he was born in the country of Bāhiya, his name was Bāhiya.
Later, he wore garments made of bark; therefore, he became known as Dārucīriya.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential narrative: During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
While listening to the Dhamma teaching of the One Possessed of Ten Powers, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge.
Having performed a work of merit and aspiring for that very status, he [practiced] for as long as he lived...
Having performed wholesome deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, at the time when the teaching of the Buddha Kassapa was declining,
he practiced the duties of a recluse together with the monks mentioned above; having fulfilled his moral conduct, upon the end of his life,
he was reborn in the world of the gods.
Having dwelt in the world of the devas for one interval between Buddhas, he was reborn in this present dispensation of a Buddha into a noble family in the kingdom of Bāhiya.
Upon reaching maturity and living the life of a householder, thinking, "I shall engage in trade," he boarded a ship bound for the Land of Gold.
Before the ship could reach its intended destination, it was wrecked in the midst of the ocean, and the great multitude became food for fish and turtles.
He was there. Having taken a piece of wood, however, he landed at the port of Suppāraka on the seventh day;

upon reaching a human habitation, thinking it improper to approach people according to the manner of a naked ascetic (acelaka), he wrapped his body in moss from a large nearby pond and took a skull that had fallen in one place.
Having taken [the bowl], he entered for alms.
When people saw him, they thought: "If there are those called 'Arahants' in the world, they must be like this.
Does the noble one not take a robe because of his austere nature, or would he accept one if it were given?"
Investigating him, they brought garments from various directions. He thought: "If I do not come by this method, they will not have confidence in me;
therefore, by whatever means necessary, it is right to deceive these people and make a livelihood.
Thus, he did not accept the garments. The people became even more exceedingly pleased and paid him great honor. He too—
Having finished his meal, he went to a nearby shrine. The great multitude followed him there and, having tended to the shrine, offered it to him.
He thought: "These people have developed such faith in me merely because of my coarse clothing;
therefore, I ought to appear in a superior manner to them. Thus, he [prepared] light garments...
Taking tree bark, having had it split and woven into cloth, he made a garment for himself, which he wore as an undergarment and a cloak,

living his life in this manner. Now, at the time of the Buddha Kassapa, when seven persons were practicing the religious life (*samaṇadhamma*), there was one monk who [was reborn] in the Suddhāvāsa Brahmā-world.

He was reborn. Immediately upon being reborn, he surveyed his own attainment of the Brahma realm and, reflecting on the place from which he had come, saw that seven persons had ascended a mountain and were practicing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

Reflecting on the places where the remaining six had been reborn, he perceived that one had attained final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*), while the other five were in the sensual-sphere deva world (*kāmāvacaradevaloka*).
Having known their state of rebirth, he would periodically direct his attention toward those five people.

At this time, however, while directing his attention with the thought, "Where indeed are they?", he saw Dārucīriya living near the port of Suppāraka, making his livelihood through the practice of hypocrisy.
Seeing him, [the Elder thought]: "Alas, this fool is lost! Previously, while practicing the duty of a recluse, because of his excessive austerity—"
"Even though he has brought almsfood from an Arahant, he does not consume it;

now, for the sake of his own belly, he wanders about deceiving the world by falsely claiming Arahantship despite being unworthy, and he does not know that the One of Ten Powers has appeared in the world.
I shall go and stir him with a sense of urgency, making him realize that the One of Ten Powers has appeared. At that very moment, [he departed] from the Brahma-world.
At the Suppāraka port, immediately following the middle watch of the night, he appeared before Dārucīriya.
Seeing a radiance in his own dwelling place, he went outside, stood there, and looking up at the Great Brahmā and raising his hands in reverential salutation, he asked, "Who are you?
[The Brahmā replied: "I am your former companion; having attained the fruit of non-returning..."
He was reborn in the Brahma-world. But our eldest brother, having attained Arahantship, has passed away into Parinibbāna;
you five have been reborn in the world of the devas. Therefore, seeing you living here by means of fraudulent practice, I have come to subdue you.
Having said this, he stated the reason: "Bāhiya, you are not an Arahant, nor have you entered the path to Arahantship."
"You do not possess that practice by which you might become an Arahant or have entered the path to Arahantship. Then,
having informed him that the Teacher had appeared and was residing in Sāvatthī, and having sent him off with the words,
"Go into the presence of the Teacher," he returned to the Brahma-world itself.
Stirred by the Great Brahmā, Dārucīriya thought, "I shall seek the path to liberation.
Traveling a road of one hundred and twenty *yojanas* in a single night’s stay, he reached the Teacher while the Blessed One was entering among the houses for alms.
Prostrating at the Teacher’s feet, he requested three times: "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma; may the Sugata teach me the Dhamma."

He made his request. The Teacher, knowing that Bāhiya’s knowledge had reached maturity at this point, instructed him with this exhortation: “Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: ‘In the seen, there shall be only the seen.

At the conclusion of the teaching, even while standing in the middle of the street, he directed his knowledge according to the instruction and attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Thus, realizing that his own duty had reached its fulfillment, he requested ordination from the Blessed One.
While seeking a bowl and robes because they were not yet complete, he gathered scraps of cloth from a rubbish heap.
Then, an unwholesome non-human being who harbored an old grudge against him, having fixed his intent upon the body of a cow with a young calf, brought about his death. The Teacher—
As he was departing from Sāvatthī, he saw Bāhiya fallen in a heap of refuse in the middle of the street.
Seeing him, he said, "Monks, take up the body of Bāhiya Dārucīriya. Having had it carried out and the funeral rites performed, he had a shrine (cetiya) erected at the crossroads.
Then, a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha: "The Tathāgata, together with the community of monks, [honored] Bāhiya..."
They performed the duty of cremating his body, took his relics, and erected a shrine;
then they thought, "Which path has he realized? Is he a novice monk or a fully ordained bhikkhu?
Taking that as the occasion, the Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, Bāhiya was wise," and expanding upon it with a further teaching on the Dhamma, [he spoke] to him...
He proclaimed the state of his final Nibbāna. Again, a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha:
"The Teacher did not teach much Dhamma to Bāhiya, yet he says he attained Arahantship. What can this mean? The Teacher said, "That the Dhamma was meager is no reason [for his attainment];
it is like an antidote for one who has swallowed poison," and he spoke this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
“Even a thousand verses composed of meaningless words are not worth a single verse-quarter which, having been heard, brings about tranquility.
At the conclusion of this teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings drank the drink of the Deathless. And this [was said] regarding the Elder Bāhiya.
Because it is included in the *Vatthu Sutta*, it has not been told in detail here.
Later, however, while sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, the Teacher established the Elder Bāhiya in the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge.
This is the story of the Elder Kumārakassapa.
217. Regarding "among those who speak with charm": this refers to those who preach the Dhamma having made it variegated.
It is said that when the Elder preached the Dhamma to even one person or two, he spoke while adorning and awakening them with many similes and reasons.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who speak with charm.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential account: During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he took rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the discourse on the Dhamma from the One Possessed of the Ten Powers, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who discourse on the mind. Having performed a work of merit, he—
Having made aspirations for various high stations, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans.
During the time of the dispensation of Buddha Kassapa, he became one of seven monks; while practicing the duties of a recluse on a mountain peak, he remained unimpaired in virtue.
Passing away from there, he was reborn in the world of the gods and, experiencing prosperity for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, [he eventually appeared] before our Teacher.
At that time, in Rājagaha, she was conceived in the womb of a certain noble maiden.
Having first requested permission from her parents for the going forth but not obtaining it, she went to her family home and became pregnant. Not knowing of this, she gratified her husband;
with his consent, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs. When the bhikkhunīs saw the signs of her pregnancy, they [reported it] to Devadatta.
They questioned her, and she said, "I am no longer a female ascetic. They questioned the One of Ten Powers, and the Teacher entrusted the matter to the Elder Upāli.
The Elder summoned the families residing in the city of Sāvatthī, as well as the laywoman Visākhā, and while investigating the case, he declared, "The pregnancy was conceived previously;
her ordination is valid. The Teacher gave his approval to the Elder, saying, "The legal dispute has been well adjudicated."
That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. Taking him, King Pasenadi of Kosala raised him;
having given him the name Kassapa, he later adorned him, led him into the presence of the Teacher, and had him ordained.
Because he had been ordained during his childhood, the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa here; this fruit or hard food..."
When it was said, "Give [it] to Kassapa," [he asked], "To which Kassapa? [The reply was], "To Kumārakassapa.

Because he had thus received that name, from then on, even in his old age, he was called by the name Kumārakassapa alone. Furthermore, they knew him as Kumārakassapa because he was the king’s foster son (*posāvanikaputta*).
Thus, from the time of his going forth, he applied himself both to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and to mastering the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*).

Then, having practiced the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) together with him on the mountain peak and attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), he was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa heaven as a Great Brahmā.
At that time, while reflecting, he saw Kumāra Kassapa and thought: "My companion [is engaged] in insight meditation..."
“...is weary; having gone there, I shall show him the gateway to the method of insight (vipassanā) and provide the means for his attainment of the paths and fruits.

While still stationed in the Brahma-world, he formulated fifteen questions and, immediately following the middle watch of the night, appeared in the Andhavana grove at the dwelling place of the Elder Kumāra Kassapa.
Seeing the light, the Elder asked, “Who is there? “It is I, who previously...”
“Having practiced the duty of a recluse together with her, he attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) and was reborn as a Brahmā in the Suddhāvāsa heaven,” he said.
[The King asked: “By what kamma have you come here? Mahābrahmā, explaining the reason for his own arrival, set forth those questions and said:
“After you have mastered these questions, go to the Tathāgata at dawn and ask them; setting aside...”
"Indeed, there is no one else capable of answering these questions for the Tathāgata," he said, and then he departed for the Brahma-world itself.
On the following day, the Elder approached the Teacher, paid homage, and asked the questions according to the very order in which they had been stated by Mahābrahmā.
The Teacher, having enabled the Elder Kumārakassapa to attain Arahatship, explained the answers to the questions. The Elder—
Having mastered [the teaching] exactly according to the method explained by the Teacher, he went to the Blind Men’s Grove, entered the womb of insight (*vipassanā*), and attained *arahantship*.

From that time forth, while delivering Dhamma discourses to the fourfold assembly, he spoke only on the mind, adorning it with many similes and reasons. Then the Teacher [spoke to him] regarding King Pāyāsi...

When the Sutta was taught, adorned with fifteen questions, the Buddha took that Sutta as the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and established the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita in the foremost position among those who deliver inspired discourses (*cittakathika*) within this Dispensation.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita.

218. Regarding the tenth [category], "of those who have attained the analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidāpatta*), this shows that among those established after having reached the four analytical knowledges, the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita is the foremost.

For this elder, by virtue of his mastery over the analytical knowledges, whether he approached various well-known great disciples to ask questions or approached the One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*) to ask questions, [he was always successful].

He asked a question concerning the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) themselves. Thus, by virtue of this mastery attained through practice, he became known as the foremost among those who have reached the analytical knowledges.
This is the sequential account regarding his questioning: for he too, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, was reborn in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī;
and on another occasion, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he [addressed] the Teacher...
Seeing the Buddha place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he performed an act of merit and aspired to that very station.
