Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, he was reborn into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. They gave him the name Koṭṭhita-māṇava.
Having reached adulthood and mastered the three Vedas, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma one day;

having gained faith, he went forth. From the time of his full ordination, while applying himself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*), he attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Having always mastered the analytical knowledges, whenever he asked a question, he did so regarding those very analytical knowledges.

She asked [the question]. Then, at a later time, the Teacher, taking this as the occasion for the discourse, established her in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) in the *Mahāvedalla-sutta*.
This concludes the commentary on the Third Chapter.
14. Etadagga Vagga (14) 4.
The Fourth Etadagga Vagga:
The Story of the Elder Ānanda
219–223. Regarding the first [ranking] of the fourth [section], concerning the phrase "of those who have heard much" (*bahussuta*) and so forth:
there were other elders as well who had heard much, who possessed mindfulness, intelligence, and fortitude, and who were attendants.

However, this venerable one, while learning the word of the Buddha, stood within the treasury of the scriptures (*bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti*) of the Teaching of the One of Ten Powers and mastered it. Therefore, he is the foremost among those who have heard much.
He was thus named. Furthermore, having received the Buddha’s word from this very elder, his retentive memory became stronger than that of other elders;
therefore, he was known as the foremost among those possessed of mindfulness (*satimantānaṃ*).
Moreover, this venerable one, while standing on a single word, would grasp sixty thousand words; he knew all the words according to the method explained by the Teacher. Therefore—

He became known as the foremost of those possessed of speed. Furthermore, that venerable one’s energy in learning the Buddha’s word, his energy in recitation, his energy in retention, and his energy in attending upon the Teacher were peerless;
therefore, he became known as the foremost of those possessed of steadfastness. When attending upon the Tathāgata, he did not do so in the manner of other attendant bhikkhus.
He attended upon [the Buddha]. For other attendants who served the Tathāgata did not do so for long, nor did they attend upon him having grasped the mind of the Buddhas.

This elder, however, from the very day he obtained the position of attendant, became one who had initiated energy and attended upon the Tathāgata having grasped his mind. Therefore, he became known as the foremost among attendants.
Regarding his answering of the question, this is the sequential narrative: It is said that one hundred thousand aeons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world.
His city was called Haṃsavatī; his father was King Nanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was a prince named Uttara. On the day his son was born...
Having gone forth after making the Great Renunciation and being devoted to striving, he gradually attained omniscience.
Having uttered the inspired utterance, "Through many births in saṃsāra...," and having spent seven days on the seat of enlightenment, he extended his foot, thinking, "I shall place it upon the earth.
Then, having split the earth, a lotus of the dimensions described below appeared.
He arose. From that time forth, the Blessed One was known as Padumuttara. Devala and Sujāta were his two chief disciples;
Amitā and Asamā were his two chief female disciples; and his attendant was named Sumana.
The Blessed One Padumuttara, providing for his father, resided in the capital city of Haṃsavatī with a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus.
His younger brother was named Prince Sumanas. The king gave him a village of revenues two hundred yojanas from Haṃsavatī.
From time to time, he would come and see both his father and the Teacher.
Then one day, when the border region rose in revolt, Sumanas sent word to the king. The king replied, "Why were you not stationed there by me? He—
Having pacified the interior [of the country], he sent word to the king, saying, "The countryside is pacified, Your Majesty.
The king was delighted and said, "May my son come quickly! He had about a thousand ministers; on the way, he consulted with them:
"If my father, being pleased, grants me a boon, what should I take? Then some of them...
“Seize elephants! Seize horses! Seize the countryside! Seize the seven treasures! they said.
Others said, “You are the sons of the Lord of the Earth; wealth is not difficult for you to obtain.
Yet even all this that has been acquired must be abandoned when departing; only merit is that which one may take with one. Therefore, while the King is granting a boon—”
“Take a boon to serve the Blessed One Padumuttara for three months,” they said. He replied, “You are my virtuous friends;
such a thought did not exist in me, but since it has been inspired by you, I shall do so.
Having gone and paid homage to his father, and being embraced and kissed on the head by his father, who said, “I grant you a boon, my son,” he [accepted].
“Great King, I wish to make my life fruitful by attending upon the Blessed One for three months with the four requisites;
O Lord, grant me this boon,” he said. “It is not possible, dear one; choose another boon.
“Lord, there are indeed only two kinds of speech among the kṣatriyas. Grant me this very boon; I have no need for anything else.”
“Father, the minds of the Buddhas are indeed difficult to know. If the Blessed One does not wish for it, what will happen even if I give it?
“Very well, Your Majesty; I shall know the mind of the Blessed One. Having said this, he went to the monastery.
At that time, having finished his meal, the Blessed One had entered the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi), while [the prince] remained in the pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷa).
He went into the presence of the monks who had assembled there. They said to him, "Prince, why have you come?
"To see the Blessed One; show me the Blessed One. "Prince, we do not obtain the opportunity to see the Teacher at our own will.
"But who, venerable sirs, does obtain it? "The Elder named Sumanatthera, Prince."
"So, venerable sir, where is the Elder? Having asked where the Elder was sitting, he went there, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One; show me the Blessed One.
Even as the prince was looking on, the Elder entered the water-kasina absorption, resolved upon the great earth as water, and [disappeared] into the earth.
Having submerged himself, he reappeared right there in the Teacher’s fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭi). Then the Blessed One said to him, “Sumanā, why have you come?
“Venerable sir, I have come to see the Blessed One,” replied the prince. “In that case, monk, prepare a seat.
Once again, while the prince was looking on, the elder took the Buddha’s seat, submerged himself within the fragrant chamber, and [reappeared].
Having appeared in the outer courtyard, he prepared a seat in the inner courtyard.
Seeing these two miraculous occurrences, the prince thought, "How great indeed is this bhikkhu!
Then the Blessed One emerged from the fragrant chamber and sat down on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Blessed One.

He offered him hospitality. When asked, "When did you arrive, Prince? he replied, "Venerable sir, when you had entered the fragrant chamber, the monks sent me to the Elder, saying, 'We do not get to see the Blessed One whenever we wish.
But the Elder showed himself with a single word; Venerable sir, that Elder [is like] yours."
“I think he is dear to the Dispensation. “Yes, prince, this bhikkhu is dear to my Dispensation.
“Venerable sir, by doing what does one become dear to the Buddhas’ Dispensation? “By giving gifts, prince, by undertaking the precepts, and by performing the Uposatha observance.
[The prince thought: “The Blessed One says that I too, like the Elder, desire to be dear to the Buddha’s Dispensation; tomorrow, for me—”
"Please accept alms," he said. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
The prince went to his own residence and, having prepared great honors throughout the entire night, provided what is known as "army-camp food" for seven days.
On the seventh day, after paying homage to the Teacher, he said: "Venerable Sir, my father has granted me three months of the rainy season for your sake."
“I have obtained the privilege of providing care; please accept my invitation for the three-month rains retreat.
The Blessed One, having reflected, “Is there indeed purpose in going there? and seeing that there was, said, “Prince, Tathāgatas take delight in empty dwellings.
The prince said, “Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Sugata! and added, “Venerable sir, I—”
Having gone ahead, he obtained a promise from the Blessed One, saying, "I shall have a monastery built; when I send for you, please come together with a hundred thousand bhikkhus.
Then, having gone into his father's presence and said, "Your Majesty, I have received a promise from the Blessed One;
when I send for him, you should dispatch the Blessed One," he paid homage to his father, departed, and at every league along the way...

While having a monastery built, he traveled a distance of two hundred yojanas. Having arrived, while searching for a site for the monastery in his own city, he saw the garden of a householder named Sobhana;
having purchased it for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and expended another hundred thousand, he had the monastery constructed.
There, he built a fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*) for the Blessed One and places for the other monks to stay by night and by day.
Having had a pavilion built of *kuṭila* wood and having completed the surrounding wall and the gateway tower, he sent word to his father:
"My task is finished; please send the Teacher.
After the King had fed the Blessed One, he said: "The Blessed One, Sumanas's task is finished; he awaits your arrival."
He said: "The Blessed One, surrounded by a retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus, traveled while staying at monasteries every yojana.
When the prince heard that 'the Teacher is coming,' he went out to meet him for a yojana, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, and having led him into the monastery, said:
'It was purchased by me for a hundred thousand, it was constructed for a hundred thousand;'"
“The garden named Sobhana—accept it, O Great Sage.
Thus he offered the monastery. On the day of entering the rains retreat, having given alms and summoned his sons, wife, and ministers, he said:
“The Teacher has come from afar to our presence; indeed, Buddhas are those who hold the Dhamma in high esteem.”
“They do not have eyes for material gain. Therefore, having put on these two robes and undertaken the ten precepts, I shall dwell right here for these three months;
you should give alms for a hundred thousand arahants in this very manner for the three months.
He then dwelt in a place adjacent to the Elder Sumanas’s residence, performing for the Elder the same duties that the Elder performed for the Blessed One.
Having seen all that he was doing, he thought, "In this place, this elder is exclusively beloved; it is fitting for me to aspire to his very position.
Then, as the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) drew near, he entered a village and gave a great almsgiving for seven days.
On the seventh day, having placed his three robes at the feet of a hundred thousand bhikkhus, he [addressed] the Blessed One.

Having paid homage, he said: "Venerable sir, this merit that I have performed for seven days starting from the gift of the camp, was not done by me aspiring for the excellence of Sakka, nor for the excellence of Māra or Brahmā; rather, it was done by me aspiring for the status of being an attendant to a Buddha.
Therefore, O Blessed One, may I too in the future become like the Elder Sumanas, an attendant to a single Buddha."
"I shall be your attendant," he said, and having prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he paid homage.

The Teacher, seeing that there would be no obstacle for him, gave a prediction and departed. When the prince heard this, thinking, "The Buddhas indeed speak without duplicity," on the following day he took the bowl and robe of the Buddha Gotama and followed closely behind him as if walking side by side.
Thus, during that appearance of a Buddha, he gave gifts for a hundred thousand years and was reborn in the heavenly realms.
During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he made an offering by giving his upper robe to an elder who was walking for alms, in order to receive the elder’s bowl.

Having been reborn again in the heavenly realms and passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī; while seated in the excellence of the upper palace, [he saw] from Gandhamādana coming through the air...
Seeing eight Paccekabuddhas approaching, he invited them and fed them;

then, having had eight leaf-huts constructed for them in his own auspicious park, he prepared eight seats made entirely of precious gems along with gemstone water-basins in his own residence for them to sit upon, and rendered service to them for ten thousand years. These are the well-known sites.
However, having given gifts for a hundred thousand eons, our Bodhisatta was reborn together with him in the Tusita heaven;
passing away from there, he was reborn in the house of the Sakyan Amitodana.
Because he was born making all his kinsmen joyful and delighted, they gave him the name Ānanda. He eventually went forth into homelessness and attained supreme enlightenment.
Having reached Kapilavatthu on his first journey and having departed from there once the Blessed One had left,
while the princes were going forth for the sake of entering the Blessed One’s retinue, he went out together with Bhaddiya and the others.
Having gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One and heard a discourse on the Dhamma from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry before long.
Now at that time, during the first twenty years after his enlightenment, the Blessed One had no fixed attendants.
At one time Nāgasamāla followed him, taking his bowl and robes; at another time Nāgita; at another time Upavāna;
at another time Sunakkhatta; at another time the novice Cunda; at another time Sāgata; at another time Rādha; and at another time Meghiya.
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was traveling along a highway together with the elder Nāgasamāla, they reached a fork in the road.
The elder stepped off the path and said, "Blessed One, I shall go by this way.
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Come, bhikkhu, let us go by this way. He replied, "In that case, Blessed One, [take] your bowl and robe..."
"Take them; I shall go by this path," he said, and began to set down his bowl and robes on the ground.
Then the Blessed One said to him, "Bring them back, monk," and having taken the bowl and robes, He departed.
As that monk was going by the other path, thieves robbed him of both his bowl and robes and split open his head. He thought, "The Blessed One..."
Thinking, "Now this is my refuge; there is no other," he approached the Blessed One while blood was still flowing.
When the Blessed One asked, "What is this, monk? he reported what had occurred. Then the Blessed One comforted him, saying, "Do not worry, monk;
it was for this very reason that we restrained you."
On one occasion, however, the Blessed One went from the Migadāya in Pācīnavaṃsa to Jantugāma together with the Elder Meghiya.

There too, after Meghiya had wandered for alms in Jantugāma, he saw a beautiful mango grove on the riverbank and said, "Blessed One, take your bowl and robe; I shall perform the duties of a recluse in that mango grove."
Although he was forbidden three times by the Blessed One, he went out; being obsessed by unwholesome thoughts, he returned and reported what had happened.
The Blessed One said to him, "It was precisely because we observed this very reason that we forbade you," and then gradually proceeded to Sāvatthī.
There, in the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber, upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him—
Seated, surrounded by the community of monks, he addressed the monks: “Monks, I am now old.
When it is said, ‘Let some monks go by this path,’ they go by another;
some set down my bowl and robe on the ground. Know, monks, that there is one monk who is my constant attendant. [To the monks...]
A sense of spiritual urgency arose in him. Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said:
"Venerable sir, it was longing for you alone that I fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable eon plus a hundred thousand kappas.
Is it not fitting that one of such great wisdom as I should be your attendant? I shall attend upon you. The Blessed One [consented].
“Enough, Sāriputta; that direction in which you dwell is indeed not empty, for your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas.
Therefore, I have need of you as my attendant,” he said, and thus declined.
By this very means, beginning with Mahāmoggallāna, the eighty great disciples arose [to offer their service], but the Blessed One declined them all.
But the Elder Ānanda remained silent. Then the bhikkhus said to him: "Friend Ānanda, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus requests a place for an attendant;
you too should request one. "Friend, what kind of place is it that is called 'obtained by request'?
Does the Teacher not see me? If the Teacher would approve, [he would say], 'Let Ānanda attend upon me.'"
“He will speak. Then the Blessed One said, “Monks, Ānanda need not be urged by others; having understood it himself, he will attend upon me.
Thereupon the monks said, “Arise, friend Ānanda! Arise, friend Ānanda!
Request the place of attendant for the One of Ten Powers. The Elder arose and made four refusals.
And with four requests, he asked for eight boons.

There are four rejections, namely: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robe he himself has received, if he will not give me almsfood, if he will not allow me to dwell in the same fragrant cell, and if he will not accept an invitation..."
“Having taken them, I will not go; in this way I shall attend upon the Blessed One.
When it was asked, “But what disadvantage, Ānanda, did you see in this? he replied: “Venerable sir, if I were to receive these requisites, there would be those who would say:
‘Ānanda enjoys the fine robes obtained by the One of Ten Powers; he enjoys the almsfood obtained by the One of Ten Powers.’”
“He dwells in one fragrant chamber and accepts invitations from one side. Receiving such gains, he attends upon the Tathāgata;
what burden could there be for one who is so attended? Thus he requested these four refusals.
These are called the four entreaties: “If, venerable sir, the Blessed One will go to the invitation accepted by me, and if I—”
"From across kingdoms and across provinces, as soon as the assembly comes to see the Blessed One, I shall have the opportunity to see the Blessed One;
whenever doubt arises in me, at that very moment I shall have the opportunity to approach the Blessed One;
and likewise, whatever Dhamma the Blessed One teaches to me in his absence, having returned, [I shall understand it]."
“I will speak thus, and in that way I shall attend upon the Blessed One. When [the Blessed One] asked, “But what benefit do you see in this, Ānanda?
he replied: “Here, venerable sir, when faithful sons of good family find no opportunity with the Blessed One, they say to me:
‘Venerable Ānanda, tomorrow may you accept almsfood at our house together with the Blessed One.’”
If the Blessed One does not go there, I shall have no opportunity to show myself to the assembly at whatever moment I desire, nor to dispel their doubts.
People will say, "What, Ānanda attends upon the One of Ten Powers?
Yet the Blessed One does not grant him even this much favor. And they will question me in the absence of the Blessed One.
“Friend Ānanda, this verse, this sutta, this Jātaka—where was it taught?
If I were not to provide the source for it, there would be those who would say: “Friend, you do not even know this much;
why then have you wandered for so long, never leaving the Blessed One’s side, like a shadow? Therefore, in his absence...
“I wish for the Dhamma already taught to be spoken again. Thus he made these four requests, and the Blessed One granted them as well.
Having thus obtained these eight boons, he became a constant attendant.
It was for the sake of that very position that he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over a hundred thousand eons. From the day he obtained the status of an attendant...
From that time on, while attending upon the One of Ten Powers with these duties— namely, the two kinds of water, the three kinds of tooth-sticks,
the massaging of hands and feet, the rubbing of the back, and the sweeping of the fragrant chamber and its courtyard—
he would spend his day thinking, "At this particular time, it is fitting for the Teacher to receive such-and-such; it is fitting to perform such-and-such."
Living in close attendance, immediately after the first watch of the night, he would take a staff-lantern and walk around the Gandhakuṭi courtyard nine times during that single night.
For he thought: "If sloth and torpor should overcome me, I might not be able to give a reply when the One of Ten Powers calls upon me.
Therefore, throughout the entire night, he held the staff-lantern in his hand.

He did not let it go. This is the extent of the story. Later, however, while residing at Jetavana, the Teacher praised the Elder Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma, in many ways and established the Elder in the foremost position among the bhikkhus in this Dispensation who were learned, possessed of mindfulness, possessed of intelligence, possessed of fortitude, and who were attendants.
The Story of the Elder Uruvelakassapa (224).
Regarding the phrase "of those with great assemblies," this shows that among those with large retinues, Uruvelakassapa was the foremost.
For while the retinue of other elders might be large at one time and small at another, for this elder it was [always] twofold...
Together with his brothers, he had a fixed retinue of one thousand ascetics.
When he ordained one person from among them, there were two thousand ascetics; when he ordained two, there were three thousand.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those with a great retinue. His clan name was Kassapa. Because he went forth at Uruvelā, [he was called Uruvela-Kassapa].
He became known as Uruvelakassapa.

This is the sequential account regarding his questioning: for he too, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, having taken rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī, reached maturity and, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, [beheld] the Teacher [bestowing a prediction upon] one...
Seeing the monk established in the foremost position among the great assemblies, [the man] thought, "In the future, it is fitting that I too become like this.

Having given a great almsgiving for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and having clothed them with the three robes, he paid homage to the Teacher and made an aspiration for the state of being the foremost among the great assemblies. The Teacher—
Having seen that there would be no obstacle, he prophesied, “In the future, under the dispensation of Buddha Gotama, you will become the foremost among the great assemblies,” and then departed.
That clansman, too, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, wandered through the realms of gods and humans;
ninety-two aeons ago from now, he was reborn as the half-brother and younger sibling of Buddha Phussa, while his father was King Mahinda. Others...
He had two younger brothers. Thus, those three brothers each obtained their respective positions.
Having pacified the rebellious border region in the manner described above, and having received a boon from their father, they chose as their boon:
"We shall attend upon the One of Ten Powers for three months. Then this thought occurred to them:

Thinking, “It is fitting for us who are attending upon the One of Ten Powers to do what is appropriate,” they appointed one minister to the position of provider, one to the position of accountant for income and expenditure, and one to the position of distributor for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha;
then, having undertaken the ten precepts themselves, they observed the training rules for three months. Those three ministers—
In this very same manner as described below, Bimbisāra, Visākhā, and Raṭṭhapāla were born during this appearance of a Buddha.
Those princes, having completed their years of training, personally honored the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with offerings of requisites;
and having performed virtuous deeds for as long as they lived, even before our Ten-Powered One had been born, they—
Having been reborn in a brahmin family, all three of them were named Kassapa according to their own lineage.
When they reached maturity, they mastered the three Vedas. The eldest brother had a retinue of five hundred young students, the middle one three hundred, and the youngest two hundred.
As they examined the essence of their own scriptures, they found that it concerned only matters pertaining to this visible world.
They saw only the present, not the future life.

Then their eldest brother, having gone to Uruvelā with his own retinue and having gone forth into the ascetic life, became known as Uruvelakassapa; he who went forth on a bend of the great river Ganges became known as Nadīkassapa;
and he who went forth at Gayāsīsa became known as Gayākassapa.
Thus, while they had gone forth into the life of a seer and were dwelling there, after the lapse of many days,
our Bodhisatta made his Great Renunciation, realized all-knowing wisdom, and in due course set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion;
having established the five bhikkhus of the group in Arahatship, he [established] fifty-five people headed by the youth Yasa.
Having also instructed sixty arahants among his companions, he sent them forth on a wandering tour for the welfare of many people,
saying, "Wander, O bhikkhus. Then, having instructed the group of Bhaddas, and perceiving the reason for Uruvelakassapa’s conversion— knowing that "when I have gone,
the three brothers along with their followers will attain arahantship"— he went alone, without a second, to Uruvelakassapa.

Having gone to the dwelling place and requested the fire-hall for the purpose of staying, he converted Uruvela Kassapa along with his followers by means of three hundred and fifty miracles, beginning with the taming of the Naga; he then ordained him.
Knowing that he had gone forth, the other two brothers also came with their own followers and were ordained; thus all of them—
"Come, monks! they became bearers of miraculous bowls and robes.
Taking those thousand ascetics with him, the Teacher went to Gayāsīsa and sat upon the flat rock;
looking about and considering, "What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for these men?", he reflected that they had lived their lives worshipping fire.
"It is fitting to show these three realms of existence as being like a house on fire," he said, and thus he taught the *Ādittapariyāya Sutta*.
At the conclusion of the teaching, all of them attained *arahantship*.

Surrounded by them, the Teacher went to the Laṭṭhivana Grove in the city of Rājagaha, because of a promise previously made to King Bimbisāra. When the King learned of the arrival of the One of Ten Powers...
Having heard this, he approached the Teacher together with twelve hundred thousand brahmins and householders;
having paid homage, he sat down to one side. The Teacher surveyed the entire assembly and, seeing the great multitude paying such respectful homage to Uruvelakassapa, thought:
"These people do not know the relative greatness of either myself or Kassapa."
Thinking, "Those who possess applied thought (savitakkā) are unable to receive the teaching," he gave a signal to the Elder,
saying, "Kassapa, cut off the discursive thoughts of your supporters. The Elder, having accepted the Teacher's word, rose from his seat,
paid homage to the Teacher with the fivefold prostration, and leaping into the air to the height of a palm tree, performed a feat of supernatural power (iddhi-vikubbana).
Having displayed himself thus, he said, "The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple. The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir;

I am his disciple. Having spoken, he descended and paid homage at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers. By this same method, on the seventh occasion, having ascended into the sky to the height of seventy palm trees and then returned, he paid homage at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers and sat down to one side.
At that time, the great multitude conceived confidence in the Teacher, thinking, "This one in the world is a Great Recluse.

Then the Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, the king, together with eleven hundred thousand brahmins and householders, was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and one hundred thousand declared themselves lay followers (*upāsaka*). Those [followers] also [belonged to] Uruvelakassapa...
The monks, numbering about a thousand in their retinue, reflected according to their own habitual tendencies:
"Our duty as renunciants has reached its culmination; what shall we do by going outside? Thus they wandered, surrounding only the Elder Uruvelakassapa.
When each of them took one dependent disciple, there were two thousand; when two [disciples] were taken from each, there were four thousand.
Those who took it up numbered three thousand. From that time on, it was considered appropriate to teach as many people as there were among their dependents.
This is the background story here. Later, while residing at Jetavana, the Teacher placed the Elder in the foremost position among those with large assemblies.

The Story of the Elder Kāḷudāyi (225). Regarding the third phrase, “those who inspire confidence in families”: this means those who cause a family to have faith. For this Elder inspired confidence in the palace of King Suddhodana himself, even though he had not yet seen the Buddha; therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who inspire confidence in families.
This is the sequential account concerning his past deeds: during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he lived in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Having been reborn in a noble family, while listening to the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who inspire faith in families.
Having performed an act of merit, he aspired to that very station.
Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, on the day our Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of his mother, he [was reborn].
He took rebirth in Kapilavatthu itself, in the house of a minister. On the very day he was born, he was born together with the Bodhisatta;
therefore, on that same day, they placed him in a bundle of fine linen and led him away to serve as an attendant for the Bodhisatta.
For along with the Bodhisatta were born the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four pots of treasure, and the elephant Ārohaṇiya.
Kaṇḍaka, Channa, and Kāḷudāyī—these seven were called "co-born" because they were born on the same day.
On the day of his naming ceremony, because he was born on a day when the entire city was filled with exultant hearts, they gave him the name Udāyī.
However, because he possessed a somewhat dark complexion, he became known as Kāḷudāyī. He played as a youth together with the Bodhisatta.
Playing, he reached maturity.

Later on, after the Bodhisatta had gone forth in the Great Renunciation and gradually attained omniscience, he turned the sublime Wheel of Dhamma and, while bestowing benefit upon the world, dwelt in dependence upon Rājagaha. In that...
At that time, having heard that Prince Siddhattha, after attaining full enlightenment, was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha,
King Suddhodana dispatched a minister accompanied by a thousand men, saying, "Bring my son here. Having traveled a road of sixty yojanas,
he arrived at the time when the One Possessed of Ten Powers was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly and teaching the Dhamma.

He entered the monastery. Thinking, "Let the message sent by the king remain for now," he stood at the edge of the assembly and, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, attained Arahatship right where he stood along with his thousand men.
Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks! and at that very moment, they all became bearers of miraculous bowls and robes.
They became like elder monks of sixty years' standing. However, from the moment they attained *arahatta*, the Noble Ones (ariyas) remain inherently equanimous;
thus, they did not report the message sent by the king to the One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*).
The king, thinking, "He neither comes nor is his message heard," dispatched another minister according to the same procedure, saying, "Come, dear one, you go."
He too, having gone with his retinue in the same manner as before, attained Arahatship and became silent.
Thus, by means of nine ministers, he dispatched nine thousand men. Having all completed their respective tasks, they became silent.
Then the king thought: "Because these people lack affection for me, they have not come here for the sake of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers."
“They said nothing; even if others go, they will not be able to bring the One of Ten Powers.
However, my son Udāyī is of the same age as the One of Ten Powers and was his playmate in the dust; he has affection for him.
Having thus summoned Kāḷudāyin, he said, “Dear son, go with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the One of Ten Powers.”
“Your Majesty, I shall bring him back after he has been permitted to go forth, just as those men who went before did,” he said. “By whatever means necessary, show me my son!
“Very well, Your Majesty,” he replied, and taking the king’s message, he went to Rājagaha.

Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he heard the teaching; together with his retinue, he attained the fruit of Arhatship and [was ordained] in the state of an *ehibhikkhu*.
He established himself there. Then he thought: "This is not yet the time for the One Possessed of Ten Powers to go to his native city;
this will be the time when the forest groves are in full bloom during the spring season and the earth is covered with green grass.
While awaiting that time, having recognized that the time had arrived—
“Neither too cold nor too hot, neither too plagued by famine nor drought;
the earth is verdant and lush— this is the time, O Great Sage!”—
with these sixty verses, he praised the journey for the sake of the Ten-Powered One’s departure for his native city.

The Teacher, thinking, "Udāyī is speaking in praise of going; this is the time to go to the city of Kapilavatthu," set out on a walking tour with a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, traveling with a steady, unhurried pace.
When the Elder Udāyī learned that the Teacher had departed, he thought, "It is fitting to give notice to my father, the Great King."
Having ascended into the air, he appeared at the king’s residence. Upon seeing the Elder, King Mahāsuddhodana was filled with joy;
he had him sit upon a magnificent couch, filled the bowl with various kinds of exquisite food prepared for himself, and offered it to him.
The Elder rose and made a gesture as if to depart. "Sit down and eat, dear one," [the king said]. [The Elder replied: "To the presence of the Teacher."
“I shall go and eat, Great King. “But where is the Teacher, dear son?
“Accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand bhikkhus, he has set out on a journey to see you, Great King.
“After you have partaken of this almsfood, carry this almsfood for him all the way until my son reaches this city. Thus spoke the Elder.
Having performed his meal duties, he took the food to be offered to the One of Ten Powers;
after delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, and even while the One of Ten Powers was out of sight, he caused the entire royal palace to attain the acquisition of faith.
Then, while everyone was looking on, he released his alms-bowl into the air and himself ascended into the sky, [carrying] the alms-food.
Taking it, he placed it in the Teacher’s hand, and the Teacher consumed that alms-food.
For sixty *yojana*s of the journey, as the Teacher traveled at a maximum rate of one *yojana* per day, the Elder brought food daily from the royal palace and gave it to him.
This is how the background story is to be understood. Then, at a later time, the Teacher [thought], "My father, the Great King, [has given] his entire residence..."
“...he inspired confidence,” meaning he established the Elder in the foremost position among those who inspire confidence in families.
Regarding the story of the Elder Bākula:
in the fourth [section], “of those with little illness” means of those free from disease. The Elder named Bākula received that name because he was raised in two different families.

Regarding his inquiry, this is the sequential narrative: It is said that in the past, more than a hundred thousand aeons ago, at the conclusion of an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*), even before the appearance of the Seven-Perfected One Anomadassi, he took rebirth in a brahmin family.
Upon reaching maturity, having mastered the Vedas, he saw no essence in the threefold Veda and, thinking, "I shall seek the goal pertaining to the future life," went to the foot of a mountain.
Having gone forth into the ascetic life, he attained the five supernormal powers and the eight meditative attainments, and spent his time sporting in jhāna.
At that time, the Bodhisatta Anomadassī, having attained omniscience, was wandering on tour surrounded by a company of noble ones.
Hearing that "the Three Jewels have appeared," the ascetic went into the presence of the Teacher; having heard the Dhamma, at the conclusion of the teaching—
Established in the refuges, he was nevertheless unable to abandon his own place. From time to time, he went to see the Teacher and listened to the Dhamma.
Then, on one occasion, wind arose in the Tathāgata’s stomach. The ascetic came to see the Teacher.
Hearing that "the Teacher is ill," he asked, "Venerable sir, what is the ailment? When it was said, "A wind in the stomach," he thought, "This is the time for me to perform an act of merit.

He went to the foot of a mountain, gathered various kinds of medicinal herbs, and gave them to the attendant elder, saying, "Take this medicine to the Teacher. As soon as the medicine was administered, the wind in the stomach [subsided].
It subsided. When the Teacher was feeling well, he went to him and said:

"Venerable Sir, since the Tathāgata has become comfortable through my medicine, by the result of that merit, may there not be even a single ailment as large as a cow's hoof-print in my body throughout all my future births. This was the wholesome deed he performed in that existence.

Passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. Wandering among gods and humans for one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeya*), during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he took rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those free from illness, he performed a service and aspired to that very status. He [lived] for the full span of his life.
Having performed wholesome deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans,

he was reborn even before the appearance of the Buddha Vipassī in a brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī. Just as in the previous case, he went forth into the ascetic life, attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna),
and dwelt at the foot of a mountain.

The Bodhisatta Vipassī, having attained omniscience, dwelt at the Khema Deer Park near the city of Bandhumatī, surrounded by a retinue of six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus, while providing for his father, the Great King.

Then this ascetic, having learned that the One Possessed of the Ten Powers had appeared in the world, came there; and having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he took refuge [in the Triple Gem].
He remained [in the order], unable to abandon his own renunciation; however, from time to time, he went to attend upon the Teacher.

Then, on one occasion—with the exception of the Teacher and the two Chief Disciples—a disease called "head-ailment" arose among the other bhikkhus due to the contact with the wind from flowering *visarukkha* trees in the Himālayas. The ascetic [went] to attend upon the Teacher.
When the ascetic arrived and saw the monks lying down with their heads covered, he asked, "Venerable sirs, what is causing discomfort for the Saṅgha of monks?

"The monks have an affliction caused by grass and flowers, friend," they replied. The ascetic thought, "This is the time for me to generate merit by performing service for the body of the Saṅgha of monks. Then, by his own spiritual power—
Having gathered various kinds of medicines and prepared them, he gave them [to the sick monk]. At that very moment, the illness of all the bhikkhus was completely pacified.

He lived out his full lifespan and was reborn in the Brahma-world. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for ninety-one aeons, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, he was reborn into a noble family in Bārāṇasī. While living the life of a householder, [he thought: "My dwelling-house..."
Thinking, "I shall go to the borderlands, gather building materials, and build a house," he set out with carpenters;
however, seeing an old great monastery along the way, he thought, "Let my house-building project wait for now—it will not go with me;
rather, by whatever means necessary, I must first accomplish the task of going there."
"It is fitting to have it made even more excellent. Having had those very carpenters fetch the building materials, he had an Uposatha hall constructed in that monastery;

he also had a dining hall, a fire-hall, a long walkway, a bathhouse, a kitchen, a privy, and a dispensary built, as well as whatever requisites, utensils, and medicines the Saṅgha of bhikkhus might require.
Having prepared everything by that name, he set it aside.

Having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*, he took rebirth in the house of a merchant in Kosambī even before our Ten-Powered Lord was born. From the day of his conception...
From that time on, that merchant’s family attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of glory. Then, after his mother had given birth to her son, she thought:

"This child is meritorious and has performed great deeds; for as long as he remains healthy and long-lived, he will be the provider of prosperity for us. On the very day of his birth, at the Mahā-Yamunā...

"He sent him for the purpose of bathing so that the boy might become clean and free from disease," [says one tradition]. "On the fifth day, having bathed his head, he sent him for the purpose of playing in the river," say the Majjhimabhāṇakas.
There, as the nurse was making the boy play by repeatedly submerging and raising him in the water, a fish saw the boy and, thinking "This is my food," opened its mouth.
He arrived. The nurse, having abandoned the boy, fled; a fish swallowed him. The meritorious being did not experience suffering;

he was as if lying down after entering his own bedchamber. Through the power of the boy, the fish, as if burning from swallowing a red-hot iron plate, traveled thirty *yojanas* with great speed and reached a fisherman living in the city of Bārāṇasī.
He entered the net. Great fish, when caught in a net, die only as they are being killed; however, this one died the very moment he was pulled out of the net by the power of the boy.
And fishermen, having obtained a great fish, usually split it open to sell it;
but because of the boy's supernatural power, they did not split it, but carried it whole on a carrying-pole, saying, "We will give it for a thousand."
They wandered about the city preaching, yet no one would take [the bowl].
However, in that city there was a merchant’s family with eighty crores of wealth who had no son.
Having reached the threshold of their gate, when they were asked, "What will you give in exchange?", they said, "A kahāpaṇa coin. Having been given a kahāpaṇa by them, it was taken.
On other days the merchant’s wife did not play with fish, but on that day she placed a fish on a wooden board and cut it open herself. Fish are indeed cut open in a loathsome manner;
however, as she was cutting it from the back, she saw a golden-colored boy within the belly of the fish and cried out, "I have found a son in the belly of a fish!"
Having cried out, she took the boy and went into the presence of her husband. The merchant immediately had the drum beaten and, taking the boy, went into the presence of the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, I have obtained a boy from the belly of a fish; what shall I do?
"This is a man of merit, who dwelt healthy within the belly of a fish; raise him," [the king] said.
The other family heard that a certain merchant’s family in Bārāṇasī had obtained a boy from the womb of a fish.
They went there. Then his mother, having seen the boy being adorned and played with, thought, "What a charming child this is!
She took him and explained the truth of the matter. The other woman said, "He is my son. "Where [is he]? [she asked].
"Where did you find them? "In the belly of a fish. "It is not your son; it is my son. "Where did you find him?
"I carried him in my womb for ten months, and then, while he was playing in the river, a fish swallowed him.
"Your son must have been swallowed by another fish, but this one was found by me in the belly of a fish."
Both went to the royal palace. The king said: "Because she carried him in her womb for ten months, it is not possible to treat her as motherless;

likewise, even those who catch fish do so by leaving the scales and bones outside, so because he was obtained from within a fish's belly, it is also not possible to treat him as motherless. Let the boy be an heir to both families."
From that time forth, both families attained the very pinnacle of gain and the highest excellence.
Because he was raised by two families, they gave him the name Bākula-kumāra.
When he reached the age of discretion, they had three palaces built for him in each of the two cities and provided him with theatrical performances.
He dwells for four months in each city. When he has stayed for four months in one city, they have a pavilion constructed within the monastery grounds and place him there along with dancers.
While enjoying these splendors, after those four months he goes to another city. The dancers residing in that city [prepare] for two...
Having traveled half the way in two months, he will arrive; so they go out to meet him, surround him, and lead him back to their own city in another two months.
The other theatrical troupes, however, turn back and go to their own cities.
Having stayed there for four months, he returns again to the other city by that same routine. Thus was his prosperity.
As he was experiencing this, eighty full years passed.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, having attained omniscience and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, reached Kosambī while wandering on his journey in due course—Bārāṇasī, according to the Majjhimabhāṇakas. And the merchant Bākula...

Hearing that "the One Possessed of Ten Powers has arrived," he took many perfumes and garlands, went into the presence of the Teacher, and having heard a discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth.
Having remained an ordinary person for only seven days, on the eighth dawn he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Then, in two cities, the women who had been his attendants during his time as a householder—
Having come from their own family homes and residing there, they made robes and sent them.
For one half-month the Elder used the robe sent by the residents of Kosambī, and for another half-month that sent by the residents of Bārāṇasī.
In this very manner, whatever was most excellent in both cities was brought specifically for the Elder. To the Elder...

While living in the midst of a household for eighty years, there was never any ailment whatsoever, even for the duration of time it takes to take a pinch of scented paste with two fingers and apply it to the nose. At the age of eighty, he entered the homeless life in perfect ease.
Even after his ordination, there was not the slightest illness nor any deficiency regarding the four requisites. Thus, even at the final stage of his life, at the very moment of his Parinibbāna—

Having preached the entire Bākula Sutta by way of illustrating his own physical and mental happiness to the naked ascetic Kassapa, who was his companion from his former home, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. Thus arose the occasion [for the discourse].
However, while the Elder was still living, the Teacher [appointed him] to a rank in the succession of Elders.
By placing the Elder Bākula in this position, the Buddha established him in the foremost rank among those free from illness within this dispensation.
[End of] the Story of the Elder Sobhita. 227.

Regarding the fifth category, "those who recollect their past lives" (pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantānaṃ): this refers to those capable of recollecting the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) in which they previously resided.

This shows that the Elder Sobhita was the foremost. It is said that when he was recollecting his past lives in successive order, he took five hundred eons of rebirth in the non-percipient realm (*asaññibhava*)—a state of mindless rebirth—as far back as he could trace them, just as one might point out a footprint in the sky.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who recollect their past lives.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential narrative: It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he took rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those bhikkhus who have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*). Having seen this, he performed a work of merit.

Having done so, he aspired to that high position. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, during the present arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī; they gave him the name Sobhita.
At a later time, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and [applied himself to] insight meditation.
Having increased his practice and attained *arahantship*, he became one who had mastered the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).

Recalling his own places of rebirth in successive order, he saw his rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as far back as the non-percipient realm (*asaññibhava*), where there is rebirth-linking without consciousness.
Beyond that, seeing no continuity of existence for five hundred eons, and seeing only the death-moment at the very end, he thought: "What..."
Reflecting on the name, he reached the conclusion by way of inference that "there will be a state of non-perception.
The Teacher, taking this as the occasion for a discourse, established the Elder in the foremost position among those who recollect their past lives.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Upāli.
228. Regarding the sixth [category], "of those who uphold the Vinaya, namely Upāli": this shows that among the monks who uphold the Vinaya, the Elder Upāli is the foremost.
It is said that the Elder, having received his meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the presence of the Tathāgata himself and having developed insight (vipassanā), attained Arahatship.
Having likewise mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka from the presence of the Tathāgata himself, [he became the foremost] regarding the Bhārukacchaka-vatthu...
He related these three stories—the story of the maternal uncle, the story of Kumāra Kassapa, and the story of the three—by correlating them with his own omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
This is the sequential account of his past deeds: it is said that during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he was born into a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
Having been reborn, one day while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.

Having performed a work of merit, he aspired to that very status. Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans, and was now conceived in the house of a barber at the time of this Buddha’s appearance.
They gave the boy Upāli the name Gaṇḍī. When he reached maturity, he became a hairdresser for six kṣatriyas.

While the Tathāgata was dwelling in the Anupiya Mango Grove, he went forth together with those six kṣatriyas who were departing to seek ordination, and thus he too was ordained. The procedure for his ordination is recorded in the Pāḷi itself.
Having thus gone forth and received full ordination, he requested a meditation subject from the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please grant me permission to dwell in the forest.
The Teacher replied, "If you dwell in the forest, my son, only one burden will increase for you;
but if you dwell in our presence, both the burden of insight and the burden of study will be fulfilled. The Elder—
Having accepted the instruction, he performed the work of insight meditation and before long attained Arahatship.
Then the Teacher himself had him master the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. Later on, he adjudicated the three cases mentioned below.
As each case was adjudicated, the Teacher gave his approval, and regarding those three adjudications—
Having established this occasion, [the Buddha] placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya.
The Story of the Elder Nandaka (229).

Regarding the statement, "Among those who instruct the bhikkhunīs, he is foremost, namely Nandaka": for while this Elder was delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, he led five hundred bhikkhunīs to the state of Arahatship during a single assembly. Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who instruct the bhikkhunīs.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential account: During the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of chief among those who instruct the bhikkhunīs.
Having performed an act of service, he aspired to that very position. For as long as he lived, he...
Having performed wholesome deeds and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in a noble family at Sāvatthī during this current appearance of a Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, he heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma; having gained faith, he went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher.
By developing insight (vipassanā), he attained arahantship and became one who had mastered the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa). He [was proficient] in the four...
When assemblies had gathered, he became known as Dhammakathikanandaka because he was able to speak while taking into account the minds of everyone present.
Meanwhile, the Tathāgata, having emerged from Cumbaṭaka on the bank of the Rohiṇī River,
took with him those five hundred Sākiyan princes who had gone forth after dissatisfaction had arisen in them, and went to Kuṇāla Lake.

Having gone there, he understood their state of spiritual agitation through the story of the Kuṇāla Jātaka; after teaching them the discourse on the Four Noble Truths, he established them in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*).
Later, by teaching the Mahāsamaya Sutta, he led them to the supreme fruit of arhatship.
The former wives of those elders, saying, "What shall we do here now? became all of one mind.
They approached Mahāpajāpatī and requested the going-forth. Those five hundred women also received the going-forth and full ordination in the presence of the Elder Nun.
Furthermore, in their immediately preceding birth, they had all been the female attendants of the Elder Nanda while he was still a prince.
At that time, the Teacher said, "Let the monks exhort the bhikkhunīs.
When it was the Elder’s turn, he realized that in a previous existence he had been their personal attendant, and he thought:

"If others who have attained the knowledge of past lives were to see me sitting here in the midst of this community of bhikkhunīs, preaching the Dhamma by bringing forward similes and reasons, [they would be amazed]."
“Having observed this situation, a bhikkhu might think: ‘Venerable Nandaka does not release the women’s quarters until this very day;
this Venerable One shines while surrounded by the harem. Therefore, instead of going himself, he sent another bhikkhu.
Moreover, those five hundred bhikkhunīs were waiting specifically for the Elder’s exhortation. By this...

For this reason, the Blessed One said to the Elder, "When your turn has arrived, do not send another, but go yourself and exhort the community of bhikkhunīs. Unable to refuse the Teacher’s word, when his own turn arrived on the fourteenth day, he gave the exhortation to the community of bhikkhunīs; and all those bhikkhunīs, adorned with the six sense bases (saḷāyatana)— [The remainder of the text follows:
...were established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, the Elder Mahākassapa was the foremost among the disciples in the practice of the dhutaṅgas.

Having given the exhortation to the bhikkhunīs, he went to the village of Pāvā. There, the Venerable Cunda the Smith prepared a meal of sukara-maddava for him. When the Elder had finished eating, he felt a slight illness. He then lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, mindful and clearly comprehending, and passed away. His body was cremated with great honor, and a stūpa was erected over his remains at Pāvā.]
Through his teaching of the Dhamma, he established them in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).
Delighted by the Elder’s Dhamma teaching, those bhikkhunīs went into the presence of the Teacher and reported the qualities they had realized.
The Teacher asked, "While whom was the Dhamma being taught when these bhikkhunīs attained the fruits of the higher paths?"

Reflecting, "May they attain [the goal]," and seeing again that "having heard this very same Dhamma teaching of Nanda, these five hundred women will also attain Arahantship," he sent them once more to the presence of the Elder on the following day for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.
Having heard the Dhamma on that following day, they all attained Arahantship. On that day, the Blessed One [bestowed] upon them...

Knowing that his teaching of the Dhamma to the bhikkhunīs who had come into his presence was fruitful, he said, "Yesterday, Nandaka’s teaching of the Dhamma was like the moon on the fourteenth day; today, it is like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Having given his approval to the Elder, and taking that very reason as the occasion (the *aṭṭhuppatti*), [he appointed] the Elder as the instructor of the bhikkhunīs.
"He placed [him] in the foremost position.
(Nanda Thera’s Story, 230).
Regarding the eighth [section], "those with guarded doors among the faculties": this refers to those who have closed the doors of the six sense-faculties; [the foremost among them was] Nanda Thera.

This shows that he was the foremost. For although there were no disciples of the Teacher who did not guard their sense-doors, the Elder Nanda, whenever he wished to look toward any of the ten directions, would not look without delimiting his field through the four kinds of clear comprehension (*catu-sampajañña*).
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who guard their sense-doors.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential account: During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he took rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.

Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties. Having performed a work of merit, he made a resolution.

He aspired for that particular station. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans and took rebirth in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī in the city of Kapilavatthu.
Then, on the day of his naming ceremony, because he was born bringing joy and satisfaction to the assembly of his kinsmen, they gave him the name Nandakumāra (the Joyful Prince).
The Mahāsatta, having attained omniscience and set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma, performed a benefit for the world by traveling from Rājagaha to the city of Kapilavatthu;
at his very first sight, he established his father in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*).
On the following day, having gone to his father’s residence and given instruction to Rāhula’s mother, he taught the Dhamma to the rest of the people as well.

He preached the Dhamma. On the following day, while the auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda’s consecration and his entry into the marriage chamber were underway, he went to the prince’s residence, had him take up the alms-bowl, and set out toward the monastery to ordain him.
The auspicious ceremony of Prince Nanda’s consecration did not trouble him as much; however, at the time of taking the bowl and departing, Janapadakalyānī—
Having ascended to the excellent upper palace and opened the lion-window, she uttered these words: "Noble son, you should come quickly.
Hearing this, he looked out under the influence of worldly desire and passion;
however, due to his reverence for the Teacher, he was unable to seize upon the sign as he pleased, and because of that, his mind became distressed. Then—
Even as he was thinking, "He will turn back at this spot; he will turn back at that spot," the Teacher led him to the monastery and ordained him.
Although he had been ordained, [the King] remained silent, unable to refuse.
From the day of his ordination, however, he remembered only the words spoken by Janapadakalyāṇī. Then she came and stood not far away.
He became as if paralyzed. Oppressed by discontent, he walked a short distance;
yet as he passed a grove or a thicket, the One of Ten Powers appeared standing right before him.
Like a hen’s feather cast into a fire, he turned back and entered his own dwelling place.
The Teacher thought: “Nanda dwells in extreme negligence; he is unable to pacify his discontent.
It is necessary to bring about the cooling of his mind. Then He said to him: “Come, Nanda, let us go on a tour of the celestial realms. The Blessed One asked:
“How shall we go to the place that must be traveled by those possessing psychic power? [He replied: “You alone—”
“Arise with the thought of going; having gone, you shall see. Through the power of the One of Ten Powers, he went on a celestial journey together with the Tathāgata.
Having observed the residence of Sakka, king of the gods, he saw five hundred nymphs.
Seeing the Elder Nanda looking at them through the lure of the sign of beauty, the Teacher said, “Nanda, are these...”
“Is a celestial nymph more delightful, or is a woman beautiful throughout the land? he asked.

“Venerable sir, compared to these celestial nymphs, a woman beautiful throughout the land looks like a monkey with its ears and nose cut off. “Nanda, such celestial nymphs are not difficult to obtain for those who practice the duty of a recluse.
Venerable Blessed One, if you will be my guarantor, I shall practice the duty of a recluse.”
"I shall do so. "Then, Nanda, perform the duties of a recluse with confidence.
If your death should occur with rebirth still pending, I am a guarantor for the recovery of these [wives] for you.
Having thus wandered on his divine tour as he pleased, the Teacher returned once more to Jetavana.
From that time on, the Elder Nanda practiced the duties of a recluse day and night for the sake of the celestial nymphs.

The Teacher commanded the monks: "Go about from place to place saying, 'It is said that a certain monk, having made the One of Ten Powers his guarantor, practices the duties of a recluse for the sake of celestial nymphs.'"
Having accepted the Teacher’s words, they wandered about within the range of the Elder’s hearing, saying: “Venerable Nanda is indeed a hireling; Venerable Nanda is indeed a mercenary;
he leads the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs; it is said that the Blessed One is his guarantor for the acquisition of five hundred Kakuṭapādī nymphs.
Thus did they speak regarding the Elder Nanda.
Having heard that, he reflected: "These monks are not talking about anything else; they are talking about me.
This is an unworthy task for me. Having thus produced this reflection, he developed insight and attained arahantship.
At the very moment he attained arahantship, a certain deity informed the Blessed One of this matter, and the Blessed One himself [also knew it].
He understood it indeed. On the following day, the Elder Nanda approached the Blessed One and said:

"Venerable sir, that for which the Blessed One was my guarantor regarding the acquisition of five hundred peahen-footed nymphs—I release the Blessed One from that promise. Thus the occasion arose. Later, the Teacher—
While dwelling in the Jetavana monastery, [the Buddha] placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who guard the doors of the sense faculties.
This is the story of the Elder Mahākappina (231).
In the ninth [section], it is shown that among those who exhort monks, the Elder Mahākappina is the foremost.
It is said that this Elder, while delivering a single discourse on the Dhamma during one assembly, led a thousand bhikkhus to Arahatship.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost of those who exhort bhikkhus.
Regarding his past deeds, this is the sequential account: for he too, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, was in Haṃsavatī...

Having been reborn in a noble family, at a later time while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being the foremost among those who exhort bhikkhus. Having performed an act of service, he aspired to that very station.
Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans until the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa.
Having taken rebirth in a noble family in Bārāṇasī, he became the leader of a group of one thousand men and built a great monastery adorned with a thousand cells.

All those people, having performed wholesome deeds throughout their lives and making the lay follower Kappina their leader, were reborn in the world of the gods together with their wives and children.
For the duration of an entire interval between Buddhas, they wandered among gods and humans.
Now, even before our Teacher was born, this Kappina took rebirth in the royal palace in the frontier city of Kukkuṭavatī; the other men were born in that same city into the families of ministers.
Among them, when Prince Kappina’s father passed away, he raised the royal parasol and became known as King Mahākappina. Previously...
At the time when he was performing wholesome deeds, the mistress of his house was reborn in a royal family of similar status and became the chief queen of King Mahākappina;
because her complexion was like that of the *anoja* flower, she was known by the name Queen Anojā.
King Mahākappina, moreover, was wealthy and learned. Rising early in the morning, he [went] through the four gates...
He quickly dispatched messengers with these instructions: “Wherever you see those who are learned and possessors of what they have heard, turn back from there and report it to me.
Now at that time, our Teacher, having appeared in the world, was residing near Sāvatthī.
At that moment, merchants living in the city of Sāvatthī took merchandise for trade and departed from Sāvatthī.
Having gone to the city and secured their merchandise, they took gifts with the thought, "We shall see the king.
Arriving at the gate of the royal palace, they heard that the king had gone to the park; so they went to the park and, standing at the gate, announced themselves to the doorkeeper.
When this was reported to the king, he summoned them. Once they had presented their gifts and stood there having paid homage, the king said, "Sirs,..."
“Where have you come from? he asked. “From Sāvatthī, Your Majesty. “Is there plenty of food in your country, and is the king righteous?
“Yes, Your Majesty. “But is there any teaching of the Buddha in your land? “There is, Your Majesty, but it is not possible to speak with mouths full of leftovers.
The king had water poured from a golden pitcher for them, and they washed their mouths.
Having rinsed their mouths and raised their hands in añjali toward the One of Ten Powers, they said, “Your Majesty, in our land a jewel called the Buddha has appeared.
At the mere sound of the word “Buddha,” joy arose that pervaded the king’s entire body.
Then he said, “Sons, say ‘Buddha! “We say ‘Buddha,’ Your Majesty,” they replied. Thus...
Having had him recite it three times, [the king thought], "The word 'Buddha' is immeasurable; it is not possible to place a limit upon it.

Becoming inspired by that very word, he gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and asked, "What further teaching is there? [The monk replied], "Your Majesty, that which is called the Jewel of the Dhamma has appeared.
Having heard that as well, he likewise obtained his consent three times and gave another hundred thousand.
Having given it, he asked again, "What else is there in the Dispensation? "The Jewel of the Sangha has arisen, Your Majesty," they replied.

Having heard that as well, he gave his assent in the same manner, gave another hundred thousand, and after writing on a letter the fact that it had been given, he sent them off, saying, "Sirs, go into the presence of the Queen.
When they had departed, he asked his ministers: "Sirs, the Buddha..."
“Since one has appeared in the world, what will you do?”— “Your Majesty, what do you intend to do?”—

“I shall go forth into homelessness.”— “We too shall go forth. Without taking leave of their homes or families, they all departed by means of those very horses upon which they had ridden when they first set out.
The merchants went into the presence of Queen Anojā and presented the letter.
Having read it, she asked, "Dear ones, the King has given you many kahāpaṇas; what have you done with them? "A pleasant message has been brought, Your Majesty.
"Dear ones, can we also be made to hear one? "It is possible, Your Majesty, but it cannot be spoken from a mouth that is defiled by food remnants."
She had water poured from a golden pitcher. Having rinsed their mouths, they reported [the matter] to the king exactly as they had been instructed.

Upon hearing this, she too was filled with joy; following that same method, she obtained a formal promise three times for each word, and by counting those promises—three for each—she gave nine hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. The merchants [took] all of them...
They received twelve hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Then he asked them, "Where is the king, dear ones?

"He has gone forth, O Queen, thinking, 'I shall go into homelessness. "In that case, dear ones, you may go," he said, and having dismissed them, he summoned the wives of the ministers who had gone with the king and said, "You know the place where your own husbands have gone."
"Mother," she asked. "We know, noble lady, that you went with the king for a pleasure excursion to the park. "Yes, mother, we did go;

but having gone there, we heard, 'A Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma has arisen, the Saṅgha has arisen,' and we went thinking, 'We shall go forth in the presence of the One Possessed of the Ten Powers. What will you do? "But what do you intend to do, noble lady?"
“I shall go forth into homelessness; I will not place upon the tip of my tongue that which has been vomited by them.
“If it is so, we too shall go forth,” they said, and having harnessed all their chariots, they departed.
The king also reached the bank of the Ganges together with a thousand ministers; at that time, the Ganges was full.
Then, seeing this, [the king thought]: "This Ganges is full and teeming with fierce fish;
there are no slaves or men who have come along with us who could build and give us a boat or a raft.
Yet the virtues of this Teacher extend from below the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence. If this Teacher is truly a Sammasambuddha..."
“Let not the hooves of these horses get wet,” they said, and so they made the horses leap over the surface of the water.
Not even the surface of the hooves of a single horse became wet; as if traveling along a royal highway, they reached the opposite bank and arrived at another great river beyond.
He asked, “What is this second one? It was called the Nīlavāhinī, and it was deep...
The gods were also half a *yojana* in width. There was no other act of truth (*saccakiriya*) there;

by that very act of truth, they crossed even that river which was half a *yojana* wide. Then, having reached the third great river named Candabhāgā, they crossed that as well by means of that same act of truth.
On that day, at the time of dawn, the Teacher emerged from the attainment of great compassion and, surveying the world, saw:
"Today Mahākappina will come into my presence to go forth, having abandoned his kingdom of three hundred leagues along with a retinue of a thousand ministers.
Seeing this, he thought, "It is fitting for me to go out to meet them," and early in the morning performed the care of his body.
Having done so, accompanied by the community of monks, he walked for alms in Sāvatthī; after his meal, having returned from the alms round,

he took his own bowl and robe, rose into the air, and sat cross-legged at the foot of a great banyan tree located on the bank of the Candabhāgā River facing the landing place where they were to cross, establishing mindfulness directed toward the front.
He emitted the six-colored rays of a Buddha. As they were crossing by that ford, they saw the Buddha’s rays streaming hither and thither;
then, beholding the face of the One Endowed with Ten Powers, which possessed the splendor of the full moon, they reached the conclusion through that very sight:
"Surely this is the Teacher for whose sake we went forth. From the place where they had seen him...

Having approached, they bowed down and paid homage to the Teacher. The King, taking hold of them by the ankles, paid homage to the Teacher and sat down to one side together with his thousand ministers. The Teacher delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to them.
At the conclusion of the teaching, they all became established in Arahatship and requested the Teacher for the going-forth. The Teacher—
“Because these people had previously given gifts of robes, they have come here having already taken their own bowls and robes. Extending his golden-colored hand, he said:
“Come, monks; the Dhamma is well-expounded. Lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
That itself was the going-forth and the full ordination of those venerable ones.
They surrounded the Teacher like monks who had been ordained for sixty years.
Queen Anojā also, accompanied by a thousand chariots, reached the bank of the Ganges;
not seeing a boat or a raft that had been brought for the king, she reflected with her own discernment: "The king must have gone after performing an act of truth."
But that Teacher did not arise solely for their sake; if that Teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), may our chariots not sink into the water!
Thus he caused the chariots to drive over the surface of the water. Not even as much as the circumference of the chariot wheels was wetted.
He crossed the second river and the third river by means of that very same declaration of truth.
And at the foot of the Nigrodha tree, Uttaramānā saw the Teacher.

The Teacher, thinking, "If these women were to see their own husbands, desire and lust would arise within them, creating an obstacle to the Path and its Fruits, and they would be unable to hear the Dhamma," acted in such a way that they could not see one another. All of them remained standing there.
Having crossed over and paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, they sat down. The Teacher delivered a discourse on the Dhamma to them.
At the conclusion of the teaching, they all became established in the fruit of stream-entry and beheld one another. The Teacher thought, "Let Uppalavaṇṇā come.
The Elder Nun arrived, ordained them all, and taking them with her, went to the nuns' quarters; the Teacher [then addressed] the thousand bhikkhus.
Having taken it, he went through the air to Jetavana.
Then, the Elder Mahākappina, realizing that his own task had reached its culmination, became free from concern;

passing his time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), whether gone to the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty dwelling, he exclaimed, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!"

He frequently uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*). The monks raised the question, "Is it not the Elder Kappina who is uttering this inspired utterance while recollecting the happiness of kingship?

They reported this to the Tathāgata. The Blessed One said, "My son has uttered this inspired utterance concerning the happiness of the Path and the happiness of the Fruit," and then spoke this verse in the *Dhammapada*:
“One who delights in the Dhamma sleeps happily with a serene mind;
the wise man always rejoices in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble One.
Then, one day, the Teacher addressed his thousand resident monks and said: “I hope, monks, that you are well?”
“The teacher teaches the Dhamma. [The Blessed One said: “The Blessed One does not teach;
he dwells at ease, devoted to the pleasant abiding in this very life, and he does not give even a mere exhortation to anyone.
The Teacher summoned him and asked, “Is it true, Kappina, that you do not give even a mere exhortation to your pupils? “It is true, Blessed One,” he replied. “Brāhmaṇa,…”
"Do not do so; from this day forward, teach the Dhamma to your pupils. "Very well, Bhante," the Elder replied, accepting the Teacher's words with his head.
