At that very same assembly, he taught the Dhamma to a thousand ascetics and led them all to Arahantship.
Later on, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the Saṅgha, [he spoke] in due order...
Placing him among those various positions, he established the Elder Mahākappina in the foremost place among those who exhort the bhikkhus.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Sāgata (232).
Regarding the tenth [category], "among those skilled in the fire-element": the Elder Sāgata is the foremost among those skilled in attaining the fire-element (*tejodhātu*).

[The Blessed One] shows this. For this Elder, by means of the attainment of the fire-element (*tejodhātu-samāpatti*), consumed the fire of the Naga Ambatittha with his own fire and rendered that Naga harmless.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those skilled in the fire-element.
Regarding his past deeds, this is the sequential account: during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he also [lived] in Haṃsavatī...

Having taken rebirth in a noble family, later on, while listening to the Teacher’s preaching of the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those skilled in the fire element (*tejodhātu*). Having performed an act of service, he aspired to that very station.
Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans until this arising of a Buddha.
He was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī, and they gave him the name Sāgata-māṇava. Later,
having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith, went forth, and after attaining the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti),
he reached mastery over them.
Then one day, while wandering on his alms-tour, the Teacher arrived near the city of Kosambī.
At that time, many travelers and wayfarers, having become hostile toward an old ferryman at a river crossing, beat him to death.
With a mind full of resentment, he made a wish; and at that very same crossing, he became a powerful Nāga king.
Having made the offering, he was reborn there. Because his mind was hostile, he caused it to rain out of season and failed to cause it to rain at the proper time;

consequently, the crops did not flourish. The inhabitants of the entire kingdom performed an annual ritual offering for the sake of appeasing him, and they built a house for him to dwell in. The Teacher also [arrived] by that same ford.
Having crossed over, surrounded by the community of monks, he proceeded with the thought, "I shall dwell for the night in that very place.

Then this elder, having heard that "the Naga king here is indeed fierce," thought, "It is fitting to tame this Naga king, to render him harmless, and thus provide a dwelling place for the Teacher. He then entered the dwelling place of the Naga king.
He sat down, having folded his legs crosswise in the *pallaṅka* posture. The nāga, becoming angry, thought, "Who is this shaveling who has entered my dwelling place and sits there?
and he emitted smoke; the Elder emitted even more smoke. The nāga burst into flames; the Elder also burst into flames even more intensely, and having done so, he consumed the nāga's fiery power.
The nāga thought, "This monk is truly great," and [fell] at the feet of the Elder.
Having prostrated, he said, "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to you. [The Elder replied,] "I have no need for going for refuge;
go for refuge to the One of Ten Powers. Having said, "Very well," he went for refuge. From that time forth, he did not harm anyone;
the rain fell properly, and the crops flourished successfully.
The residents of Kosambī, having heard that the noble Sāgata had tamed the Ambatitthaka Nāga, awaited the arrival of the Teacher and prepared a great honor for the One of Ten Powers.

Having performed this great honor for the Dasabala, and at the word of the Chabbaggiyas, they prepared dove-colored broth in all their houses; then, on the following day, [they waited] for the Elder Sāgata.
As he was walking for alms, people gave him small portions from house to house.

When the Elder had not yet been given the training rule, he accepted small portions from people as they requested them, drinking a little at each house; then, having gone only a short distance, he lost his mindfulness due to hunger and fell in a place of refuse.
When the Teacher had finished his meal and was departing, he saw him; having him taken hold of and brought back to the monastery, he rebuked him and laid down a training rule.
On the following day, that man regained his mindfulness, heard what he had done, and confessed his transgression.
Having asked the Ten-Powered One for forgiveness, he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*); increasing his insight (*vipassanā*), he attained Arhatship.
Thus the origin of the matter arose in the Vinaya; it should be understood in detail according to the method presented therein.

Later, however, while the Teacher was seated in the Great Monastery at Jetavana, he established the Elders in their respective positions in succession, and placed the Elder Sāgata in the foremost position among those skilled in the fire-element (tejodhātu).
Rādha Thera’s Story (233).

In the eleventh [section], "Among those who possess ready wit," it is shown that among the monks who serve as conditions for the Teacher’s inspired discourse on the Dhamma and who generate such wit, Rādha Thera is the foremost. For this Thera, regarding the manifestation of wrong view...
And by relying on that faith which is capable of supporting the Dhamma, ever-new discourses on the Dhamma inspired the Teacher of the Ten Powers.
Therefore, the Elder became known as the foremost among those who possess ready wit (*paṭibhāneyyaka*).
This is the sequential account regarding his past deeds: for he too, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, was in Haṃsavatī...

Having been reborn in a noble family, later on, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of being the foremost among those possessed of ready wit. Having performed an act of service, he aspired to that very station.
After serving the Tathāgata for as long as he lived, and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, during this present arising of a Buddha—
He took rebirth in a brahmin family in the city of Rājagaha, and they gave him the name Rādha Māṇava.

When he was advanced in years, being held in low esteem by his own sons and wife, he thought, "I shall go forth and spend my time in that state," and so he went to a monastery and requested ordination from the elders. However, because he was an old and aged brahmin, no one would ordain him.
Thus he desired. Then one day, the brahmin went into the presence of the Teacher; having exchanged greetings, he sat down to one side.
Seeing his excellence of spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), the Teacher, wishing to initiate a conversation, asked:
"Brahmin, do your sons and wife look after you? "How could they, Master Gotama? I am old; they do not look after me when I am outside."
“They have carried him away. “But, brahmin, is it not fitting for you to go forth? “Who, Master Gotama, would ordain me?
Because of my advanced age, no one wishes to have me. The Teacher gave a sign to the Elder Sāriputta.
The Elder, having accepted the Teacher’s word with his head, ordained the Brahmin Rādha and thought: “The Teacher—”
"Since he has caused this brahmin to go forth with such reverence, it would not be right for me to treat him with neglect," he thought.

Taking the Elder Rādha with him, he went to the village monastery. There, because the Elder had only recently gone forth and was one who obtained requisites with difficulty, he gave his own alms-bowl as a lodging for him;
and having given even his own excellent alms-food to him, he himself—
He went for alms. Having obtained suitable lodgings and suitable food, the Elder Rādha took a meditation subject from the Elder Sāriputta and before long attained Arahantship.
Then the Elder, taking him with him, came to see the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher, though already knowing, asked: "He who [was] yours..."
“Sāriputta, I have given [the status of] one who is dependent; what kind of person is he? He does not grow weary. “Venerable sir, such a one would indeed be a bhikkhu who delights in the Teaching.
Then, a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha: “The Elder Sāriputta is grateful and appreciative. Hearing this, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, it is not surprising that Sāriputta is now grateful and appreciative;
in the past, even when he was reborn with a non-causal rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-paṭisandhi*), he was likewise grateful and appreciative. “At what time, Blessed One?
“In the past, monks, five hundred carpenters entered a great forest at the foot of a mountain.”
Having cut the timber and materials, they bound together a great raft and launched it into the river.
Then a certain noble elephant, at a certain uneven spot, grasped a branch with his trunk;
unable to withstand the force of the snapping branch, he planted his foot upon a sharp stump. His foot was pierced, and agonizing pains arose. He was unable to proceed.

Unable to do so, he lay down right there. After a few days had passed, seeing those carpenters passing by his side, he thought, "Depending on these men, I shall obtain my livelihood," and followed after them.
When they turned back and saw the elephant, they fled in fear. Knowing that they were fleeing, he stood still; when they stopped again, he pursued them once more.
The eldest carpenter thought: "While we are standing still, this elephant pursues us;
when we flee, he stops. There must be a reason for this. They all climbed various trees and sat waiting for his approach.
He came into their presence and, showing them his foot, turned it over.
He lay down. Then a thought occurred to the carpenters: "He is coming because he is ill, not for any other reason.
Going to him and seeing a splinter stuck in his foot, they realized, "It is for this reason he has come.
They drove a wedge into the tip of the splinter with a sharp axe, bound it firmly with a strong rope, and pulled it out.
They drew it out. Then, having pressed the opening of the wound, they removed the pus and blood, washed it with a decoction of *kasāva*, and applied a medicine they knew well;
in no long time, they made him well again.
When the elephant king had recovered from his illness, he thought: "These men have been very helpful to me; it is by depending on them that I have my life."
“Having received this, it is right for me to be grateful and mindful of what has been done for me,” he thought.
He went to his own dwelling place and brought back the white young scent-elephant.
When the carpenters saw the young elephant, they were exceedingly joyful, thinking, “Our elephant has even come bringing his son with him! Then the elephant-king thought: “In me…”
Thinking, “If I remain here, they will not know the reason for my arrival and will wonder, ‘Why has he come?
he departed from his standing place. The young elephant calf followed closely behind his father.
When the great elephant perceived that he had arrived, he gave a signal with his voice to turn him back. Having heard his father’s words, the calf turned back toward the carpenters.

He went into his presence. The carpenters, realizing, "This one must have come to give us this young elephant calf," sent him back, saying, "There is no business for you to do in our presence; go back to your father's side.
Although the elephant king had come to him three times, he sent him back again to the vicinity of the carpenters.
From that time on, the carpenters took the elephant calf under their own care and looked after it.
At mealtime, they gave him a morsel of food each, and he had as much food as he required.
He would bring the building materials that were being hewn inside the house by the carpenters and pile them up in the courtyard. In this very manner, he also [brought other materials].
He performs a service.
By citing this instance, the Teacher illustrates that even in the past, Sāriputta was grateful and mindful of benefits.
For at that time, the Elder Sāriputta was a great elephant, while the monk who had abandoned his energy was a young elephant cub, as related in the introductory narrative (Nidāna).
It was so. However, having reached the *Saṃyuttanikāya*, the entire *Rādhasaṃyutta* is found there, and in the *Dhammapada*:
“As one would [seek] a discoverer of hidden treasures, so should one associate with a wise person who points out faults, who speaks with censure, and who is discerning—such a one is a true sage.”
“For one who associates with such a person, it is better, not worse.”—This verse is known as the Elder’s Dhamma-teaching.
Later, however, when the Teacher was assigning the Elders to their respective positions in succession, he placed the Elder Rādha in the foremost position among those of ready wit.
This is the story of the Elder Mogharāja.
234. Regarding the twelfth [quality], "among those who wear coarse robes": this shows that Mogharāja is the foremost among those who wear coarse robes.
For this elder wore a refuse-rag robe (*paṃsukūla*) endowed with the three kinds of coarseness—coarseness in its cutting, coarseness in its stitching, and coarseness in its dyeing.
Therefore, he became known as the foremost among those who wear coarse robes.
Regarding his performance of the question, this is the sequential account:
During the time of Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn into a noble family in Haṃsavatī.

Later, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the position of foremost among those who wear coarse robes, and he performed a work of merit.

Having done so, he aspired to that position. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, he took rebirth in the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana in the house of a minister even before the appearance of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Later, having reached maturity, while serving King Kaṭṭhavāhana, he obtained the position of minister.
At that time, Kassapa, the One Endowed with the Ten Powers, appeared in the world.
King Kaṭṭhavāhana, having heard that "a Buddha has indeed arisen in the world," summoned him and said: "Dear son, it is said that a Buddha has arisen in the world.
It is not possible for both of us to empty this frontier city all at once; therefore, you go first to the Middle Country."
"Knowing that the Buddha has appeared, bring this One of Ten Powers to this city," he said, and dispatched him along with a thousand men.

He traveled by stages to the presence of the Teacher; having heard a discourse on the Dhamma and gained faith, he went forth right there and practiced the ascetic life for twenty thousand years. The men who had gone with him—
But they all turned back and returned once more to the presence of the king.

This elder, having perfected his moral virtue (*sīla*), passed away and, wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas, took rebirth in the family of a brahmin in Sāvatthī even before our Ten-Powered One was born; he was the young brahmin Mogharāja.

They gave him that name. King Kaṭṭhavāhana, having performed meritorious service for the Blessed One Kassapa, passed through one interval between Buddhas wandering among gods and humans together with his retinue;
even before our own Dasabala was born, he took rebirth in Sāvatthī in the home of the family priest, and they gave him the name Bāvari Māṇava. At a later time, he...
Having mastered the three Vedas, he traveled about teaching the craft to sixteen thousand young brahmins.
Then, during the time of King Pasenadi of Kosala, they appointed him to the position of royal chaplain upon the death of his father.
At that time, this young brahmin Mogharāja was also receiving his training in the presence of the brahmin Bāvari.
Then one day, while the brahmin Bāvari was reflecting in solitude upon the essence of his own craft, he saw no essence pertaining to the future life.
Thinking, "Having gone forth into homelessness, I shall seek that which pertains to the future life," he approached the King of Kosala and requested permission for his renunciation.
Having been granted permission by the king, he set out surrounded by sixteen thousand young brahmins.
He went forth for the sake of the going-forth. The King of Kosala also sent a minister along with him, giving him a thousand kahāpaṇas, saying:
"In whatever place the teacher goes forth, go there and secure a dwelling for him.
While the brahmin Bāvari was looking for a suitable location, he turned back from the Middle Country toward the kingdoms of Assaka and Mūḷaka.
And he established his own dwelling place on the banks of the Godhāvarī River within the Sīma.
Then, a certain man who had gone to visit the Jaṭilas, being permitted by them to do so on a piece of land belonging to them, established his own dwelling place there.
Seeing what he had built, another hundred families constructed a hundred houses. All of them—
Having assembled, they said, “We dwell on land belonging to the noble ladies; there is no reason for us to live here for nothing.
We shall provide you with a comfortable dwelling. Thus, each one deposited a single kahāpaṇa coin in the residence of the brahmin Bāvari.
The coins brought by everyone amounted to approximately one hundred thousand. The brahmin Bāvari asked, “For what purpose have these been brought?”
He said, "Venerable sir, it is for the sake of providing a comfortable dwelling.
[The Elder replied,] "If I were in need of gold and bullion, I would not have gone forth after abandoning such a great heap of wealth. Take these coins and go.
[They replied,] "We do not take back what has been relinquished by the Noble One; however, according to this very arrangement, every year—"

"We shall bring it; having taken these, may the noble one give alms. The brahmin consented and distributed them through the channels of charity to the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and the beggars.
His status as a donor became renowned throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa.
Subsequently, in the kingdom of Kāliṅga, in a village named Dunniviṭṭha, there was a brahmin born into the lineage of the brahmin Jūjaka.
The brahmin woman, rising again and again, urged the brahmin: "Bāvari, it is said that he is giving alms;
go and bring back gold and bullion from there. Being thus urged by her, unable to remain steadfast, he went into the presence of Bāvari.
Having given alms to Bāvari, he entered the leaf-hut and lay down, recollecting the gift.
He went. Having gone, he said, "Give me alms, brahmin; give me alms, brahmin. [The other replied], "Brahmin, you have come at an improper time;
I have already given to those who arrived as supplicants. Now there are no kahāpaṇas.
[The first replied], "Brahmin, I have no need for many kahāpaṇas; it is not possible for one giving such an amount of alms as you..."
"I must be without kahāpaṇas; give me five hundred kahāpaṇas. "Brāhmaṇa, even those five hundred are not here;
when the time for giving arrives, you shall receive them. "But shall I come to your time for giving?
[The Buddha] then made a sand stupa at the door of the brāhmaṇa Bāvari’s leaf-hut and scattered red-colored flowers all around it.
Spreading out his sacrificial grass as if muttering a mantra, he moved his lips repeatedly and said, "May his head split into seven pieces!
Bāvarī the Brahmin thought: "This Mahātapo has been practicing asceticism for seven days and now says to me, 'May his head split into seven pieces! But what must be given to him by me?"
"I have no five hundred kahāpaṇas; he will certainly have me executed.
While he lay there thus pierced by the arrow of grief, immediately after the first watch of the night had passed, Bāvari’s mother was reborn as a deity in his very next existence.
Seeing that her son was pierced by the arrow of grief, she came and said: "Dear son, this man [will perform] either the head-reading or the splitting of the head..."
“Or perhaps he does not know; you too do not know whether Buddhas have appeared in the world.
If you have any doubt, go to the presence of the Teacher and ask him; he will explain this matter to you.
From the moment the brahmin heard the deity’s words, he found comfort. When dawn rose on the following day, he [instructed] all his disciples...
Having summoned them, he said: "Sons, it is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world.
Go quickly, and having ascertained whether he is truly a Buddha or not, return and inform me; I shall go into the presence of the Teacher.
However, because of my advanced age, a threat to my life is difficult to foresee; therefore, you must go into his presence and [inquire] with such and such questions."
"Ask your question according to the proper method. Having thus formulated what is known as the "Question of the Splitting of the Head," he presented it.

Then he thought: "All these young men are wise; having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, they might reach the culmination of their own purpose and either return to my presence or not. Then, [he spoke] to his own nephew...
He gave the young man Ajita the instruction: “You must certainly come into my presence;

having acquired whatever qualities there, you should report them to me. Then those sixteen thousand matted-hair ascetics, with the young man Ajita as their leader, together with sixteen senior disciples, set out, thinking, “We shall ask the Teacher a question.”
While traveling on their journey, wherever they went, when asked, "Venerable sirs, where are you going? Where are you going?
they replied, "We are going into the presence of the One of Ten Powers to ask him a question. Gathering a great assembly from Koṭi onwards, they traveled along a road of many hundreds of yojanas.
The Teacher thought, "On the day of their arrival, there will be no opportunity for anyone else."
Thinking, "This place is suitable for this assembly," he went and sat down on a stone slab at the Pāsāṇacetiya.
Ajita the young brahmin, together with his followers, climbed onto that stone slab;
having beheld the excellence of the Teacher’s physical form, he thought, "This man shall become a Buddha in this world, one whose veil is rent. Then, regarding the questions sent by his own teacher:
He departed as if asking with his mind.
On that day, the assembly gathered at that place extended for twelve yojanas.
Among those sixteen pupils, the young brahmin Mogharāja was stiff with pride, thinking, "I am the most wise of all," and this thought occurred to him:
“This young man Ajita is the eldest of all; it is not fitting for him to ask me my question first. Feeling ashamed, he did not ask his question first.
When the other had asked his, he became the second and asked the Teacher a question. The Teacher said, “Mogharāja, the young man, is stiff with pride; his knowledge has not yet matured.”
Thinking, "He is reaching maturity; it is fitting to restrain his pride," he said, "Stay where you are, Mogharāja;
let others ask their questions first. Having received this slight from the Teacher, he thought:
"For so long I have wandered about thinking there was no one wiser than myself, yet these Buddhas do not speak without knowing."
They did not speak. Thinking, "The Teacher must have seen fault in my question," he remained silent.
When the eight men had asked their questions in succession and were unable to endure it further, he rose again as the ninth.
Once more, the Teacher rebuked him.
Again, remaining silent, he thought, "Now I shall no longer be able to remain the youngest member of the Saṅgha," and so, becoming the fifteenth, he asked a question.
Then the Teacher, knowing the maturity of his wisdom, explained the answer.
At the conclusion of the teaching, he attained Arahatship together with his retinue of one thousand matted-hair ascetics. In this very same manner, the others [also attained it].
Fifteen thousand matted-hair ascetics attained arahantship.
All of them were as if "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordinations, wearing robes and bowls produced by supernormal power (iddhimaya). However, the remaining people are not mentioned.
From that time on, this Elder Mogharāja wore a robe endowed with three kinds of coarseness. Thus the story originated in the Pārāyana. The Teacher—
Later, however, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, as he was establishing the elder monks in their respective ranks,
he placed the Elder Mogharāja in the position of being foremost among those who wear coarse robes in this Dispensation,
saying: "This is the foremost, O bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who wear coarse robes, namely Mogharāja."
Commentary on the Fourth Chapter.
The commentary on the Elder’s Collection (*Therapāḷi*), consisting of approximately forty-one suttas, is finished.
14. The Chapter on the Foremost (*Etadaggavagga*).
(14) 5. The Fifth Chapter on the Foremost:
The Account of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. 235.
In the first [section] of the Therīgāthā, namely "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī," it is shown that the elder nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is foremost among those of long-standing seniority.
Regarding her performance of the question, this is the sequential narrative: It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.

On another occasion, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of foremost among those long-ordained. Having performed an act of service, she [aspired to] that very station.
She made this aspiration. Having given alms and guarded her virtue for as long as she lived, when she passed away from there, she was reborn in the world of the gods.
Then, after one interval between Buddhas, having descended from the world of the gods, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the senior slave among five hundred female slaves.
Then, at the time of the commencement of the rains retreat, five Paccekabuddhas [emerged] from the Nandamūlaka mountain slope.

Having descended at Isipatana and wandered for alms in the city, they returned to Isipatana itself and thought, "We shall request manual labor for the sake of a hut for the commencement of the rains retreat. Why?
Because one who enters the rains retreat—even if practicing the Nālaka method—must dwell in a lodging provided with one of the five types of roofing and equipped with a closed door.
One must enter the rains residence. For this has been said: "Monks, one who does not have a lodging should not enter the rains residence;
whoever should do so incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Therefore, when the time for the rains has arrived, if one obtains a lodging, that is well.
If one does not obtain one, one should build it even by seeking manual labor. By one who cannot find manual labor, it should be built by oneself.
This must be done; however, one who does not possess a dwelling should not enter the rains residence. This is the natural order of things (*anudhammatā*).
Therefore, those *paccekabuddhas*, thinking, "We shall ask for manual labor," put on their robes and entered the city in the evening, standing at the gate of the merchant’s house.
The eldest female slave, taking a water-pot, was going to the watering-place when she [saw] the *paccekabuddhas*...
He saw them entering the city. When the merchant heard the reason for their arrival, he said, "We have no room; you may go.
Then, as they were departing from the city, the eldest female slave saw them entering while carrying a water-jar.
She set down the jar, paid homage, bowed low, and looking up, said, "Noble sirs, you have already left the city as soon as you entered; why [are you back]?"
“Is it so? he asked. “We have come to request manual labor for the hut for entering the rains retreat,” they replied.
“Was it obtained, venerable sir? “It was not obtained, lay follower. “But must this hut be built only by the wealthy, or can it also be built by the poor?
“It can be built by anyone. “Very well, venerable sir, we shall build it; tomorrow, give me alms.”
Having invited them with the words, "Take [some]," she took a water-jar again and stood on the path at the ford where they were coming from.
As each of the remaining slave-girls arrived, she said to them, "Stop right here. When they had all arrived, she said:
"Women, will you always perform the work of another's slave, or do you wish to be released from the state of slavery? "We wish to be released this very day, noble lady."
"If that is so," she said, "I have invited the Paccekabuddhas for tomorrow's meal because they received no manual labor from me;
please ensure they receive manual labor for one day from your husbands. They agreed, saying, "Very well," and when their husbands returned from the forest in the evening, they informed them.
The husbands said, "Very well," and gathered at the door of the eldest slave's house.
Then the eldest female slave explained the benefits, saying, "Sons, tomorrow provide manual service for the Paccekabuddhas.
She then exhorted those who were unwilling with firm admonitions and caused them all to agree.
On the following day, after she had given food to the Paccekabuddhas, she gave instructions to all the sons of the slaves.
They entered the forest immediately, gathered the necessary materials, and in groups of one hundred each, they constructed individual huts equipped with walking-paths and other amenities.

Having provided beds, stools, drinking water, and washing water, they obtained the promise of the Paccekabuddhas to reside right there for the three-month rains retreat, and established a system of taking turns to provide alms. As for their own...
On the day of the fast, she was unable to provide it herself; therefore, her eldest female slave would bring it from her own home and give it to her.
Having thus cared for them for three months, the eldest female slave had each of the other slaves prepare a garment; there were five hundred thick garments in total.
She exchanged these and, having made them into the three robes (*tricīvara*) for the five *paccekabuddhas*, she gave them to them. The *paccekabuddhas*...
While they were still looking on, they traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana.
Having performed wholesome deeds throughout their lives, they all were reborn in the world of the devas.
Of those women, the eldest passed away from there and was reborn in the house of the chief weaver in a weavers' village not far from Bārāṇasī. Then, one day—
The five hundred *paccekabuddhas*, sons of Padumavatī, having been invited by the King of Bārāṇasī, arrived at the royal gate;
but seeing no one even looking toward them, they turned back, departed through the city gate, and went to that weaver’s village.
When that woman saw the *paccekabuddhas*, she felt great affection for them, paid homage to them all, and gave them almsfood. They finished their meal...
Having done so, they went to Gandhamādana.

She too, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as she lived, while wandering through the realms of gods and humans, took rebirth even before our Teacher was born, in the house of Mahāsuppabuddha in the city of Devadaha; they gave her the name Gotamī.
Mahāmāyā had a younger sister. When the brahmins who were masters of mantras examined their physical marks, they prophesied:
"The children dwelling in the wombs of these two women shall both become universal monarchs (cakkavatti).
When they reached marriageable age, King Suddhodana performed auspicious ceremonies for both and brought them to his own home. Later on—
Our Bodhisatta, having descended from the Tusita heaven, took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.
On the seventh day after his birth, Mahāmāyā passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven.
King Suddhodana then established Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the Bodhisatta’s maternal aunt, in the position of chief queen. At that time...
Prince Nanda was born. Having entrusted Prince Nanda to the nurses, Mahāpajāpatī herself attended to the Bodhisatta.

At another time, after the Bodhisatta had gone forth on the Great Renunciation and attained omniscience, he performed a benefit for the world and, arriving in due course at Kapilavatthu, entered the city for alms. Then his father, King Suddhodana—
Having heard a discourse on the Dhamma right there in the street, he became a stream-enterer. Then, on the second day, Nanda went forth, and on the seventh day, Rāhula.
At a later time, the Teacher was dwelling in the Gabled Hall near Vesālī.
At that time, King Suddhodana, while beneath the white parasol, realized Arhatship.
He attained final Nibbāna. At that time, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī conceived the desire for the going forth.
Then, on the banks of the Rohiṇī River, at the conclusion of the *Kalahavivāda Sutta*, all five hundred young women who had been her personal attendants, being of one mind, said:
"Let us go to Mahāpajāpatī and all together go forth in the presence of the Teacher."
With Mahāpajāpatī as their leader, they went into the presence of the Teacher and desired to go forth. However,
since Mahāpajāpatī had previously requested ordination from the Teacher on one occasion and had not received it,
she summoned a barber, had her hair cut, donned the saffron robes, and taking all those Sakyan women with her, departed for Vesālī.
Having gone there, the Elder Ānanda requested the One of Ten Powers on her behalf, and she received both the going-forth and full ordination by means of the eight weighty rules (*garudhamma*).
All the others, however, were ordained together as one. This is the summary here; the detailed account of this matter has indeed come down in the Pāḷi.
Having been thus ordained, Mahāpajāpatī approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side;
then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma. Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, she attained arahantship.
The remaining five hundred bhikkhunīs attained arahantship at the conclusion of the Nandakovāda Sutta.

Thus this matter arose. Later on, while the Teacher was seated in Jeta’s Grove, he established the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks and placed Mahāpajāpatī in the foremost position among those long-standing in the faith.
This is the story of the Elder Nun Khemā.

236. In the second case, "Khemā" is the name of the bhikkhunī. From this point forward, in her formal inquiry (pañhakamma), we shall not state "this is the sequential narrative," but shall speak only of what must be said, beginning with the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra).
It is said that in the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in Haṃsavatī as one belonging to another family.
Then, one day, having seen the Blessed One’s chief female disciple, the elder nun named Sujātā, wandering for alms, [she made her aspiration].
Having given three sweetmeats and on that very day having offered her own hair as a gift to the Elder Nun, she made a resolution, saying:

"In a future arising of a Buddha, may I possess great wisdom like yours. Remaining diligent in wholesome deeds for the rest of her life, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, and during the time of Kassapa Buddha, [she was born] in the household of King Kiki.
Having taken rebirth in the house of the King of Kāsi and become one of seven sisters, she lived the celibate life of a maiden within the household for twenty thousand years.
Together with those sisters, she had a residence built for the One of Ten Powers;
then, wandering among gods and humans for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, she was born in this present dispensation of the Buddha in the kingdom of Madda.
She took rebirth in the royal palace in the city of Sāgala, and they gave her the name Khemā.
Her complexion was like that of molten gold. When she reached maturity, she went to the household of King Bimbisāra.
While the Tathāgata was dwelling at Veḷuvana near Rājagaha, she heard: "The Teacher, it is said, demonstrates the defects in material form."
Intoxicated by the pride of her beauty, she did not go to see the One of Ten Powers out of fear that he might point out the defects in her form, thinking, “He might show me my faults.

The King thought: “I am the foremost attendant of the Teacher, yet the chief consort of a noble disciple such as myself does not go to see the One of Ten Powers; this does not please me. He then had the Veḷuvana Monastery decorated by poets...
Having had the park decorated, he said, "Sing in the vicinity of Queen Khemā's hearing.
Having heard the description of the park, she desired to go and questioned the king. The king said, "Go to the park, but you shall not return until you have seen the Teacher.
Without giving the king a reply, she set out on the road. The king—
He said to the men who were going with her: "If the Queen, while returning from the park, sees the One of Ten Powers, that is well.

But if she does not see him, you must show him to her by royal command. Then the Queen, having wandered in the park for part of the day, began to return without having seen the One of Ten Powers. Thereupon, the king’s men—
Against her own will, they led the queen into the presence of the Teacher.
When the Teacher saw her approaching, he used his supernormal power to create a celestial nymph (*devaccharā*), who appeared as if she were holding a palm-leaf fan and fanning him.
Seeing this, Queen Khemā thought: "I have lost my pride; indeed, such [beauty] as this..."
"Women resembling celestial nymphs stand not far from the One of Ten Powers;
I am not even fit to be their attendant, for having fallen under the sway of an evil mind due to pride and intoxication, I have been lost.
Having grasped that sign, she stood there gazing at that very woman. Then, while she was still looking on, by the power of the Tathāgata’s resolve—
That woman, having passed her first stage of life, appeared as if she were standing in middle age;
and having passed middle age, she appeared as if she were standing in her final stage of life—her skin became wrinkled, her hair turned grey, and her teeth became broken and sparse.
Then, even as she was looking on, [the fan] turned over together with its palm-leaf handle and fell down. Thereupon, because of her perfection of past causes, Khemā—toward that...
As soon as that object entered her field of perception, she thought: "Even such a body as this meets with such a calamity;
my own body, too, will surely meet with the same end. At the very moment she had thought this, the Teacher spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:
“Those who are stained by passion follow the stream,
like a spider following the web it has spun itself;
having cut even this asunder, the wise go forth.”
"Having abandoned all suffering, they are free from longing.
At the conclusion of this verse, while she remained standing on that very spot, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
It is said that one who has attained Arahantship while living in the midst of a household must either attain final Nibbāna on that very day or go forth into the homeless life.
She was there; however, having realized that her own life-forces (*āyu-saṅkhāra*) were still active, she thought, "I shall ask for permission to go forth.
She paid homage to the Teacher and went to the royal palace, where she stood without even saluting the king. The king understood by her gesture alone:
"She must have attained the Noble Dhamma. Then he said to her, "Queen, have you gone to see the Teacher?"
“Great King, your vision is limited; however, I have clearly beheld the One Possessing the Ten Powers. Grant me permission to go forth.
The king, accepting her request by saying, “Very well, lady,” had her carried to the nunnery in a golden palanquin and ordained her.
Then it was said of her: “The Elder Khemā attained Arahantship while remaining in the state of a householder.”

Her state of great wisdom became manifest. This is the background story here. Later, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher, as he was appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective ranks, placed the Elder Khemā in the foremost position among those of great wisdom.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Uppalavaṇṇā.
237. Regarding the third, the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā: she received this name because her complexion was exactly like the interior of a blue lotus (*nīluppala*).
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
Later, having gone into the presence of the Teacher along with a great multitude to hear the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher [bestowing a boon] upon a certain bhikkhunī.

Seeing him being placed in the foremost position among those possessing supernormal powers (*iddhimant*), she gave a great alms-offering for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and aspired to that very status.
Having performed wholesome deeds throughout her life, she passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans until,
during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took rebirth in the home of King Kiki of Kāsi in the city of Bārāṇasī.
Having lived as one of seven sisters and practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years,
she built a dwelling for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and was reborn in the world of the devas.
Passing away from there, as she returned once more to the human world, she was in a certain village in a position of livelihood where she had to work with her own hands.
She was reborn there. One day, while going to the field-hut, she saw a lotus flower that had bloomed at dawn in a certain lake along the way.

She entered the lake, took that very flower and a lotus leaf for the purpose of putting rice into it, and having cut off heads of rice in the field, sat down in the hut and parched the grains. Then, [she prepared] five...

She was counting the handfuls of parched grain. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha who had emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana arrived and stood not far from her.
Seeing the Paccekabuddha, she took a lotus flower along with the parched grain, descended from the hut, placed the parched grain into the Paccekabuddha’s bowl, and [offered it] with the lotus flower.
She covered her bowl and gave it to him. Then, after the Paccekabuddha had gone a short distance, this thought occurred to her:
"Those who have gone forth are indeed without need for flowers; I shall take these flowers and wear them.
Having approached and taken the flowers from the Paccekabuddha’s hand, she thought again: "If the noble one had been without need of flowers..."

Thinking, "He did not allow me to place it on the head of his bowl; surely there must be some purpose for the noble one," she went back again, placed it on the head of the bowl, and having asked the Paccekabuddha for forgiveness, she said:
"Venerable sir, by the merit of these fried grains, may I have sons equal in number to the grains;
and by the merit of this lotus flower, may a lotus flower spring up at every step in each place where I am reborn."
"May you arise! she made this aspiration. Even as she watched, the Paccekabuddha traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana;
there, he placed that lotus near the foot-wiping cloth at the base of the staircase used by the Paccekabuddhas for ascending the Nandamūlaka cave.
By the result of that deed, she took rebirth in the world of the gods, and from the moment of her conception...
At every step, a great lotus flower rose up for her. Having passed away from there, she was reborn within the calyx of a lotus in a certain lotus pond at the foot of a mountain.
A certain ascetic lived depending on that place;
he would go to the lake early in the morning to rinse his mouth, and seeing that flower, he thought: "This flower is larger than the others; as for the rest..."
"Yet these others have blossomed; this one must be merely a bud, so there must be a reason for it. Having descended into the water, he took that flower.
As soon as it was taken by him, it blossomed. The ascetic saw the maiden lying within the interior of the lotus.
From the moment he saw her, he felt a motherly affection for his daughter and, together with the lotus, carried her to the leaf-hut.
Having led her there, he had her lie down upon a couch. Then, by the power of her merit, milk flowed from her thumb.
When that flower withered, he brought another fresh flower and had her lie down upon it.
From the time she became capable of running about and playing, a lotus flower would arise at every step she took, like a heap of saffron powder.
Her bodily complexion became radiant; she had not yet attained the splendor of a goddess, but she had transcended the appearance of a human being.
While her father had gone out for the sake of gathering fruits, she remained behind in the leaf-hut.
Then one day, when she had reached the age of maturity and her father had gone out for the sake of gathering fruits, a forest-dweller [approached] her.
Seeing him, she thought, "Human beings do not possess such a form; I shall test him.
She sat waiting for the ascetic's arrival. When her father approached, she went out to meet him and took the goatskin water-pot from his hand.
Once he had returned and sat down, she performed the duties of hospitality for him. At that time—
The forest-dweller, recognizing him as a human being, paid homage to the ascetic and sat down.
The ascetic invited the forest-dweller to partake of forest roots, fruits, and water, and asked him, "O man, will you dwell in this very place, or will you depart?
"I shall depart, venerable sir; what would I do staying here? [The ascetic replied: "This is the reason you have seen."
“Having gone from here, will you be able to tell [him]? “If the noble one does not wish it, for what reason would I tell him?
Having paid homage to the ascetic, he departed, making marks on branches and marks on trees so that he might recognize the path upon his return.
He went to Bārāṇasī and saw the king. The king asked, “Why have you come? “I have come, Your Majesty, to inform you—”
"I have come from the foot of the mountain after seeing a wondrous woman-jewel," the forest-dweller said,
recounting the entire account. Having heard his words, he went swiftly to the foot of the mountain, established his camp in a nearby location,
and together with the forest-dweller and other men, performed the meal-offering for the ascetic.
Having gone there at the time he was seated, he paid homage, exchanged friendly greetings, and sat down to one side.
The king placed the ascetic’s requisites at the feet of the ascetic and said, "Venerable sir, what shall we do in this place?
Let us go. "Go, Great King," he replied. "Yes, I am going, venerable sir; but as for the noble one—"
“We have heard that there is a group of dissimilar companions nearby; this is unsuitable for those who have gone forth.
Let her come with us, venerable sir. “The minds of humans are indeed difficult to satisfy; how will she live in the midst of so many?
“From the moment it pleases us, venerable sir, I shall establish her in the position of seniority over the rest and look after her.”
Having heard the king’s words, he called his daughter by the name she had been given in her childhood:
“Amma Padumavatī! At that single word, she emerged from the leaf-hut, paid homage to her father, and stood before him.
Then her father said to her: “Amma, you have reached marriageable age; ever since the time you were seen here by the king—”
"It is not fitting for you to live here; go with the king, mother. She replied, "Very well, father," and having accepted her father's words, she stood there bowing and weeping.

The king, thinking, "I shall win her father's heart," placed her right there upon a heap of kahāpaṇa coins and performed the consecration ceremony. Then, taking her with him, he brought her to his own city.
From the moment she arrived, he would not look at the other women but took his pleasure with her alone.
Those women, overcome by jealousy and wishing to create a rift between her and the king, said this: "Great King, she is not of human birth.
Where indeed have you ever seen lotuses springing up in places frequented by humans? Surely..."
“This is a female spirit; drive her out, Great King! When the king heard their words, he remained silent.
Later, however, his border region rose in rebellion. Thinking, “Padumavatī is heavily pregnant,” he left her in the city and departed for the border.
Then those women, having given a bribe to her nurse, [said]: “To this woman...”
They said, “Take away the newborn boy immediately, smear a piece of wood with blood, and place it near her.

Not long after, Padumavatī’s delivery occurred; Prince Mahāpaduma alone had taken rebirth in her womb, while the remaining four hundred and ninety-nine children [were born from the other queens]. From the mother’s womb of Prince Mahāpaduma...
When he had gone out and was lying down, they were reborn as moisture-born beings.
Then, knowing that "he has not yet regained consciousness," his attendants smeared a wooden stick with blood, placed it near him, and gave a signal to those women.
Those five hundred women each took a child and [gave them] to the woodworkers.
Having sent for a chest and had it brought, they each laid the infants they had taken there inside,
sealed the exterior, and set it aside. Padumavatī,
having regained consciousness, asked her attendant, "What have I given birth to, mother?"
Having intimidated her, she said, "Where will you get a child? and placed before her a piece of wood smeared with blood, saying, "This is the child who emerged from your womb.
Upon seeing it, she became distressed and said, "Quickly split this apart and remove it;
if anyone should see it, it would be a cause for shame. She [the other woman] heard her words...
Having heard this, as if desiring his welfare, they split the wooden block and threw it onto the hearth.
The king, having arrived from the borderlands and established his camp outside the city while awaiting the auspicious conjunction of the stars, sat there.
Then those five hundred women came out to meet the king and said: "O Great King, you..."
"You do not believe us; what we have said seems groundless to you.
Summon the queen’s attendant and question her; the queen has given birth to a wooden doll.
Without investigating the matter, the king concluded, "She must be of non-human origin," and expelled her from his house. At the very moment she departed from the royal palace...
The lotus flowers vanished, and the complexion of her body became discolored. She set out alone along the middle of the street.
Then, an elderly woman of mature years saw her and, feeling a motherly affection for her like that for a daughter, said, "Where are you going, dear?
"I am a newcomer; I am wandering about looking for a place to stay. "Come here," she replied.
Saying, "Mother," she gave her a place to live and prepared food for her.
As she was living there according to this very routine, those five hundred women became of one mind and said to the king:
"Great King, when you have gone to war, we [have made an agreement] with the goddess of the Ganges: 'If our lord returns victorious from battle...'"
“Once he has arrived, we shall perform the offering ceremony and then enjoy a water-sport”; this was their wish, and “O King, let us inform you of this matter.
Delighted by their words, the king went to the Ganges to engage in the water-sport.
They too, having each concealed the casket they had taken, took it with them, went to the river, and [placed] those caskets...
Having put on [the garments] for the purpose of concealment, they repeatedly threw them into the water and released them into baskets.
All those baskets went along together and became snagged in a net spread out in the lower current.
Then, after the king had finished playing in the water, as they were hauling up the net at the time of his departure, they saw those baskets and brought them into the presence of the king.
Seeing the caskets, the king asked, "What is this, dear ones, in these caskets? "We do not know, Your Majesty," they replied.
He had the caskets opened for him to look at; first, he had the casket of Prince Mahāpaduma opened.
On the very day they had been placed within those caskets, milk had issued from their thumbs through the power of their merit.
Sakka, the king of the gods, in order to remove the king’s doubts, had letters inscribed inside the casket:
“These princes were born from the womb of Padumavatī as the sons of the King of Bārāṇasī;
then her five hundred co-wives placed them in caskets and cast them into the water. The king [learnt] this matter.”
"Let him know! As soon as the basket was opened, the king read the letters and, seeing the boy, lifted up Prince Mahāpaduma and said, "Yoke the chariot with speed and prepare the horses;
today, having entered the city, I shall do what is pleasing to certain women. Having ascended the palace, he placed a bundle of a thousand coins upon the neck of an elephant.
Setting aside the drum, he had it proclaimed: "Whoever sees Padumavatī, let that person take this thousand [pieces of gold].
Hearing that announcement, Padumavatī gave a signal to her mother: "Mother, take the thousand from the neck of the elephant.
"I do not dare to take such a thing," she replied. When this was said a second and a third time, [the mother asked: "What shall I say so that I may take it?"
“Mother,” she said. “My daughter sees Queen Padumavatī,” he replied, and added, “Take her.
She thought, “Let it be this or that,” and having gone there, she took a thousand-fold cloak. Then people asked her, “Mother, do you see Queen Padumavatī?
She said, “I do not see her; my daughter, they say, sees her. They asked, “Where is she?”
Saying, "But she is here, mother," they went with her; recognizing Padumavatī, they fell at her feet.

At that time, knowing, "This is Queen Padumavatī," she said, "Alas, what a grievous deed has been committed by this woman, who, being the chief queen of such a king, dwells in such a place without protection! Those royal guards also—
Having had Padumavatī’s residence surrounded with white curtains and having stationed guards at the doors, they informed the king.
The king sent a golden palanquin. She said, "I will not go in this manner;
from my own dwelling place all the way to the royal palace, let fine cloth and painted rugs be spread along the path, and above that, [let it be covered] with a canopy variegated with golden stars."
"Having had a canopy spread for my carriage and having had all the ornaments provided for my adornment, I shall go on foot;
in this way, the citizens will behold my splendor," she said. The king replied, "Do as Padumavatī wishes.
Thereupon, Padumavatī, having adorned herself with every ornament, set out on the road, thinking, "I shall go to the royal palace."
Then, at every place she stepped upon, the fine cloth and painted rugs were torn asunder and lotus flowers sprang up.
Having displayed her own prosperity to the great multitude, she ascended the royal palace and caused all the painted rugs to be given away,
making them the means of sustenance for that old woman.
The king also summoned those five hundred women and said, "I give these to you, O Queen, as your slave-girls.
"Very well, Great King; let it be made known throughout the entire city that these have been given to me," she replied. The king had a drum beaten through the city, proclaiming:
"These five hundred women who deceived Padumavatī are being given to her as her very own slave-girls."

“[They] have been given,” he said. She, realizing that her slave-status had been recognized by the entire city, asked the king, “Your Majesty, may I be permitted to make my own female slaves free? “It is your wish, Queen,” [the king replied].
This being so, she summoned those very five hundred women who had been given to her as her own slaves by Queen Padumavatī through the sounding of the drum.
"All have been made free; strike the drum again," he said.
Once their status as free persons was established, she gave those six hundred and ninety-nine sons into the hands of those very women to raise, while she herself took Prince Mahāpaduma alone.
Later, when those princes reached the age for play, the king [prepared] various places for recreation in the pleasure garden.

They had it made. When they were all sixteen years of age, while playing together in the park at a lucky lotus pond covered with lotuses, they saw that new lotuses had blossomed and old lotuses were falling from their stalks.
Seeing this, they thought: "If such decay as this comes even to these things that are not subject to grasping, how much more so for our own bodies?"

"Even this will have such a destiny," he thought; taking this as his object of meditation, they all developed the knowledge of *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) and, rising up repeatedly, sat cross-legged upon the hearts of lotus flowers.
Then, the king’s men who had come with them, realizing that much of the day had passed, said, "Noble sons, your time has come."
"Do you know? they asked. They remained silent. Those men went and reported to the king:
"Your Majesty, the princes are sitting upon lotus calyxes; even when we speak, they do not utter a word. "Let them sit as they please," [the king replied].
Thus, having been placed under guard all night long, they sat in the very manner of those on lotus calyxes.
They woke Aruṇa. On the following day, men approached him and said, “Your Majesty, please know the time.
“We are not kings,” he replied, “we are called Paccekabuddhas. “Noble sirs, you speak heavy words;
those called Paccekabuddhas are not like you, who wear hair and beard two finger-breadths long and carry eight requisites fastened upon your bodies.”
"So be it," they said. They touched their heads with their right hands;

at that very moment, the marks of householders vanished, and the eight requisites appeared already fastened upon their bodies. Then, even as the great multitude looked on, they departed through the air for the Nandamūlaka cave.
Queen Padumavatī, too, having fallen into heart-rending grief at the thought, "Having been one with many sons,
I have become childless," passed away from that very sorrow and was reborn in a village near the gate of the city of Rājagaha in a place where she lived by performing manual labor with her own hands.
Later, having gone to her family home, one day, while carrying rice-gruel to her husband's field—
Seeing eight paccekabuddhas traveling through the air at the time for the alms-round among their own sons, he went very quickly and informed his master: "Look, sir, these are paccekabuddhas;
let us invite them and feed them. He replied: "These are merely 'ascetic-birds' who wander about in this way elsewhere as well; they are not paccekabuddhas."
While they were still speaking, they descended to a place not far away.
That woman, having given them her own meal of rice and hard food on that day, said, "May eight people also take alms from me tomorrow. "Very well, laywoman;
let your hospitality be just this much, and let there be only eight seats," [they replied], having seen many other Paccekabuddhas as well.
“May you gladden your heart. On the following day, she prepared eight seats and arranged offerings of honor for the eight [Paccekabuddhas] and sat down.
The Paccekabuddhas who had been invited gave notice to the others: “Venerable sirs, do not go elsewhere today;
let all of you together receive the hospitality of your mother. Having heard their words, they all came through the air together.
They appeared at the door of her mother’s house. She, having first regained her composure, was not shaken even upon seeing many of them;

she ushered them all into the house and had them sit upon seats. As they were taking their seats one after another, the ninth man prepared eight other seats and sat himself upon the foremost seat. As long as the seats continued to multiply, so it went on.

The household flourished. While all of them were thus seated, that woman gave the hospitality she had prepared for the eight *paccekabuddhas* to the five hundred as well, providing as much as they required.
Then, bringing eight handfuls of blue lotuses, she placed them at the feet of the very *paccekabuddhas* she had invited and said: "Venerable sirs, in whatever place I am reborn..."
“May the complexion of my body be like the color of the interior of these blue lotuses,” she made this aspiration.
After the Paccekabuddhas had offered their blessing to her mother, they departed for Gandhamādana itself.
She too, having performed wholesome deeds throughout her life, passed away from there and was reborn in the deva world; then, during the arising of this Buddha, she was born in Sāvatthī.
She took rebirth in a merchant’s family, and because her complexion was like the interior of a blue lotus, they gave her the name Uppalavaṇṇā.

When she reached maturity, all the kings and merchants of the entire Jambudīpa sent messengers to the merchant, saying, "Give us your daughter. There was no one who did not send such a message. Then the merchant—
He thought, “I will not be able to win over the minds of everyone; however, I shall employ a certain stratagem.
Having summoned his daughter, he said, “My dear child, will you be able to go forth into the religious life?
Because she was in her final existence, her father’s words were like a hundred-fold refined oil poured upon her head; therefore, she said to her father, “Father, I will go forth.”
He said: Having paid her honor, he led her to the nunnery and ordained her. Not long after she had been ordained, it was her turn to take charge of the Uposatha hall.
She lit a lamp, swept the Uposatha hall, and having taken a sign from the flame of the lamp, she gazed at it again and again;
thus, having produced jhāna with the fire-kasiṇa as its object, she [attained that very state].

Having made this her foundation, she attained arahantship. Simultaneously with the attainment of the fruit of arahantship, she became one who had mastered the exercise of supernormal powers (*iddhi-vikubbana*).
Later, on the day the Teacher performed the Twin Miracle, she let out a lion’s roar, saying, "Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle.
Taking this as the occasion for a discourse, the Teacher [spoke] at the Jetavana Monastery.
Seated there, as he was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective ranks, he placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those possessing supernormal powers.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā (238).
Regarding the fourth [category], "among those who uphold the Vinaya, namely Paṭācārā": the Elder Nun Paṭācārā is the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
[The Buddha] shows this. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
Later, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Having performed a meritorious deed, she aspired to that very position. She [remained so] for as long as her life lasted...
Having performed wholesome deeds, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans; then, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took rebirth in the household of King Kikī of Kāsī.
There, as one of seven sisters, she practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years and constructed a monastery cell for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Subsequently, having been reborn in the world of the gods, she remained there for the duration of one interval between Buddhas.
Having experienced prosperity, she took rebirth in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the house of a wealthy merchant in Sāvatthī.
Later, when she had reached maturity, she formed an intimate relationship with a certain laborer in her own home.
Subsequently, as she was about to go to a family of equal status, she gave notice to the man with whom she had been intimate, saying: "No..."
"From this day forward, you shall not be permitted to see me even by a hundred intermediaries;

if you have business, take me now and go. He replied, "So be it," and taking suitable valuables for his journey, he took him and retreated from the city three or four *yojanas* away, settling there in a village.
Then, later on, a fetus took root in her womb. When the fetus was fully developed, she said, "This is a time of need for us;
let us go to our family home, my lord. He replied, "Let us go today," or "Let us go tomorrow," and being unable to go, he let the time pass.
She, having understood his reason, thought, "This fool will not take me away."
When he had gone outside, she set out on the path, thinking, "I shall go alone to my family home.

He returned and, not seeing her at home, questioned his neighbors; hearing that she had gone to her family home, he thought, "Because of me, this daughter of good family has become destitute," and following her footprints, he arrived there. On the very way, she went into labor.
Then they thought, "The very purpose for which we were going has been accomplished even on the way;
what shall we do now by going further? and they turned back. Again, a fetus was conceived in her womb;
this should be detailed in the same manner as before.
But on the way, as soon as she gave birth, a great cloud arose in the four directions.
She said to that man, "Husband, a cloud has arisen in the four directions at an improper time; let us strive to make a dwelling place for ourselves.
He replied, "I shall do so," and having built a small hut with sticks, he [prepared] grass for the roof.
Thinking, “I will fetch it,” she cut some grass at the foot of a large anthill. Then a black snake lying within the anthill bit her on the foot;

she fell down right there. She spent the entire night thinking, “He will be back now, he will be back now,” until she finally thought, “Surely he has gone, leaving me behind on the road because he thought, ‘She is helpless.’”
When light appeared, she looked along the path of his footprints; seeing that he had fallen at the base of an anthill, she lamented, "The man has perished because of me!
Then, taking the young boy on her hip and making the elder one grasp her fingers, she proceeded along the road.
On the way, seeing a shallow river, she thought, "I must carry both children across at once."

"I shall not be able [to carry them both]," she thought. So, having left the elder child on this side of the bank, she took the younger one to the other side, laid him down upon a pillow made of rags, and returned.
Thinking, "I will take the other one and go," she descended into the river.
When she reached the middle of the river, a hawk, perceiving the child to be a "lump of meat," swooped down to strike him.
She approached. Stretching out her hand, she startled the bird away.
Seeing that movement of her hand, the young boy, thinking "she is calling me," descended into the river and fell into the current, being carried away with it.
Even before she had reached him, the bird seized the young boy and flew off. Overcome by intense grief, she [followed] along the way.
Singing this song of lamentation, she went along, saying:
"Both sons are dead; my husband is dead on the road.
Lamenting in this way, she reached Sāvatthī, and although she went to the family circle, she entered her own home solely under the influence of grief.
Unable to determine [the location], she asked back, "In this place there is such-and-such a family; which house is it?
"What will you do by asking about that family? Their dwelling house collapsed from the force of the wind, and they all met their end right there.
Now, both the small and the great are on a single funeral pyre."
“They are setting it on fire; look, this column of smoke is appearing! Upon hearing these words, she was unable to hold back the lower garment she was wearing.
As if her very life had been extinguished, she threw up her arms and wept.
Having gone to the place where her kinsmen’s funeral pyre stood, she completed that song of lamentation and, wailing, cried out:

“Both my sons have died; my husband has perished on the road; my mother, father, and brother—all are being burned upon a single funeral pyre,” she said. Even when given a garment by another person, she tore it apart again and again and threw it away. Then, wherever she was seen— [The text continues: ...in whatever place she was seen... [she would tear it up and discard it]. Finally, she was caught in that very spot. She was seized and brought before the king. When questioned, she spoke thus: “O King, I am not a thief; I am a madwoman. I do not know what I say. My mind is deranged; I am distraught. I am not a thief. When the king heard this, he had her released. He gave her abundant wealth and sent her away. Thus, through the power of her previous wholesome kamma, she was born into a wealthy family. Because she had torn up and discarded the garments given to her, she became a madwoman. Because she had spoken the truth, she was released from the king’s hands and attained great wealth. Thus, monks, the fruit of even a small deed done with a pure mind is great in this very life. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: “We shall perform even small deeds with a pure mind.
