She spoke thus. Even when given a garment by another person, she tore it apart again and again and threw it away.
A great crowd followed her about. Then, because they thought, "She moves about without wearing a cloth (paṭa)," they gave her the name Paṭācārā.
And because that shameless conduct of hers, due to her nakedness, became public knowledge, they gave her the name Paṭācārā, thinking, "Her conduct (ācāra) has fallen away (paṭita)."
One day, while the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma to a great multitude, she entered the monastery and stood at the edge of the assembly.
The Teacher, having suffused her with the pervasion of loving-kindness (*mettā*), said: "Regain your mindfulness, sister! Regain your mindfulness, sister!
Upon hearing the Teacher’s words, a powerful sense of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) arose within her, and right there—
She sat down on the ground. A man standing nearby threw her an upper garment and gave it to her.
Having put it on, she listened to the Dhamma. According to her disposition, the Teacher spoke these verses from the *Dhammapada*:
“Sons are no refuge, nor father, nor even kinsmen;”
For one seized by the End-maker, there is no protection among kinsmen.
"Knowing this fact, the wise person, restrained by virtue,
should quickly purify the path leading to Nibbāna."
At the conclusion of that verse, she established herself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*) right where she stood;

she then approached the Teacher, paid homage, and requested the going forth (*pabbajjā*). The Teacher consented to her going forth, saying, "Go to the nunnery (*bhikkhunūpassaya*) and receive the going forth.
Having gone forth, before long she attained *arahantship* and, while mastering the Buddha’s word, [studied] the Vinaya Piṭaka.

She attained mastery. Later on, while the Teacher was seated in Jeta’s Grove, he established the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks and placed Paṭācārā in the foremost position among those who uphold the Vinaya.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā.
239. Regarding the phrase "among the preachers of the Dhamma": this indicates that among the bhikkhunīs who preach the Dhamma, Dhammadinnā was foremost.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in Haṃsavatī in a position dependent on others;
having performed a work of merit for the Elder Sujāta, the chief disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara, she aspired to that very status.

Having performed wholesome deeds for as long as she lived, she was reborn in heaven. All of this should be understood through the power of the resolution (abhinīhāra) made by the Elder Nun Khemā, as described below.

However, during the time of the Buddha Phussa, while she was living in the house of a steward appointed to oversee the almsgiving for the Teacher’s three half-brothers, when told, “Give one,” she gave two. In this way, she never failed in anything.
Having given [this gift], after ninety-two aeons had passed, she took rebirth in the household of King Kiki of Kāsī during the time of Buddha Kassapa;
there, as one of seven sisters, she practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years,
constructed a dwelling-vihāra for the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus, and spent an entire interval between Buddhas among gods and humans.
Wandering through existence, she took rebirth in a noble family during this dispensation of a Buddha;
later, she entered the household of the merchant Visākha. This merchant Visākha was a friend of King Bimbisāra;

having gone with the king to his first audience with the One of Ten Powers and having heard the Dhamma, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and at a later time, he realized the fruit of non-returning.
So that day, having gone home, he ascended the palace without even placing his hand in the hand of Dhammadinnā as she stood at the top of the stairs with her hand extended.
Even while eating, he did not speak, saying, "Give this," or "Take that.
As Dhammadinnā took the serving ladle and served him, she thought: "This man does not take my hand..."
"Even when she was giving me food, she did not even touch my hand; even while eating, she said nothing at all. What fault could there possibly be on my part?
Then, after he had finished eating, he asked her, "Noble lady, what fault is there on my part? [She replied: "Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you.
However, from today onward, because of our intimacy, I shall no longer sit or stand near you, nor shall I have food brought for you."
He is incapable of eating or consuming it. "If you wish, stay in this house;
if you do not wish, take whatever wealth you require and go to your own family home.
"Noble sir, that being the case, I will not wander about carrying on my head what has been spat out and vomited by you; for me..."

“Please grant me the going forth. Visākha said, “Very well, Dhammadinnā,” and having informed the king, he sent Dhammadinnā in a golden palanquin to the nuns’ residence for the purpose of her ordination.
Having gone forth, she thought: “This merchant, while remaining right in the midst of his home, has brought an end to suffering.”
"Since the time I received the going-forth, it is fitting that I too should bring an end to suffering.
Having said this, she went to her preceptor and teacher and said, "Venerable ladies, my mind does not delight in a crowded place; I am going to a village residence.
The elder nuns, being unable to restrain her mind because she had gone forth after leaving behind a great family, [consented].

Taking her with them, they went to a village monastery. Because she had previously practiced the crushing of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*), she attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long.
Then this thought occurred to her: "My task has reached its culmination;
what shall I do by staying here? I shall go to Rājagaha itself; there, supported by me, my large circle of kinsmen will perform meritorious deeds."
Having taken the elder nuns, they returned to the city itself.
Visākha, learning that she had arrived, thought, "She has come quickly; perhaps she is weary?
So in the evening, he went to her presence, paid homage, and sat to one side, thinking, "It is improper to ask about a state of weariness."
He asked questions concerning the five aggregates and so forth; Dhammadinnā answered each question as it was posed, like one cutting the stalk of a blue lotus with a sword.

Having recognized the sharpness of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā’s knowledge, the lay follower questioned her in all aspects regarding the three paths in the order of his own attainment, and by way of mastery—
He also asked about the path of arahantship. The Elder Dhammadinnā, realizing that the lay follower’s range extended only as far as the fruit of non-returning, turned him back, saying:
"Friend Visākha, you have overstepped the bounds of the questions; you were not able to grasp their limit. For, friend Visākha, [the Dhamma] has Nibbāna as its ultimate goal."
“The holy life has Nibbāna as its goal and Nibbāna as its consummation.
And if you wish, friend Visākha, you should approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter. You should remember it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to you,” he said.
Visākhā went into the presence of the Teacher and related the entire sequence of questions and answers.
Having heard his words, the Teacher said, "My daughter has no craving for the aggregates of the past, future,
or present," and spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:
“He who has nothing before, after, or in between;
who is without possessions and without grasping—him I call a brahmin.
Then, having given his approval to Dhammadinnā, he said this to the lay follower Visākha: “Visākha, she is wise.”
“Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is of great wisdom; Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is of great wisdom.
If you had asked me this same question, Visākha, I would have answered it exactly as it was answered by the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā.
Such is its meaning, and so you should remember it. Thus did this account arise.
Later on, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order of seniority.
Taking this very *Cūḷavedalla* as the occasion for his discourse, he established the Elder Nun in the foremost position among those who preach the Dhamma in this Dispensation.
Thus ends the story of the Elder Nun Nandā.
240. Regarding the sixth [discourse], "Among those who meditate, this one is Nandā": this indicates that among those who delight in meditation (*jhānābhirata*), the Elder Nun Nandā was supreme.
It is said that during the time of Buddha Padumuttara, she took rebirth in a noble family in Haṃsavatī;
later, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being foremost among those who delight in meditation.

Having seen this, she performed meritorious deeds and aspired to that particular position. Thereafter, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, she took rebirth in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī even before our Teacher was born;
they gave her the name Nandā Tissa. She is also called Rūpanandā. Later on...
By virtue of her supreme beauty, she was known as Janapadakalyāṇī.
After our Teacher, the One of Ten Powers, had attained omniscience, she gradually returned to Kapilavatthu, ordained Nanda and Rāhula, and departed;
then, at the time of the passing away of King Mahāsuddhodana, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī—

Knowing that Rāhula’s mother had gone forth and been ordained in the presence of the Teacher, [Mahāpajāpatī] thought, "What business do I have here from this time of their ordination onwards? She went to Mahāpajāpatī and was ordained herself.
From the day she was ordained, thinking, "The Teacher censures physical beauty," she did not go to attend upon the Teacher; however, when her turn for exhortation arrived—
She sent another woman and had her bring back the instruction. The Teacher, knowing that she was intoxicated with the pride of her own beauty, said:

"Let them come and receive the instruction from me personally; no other woman should be sent by the bhikkhunīs. Thereupon, Rūpanandā, seeing no other way and being unwilling to go herself, went to receive the instruction.
The Teacher, by means of his psychic power (*iddhi*) in accordance with her own conduct, manifested a female form and acted as if he were fanning himself with a palm-leaf fan.
Seeing this, Rūpanandā thought: "I have been coming here only because I am negligent without cause;
even women such as these move about with confidence in the presence of the Teacher. My own beauty is not even a fraction of their beauty."
“It is not worth a sixteenth part [of the merit]; having not known this, I have not come for all this time,” she said, and standing there, she gazed at that very female form.
Because of her perfection in past causes, the Teacher recited the verse from the *Dhammapada*: “A city made of bones... and continued:
“Whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down...”
He preached a discourse. At that very moment, having established the contemplation of the destruction and vanishing of that same form, she attained Arahatship.
In this instance, this account is not elaborated upon because it is identical to the story of the Elder Nun Khemā given below.
From then on, Rūpanandā became pre-eminent among those who delight in meditation. Later, the Teacher—

Seated in the Jeta Grove, as he was establishing the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks one after another, he placed the Elder Nun Nandā in the foremost position among those who practice meditation.
This is the story of the Elder Nun Soṇā.
241. "Of those who have aroused energy" (āraddhavīriyānaṃ) in the seventh [verse] indicates that Soṇā was the foremost among those whose energy is exerted and perfected.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Later, while listening to the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being the foremost among those who have aroused energy.

Having performed the formal act of authorization, she aspired for that high station. After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she took rebirth in a noble family in Sāvatthī during this current dispensation of a Buddha.
Later, having lived the life of a householder and obtained many sons and daughters, she established them all individually in their own domestic lives.
From that time on, thinking, "What will she do for us?", they did not even form the perception that she was their mother when she came before them.
When Soṇā, who had many sons, realized their lack of respect toward her, she thought, "What is the use of living as a householder?
and having gone forth, she entered the religious life. Then the bhikkhunīs said to her, "This woman does not know the proper conduct (*vatta*)."

They inflicted punishment on her, saying, "She does what is improper. When her sons and daughters saw her undergoing that punishment, they mocked her wherever they saw her, saying, "Even to this day she does not know even a fraction of the training rules.
Hearing their words, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and thought, "It is right for me to purify my own destiny," and even while sitting in her place...
Even while staying in her place, she recited the Thirty-two Aspects (dvattiṃsākāra).
Just as she had previously been known as the Elder Nun Bahuputtikasoṇā, afterwards she became renowned as the Elder Nun Āraddhavīriyasoṇā.
Then one day, as the nuns were going to the monastery, [she said]: "You should heat water for the community of nuns."

Having said, "Soṇa," they departed. She, too, even before the water was heated, walked back and forth in the fire-hall, increasing her insight (vipassanā) while reciting the thirty-two aspects (dvattiṃsākāra).
While seated in the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭī), the Teacher spoke this illuminating verse:
“But he who should live for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma, one day’s life seeing the supreme Dhamma is better.
At the conclusion of this verse, having attained Arahatship, she thought: “I have attained Arahatship; I am now a stranger.”
“Furthermore, if she were to speak something out of contempt for me without first reflecting, she might generate much demerit; therefore, it is appropriate to perform a test.
She placed the water vessel on the hearth but did not place a fire beneath it.
When the bhikkhunīs arrived and looked at the hearth, they did not see a fire and said, “This old woman [has provided] water for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs...”
"We told her, 'Heat it,' yet even now she does not even make a fire on the hearth," they said.
"Noble lady, what use have you for fire? Desiring to bathe in warm water, take water from the vessel and bathe," [they replied].
Thinking, "There must be a reason for this," they went and dipped their hand into the water; perceiving its warmth, they brought a single jar.
They took water, and each place they drew from was replenished.

Then, realizing that she had all along been established in Arahatship, the younger nuns first prostrated themselves at her feet with the fivefold salutation and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Venerable lady, for so long we have spoken to you repeatedly, without considering you and causing you distress; please forgive us."
Even those who were older sat in the *ukkuṭika* posture and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Forgive us, Noble Lady.

From that time on, the Elder Nun's virtue became well-known: "Although she went forth at an advanced age, through her state of aroused energy, she established herself before long in the supreme fruit.
Later, while the Teacher was seated in Jeta’s Grove, he [placed] the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks...
By placing her thus, he established the Elder Nun Soṇā in the foremost position among those who have aroused energy.
[End of] the Story of the Elder Nun Bakulā (242).
In the eighth [category], regarding "those with the divine eye," namely Bakulā: Bakulā the Elder Nun is foremost among those with the divine eye.
[The Buddha] shows this. It is said that in the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being foremost among those with the divine eye.
Having performed a meritorious deed, she aspired to that very station. For one hundred thousand aeons, she [dwelt] among the devas.
Having wandered through births among humans, she was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during the present dispensation of a Buddha.
Later, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, she gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and before long attained Arahantship.
From that time on, she became one who had mastered the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). Later, while the Teacher was seated in the Jeta Grove—
While assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order of seniority, [the Buddha] placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye.
This is the story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesā (243).
Regarding the ninth category, "among those of quick higher knowledge": Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā is the foremost among the bhikkhunīs of quick higher knowledge.
[The Buddha] shows this. For she too was born into a noble family in Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha.

Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and seeing the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge, she performed a work of merit and aspired to that very station.
After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, during the time of Kassapa Buddha...
Having been among the seven sisters in the household of King Kiki of Kāsi,
she observed the ten precepts for twenty thousand years while leading the celibate life of a maiden;

having built a dwelling-vihara for the Saṅgha and wandered among gods and humans for the duration of one Buddha-interval, she was now born into a merchant family in the city of Rājagaha during this present appearance of a Buddha.
She took rebirth, and they gave her the name Bhaddātissā.
On that very same day, a son was born in that city to the family priest.

At the moment of his birth, starting from the royal palace and throughout the entire city, weapons burst into flame. Early in the morning, the priest went to the royal court and [addressed] the king...

He asked after his well-being. The king said, "How could there be well-being for me, teacher? Today throughout the entire night, seeing weapons blazing within the royal palace, we were overcome with fear. [The teacher replied,] "Great King, do not worry on that account;
it was not only in your own house that the weapons blazed; it happened thus throughout the entire city. "For what reason? [he asked.]
“Teacher? [The astrologer replied: “In our house a boy was born under the constellation of thieves;
he has arisen as an enemy to the entire city, and this is his omen. There is no danger for you, but if you wish, we shall take him away. [The king said:
“If there is no affliction for us, there is no need to take him away. The chaplain [thought]: “My son...”
"Since he has come here having been called by his name," they gave him the name Sattuka.
Bhaddā grew up in the merchant’s house, and Sattuka grew up in the chaplain’s house.
From the time he was able to play by running about and leaping, whatever he saw in his place of wandering, he would bring it all back to his parents.
He filled his house. His father was unable to dissuade him even after speaking to him with a thousand reasons.

Later, however, realizing that he could not be restrained by any means once he had reached maturity, [the father] gave him two blue garments, placed in his hands the tools for breaking through walls and a windlass, and said: "You..."

"Live by this very work," he dismissed him. From that day forward, the man cast his snare-trap and, having climbed the palaces of various families, would break into them and take the goods left by other households as if they were his own;
there was no house in the entire city that was not plundered by him. One day...
As the king was traveling through the city in his chariot, he asked the charioteer:

"Why is it that in this city, in this house after that, only a breach is seen? "Your Majesty, there is a thief named Sattuka in this city who breaks through walls and carries off the property of families. The king summoned the city guardian and said: "It seems, in this..."
“There is a thief in this city named so-and-so; why do you not arrest him? he asked.
“Your Majesty, we are unable to find that thief along with his stolen goods,” they replied. “If you arrest that thief today, you shall live.
If you do not arrest him, I shall have the king’s command executed against you. “As Your Majesty commands,” the city guard replied, and having dispatched men throughout the entire city, he—
Having broken through a wall and stolen another’s goods, he was caught in the very act of fleeing; the king then had him brought before him.
The king said, "Take this thief out through the southern gate and execute him.
Having assented to the king's command, the city guardian seized the thief and, having him beaten with a thousand lashes at every crossroads, led him toward the southern gate.
At that time, this daughter of a merchant named Bhaddā, having opened the lion-window at the sound of the great crowd’s clamor and looking out, saw the thief Sattuka being led away in such a manner;
clutching her heart with both hands, she went and lay down face-down upon the royal couch. And she was the only daughter of that family, therefore—
Her relatives were unable to endure even the slightest facial expression [of distress]. Then her mother, seeing her lying upon the bed, asked, "What are you doing, my child?
"I saw this thief being led away after having been condemned to death, mother.
"Yes, mother. "If I obtain him, I shall live; if I do not obtain him, death is all that remains for me. They [then searched] for her in many ways...
Being unable to persuade her, they concluded that "life is better than death.
Then her father went to the city guard, gave him a bribe of one thousand pieces, and said, "My daughter’s heart is set upon the thief; release him by whatever means possible.
He replied, "Very well," and having agreed with the merchant, he took the thief and—up to this point—[acted].
Without letting the sun set on this side or that, he had one man brought out from the prison once the sun had set;
he released Sattuka from his bonds and sent him to the merchant’s house, while binding the other man with those very same bonds.
Having led him out through the southern gate, he had him executed. The merchant’s servants also took hold of Sattuka.

They arrived at the merchant’s residence. Seeing them, the merchant thought, "I shall fulfill my daughter's wish," and had Sattuka bathed with scented water, adorned him with every ornament, and sent him up to the palace.
Bhaddā, thinking, "My desire is fulfilled," adorned herself with many ornaments and attended upon him.
After Sattuka had spent a few days there, he thought: "This woman's jewelry will be mine;

it is right that I obtain these ornaments by some means. While she was sitting comfortably nearby, he said to Bhaddā, "I have a certain thing to say to you. The merchant's daughter, having received her thousand-fold gain, [listened].
With a heart full of joy, she said, "Speak with confidence, noble lady.
You thought, "It is by depending on her that he has obtained his life," but as for me, the very moment I was seized, I made a supplication to the deity dwelling on the Corapātapa mountain:
"If I shall receive my life back, I will offer you a sacrificial gift. It is by depending on her that I have received my life.
“Having received it, quickly prepare the offering.

Thinking, “I shall fulfill his wish,” Bhaddā prepared the offering, adorned herself with all her finery, mounted a single carriage with her husband, and set out for the Corapapāta mountain, intending to perform the offering to the mountain deity. As they began to ascend, Sattuka thought:
Thinking, “While everyone else is climbing up, there will be no opportunity for me to take this ornament,” he had that very offering bowl taken [by her] and climbed the mountain.
Even while conversing with Bhaddā, he did not speak pleasant words. She, by his mere gesture, understood his intention.
He understood. Then he said to her: "Bhadde, take off your upper garment and make a bundle here of the ornaments you have put on your body.
She asked, "Master, what is my offense? He replied, "What, you foolish girl, do you think I have come for the sake of a sacrificial offering (*balikamma*)?
For I would tear out the liver of this deity and give it to her under the pretext of a sacrificial offering."
"But I have come wishing to take your ornaments. "Noble sir, whose ornaments are they? Whose are mine?
"We do not know such things as 'this belongs to you' and 'this belongs to me. "Very well, noble sir;
however, fulfill one request of mine: let there be a procession of me, both before and behind, in the manner of one being adorned."

“Give me a hug,” she said. He consented, saying, “Very well. Knowing that he had agreed, she embraced him from the front and, as if embracing him from behind, pushed him over a mountain precipice. As he fell, he was reduced to dust and ashes even in mid-air.
Seeing the strange turn of events she had wrought, a deity dwelling on the mountain spoke these verses in praise of his virtues:
“A man is not wise in all circumstances;
even a woman may be wise and discerning in various matters.
A man is not wise in all circumstances.”
"A wise woman can reflect even for a moment.
Then Bhaddā thought: "It is not possible for me to go home again by this same method;
I shall go from here and enter one of the religious orders. Having gone to the Nigaṇṭha monastery, she requested ordination from the Nigaṇṭhas. Then...
They said to her, "By what method shall your going-forth (pabbajjā) take place? She replied, "Do exactly that which is the most excellent for your own going-forth.
Saying, "Very well," they plucked out her hair with a palm-leaf fan and ordained her.
As her hair grew back, it increased in curls, turning in spirals like a mass of coils; for that reason, she was known as Kuṇḍalakesā.

She was born with that name. Having mastered every craft in her own place of ordination, she realized, "There is no excellence beyond this," and so she wandered through villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
Wherever there were wise men, she went to each of those places and mastered every craft they knew. Then, because of her training in many fields, [she became renowned].

They were not capable of giving her a rebuttal. Seeing no one capable of conversing with her, whatever village or town she entered, she would heap up a pile of sand at its gate and plant a branch of a rose-apple tree (*jambu*) there.
Standing nearby, she would say to the children: "Whoever is able to refute my argument, let him trample this branch."
She gave her consent. Even for seven days, they did not crush her; then, taking her, he departed.
At that time, our Blessed One, having appeared in the world, was dwelling at Jetavana near Sāvatthī.
And Kuṇḍalakesā, having gradually reached Sāvatthī, as she was entering the city, according to the ancient custom—
Having placed a branch upon a heap of sand and given a signal to the children, he entered [the city].
At that time, as the Dhammasenāpati was entering the city alone while the Saṅgha of bhikkhus had already entered, he saw the Jambu branch on the sand-mound and asked, "Why has this been placed here?
The children explained the reason without omitting any detail. This being so, [he thought: "This..."
"Seize it and crush it, children! When they heard the Elder’s words, some did not dare to crush it, while others crushed it at that very moment, reducing it to powder and dust.
As Kuṇḍalakesā was coming out after finishing her meal, she saw that branch crushed and asked, "Whose work is this? Then the Dhammasenāpati—
They reported that he had caused it to be made. She thought, "He will not be able to crush this branch without knowing his own strength;
he must certainly be a great man. But as I am small, I would not look well [if I went out];
it is better for me to enter the village itself and give notice to the assembly. Having reflected thus, she did so. [In that place] where eighty thousand families resided...
It should be understood that everyone in the city recognized one another through their mutual resemblance.
The Elder, having finished his meal, sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Then Kuṇḍalakesā, surrounded by a great crowd, approached the Elder, exchanged greetings, and standing to one side, said: "Venerable sir, by you [the branch]..."

“Did you have it ground? he asked. “Yes, I had it ground,” he replied. “If that is so, let there be a debate between us, venerable sir. “Let there be one, good man. “Who shall ask the questions and who shall provide the answers?
“The question has come to us; however, you must ask what you know. With the permission granted by the Elder, she [asked] everything...
She asked him a question concerning his own knowledge, and the Elder answered everything. Having asked all her questions, she became silent.
Then the Elder said to her: “You have asked many things; let us also ask one question.
“Ask it, venerable sir,” she replied. “What is ‘one’? She said, “I do not know, venerable sir. [The Elder said: “You—”
"You do not know even this much; what else will you know? She fell at the elder's feet and said, "Venerable sir, I go for refuge to you.

He replied, "I have no kamma of going for refuge. The Supreme Person in the world with its devas dwells in the head monastery; go for refuge to him. She said, "I shall do so, venerable sir," and in the evening time—
At the time for the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, she went into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and stood to one side.
The Teacher, in accordance with the temperament of her who had crushed the conditioned formations, spoke this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
“Even if there were a thousand verses composed of meaningless words;”
“A single verse-line is better, hearing which one attains peace.
At the conclusion of that verse, while she remained standing right where she was, she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and requested ordination.
The Teacher accepted her ordination. She went to the nuns’ quarters and was ordained. Later on—
In the midst of the fourfold assembly, this discussion arose: “How great indeed is Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā, who attained Arahatship at the conclusion of a four-line verse!
The Teacher, taking that as the occasion for a discourse, established the Elder Nun in the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge.
The Story of the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kāpilānī (244).
In the tenth verse, it is shown that among those who recollect the continuity of the aggregates in which they dwelt in former lives, Bhaddā Kāpilānī was the foremost.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī and [served] the Teacher...
While listening to the Dhamma teaching, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being foremost among those who recollect their past lives (*pubbenivāsa*).
Having performed an act of merit, she aspired for that very station.
After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she took rebirth in a noble family in Bārāṇasī during a time when no Buddha had yet appeared.
While she was quarreling with her own mistress-sister, when that sister gave alms-food to a paccekabuddha, she thought, "By giving this man his alms-food, she brings him under her control.
So, taking the bowl from the paccekabuddha’s hand, she threw away the cooked rice, filled it with mud, and gave it back. The great multitude reviled her, saying, "This woman is a fool!"
“You do nothing at all to her with whom you quarreled; what has the Paccekabuddha done wrong to you?

she said. Ashamed by their words, she took the bowl again, removed the dregs, washed it, rubbed it with fragrant powder, filled it with the four sweet substances, and lit it so that it shone like the interior of a lotus with the clarified butter poured over it.
Having placed it in the hand of the Paccekabuddha, he made this aspiration: "Just as this alms-food has become radiant, so may my body become radiant.
All of this is to be understood in the same manner as described in the account of the Elder Mahākassapa.
The Elder Mahākassapa, however, took the southern road and went into the presence of the One of Ten Powers to the foot of the Bahuputtaka Nigrodha tree.
Having departed, Bhaddā Kāpilānī took the wrong path and went to the park of female wanderers because the going forth for women had not been permitted.
However, when Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī obtained both the going forth and full ordination,
that elder nun received the going forth and full ordination from her, and at a later time...
While practicing insight meditation, she attained arahantship and became proficient in the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).
Then, while seated in the Jeta Grove, the Teacher, as he was establishing the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks,
placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those who recollect past lives.
The Story of the Elder Nun Bhaddākaccānā (245).

Regarding the phrase "of those who have attained the great higher knowledges" (*mahābhiññāppattānaṃ*): it shows that Bhaddā Kaccānā is the foremost among those who have attained the great higher knowledges (*mahatiyo abhiññāyo*).
For in the case of a single Buddha, only four individuals possess the great higher knowledges, and not the remaining disciples.
For the remaining disciples are able to recollect only one hundred thousand eons, and not beyond that.
However, those who have attained great supernormal knowledge recollect more than one hundred thousand eons—an incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya).
Even in the dispensation of our own Teacher, the two chief disciples, the Elder Bākulatthera and Bhaddā Kaccānā—these four were able to recollect this much.
Therefore, this elder nun became known as the foremost among those who have attained the great direct knowledges (*mahābhiññā*). "Bhaddā Kaccānā" was her name.
For her bodily complexion was like that of excellent gold (*bhaddakañcana*), the finest of metals;
thus she received the name Bhaddakañcanā, and later she came to be designated simply as Kaccānā. This is a synonym for the Mother of Rāhula.
For during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.

Later, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being foremost among those who have attained great direct knowledge (mahābhiññā).
Having performed an act of service, she aspired to that very status. For a hundred thousand aeons...
Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans, she took rebirth in the home of the Sakyan Suppabuddha during this arising of a Buddha;
they gave her the name Bhaddā Kaccānā Tissa.
When she reached maturity, she went to the home of the Bodhisatta. Later, she bore a son named Rāhula Kumāra.

He was born. On the very day of his birth, the Bodhisatta went forth, attained omniscience at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and while performing acts of benefit for the world, eventually returned to Kapilavatthu and showed favor to his kinsmen.
Later, after the Great King Suddhodana had passed away into Parinibbāna, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, together with five hundred women, [approached] the presence of the Teacher.
She went forth. Rāhulamātā and Janapadakalyāṇī also went to the elder nun and went forth.
From the time she went forth, she became well known as the Elder Nun Bhaddakaccānā.

Later on, having developed insight and attained Arahatship, she gained mastery over the supernormal powers; while sitting cross-legged, with a single act of attention, [she could perceive] more than a hundred thousand eons...
She recollects incalculable [aeons]. When that quality of hers became manifest, the Teacher, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective ranks;
he placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those who have attained the great direct knowledges (*mahābhiññā*).
This is the story of the elder nun Kisāgotamī.
246. Regarding the twelfth [verse], "to those wearing coarse robes": this indicates that Kisāgotamī was foremost among those who wore rag-robes (paṃsukūla) endowed with the three kinds of coarseness.
"Gotamī" is her name; however, because her physical constituents were somewhat emaciated, she is called "Kisāgotamī.
She too, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, having been reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī, [heard] the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma...
Hearing the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhunī as the foremost among those who wear coarse robes, she performed an act of merit and aspired to that position.
After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand kappas, she was reborn in this current Buddha-epoch into a poor family in Sāvatthī; and when she reached maturity—
She went to one family. There, they treated her with contempt, saying, "She is the daughter of a poor family.
Later, she gave birth to a son; then they showed her respect.
However, when that boy reached the age of playfulness and died while running about and playing, grief arose within her. She thought, "In this very [place]..."
“Having been one who received honor in the home through wealth and gain, from the time my son was born I have attained honor;
yet these people would even strive to cast my son out! Taking her son on her lap, she wandered from door to door, saying, “Give medicine for my son.
Wherever she was seen, people asked, “Where is there medicine for one who is dead?”
"Have you seen him before? they asked, clapping their hands and making jokes. She did not respond to their talk at all.
Then, a certain wise man, seeing her, thought: "She must have reached a state of mental distraction due to grief for her son;
no one else will know the remedy for this, only the One Possessed of the Ten Powers (the Buddha) will know."
He spoke thus: “Mother, there is no one else who knows the medicine for your son;
however, the Supreme Person among the world with its devas, the One Possessing Ten Powers, dwells at Dhuravihāra. Go to him and ask.
Thinking, “The man speaks the truth,” she took her son and went to the edge of the assembly while the Tathāgata was seated upon his Buddha-throne.
Standing there, she said, "Venerable Sir, please give medicine for my son.
Seeing her underlying potential (*upanissaya*), the Teacher said, "It is well done by you, Gotamī, that you have come here seeking medicine.
Go, enter the city, and having wandered through the entire city starting from the gate, go to whichever house someone has previously died."

“There is none; therefore, bring some white mustard seeds,” he said. “Very well, Bhante,” she replied with a joyful heart, and entering the city, at the very first house she said, “The One of Ten Powers is having white mustard seeds brought for my son’s medicine;
give me some white mustard seeds. “Here you are, Gotamī,” they said, and bringing it out, they gave it to her. I [acted] in this way to take [the seeds].
“I am unable; there has never been anyone who died in this house, has there? “What are you saying, Gotamī?
Who is able to count those who have died here? “In that case, enough! I will not take it.
The One of Ten Powers makes me take it from where no one has ever died before,” she said. Following this very method, she went to the third house and thought:

Thinking, “This very rule shall apply throughout the entire city; this must have been seen by the Buddha, who is compassionate for our welfare,” she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
She then went out from there, proceeded to the raw charnel ground, took her son by the hand, and said: “My little son, I thought that this death would happen to you alone, but it is not so.”
"This is a law common to all people, even to you," he said, and having abandoned his son in the raw charnel ground,
he spoke this verse: "It is not the law of the village, nor the law of the town,
Nor is it the law of a single family."
“For the entire world, including the devas, this is the very nature of things: namely, impermanence.
Having spoken thus, she went into the presence of the Teacher. Then the Teacher said to her, “Gotamī, have you obtained the white mustard seed?”
She said, "Venerable sir, my work with the white mustard seeds is finished; please give me a support.
Then the Teacher spoke this verse from the *Dhammapada*:
"For a person who is intoxicated by children and cattle, whose mind is distracted..."
“Like a great flood sweeping away a village, death carries one off.
At the conclusion of this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry right where she stood; she then requested the going forth, and the Teacher granted her permission.
She circumambulated the Teacher three times, paid homage, and [proceeded] to the nunnery.
Having gone forth and received full ordination, before long she applied herself to wise attention and increased her insight.
Then the Teacher spoke this verse of illumination to her:
“Though one should live for a hundred years, not seeing the deathless state;”
"One day’s life is better for one who sees the deathless state.
At the conclusion of that verse, she attained arahantship. Having become preeminent in the use of requisites, she wandered about wearing a robe made of three coarse materials.
Later, while the Teacher was seated in Jeta’s Grove, he addressed the bhikkhunīs:
While assigning them to their respective positions in order, he placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes.
[This concludes] the story of the Elder Nun Siṅgālakamātā (247).
In the thirteenth [section], "of those resolved upon faith" (*saddhādhimuttānaṃ*) means of those who are firmly intent upon the characteristic of faith; [the foremost was] Siṅgālakamātā.
He indicates that she is foremost. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being foremost among those resolved through faith.
Having performed an act of service, she aspired to that very status. For one hundred thousand aeons, she [dwelt] among gods and humans.
Having wandered through the cycle of existence, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha into a merchant family in the city of Rājagaha.
Having married into a family of similar status, she gave birth to a son, whom they named Siṅgālaka-kumāra.
For that very reason, she became known as Siṅgālakamātā (Mother of Siṅgālaka). One day, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she acquired faith.
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher, she went forth. From the time of her going forth, she acquired an extraordinary degree of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
Whenever she went to the monastery to hear the Dharma, she would stand gazing at the excellence of the Ten-Powered One’s physical form.
The Teacher, knowing that she was firmly established in the characteristic of faith, made himself agreeable and inspiring to her.
She taught the Dhamma. That elder nun also, making the characteristic of faith her primary focus, attained Arahatship.
Later, while seated in the Jeta Grove, the Teacher established the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks and placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those resolved through faith.
Commentary on the Fifth Chapter.
The commentary on the Thera-vagga, adorned with thirteen suttas, is finished.
14. The Chapter on the Foremost (Etadagga-vagga).
(14) 6. The Sixth Chapter on the Foremost:
The Story of Tapussa and Bhallika. 248.
In the first section of the *Upāsakapāḷi*, regarding "those going for refuge for the first time," this refers to the very first instance of going for refuge.
This indicates that among those traveling, these two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, were at the forefront.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, they took rebirth in noble families in Haṃsavatī;
later, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, they saw the Teacher designate two lay followers as foremost among those who first go for refuge, and they performed a work of merit.

Having done so, they made a wish for that very position. After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, they were reborn even before our Bodhisatta attained omniscience, in the house of a householder in the city of Asitañjana.
The elder brother was named Tapussa, and the younger was named Bhallika.
At a later time, while living as householders, they traveled about from time to time performing the work of merchants, having yoked five hundred carts.
At that time, our Bodhisatta, having attained omniscience and dwelt at the seat of enlightenment for seven weeks, sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree on the eighth week. In that [time]...
At that time, those merchants arrived at that place with about five hundred wagons.
In their immediately preceding existence, their mother had been reborn as a deity in that very spot. She thought: "Now it is necessary to obtain food for the Buddhas;
it is not possible to continue beyond this point without sustenance. And these are my sons."
“They travel by this path; it is fitting that we cause almsfood to be given to the Buddhas today.
Thus he brought about the halting of the oxen yoked to five hundred carts. They wondered, “What is this? and observed various omens.
Then, perceiving their weariness, he resolved his mind upon the body of one man and asked, “What—”
“What is the cause of your exhaustion? You have no other obsession with yakkhas, bhūtas, or nāgas;
rather, in a previous existence I was your mother, and in this place I have been reborn as a terrestrial deity.
This King of Ten Powers is sitting at the root of the Rājāyatana tree; give him your first alms-food.”
Having heard her words, they became joyful in heart;
taking some stirred milk-rice and honey-cakes in a golden bowl, they went into the presence of the Teacher and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept this food.
The Teacher looked back upon the practice of past Buddhas, and then the Four Great Kings presented him with bowls made of rock crystal.
The Teacher, thinking, "May this be of great fruit for them," resolved that the four bowls should become "but one bowl.
At that moment, those merchants placed the stirred drink and the honey-cake into the Tathāgata’s bowl;
when he had finished eating, they gave him water, and at the conclusion of the meal, they paid homage to the Teacher and stood to one side.

They sat down. Then the Teacher taught them the Dhamma; at the conclusion of the teaching, both individuals, having established themselves in the two-fold refuge through the words of the Teacher, paid homage to him and, desiring to go to their own city, said, "Venerable Sir, give us a cetiya for our veneration.
The Teacher stroked his head with his right hand and—

He gave eight hair-relics to both men. Both men, having placed the hair-relics in golden caskets, brought them to their own cities and established a shrine for the living hair-relic at the gate of the city of Asitanjana.
On fast days, rays of blue light emanate from the shrine. Thus this story originated. The Teacher [spoke].
Later on, however, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, as the Buddha was assigning lay followers to their respective ranks of eminence,
he placed these two people in the foremost position among those who first went for refuge.
Thus ends the story of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.
249. Regarding the second [simile], "of donors," it shows that Sudatta, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, was the foremost among those who delight in giving.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, having been reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma.
While listening, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain lay follower to the position of being the foremost among donors, and he performed a work of merit.

Having performed that deed, he aspired for that very station. After wandering among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the city of Sāvatthī, in the house of the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi; they gave him the name Sudatta.
Later, when he was established in the life of a householder, he became a donor and a lord of giving, and by virtue of that very quality, his name became widely renowned.
There was one named Anāthapiṇḍika. Taking merchandise with five hundred carts, he went to the house of a merchant who was his dear friend in Rājagaha.

Having heard there that the Buddha, the Blessed One, had appeared, he approached the Teacher at the time of the powerful dawn through a gate opened by the power of a deity. Having heard the Dhamma, he attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having established himself, on the following day he gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Having obtained the Teacher’s consent for his arrival at Sāvatthī, he gave one hundred thousand pieces of gold for every forty-five *yojana*s along the road;
having had monasteries built at intervals of one *yojana* and having covered Jetavana with a layer of ten million pieces of gold, [he honored it] with eighteen...

Having purchased [the site] for eighteen crores and having had the monastery built for eighteen crores, when the monastery was finished, he provided whatever was desired as alms to the four assemblies before and after their meals; thus, with eighteen crores, he completed the festival of the monastery.
The festival of the monastery reached its conclusion in nine months, though others say "in five," or "in three months."
However, there was no disagreement among any of the teachers.
Thus, having disbursed fifty-four koṭis of wealth, he constantly maintained such a distribution of gifts within his household.
Daily, there were five hundred *salāka*-meals, five hundred fortnightly meals, and five hundred *salāka*-sacrifices.
There were five hundred portions of rice for the fortnightly offerings, five hundred portions for the regular daily meals,
five hundred portions for guests, five hundred portions for those departing, five hundred portions for the sick, five hundred portions for those attending to the sick,
and five hundred seats were always prepared in the house. Later on, while the Teacher was seated in Jeta’s Grove...
While arranging the lay followers (upāsakas) in successive ranks, he placed [Citta] in the foremost position among donors.

This is the story of the householder Citta (Cittagahapativatthu). Regarding the third [category], "among those who preach the Dhamma": among the lay followers who preach the Dhamma, the householder Citta is the foremost.
[The Buddha] shows this. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
Later, while listening to a discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain lay follower to the position of foremost among those who preach the Dhamma.
Having performed a meritorious deed, he aspired to that very status. For a hundred thousand aeons, he [repeatedly] existed among gods and humans.
Having wandered through the cycle of existence, he was reborn during the time of Buddha Kassapa in the house of a deer-hunter.
Later, when he was capable of working in the forest, one day while it was raining, he took a spear and went into the woods to kill deer.
While looking for the forms of deer, he saw [a being] on an unprepared mountain slope, wearing a head-covering and a rag-robe (paṃsukūla), seated upon a stone slab.
Seeing a single bhikkhu seated there, she formed the perception that "this noble one must be sitting alone performing the duties of a recluse.
She hurried home, had meat brought from yesterday’s supply cooked on one hearth and rice cooked on another;
then, seeing two bhikkhus wandering for alms, she took their bowls, seated them on prepared seats, and served them.
Having caused alms to be collected and having instructed others, saying, "Noble ladies, serve the meal," he placed that food in a jar,
sealed the mouth with a leaf, and set out carrying the jar. Along the way, he gathered various kinds of flowers, took them in a leaf-bag,
went to the place where the Elder was sitting, lowered the jar, and set it aside to one side.
Having said, “Venerable sir, please show me your favor,” he took the elder’s bowl, filled it with food, and placed it in the elder’s hand.
After worshipping the elder with those mixed flowers, he stood to one side and thought:
“Just as this offering of flowers together with this delicious alms-food has gladdened my heart, so may it be in every place where I am reborn.”
“Let ten thousand gifts come to me, and let there fall a rain of five-colored flowers,” he said.
The Elder, perceiving his spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), explained and gave him the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of the thirty-two parts of the body.
Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he was reborn in the world of the devas; in the place where he was reborn, a rain of divine flowers fell to the depth of his knees.
It rained, and he himself was endowed with a form superior to that of other deities.

After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one *buddhantara*, he was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in the merchant family of Macchikāsaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha.
At the time of his birth, a rain of five-colored flowers fell throughout the entire city to a depth reaching the knees.
Then his parents, thinking, "Our son has come having taken his own name for himself, and on the very day he was born,
the entire city became adorned with flowers of five colors," gave him the name Cittakumāra.
Later, when he was established in the life of a householder, upon the passing of his father, he attained the position of chief merchant (*seṭṭhi*) in that city.
At that time, Mahānāma Thera, one of the group of five elders, went to the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa.
The householder Citta, having gained confidence in his deportment, took his bowl, brought him to his home, and honored him with almsfood.
When the meal was finished, he led him to a park called Ambāṭakārāma and provided him with a place to stay there.
Having had a fixed portion of alms-food prepared for himself at his own house, he obtained the Elder’s consent to stay there.
The Elder, perceiving his underlying potential (*upanissaya*), taught him the Dhamma by expounding specifically on the analysis of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatanavibhatti*).

Because of his state of having crushed the conditioned formations (*madditasaṅkhāratā*) from previous lives, the householder Citta attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) before long. Then, one day—

The Elder Isidatta went there and stayed in that place. At the conclusion of the meal in the merchant’s residence, when he was requested by the Venerable Elder—who was unable to answer the question—to explain the lay follower’s inquiry, he answered it.
Once the Elder recognized that he had previously been his householder friend, he thought, "I should not remain here any longer," and departed at his pleasure. On another day, again—
The householder merchant requested the Elder Mahānāma to perform a miracle of supernormal power.
He, for his part, having displayed for him the miracle of the attainment of fire, thought, "It is no longer fitting to dwell here," and departed as he pleased.
Then one day, the two Chief Disciples, accompanied by a retinue of a thousand bhikkhus, went to the Ambāṭaka Monastery. The merchant—
The householder prepared a great reception for them. Unable to endure this, the Elder Sudhamma reviled the merchant with the words "sesame-finger-mark" and was dismissed by him.
Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and received his instruction, he stood firm in the teaching of the One of Ten Powers.
After apologizing to the householder Citta, while dwelling right there in the Ambāṭaka Grove, he developed insight (*vipassanā*).
He attained arahantship. Then the lay follower thought: “I have spent a long time without seeing the One of Ten Powers;
it is improper for me to go into the presence of the Teacher empty-handed. So, taking five hundred carts laden with oil, honey, molasses, and other provisions, he said:
“Whoever wishes to see the One of Ten Powers, let them come along with me.”
Having caused a drum to be beaten in the city, surrounded by two thousand men, he set out to see the Teacher.
Along the thirty-yojana path, deities presented him with offerings. Having approached the presence of the Teacher, he paid homage to the Teacher by prostrating himself at the five points;
at that moment, a rain of five-colored flowers fell from the sky.
The Teacher, in accordance with his disposition, taught him specifically the Analysis of the Six Sense Bases.
Even as he gave alms to the One Possessing Ten Powers for nearly half a month, the rice, oil, honey, molasses, and other provisions brought from his own residence were not exhausted;
the offerings sent by the residents of Rājagaha alone were sufficient. Having seen the Teacher, he—his own...
As he was going to the city, he gave everything brought by the carts to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
As soon as the carts became empty, deities filled them with the seven treasures. Among the great crowd, this talk arose:
“How indeed this householder Citta has attained honor and respect! Hearing that, the Teacher spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:
“Endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, possessed of fame and wealth,
whatever region he frequents, there he is honored.
From that time forth, he wandered about surrounded by five hundred lay followers who were noble disciples.
Later on, when the Teacher was assigning the lay followers to their respective ranks,
he established this account as the occasion for the *Cittasaṃyutta* and placed him in the foremost position among those who preach the Dhamma.
This is the story of Hatthaka Āḷavaka.

251. Regarding the fourth [case], "by means of the four bases of sympathy" (*saṅgahavatthu*) indicates that among those who gather a following by means of the fourfold bases of sympathy, Hatthaka Āḷavaka is the foremost.
It is said that he was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha;
later, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he [saw] the Teacher with the four bases of sympathy.
Seeing a single lay follower endowed with such qualities being appointed to a high position, he performed an act of merit and aspired to that same rank.

After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, he took rebirth in the city of Āḷavī in the province of Āḷavī within the household of King Āḷavaka; he was to be sent to King Āḷavaka the following day along with his meal-servant.
In this regard, the following is the sequential account: One day, it is said, King Āḷavaka went to the forest for deer-hunting;
having pursued a deer, killed it, and cut it up, he hung it from the tip of his bow and returned.
As he was coming back, his body exhausted by the wind and heat, he entered and sat down at the foot of a banyan tree that provided shade. Then...
After dispelling his distress for a moment, as he was departing, a deity dwelling in a tree seized him by the hand, saying, "Stop! Stop!
You are my prey! Because he was held so firmly and saw no other way out, he said, "I shall send you one bowl of rice along with one man every day," and then went to the city. From that time forth...
He sent a meal of rice porridge with each prisoner from the jail.

Following this very method, when the men in the jail were exhausted, they thought, "If we take the elderly men, there will be an upheaval in the kingdom," so they refrained from taking them and began to seize young boys.
From that time on, the mothers of children and pregnant women in the city...
And they were going to another kingdom.
At that time, as the Teacher was surveying the world at dawn, he saw that Prince Āḷavaka possessed the necessary support for attaining the three paths and fruits;
[he perceived] that this prince, having made his aspiration for a hundred thousand eons, had passed away from the deva-world.
Thinking, “He was reborn in the house of King Āḷavaka; since they will not find another boy,
tomorrow they will take this boy along with their meal for the beggars,” at evening time he went to the gate of the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka in the guise of a stranger,
and [addressed] his doorkeeper, the yakkha named Gadrabha, for the purpose of entering the abode.
He entreated him. He replied, "Blessed One, you may enter; however, it would be improper for me not to inform Āḷavaka.
He went into the presence of Āḷavaka, who had gone to a gathering of yakkhas in the Himalayas.
The Teacher also entered that abode and sat upon the seat-couch where Āḷavaka used to sit.

At that time, as the Sātāgira and Hemavata deities were traveling through the upper reaches of Āḷavaka’s abode on their way to the assembly of yakkhas, they wondered, "What is the cause of our failure to proceed?

While reflecting thus, they saw the Teacher seated in Āḷavaka’s abode. Having gone into the presence of the Teacher and paid homage to him, they proceeded to the assembly of yakkhas and [approached] Āḷavaka.
They expressed their joy, saying: "It is a gain for you, friend Āḷavaka, that the Supreme Person in the world with its devas is sitting in your abode;
go and listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. Having heard their words, he thought:
"These are telling one shaven-headed ascetic that he is sitting on my couch," and he was displeased.
Overcome by anger, he thought, "Today I shall have a battle with this ascetic;
there, you must be my allies! Raising his right foot, he stepped upon a mountain peak sixty yojanas in height, which shattered and split in two.
From this point onward, the battle with Āḷavaka should be related in detail. Āḷavaka...

However, although he fought with the Tathāgata in various ways throughout the entire night, being unable to do anything at all, he approached the Teacher and asked eight questions, which the Teacher answered. At the conclusion of the teaching, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
One who wishes to explain this in detail should consult the commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta.
On the following day, when the dawn had risen and it was time to collect the morning meal, they informed the king that they could not find a boy suitable to be taken throughout the entire city.
The king said, "But there may be one, dear ones, in a place where it is improper to take him. "Yes, Your Majesty;
today a son has been born in the royal household. "Go then, dear ones; as long as we live, we shall obtain our son."
"Send him with a bowl of gruel. While the queen was wailing, they took the child and went with the bowl of gruel to the gate of Āḷavaka’s abode, saying, "Come, noble sir, accept your portion.
When Āḷavaka heard their words, he sat down with his head bowed in shame because he was a noble disciple. Then the Teacher—
He said, “Now, Āḷavaka, you have no need for shame; take the boy and place him in my hand.
Those royal officers placed the young Āḷavaka in the hands of Āḷavaka; Āḷavaka took him and placed him in the hand of the One of Ten Powers.
The Teacher accepted him and then placed him back in the hand of Āḷavaka. Āḷavaka [took him].
Having taken him, he placed him in the hands of the king’s men. Because he had passed from hand to hand, they gave him the name “Hatthaka Āḷavaka.
Then those royal men, with joyful minds, took him and went into the presence of the king.
Upon seeing him, the king perceived that he was not accepting his food today and asked, “Why, dear ones, have you come in this manner?”

He said, "Your Majesty, there is joy and prosperity for the royal family! The Teacher, having sat in the abode of Āḷavaka, tamed Āḷavaka, established him in the status of a lay follower, and gave the youth to us.
Then the Teacher, having had Āḷavaka take his bowl and robe, set out toward the city of Āḷavī. As he approached the city, Āḷavaka drew back as if out of shame.
The Teacher looked at him and asked, “Are you ashamed, Āḷavaka? “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied.
“Because of me, the city-dwellers have met with the death of mothers, the death of fathers, and the death of children and wives. When they see me, they will strike me with sticks and clods of earth.
Therefore, venerable sir, I am retreating. “Āḷavaka, there is no fear for you as you go with me.”
Having said, "Do not be afraid; come with confidence," he stood in a grove of trees not far from the city.
King Āḷavaka, taking the citizens with him, went out to meet the Teacher.

The Teacher taught the Dhamma to the assembled multitude, and at the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the drink of the Deathless. They [then] addressed Āḷavaka right there.
Having established a dwelling place for him, they instituted an annual offering ceremony.
Āḷavaka, too, protected the citizens with righteous guardianship.
When that Prince Āḷavaka reached maturity, he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and realized the three paths and fruits. He was, at all times, among the noble disciple lay followers...

He wandered about surrounded by five hundred [attendants]. Then one day, having gone into the presence of the Teacher together with those lay followers and having paid homage, he sat down to one side.
Seeing that the assembly was well-disciplined, the Teacher said: "Āḷavaka, your assembly is large;
how do you sustain it? [He replied: "Blessed One, I sustain those who find satisfaction in giving by means of giving."
"I win over one who is pleased by kind words with kind words; I win over one who is pleased by the accomplishment of their needs when those needs arise by the accomplishment of those needs;
I win over one who is pleased by equality of status through equality of status.
Thus did this matter arise. Then, at a later time, the Teacher sat in Jeta’s Grove.
When establishing lay followers in their respective positions, he placed Hatthaka Āḷavaka in the foremost rank among those who attract assemblies by means of the four bases of sympathy.
This is the story of Mahānāma the Sakyan.
252. Regarding the fifth [case], "of those who give superior food," this shows that the Sakyan Mahānāma was the foremost among those who give superior flavors.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.

While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain lay follower to the position of being the foremost among those who give superior flavors, and he performed a meritorious deed [in emulation].

Having performed that deed, he aspired for that very station. After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, he was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in the Sakya royal family at the city of Kapilavatthu.
Upon reaching maturity, at his very first sight of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, he established himself in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti).
Then, on one occasion, after spending the rains retreat at Verañjā, the Teacher traveled by stages to the city of Kapilavatthu and stayed at the Nigrodha Monastery.

Having heard that the Teacher had arrived, Mahānāma went into the Teacher’s presence, paid homage to him, and sitting to one side, spoke thus to the Teacher: “Blessed One, I have heard this: ‘The Saṅgha of bhikkhus...’”
“It is said that you are weary from wandering for alms in Verañjā;
grant me your promise to sustain the community of monks for four months, and I shall infuse vital essence into the bodies of the Saṅgha. The Teacher consented.
Having understood the Teacher’s consent, starting from the following day, he [served] the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
Having tended to him with superior delicacies, the four sweet foods, and so forth, he again obtained a promise for four months;
having fulfilled those eight months, he again obtained a promise for four months, and thus tended to him for an entire year.
After that, the Teacher did not accept any further promise. But from then on, Mahānāma [tended] to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus as they arrived one after another.
In that very same manner, he continued to offer his hospitality. His virtue became renowned throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa.
Thus did this story originate. Later, however, while seated in the Jeta Grove, the Teacher placed Mahānāma the Sakyan in the foremost position among those who give choice gifts.
253. The Story of the Householder Uggata.

Regarding the sixth [verse], "of those who give what is pleasing": this shows that the householder Uggata was the foremost among those from Vesālī who give food that is pleasing—that is, food according to one's heart's desire.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was reborn into a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
Later, while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher designate a certain lay follower as the foremost among those who give what is pleasing.

Having performed a meritorious deed, he aspired to that very position. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha into a merchant family in Vesālī. Of him—
At the time of his birth, his name was not yet determined. Later, however, both his physical form became exalted and prosperous;
like a decorated archway or a raised banner-cloth, it shone with great brilliance. His virtues, too, became exalted.
Because of this exaltation of both these qualities, he became known as Ugga-Setthi. And he [was a follower] of the One Possessing Ten Powers.
Having established himself in the fruit of stream-entry at the very first sight [of the Buddha], he later realized all three paths and fruits.

Having paid homage, he took the Teacher’s bowl, led him into the house, and had the Teacher sit upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, while the rest of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus were seated on the remaining seats.

Having thus informed the Teacher, from that time forward, whatever was pleasing to him, he gave that very thing to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.

Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, and seeing the Teacher appoint a certain lay follower to the position of being the foremost among those with unwavering confidence (*aveccappasanna*), he performed a work of merit and aspired to that very station. For a hundred thousand aeons...
Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans, he was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in Sāvatthī into a family of wealthy merchants; they gave him the name Sūrambaṭṭha.
Later, when he had reached maturity and established himself in the life of a householder, he lived as an attendant to followers of other sects.

“...to see one another. Then Nakulamātā, the housewife, said this to the Blessed One:

"...and to see the Dhammas as mutually related, and to see the future life as mutually related.

I shall come,” and went to the city of Sāketa together with Migāra the merchant. The merchant Dhananjaya said, “Migāra the merchant…”
Having heard that he had come taking the King of Kosala with him, he went out to meet him, took the king by the hand, and led him to his own residence.

Immediately, he prepared dwelling places for the king, the royal army, and Migāra the merchant, as well as garlands, perfumes, food, and all other necessities. "This is what he ought to receive; this..."
"He knows all this for himself. Those people thought, "The merchant is showing honor only to us.
Then one day, the king sent a message to the merchant Dhananjaya: "It is not possible for the merchant to continue supporting and maintaining us for a long time;
let him know that it is time for the girl to depart. He [the merchant] also [received] the king's message.
He sent word: “The rainy season has now arrived; it is not possible to travel for four months.
Whatever your army requires shall be my responsibility. Let the King go only when he is sent by me.
From that time on, the city of Sāketa became like a village where the constellations are always visible. Thus, three months passed.
But the great *mahālatā* cosmetic preparation for the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya was not yet finished.
Then his overseers of the workshops came and reported: "There is nothing remaining that is not present;
however, there is a shortage of firewood for cooking the meal for the army. [He replied: "Go, dear ones, and separate the elephant stable from the horse stable."
“Cook the meal. Even as they were cooking in this manner, half a month passed by. Then they reported again:
“Master, there is not enough wood. “Sirs, at this time it is impossible to obtain wood;
however, open the storehouse for cloth, take some thick cotton cloths, make wicks from them, soak them in oil in an oil-vessel, and cook the meal.”
In this manner, four months passed while they were cooking.
Then, the merchant Dhanañjaya, knowing that his daughter’s great *mahālatā* ornament was finished, thought, “Tomorrow I shall send the girl,” and seating his daughter beside him, said:
“My dear, for one living in her husband’s family, such and such... [and so forth].”
"It is fitting to train in proper conduct," he gave this advice.
This merchant Migāra, sitting in the adjacent room, overheard the advice of the merchant Dhanañjaya. That merchant also advised his daughter thus:
"Dear girl, while living in your father-in-law's house, you must not let the internal fire go out to the outside, nor must you let the external fire enter within."
"It should be given only to one who gives; it should not be given to one who does not give. It may be given both to one who gives and to one who does not give.
One should sit comfortably, enjoy [the food] comfortably, and lie down comfortably.
One should tend the sacred fire and pay homage to the deities within."
Having given this tenfold exhortation, on the following day he assembled all the troops and,
standing in the midst of the royal army, took eight householders as sureties, saying, "If any fault should arise regarding my daughter’s destination, you must clear her. Then,
having adorned his daughter with a magnificent garland and ornament worth nine crores, [he gave] the cost of the bath-powder...
Having given one hundred and fifty-four carts as wealth for his daughter, and having provided five hundred female slaves bound to accompany her on her journey,
five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses, and a hundred of every kind of requisite, he dismissed both the King of Kosala and the merchant Migāra.
Then, at the time of his daughter’s departure, he summoned the men appointed to guard the boundary and said, "Sirs, my..."

Since there is a need for cows to provide milk for my daughter’s sustenance and for bulls to draw her carriage, I have had the Vajra Gate opened along my daughter’s route and filled it with eight broad bulls from the herd.
Furthermore, three *gāvutas* away there is a ravine called Asuka; when the lead of the herd reaches that place, by the signal of a drum—
“Shut the iron gate! They accepted the merchant’s words with “Very well” and did so.
When the iron gate was opened, the cows emerged in great numbers indeed.
But when the gate was shut, by the power of Visākhā’s merit, both the strong bulls and the tame oxen leaped over the outside and set out upon the road. Then—
When Visākhā reached the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, she thought, “Shall I enter sitting in a covered carriage, or shall I stand in the chariot?
Then it occurred to her, “If I enter in a covered carriage, the excellence of my great and magnificent ornaments will not be visible. So, displaying herself to the entire city, she entered.
Standing in his chariot, he entered the city. The residents of Sāvatthī, seeing Visākhā’s splendor, said, "This one, it seems, is indeed named Visākhā;

this prosperity is truly worthy of her. Thus, she entered the house of the merchant Migāra with great magnificence. On the day of her arrival, all the inhabitants of the city said, "To us, Dhanañjaya the merchant..."
Upon their arrival in her own city, she paid them great honor, and they each sent back gifts according to their means.
Visākhā had every gift that was sent distributed throughout that very city among various families everywhere.
Then, toward the end of the night, a certain mare of noble breed gave birth.
That female slave had torches taken by her servants, went there, bathed Vaḷava with hot water,
rubbed him with oil, and returned to her own residence. Meanwhile, the merchant Migāra,
performing the marriage festivities for his son for seven days, did not even notice that the Tathāgata was staying at the Dhura Monastery.
Without paying them any mind, on the seventh day, filling his entire residence with naked ascetics, he sent a message to Visākhā, saying: "Let my daughter come; let her pay homage to the Arahants.
Upon hearing the word "Arahants," the noble female disciple, a stream-enterer, became joyful and elated; she went to the place where they were seated and looked at them.
“Arhats do not act in such a manner; why has my father-in-law summoned me to the presence of those who are devoid of shame and moral dread?
Having thus reproached herself with “Shame! Shame! she returned to her own dwelling place.
When the Naked Ascetics saw this, they all rebuked the merchant at once, saying: “Householder, did you find no one else?”
"Why have you allowed this disciple of the ascetic Gotama, who has such ill fortune, to enter this house? Quickly drive her out of this house!
Then the merchant thought, "I cannot drive her out of this house at their word;
she is the daughter of a great family. Having reflected thus, he said: "Teachers, whether they know it or not, those who are young..."

"Let them do so; you, however, remain silent. Having thus dismissed the naked ascetics and had [Visākhā] seat him upon a great couch, he took a golden spoon and, while being served by Visākhā, partook of the milk-rice mixed with honey and water from a golden bowl.
At that time, a certain elder monk wandering for alms arrived at the gate of the merchant’s house while on his round.
Seeing this, Visākhā thought, "It is not proper for me to inform my father-in-law," and she stood aside in such a way that he would see the Elder.
