But that fool, even upon seeing the Elder, acted as if he did not see him and continued eating his rice gruel with his head bowed down.
Visākhā, realizing, "Even though my father-in-law has seen the Elder, he pays no heed," approached the Elder.
“Please accept this, venerable sir; my father-in-law eats old food,” he said. When the Nigaṇṭhas had already spoken, he consented;
but at the very moment it was said, “He eats old food,” he withdrew his hand and said, “Take this milk-rice away from here, and take this out of this house.
For in such an auspicious house, he is eating what is impure.”
He said, "She gives him a name. Now, in that household, all the slaves and laborers belonged to Visākhā;
who would dare to seize her by hand or foot? Indeed, there was not even one capable of speaking to her face-to-face.
Then, having heard her father-in-law's words, Visākhā said: "Father, we do not depart merely because of these words."
"I was not brought here by you like a water-carrier girl from a watering place.

Daughters whose parents are still living do not depart on the basis of such a thing alone; for this very reason, on the day my father came here, he summoned eight householders and said to them, 'If any fault arises concerning my daughter, you must clear her.'"
He placed it in his hand. Having summoned them, he said, "Have the merits and demerits of my case investigated.

Then the merchant, thinking, "She speaks well," summoned eight householders and said, "On the seventh day, while I was sitting in my auspicious house before the term was complete, this girl called me a 'consumer of filth. Thus...
“Is it true, mother? “Dear child, my father-in-law must have been wishing to eat impure food; however, I did not say so after doing this.
But when a certain alms-collecting elder stood at the door of our house, this man was eating rice porridge with little water and honey, yet he paid no attention to him.
For that reason, I said, ‘Please wait, venerable sir, for my father-in-law—’”
"He does not perform merit in this present life; he merely consumes his past merit"—this much she says.
"Noble sir, there is no fault here; our daughter is stating the reason. Why are you angry?
"Noble lady, let us set aside that fault for now; however, on the very day this girl arrived, she gave a signal to my sons without [consulting] me."
"He went to his desired place. "Is that so, mother? "Dear ones, I am not going to my desired place.
However, it is improper for a seat to be provided in this house without even acknowledging that a noble mare has given birth.
Therefore, having had torches taken and being surrounded by female slaves, I went there myself and caused the necessary care to be given to the mare after her birth."
“Noble lady, our daughter committed an act in your house that even your slave-girls would not do; what fault do you see in this?
“Noble lady, let us set that merit aside for now. However, on the day she arrived here, her father gave her this instruction:
‘The fire within must not be carried outside. But how could we possibly [extinguish] the fire from both neighboring houses?”
"Did he say, 'Wear it without having given it'? "Indeed he did, mother. "Dear, my father was not speaking with reference to this fire;
rather, whatever secret talk arises within the household concerning mothers-in-law and others must not be told to the male and female slaves.
For such talk, when allowed to grow, leads to quarreling. It was with reference to this that my father spoke, dear."
“Venerable lady, let that be for now; her father said, ‘External fire must not be allowed to enter within.
How can we possibly bring in external fire when the internal fire has been extinguished? “Is that so, my child?
“Father, he did not say this with reference to this fire; rather, it was regarding the fault committed by the slaves and laborers.”
It has been said: "That which has been spoken should not be told among human beings...
[and so on]. Furthermore, when it was said by him, "It should be given only to those who give," this was said with reference to those who, having taken borrowed requisites, return them.
"Those who do not give"—this too was said with reference to those who, having taken borrowed requisites, do not return them; to such people, [the requisites] should not be given.

“Whether they give or not, it should be given”—this was said with reference to the fact that when impoverished kinsmen or friends arrive, one ought to give regardless of whether they are able to reciprocate.
“One should sit comfortably”—this too was said with reference to the fact that it is improper to sit in a place where one should rise upon seeing one’s mother-in-law or father-in-law.

The phrase “one should eat comfortably” is said with reference to the fact that it is appropriate for one to eat after one’s parents-in-law and husband have first eaten; having served them and ascertained whether everyone has received their portion, one may then eat oneself afterwards.
The phrase “one should lie down comfortably” likewise means that one should not go to bed and lie down before one’s parents-in-law and husband;
rather, after performing whatever duties and services are appropriate for them, one may then lie down oneself afterwards.
This was said with reference to what is "proper.

However, the statement "The fire must be tended" was said with reference to the idea that one ought to regard one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband as if they were a mass of fire or like a king of the *uraga* nāgas.
Let these qualities suffice for now; but what is the purpose of this [practice] wherein her father causes her to worship the internal deities?
"Is it really so, mother? "Yes, dear ones; for this too was said by my father with reference to this very matter:

'From the time one begins to live the life of a householder independently, whenever one sees a renunciant who has arrived at the door of one's own house, it is proper to eat only after first giving whatever hard or soft food is available in the house to those renunciants. Then they said to her:
“But, Great Merchant, it seems that upon seeing those who have gone forth, you prefer not to give,” he said.
Seeing no other reply, he sat with his head bowed.
Then the householders asked him, “Is there some other fault in our daughter, Merchant? “There is none.”
"Noble lady. But why did he have her, who was faultless, driven out from her home for no reason? At that moment Visākhā said:
"First of all, it was not proper for me to go at my father-in-law's word;
however, on the day of my arrival, my father placed me in your hands in order to clear me of any fault or defect."
"Now it is easy for me to go," he said, and commanded his male and female slaves, "Prepare the carriages and other conveyances.
Then the merchant, taking those householders with him, said, "Mother, I spoke without knowing; please forgive me.
She replied, "Sirs, I shall indeed forgive you as far as it is possible for you to be forgiven; however, regarding one who possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha's teaching—"
“I am the daughter of a noble family; we do not live without the Saṅgha of monks.
If I may be allowed to look after the Saṅgha of monks according to my own wish, I shall stay. “Dear child, look after your recluses as you wish.
Then, Visākhā, having invited the One of Ten Powers, on the following day filled her residence with offerings for the Buddha and his retinue.
He had the community of monks take their seats. The assembly of naked ascetics, having heard that the Teacher had gone to Migāra-seṭṭhi’s house, went there, surrounded the house, and sat down.
Visākhā, having offered water for the guest-offering, sent a message saying, "All the hospitality has been prepared;
let my father-in-law come and serve the One of Ten Powers. He [sent word] to the Nigaṇṭhas...
Having heard the message, he said, "Let my daughter serve the Fully Enlightened One.
After Visākhā had served the One of Ten Powers with various choice flavors and the meal was finished, she sent a message again:
"May my father-in-law come and hear the Dhamma talk from the One of Ten Powers. Then [the Buddha] said to her, "It would now be most inappropriate not to go."
As he was going out, desiring to hear a discourse on the Dhamma, naked ascetics said to him, “Sit outside the curtain and listen to the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama.
Having already gone ahead, they had enclosed the area with a curtain.
The merchant Migāra went and sat outside the curtain. The Tathāgata said, “Whether you sit outside the curtain or behind the wall...”
"Or sit on another mountain, or even in another world-system; I am called a Buddha, and I am able to make my voice heard by you.
Speaking thus, as if shaking a golden-colored *amba* tree by its trunk, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.
At the conclusion of the teaching, the merchant was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*), and having lifted his curtain, he [approached] the Teacher.

Having prostrated with her five limbs touching the ground at the feet of the Teacher, she placed Visākhā in the position of her own mother right there in the presence of the Teacher, saying, "From today onward, Mother, you are my mother. From that time forth, she became known as Visākhā Migāramātā.
One day, while the festival of the constellations was being celebrated, she went out surrounded by her female slaves, thinking, "There is no merit to be found within the city."
While going to hear the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she thought, "It is improper to go into the presence of the Buddhas with an arrogant appearance.
Thus, she removed her great womanly ornaments, placed them in the hand of a maidservant, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
The Teacher delivered a discourse on the Dhamma. At the conclusion of that teaching, she [addressed] the One of Ten Powers...
Having paid homage, she set out toward the city. That maidservant, however, not having noticed where she had placed the ornaments she herself had taken, turned back to retrieve them.
Then Visākhā asked her, "But where did you place that? "In the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber, mistress," she replied. "Very well, girl; go and bring it."
"From the time it was placed in the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber, it has been improper for us to continue having it brought here.
Therefore, we shall dispose of it and perform an act of penance (*daṇḍakamma*). Furthermore, when it is kept there, it becomes an impediment for the noble ones (*ayya*).
On the following day, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), arrived at the door of Visākhā’s residence. In the residence...
and seats were arranged. Visākhā took the Teacher’s bowl, led the Teacher into her house, and had him sit upon the very seats that had been prepared.
When the Teacher had finished his meal, she brought that ornament, placed it at the Teacher’s feet, and said, “Venerable Sir, I give this to you. The Teacher replied, “An ornament, indeed...”
"It is not permitted for those who have gone forth," he refused. "Venerable sir, I know this;
however, after having this appraised and taking the wealth, I shall have a fragrant chamber built for you to dwell in. Then the Teacher consented.
She too, having had it appraised and taken nine crores of wealth, [built] for the Tathāgata at the Pubbārāma Monastery, which was adorned with a thousand cells...

She had a fragrant chamber for her robes constructed. At the time of the morning meal, however, Visākhā’s residence was filled with the radiance of the saffron robes and the fragrance of the scent of the seers, just like the house of Anāthapiṇḍika.
In her home as well, all the meals were already prepared. Having provided material support to the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus at the time of the morning meal, she [attended] after the meal...
Having had medicines and the eight kinds of drinks prepared, she went to the monastery, gave them to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
and afterwards returned after hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse. Later,
when the Teacher was assigning the laywomen to their respective ranks, he placed Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, in the foremost position among donors.
Khujjuttarā-Sāmāvatī-vatthu (260–261). Regarding the third and fourth [suttas]:
"Among those who are learned, namely Khujjuttarā; among those who dwell in loving-kindness, namely Sāmāvatī.
This shows that Khujjuttarā is the foremost among female lay disciples who are learned, and Sāmāvatī is the foremost among those who dwell in loving-kindness.
It is said that both of them, having taken rebirth in noble families in Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha,
went to the monastery later on, thinking, "We shall listen to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma. There, Khujjuttarā,
seeing the Teacher appointing a certain laywoman to the position of being foremost among those of great learning, performed a work of merit and [attained] that station.
Sāmāvatī, too, having seen one laywoman placed in the foremost position among those who dwell in loving-kindness,
performed meritorious deeds and aspired to that same station. After both of them had practiced virtue throughout their lives and were reborn in the world of the gods,
a hundred thousand aeons passed while they continued to wander among gods and humans.
Now, even before our Teacher was born, a disease called "serpent-wind" broke out in the kingdom of Allakappa.
In every single house, ten, twenty, or even thirty people would die at once;
however, those who went to another kingdom would regain their lives. Having learned of this, a certain man took his wife and children and [set out for] another kingdom.
“I shall go,” he said, and departed from there. Then the provisions he had taken for his journey in his house were completely exhausted even before they had crossed the wilderness on the way.
Their physical strength failed them; at times the mother would lift up the son, and at times the father.
Then his father thought: “Our physical strength has failed us; while traveling by lifting our son, we shall [perish].”
"We shall not be able to cross the wilderness. Without informing his mother, he acted as if delayed by the business of water;
having seated his son on the path, he set out alone.
Then his wife, standing and watching for his arrival, not seeing her son in her hand, went forth crying out, "My lord, where is my son? and said, "Where is my son?"
“What use have you for a son? We shall obtain a son while we are still alive.
She said, “This man is truly reckless! and added, “Go away; I will not go with such a person as you.
He replied, “My lady, I acted without due reflection; please forgive me,” and having taken his son, he returned.
Having crossed that wilderness, they reached a herdsmen’s settlement in the evening. On that day, the residents of the herdsmen’s settlement had cooked rice gruel without water.

Seeing them, [the herdsmen thought], "These people are extremely hungry," and filling a large vessel with the gruel, they poured a ladleful of ghee over it and gave it to them. While they were eating that gruel, [the Buddha said:]
That woman ate within moderation, but the man, having eaten beyond measure, was unable to digest it and passed away immediately after the first watch of the night.

As he was dying, due to his lingering attachment to those things, he took rebirth in the womb of a female dog in the house of the cowherds. Not long thereafter, the female dog gave birth. The cowherd...
Having seen that dog, which was full of splendor, he enticed it with alms-food and, seizing upon the affection that had arisen within himself, he lived solely on faith.
Then one day, at the time for the alms-round, a paccekabuddha arrived at the gate of the cowherd’s house.
Seeing him, the cowherd gave him alms-food and obtained his promise to stay, depending upon him. Thus the paccekabuddha—
He took up residence in a forest thicket not far from the cowherd’s settlement.

As the cowherd went to his presence, he would go along taking that dog with him; and along the way, in places where there were wild beasts, he would strike a tree or a rock for the sake of making the wild beasts flee, and the dog [observed] his manner of acting.
He established [this]. Then one day, that cowherd sat near the Paccekabuddha and said, "Venerable sir, we do not have you visiting us at all times. However, this dog is clever;
you should come to our house door whenever he perceives that you have arrived. One day, [the cowherd] said, "Come, taking the Paccekabuddha with you."
He sent a dog. Having heard his command, the dog went at the time for alms-round and lay down on its chest at the feet of the paccekabuddha.
The paccekabuddha, knowing that "this one has come into my presence," took his bowl and robe and set out on the path.
In order to test him, the king stepped aside and took another path; the dog—
Standing in front, he stepped aside at the moment the cowherd set out upon his path.
And at whatever spot the cowherd struck a tree or a stone for the purpose of scaring away wild beasts, as soon as the dog reached that place, it let out a great howl.
By that sound, the wild beasts fled. At the time of the meal, the Paccekabuddha too—
He gave him a large, affectionate lump of food. By receiving that alms-food, he too felt even greater affection for the Paccekabuddha.
When three months had passed, the cowherd gave the Paccekabuddha a cloth sufficient for a triple robe and said, "Venerable sir, if it pleases you, stay right here;
if it does not please you, go wherever you wish. The Paccekabuddha—
He shows the manner of going. That cowherd, having followed the Paccekabuddha, turns back.
The dog, knowing that the Paccekabuddha was going elsewhere, died with intense grief arising from his lack of affection, which reached the point of splitting his heart;
he was reborn in the city of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa). Then, at the time when [the cowherd] was traveling together with the Paccekabuddha, there was a loud noise...
Because he had caused the wild beasts to flee while conversing with the deities, his voice stood resounding, covering the entire city of the gods.
He received that very name and became known as the divine son Ghosaka.
Then, while he was enjoying such prosperity, there was a king named Udena ruling in the city of Kosambī on the human path.
He practiced accordingly. The background story for this should be understood in the same manner as related in the commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra-sutta in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa.
While he was ruling the kingdom, the deva-son Ghosaka passed away and took rebirth in the womb of a certain courtesan in Kosambī.
When ten months had elapsed, she gave birth; and having realized it was a son, she [threw him] onto a rubbish heap.
He had [the child] abandoned. At that moment, the steward of the Kosambi merchant, going to the merchant’s house early in the morning, saw that the place was surrounded by crows.
Having gone there and seen the boy, he thought, "This boy must be one of great merit," and sent a man to the house with his hand [as a sign]. He then went to the merchant’s house. The merchant also—
On his way to the royal palace at the time for attending upon the king, he saw the family priest on the road and asked, "What is the constellation today?
Standing right there, the priest calculated and said, "It is such-and-such a constellation;
a child born today under this constellation will obtain the position of a treasurer in this city. Having heard his words, he...
He sent him home in haste, saying: "This chaplain has two things he cannot do; my wife is heavily pregnant.
Find out for now whether she has given birth or not. They went, found out, and said: "Noble sir, she has not yet given birth. "In that case, go;
search this city today for a newborn boy. As they were searching, [they found one].
When they saw that boy in the house of the merchant’s overseer, they informed the merchant.
He said, "In that case, go, men, and summon that overseer. They summoned him.
Then the merchant asked him, "I hear you have a boy in your house? "Yes, sir," he replied. "Give that boy to us," the merchant said.
“I will not give it, noble lady,” he replied. “Well then, take a thousand [pieces] and give her,” she said.
Thinking, “Whether she lives or dies is difficult to know,” he took the thousand and gave them.
Then the merchant thought: “If my wife gives birth to a daughter, I shall make this very boy my son.”
"If she gives birth to a son, I shall kill him. Having thought this, he maintained her in his house. Then, after a few days had passed, his wife gave birth to a son.
Thereupon, the merchant, thinking, "In this way they will trample and kill him," said, "Lay this boy down at the gate of the diamond-stone. They laid him there. Then the bull, the leader of the herd—
Seeing him as he first emerged, [the cow] stood with him between her four legs, thinking, "In this way, others will not trample him.
Then, when the cowherds saw him, they thought, "This child must possess great merit, since even an animal knows his virtue; we shall look after him," and they led him to their own home.

The merchant, investigating the matter of his death and hearing that he had been taken away by cowherds, again gave a thousand pieces of money, issued orders, and had him discarded in the raw charnel ground. At that time, a goat-herd was grazing goats near the cemetery on the merchant’s property.
Then, one milch-goat, through the merit of the boy, left the path and went toward the boy.
Having given the milk, she departed. Then, returning, she went there in the same manner and gave him the milk once more.
The goat-herd thought, "This she-goat has left this place and gone even before dawn; what could this mean?
Going there and looking about, he saw the boy and thought, "This boy possesses great merit; even animals recognize his virtue. I shall take care of him."
Saying "No," he took him and went home.
On the following day, the merchant, looking to see whether the boy was dead or not, learned that he had been taken by the goat-herd;
he gave him a thousand pieces of money, gave orders, and said: "Tomorrow, the son of a certain caravan leader will enter this city."
"Take this boy and place him on the path of the wheels; thus the cart wheel will pass along, cutting through him," he said.
When it was placed there, the oxen of the caravan leader’s son’s first cart saw it and stood still, planting their four feet like pillars.
The caravan leader asked, "What is the reason for their standing still? regarding their cause for stopping.
Looking about, he saw the boy and thought, "This is a boy of great merit; it is fitting that I should look after him. Taking him, he departed.
The merchant, meanwhile, keeping watch to see whether the boy was dead or alive within his range of vision, learned from the caravan leader that he had been taken away.
He gave a thousand pieces of money to the leader as well, issued orders, and had the boy thrown over a precipice in a place not far from the city. He—
As he fell there, he landed in a single-hall workshop belonging to some reed-makers. By the power of his merit, that hall became as soft to the touch as a hundred-fold beaten cotton ball.
Then the chief of the reed-makers, thinking, "This child is meritorious;
it is right to look after him," took him and went home. At the spot where the merchant’s son had fallen from the precipice—
While he was searching for someone who had either stolen it or knew its whereabouts, he learned that it had been taken by Naḷakāra the chief;
knowing this, he gave him a thousand pieces of money as well and issued an order.
Later on, both the merchant’s own son and the other boy reached maturity. Then the merchant [again] regarding the boy Ghosaka...
While contemplating a means for his death, he went to the house of his own potter and said, "My good man, there is a certain unworthy son in my house;
it is necessary to kill that boy by any means possible in secret.
Covering both his ears, the potter replied, "It is not right to speak such a grave word as this."
He said: Then the merchant, thinking, "This man will not do it for nothing," said, "Come now, sir, take a thousand [pieces] and carry out this work.

For a bribe indeed breaks what has not been broken; therefore, having received and accepted the thousand, he said, "Noble sir, on such-and-such a day I shall apply the ointment to the pit; at that time, that boy..."
"Send him at such-and-such a time," he said. The merchant, having accepted his word, began counting the days from then on;
when he realized that the day specified by the potter had arrived, he summoned Prince Ghosaka and said, "Dear son, on such-and-such a day we have need of many vessels; you [must go] to our potter..."
"Go to him and say, 'It seems your father has told you something; complete it today.
He replied, "Very well," and accepted his words, then departed.
Now, on the way, the merchant's own son, who was playing with marbles, saw him and went toward him in haste, saying, "I..."
"Brother," he said, "you have won this much while playing with the children; having lost it to me, give it back.
He replied, "I have no time now; my father has sent me to the potter on urgent business.
The other said, "I will go there myself, brother; you play with these children until my turn comes."

"Bring it back and give it to me," he said. "In that case, go then," [the potter replied], and having delivered his own message to him, he played with the children. That prince also went to the potter and reported the message.
He said, "Very well, dear boy, I shall prepare it," and having ushered the prince into the workshop, he took a sharp adze.
Having cut it into pieces, he placed them in a jar, closed the mouth of the jar, set it inside another vessel, and lit a fire beneath it.
Prince Ghosaka, having won many games, sat waiting for his younger brother’s arrival.
Perceiving that he was taking a long time, he wondered, "Why is he so late? and went toward the vicinity of the potter's house. Somewhere...
Seeing him, [the man] thought, "He will go home," and turning back, he went to his house.
When the merchant saw him coming from afar, he thought, "What could be the reason?
I sent this man to the potter for the purpose of killing him, yet now he is returning here again. As he was still approaching, [the merchant...]
“Why, dear one, did you not go to the potter’s place? he asked. “Yes, father, we did not go,” he replied.
“For what reason, dear one? He then related both the reason for his own turning back and the reason why his younger brother had gone there.
From the moment the merchant heard those words, he felt as if he were submerged by the great earth, and cried out, “What—”

“Do you say this? With a mind full of agitation, he hurried to the potter and, because it was something he could not have told anyone else, cried out, “Look, sir! Look, sir! “What are you making me look at?
“This work is finished. He turned back right there and went home. From that time on, for him—
A mental illness arose in him.
At that time, not eating with him and breaking his fast, he thought, "By whatever means possible,
it is right for me to see an opening in my son's enemy," and having written a letter, he summoned Prince Ghosaka.
“Take this letter and go to the village named so-and-so; there is our agent there.
Go to him, give him this letter, and say: ‘Please carry out the message on this letter with haste.
On the way, there is a certain merchant named our friend, the village headman; go to his house and [eat] food.”
“Eat and then depart,” he gave as his oral instruction. Having paid homage to the merchant and taken the letter, he set out;

on the way, he went to the residence of a village headman, asked for his house, and having sat down outside the gateway while the man was having his beard groomed, he paid homage and stood there. “From where...? [he asked.]
When he was asked, "Are you coming, dear? he replied, "I am the son of the Kosambi merchant, dear.

At that moment, the merchant was overjoyed and delighted, thinking, "He is the son of our friend, the merchant. And at that very instant, a maidservant belonging to the merchant's daughter was going to fetch flowers for the merchant's daughter.
Then the merchant said to her, "Mother, setting aside this work, wash Ghosaka Kumāra’s feet, spread out his bed, and give it to him.
She did so, went to the shop, and brought flowers for the merchant's daughter.
When the merchant's daughter saw her, she became angry and said, "You have been dawdling outside for a long time today! What is the matter with you?"
“How long has he been here? she asked. “Do not speak thus, noble lady; I have never seen anyone like him before.
It is said that he is the son of a merchant who was a friend of your father. His physical perfection cannot even be described.
When I went to fetch flowers, the merchant told me: ‘Wash the feet of that young man, spread out his bed, and...’”
"Give me [a drink]," she said; "therefore, I have been delaying outside for a long time. That merchant’s daughter had been the mistress of that young man's household during his fourth existence;

therefore, from the moment she heard those words, she was no longer aware of whether she herself was standing or sitting. Taking that very maidservant with her, she went to the place where he was lying down.
Having gone there and observed him sleeping, and seeing a leaf upon his garment, he thought, "What indeed is this leaf?
Without waking the prince, he took the leaf and read it, thinking, "This man has come here having himself taken a death-warrant.
While the prince was still asleep, he tore that leaf and said, "By me, in your presence..."
"My son has been sent: my friend, the village headman, has a daughter who has reached marriageable age.

You must quickly take wealth and produce from our place of business and, for a total of one hundred thousand, take my son’s hand in marriage with the daughter of that village headman and perform the auspicious ceremony.
Once the ceremony is completed, [report] 'This was done by me according to this procedure.'"
"Send a message to me; I shall know what must be done for you here.
Having written this on a letter and affixed his own seal, he first bound it to the hem of his garment according to the established custom.
That prince, having stayed there that day, requested leave from the merchant the following day and [approached] the official...
Having gone to the village, he delivered a letter. The official read the letter, assembled the villagers, and said: "Do not disregard me;
my master has sent me here to bring a maiden for his eldest son at a cost of a hundred pieces of gold.
Quickly gather all the requisites for the auspicious ceremony in this place. Thus he arranged for all the festive honors.
Having made preparations and sent a message to the village headman, and having received his consent,
he completed the auspicious ceremony with all his wealth and then dispatched a letter to the Kosambi headman, saying: "Having heard the message in the letter sent by you,
I have performed this and that."
Upon hearing that message, the merchant felt as if he were consumed by fire; thinking, "Now I am lost," he was stricken with the disease of internal hemorrhaging.
He resolved, "By whatever means possible, I shall summon him and make my property ownerless.
Thus he said, "Ever since the completion of Maṅgala’s festival, why has my son been away? Let him return quickly!"
He sent a message. Upon hearing the message, when the prince was about to depart, the merchant’s daughter thought:
"This fool does not realize that he obtained this prosperity by depending on me; I must do whatever is necessary to find a means to prevent his departure.
Then she said to him: "Prince, do not go with such haste; when going to your family village..."
"It is fitting for you to go, having made a solemn vow to yourself.
The merchant of Kosambī, perceiving his son's delay, sent a message again: "Why does my son delay?
I have fallen ill with dysentery; it is fitting that he come and see me while I am still alive."
At that time, the merchant’s daughter informed him: “This is not your father; you have merely formed the perception that he is your father.
He sent a letter to the official for the purpose of having you executed.
I removed that letter and, having written another message, I brought about this prosperity for you. He intended to leave you childless.”
“Summon him and wait for his death. Then, having heard that he had already passed away while still living, he went to the city of Kosambī.

The merchant’s daughter also gave him a signal outside, saying, “As you enter, enter as if you were establishing your own protection throughout the entire house. She herself, together with the merchant’s son...
Having entered, he raised both hands and, as if weeping, went to the presence of the merchant who was lying in a dark place and struck him in the chest with his head.
Because of his weakness, the merchant died from that very blow.
The prince, having performed the funeral rites for his father, said: "You say of me that I am the son of the Great Merchant."

He gave a bribe to the king’s footmen. Then, on the seventh day, the king sent word, saying, “It is necessary to find someone worthy of the position of treasurer; find out whether the treasurer has sons or not.
The king’s footmen told the king that the treasurer had sons. The king accepted this, saying, “Very well,” and [appointed] him to the position of treasurer.
He gave [the gift]. He became known as Ghosaka the merchant. Then his wife said to him:
"Noble son, you too were born of low birth, and I was reborn into a poor family. Yet, by virtue of wholesome deeds performed in the past, we have obtained such prosperity;
let us now also perform wholesome deeds. Having agreed, saying, "Very well, dear lady," he [gave] a thousand [pieces of money] every day.
Having distributed [the wealth], he established a gift.

At that time, of those two women, Khujjuttarā, having passed away from the deva-world, took rebirth in the womb of a nurse in the house of the merchant Ghosaka. Because she was hunchbacked at birth, she was called Khujjuttarā.

They gave her that name. Sāmāvatī, too, having descended from the world of the devas, took rebirth in the house of the merchant Bhaddavatiya in the city of Bhaddiya in the kingdom of Bhaddavati; they gave her the name Sāmā.
Later on, a fear of famine arose in that city, and people, terrified by the fear of famine, fled in every direction. At that time, this merchant Bhaddavatiya—
He consulted with his wife: "My dear, no end to this fear of famine is in sight.
Let us go to our friend, the merchant Ghosaka, in the city of Kosambī; he will not neglect us when he sees us.
It is said that the merchant had never seen that friend before, and therefore he spoke thus. Having sent the other people back, he—
Taking his wife and daughter, he set out on the road to the city of Kosambī.
The three of them, experiencing great suffering along the way, eventually reached Kosambī in due course and took up residence in a certain hall.
Meanwhile, the merchant Ghosaka caused a great almsgiving to be distributed at the door of his own house for the poor, the needy, the destitute, and beggars.
Then the merchant Bhaddavatiya thought: "It is not possible for us to show ourselves to our friend while in this miserable guise;
when our bodies have returned to their natural state, we shall see the merchant well-dressed and well-robed.
So both of them sent their daughter to the head of the almsgiving of the merchant Ghosaka. She went there for the purpose of bringing her own food.
Taking her bowl, she went to the head of the almsgiving line and stood in one spot with an air of modesty. Seeing her, the distributor of gifts thought:
"The other people go taking [the food] while making a great clamor, like fishermen hauling in a catch;
but this girl must be a daughter of noble family, for she possesses the excellence of personal refinement."
Then he said to her, "Mother, why do you not take [this food] and go, like the other people?
"Father, how could I enter such a crowded place? "But mother, how many people are there with you?
"There are three, father. He gave her three portions of rice. She gave that food to her mother and father; for a long time, the father—
Because she was hungry, she ate an excessive amount and passed away. On the following day, she went again and took only two morsels of food.
That very day, the merchant’s wife, exhausted from eating too much and due to the grief over the merchant’s death, passed away immediately after the first watch of the night.
On the next day, the merchant’s daughter took only a single morsel of food.
She took them. The alms-collector, having observed her conduct, asked, "Mother, on the first day you took three morsels of alms, on the next day two, and today you take only one.
What is the reason for this? She explained the reason to him. He then asked, "Mother, where do you live? In which village do you dwell? She told him that reason in full detail as well.
He spoke: "Mother, this being so, you were indeed called our merchant’s daughter; furthermore, I have no other girl.
From now on, Mother, you are my daughter. Having thus adopted her as his daughter, he took her.
Rising up again and again, she heard the great clamor at the alms-giving and asked, "Father, why is there this loud noise and great shouting?"
He said, "Mother, it is not possible to make a small noise in the midst of a great crowd. I know a way for this, dear father.

"What should be done, mother? [he asked]. "Having built a fence all around and fitted two doors, and having had vessels placed inside, one should enter through one door, take the food, and [exit] through the other door."
"Go forth, dear ones," he said. "Very well, mother," they replied, and from the following day onward, they acted accordingly.
From that time on, the assembly for giving was as silent as a lotus pond when its creatures are settled.
Then, the merchant Ghosaka, who had previously heard a loud and great clamor at the assembly for giving, did not hear it this time.
Having summoned the superintendent of alms-giving, he asked: "Did you not cause alms to be given today? "It was given, venerable sir.
"Then why is the sound of the alms-offering not heard as it was before? "Yes, venerable sir, I have a daughter;
standing by the means she suggested, I caused the alms-offering to be made without noise. "You have no such daughter," [the king said].
"From where did you obtain this daughter? He, being unable to deceive him, told the merchant everything regarding the manner of his daughter's arrival.
"But why, sir, did you commit such a grave act?
You did not inform me that my daughter had been living in your presence for all this time; quickly order her to come to our house!"
Having heard his words, he gave the order reluctantly. From that time forth, the merchant,
treating her as if she were his own daughter, thinking, "I shall provide honor for my daughter," made five hundred young maidens of equal age and from families of similar status her retinue.
Then one day, King Udena, while wandering through the city, saw Sāmāvatī playing, surrounded by those young girls.
Having asked, "Whose daughter is this girl? and having heard that she was the daughter of the merchant Ghosaka, he inquired whether she had a husband or not.
When it was stated that she was without a husband, he said, "Go and tell the merchant: 'Bring your daughter [to me].'"
"The king desires her. Upon hearing this, the merchant said, "We have no other daughters;
we cannot give away our only child while she still has co-wives. When the king heard these words, he sent the merchant and the merchant's wife outside and had the entire house sealed.
As Sāmāvatī was returning from playing outside, she saw her parents sitting outside.
Seeing them, he asked, "Mother and father, why are you sitting here? They explained the reason to him. He said, "Mother and father, why do you not know this reply:
'My daughter, while living in her husband's household, will not be able to live alone;
if you provide her with five hundred young women as attendants, she will be able to live there'?"
"Now speak thus, dear ones. "Very well, mother; we did not know your mind," they said, and so they spoke accordingly.
The king, becoming even more confident, said, "Let there be a thousand; bring them all.
Then, under an auspicious constellation and moment, he brought her to the royal palace with five hundred women as her retinue.
They led her away. The king, making those five hundred women her retinue, performed the consecration for her and had her dwell separately in a palace of her own.

At that time, in Kosambī, there were three people—the merchant Ghosaka, the merchant Kukkuṭa, and the merchant Pavārika—who were friends with one another. Those three men looked after five hundred ascetics. The ascetics, too—
Having lived in their presence for four months, they dwell in the Himalayas for eight months.

Then one day, while those ascetics were returning from the Himalayas, exhausted and thirsty in a great wilderness, they came upon a large banyan tree and sat down there, seeking hospitality from the deity dwelling therein. The deity—
Extending her hand, adorned with every ornament, she gave them water for drinking and other refreshments, thereby dispelling their fatigue.
Awestruck by the power of the deity, they asked:
"O deity, what deed did you perform to obtain this prosperity? The deity replied: "In the world, a Blessed One named Buddha has appeared."
He is currently staying at Sāvatthī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika attends upon him.
On the Uposatha days, after giving his own hired laborers their regular food and wages, he would have them observe the Uposatha.
Then one day, having arrived at midday for my morning meal, I did not see any of the laborers performing work, and [thought]: "Today the people..."
"Why do they not perform the work? I asked. They explained this matter to me.
Then I said, "Now half a day has passed; is it possible to observe half of the Uposatha?
Thereupon, having informed the merchant, he replied, "It is possible. So, having undertaken the Uposatha for half a day, on that very day—
Having passed away, they obtain this prosperity.

Then those ascetics, having conceived joy and gladness upon hearing that "the Buddha has indeed appeared," and though they desired to go from there to Sāvatthī, thought, "Our chief patrons have been very helpful to us;
we shall inform them of this matter as well," and [went] to Kosambī.
Having arrived and received great honor and respect from the merchants, they said, "We shall depart this very day. When asked, "Venerable sirs, why are you in such a hurry?
Do you not usually stay for four or five months before departing? they related what had occurred.
And when they were told, "In that case, Venerable sirs, let us go together," they replied, "We are going; as for you..."
“Come slowly,” they were told. Having gone to Sāvatthī and gone forth in the presence of the Blessed One, they attained arahantship.
Later, those two merchants, accompanied by five hundred carts each, went to Sāvatthī;
having pitched camp not far from the Jeta Grove, they approached the Teacher, prostrated themselves with the fivefold salutation, and—
They sat down to one side. The Teacher taught the Dhamma to them according to their individual dispositions.

At the conclusion of the teaching, all three were established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). Having invited [the Buddha] for the following day’s meal, they gave a great almsgiving (*mahādāna*) on the next day to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
Following that same procedure, they invited him for the following day as well, and for half a month they provided food for the camp (*khandhāvāra-bhatta*).
Having given their names, they requested the Teacher to come to their own city. The Teacher said, "Tathāgatas take delight in empty dwellings.
They replied, "Understood, Bhante," and added, "You should come at our message being sent.
Having paid homage to the Teacher and circumambulated him three times, they departed for their own city.
Having arrived, those two men also each had a monastery built in their own park. The one built by the merchant Ghosaka became known as the Ghositārāma;
the one built by the merchant Kukkuṭa became known as the Kukkuṭārāma; and the one built by the merchant Pāvārika became known as the Pāvārikambavana.
After having these monasteries constructed, they sent a messenger to the Teacher, saying: "Teacher..."
“Please come to this city to show us favor. The Teacher, intending to go to Kosambī, set out on a journey accompanied by a great community of monks.
On the way, perceiving that the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya possessed the necessary conditions for attaining Arahatship, he halted his progress and went to the town named Kammāsadamma in the kingdom of Kuru.
At that time, Māgaṇḍiya, having burned offerings outside the village throughout the entire night, was entering the village early in the morning.
As the Teacher was entering the village for alms on the following day, he presented himself on the path before the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya.
Upon seeing the One of Ten Powers, he thought: "For all this time, because of my daughter’s perfection of beauty..."
"I have been wandering about seeking a boy like him; even though he was endowed with such physical beauty, I desired one who had already taken up the life of a renunciant.
This renunciant here is handsome and lovely to behold, and is truly a suitable match for my daughter.
With these words, he went quickly home. It is said that this brahmin had a family tradition of renunciation from former times, and because of that—
Upon seeing him who had gone forth, his heart was inclined toward him. He addressed the brahmin lady:
"My dear, I have never before seen such a one as this renunciant—golden-hued and with the appearance of Brahmā; he is truly worthy of my daughter.
Quickly adorn my daughter for me. Even as the brahmin lady was adorning her daughter, the Teacher stood at his own place.
Having shown the foot-relic shrines (*padacetiyāni*), he entered the city.
Then, as the brahmin was entering the village on his way back to that place with his wife and daughter, he looked here and there because he had arrived late;
not seeing the One of Ten Powers (*dasabala*), he rebuked his wife.
“There is no good reason for you; while you were still making a fuss, he went forth and departed.
“Brahmin, let it be that he has gone; in which direction did he go?
“In this direction,” she replied, and as she looked toward the place where the Teacher had gone, she saw the footprints and said, “Bhadde, these are the footprints of that man.”
"He will have gone from here," he said. Then, O Brahmin lady, seeing the Teacher’s footprint shrine, she thought, "How foolish this Brahmin is, not even knowing the meaning of his own own book!
And mocking him, she said: "How very foolish you are, Brahmin, to think that you shall give your daughter to such a man as this!"
You say this. For such a footprint as this does not belong to a person who is stained by lust, corrupted by hatred, or deluded by ignorance.
But behold, Brahmin, this is the footprint of the All-Knowing Buddha, whose veil has been removed from the world:
“For one who is stained, the footprint would be crouching;”
For the wicked man there is a downward-dragging foot;
for the deluded man there is a sudden pressing down;
such is the foot of one whose veil has been lifted.
Even though the brahmin woman spoke at such length, he did not listen and said, "You are indeed fierce and talkative.

While the two of them were still quarreling with one another, the Teacher, having walked for alms and finished his meal together with the community of monks, departed from within the very range of the brahmin’s sight. The brahmin [saw] the Teacher from afar...
Seeing him approaching, he sent away the brahmin woman and, standing before the One of Ten Powers with a face beaming with joy, cried out, "O renunciant!
This is that man! Since early morning I have been wandering about searching for you;
in this Jambudīpa, there is no woman equal in beauty to my daughter, nor is there any man equal in beauty to you."
“There is no such thing; I give my daughter to you for your support, so take her,” he said.

Then the Teacher replied to him: “Brahmin, even though daughters of the gods—dwellers in the realm of desire, possessing supreme beauty, and having come to tempt me while standing near me and speaking in various ways—did not please me, how much less [this woman]?”
Having said, "I shall take this one," he spoke this verse:
"Having seen craving, aversion, and passion,
there was no desire even for sexual union."
"What is this of mine, filled with urine and excrement?
I would not even wish my feet to touch it.
Māgaṇḍiyā thought: "It is indeed appropriate for one who has no interest to say 'enough. But this man..."

Having described the body as being "full of urine and excrement," she said, "I would not even wish to touch its feet," and harbored a grudge, thinking, "If I obtain a position of authority, I shall see to it that he is ruined.
The Teacher, disregarding her, began to teach the Dhamma to the brahmin according to his temperament. At the conclusion of the teaching, both husband and wife—
Having established themselves in the fruit of non-returning, they thought, “Now we have no further need for the household life.
They gave their daughter Māgaṇḍiyā in marriage to her younger paternal uncle, and both went forth into homelessness and attained arahantship.
Then King Udena, having conducted business with Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, brought the maiden Māgaṇḍiyā into his home by means of royal power.
Having performed the consecration, he gave her a separate palace as a residence for herself and her retinue of five hundred women.
The Teacher, meanwhile, traveling by stages on his journey, arrived at the city of Kosambī.
Upon hearing that the Teacher was approaching, the merchant went out to meet him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and sat to one side; then he addressed the Blessed One.
They said this: “Venerable sir, these three dwellings have been built for you;
please accept them, venerable sir, for the sake of supporting the Saṅgha from the four quarters. The Blessed One accepted the dwellings.
Then those three merchants, having invited the Teacher for the following day’s meal and paid homage to him, went to their own homes.
When Māgaṇḍiyā heard that the Teacher had arrived, she summoned some rogue ruffians who were disreputable and broken,
gave them a bribe, and sent them away, saying, "You must abuse the ascetic Gotama in this and that manner.
When the Teacher entered the village, they abused him and his retinue with various kinds of insults.
The Venerable Ānanda said to the Teacher, “Bhante, we shall not dwell in such a place of abuse;
let us go to another city. The Teacher replied, “Ānanda, the Tathāgatas are unshaken by the eight worldly conditions.
This noise will not last beyond seven days; it will fall back upon those very who revile us. Do not worry about this.”
The three guild-presidents of the city, having ushered the Blessed One in with great honor, gave a great almsgiving.
As they continued giving alms one after another, a month passed; then it occurred to them:
"Buddhas indeed arise out of compassion for the entire world; let us give opportunity to others as well. Thereupon, even the inhabitants of the city of Kosambī...
They made way for the people. From that time on, the citizens also gave great alms in their respective streets and community groups.
Then one day, the Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, sat down in the house of the chief florist.
At that moment, Khujjuttarā, Sāmāvatī’s attendant, took eight kahāpaṇas and went to that house for flowers.
She arrived. When the head gardener saw her, he said, "Sister Uttara, today you have no time to give flowers;
I am serving the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. You too must be a helper at the distribution of food;
in this way, you will be released from having to perform services for others hereafter. Then Khujjuttarā herself—
Having eaten the food she had received, she performed services for the Buddhas in the meal-hall. She mastered everything of the Dhamma spoken by the Teacher during the course of his seated discourse.
Furthermore, having heard the words of thanksgiving, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
On other days she would go after giving four kahāpaṇas and taking flowers; but on that [day], however—

On that day, having seen the truth and not giving rise to desire for another's property, he gave all eight kahāpaṇas, filled his basket, took the flowers, and went into the presence of Sāmāvatī. Then she asked him:
"Mother Uttarā, you do not bring many flowers on other days; but today there are many."
“Has the King become even more favorably disposed toward us? Because she was incapable of speaking falsehoods, she did not conceal what she had done in the past and told everything.
When asked, “Then why have you brought so many flowers today? she replied:
“Today, having heard the Dhamma from the One of Ten Powers, I have realized the Deathless; therefore, I do not deceive you. Thus she spoke.
Having heard this, they all extended their hands, saying, "Mother Uttara, give us also the Deathless Dhamma you have attained.
She replied, "Noble ladies, it is not possible to give it in that way; however, I shall teach you the Dhamma according to the method explained by the Teacher.
When the cause exists within yourselves, you will attain that Dhamma. She said, "In that case..."
“Mother Uttara, tell us,” they said. “It is not possible to speak in such a manner; prepare a high seat for me and you yourselves sit on low seats,” she replied.
Those five hundred women gave a high seat to Khujjuttarā and, taking low seats themselves, sat down.
Khujjuttarā, established in the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of one still in training (*sekkha*), [proceeded] to them...
He taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, with Sāmāvatī as their leader, they all became established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).

From then on, having removed Khujjuttarā from her duties of service, they said to her, "Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, bring it back and teach it to us. And from that time forth, Khujjuttarā did exactly so.
But why was she reborn as a slave? It is said that during the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, she performed service for a certain novice nun.
By that kamma, she was reborn as a slave to others for five hundred births.
And why was she hunchbacked? It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, she was living in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī.

Having seen a certain Paccekabuddha named Khujjadhātuka who was a frequent visitor to the royal palace, she mocked him in front of the women with whom she lived and moved about in a hunchbacked manner. Therefore, she was reborn as a hunchback.
But what did she do to be born so wise? While the Buddha had not yet appeared, she lived in the household of the King of Bārāṇasī and [performed] eight...
Seeing a Paccekabuddha departing after taking a bowl filled with warm milk-rice from the royal palace,
she said, "Venerable sir, please set this down here before you go," and having removed eight golden bracelets, she gave them to him.
Through the result of that deed, she was reborn endowed with wisdom.
Then those five hundred women who were Sāmāvatī’s attendants, although they had already penetrated the Truths, because of the king’s lack of faith,
did not obtain the opportunity to see the Buddha from time to time when they went into the presence of the Teacher.
Therefore, when the One of Ten Powers entered the street, as there was no room at the windows, they made a hole in each of their own rooms.
Having done so, they looked out from there. Then one day, Māgaṇḍiyā, having stepped down from the terrace of her own palace and walking about, went to their dwelling place;

seeing a gap in the wall, she asked, "What is this? Not knowing that the Teacher harbored a deep-seated enmity toward her, they replied, "The Teacher has come to this city; we are standing here [watching] the Teacher."
When they said, "We shall both see him and pay him honor," he thought, "Now I shall know what must be done for him;

these women are his attendants, and I shall also know what must be done for them. Having gone there, when he was alone with the king, he said, "Great King, Sāmāvatī and her companions have external designs; in just a few days they will take your life. Sāmāvatī—"
“Together with her retinue, she feels neither affection nor love for you;
rather, when she sees the ascetic Gotama walking along the middle of the street, even though there is no room at the windows, she breaks them open to make space and gazes out,” he said.
The king did not believe it, thinking, “They would not do such a thing. Even when it was told again, he still did not believe it.
When he had spoken thus three times, the king still did not believe him, so [the minister] said: "Great King, if you do not believe my words, go to their dwelling place and investigate for yourself.
The king went there and, seeing a hole in the walls of the rooms, asked, "What is this?
When the matter was explained to him, he did not become angry with them; instead, without saying anything, he had the holes closed up.
From that time on, the king had latticed windows with openings above installed in their palaces.
Being unable to provoke the king’s anger for that reason, she said, "Your Majesty, we shall know whether these women have affection for you or not;
send eight cocks and have them cooked for your sake. The king—
Having heard her words, [the king] sent eight cocks to Sāmāvatī with the instruction, "Let her cook these and send them.
But Sāmāvatī, a noble female disciple who had attained the fruit of stream-entry, said, "What need is there to cook living cocks? and refused even to touch them with her hand.
Māgandiyā said, "Very well, Great King; let these very same cocks be for the cooking of the ascetic Gotama."
“Cook them,” she said. The king did so. On the way, however, Māgandiyā had chickens slaughtered and sent word, saying, “Have these chickens cooked and give them to the ascetic Gotama.

Because they were dead and because they had been sent specifically for the One of Ten Powers, she cooked them and sent them to the One of Ten Powers. Māgandiyā said, “See this, Great King! and even with that much...
She was unable to provoke the king to anger.
However, this Udena stayed for seven days at the dwelling place of each of them in turn.
Then Māgandiyā, having had a young black snake placed inside a bamboo tube, set it up at her own dwelling place. [She informed] the king...
It was his custom to always take his *hatthikanta* lute with him wherever he went.
When Māgaṇḍiyā arrived before the king, she placed that young snake inside the lute and had her hole closed up.
Then, as he was going to Sāmāvatī’s presence, [she said], "Great King, the one named Sāmāvatī... [to the ascetic].
“Gotama’s partisans do not count you; whatever he does, he thinks only of your faults. Be vigilant!
she said. After spending seven days in Queen Sāmāvatī’s residence, the king went again on the seventh day to Māgaṇḍiyā’s dwelling.
As soon as he arrived, she asked, “Great King, I hope Sāmāvatī has found no opportunity against you?”
As if saying, "He does not search," she took the lute from the king's hand, played it, and asked, "What is it, Great King, that moves about within here?
Having thus made an opening for the snake to emerge, she cried out, "Aha! There is a snake inside!
and casting away the lute, she fled. At that moment, the king was like a bamboo grove set ablaze, or like salt cast into [boiling water].
Boiling with anger like a cauldron over a fire, he said, "Go quickly and summon Sāmāvatī along with her retinue!
The king’s men went and summoned her.
Having perceived the king’s state of wrath, she gave a signal to the other women: "The king wishes to have you all executed."
He said, "Summon them; today, during the day, you must pervade the king with a specific radiation of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

The king had those women summoned, and having placed them all in a row, he took up his great bow, fitted it with a poisoned arrow, drew the string, and stood ready. At that moment, all those women, headed by Sāmāvatī—
They pervaded him with loving-kindness in limited measure. The king was unable either to shoot the arrow or to withdraw it;
sweat poured from his limbs, his body trembled, saliva fell from his mouth, and he could no longer see what he should grasp.
Then Sāmāvatī asked him, "Are you weary, Great King? "Yes, Queen, I am weary; be my support."
“Excellent, Great King! Aim the arrow at the face of the great earth. The king did so. She made this resolve:
“May the arrow be released from the king’s hand. At that very moment, the arrow was released.
At that same instant, the king submerged himself in the water, and returning with his hair still wet and his clothes still damp, he fell at Sāmāvatī’s feet and said, “Forgive me, Queen!”
"Without investigating, you have done this at the word of those who seek to cause division," he said. "I forgive you, Your Majesty," she replied.
"Very well, Queen; it is only when you have forgiven me in this way that it is truly so.
From now on, give alms to the One of Ten Powers according to your pleasure, and after the meal, go to the monastery and listen to the Dhamma discourse. From today onward for you..."
"I grant you this favor. "In that case, Your Majesty, from this day forward, please request one monk and bring him here, so that he may teach us the Dhamma.
The king went into the presence of the Teacher and, making his request, obtained the Elder Ānanda.
From then on, those five hundred women had the Elder summoned, paid him honor and respect, and once their meal was finished—
They mastered the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder.
One day, inspired by the Elder’s expression of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*), they gave him five hundred upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*).
It is said that in the past, during his time as a tailor, the Elder had given a palm-tree’s worth [of cloth] together with a single needle to a certain Pratyekabuddha.
He gave her a piece of cloth. By the fruit of that needle, he became one of great wisdom in this present existence;
and by the fruit of that piece of cloth, in this very same manner, he obtained garments five hundred times.
Then Māgaṇḍiyā, seeing no other task to be done, said, "Let us go to the garden, Great King. "Very well," [he replied].
“‘Queen! Having understood that the king had accepted her proposal, she summoned her younger brother and said:

‘When we have gone to the pleasure grove, go to Sāmāvatī’s residence, shut Sāmāvatī and her attendants inside, say “By the king’s command,” close the door, wrap it with straw, and set fire to the house. Thus spoke Māgaṇḍiya.
Having heard her words, he did exactly so. On that day, due to the power of the *upapīḷaka* karma they had previously committed, none of those women were able to enter meditative absorption;
instead, they were all consumed by fire at once, like a handful of chaff.
Their guards went to the king and reported, "Your Majesty, they have done this."
The king, searching for who had done it, learned that it was caused by Māgaṇḍiyā. Having summoned her, he said:
“Lady, you have performed a praiseworthy deed by carrying out what ought to have been done by me;
since you were striving for my death as you rose up again and again, you have been executed. I am pleased; I shall grant you prosperity, so summon your kinsmen.”
He said: Having heard the king’s words, she treated even those who were strangers as her own kin and summoned them.

When the king learned that they had all assembled, he had them buried up to their necks in pits dug in the royal courtyard and, while their heads remained above ground, had them ploughed with large iron ploughs until his heads were split open.
He also had Māgaṇḍiya cut into pieces and baked in a bread-pastry pan.
But what was the deed for which Sāmāvatī, together with her retinue, was consumed by fire?
It is said that before the Buddha had appeared, she, having sported in the Ganges with those five hundred women, stood on the outer bank;
when it became cold, she saw the leaf-hut of a Paccekabuddha not far away, and without cleaning the interior, she set fire to the outside.
They were visible. Inside the leaf-hut, the Paccekabuddha was seated, having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
When those flames had been extinguished, they saw the Paccekabuddha and thought, "What have we done?
This Paccekabuddha is the King’s personal attendant; seeing him, the King will be angry with us. We must now clean it up."
"It is fitting," they said, and having added other pieces of wood, they set fire to it.
When the flames were extinguished, the Paccekabuddha emerged from his meditative attainment and, while they were looking on, shook out his robes, rose into the air, and departed.
Because of that deed, they were cooked in hell, and due to the remainder of that karma, they have now met with this misfortune in the midst of the four assemblies.
Then this discussion arose: “Khujjuttarā was indeed one of great learning;
while remaining in the female form, she taught the Dhamma to five hundred women and established them in the fruit of stream-entry.
And Sāmāvatī, by pervading with loving-kindness the arrow discharged at her by the king, warded it off. Thus the great multitude spoke of her virtues as well.

Thus this story arose. Later, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher took that very incident as the occasion for a discourse and established Khujjuttarā in the foremost position among those of great learning, and Sāmāvatī in the foremost position among those who dwell in loving-kindness.
This is the story of Uttarā, the mother of Ānanda.

262. Regarding the phrase "of those who meditate" (*jhāyinīnaṃ*): this indicates that among the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*) who delight in meditation, Uttarā, the mother of Nanda, was the foremost.
It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.

While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain female lay disciple to the position of being the foremost among those who delight in meditation; having seen this, she performed a work of merit (*adhikārakamma*).

Having done so, she aspired for that high station. After wandering among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, during this current appearance of a Buddha, she took rebirth in the womb of the wife of Puṇṇasīha—who was living in dependence on the merchant Sumanaseṭṭhi in the city of Rājagaha; they gave her the name Uttarā.
Then, on a certain festival day of the constellations, the merchant of Rājagaha summoned Puṇṇa and said:
"Dear Puṇṇa, what will a festival or an observance day do for one who is poor? Nevertheless, say this:
'Will you spend the festival by taking the festival expenses and playing, or will you take strong oxen, a plowshare, and a yoke and go to plow?'"
“I will consult with my wife and then let you know, noble lady,” he said, and he reported those words to his wife.
She replied, “The master is called a ‘wealthy man’ because he is powerful;
for him to converse with you is fitting, but you must not abandon your own farming work. Having heard her words, he took his farming implements and went to plow.
On that very day, the Elder Sāriputta, having emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), reflected, "Whom should I assist today?

Perceiving Puṇṇa’s spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he took his bowl and robes at the time for alms-round and, while proceeding to the field where Puṇṇa was plowing, showed himself not far away. Upon seeing the Elder, Puṇṇa [abandoned] his plowing.
Leaving him behind, he went into the presence of the Elder and paid homage by prostrating himself at the five points.
The Elder looked at him and asked for water. It occurred to him, "The noble one must wish to wash his face.
Then, going quickly, he brought a tooth-stick, made it permissible, and gave it to the Elder. While the Elder was chewing the tooth-stick...
Taking the water-strainer out together with his bowl, he filled it with water and brought it back.
The Elder washed his face and set out on the path for alms. Puṇṇa thought:
"On other days the Elder does not take this path, but today he will have taken it for the sake of showing me favor. Oh, that my wife..."
“Place food brought for my sake into the elder’s bowl.
Then his wife, thinking, “Today is an auspicious day,” prepared hard and soft foods according to her own means early in the morning;
taking them, she was on her way to her husband’s field when she saw the elder along the path and thought:
—“On other days, when I see the Elder, I have no gift to give; and even when there is a gift to give, I do not see my noble master.
But today, the meeting of both has occurred. I shall prepare more for my husband and bring it back later;
for now, I will give this food to the Elder. Having thus formed [this resolve] associated with the three types of volition, she...
Having placed that food in the Elder Sāriputta’s bowl, she said, "May I be released from such a life of poverty.
The Elder, saying, "May your aspiration be fulfilled," offered his blessing of appreciation (anumodana) for her, then turned back and went to the monastery.
She too, having returned once more to her own home, prepared food for her husband, took it with her, and went to the field where they were plowing.
Fearing her husband’s anger, she said, "Husband, please wait for me today for one day.
"For what reason? he asked. She replied, "Today, while bringing food, I saw an elder on the road;
I placed your portion of almsfood into the elder's bowl, then returned home, cooked more food, and have now come back with it. "That is pleasing," he said.
"Bhadde, you have done well; I too have given the elder tooth-sticks and water for rinsing his mouth early this morning.
Today has dawned auspiciously for us, as everything belonging to the elder has come entirely under our control.
Thus, the minds of both people became exactly the same. Then Puṇṇa, having finished his meal, placed his head upon his wife's thigh.
He lay down for a moment. Then sleep came over him. After sleeping a little and waking up, he looked toward the place where he had been plowing;
every spot he looked upon appeared as if strewn with great *kosātaki* flowers.
He said to his wife, "My dear, what is this that today this plowed field appears as if it were golden in color?"
“Noble lady, today your eyes seem to be rolling about from being exhausted all day long.
“Bhadde, do not believe me; look for yourself. At that moment, she looked and said, “Noble lady, tell your true nature; it will be exactly so.
Puṇṇa rose up, took a piece of wood, and struck it against the tip of the ploughshare; it was like a ball of sugar [sticking] to the tip of the ploughshare.
Having approached, he stood there. He called his wife and said:
"My dear, the seed sown by others indeed bears fruit after three or four months;

but as for us, the seed of faith planted within our noble Elder Sāriputta has surely borne fruit this very day. Even in a space the size of a handful of soil, [there is] not even a single myrobalan..."
“There is no such thing as a lump of dust that is not gold. “Now what shall we do, noble sir?
“My dear, it is impossible to have stolen and consumed this much gold,” he said.
Leaving his wife at that spot, he filled the bowl he had brought back with food, then filled it with gold, and went to inform the king: “A certain man has brought a golden bowl...”
“...and stood there holding it. The king summoned him and asked, “My dear son, where did you get this?
He replied, “Your Majesty, one plowed field of mine has turned entirely into gold; please send someone to have it brought back.
“What is your name? “I am named Puṇṇa, Your Majesty. “Go, my man, yoke the carts and [take Puṇṇa]...”
"Bring gold from the plowed spot!

When the king's men who had gone with the carts said, "This is the King’s merit," they took handfuls of gold; yet every handful they took turned out to be nothing but clods of earth from the plowed field.
They went and reported this to the king. [The king said: "In that case, go and say, 'This is Puṇṇa’s merit.'"
Having said, "Take it," whatever was taken was indeed gold. They brought all that gold and made a heap in the royal courtyard.
The heap was as high as a palm tree. The king summoned the merchants and asked, "In whose house is there so much gold?
"There is none, Your Majesty, in anyone's house. [The king said: "Of such [an amount]..."
"But what should be done for the owner of this wealth? "It is fitting, O King, to make him the chief treasurer (dhanaseṭṭhi)," they said.
"In that case, appoint Puṇṇa as the chief treasurer of this city," he replied;
and having given all that gold to him, he bestowed the position of treasurer upon him on that very day. As the treasurer, he performed auspicious ceremonies for seven days.
He gave a great alms-offering to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
On the seventh day, during the Buddha’s expression of gratitude for the meal, both Puṇṇa the merchant, his wife, and his daughter were all established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Later, when the merchant of Rājagaha heard that Puṇṇa the merchant had a daughter who had reached marriageable age, he [approached] his own...
For the sake of his son, he sent word to his house. Having heard that message, the other sent back a reply: "I will not give my daughter. The merchant Sumanas sent word again:
"Having lived in dependence upon my house, you have now become a master all at once and yet do not give me your daughter! Then the merchant Puṇṇa said:
—“This merchant has indeed spoken of you according to your true nature; however, one should not assume that every man is always like this.
For I am now able to take such a man as a slave, yet I do not violate your birth or your clan.
Moreover, my daughter is a stream-enterer, a noble disciple, who [attends] daily...”
“I perform worship with flowers worth a kahāpaṇa; I will not send such an offering to the house of one who holds wrong views like you.
Having thus understood the merchant Puṇṇa’s refusal, the merchant of Rājagaha sent another message:
“Do not break our ancient bond of trust. I [will provide] for my daughter-in-law daily...”
“I shall have flower garlands prepared for two kahāpaṇas. Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he sent his daughter to that man’s house.
Then one day, Puṇṇa the merchant’s daughter, Uttarā, spoke thus to her husband: “I [myself]...”
"For eight days of the month, I regularly perform the Uposatha observance in my family home;
now, if you would accept it, I would resolve to observe the Uposatha precepts even here. He replied, "It is not possible," and did not accept her offer.
Unable to persuade him, she remained silent. Later, during the rainy season, she thought, "I shall observe the Uposatha."

Even then, she did not obtain permission. When two and a half months of the rainy season had passed and only half a month remained, she sent a message to her parents: "I have been cast into prison by you;
during all this time, I have not been able to observe the Uposatha precepts for even a single day. Give me fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas."
"Send them. Having heard her daughter's message, they sent them off without even asking "For what reason?
Uttarā took those kahāpaṇas and, having summoned a courtesan named Sirimā who lived in that city, said:
"Mother Sirimā, for this half-month I shall observe the precepts of the Uposatha; you [should take] these fifteen..."
"Take these thousand kahāpaṇas and attend upon the merchant’s son for this half-month.

She accepted, saying, "Very well, noble lady. From then on, thinking, "I shall enjoy myself with Sirimā," the merchant’s son accepted the observance of the Uposatha from Uttarā for the remaining half-month.
Knowing that he had accepted [her request], she would go every day at dawn, surrounded by her retinue of female slaves, and personally prepare hard and soft foods for the Teacher.

When the Teacher had finished his meal and returned to the monastery, she would resolve upon the factors of the Uposatha, ascend to her magnificent palace, and sit there reflecting upon her own moral precepts (*sīla*). She continued in this manner for half a month.
Having passed the Uposatha day, on the day of dismissal, she moved about early in the morning preparing rice gruel, solid food, and other provisions.

At that time, the merchant’s son, having gone to the upper story of the excellent palace together with Sirimā, stood opening the lattice window and looking out over the interior courtyard. Uttarā looked upward through the opening of the window. The merchant’s son—
Looking at Uttara, he smiled, thinking, "Alas, this woman is surely destined for hell;
having abandoned such great prosperity, she wanders among slave-girls for no reason at all, her mortar smeared with oil-cake.
Knowing his state of negligence, Uttara thought, "This fool will surely believe that his own prosperity is permanent for all time," and so she herself—
She smiled. Then Sirimā, thinking, “While I am standing here, this slave-girl is smiling with my husband,” became angry and descended with haste.

Uttarā, by the very manner of her arrival, realized, “This foolish woman, having lived in this house for only half a month, has come to perceive it as her own home,” and at that very moment [she entered] the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*).

Having entered [the meditative attainment], he remained there. The maidservant Sirimā also came through the midst of the other servants, took a ladle, filled it with boiling oil at the place where cakes were being fried, and poured it over Uttara’s head.
Due to the radiation of the jhāna of loving-kindness (*mettā*), the boiling oil poured on Uttara’s head turned back and flowed away like water poured onto a lotus leaf.
At that moment, the female slaves standing near Sirimā looked at her and rebuked her in her presence, saying, "O lady, you have come here having taken wages from our mistress's hand;
while living in this house, you must strive to become like our mistress!
At that moment, Sirimā [realized] her own status as a newcomer.
She understood. Going from there, she fell at Uttara’s feet and said, “Noble lady, I acted without due consideration;
please forgive me. “Dear Sirimā, I will not forgive you in this place;
I am the daughter of the Ten-Powered One, and I shall only forgive you when the Ten-Powered One himself forgives.”
The Teacher, accompanied by the community of monks, arrived and sat upon the seat prepared in the residence of Uttarā.
Sirimā went there, prostrated at the feet of the Teacher, and said, "Venerable sir, I have committed an offense against the noble lady Uttarā.
She says, 'When you have forgiven her, I shall forgive her. May the Blessed One forgive me. "I forgive you," [the Teacher replied].
