They were Sirimā and Uttara. At that time, she went to him and asked for his forgiveness. And on that very day, having heard the Dasabala’s expression of gratitude after the meal, Sirimā said:
"Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the wicked with goodness."
"One should conquer the miser with generosity, and the liar with truth.
At the conclusion of this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). She invited the One of Ten Powers and on the following day gave a great alms-offering.
Thus did this story originate. Later, however, while the Teacher was seated in Jetavana, he addressed the female lay disciples (*upāsikāyo*):
While assigning them to their respective positions, he placed Uttara, the daughter of Nanda, in the foremost place among those who practice meditation (*jhāyin*).

[This concludes] the story of Suppavāsā (263). Regarding the sixth [title], "among those who give choice food": this refers to the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*) who provide superior flavors; [the foremost among them was] Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyas.
This indicates that she was foremost among those who give choice gifts. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī.
While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain female lay disciple to the position of being foremost among those who give choice gifts.
Having performed a meritorious deed, she aspired to that very status. For a hundred thousand aeons, she [dwelt] among gods and humans.
Having wandered through the cycle of existence, she was reborn in this present dispensation of a Buddha in a kṣatriya family in the city of Koliya;
they gave her the name Suppavāsā Tissa. When she reached maturity, she went to the home of a Śākya youth.
Upon her very first sight of the Teacher, she heard his discourse on the Dhamma and became established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Later, she [gave birth to] a boy named Sīvali.
She gave birth. The background for this has already been explained in detail below.
On one occasion, she provided various kinds of choice and excellent food to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
When the Teacher had finished his meal, while delivering the blessing of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*), he taught this Dhamma to Suppavāsā: "Food..."
When a noble female disciple gives while in the state of Suppavāsā, she gives five things to those who receive:
she gives life, she gives beauty, she gives happiness, she gives strength, and she gives eloquence.
Having given life, she partakes in life—whether divine or human... [and so on] ...having given eloquence, she partakes in eloquence—whether divine.

“or of a human. Thus this matter arose. Later on, while sitting in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher, as he was assigning the laywomen to their respective ranks, placed Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyans, in the foremost position among those who give choice food.
Suppiyā’s Story (264).

Regarding the phrase “of those who attend to the sick” (*gilānupaṭṭhākīnaṃ*): it shows that among the female lay followers (*upāsikā*) who attend to the sick, the female lay follower Suppiyā was the foremost.
It is said that in the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in Haṃsavatī; later on—
While listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain laywoman to the foremost position among those who attend to the sick;
having performed a meritorious deed, she aspired to that very station.
After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a noble family in Bārāṇasī; she was Suppiyā by name.
...gave her a name. Later, the Teacher, accompanied by the community of bhikkhus, arrived at Bārāṇasī.
Upon seeing the Tathāgata for the first time, she heard the Dhamma and was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti).
Then, one day, having gone to the monastery to hear the Dhamma, while walking on a tour of the monastery grounds, she saw a certain bhikkhu.
Seeing the sick man, she paid homage to him, offered him hospitality, and asked, "Venerable sir, what does your honor require?
"I require some broth, laywoman," he replied. "Very well, Bhante; I shall send it," she said, and after paying homage to the Elder, she went into the city.
On the following day, she sent a female slave to the market for the sake of meat that was being prepared. She [searched] throughout the entire city...
Not obtaining meat that was already prepared, she spoke of the fact that it could not be found. The laywoman thought: "I said I would send some delicacy to the Noble One;
if I do not send it, the Noble One will suffer from not finding anything elsewhere. No matter what, it is right to send something.
Entering her room, she cut flesh from her own thigh and gave it to a maidservant, saying: "This..."
“Take some meat, prepare it with the necessary ingredients, make it into a broth, bring it to the monastery, and give it to the noble one.
If he asks you why, tell him, ‘I am ill. She did exactly as she was told.
The Teacher, knowing the reason for this, on the following day at the time for the alms-round, surrounded by the community of monks, [went to] the laywoman...
He went home. Having heard that the Tathāgata had arrived, she addressed her husband:
"Noble son, I am unable to go into the presence of the Teacher; you go, bring the Teacher into the house, and have him sit down.
He did so. The Teacher asked, "Where is Suppiyā? "She is ill, Bhante," they replied. "Call her here," he said.

Then they went and said, "The Teacher calls for you. She thought, "The Teacher, who is compassionate and seeks the welfare of the whole world, would not call me without seeing some reason for it," and she rose from her bed in haste.
Then, by the power of the Buddha, at that very moment her wound healed and her skin became more beautiful than it was in any other place.

Her complexion was serene. At that moment, the female lay devotee smiled, prostrated herself before the One of Ten Powers with the five-limbed salutation, and sat down to one side. The Teacher asked, "What is it that makes this female lay devotee unwell?
She related everything she had done. Having finished his meal, the Teacher went to the monastery and, having caused the community of monks to assemble, said:
Having rebuked that bhikkhu in many ways, he laid down a training rule. Thus this matter arose.
Later, while sitting in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher, as he was assigning the laywomen to their respective ranks, placed the laywoman Suppiyā in the foremost position among those who tend to the sick.

265. Regarding the eighth [section], "of those with confirmed confidence" (*aveccappasannānaṃ*): this indicates that among the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*) who possess unshakable confidence attained through realization, Kātiyānī was the foremost.
It is said that she was reborn into a noble family in Haṃsavatī during the time of Buddha Padumuttara.
Seeing the Teacher place a certain female lay devotee in the foremost position among those with unwavering confidence, she performed meritorious deeds and aspired to that very status.
After wandering through existences among gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in the city of Kuraraghara; they gave her the name Kātiyānī.
In the course of time, when she reached maturity, she became a close friend of Kāḷī, the resident of Kuraraghara. Later,

when the Elder Kuṭikaṇṇa Soṇa was requested by his mother, "Preach the Dhamma to me also according to the method taught by the One of Ten Powers," he sat upon the decorated Dhamma-seat within the city during the night and made his mother a bodily witness [of the Dhamma].
Having given this teaching on the Dhamma, he began [his discourse]. At that time, the laywoman Kātiyānī went with Kāḷī and stood at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma.
At that moment, about five hundred thieves, thinking it was daytime within the city, dug a tunnel starting from the wall and reached the house of this Kātiyānī. Their chief thief—
Without entering with them, and for the purpose of investigating, "What indeed is this assembly gathered for?", he went to the place where the Elder Soṇa was preaching the Dhamma;
standing at the edge of the assembly, he stood behind the back of Kātiyānī.
At that time, Kātiyānī addressed her maidservant: "Go, girl, enter the house and bring the oil for the lamp."
"Having lit a lamp, we shall listen to the Dhamma. She went home, saw the thieves digging a tunnel, and returned without even taking the lamp oil, reporting to her mistress:
"Lady, there are thieves in the house digging a tunnel.
Upon hearing this, the chief of the thieves thought: "If she takes this news and goes home, [our plans will be ruined]."
“Right here I shall cut him in two with my sword. But if he listens to the Dhamma by means of the very sign he has grasped, I shall have the goods seized by the thieves returned to him.

When the maidservant Kātiyānī heard the slave’s words, she said, “Mother, do not make a sound; for when thieves steal, they take only what they themselves see. As for me, today I am hearing something rare to hear.”
“I am listening; do not create an obstacle for the Dhamma,” she said. Having heard her words, the chief robber thought:
“If we were to steal goods from the house of one who stands with such an intention, we would be as if entering the great earth.
He went there immediately, had the goods seized by the robbers discarded, and returned together with them.
While listening to the Dhamma, he stood at the edge of the assembly. At the conclusion of the Elder’s teaching, the female lay follower Kātiyānī was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Then, when the dawn had risen, the chief of the bandits went and fell at the feet of the female lay follower, saying, "Noble lady, for all of us..."
"I do not forgive you," she said. "But what have you done to me? He then confessed every fault he had committed.
"In that case, dear ones, I forgive you," she replied. "Noble lady, it is not right for us to be forgiven in this way;
rather, please grant the going-forth to all of us in the presence of your son, the Elder. She then took them all with her.
He ordained them in the presence of the Elder Kuṭikaṇṇa-Soṇa. Those bandits, having been ordained in the presence of the Elder, all attained arahantship. Thus this story originated.

Later on, while residing at Jetavana, the Teacher, while establishing the female lay disciples (upāsikā) in their respective ranks, placed the lay disciple Kātiyānī in the foremost position among those possessed of verified confidence (aveccappasanna).
Nakulamātā’s Story (266).

Regarding the ninth [story], "of the trustworthy ones" (*vissāsikānaṃ*): this indicates that among the female lay followers (*upāsikā*) who were engaged in conversation about trustworthiness, the housewife Nakulamātā was the foremost.
Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated below in the *Upāsaka-pāḷi*.
It should be understood that here, the story is to be told by making Nakulamātā the central figure.
(267) Regarding the tenth case, "those who have faith through hearsay": this refers to those endowed with faith arisen solely through hearsay.

Among the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*), he shows that the female lay disciple Kāḷī of Kuraraghara was the foremost. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born in the city of Kuraraghara in Haṃsavatī;

while listening to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain female lay disciple to the position of being foremost among those who have faith through hearsay (*anussava*). Having performed a meritorious deed (*adhikārakamma*) for that purpose, she—

She aspired for that state. After wandering among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a noble family in the city of Rājagaha; they gave her the name Kāḷītissā.
When she reached maturity, she went to a noble family in the city of Kuraraghara. Then, through living with him, she conceived a child.
When her pregnancy was full, thinking, "It is improper for the delivery of a child to take place in another's house," she returned to her own home city.

Shortly after midnight, while standing in the sky above her palace, she heard the praises of the Triple Gem being spoken by Sātāgira and Hemavata. Having developed a faith based on hearsay, she [approached] the Teacher...
She established herself in the fruit of stream-entry by the mere sight [of the Buddha];
later, however, she gave birth to a child—all of which has already been explained in detail below.

Later on, while sitting in the midst of the community of monks at Jetavana, the Teacher, as he was assigning the laywomen to their respective ranks, placed this laywoman in the foremost position among those who gained faith through hearsay.
The commentary on the *Upāsikāpāḷi*, consisting of ten suttas, is completed. And with this,
[the commentary] on the *Manorathapūraṇī*,
the commentary on the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, [is finished].
The entire commentary on this *Agga-pāḷi* is concluded.

"For which reason the worldling... means that this reason exists: "it is possible" (*ṭhānam etaṃ vijjati*).

For by means of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*), he might grasp some conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*) among the conditioned formations belonging to the three planes as permanent; this is the meaning.
However, because the formations of the fourth plane are characterized by an abundance of heat—like a ball of iron heated all day for flies, or [because they are repulsive] to views or others—...
They do not become objects for unwholesome states. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood regarding any formation [being grasped] as "pleasure," and so forth.
"Would grasp it as pleasure": this is said with reference to the grasping of a self-view (*attadiṭṭhi*), such as "the self is exclusively happy and healthy after death.
However, even when overcome by feverish distress, a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) does not grasp anything with a mind dissociated from wrong view.
Just as a refined brahmin, terrified of a rutting elephant, would avoid dung, one who seeks the subsiding of feverish distress regards no formation whatsoever as pleasant.
In the section on the self,
instead of saying "any formation" (*saṅkhāra*), it is said "any phenomenon" (*dhamma*) for the purpose of including the designations such as the *kasiṇas*.
Here too, the delimitation should be understood according to the four planes for the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), and according to the three planes for the worldling (*puthujjana*).
Alternatively, in all instances, it is appropriate to delimit even the noble disciple according to the three planes alone.
For whatever the worldling grasps, from each of those the noble disciple undoes the grasp. Indeed, whatever the worldling...
One grasps [them] as permanent, pleasant, and self; the noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), grasping them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, unravels that grasping.
Thus, in these three suttas, what is called "the unraveling of the ordinary person’s (puthujjana) grasping at a self" is explained. 271. Regarding the terms "mother," etc.:
she who gives birth is the mother; he who fathers is the father; one who has become a human being and is an arahant with taints destroyed (khīṇāsava) is an arahant.
This is what is intended. But could a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) take the life of another? That too is impossible.

Even if someone were to say to a noble disciple who has passed into another existence and does not recognize his own status as a noble disciple, "Kill this ant and you shall attain the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) throughout the entire interior of the world-system," [he would never do so].
He would not deprive him of life. Even if they were to say to him, "If you do not have him killed, we shall cut off your head," they might indeed cut off his own head, yet he would not kill him.
However, this was said for the purpose of showing the great culpability of the state of being an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and to demonstrate the great power of a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).

This is the intended meaning here: the state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*) is blameworthy, for it is precisely because of this that a worldling might even commit such immediate transgressions (*ānantariya*) as matricide and so forth.
And the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) possesses great power, in that he does not perform these deeds.

"Corrupt in mind" means having a mind corrupted by a murderous intent. "Should shed blood" means that he should shed even as much blood as could be drunk by a tiny fly from the body of one who is still living.

275. "He should cause a schism in the Saṅgha" means that he should cause a schism in the Saṅgha—consisting of those who share the same communion and reside within the same boundary—by means of five causes.

And this has been said: "Upananda, the Saṅgha is split by five ways: by formal act (kamma), by recitation (uddesa), by deliberation (voharanta), by proclamation (anussāvana), and by the drawing of lots (salākaggāha)."
Therein, "by means of a formal act" (*kammena*) refers to any one of the four formal acts, such as the *apalokana* (announcement) and so forth.
"By means of a recitation" (*uddesena*) refers to any one of the five recitations of the *Pātimokkha*. "Speaking" (*voharanto*) means conversing;

that is, pointing out the eighteen grounds for schism, such as declaring what is non-Dhamma to be Dhamma, and so forth, through various specific instances. "By means of a proclamation" (*anussāvanena*) refers to [the phrase] "Is it not... and so on.
“You know my noble birth, my state as one who has gone forth, and my great learning;
it is not fitting for you even to conceive the thought that someone like me would cause the Teacher’s dispensation to fall into unrighteousness (uddhamma) and anti-discipline (ubbinaya).
Is Avīci cool to me like a grove of blue lotuses? Do I not fear the states of misery?”—in such a manner [he spoke] into his ear.

"By making a verbal declaration and by means of an announcement. "By the taking of voting tickets (*salākaggāha*)" means: having thus announced it, having steadied their minds, and having made them firm in their resolve not to turn back, [the monk says] "Take this voting ticket," and thus by the taking of the voting tickets.

In this context, the formal act (*kamma*) itself, or the recitation (*uddesa*), is the criterion; however, the preliminary announcement and the taking of the voting tickets are merely the prior stages. This is by way of illustrating the eighteen grounds (*vatthu*).
For when one who is speaking proclaims [the proposal] there in order to generate consent, even if the voting sticks have been taken, the Saṅgha remains undivided.
But when four or more have thus taken the voting sticks and perform a separate formal act (*kamma*) or recitation (*uddesa*), then the Saṅgha is said to be divided.
Thus, a person endowed with right view might cause a schism in the Saṅgha.

This is not possible. Up to this point, the five deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma)—such as matricide and so forth—which an ordinary person (puthujjana) commits but a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) does not, have been shown. To clarify them:
“By way of the deed, by way of the door, and likewise by way of its duration in an aeon (kappa-ṭṭhitiya);”
“The exposition should be understood through the *pākasādhāraṇa* (common results) and so forth.
Regarding that, first, from the perspective of the action (*kamma*):

here, for one who has become a human being, the act of depriving of life a mother or a father who have also become human beings—even if their gender has changed—constitutes an immediate (*ānantariya*) deed; its result...
Even one who thinks, "I shall ward it off," and fills the entire Cakkavāḷa with golden stūpas the size of the Mahācetiya,

and even after giving a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha of monks seated and filling the entire Cakkavāḷa, and even after wandering about without letting go of the corner of the Blessed Buddha’s outer robe,
is reborn in hell alone upon the dissolution of the body. But he who is himself a human being...

If one deprives of life a mother or a father who has become an animal, or if one, being oneself a human being, deprives of life a human being who has become an animal, or if one, being an animal, deprives of life another animal—his action is not an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense;
however, it is grave, and it remains as having reached the level of an *ānantariya*. This question, moreover, is stated with reference specifically to those of human birth.
In this regard, the "sheep tetrad," the "battlefield tetrad," and the "thief tetrad" must be explained.

For even with the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) "I shall kill a sheep," if one kills a mother or a father who is actually a human being standing in the place of the sheep, one incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*).
Likewise, one who kills a sheep with the intention of killing a sheep, or with the intention of killing a mother or father, [incurs the respective result].

One does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) for killing one's mother or father with a mistaken intent; however, if one kills one's mother or father while intending them to be so, one certainly incurs it.
This same principle applies to the other two tetrads as well. And just as it is with respect to one's mother and father, these tetrads should be understood in the same way regarding an *arahant*.
Furthermore, one incurs an immediate retribution only by killing a human *arahant*, not one who is a *yakkha* or a spirit. As for the kamma...

It is grave, indeed equivalent to an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. Regarding a human *arhat*, even if a blow with a weapon or poison is administered while he is still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), if he attains *arahatta* and dies by that very means, he is indeed a murderer of an *arhat*.
However, if one who was an ordinary person at the time of giving a gift enjoys that gift after having attained *arahatta*, it belongs to the ordinary person alone.

That [offense] is considered given. For one who kills other noble persons (ariyapuggala), there is no immediate retribution (ānantariya); however, the karma is grave, being equivalent to an immediate offense.
Regarding the shedding of blood:
because the Tathāgata possesses an indestructible body, it is the flowing of blood resulting from the cutting of the skin through the assault of another.
There was no [external] wound; rather, the blood merely collected in one spot inside the body.
Even a splinter from a stone hurled by Devadatta, having broken off, struck the edge of the Tathāgata’s foot;
his foot became filled with internal blood as if struck by an axe. One who acts in such a manner incurs an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense. Jīvaka...
However, by the Tathāgata’s own consent, he had the skin cut with a knife, extracted the corrupted blood from that place, and made it healthy.
For one who acts in this way, there is only merit-making.
Now, as for those who, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, destroy a stūpa, cut down a Bodhi tree, or take action against the relics—
What happens for them? It is a grave offense, similar to an *ānantariya* (immediate) transgression.
However, it is permissible to cut down a branch of the Bodhi tree that is obstructing a stupa containing relics or an image.

Even if birds perched there void excrement upon the shrine (*cetiya*), it is still permissible to cut it down; for the body-relic shrine (*sarīracetiyam*) is more venerable than a shrine of use (*paribhogacetiyam*).
It is more significant. One may break open the site of a cetiya and even cut down and carry away the root of a Bodhi tree.
However, one is not permitted to cut down a branch of the Bodhi tree that obstructs the Bodhi-house for the sake of protecting that house.
For the house exists for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. The same principle applies to the seat-house (*āsana-ghara*). But in whichever seat-house...
When the relic (dhātu) has been enshrined, it is permissible to cut a branch from the Bodhi tree for its protection.
It is likewise permissible to cut a branch that draws away sap or one that is rotten for the purpose of tending to the Bodhi tree; this brings merit just like the tending of one's own body.

Even in the case of a schism in the Sangha, when the Sangha residing within the boundary (sīmā) has not assembled, it is [permissible] to take a separate assembly and perform the formal acts of proclamation and the distribution of voting sticks.
Whether one is performing an act of schism or reciting the *uddesa* while there is actually a schism, and it is an *ānantariya* (immediate) offense;
however, if one acts with the perception that the community is united, it is permissible—thus, for one acting with such a perception, there is only the schism itself, but no *ānantariya* offense.
Likewise for a quorum of fewer than nine; at the very minimum, for one who splits the Saṅgha consisting of nine persons:
It is an immediate offense (*ānantariyakamma*). For those who follow him and speak what is contrary to the Dhamma, it is a highly blameworthy act;
however, for those who speak according to the Dhamma, they are blameless. Regarding the schism of the Saṅgha involving nine persons, this is the Sutta:
"On one side, Upāli, there are four; on the other side, four; the ninth proclaims [the division] and distributes voting tickets, saying: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya...'"
“This is the Teacher’s instruction; take this up, approve of this. In this way, Upāli, there is both a schism in the Saṅgha and a formal split of the Saṅgha.
Or, Upāli, with nine or more than nine [monks], there is both a schism in the Saṅgha and a formal split of the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, among these five [factors], the split of the Saṅgha is verbal action (vacīkamma), while the remaining ones are bodily actions (kāyakamma).
Thus should the exposition be understood by way of action.

By way of door: all of these arise from both the body-door and the speech-door. However, among these, the first four, even though they arise from the speech-door by means of commanding, science, and instigation, [result] only in the body-door.

They fulfill [the requirements]. For one who effects a schism in the Saṅgha by means of hand gestures, even though the breach originates from the door of the body, it fulfills [the offense] through the door of speech alone;
thus should the analysis here be understood also by way of the doors.
Regarding "lasting for an eon" (*kappaṭṭhitiyo*): here, it is the schism in the Saṅgha itself that lasts for an eon. For when an eon is established, or during the middle of an eon...
Or, having caused a schism in the Saṅgha, one is liberated only when the aeon (kappa) is destroyed.
For even if one causes a schism in the Saṅgha today with the thought, "The aeon will be destroyed tomorrow," one is liberated on that very day; one suffers in hell for only a single day.
However, such a thing does not happen. The remaining four deeds are indeed immediate (ānantariya), and they do not persist for the duration of an aeon. Thus it is here.
The exposition should also be understood by way of its duration for an eon (*kappa-ṭṭhitika*).
As for "manifest" (*pākata*): for one who has performed all five of these deeds, it is the schism of the Saṅgha alone that ripens by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
the remaining deeds are reckoned as "deeds that have been done but whose result has not yet occurred," and so forth.
In the absence of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, there is the shedding of blood [of a Buddha]; in the absence of that, the murder of an Arahant;
in the absence of that, if the father is virtuous and the mother is immoral—or if she is not likewise virtuous—then patricide ripens by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
If the mother is virtuous, then matricide [ripens]. When both are equal in virtue or in immorality, it is matricide alone that ripens by way of rebirth-linking.
It ripens. For a mother performs difficult tasks and is of great benefit to her children. Thus, in this context, the exposition should be understood even from what is evident.
Regarding "by commonality and so forth": the first four [offenses] are common to all, whether householders or those gone forth.
However, as for schism in the Saṅgha: "Upāli, it is not a bhikkhunī who causes a schism in the Saṅgha, nor a female trainee, nor a male novice, nor a female novice..."
"A lay follower (upāsaka) does not cause a schism in the Saṅgha, nor does a female lay follower (upāsikā).

It is a bhikkhu, Upāli, who—being of regular status (pakatatta), belonging to the same communion (samāna-saṃvāsaka), and standing within the same boundary (sīmā)—causes a schism in the Saṅgha. Because of this statement, it belongs only to a bhikkhu of the aforementioned type and not to anyone else;
therefore, it is not common [to all]. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), all these [defilements] are accompanied by painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) and associated with hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha).
Thus, in this context, the analysis should also be understood by means of the common [characteristics] and so forth.

276. "Another Teacher": the meaning is that it is impossible for him to take another founder of a sect—even in another existence—thinking, "This teacher is my teacher," on the grounds that "this teacher is unable to perform the duties of a Teacher.

277. "In a single world-system" means in a ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*). For there are three fields: the field of birth (*jātikhetta*), the field of authority (*āṇākhetta*), and...
"Field of objects" (*visaya-khetta*). Therein, the "field of birth" (*jāti-khetta*) refers to the ten-thousandfold world system (*dasasahassī lokadhātu*).

For that [world system] shakes at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb, at the time of his emergence [from it], at the time of his full enlightenment (*sambodhi*), at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the relinquishing of the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*), and at his final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*).

However, a hundred thousand million world systems (*cakkavāḷa*) is called the "field of authority" (*āṇā-khetta*). For [within this field], the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta*, the *Moraparitta*, the *Dhajagga-paritta*, the *Ratana-paritta*, and so forth—
Herein, the command operates. However, there is no limit to the extent of its objective field. For regarding the Buddhas, it is said:

"As far as knowledge extends, so far does the knowable extend; as far as the knowable extends, so far does knowledge extend. The knowable is coextensive with knowledge; knowledge is coextensive with the knowable.
Thus, for them, there is nothing that is not within their range.
Regarding these three fields, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise in another world-system apart from this Cakkavāḷa; however, there is one stating that they do not arise [there].
For there are three Piṭakas—the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka—and three Councils—the Council of the Elder Mahākassapa and the Council of the Elder Yasa.

The Recitations: the recitation of the Elder Moggaliputta. Regarding these three recitations, once the word of the Buddha has been established in the Tipiṭaka, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise elsewhere outside this Cakkavāḷa; however, there is [a sutta] stating that they do not arise.
"Neither before nor after" means not earlier and not later; they do not arise simultaneously. They arise either before or after.

This has been stated. In this context, "prior" should not be understood as the period from the time he sat at the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka) with the resolve, "I shall not rise until I have attained enlightenment," back to his taking rebirth in the mother’s womb.

For at the very moment of the Bodhisatta’s conception, the delimitation of his field was accomplished by the shaking of ten thousand world-systems; it is within this interval [that the prior lives are to be understood].

The arising of another Buddha is indeed precluded. It should not be understood that this preclusion lasts from the time of the final *parinibbāna* until even a relic the size of a mustard seed remains; for as long as the relics remain, the Buddhas are truly present.
Therefore, within this interval, the arising of another Buddha is indeed precluded. However, at the *parinibbāna* of the relics...
Once one Buddha has arisen, the arising of another Buddha is not prevented.
But why do they not arise neither before nor after one another? Because it would lack wonder.
For Buddhas are wonderful persons. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, one person, appearing in the world, appears as a wonderful person. Who is that? [And so forth.]
"A single person? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For if two, four, eight, or sixteen were to arise together, they would not be marvelous. Indeed, in a single monastery, even for two shrines, the gain and honor are not great;
and just as monks, when numerous, have become commonplace, so too would Buddhas be.
Therefore, they do not arise.

Furthermore, because there would be no distinction in the teaching: for if one person were to teach a Dhamma such as the foundations of mindfulness, that same Dhamma would have to be taught by another who had also arisen [in the world];
consequently, it would not be marvelous. But when one person teaches the Dhamma, the teaching itself is truly marvelous.
And because of the existence of dispute. For if many Buddhas were to arise, the disciples of many teachers would dispute among themselves like this:
"Our Buddha is handsome," or "Our Buddha has a sweet voice, is successful, and is meritorious.
Therefore, for that reason as well, they do not arise [simultaneously].
Furthermore, this reason was explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda.
For it is said there: "Venerable Nāgasena, this has also been stated by the Blessed One:
'It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously and at the same time in one world-system.'"
‘This is not possible. Yet, venerable Nāgasena, all the Tathāgatas, when teaching, teach the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
when explaining, they explain the four noble truths;
when training, they train in the three trainings; and when instructing, they instruct in the practice of diligence. If—
"Venerable Nāgasena, for all Tathāgatas there is one summary, one teaching, one training, and one instruction;
for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise simultaneously? Even with the arising of a single Buddha, this world becomes filled with light;
if there were a second Buddha as well, this world would become even more intensely illuminated by the radiance of both."
“I would become filled with radiance. And two Tathāgatas, when exhorting me, would exhort me happily;
when instructing me, they would instruct me happily. In this matter, teach me the reason so that I may become free from doubt.
“Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the domain of a single Buddha; it possesses the virtues of a single Tathāgata alone.”
It sustains [them]. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him;
it would shake, tremble, waver, incline, lean, bend, scatter, be dispersed, and be utterly destroyed, and it would not remain stable.
"Great King, it is as if there were a ship capable of supporting only one person. When that one person has boarded, it..."

It would be capable of carrying [one person]. Then a second man were to come, similar in lifespan, complexion, age, size, and in every limb and member—whether lean or stout—and he were to board that boat.
Would that boat, Great King, be able to carry both of them? "No indeed, venerable sir; it would move, shake, bend, incline, and lean over."
"It would scatter it, blow it away, and destroy it; it would not remain in its place, but would sink into the water.
"In the same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the domain of a single Buddha; it sustains the qualities of only one Tathāgata.
If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system would not be able to sustain him."
It would move... [and so on] ... it would not come to rest.
"Or again, Great King, suppose a man were to eat as much food as he desired, filling his throat until it was completely full.
He, being satiated, nourished, fulfilled, and without gaps, becoming lethargic and with his limbs unable to bend, would [be unable to move] that same amount again."
“Would he eat his meal? And would that man, Great King, be happy? “No indeed, venerable sir; he might die after eating only once.
“In the same way, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system is the domain of a single Buddha’s sustaining power...
[it would not be possible for it to endure otherwise].”
“Venerable Nāgasena, does the earth tremble because of the excessive burden of the Dhamma?
In this case, O Great King, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to their very rims.
If one were to take the jewels from one cart and pour them into the other, would that cart, O Great King, [bear the weight] of the jewels of both carts?”
"Could it bear it? "No, venerable sir; its nave would burst, its spokes would break, its rim would warp, and its axle would snap.
"But, Great King, does a cart break because of the excessive weight of its jewels?
"Yes, venerable sir. "In the same way, Great King, the earth trembles because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma."
“Furthermore, Great King, this reason has been set forth to illustrate the power of the Buddhas.
Listen now to another appropriate reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise simultaneously.
If, Great King, two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise at the same moment, a dispute would arise within the assembly: ‘The Buddha belongs to you;’”

‘Our Buddha’—thus they would become divided into two factions. Just as, Great King, when a dispute arises between the retinues of two powerful ministers, they become divided into two factions, saying, ‘Your minister is ours;
our minister is yours,’ even so, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, there would be a dispute among their retinues.
If two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise simultaneously, they would each say, "The Buddha is yours; the Buddha is ours," and thus they would become divided into two factions.
Listen to this first reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same moment.
Furthermore, Great King, listen to another subsequent reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Ones do not arise at the same moment.
They do not arise. Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Ones were to arise simultaneously, then the statement that "the Buddha is supreme" would be false;

likewise, the statements that "the Buddha is the eldest," "the Buddha is the best," "the Buddha is distinguished," "the Buddha is the highest," "the Buddha is preeminent," "the Buddha is peerless," "the Buddha is equal to the unequaled," and "the Buddha is without equal" would be false.
If it were otherwise, the statement that "the Buddha is peerless," "the Buddha is matchless," and "the Buddha is without equal" would be false.
Great King, you should also accept this reason according to its true meaning: the reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise simultaneously.

“Furthermore, Great King, it is the natural disposition of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world at a time. Why? Because of the greatness of the qualities of an omniscient Buddha.
Whatever is great, Great King, is singular. The earth, Great King, is great, yet it is only one. The ocean...”
He is great and he is unique. Sineru, the king of mountains, is great and it is unique. Space is great and it is unique. Sakka is great and he is unique.
Brahmā is great and he is unique. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is great and he is unique.
Wherever they arise, there is no room for others. Therefore, the Tathāgata...
“An Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, arises alone in the world. “Well explained, venerable Nāgasena, is the question by means of similes and reasons.
“In one world-system” means in one *cakkavāḷa*. By this very term, ten thousand *cakkavāḷas* are [implied] below.
Those [world-systems] that have been grasped may also be delimited by a single world-system (cakkavāḷa) alone.

For Buddhas, when arising, arise only in this very world-system; however, once the place of arising has been excluded, it follows as a matter of course that they do not arise in other world-systems beyond this one.
Commentary on the First Chapter. 15.
The Text of the Impossibilities (Aṭṭhānapāḷi). 2. Commentary on the Second Chapter of the Text of the Impossibilities.

278. Regarding the phrase "neither before nor after": here, "before" refers to the period prior to the manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*), and "after" refers to the period subsequent to its disappearance. In this regard, the disappearance of the Wheel-Treasure occurs in two ways:

either through the death of the Universal Monarch (*cakkavatti*) or through his renunciation of the world. Furthermore, as it is disappearing, whether due to death or renunciation, on the seventh day—
When the day has passed away, the appearance of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) thereafter is no longer obstructed.
But why do two wheel-turning monarchs not arise simultaneously in a single world-system (cakkavāḷa)?

Because it would prevent disputes, because of their marvelous nature, and because of the great power of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana). For if two were to arise, [the thought would occur]: "Our king is great; our [king is great]."

A dispute might arise as to whether [he] is a great king, and it would not be extraordinary to say, "In one continent there is a wheel-turning monarch; in another continent there is a wheel-turning monarch.

Furthermore, even that great majesty which is capable of bestowing sovereignty over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands would diminish. Thus, from the perspective of ending disputes—
Due to the marvelous nature of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*) and its great power, two do not arise simultaneously within a single world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

As for the statement, "Could a woman be an *arhat*, a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*)?", let alone the state of Buddhahood—which involves generating the qualities of omniscience and being capable of delivering the world—such a thing does not even come to pass for a woman through mere aspiration. [The factors are:
human birth, possession of the male gender, the cause, and seeing the Teacher.
“Going forth, the perfection of virtues, the requisite qualification, and zeal—through the convergence of these eight factors, the resolution succeeds.
These are indeed the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration. Thus, for a woman who is incapable of fulfilling even the aspiration...
“Whence can there be the state of a Buddha? It has been said: “It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a woman should be an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha.

Since a mass of merit fulfilled in every way produces only a personal existence (attabhāva) fulfilled in every way, it is only a man who becomes an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, and not a woman.

280. Also, in such cases as "He shall be a wheel-turning monarch," because the marks do not reach fulfillment due to the absence in a woman of such things as the male organ concealed in a sheath, because the possession of the seven jewels does not come to pass due to the absence of the woman-jewel, and because there is no personal existence superior to all men;
therefore, "Bhikkhus, this is impossible, this has no occasion... [is said].
“Whatever woman might be a universal monarch (cakkavattī) king,” so it was said. 281.
And because the three positions—such as that of Sakka and the others—are supreme, whereas the female gender is inferior, therefore even those [positions] such as that of Sakka are prohibited for her.
But is it not the case that, just as the female gender does not exist in the Brahma-world, so too the male gender does not exist there? Therefore, “whatever man... [and so forth].
"One should not say: 'It is possible that she might exercise the status of a Brahmā'—this is not something that should not be said.
Why? Because a person here is reborn there. For by 'the status of a Brahmā,' the state of a Mahābrahmā is intended.
And here, a woman, having developed jhāna and passed away, is reborn into the company of the Brahmapārisajja devas."
It is not [the case that] a Great Brahmā [arises there]. However, it cannot be said that "a man does not arise there.
Even though both are equally devoid of sexual characteristics (*liṅga*), the Brahmās there have the form of men, not the form of women. Therefore, this is well-stated.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Of bodily misconduct," etc., just as the seeds of the *nimba* tree, the *kosātaki* creeper, and so forth do not produce sweet fruit, [so too does misconduct not produce pleasant results].
Just as [seeds] produce what is unpleasant and not sweet, so too bodily misconduct and the like do not produce a sweet result,
but produce only what is not sweet. And just as seeds such as sugarcane and rice produce fruits that are sweet and of excellent taste,
not unpleasant or bitter, so too bodily good conduct and the like produce only a sweet result.
It is not unpleasant. And this has also been said:
“As one sows the seed, so one reaps the fruit;
the doer of good reaps good, and the doer of evil reaps evil.”
Therefore, it was said: “Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who is possessed of bodily misconduct... and so forth.
(290–295) Regarding the phrases “one possessed of bodily misconduct,” etc., there are five kinds of possession (*samaṅgitā*):

possession by way of accumulation, possession by way of volition, possession by way of kamma, possession by way of result, and possession by way of manifestation. Therein, at the moment of accumulating wholesome or unwholesome kamma...

It is called "endowment with accumulation. Likewise, it is "endowment with volition. As long as beings have not attained Arahatship, all beings are called "endowed with volition" by virtue of being endowed with volition accumulated in the past. This is endowment with volition.
As long as they have not attained Arahatship, all beings [possess] that which was accumulated in the past...
With reference to karma that is subject to ripening (*vipākāraha*), beings are called "possessors of karma" (*kammasamaṅgin*). This is the state of possessing karma.
The state of possessing fruition (*vipākasamaṅgitā*) is to be understood as occurring only at the moment of fruition itself.

However, as long as sentient beings have not reached Arahantship, for them—falling from here and there and being reborn in hell—the hell appears through its manifest modes such as masses of flames and cauldrons of molten iron.

For those entering the womb, the sign of rebirth appears as the mother’s womb; for those arising among the devas, it appears in the form of the wish-fulfilling tree, celestial mansions, and so forth, as the deva-world.
Thus, their state of being "possessed of appearance" (upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā) consists in their not being freed from the appearance of this sign of rebirth.
That [state] wavers, while the others are immovable. For even when hell appears...
The world of the devas appears; when the world of the devas has appeared, hell also appears.
When the human world appears, the animal realm also appears; and even when the animal realm has appeared, the human world continues to appear.
Here is an illustration of this: it is said that at the foot of Mount Soṇa, in the Acela Monastery, there was a certain Dhamma-preacher named the Elder Soṇa.

His father was named Sunakhavājika. Although the Elder tried to dissuade him, being unable to establish him in self-restraint, he ordained him against his will in his old age, thinking, "May this poor man not perish.
As he lay on his sickbed, hell appeared before him; large dogs came from the foot of Mount Soṇa and surrounded him as if desiring to devour him.
Terrified by such great fear, he cried out, "Save me, dear Soṇa! Save me, dear Soṇa! "What is it, Great Elder? [Soṇa asked.
"Do you not see, dear one? [the father replied], and he explained what was happening. The Elder Soṇa thought, "How indeed can my father, who is like me, be reborn in hell?
I shall be his support," and having had the novices bring various flowers, he—
Having performed a worship of floor-coverings and a worship of seats in the Cetiyaṅgaṇa and Bodhiyaṅgaṇa, he had his father carried on a couch to the Cetiyaṅgaṇa;
having seated him upon the couch, he said, "Mahāthera, this offering has been made for your sake.
'This is my gift for the Blessed One,' saying this, pay homage to the Blessed One and gladden your heart."
He said: When the Elder Mahāsoṇa saw the offering and performed it in that manner, his mind was filled with serene confidence.

At that very moment, the celestial realm appeared before him. The Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove, as well as the celestial palaces and divine dancers, seemed to stand surrounding him. He then said to the Elder, "Come, Soṇa! Come, Soṇa!"
"What is this, Great Elder? "These mothers of yours are coming. The Elder thought, "Heaven has presented itself before the Great Elder.

Thus, it should be understood that possession through presence (*upaṭṭhānasamaṅgitā*) is unstable. Among these types of possession, here it is stated as "one possessed of bodily misconduct" and so forth, by way of possession through the volition of accumulation (*āyūhanacetanā-kamma-samaṅgitā*).
Regarding this, some teachers say: "At the very moment one accumulates karma, heaven is already barred for them.
Others, however, say: "Accumulated karma is of two kinds: that which receives an opportunity for fruition and that which does not.
In this regard, at the very time when the karma receives an opportunity for fruition, heaven is barred for them."
The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.
The commentary on the *Aṭṭhāna-pāḷi* is finished.
16. The *Ekadhamma-pāḷi*.
(16) 1. Commentary on the First Chapter of the *Ekadhamma-pāḷi* 296.

In the *Ekadhamma-pāḷi*, "one thing" (*ekadhammo*) means a single nature. "For the sake of absolute disenchantment" (*ekantanibbidāya*) means for the purpose of becoming thoroughly disenchanted with the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), for the purpose of weariness.
"For the sake of dispassion" (*virāgāya*) means for the purpose of becoming dispassionate toward the round of existence, or for the fading away of the defilements such as lust (*rāga*).
"For the sake of disappearance. "For the sake of cessation" means for the sake of the cessation of lust and the other defilements, that is, for the purpose of making them no longer arise;

or else, for the sake of the stopping of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*) itself. "For the sake of peace" means for the sake of the pacification of the defilements. "For the sake of direct knowledge" means for the sake of knowing directly by applying the three characteristics, such as impermanence and so forth.
"For the sake of enlightenment" means for the sake of awakening to the Four Truths. "Enlightenment" is said to be... [in] the four...
Or for the purpose of penetrating the knowledge of the four paths as it was spoken thus: "knowledge of the paths.
"For the sake of Nibbāna" means for the purpose of realizing unconditioned Nibbāna.
Thus the Blessed One praised the meditation subject of the recollection of the Buddha with these seven phrases. Why?
It was for the purpose of generating enthusiasm among the people, like a merchant of "poison-thorns" (visa-kaṇṭaka) does for his own merchandise.

A merchant of poison-thorns is said to be a sugar merchant. It is said that he, having taken sugar, molasses, candied sugar, granulated sugar, and so forth by cart, went to a frontier village and proclaimed, "Buy poison-thorns! Buy poison-thorns! Hearing this, the villagers—
“Poison is indeed hard and terrible. Whoever eats it dies; even a thorn, having pierced, kills. Both of these are hard. What benefit is there in this?
Thus they bolted the doors of their houses and sent the children away.
Seeing this, the merchant thought, “These villagers are skilled in business dealings; come now, I shall have them take [the goods] by means of a stratagem. [He said: “It is exceedingly sweet...”
"Take it! Take it very cheaply! Sugar, molasses, and candied sugar are being sold at a low price;

they can even be obtained for counterfeit coins and fake kahāpaṇas," he proclaimed. Hearing this, the villagers went off in groups, joyful and exultant, and having paid much for the goods, they took them.
In this context, the Blessed One’s discourse on the meditation subject of recollecting the Buddha is like the merchant of poison-thorns shouting,
"Buy poison-thorns! Just as the merchant, after describing the qualities of the poison-thorns, incites the great crowd to take them, so too,
by praising the meditation subject of recollecting the Buddha with these seven terms, he incites that great crowd.
"What is the one thing?"—this is a question asked with the desire to explain. "Recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*) means the recollection that has arisen concerning the Buddha;
it is a designation for mindfulness having the qualities of the Buddha as its object. Furthermore, this meditation subject of recollecting the Buddha is twofold:
for the purpose of gladdening the mind and for the purpose of insight (*vipassanā*). How so? For when [the mind] is directed toward objects of foulness (*asubha*),...
When a bhikkhu who is developing one [meditation subject] finds his mind disturbed, becomes disenchanted, loses interest,
does not enter the path, and wanders hither and thither like a wild bull,
at that moment he should abandon his original meditation subject and recollect the mundane and supramundane qualities of the Tathāgata by way of the formula beginning, "Such is he, the Blessed One."
As he thus recollects the Buddha, his state of mind becomes serene and free from hindrances.
Having thus tamed that mind, he again directs his attention to the original meditation subject. How?
Just as a strong man, while cutting down a great tree for the sake of rafters or roof-peak supports, does not even notice the striking of the axe-blade upon the mere cutting of branches and foliage;
Just as one who is unable to fell a great tree when it has grown out of control might nevertheless not give up the task,
but go instead to a blacksmith’s shop, have a sharp axe made, and then fell that tree again— it is in this way that this should be understood.
Having thus tamed his mind by means of the recollection of the Buddha, he then brings the original meditation subject to mind once more.
Having produced the first jhāna with an impurity as its object and having reflected upon the factors of that jhāna, he enters the plane of the noble ones.
Thus, for the time being, it serves to gladden the mind.
But when he recollects the Recollection of the Buddha, recollecting in the manner beginning, "Who is this Blessed One?", and so forth?

While investigating whether it was a woman or a man, or perhaps one among the gods, humans, māras, or brahmās, he saw that it was none other than his own mind associated with mindfulness that had recollected;

and he saw that this mind is, in terms of the aggregates, the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), while the feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). By that...
"Perception associated [with consciousness] is the aggregate of perception; the co-nascent contact and so forth are the aggregate of formations—these are the four immaterial aggregates.

Having thus defined the immaterial, while searching for its support, he sees the heart-base (hadayavatthu), as well as the four great elements that are its support, and the remaining derived matter that arises dependent upon them.
Having grasped it and defined it as “all this is the aggregate of form,” one defines form and non-form in brief as “this form and the preceding non-form.

Then, having further defined the five aggregates in detail, and again defining them in brief as “all these five aggregates are the truth of suffering,” one defines craving— which brings that suffering about— as the truth of origin.
The cessation of that [craving] is the truth of cessation; the way leading to the full understanding of cessation is the truth of the path.

Having thus defined the four truths during the preliminary stage, he enters the plane of the Noble Ones in due order. At that time, this meditation subject for him is called "for the purpose of insight" (*vipassanā*).
This section on absorption (*appanā*), beginning with "This indeed," should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
297. This same method applies to the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*) and the others as well. Herein, however, this is the etymological explanation:

the recollection that has arisen with reference to the Dhamma is "recollection of the Dhamma"; this is a designation for mindfulness having the qualities of the Dhamma, such as being well-expounded, as its object.

The recollection that has arisen with reference to the Sangha is "recollection of the Sangha"; [this is a designation for mindfulness] having the qualities of the Sangha, such as being well-practiced, as its object.

This is a designation for mindfulness (*sati*). Mindfulness arisen with reference to virtue (*sīla*) is "recollection of virtue" (*sīlānussati*); this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of virtue such as being unbroken and so forth.

Mindfulness arisen with reference to generosity (*cāga*) is "recollection of generosity" (*cāgānussati*); this is a designation for mindfulness having as its object the qualities of generosity such as being free from attachment and so forth.
Mindfulness arisen with reference to deities (*devatā*) is "recollection of deities" (*devatānussati*); [this refers to] deities standing in the position of witnesses.
This is a designation for mindfulness whose object is one’s own qualities such as faith and so forth. Mindfulness arisen with reference to inhalation and exhalation is *ānāpānassati*;
this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the sign of the in-breath and out-breath.
Mindfulness arisen with reference to death is *maraṇassati*; this is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the cutting off of the life-faculty.
"Body-contemplation" (*kāyagatā*) means that mindfulness has gone to the form-body consisting of the distinctions of hair and so forth, or it has gone to the body;

thus, while it should be called "body-contemplated mindfulness" (*kāyagatā-sati*), it is stated as "body-contemplated mindfulness" (*kāyagatāsati*) without shortening the vowel. This is a designation for mindfulness whose object is the sign of the bodily parts such as hair.
"Recollection of peace" (*upasamānussati*) is the recollection arisen with reference to peace; it is [the name] for mindfulness whose object is the pacification of all suffering.
This is a designation for mindfulness. Alternatively, tranquility is twofold:
absolute tranquility and the tranquility of destruction. Therein, absolute tranquility is Nibbāna, and the tranquility of destruction is the Path.
Thus, the mindfulness that arises in one who recollects these two kinds of tranquility is "recollection of tranquility"; this is the meaning here. Thus, among these ten meditation subjects...
Mindfulness of breathing, mindfulness of death, and mindfulness directed to the body—these three are exclusively subjects for insight;
the remaining seven are subjects both for gladdening the mind and for insight.
This concludes the commentary on the first chapter.
16. Ekadhammapāḷi (16) 2.
Commentary on the Second Chapter of the Ekadhammapāḷi 298.
In the second [sutta], "wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is a designation for all sixty-two kinds of wrong view. "Of one with wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhikassa*) means of one who is possessed of that view.
299. “Right view” (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is a designation for all five kinds of right view. “Of one possessing right view” means of one endowed with that view. 302.
“Unwise attention” (*ayoniso manasikāra*) means attention that is not a skillful means. 303.
“Wise attention” (*yoniso manasikāra*) means attention that is a skillful means. In this regard, for one who attends unwisely, [states] previously unarisen...
Wrong view arises; once arisen, it increases until one enters the fixed course of rightness (*niyāma*). Once the fixed course has been entered, it is said to have fully increased.
For one who attends appropriately (*yoniso manasikaroto*), unarisen right view arises;
once arisen, it increases until the path of arahantship. Upon attaining the fruit of arahantship, it is said to have fully increased.
304. “Bhikkhus, regarding the statement ‘beings possessed of wrong view’: herein, some wrong view both obstructs heaven and obstructs the Path;
some obstructs the Path but does not obstruct heaven; and some obstructs neither heaven nor the Path.
In this regard, the threefold [wrong view] consisting of the view of no cause, the view of non-action, and the view of nihilism—”
It is both an obstruction to heaven and an obstruction to the Path. Wrong view consisting of the ten bases of grasping at extremes is an obstruction to the Path alone, not an obstruction to heaven.
The twenty-based view of individuality (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) is neither an obstruction to heaven nor an obstruction to the Path.
Having set aside this classification, however, in this sutta it says: "Bhikkhus, those possessed of wrong view..."
According to the scriptures, there is no view whatsoever—down to the twenty-based view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)—that is capable of leading one to heaven;
rather, it is said that such views cause one to sink exclusively into hell.
For just as even a pebble the size of a mung bean or a bean, when thrown into water, does not float but sinks straight to the bottom, so too is it with these views.
In the same way, even the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is not capable of leading one to heaven; rather, it causes one to sink exclusively into the states of misery (*apāya*).

305. Regarding the phrase "endowed with right view" (*sammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgatā*): here, right view is fivefold—namely, the right view of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata-sammādiṭṭhi*), the right view of meditative absorption (*jhāna-sammādiṭṭhi*), the right view of insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*), the right view of the path (*magga-sammādiṭṭhi*), and the right view of the fruit (*phala-sammādiṭṭhi*).

In this regard, the right view of being the owner of one’s kamma draws one toward a state of prosperity; the right view of meditative absorption (jhāna) grants rebirth-linking in the fine-material or immaterial realms;
the right view of the path destroys the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa); and the right view of the fruit wards off further becoming.
What does the right view of insight (vipassanā) do? It too does not draw about rebirth-linking. Thus says the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya.
Furthermore, he said: "If right view through insight (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi), when developed, is able to bring about Arahantship in this very life, that is well;
but if it is not able to do so, it gives [the practitioner] seven more existences, friend.
Thus, this right view has been described as both mundane and supramundane. However, in this context, it should be understood as being only the mundane kind which brings about further existence.
306. Regarding the phrase "whatever bodily action is undertaken and performed in accordance with one's view":
here, "in accordance with one's view" (*yathādiṭṭhi*) means corresponding to whichever view [one holds]. "Undertaken" (*samatta*) means fulfilled.
"Performed" (*samādinna*) means grasped. Thus, this is bodily action established upon a view, bodily action co-nascent with the view, and bodily action conformable to the view.
It is threefold. Therein, for one who holds the view:

"For one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, there is no evil on that account, nor is there any consequence of evil"—the bodily action consisting of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct belonging to such a person is called "bodily action based on a specific view. [Furthermore,] for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given...

Regarding the view: "For one who engages in sexual misconduct, there is no evil on that account, nor is there any arrival of evil," bodily action born together with this view—this is what is called "bodily action born together with wrong view" (*diṭṭhisahajāta-kāyakamma*).

Furthermore, when that very same [action] is fulfilled, undertaken, grasped, and adhered to, it is called "bodily action conforming to wrong view" (*diṭṭhānulomika-kāyakamma*). This applies likewise to vocal action and the others.

The same method applies here. Just as the construction was made in this context regarding bodily action—"For one who kills a living being, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, there is no evil resulting from that"—so too it should be applied to verbal and mental actions:
"For one who speaks falsehood, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, or has a mind of ill will..."
The construction should be made thus: "And for one who possesses wrong view, there is no evil resulting from that cause.
Regarding the phrases "and whatever volition," and so forth: it is precisely the volition co-arising with the view that is called "volition";

it is precisely the aspiration co-arising with the view that is called "aspiration"; and the fixing of the mind by way of that volition and aspiration is called "resolution. By means of those [factors], volition and the rest...
The associated factors such as contact (phassa) and so forth are called volitional formations (saṅkhāra).
"For his view, monks, is evil" means that the view of that person is evil and base. "Planted" means sown. "He takes up" means he grasps.
"For the sake of bitterness" is a synonym for the former [term].
“Endowed with beauty, fragrance, and flavor, this mango tree was once so;
receiving such honor as that, why has the mango now become bitter-fruit?
O Dadhivāhana, surrounded by *pucimanda* trees, [why is this mango so?]”
"The root is entwined with the root, the branch is joined with the branch;

through dwelling together with what is unpleasant, therefore it has bitter fruit"—as it is said in the passage where this was recited, so here too "bitter" (kaṭuka) should be understood as "pungent" (tittaka). "Because of its unpleasantness" (asātattāya) means because of its lack of sweetness.
Regarding this *Bījūpama-sutta*, the Elder Teachers of old said: "By the term 'view' (*diṭṭhi*), fixed wrong view is intended.
However, having rejected that, it was stated: "All sixty-two types of speculative views (*diṭṭhigata*) are included. In the immediately following sutta:
"For one who abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, and from sexual misconduct, there is no..."

In this context, one should understand [the factors] by applying bodily actions and so forth as they abide according to one's view, following the method beginning with the words, “merit on that account,” and so on.
However, here it should be understood that "aspiration" refers specifically to the stabilization of the mind conascent with right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
Furthermore, in this instance, right view is explained as being both mundane and supramundane. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Commentary on the Second Chapter. 16.
The Discourse on a Single Dhamma (16). 3.
Commentary on the Third Chapter of the Discourse on a Single Dhamma.
308. Regarding the first [clause] of the third [section]:
"one of wrong view" means one whose view is not according to reality. "One of perverted vision" means one who has a perverted vision by means of that very same wrong view.

"Having turned away from the true Dhamma" means having turned away from the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action. "He establishes in the non-Dhamma" means he establishes in the non-Dhamma consisting of the ten courses of unwholesome action.
And here, by "one person," Devadatta along with the six teachers and others of similar kind should be understood.

309. In the second [verse], "one of right view" means one who possesses the view according to reality. "One of non-perverted vision" means one who, by that very same right view, possesses vision free from perversion.
"Unrighteous things" refers to the ten courses of unwholesome action. "The True Dhamma" refers to what is comprised of the ten courses of wholesome action.

Regarding the true Dhamma (*saddhamme*): as for the "single individual" (*ekapuggalo*) here, when a Buddha has not yet appeared, such as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) or an omniscient Bodhisatta, these are what are found;
but when a Buddha has appeared, it refers both to the Buddha and to his disciples.
310. In the third [case], "having wrong view as supreme" (*micchādiṭṭhiparamāni*) means those for whom wrong view is supreme (*paramā*).

For there are five deeds of immediate retribution (ānantariya-kamma) that are called "greatly blameworthy," and the intention is that wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) alone is even more greatly blameworthy than those.
Why? Because they have a limit. For it is said that four of the deeds of immediate retribution cause rebirth in hell;
the act of schism in the Saṅgha likewise results in remaining in hell for an eon (kappa). Thus, these have a limit.
There is a limit that can be discerned; however, there is no boundary for fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi*).
For it is the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); for one possessed of it, there is no emergence from existence. It even leads those who think it should be heard to practice wrongly.
And for one possessed of it, there is neither heaven nor the path. At the destruction of an eon...
Even when the Brahma-world has arisen for the great multitude, one who holds a fixed wrong view does not arise there, but is reborn in the back of the world-sphere (piṭṭhicakkavāḷa).
But does the back of the world-sphere not burn up? It does burn up;
yet they say that even while it is burning, this person is cooked in a single spot in the sky.
311. Regarding the fourth [case], Makkhali is a founder of a sect who received that name based on his saying, "Do not stumble" (*mā khalī*).
"At the river-mouth" (*nadīmukhe*) means at the place where two rivers meet. This is merely an illustration;
it applies also to two ravines, two bodies of water, the ocean and saltwater, and the ocean and a river—whichever of these it may be.
Any place where fish congregate, or any other such water. They cast a fish-net.

"Should set" means they should spread it. For people, having made a fish-net capable of holding one, two, or three jars by means of reeds, sugarcane, bamboo, or *palāsa*-twig stakes, and having tied its rim with a rope, lead it to the mouth of a river and [place it] between two...
In mountain passes, they crush stumps and bind them there with ropes; it was with reference to this that it was said.
For when one has entered therein, there is no escape even for a small fish. *Anayāya* means for non-prosperity.
*Byāsanāya* means for destruction. *Makkhali moghapuriso*: this Makkhali Gosāla is an empty man, a man who casts people away.

"I think he has arisen in the world" means that he has appeared in the world like a human trap, for the purpose of obstructing the great multitude from traveling along the path leading to heaven and liberation. 312.
Regarding the fifth [offense] and those following, "in a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, O Bhikkhus": this refers to what is called a poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya.
The teaching of the outsiders. For there, the Teacher is not omniscient, the Dhamma is poorly expounded, and the community practices wrongly.
"And he who exhorts" refers to the teacher-person who exhorts. "And whom he exhorts" refers to the pupil whom he exhorts.
"And he who, being exhorted, practices accordingly" refers to the pupil who, having been exhorted by the teacher, practices in that manner.

Acting upon his words, one proceeds toward becoming such [a person]. "They produce much demerit" means that the instigator, by inciting a hundred people to kill living beings and so forth, incurs demerit equal to that of all of them through their unwholesome action.
Therefore he said: "They all produce much demerit."

313. "Well-expounded" (*svākkhāta*) means well-proclaimed and well-taught. For in such a Dhamma and Vinaya, the Teacher is omniscient, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the community is practicing rightly.
By encouraging others—seeing monks who have entered for alms and exhorting them toward rice gruel, solid food, and so forth—one causes all of them to generate much merit.
Through the merit of the donors, they themselves attain merit equally. Therefore it is said: "They generate much merit.
(314) "The donor must know the measure" means that the individual donor must know the proper amount; he should give according to that measure and not give more than what fills [the recipient's need].
For instead of saying "it should not be given," it is said "it should be given in small measure" by way of the proper amount.
It has been said. Why? For even if one gives more after having filled [the bowl], there is no superior human excellence, divine excellence, or the excellence of Nibbāna resulting from that excess.
"Not by the recipient" means that for the recipient, once they have known the proper measure, there is no further duty of receiving.
Why? Because for him, once he has known the measure, it must be fulfilled based on the principle of receiving only what is measured.
There is no such thing as a practice of fewness of wishes. Whatever one receives, that much should be accepted;
for the root of taking more than necessary will lead to the burdening of wives and children. 315.
"The recipient must know the measure" means that the person receiving must know the proper amount. How so?
In that case, one must understand the donor’s capacity, understand the nature of the gift, and understand one’s own strength.
For if the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a little, one should accept only a little according to the donor’s capacity.
If the gift is meager but the donor wishes to give much, one should accept only a little according to the nature of the gift.
Even when there is much property to be given and the donor wishes to give much, one should accept only according to measure, having understood one’s own capacity.
For by accepting in this way, knowing the proper measure, one fulfills the practice of fewness of desires.
Unarisen gain arises, and arisen gain becomes stable. Those without confidence become confident, and those already confident attain even greater confidence.
He becomes an eye for the great multitude and ensures that the Dispensation endures for a long time.

In this regard, there are these instances: it is said that in the Rohaṇa province, at the Kuṭimbīya Monastery, a certain young monk during a time of famine took a ladleful of rice from the house of a laborer in that village for the purpose of eating, and as he was about to depart—
He received only a single ladleful of rice. One day, seeing a guest at that house, he took only that one ladleful of rice for him.

When asked, "For what reason?", he explained the matter; the noble youth was filled with faith and said at the king’s gate to his friends and ministers, "Such is the venerable one who visits our family."
All of them, inspired by his quality of fewness of desires, provided sixty full meals on that very same day.
Thus, one who is of few desires brings about unarisen gain.
King Saddhātissa, having tested his junior attendant, the minister Tissa, had him cook a partridge.

He had it brought. Then, at the time of eating, thinking, "I shall eat after giving the first portion," he was giving a quail’s meat to the novice Bhaṇḍagāha, the attendant of the Great Elder, in the Aṭṭhaka Sāla Pariveṇa.
While the novice accepted only a small amount, the king, becoming confident in his virtue of fewness of desires, said, "I am pleased, dear one; I give you eight meals as your regular portion."
"Great King, I give these eight to my preceptor. "I give another eight as well. "I give those to our teacher.
"I give another eight as well. "I give those to those who share the same preceptor.
"I give another eight as well. "I give those to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. "I give another eight as well. The novice accepted them. Thus it was for him.
“Gains that have arisen become stable;
those without faith gain confidence. Regarding this, it is said: once, while feeding brahmins, the Brahmin Dīgha was unable to satisfy them even after giving five platters of food to each.
Then one day, thinking, “These ascetics are indeed few in their desires,”...
Having heard this, in order to investigate the matter, he had food prepared and went to the monastery at the time when the Saṅgha of monks was finishing their meal.
Seeing about thirty monks eating in the dining hall, he took a single bowl of food and approached the senior elder of the Saṅgha.
The elder gestured with his finger and took only a small amount.
In this very manner, a single bowl of rice reached everyone.

Then the brahmin, convinced that "the virtue of these recluses is indeed true," being inspired by their fewness of desires, bestowed a thousand [pieces of gold] and had a shrine constructed in that very monastery.
Thus, those who were not yet inspired become inspired.

Regarding the phrase "those who are already confident become even more confident," there is no need for a specific external object here. For when those who are already confident see one who possesses few desires (*appiccha*), their confidence increases all the more.

However, when the general public sees one like the Elder Majjhantika Tissa who possesses few desires, they think, "I too shall be one who possesses few desires"; thus, such a person is said to be "the eye of the world" for the sake of those with few desires.

Furthermore, because of the statement, "Bhikkhus, having few desires leads to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the True Dhamma," one who possesses few desires is said to ensure that the Dispensation endures for a long time.
