Regarding "no donor": in this well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, there is no requirement for a donor to know a specific measure [of what to give].
Whatever gift one possesses, it is appropriate to give that much without restriction.
For by giving without restriction, one attains—without restriction—the excellence of human life, the excellence of the devas, and the excellence of Nibbāna.
One obtains what is ever higher and more sublime. 316.

As for the one who has aroused energy, thinking "one dwells in suffering," he who devotes himself to such practices as the fivefold self-mortification by burning, the leaping from mountain peaks, the falling into abysses, the revolving in the sun's path, and the exertion in the squatting posture, dwells in suffering even in this very life;
this is the case for one who has undertaken such [austerities] in an external discipline.
By the ripening of such ascetic practices, one is reborn in hell and dwells in suffering even in the future life. 317.
As for the statement, "He who is indolent dwells in suffering," he too dwells in suffering both in this present life and in the future life.
How so? For one who, from the time of going forth, lacks wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) toward the word of the Buddha...
He does not learn; he does not perform the duties toward his teacher and preceptor; he does not perform the duties at the shrine courtyard or the Bodhi-tree courtyard.

Having consumed the gifts of the faithful from the people with an unreflective enjoyment, and having spent the day pursuing the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of reclining, when he awakes, he indulges in three types of thoughts. In just a few days, he falls away from the state of a bhikkhu.
He falls away. Thus he dwells in suffering even in this very life. Furthermore, because he has gone forth but has not properly practiced the duty of a recluse, it is said:
"Just as kusa grass, if grasped incorrectly, cuts the hand itself, So the ascetic life, if wrongly undertaken, drags one down to hell."
He takes rebirth only in the states of misery (*apāya*). Thus, he dwells in suffering even in the future life.
318. As for the one who is lazy, thinking "I shall dwell in happiness," he performs various ascetic practices from time to time as previously described;
then, from time to time, dressed in white garments, wearing garlands, scents, and ointments, and eating sweet food...
Eating and lying on soft beds, he dwells in happiness both in this very life and in the future.
Because he did not grasp that practice of asceticism too tightly, he does not experience excessive suffering in hell;
therefore, it is said that he dwells in happiness in the future life.

319. "He who has aroused energy dwells in happiness": for one who has aroused energy, from the time of going forth, becomes a fulfiller of the duties, masters the word of the Buddha, and applies himself to wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*).
Then, as he reviews both the fulfillment of his duties, the mastery of the Buddha’s word, and the performance of the ascetic’s practice (*samaṇadhamma*), [he dwells in happiness].
The mind becomes serene. Thus one dwells in happiness in this very life.

Furthermore, for one who is unable to attain Arahantship in this present life, it is said that they "dwell in happiness even in the future life" because they become one of quick higher knowledge in their rebirth state.
320. "Bhikkhus, just as even a small amount of excrement is foul-smelling"—this Sutta is the origin of the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
It has been stated. From what occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*) did it arise? It arose from the *Sattuppāda-sutta* in the Ninth Chapter (*Navaka-nipāta*).
For while the Tathāgata was explaining that matter, he said: "Nine persons have been released from hell, released from the animal realm, and released from the sphere of hungry ghosts.
Then this thought occurred to him: "If my sons were to hear this teaching of the Dhamma..."

Thinking, "Having heard that hell has been exhausted, the animal womb has been exhausted, the realm of hungry ghosts has been exhausted, and the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the fallen states have been exhausted, they will not think to strive for the sake of the higher paths and fruits," I shall arouse a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in them.
For the purpose of arousing such urgency, he began this sutta with the words, "Just as if, monks... In this context, "insignificant" means...
Even a mere trifle, the size of a small particle—even if one were to take it with the tip of a blade of kusa grass and smell it—it would indeed be foul-smelling.
"I do not praise even a trifling existence" means that I do not praise rebirth in existence (bhava) for even a moment.
Now, showing a simile for this, he said: "even for as long as a finger-snap. This refers to the very shortest duration.
By "a moment" (kāla), it is meant even the time it takes to strike with two fingers joined together.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout. This concludes the commentary on the Third Chapter.
16. Ekadhammapāḷi (16) 4.
Commentary on the Fourth Chapter of the Ekadhammapāḷi 322.
Regarding the first [sutta] of the fourth chapter: "In Jambudīpa" means a continent (dīpa) known and made manifest by the rose-apple tree (jambu), thus it is called Jambudīpa.
It is said that on this island there is a great rose-apple tree named Mahājambū, which serves as its distinguishing mark;
it grows on the Himavanta mountains, stands for an eon, is five hundred yojanas in height, has branches fifty yojanas long, and a trunk fifteen yojanas in girth.
Because of this tree, this island is called Jambudīpa. And just as the rose-apple tree on this island endures for an eon, so too does the kadamba tree endure for an eon in Aparagoyāna.
In Uttarakuru there is the Kappa-rukkha tree; in Pubbavideha, the Sirīsa tree; among the Asuras, the Cittapāṭali tree; among the Supaṇṇas, the Simbali tree;
and among the Devas, the Pāricchattaka tree—all these also endure for an eon.
“The Pāṭali, the Simbali, the Jambū, and the Pāricchattaka of the Devas;”
“The *kadamba*, the *kapparukkha*, and the *sirisas* tree is the seventh.
“Delightful groves” (*ārāmarāmaṇeyyaka*) means the delightful quality of flower-groves and fruit-groves, such as Veḷuvana, Jīvakambavana, Jetavana, and Pubbārāma.
Such things are insignificant and limited in this Jambudīpa; the meaning is that they are not many. The same applies to the remaining terms.

This is the method. Herein, "delightfulness of woods" should be understood as forest groves located in places such as the Vaṅka mountain, the Himālaya mountains, and so forth, resembling the Nāga-forest, Sāla-forest, Campaka-forest, and others.
"Delightfulness of ground" refers to level ground locations similar to the Jeta Grove monastery, the Magadha country, and so forth.
"Delightfulness of lotus ponds" refers to those similar to the lotus pond at the Jeta Grove, the Gaggarā lotus pond, and others.
The site for the arrangement of lotus ponds having circular, square, elongated, curved, and other such shapes.
"Ukkūlavikūla" means both high ground (*ukkūla*) and low ground (*vikūla*); therein, high ground is elevated terrain, and low ground is depressed terrain.

"Nadīvidugga" is the place where rivers have split apart; because it is difficult to traverse, it is called a river-difficulty (*nadīvidugga*). "Khāṇukaṇṭakaṭṭhāna" refers to places with stumps and thorns.
It is a place where stumps, thorns, and the like—both those native to the region and those being brought from elsewhere—are established.
"Mountainous unevenness" means the ruggedness of mountains. As for those that grow in water, they are indeed more numerous.
It is said that Suvaṇṇabhūmi is about seven hundred yojanas from here; a ship traveling with a favorable wind takes seven days and nights to reach it.
Now at one time, as the ship was thus proceeding, it traveled for seven days only along the back of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa fish.
In this way, the great abundance of water-dwelling beings is to be understood.
Furthermore, this matter is to be understood through the limited extent of dry land and the vastness of the water.
Just as if there were a single lotus-stalk in a great lake, with four leaves and a single unopened lotus bud in the middle;

even so, the four continents are like the four leaves, Mount Sineru is like the unopened lotus bud in the middle, and the remaining space surrounded by water is like the water. Its vastness is as follows:
It is manifest to those possessing psychic power (iddhimanta). For when they travel through the air, the four great continents appear to them like four petals;
Mount Sineru appears like a lotus bud in the center; and the remaining space surrounded by water appears like water.
Since it is born within such a vast expanse of water, it should be understood that the "water-born" (odakā) are more numerous.
323. Regarding the second [offense] and those following, "except for humans" (*aññatra manussehi*): here, the four states of misery (*apāya*) are intended by "except for humans.
"In the Middle Countries" (*majjhimesu janapadesu*): to the east there is a market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that is Mahāsālā;
further beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side of them is the Middle Country. To the southeast... [text continues].
There is a river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the middle country.
In the southern direction there is a market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the middle country.
In the western direction there is a brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the middle country. In the northern direction...
"In this direction there is a mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the middle.
This is the meaning of "districts thus delimited. For this district is shaped like a drum;
it is eighty leagues long in some places, a hundred leagues in some places, two hundred leagues in some places, but three hundred leagues along its middle.
With its surrounding boundary, it is nine hundred yojanas in extent. Within this area, these beings are reborn:
Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, attendants of the Buddha, disciples of the Buddha, the Mother of the Buddha, the Father of the Buddha, and Wheel-turning Monarchs.
Furthermore, a "Middle Country" is also obtained by taking various sub-regions; for indeed, the entire Jambudīpa [may be considered as such].

The "Middle Country" (majjhimapadesa) refers to the remaining islands as bordering regions. In the island of Tambapaṇṇi, Anurādhapura is called the Middle Country, while the rest is considered a border region;
such is the method to be understood. 324.

Regarding the terms "wise, not dull, and not deaf-mute," this refers here to the wisdom of the ownership of one's actions (kammassakata-paññā), the wisdom of meditative absorption (jhāna-paññā), and the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā).
Those endowed with path-wisdom and fruition-wisdom are called "possessed of wisdom," and are called "unconfused" and "not dull.
Those from whose mouths no "slime" (eḷā) drips are called "aneḷamūga"; the meaning is that they have faces free from fault, being "aneḷamukha.
"Capable" means competent, endowed with both physical strength and the power of knowledge. "To understand the meaning" refers to [discerning] what is beneficial and what is not beneficial.
"To know what is a cause and what is not a cause. "Lacking wisdom" (*duppaññā*) means having little wisdom or no wisdom at all. "Dull-witted" (*jaḷā*) means sluggish and utterly deluded.

(325) "By means of the noble eye of wisdom" (*ariyena paññācakkhunā*) means by means of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). "Enveloped in ignorance" (*avijjāgatā*) means possessed by the darkness of ignorance.

(326) "Those who obtain the sight of the Tathāgata" means those who, having understood the qualities of the Tathāgata, obtain the opportunity to see the Tathāgata with visual consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
327. “Proclaimed by the Tathāgata” means proclaimed, made known, and spoken by the Tathāgata. “For the sake of hearing” means for the purpose of hearing with the auditory consciousness.
328. “They bear [it in mind]” means they do not forget it. 329.
“They examine the meaning of the teachings they have borne in mind” means that, having become proficient in the text, they examine what is the true meaning and what is not.

330. "Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma" means having known both the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and the canonical text (*pāḷi*). "Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" means fulfilling the practice that is in conformity [with the Dhamma].
331. "In instances that inspire spiritual urgency" means in causes that give rise to a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*). "They are stirred" means they attain a sense of urgency. 332.
"They strive methodically" means they exert the energy of striving by means of the proper method (*upāya*).

333. “Having renunciation as its object” (*vavassaggārammaṇa*): renunciation (*vavassagga*) is said to be *nibbāna*; the meaning is, “having made that the object. “They obtain concentration” (*samādhiṃ labhanti*): they attain both the concentration of the path (*maggasamādhi*) and the concentration of the fruit (*phalasamādhi*).
334. “Of the best foods and best flavors” (*annaggarasaggānaṃ*): of the most excellent foods and the most excellent tastes. “They subsist by gleaning” (*uñchena yāpenti*):
they subsist by the practice of gleaning, or by roots and fruits from the forest, or by food brought in an alms-bowl (*kapāla*). And here—

If, when a thought arises for the sake of any kind of food, whether hard or soft, one does not obtain it at that very moment, this person is said to be "one who does not obtain the finest and most excellent flavors.

Furthermore, even if one obtains it at that very moment, if upon looking at it the color, fragrance, and taste become unpleasant, this person too is said to be "one who does not obtain the finest and most excellent flavors. But as for the one...
They obtain color, fragrance, and flavor; they are pleasing—this is what is called "one who obtains the finest and most excellent flavors of food.
At the highest limit, this refers to a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*); at the lowest limit, it should be understood as King Dhammāsoka.
In brief, that meal for which a single bowl is worth one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] is called the "finest and most excellent flavor of food. Furthermore, that which...
When people see the Saṅgha of bhikkhus wandering for alms, they give them food that is most excellent and refined;
what is this called? This is called the "supreme essence of food" (annaggarasagga) in comparison to those who subsist on gleanings gathered in a bowl. 335.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "the essence of the meaning" (attharasa), the "essence of the meaning" refers to the four fruits of asceticism (sāmaññaphala); the "essence of the Dhamma" refers to the four paths (magga); the "essence of liberation" (vimuttirasa) refers to the deathless Nibbāna. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
Commentary on the Fourth Chapter.
The Summary of Jambudīpa is finished.
17. Commentary on the Chapter on Qualities Inspiring Confidence.
366. Regarding the passage beginning with *addhamidaṃ*, the word *addha* is a synonym for "one side" (*ekamsa*).
Thus, it means: "This is one side of gains; this is the certainty regarding gains. The phrase *yadidaṃ āraññikattaṃ* refers to that state of being a forest-dweller. This is what is meant:
the state of being a forest-dweller is indeed one side of gains—that is, its inevitable occurrence—such that it is not possible for a forest-dweller to [avoid] gain.
"He does not obtain": for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, thinking "I shall act in a manner befitting my dwelling in the forest," does not commit what is called evil;

then the great multitude, having conceived respect for him, thinking "This bhikkhu is a forest-dweller," honors him with the four requisites. Therefore it was said: "Bhikkhus, this is half of gains, namely..."
"Being a forest-dweller": the same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Herein, "erudition" (*bāhusacca*) means the state of being well-versed in the scriptures.

"Stability" (*thāvareyya*) means the state of having attained stability due to having gone forth for a long time. "Perfection of deportment" (*ākappasampadā*) means the excellence of deportment, such as the manner of wearing the robes.
"Perfection of retinue" (*parivārasampadā*) means having a pure retinue. "Son of good family" (*kolaputti*) means the state of being a son of noble family.
"Beauty of complexion" means the possession of a perfect physical form. "Eloquence" means sweetness in the delivery of speech.

"Freedom from illness" means the attainment of health. For a healthy bhikkhu, by virtue of his own bodily well-being, becomes one who fulfills both the task of insight (vipassanā) and the task of study (gantha); thus, gain arises for him.
The sixteen qualities that produce confidence are concluded.
18. Commentary on the Chapter on Another Grouping of the Flicker of a Finger-Snap (Apara-accharāsaṅghātavagga). 382.
"Even for the duration of a finger-snap" (*accharāsaṅghātamattam*): this sutta was also spoken on the very same occasion as the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*) regarding the simile of the mass of fire.
For when loving-kindness has reached absorption (appanā), there is no talk at all regarding its result (vipāka).

It should be understood that this teaching was undertaken on account of that very circumstance. In this context, "first" means "first by way of numerical sequence," or "this is first because it is attained first"—the meaning is exactly as stated in the *Vibhaṅga*.
As for "jhāna," jhāna is twofold: contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and...
"And contemplation of characteristics. In this context, "contemplation of the object" refers to the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
For these are called "contemplation of the object" because they contemplate objects such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.

"Contemplation of characteristics" refers to insight (*vipassanā*), the path, and the fruit. For insight contemplates the characteristic of formations (*saṅkhāra-lakkhaṇa*) by way of impermanence and so forth.

What is called "contemplation of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*)? However, since the function of contemplating characteristics is accomplished by the Path through insight (*vipassanā*), the Path is "contemplation of characteristics.
The Fruit is called "contemplation of characteristics" because it contemplates Nibbāna itself, which has the characteristics of emptiness, signlessness, and desirelessness.
In this context, however, "contemplation of the object" (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) refers to this.
This is what is intended. What need is there to mention those who cultivate it? Those who cultivate this first jhāna—those who practice it repeatedly—for them there is nothing further to be said.
The rest here should be understood according to the method already stated below.
Regarding the phrases "the second," and so forth, the meaning should be understood by the method beginning with "the second because of its numerical sequence," and so on.
386–387. *Mettā* is the pervading of benevolence toward all beings. *Cetovimutti* is liberation of mind. Here, it is specifically *mettā* that has reached absorption (*appanā*) which is intended.

The same method applies to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others as well. Furthermore, these four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), they are the footings of the round, they are the footings of insight (*vipassanā*), they are pleasant dwellings in this very life, and they are the footings of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
They are either the bases for cessation or not; however, they are not supramundane. Why? Because they have sentient beings as their object.

390. "Contemplating the body in the body" refers to: the section on mindfulness of breathing, the section on postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, the section on attention to repulsiveness, the section on attention to elements, the nine cemetery contemplations, and the four blue-lotus kasiṇas and so forth by way of internal preparation.
Contemplating that very body with wisdom in this eighteenfold body, he "dwells"—that is, he conducts himself and proceeds.
By this, the mode of conduct of the bhikkhu who is developing the foundation of mindfulness through body-contemplation in its eighteen aspects is described.
"Ardent" means by means of the energy for developing that very aforementioned foundation of mindfulness.

"Endowed with energy. "Clearly comprehending" means understanding correctly through the wisdom that encompasses the eighteenfold mindfulness foundation of body-contemplation (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*).
"Mindful" means being possessed of the mindfulness that encompasses the eighteenfold body-contemplation.
"Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world" means having removed both craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure and dejection regarding that very world known as the body.
It is said that "having removed and suppressed the grief associated with aversion, he dwells contemplating the body in the body.
Up to this point, it should be understood that only the pure contemplation of form (*rūpa*) has been explained by way of the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body.
Regarding "contemplating feelings in feelings": among feelings distinguished as pleasant and so forth, when experiencing a pleasant feeling... [he knows,] "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling."

He understands: "I experience a feeling. Whether it be a painful feeling, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, a worldly pleasant feeling, an unworldly pleasant feeling, a worldly painful feeling, an unworldly painful feeling, a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, or an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—while experiencing such an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling...
"‘I experience,’ thus he understands"—thus it is said while contemplating the ninefold feeling.

However, in this context, the meaning should be understood by way of the energy, wisdom, and mindfulness that grasp the development of the foundation of mindfulness through the contemplation of the ninefold feeling, beginning with the words "ardent," etc.
And herein, "the world" should be understood as feeling.
The same method applies to mental states (*cittadhamma*) as well. Herein, regarding "contemplating the mind in the mind" (*citte cittānupassī*), the meaning is:
when the sixteenfold classification of the mind has been detailed thus—"one understands a lustful mind as a lustful mind"—one contemplates that very mind by means of apprehensive contemplation.
Regarding "contemplating mental states in mental states" (*dhammesu dhammānupassī*), [it refers to] the five hindrances, the five aggregates of clinging, and so forth.

The meaning is that one contemplates those phenomena by means of the contemplation that grasps phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) among the phenomena taught in five ways according to their divisions— namely, the six internal and external bases, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the four noble truths. Here, however,
in the foundations of mindfulness consisting of the contemplation of feelings and the contemplation of the mind, there is only the pure comprehension of the formless (*arūpa*).
Thus, the investigation of the material and immaterial in the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of phenomena has been explained.
Therefore, it should be understood that these four foundations of mindfulness are taught as being a mixture of both mundane and supramundane. 394.
"Of those that have not arisen" means of those that have not yet come into being. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means those produced by lack of skill.

Of states such as greed and so forth. "For the sake of non-arising" means for the purpose of their non-production. "He generates desire" means he arouses wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act.
"He exerts himself" means he applies effort and strives. "He rouses energy" means he performs physical and mental energy.
"He uplifts the mind" means he raises the mind by means of that very co-nascent energy. "He strives" means...
He exerts the energy of striving.
"Of those that have arisen" means of those that have been born or produced. "Of wholesome states" means of states such as non-greed and so forth, which have arisen through skill.

"For their stability" means for the purpose of their remaining. "For their non-confusion" means for the purpose of their not being lost. "For their further increase" means for their repeated occurrence.
"Vepullāya" means for the sake of vastness. "Bhāvanāya" means for the sake of development. "Paripūriyā" means for the sake of fulfillment.
This, first of all, is the single-word extraction of the meaning of the four right endeavors (*sammappadhāna*).

Furthermore, this discourse on the right endeavors is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Therein, the mundane occurs throughout the entire preliminary stage; it should be understood as occurring precisely at the moment of the mundane path according to the method of the *Kassapa-saṃyutta*. For it is said therein:
“Friends, there are these four right endeavors. What are the four? Here, friends, a bhikkhu arouses ardor, thinking:
‘Unarisen evil unwholesome states might arise in me, which would lead to my harm. He arouses ardor, thinking:
‘Evil unwholesome states that have arisen in me, if not abandoned, might lead to my harm. He arouses ardor, thinking: ‘Unarisen...’”
“One makes an effort, thinking: ‘If unarisen wholesome states do not arise, they would lead to my harm’;
one makes an effort, thinking: ‘If arisen wholesome states cease, they would lead to my harm.
And here, ‘evil unwholesome states’ should be understood as greed and so forth. ‘Unarisen wholesome states’ refers to serenity and insight.”

And there is the path. What are called "arisen wholesome states" are simply serenity and insight. As for the path, once it has arisen, there is nothing that ceases while leading to what is unbeneficial;
for it ceases only after having provided the condition for the fruit.
Or, if it was stated that in the previous case too only serenity and insight are to be understood, that is not correct.
Thus, the discourse on the mundane right exertions (sammappadhāna) is to be understood in its entirety according to the method in the Kassapa-saṃyutta.
However, at the moment of the supramundane path, this single energy receives four names by way of accomplishing four functions.
In that context, regarding the phrase "of unarisen evil states," it should be understood according to the method stated in such passages as "unarisen sensual desire" and so forth.
The meaning should be understood. Regarding the phrase "of evil states that have arisen," there are four kinds of "arisen":

arisen as currently occurring (*vattamānuppanna*), arisen as having occurred and passed away (*bhutvāvigatuppanna*), arisen by providing an opportunity (*okāsakatuppanna*), and arisen by reaching its plane (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*).

Among these, those defilements that exist and are possessed of arising and so forth are called "arisen as currently occurring. However, when karma has impelled and has experienced the flavor of the object...
Having ceased its maturation, it is called "passed away"; having arisen and then ceased, karma is called "passed away.
Both of these come to be designated as "arisen after having passed away" (*bhūtvā-vigata-utpanna*).
When wholesome or unwholesome karma obstructs the maturation of other karma and creates an opportunity for its own maturation, the maturation arises once that opportunity has been made.
That which is said to have "arisen from the making of an opportunity" refers to what is called *okāsakatuppanna*.
The five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*), however, are known as the "ground" for insight (*vipassanā*); they are divided into past, future, and present.

Regarding these, it cannot be said whether the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) latent within them are past, future, or present. For even those tendencies latent in past aggregates remain unabandoned.
They exist; they remain unabandoned even when latent in future aggregates, and they remain unabandoned even when latent in present aggregates.
This is what is called "arisen by way of having acquired the plane. Therefore the ancients said:
"Defilements that have not been eradicated in their respective planes are reckoned as 'arisen by way of having acquired the plane.'"

Furthermore, there are four kinds of arisen [defilements]: arisen as manifest activity (*samudācāruppanna*), arisen by way of seizing an object (*ārammaṇādhiggahituppanna*), arisen without being suppressed (*avikkhambhituppanna*), and arisen without being eradicated (*asamugghātituppanna*).
Among these, that which is currently occurring at this very moment is called "arisen as manifest activity.
Once the eyes have been opened and the sign of the object has been grasped, the defilements will not arise at any subsequent moment of recollection.
It should not be said [that defilements will arise]. Why? Because the object has been seized. How so?
Just as it cannot be said that milk will not flow from a milky tree at the spot where it has been struck again and again with an axe, so it is here.
This is called "arisen by seizing the object. However, it cannot be said that "defilements un-suppressed by attainment will arise in this particular place."

They must be said [to exist]. Why? Because they have not been suppressed. How so? Just as if one were to strike a milky tree with an axe, it cannot be said that "milk will not come out from this particular spot," so it is here. This is what is called "arisen without being suppressed.
However, defilements that have not been eradicated by the Path arise even for one reborn in the peak of existence; thus, it is according to the previous method.
This should be expanded in detail. This is what is called "arisen but not eradicated.

Among these types of arisen states, there are four kinds of arising that are not to be abandoned by the Path: arisen as currently occurring (*vattamānuppanna*), arisen as having been experienced and passed away (*bhutvāvigatuppanna*), arisen as providing space (*okāsakatuppanna*), and arisen as active manifestation (*samudācāruppanna*).
Then there is arisen by way of having acquired the plane (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*) and arisen by way of having grasped the object (*ārammaṇādhiggahituppanna*).
That which is to be abandoned by the path is fourfold: arisen but not suppressed, and arisen and not eradicated.
For when the path arises, it abandons these defilements. Those defilements which it abandons cannot be said to be past, future, or present.
And this has also been said:
“If he abandons defilements in the past, then he is merely exhausting what is already exhausted, ceasing what has already ceased, bringing to its end what has already come to an end;

he abandons that which is past and non-existent. If he abandons defilements in the future, then he abandons what is unborn, what is unproduced, what has not arisen, what has not become manifest; he abandons that which is future and non-existent.”
One abandons that. If one abandons defilements in the present, then surely one who is lustful abandons lust; one who is hating abandons hatred; one who is deluded abandons delusion;
one who is fettered abandons conceit; one who is misapprehending abandons wrong view; one who has fallen into uncertainty abandons doubt;
and one who has become entrenched abandons the underlying tendency. Thus dark and bright states proceed coupled together; this is the development of the path associated with defilement.
"It happens... [and so on] "...therefore, there is no cultivation of the path, no realization of the fruit, no abandoning of the defilements, and no penetration of the Dhamma.
"There is cultivation of the path... there is penetration of the Dhamma. "How so?
It is just as if there were a young tree... [and so on] ...they do not become manifest because they have not yet become manifest."
Thus, while the tree with unripened fruit is mentioned in the Pāḷi, the tree with ripened fruit must now be illustrated.

Suppose there were a young mango tree bearing fruit, and people were to eat its fruits, fill their baskets by dropping the remainder, and then another person were to cut it down with an axe. By that act, neither the fruits already past would be lost, nor...
Neither those of the future nor those of the present have been destroyed. For those of the past have already been enjoyed by humans;
those of the future have not yet arisen and cannot be destroyed. Furthermore, at the very moment the tree was cut down, there were no fruits existing at all;
thus, even those of the present were not destroyed. However, had the tree not been cut down, then its earth-essence and...
Just as those fruits that might have arisen depending on water are destroyed;

for they do not arise even though they were about to be born, they do not come into being even though they were about to be produced, and they do not manifest even though they were about to become manifest—exactly so, the Path neither abandons nor does it not abandon the defilements classified as past and so forth. For those defilements which, by means of the Path...
When the aggregates have not been fully understood, their arising may occur;

but because the aggregates have been fully understood through the Path, those defilements do not arise even though they were not yet born, they do not manifest even though they were not yet produced, and they do not become apparent even though they were not yet manifested.
This is like a woman whose infant has died so that she does not give birth again, or like those who have drunk medicine for the purpose of pacifying their diseases.

Or rather, this meaning should be clarified as follows: It cannot be said that the path abandons those defilements which are past, future, or present; yet it is not the case that the path does not abandon defilements.
Rather, it is with reference to those defilements which the path abandons that the words "of arisen evil" and so forth were spoken.
And it is not only defilements that the path abandons; rather, because of the non-abandonment of defilements, those aggregates of clinging that would otherwise arise are also abandoned.

For this has been said: "By means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, through the cessation of volitional consciousness, whatever name-and-form would have arisen in the beginningless round of existence—setting aside the seven [remaining] births—"

"Herein these cease"—this is the full detail. Thus, the path emerges from both the appropriated and the unappropriated. However, by way of existence (*bhava*), the stream-entry path emerges from the existence of the states of deprivation;
the once-return path, from one part of the existence of happy destinies; the non-return path, from the existence of sensual desire within happy destinies;
and the arahant path, from the existence of the fine-material and immaterial realms. Some also say that it emerges from all existences whatsoever.
Now, how at the moment of the Path (magga) is there development for the arising of what has not yet arisen, or how is there stability for what has already arisen?
It is precisely through the occurrence of the Path itself. For when the Path occurs, it is called "unarisen" because it has never arisen before.
Indeed, having gone to a place never visited before, or having experienced an object never experienced before, [it is said to arise].
People say: "We have come to a place not yet reached; we are experiencing an object never experienced before.
Whatever its occurrence is, that itself is called its "stability" (*ṭhiti*); thus it is appropriate to say, "he develops [it] for the sake of stability.
In this way, at the moment of the supramundane path, this energy of the bhikkhu [is applied] to unarisen evil, unwholesome states...

It receives four names, beginning with “for the non-arising [of unwholesome states],” and so forth. This concludes the discussion on the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) at the moment of the supramundane path.
However, in this sutta, the right efforts are explained as being a mixture of both mundane and supramundane. 398–401.
Regarding the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), concentration that proceeds by depending on desire is “concentration of desire” (*chandasamādhi*); it is the state of striving (*padhāna*).

Formations (*saṅkhārā*) are the formations of striving. "Endowed" means possessed of those qualities. A "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*) is either a basis for success or that which has become success itself.
The same method applies to the remaining [bases] as well. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*.
Its meaning is also elucidated in the *Visuddhimagga*. In this regard, when this bhikkhu [takes] one from among zeal and the others...
By relying on the burden (*dhura*) and increasing insight (*vipassanā*), one attains Arahatship;

at that time, for such a person, the first basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) was mundane in its prior stage and supramundane in its subsequent stage. The same applies to the remaining ones. In this sutta as well, only the mundane and supramundane bases of psychic power are discussed. 402–406.
Regarding the passage beginning with "he develops the faculty of faith" (*saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti*): faith itself exercises the function of a lord (*indaṭṭha*) over its own burden of faith.
The faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*). The same method applies to the faculties of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and the rest. Regarding the phrase "he develops":
here, a beginner practitioner (*yogāvacara*), by purifying the faculty of faith through three causes, is said to "develop" the faculty of faith.
The same method applies to the faculties of energy and the rest. For this has been said:

“By avoiding persons lacking faith, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons endowed with faith, and by reflecting upon the discourses that inspire confidence—in these three ways, the faculty of faith is purified.

By avoiding persons who are indolent, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who have aroused energy, and by reflecting upon the right efforts—in these three ways, the faculty of energy is purified.”

“By avoiding persons who are muddle-minded, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who are established in mindfulness, and by reflecting upon the foundations of mindfulness—in these three ways, the faculty of mindfulness is purified.

By avoiding persons who are unconcentrated, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons who are concentrated, and by reflecting upon the meditative absorptions and liberations—in these three ways, the faculty of concentration is purified.”

“By avoiding persons of poor wisdom, by serving, associating with, and attending upon persons possessed of wisdom, and by reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge— in these three ways the faculty of wisdom is purified. And here,
“reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge” means reflecting on the subtle and delicate distinctions between the aggregates,
the bases, the elements, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the paths, and the fruits.

This is the meaning. For by means of these three sets of three causes, a beginner practitioner who has not yet formed a fixed conviction, having established a conviction regarding the burden of faith and so forth, develops [the faculties] and, turning away [from the round of existence] at the conclusion, attains Arahantship.
Up until the path of Arahantship, he is said to be developing these faculties; once the fruit of Arahantship is attained, his faculties are fully developed.
Thus it is said. In this way, these five faculties are also described as being both mundane and supramundane.
Regarding the powers beginning with the power of faith (*saddhābala*), faith itself is called "power" in the sense of being unshakable; thus it is the power of faith.

The same method applies to the power of energy (*vīriyabala*) and the others. For herein, faith is not shaken by lack of faith, energy is not shaken by laziness, and mindfulness is not shaken by forgetfulness.

It does not waver: concentration does not waver in the face of restlessness, and wisdom does not waver in the face of ignorance; thus, all of them are called "powers" (*bala*) in the sense of being unshakable.
Furthermore, the method of cultivation (*bhāvanānaya*) here should be understood according to the same method explained under the cultivation of the faculties (*indriyabhāvanā*).
These [powers] are described as being both mundane and supramundane.

418. Regarding the phrase "he develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness," here follows the method of development together with a commentary on the meaning, based on the case of clansmen who are beginners.

First, this is the commentary on the meaning of the seven initial terms stated in the sequence beginning with "the enlightenment factor of mindfulness": as for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, it is "mindfulness" in the sense of remembering; and furthermore, this...
It has the characteristic of attending, or the characteristic of not wobbling. And this has been said:
"Just as, great king, the royal treasurer does not allow the king’s property to be lost, saying, 'So much, great king, is the silver; so much is the gold;

so much is the property,' even so, great king, when mindfulness arises, it does not allow what is wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and bright, with their counterparts, to be lost."
“He does not confuse the Dhamma; these are the four foundations of mindfulness,” so it is said at length. Its function is non-confusion;
for this is the characteristic stated by the Elder in terms of its activity. Alternatively, its function is non-forgetfulness, and it is manifested as being directed toward the objective field.
Mindfulness itself is the enlightenment factor, thus it is the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*).
In this context, it is a *bojjhaṅga* because it is a factor (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or a factor for enlightenment. What is meant?

It refers to that collection of states (*dhammasāmaggī*) which, arising at the moment of the mundane or supramundane path, serves as the antidote to numerous calamities—namely, lethargy and agitation, the foundations [of those], the accumulation [of karma], indulgence in sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism—and which consists of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Because the noble disciple awakens by means of the harmony of the Dhamma, it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*).
"He awakens" means that he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or that he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or that he realizes Nibbāna itself; this is what is meant.
As it has been said: "Having developed the seven factors of awakening, he fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment."

It is a "factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because it is a factor of that awakening (*bodhi*) which is defined as the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), just like the factors of meditation (*jhānaṅga*) or the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*).

Furthermore, since the noble disciple is called "awakening" (*bodhi*) on account of this aforementioned harmony of states by virtue of his awakening through it, it is a "factor of enlightenment" because it is a factor of him, just like the factors of an army or the factors of a chariot. Thus said the teachers of the commentaries.
“Or, they are called ‘factors of enlightenment’ because they are the factors for a person who is awakening.
Furthermore: “In what sense are they ‘factors of enlightenment’ (bojjhaṅga)? They are factors of enlightenment because they conduce to enlightenment;

they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken after; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken thoroughly; they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken fully.”
The meaning of the enlightenment factor (*bojjhaṅga*) should also be understood by way of this analysis of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

A factor of enlightenment that is praised and beautiful is a "perfect enlightenment factor" (*sambojjhaṅga*); mindfulness itself as a perfect enlightenment factor is the "mindfulness-enlightenment-factor" (*satisambojjhaṅga*), which is that mindfulness-enlightenment-factor. Regarding the "investigation-of-phenomena-enlightenment-factor" and so forth:
it investigates the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths, thus it is "investigation-of-phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*). It has the characteristic of thorough investigation.
Its essence is illumination; its manifestation is non-delusion. Because it is heroic and because it must be exerted according to method, it is called energy (*vīriya*).
It has the characteristic of uplifting; its essence is supporting; its manifestation is non-sinking. It gladdens, thus it is called rapture (*pīti*).
Its characteristic is pervading, or its characteristic is satisfaction; its essence is the gladdening of body and mind; its manifestation is their very elation.
Tranquility (*passaddhi*) is so called because it allays agitation of body and mind. It has the characteristic of peace; its function is to crush agitation of body and mind;

it is manifested as the state of non-distraction and coolness of body and mind. Concentration (*samādhi*) is so called because of its nature of centering. It has the characteristic of non-distraction, or the characteristic of non-dispersal;
its function is to unify the mind and mental factors; it is manifested as the steadiness of the mind. [It is so called] because of its nature of looking on with equanimity...
Equanimity (*upekkhā*). It has the characteristic of reflecting or the characteristic of evenness. Its function is to prevent deficiency or excess, or its function is to cut off partiality.
It is manifested as a state of neutrality. The rest is exactly as previously stated. "Develops" means he cultivates or increases; the meaning is that he causes it to arise.
In this regard, it should be understood that four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*): mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).
Avoiding persons who are unmindful, associating with persons who are established in mindfulness, and being intent upon that [mindfulness]. For,
by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances beginning with "the excellent" (*abhikkanta*),

by avoiding persons who are unmindful— like crows cast out from a meal— and by associating with persons who are established in mindfulness— like the Elder Tissa Datta, the Elder Abhaya, and others— ...

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises for the purpose of arousing mindfulness during standing, sitting, and so forth, and through the mind’s inclination, leaning, and tendency toward mindfulness.

Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, having aroused the enlightenment factor of mindfulness by these four means, making that his primary task and establishing his resolve upon it, gradually attains Arahantship. He, until—
One is said to develop the mindfulness enlightenment factor during the path of arahantship; when the fruit is attained, it is said to have been developed.
Seven things lead to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor:

thorough inquiry, making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, avoiding persons of poor wisdom, associating with persons of wisdom, reflecting on the conduct of those with deep knowledge, and [reflecting on] the profound course of wisdom.

"Being intent upon that": therein, "being inquisitive" means an abundance of inquiry based on the meaning of the aggregates, elements, bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path-factors, jhānas, serenity, and insight.
"Making the basis pure" means making the internal and external bases clear. For when his—
When the hair of the head, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body has developed blemishes and is smeared with sweat and dirt,
then the internal basis is unrefined and impure. However, when the robe is worn out,
soiled, or foul-smelling, or when the lodging is dirty, then the external basis is unrefined and impure.
Therefore, by cutting off the hair and so forth, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives, and by anointing and bathing, the internal basis must be made clear.
By means of needlework, washing, dyeing, and polishing, the external basis must be made clear. For when these internal and external bases are not clear, [defilements] arise...
Knowledge regarding the mind and mental factors is also unclear and impure, like the radiance of a lamp flame produced by means of impure wicks,
oil, and so forth. However, when knowledge arises regarding internal and external bases that have become clear,
that knowledge is also clear, just as it would be by means of pure wicks, oil, and so forth.

It is like the radiance from the flame of a lamp that has been lit. Therefore it was said: “The act of making the basis pure leads to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment.
“Balancing the faculties” means making the faculties, beginning with faith, equal in strength. For if...

The faculty of faith becomes strong while the others are weak; consequently, the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing.
Therefore, by means of reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena, or by attending to them in such a way that [faith] becomes strong—
Likewise, when [an unwholesome state] has arisen, it should be abandoned through non-attention; the story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration of this here.

However, if the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is too strong, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution, nor can the others perform their respective functions.
Therefore, that [excess of energy] must be diminished by the cultivation of tranquility (*passaddhi*) and the other [factors]. In this regard, there is the case of the Elder Soṇa.
The basis must be shown. In the same way, when one among the others is predominant, it should be understood that the remaining factors are incapable of performing their own respective functions.
In particular, however, they praise the balance between faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy. One who possesses strong faith...
For one of dull wisdom has blind faith; he places his trust in what is not a proper object. One of strong wisdom but weak faith sides with the "hypocrite's faction" (kerāṭika-pakkha);

like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable. By leaping too far ahead, thinking that "merit is achieved by the mere arising of a thought," one fails to perform acts such as giving and is reborn in hell. Through the balance of both, [one succeeds] only when there is a proper object.
It becomes serene. However, when strong concentration is joined with weak energy, because concentration belongs to the side of indolence, indolence overcomes it.
When strong energy is joined with weak concentration, because energy belongs to the side of agitation, agitation overcomes it.
But concentration joined with energy does not allow one to fall into indolence, and energy joined with concentration [does not allow one to fall into agitation].
One does not fall into restlessness. Therefore, both of these must be made equal; for it is through the balancing of both that absorption (*appanā*) occurs.
Furthermore, for one whose work is concentration, even strong faith is appropriate; for by believing and resolving in this way, one will reach absorption.
As for concentration and wisdom, for one whose work is concentration, a strong degree of one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) is appropriate; for in this way—

Thus he attains absorption (*appanā*). For one whose work is insight (*vipassanā*), wisdom (*paññā*) must be strong; for in this way, he reaches the penetration of the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-paṭivedha*).
However, absorption occurs even through the balancing of both [tranquility and insight]. Yet, mindfulness (*sati*) must be strong in all cases.
For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation (*uddhacca*) due to the influence of faith, energy, and wisdom, which belong to the side of agitation.
And by means of concentration on the side of diligence, one protects against falling into sloth.
Therefore, like salt seasoning all sauces, or like a minister who performs all duties for a king, mindfulness is to be desired in every situation.
Thus he said: "Mindfulness has been declared by the Blessed One to be beneficial in all circumstances. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge."
"And mindfulness has the manifestation of protection; for without mindfulness, there is no exerting or restraining of the mind.
Avoidance of persons of poor wisdom means staying far away from dull-witted individuals who have not penetrated the analysis of the aggregates and so forth.
Service to persons of wisdom means [relying on] those who possess the discernment of the fifty characteristics of equanimity.

Associating with persons endowed with the wisdom of rise and fall; reflection on the course of profound knowledge means reflecting on the distinctions of the profound wisdom that occurs regarding the profound aggregates and so forth;
inclination toward that means having a mind that is bent, slanted, and inclined toward the arousing of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor while standing, sitting, and so forth.

Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, having aroused the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment by these seven means, making that his primary task and establishing his resolve upon it, gradually attains Arahantship.
He is said to be "developing" the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment up until the path of Arahantship; once the fruit is attained, it is said to be "developed."
Eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy:
reflecting on the fear of the states of misery; seeing the benefits; reflecting on the path to be traveled; honoring the alms-food received; reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance;

reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher; reflecting on the greatness of one’s birth; reflecting on the greatness of one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life; [reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma; reflecting on the greatness of the Sangha].
Avoiding lazy persons, associating with persons who have aroused energy, and being intent upon that [energy]. In this context,
even at the time of experiencing great suffering in the hells— starting from the time one is subjected to the fivefold torture—
and even when caught by nets, hooks, and the like in the animal realm, or when pierced by lashes, thorns, and so forth...

Furthermore, even at times such as when carrying a cart, or during the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) for many thousands of years or even an entire interval between Buddhas while suffering from hunger and thirst,
or among the Kālakañjika asuras while experiencing the sufferings of wind, heat, and so forth with a physical body only a fathom-and-a-half or two fathoms in height consisting of mere skin and bone—
it is not possible [to lose] the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga).

“...to arouse [it]. This very moment is yours, O bhikkhu. Thus, even for one reflecting on the fear of the states of misery (*apāya*), the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*) arises.
It also arises for one who sees the benefit, thinking: “The nine supramundane states cannot be attained by one who is lazy;
they can only be attained by one who has initiated energy. This is the benefit of energy. [It arises] through all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples...
"It must be traveled along the path already traversed, and that cannot be done by one who is indolent"—thus it arises even for one reflecting on the route of travel.

"Those people who attend upon me with alms-food and so forth are neither my relatives, nor my slaves or laborers, nor do they give these choice alms-foods and such thinking, 'We shall live depending on him. Rather, it is because of their own deeds..."

They give things while hoping for great fruit. It was not with the thought, “Having used these requisites, he will dwell in comfort, possessed of physical strength,” that the Teacher authorized these requisites for you;
rather, it was with the thought, “While using these, he will perform the duty of a recluse and be liberated from the suffering of the round” that those requisites were authorized.

"Therefore, if you dwell indolent, you will not honor that almsfood. For it is only for one who has aroused energy that there is what is called 'honoring almsfood,'" thus it arises even for one reflecting on the honoring of almsfood,
as it did for Mahāmitta Thera and Piṇḍapātika Tissa Thera.
It is said that the Elder Mahāmitta was residing at the Kassaka Cave. In the village where he went for alms, a certain great female lay devotee looked after him, treating him as her own son.
One day, while going to the forest, she said to her daughter: "My dear, in such-and-such a place there are old rice grains;
in such-and-such a place there is milk; in such-and-such a place there is ghee; in such-and-such a place there is molasses."
“When your brother, the noble Mitta, arrives, cook a meal and give it to him along with milk, ghee, and sugar;
after giving it, you may eat as well. But yesterday, I ate the leftover cooked rice with sour gruel.
“What will you eat during the day, mother? [He replied: “I shall eat broken rice with vegetables added.”
“Mother, cook some sour gruel and set it aside.
When the Elder heard that sound while putting on his robe and taking out his bowl, he admonished himself:
“It seems the Great Laywoman is eating discarded rice with sour gruel; even during the day she will be eating sour gruel made from broken leaves.”
However, she mentions old rice and other such things for your sake. Relying on that, she does not expect a field, a dwelling, food, or clothing;
rather, desiring the three types of success (*sampatti*), she gives.
Will you be able to grant her those successes, or will you not? This, moreover—
“Alms-food cannot be accepted by you while you are still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion. Having thus spoken, he placed the bowl into its bag, released the cord, and turned back.
He went straight to Kassakalena, set the bowl down beneath his bed and the robe on the robe-stand, and resolved upon energy, vowing: “I shall not leave until I have attained arahantship.”
He sat down. Having lived for a long time with diligence, that bhikkhu increased his insight;
having attained Arahantship even before breakfast, he emerged with a smile like a blooming lotus, a great one whose taints were destroyed.
The deity dwelling in the tree at the entrance of the cave said:
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
You whose taints are exhausted—you are worthy of offerings, O Blessed One.
Having uttered this inspired utterance, he said: “Venerable sir, having given almsfood to Arahants like yourself who have entered for alms, [one gains great merit].”
“Old women will be freed from suffering,” he said. The Elder rose, opened the door, and looking for the time, realized it was already dawn;
taking his bowl and robe, he entered the village.
The girl, having prepared the meal, thought, “Now my brother will come; now my brother will come.”

She sat watching for the door. When the elder arrived at her house, she took his bowl, filled it with a portion of milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The elder, having offered a blessing of "May there be happiness," departed.
She remained standing, watching him, for at that time the elder’s complexion was exceedingly pure.
His faculties were serene, and his face shone exceedingly, like a ripe palm fruit released from its bond.
When the great female lay follower returned from the forest, she asked, "What is it, my dear? Has your brother come? She related the entire account to her.
The lay follower, realizing that today her son’s duty of going forth had reached its culmination, said:
“Does your brother, mother, take delight in the Buddha’s teaching? Is he not weary of it? she asked.
The story of the Elder Piṇḍapātika Tissa should be understood as follows:
It is said that in Mahāgāma there was a certain poor man who made his living by selling wood. Because of that very occupation, he received the name Dārubhaṇḍaka Mahātissa.
He was born with that name. One day he said to his wife, "What is the point of our living?
The Teacher has declared that the fruit of giving to the poor is great; yet we are unable to give regularly.
Let us give at least a meal on the fortnight days, and furthermore, let us provide the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) as it arises. She agreed, saying, "Very well, husband."
On the following day, she provided the fortnightly meal according to what was available. At that time, it was a period free from danger for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus due to their provisions;

however, after eating choice foods, the young novices would think, "This fortnightly meal is coarse food," and having taken only as much as they could carry, they would discard it right before their eyes and go away.
When that woman saw him, she told her husband, "She is throwing away what was given by me," yet she felt no remorse.
Her husband said, "Because of our poverty, we have not been able to let the noble ladies enjoy themselves with ease.
What indeed must we do to win the favor of the noble ladies? Then his wife said to him, "What..."
“Master,” he said, “there are no such things as those who are unfortunate along with their children. Here is your daughter;

having placed her in one family and received twelve kahāpaṇas, bring back a milk-cow. We shall give the noble ladies their milk-tickets and alms-food, and in this way we will be able to win their favor.
Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he did exactly so.
By virtue of their merit, that cow gave three measures of milk in the evening and three measures in the morning.

Having made curds from what was received in the evening, they then prepared clarified butter (*sappi*) from the fresh butter taken from it; thus, they provided meals with milk and a sprinkling of clarified butter.
From that time on, only those possessed of merit received such meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) in his house.

So one day he said to his wife: "We have been freed from the shame of having a daughter, and the food in our house has become fit for noble ladies to consume. Until I return, do not neglect this virtuous practice.
I shall do something and liberate my daughter. He went to a certain place and engaged in sugarcane-pressing work.
Having worked for six months and received twelve kahāpaṇas, he thought, "This much is sufficient for the sake of ransoming my daughter.
Binding those kahāpaṇas in a cloth-bag, he set out on the road, thinking, "I shall go home.
At that time, the Elder Piṇḍapātika Tissa, a resident of the Ambariya Mahāvihāra, was going to the Tissamahāvihāra.
Thinking, "I shall pay homage to the cetiya," he set out for Mahāgāma from his own residence by way of that very same path.
Seeing the Elder from afar, the lay follower thought, "I will not go alone; I shall go together with this noble one, listening to a discourse on the Dhamma.
For those possessed of virtue are always difficult to find. With haste, he approached the Elder.
Having paid his respects and walking along with him, as the time was drawing near, he thought:

"I have no wrapped food in my hand, yet it is now the Venerable's time for alms; however, this travel-provision is in my hand, so when we reach a village gate, I will give alms-food to the Venerable."
As soon as his mind had thus arisen, a certain man arrived at that place carrying a wrapped meal.
Seeing him, the lay follower said, "Venerable sir, please wait a moment," and approaching him, he said, "Sir, I will give you a kahāpaṇa;
give me this wrapped meal. He thought, "This meal [is for] this..."
Thinking, "At other times even a single month's wage is not worth [this], yet he gives me a kahāpaṇa all at once;
there must be a reason for this," she said, "I do not give for a kahāpaṇa. When he replied, "In that case, take two;
take three," in this manner he became desirous of giving her all those kahāpaṇas. The other, perceiving that "he has others as well,"...
“I will not give it,” he said. Then he said to him: “If I had others, sir, I would give them too.
But I do not take it for my own sake; a noble gentleman was seated by me at the foot of this tree, and it will be for your welfare as well.
Give me the meal. “In that case, sir, take it; bring a kahāpaṇa coin for you.”

Having taken a kahāpaṇa coin, he gave him a meal in a leaf-wrapped bundle. The lay follower took the food, washed his hands, approached the elder, and said, "Please bring forth your bowl, venerable sir. The elder brought forth the bowl;
when half the food had been given, he closed it. The lay follower said, "Venerable sir, this is the portion for only one person; it is not possible for me..."
"Please eat from this. I have sought out and obtained this specifically for your sake;
take it, out of compassion for me. The Elder, thinking, "There must be a reason for this," accepted it and consumed everything.
The lay devotee strained water with a water-strainer and gave it to him. Then, when the Elder had finished his meal, they both set out on the road together.
The Elder asked the lay follower, "For what reason do you not eat? He related to him his entire account of the journey there and back.
Having heard this, the Elder was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and thought: "A difficult task has been performed by this lay follower;
having partaken of such alms-food as this, I must be grateful to him. [I must provide him] with suitable lodgings."
"Having attained [the goal], I shall not rise from this very seat until I have reached Arahantship,
even if my skin, flesh, and blood dry up. He went to the Tissamahāvihāra,
performed the duties for new arrivals, entered his assigned lodging, spread out his rug, and sitting there, he took up his own original meditation subject.
He took it up. During that night, however, he was unable to produce even a mere radiance.
From the following day onward, having severed the impediment of wandering for alms, he contemplated that very meditation subject in direct and reverse order.
Contemplating in this manner, at dawn on the seventh day, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and he thought: "It has been exceedingly difficult for me..."
"My body is exhausted; will my life continue for long, or will it not?
Then, seeing that his life would not continue, he put away his bedding, took his bowl and robe, went to the center of the monastery, had the drum beaten, and assembled the community of monks.
The senior elder of the Saṅgha asked, "By which monk was the Saṅgha convened? "By me, venerable sir," he replied. "For what purpose, good man?
"Venerable sir, there is no other business; however, those who have doubts regarding the path or the fruit, let them question me.
"Good man, such monks do not speak of qualities they do not possess. As for us..."
There is no doubt about this. But what was the cause of your spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), and by what condition did you attain *arahantship*?

"Venerable sir, in this great village, in the Valliyavīthi street, there was a lay follower named Dārubhaṇḍakamahātissa who, having set aside his own daughter, took twelve kahāpaṇas and with them [bought] a single milk-cow."
Having taken the voting tally for the Saṅgha’s milk-rice offering, he thought, "I will ransom my daughter.
After working for six months at the weaver's workshop and receiving twelve kahāpaṇas, he set out for his own home thinking, "I will ransom my daughter.
On the way, seeing me at the time of the alms-round, he gave all those kahāpaṇas to me.

"Having received the food in the bowl, he gave it all to me. After I had consumed that alms-food and come here, having obtained a suitable dwelling, I attained a state of distinction, thinking, 'I shall perform the act of honoring the alms-food,' Venerable Sir.
Upon hearing this, the fourfold assembly gathered at that place gave the Elder a cry of "Well done! in their own nature.
He was no longer capable of remaining composed. As the Elder sat in the midst of the Saṅgha and continued speaking, he made this resolve:
"May my gabled house shake at the very moment it is touched by the hand of Mahātissa of the Wood-workers' Guild.
Having thus resolved, he attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
When King Kākavaṇṇatissa heard that a certain elder had attained final nibbāna, he went to the monastery, paid him honor and respect, prepared a gabled chamber, and placed the elder therein.
As he was lifting it up, intending to say, "Now we shall go to the site of the funeral pyre," he was unable to move it.
The king questioned the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: "Venerable sirs, is there [anything remaining] by the elder?"

"Has anything been said? The monks explained the manner in which the Elder had spoken. The king summoned that lay follower and asked, "Seven days ago, did you give a packet of food to a certain monk traveling along the road?
"Yes, Your Majesty," he replied. "By what method was it given? He related the entire account of how it had happened.
Then the king sent him to the place where the elder’s gabled chamber was, saying, “Go and identify whether it is that elder or another.
He went there, lifted the curtain, and upon seeing the elder’s face, recognized him.
Holding his heart with both hands, he went back to the king and said, “Your Majesty, this is my noble master. Then the king—
He had a great adornment prepared. When the Elder had returned after being adorned, the king said, "Go, brother Mahātissa; tell my lady, 'Lift up the gabled chamber.

The lay devotee replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and having gone and bowed at the Elder's feet, he lifted it with both hands and placed it upon his own head. At that very moment, the gabled chamber rose into the air.
Having leaped up, it alighted upon the top of the funeral pyre. At that moment, flames of fire rose up spontaneously from all four corners of the pyre.
"Indeed, this inheritance of the Teacher is great; namely, the so-called seven treasures of the noble ones (ariyadhana), which cannot [be taken by force]."

It arises for one who reflects on the greatness of the inheritance: "Just as parents treat a son who has gone astray as 'this one is no son of ours' and exclude him, so that he does not receive their inheritance after their passing, even so the indolent person does not receive this inheritance of the noble wealth;
only one who has aroused energy receives it."
“Indeed, your Teacher was great.

For at the time of his conception in his mother’s womb, at his Great Departure, at his Perfect Enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the Twin Miracle, at the descent from the deva realm, at the relinquishing of the life-force, and even at the time of his Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system shook.
Is it fitting for you [to disparage] such a Teacher?”
It also arises for one who reflects upon the greatness of the Teacher, thinking: "Having gone forth in the Dispensation, how could I become lazy?
Furthermore, it arises [when reflecting]: "By birth, you are not of lowly origin;
you are born into the unbroken royal lineage of Okkāka descending from Mahāsaṃmata, the grandson of Great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of the auspicious Rāhula."
"Having become a son of the Conqueror of such a kind, it is not fitting for me to dwell in indolence"— thus it arises even when one reflects upon the greatness of one's birth.
"Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and the eighty great disciples likewise penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone."
It also arises for one reflecting on the greatness of one’s fellow celibates (sabrahmacārīmahatta) thus: "Do you follow the path of these fellow celibates, or do you not?
It also arises for one who avoids lazy persons whose physical and mental energy have been abandoned, resembling pythons that remain with their bellies full.
It arises even for one who associates with persons who have aroused energy and are resolute, and even when one’s mind is inclined, directed, and biased toward the arousal of energy while standing,
sitting, or in other postures. Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner,
having aroused the energy enlightenment factor by means of these eleven causes, should take that very thing as his burden and establish his resolve upon it.
In due course, he attains Arahatship. From the time he begins developing the energy factor of enlightenment up until the path of Arahatship, it is said that he is "developing" it;
once the fruit is reached, it is said to be "developed.
Eleven things lead to the arising of the joy factor of enlightenment: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, and recollection of virtue...
The recollection of the deities of generosity, the recollection of peace, avoidance of persons who are harsh, association with persons who are gentle,
reflection on discourses that inspire confidence, and devotion to those [qualities].
For one who recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of rapture (pītisambojjhaṅga) pervades the entire body up to the stage of access concentration.

It arises for one who recollects the virtues of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha; for one who reviews the fourfold purity of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) that has been guarded and kept unbroken for a long time;
for a layperson who reviews the ten precepts or the five precepts;

and for one who, during times of famine or fear and so forth, has given choice food to fellow practitioners of the holy life and reflects on that generosity, thinking, "In such-and-such a way we gave."
Also for one who reflects; for a householder as well, when reflecting on the gift given to those possessed of virtue at such times;
for one who reflects on the presence within oneself of those very qualities endowed with which others attained the state of the devas;
and for one who reflects that even for sixty or seventy years the defilements do not manifest because they have been suppressed by meditative attainment.
Even while avoiding harsh persons— who, like dust on the back of a donkey, are indicated by their lack of reverence in visiting shrines,
the Bodhi tree, or elders due to an absence of serene confidence and affection toward the Buddha and the rest—

and even while attending upon gentle persons who possess abundant confidence in the Buddha and the rest and have supple minds, one [should listen] to the inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem.
It arises for one who is reviewing [the jhāna], and it also arises for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of rapture while standing,
sitting, and so forth. Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, having aroused the enlightenment factor of rapture through these eleven causes,
making that his primary task and establishing his resolve upon it, gradually attains Arahantship.
Thus, from the path of stream-entry up to the path of arahantship, one is said to "develop" the enlightenment factor of rapture; when the fruit is attained, it is said to be "developed.
Seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility:
the practice of refined food, the practice of a pleasant climate, the practice of a comfortable posture, the application of equanimity, and the avoidance of persons with agitated bodies.
Associating with persons whose bodies are tranquil, and being intent upon that [tranquility].

For tranquility arises even in one who eats refined, smooth, and suitable food, and even in one who resorts to a suitable climate and posture among the seasons of cold and heat and the postures such as standing. Whoever—
However, one who is of the nature of a Great Man (mahāpurisa) is capable of enduring all postures; this statement was not made with reference to such a person.
It arises only for one who possesses both similar and dissimilar [states], and who, having avoided the dissimilar postures, cultivates those that are similar.
"The practice of equanimity" refers to the reflection on one's own and another's ownership of kamma.

It arises through this application of equanimity. It arises for one who avoids a person whose body is agitated—such as one who wanders about harassing others with clods, sticks, and so forth—and for one who associates with a person whose feet and hands are restrained and whose body is tranquil;
and also for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of tranquility during standing, sitting, and other postures.

It arises. Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, having aroused the tranquility enlightenment factor by means of these seven causes, making that his primary task and establishing his resolve upon it, gradually attains arahantship.
He is said to "develop" the tranquility enlightenment factor up until the path of arahantship; once the fruit is attained, it is said to have been "developed."
Eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration:
making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, skill in the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time,

gladdening the mind at the proper time, maintaining equanimity at the proper time, avoiding persons who are not concentrated, [associating with persons who are concentrated, listening to the true Dhamma, and reflecting on the Dhamma].
Serving persons who are concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and being intent upon them.
Therein, the purification of the basis and the balancing of the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated.
Skill in the sign means skill in apprehending the kasiṇa sign. "Upholding the mind at the proper time" means:
