At whatever time the mind is sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, at that time its uplifting occurs through the arousal of the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture.

"Restraint of the mind at the proper time" means: at whatever time the mind is agitated due to over-exertion of energy and so forth, at that time [its restraint occurs] through the arousal of the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Its restraint. "Encouragement at the proper time" means that when the mind becomes disenchanted due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom or because it has not attained the bliss of tranquility, one should, at that time, stir it with a reflection on the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four—and the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*).
The fifth is: suffering rooted in the round of existence in the past, suffering rooted in the round of existence in the future, and suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
Furthermore, one generates confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem. This is called "encouragement at the proper time.
Equanimity at the proper time means that, having relied upon right practice, at whatever time one is neither sluggish nor agitated.

When the mind proceeds evenly upon its object, free from relish and having entered the path of serenity (*samatha*), it then no longer requires the application of exertion, restraint, or encouragement, just as a charioteer does not need to intervene when his horses are moving evenly.
This is called "equanimity at the proper time" (*samaye ajjhupekkhanatā*).
Avoidance of persons who are not concentrated refers to those whose minds are distracted and who have not yet attained access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*).

It is the avoidance from afar of certain types of persons. "Associating with persons who are concentrated" means attending upon, cultivating, and revering those whose minds are concentrated through either access concentration (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*).
"Being intent upon that" means having a mind that is inclined, directed, and leaning toward the production of concentration itself while standing, sitting, and so forth.
For one who practices in this way, this [concentration] arises.

Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, having aroused the concentration enlightenment factor by means of these eleven reasons, makes that his primary task and establishes his resolve upon it, gradually attains Arahantship.
He is said to "develop" the concentration enlightenment factor up until the path of Arahantship; once the fruit is attained, it is said to be "developed."
Five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor:

neutrality toward beings, neutrality toward formations, avoidance of persons who are partial toward beings and formations, association with persons who are neutral toward beings and formations, and devotion thereto.
Therein, one arouses neutrality toward beings in two ways: "You [should consider] yourself..."

"You have come by means of your own karma and you will go by means of your own karma; he too has come by means of his own karma and will go by means of his own karma—whom do you cherish? Thus, by reflecting on the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatā*), and "In the ultimate sense, there is no self at all—whom do you cherish?
Thus, by reflecting on the absence of a sentient being (*nissatta*); [one reflects] in these two ways.

He arouses equanimity toward conditioned phenomena by reflecting on their ownerlessness thus: "This robe will gradually undergo changes in appearance and reach a state of decay until, having become a mere foot-wiping cloth, it must be discarded at the end of a staff;
yet if it had an owner, its owner would not allow it to perish in this way. Thus, by reflecting on the state of being without an owner.
And: "This is not for long; it is only temporary"—thus, by reflecting on its temporary nature.
And just as with the robe, so too should the application be made regarding the bowl and other requisites.
Regarding the phrase "avoiding persons who cherish the seven formations": here, a person—whether a householder or one gone forth—who cherishes his own children, daughters, and so forth...

Or, having gone forth, he treats his own pupils, co-residents, and others as his own; he performs for them with his own hands such tasks as cutting hair, sewing needles, washing robes, dyeing, and boiling bowls.
Not seeing them even for a moment, he looks here and there like a startled deer, wondering, "Where is that novice? Where is that young man?
Or, for the sake of having someone else perform tasks such as cutting hair, [he says], "Wait a moment, [send] so-and-so..."
Even when requested, "Please give it," he does not give it, saying, "We do not perform that work ourselves; you will only weary yourselves by taking it," such a person is called a *sattakelāyana*.

Furthermore, one who treats robes, bowls, water-pots, walking sticks, and so forth as his own private property, and does not even allow another’s hand to touch them, yet when asked for them on loan, says, "We too are guarding this as our wealth..."
"If we do not enjoy [these things], what shall we give to you?"—this is called one who "clings to formations.
However, he who is neutral and indifferent toward both of these two bases is called "neutral toward beings and formations.
Thus, this factor of enlightenment of equanimity belongs even to one who avoids from afar such a person who clings to beings and formations.
It arises even for one who associates with a person neutral toward the seven formations, and even for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and leaning toward their production while standing,

sitting, or otherwise engaged. Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, having aroused the equanimity enlightenment factor by these five means and having made that his primary task, establishes his resolve and gradually attains Arahantship.
Thus, from the path of stream-entry up to the path of arahantship, one is said to "develop" the enlightenment factor of equanimity; when the fruit is attained, it is said to be "developed.
In this way, these seven factors of enlightenment are described as being a mixture of mundane and supramundane. 419.
"He develops right view": he cultivates right view, which is the first constituent of the eightfold path.
[He] increases [it]. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Herein, right view has the characteristic of right seeing;
right intention has the characteristic of right directing; right speech has the characteristic of right embracing; right action has the characteristic of right originating;
right livelihood has the characteristic of right cleansing; right effort has the characteristic of right exerting; right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishing.
Right mindfulness. Right concentration has the characteristic of right concentrating.
Each of these [factors] has three functions. To illustrate:
first, right view abandons wrong view along with its own opposing defilements, takes cessation as its object, and [supports] the associated states.
And one sees [the truth] through non-delusion, by way of dispelling the delusion that conceals it.
Right intention and the others likewise abandon wrong intention and so forth, and take cessation as their object.
Specifically, however, in this context, right intention correctly directs the co-nascent states, right speech correctly grasps them, and right action...
Right view correctly causes [the other factors] to arise; right livelihood correctly purifies them; right effort correctly exerts them;
right mindfulness correctly establishes them; and right concentration correctly steadies them.
Furthermore, this so-called right view is of various moments and various objects in the preliminary stage, but at the time of the path, it is of a single moment.
They have a single object. As for their function, however, they receive four names beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering.
Right intention and the others are, in the preliminary stage, of different moments and different objects; at the time of the path, they are of a single moment and a single object.
Among them, right intention receives three names according to its function: the intention of renunciation, the intention of non-cruelty, and the intention of non-ill-will.

The three beginning with right speech (*sammāvācā*) are both abstinences (*virati*) and volitions (*cetanā*) during the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Path (*magga-khaṇa*), they are only abstinences.

As for right effort (*sammāvāyāma*) and right mindfulness (*sammāsati*), these two also receive four names according to their functions by way of the right exertions (*sammappadhāna*) and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*), however, is simply right concentration both during the preliminary stage and at the moment of the Path.

Thus, among these eight states, right view was taught first by the Blessed One because it is of great assistance to the yogi practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna. For this has been called "the lamp of wisdom" and "the sword of wisdom.
Therefore, by means of this right view—consisting of insight-knowledge in the preliminary stage—one dispels the darkness of ignorance.
Slaying the thieves of the defilements, the practitioner of yoga reaches Nibbāna by means of safety. Therefore it was said:
"Right view is taught first because it is of great benefit to the yogi who has set out for the attainment of Nibbāna.
Right intention, however, is of great benefit to that [right view], and therefore it is mentioned immediately after it. For just as a money-changer, with his hand...
Just as one who, turning a coin over and over again, looks at it with the eye and knows, "This is counterfeit;

this is genuine," so too the practitioner of yoga, having reflected and reflected with initial thought (vitakka) in the preliminary stage, looking with the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā), knows, "These phenomena belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara);
these phenomena belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), etc. Or, just as by a man...
Just as a carpenter, having taken hold of a large tree at its base and turned it over and over again, fashions it with an axe and brings it to its intended use;
so too, the practitioner of yoga, having reflected upon the phenomena provided by thought over and over again, delimits them with wisdom according to the method:
"These phenomena belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), these phenomena belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)," and so forth, and then applies them to his task.
It brings [them] near. Therefore it was said: "But right intention is helpful to that [right view]; therefore it is mentioned immediately after it.

And this [right intention], just as it is helpful to right view, is likewise helpful to right speech. As it is said: "Householder, having first thought and reflected, one subsequently utters speech. Therefore, right speech is mentioned immediately after that.

However, because people first agree by means of speech, saying, "We shall do this and that," and then engage in worldly tasks, speech is thus an aid to bodily action; therefore, right action is mentioned immediately after right speech.

Furthermore, it is only for one who abandons the fourfold misconduct of speech and the threefold misconduct of body and fulfills both types of good conduct that they fulfill the morality consisting of the eight factors of right livelihood, and not for anyone else; therefore, right livelihood is mentioned immediately after those two.
Thus, it is not proper for one who lives by a pure livelihood to remain complacent, thinking "my livelihood is purified," and to dwell in negligence;
rather, immediately after that, right effort is taught to show that this energy must be exerted in all postures.

Next, right mindfulness (sammāsati) is taught immediately after that in order to show that even for one who has initiated energy, mindfulness must be well-established upon the four foundations, namely the body and so forth.

Since mindfulness thus well-established is capable of concentrating the mind on a single object after having investigated the courses of those phenomena that are either helpful or unhelpful to concentration,
right concentration (sammāsamādhi) follows immediately after right mindfulness.
It should be understood that it has been "taught. Thus, this Eightfold Path has also been explained as a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
427. Regarding the passage beginning with "perceiving forms internally," one is said to "perceive forms internally" by means of preliminary work (*parikamma*) upon internal forms.
For when performing preliminary work on blue internally, one does so either upon the hair, or upon bile, or upon the pupil of the eye.
When performing yellow preparatory work, he does it on the fat, the skin, the palms and soles of the hands and feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes;
when performing red preparatory work, he does it on the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes;
when performing white preparatory work, he does it on the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes.
Or he does so. However, that [image] is not well-blue, well-yellow, well-red, or well-white; it remains simply impure.
"One sees forms externally" refers to one for whom such preliminary work (*parikamma*) has arisen internally, while the sign (*nimitta*) is external.
Thus, by way of the preliminary work being internal and the absorption (*appanā*) being external, [he practices] "internally..."
"One percipient of forms sees forms externally"—this is what is said. "Limited" means unextended.
"Beautiful or ugly" means they are either beautiful or ugly; it should be understood that this base of mastery is stated specifically by way of their being limited.
"Having mastered them" means, for example, as if a person with a good appetite, having received only a spoonful of food, [were to think]: "What..."

Just as one who has gathered [food] together, thinking, "There is something here to be eaten," makes it into a single mouthful, even so a person preeminent in knowledge, possessing clear wisdom, thinks, "What is there to be attained in this limited object?
This is no burden for me," and having mastered those forms, he enters attainment; herein, absorption occurs simultaneously with the arising of the sign.
The meaning is "he causes [them] to reach. By the words "I know, I see," however, his mental application (*ābhoga*) is expressed.

And that [application] belongs to one who has emerged from attainment, not while within the attainment itself. "He possesses such perception" means he possesses such perception both by way of the perception of application and the perception of jhāna.
For the perception of mastery exists for him even while within the attainment, but the perception of application exists only for one who has emerged from the attainment.
“Immeasurable” (*appamāṇāni*) means having increased measure; the meaning is “vast. Regarding the word “having overcome” (*abhibhuyya*):
here, just as a gluttonous man, having received one large portion of food, does not regard it as large, thinking, “Let there be more;
what will this do for me?,” even so, a person supreme in knowledge, possessing clear wisdom, [does not regard the objects as large]. What...
"This must be attained here; this is not immeasurable, nor is there any burden for me in achieving one-pointedness of mind"—having thus overcome those [hindrances], he attains absorption.
The meaning is that he reaches absorption right along with the arising of the sign (*nimitta*).
"Perceiving the formless internally" means being devoid of the preliminary perception regarding internal form, either due to non-attainment or due to lack of interest.

“He sees forms externally”: one for whom even the preliminary work (*parikamma*) and the sign (*nimitta*) have arisen only externally is thus said to “perceive internally the ideation of the formless and see only forms externally,” by way of both the external preliminary work and absorption (*appanā*).
The rest here is exactly according to the method explained in the fourth base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*). Among these...
However, among the four types of persons, the limited [object] is presented for one of discursive-thought temperament, the immeasurable for one of delusion temperament,
the beautiful for one of hatred temperament, and the ugly for one of lust temperament. For these [objects] are suitable for them,
and that suitability has been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the "Description of Temperaments."
In the context of the five bases of mastery (*pañca abhibhāyatana*) and so forth, the term "blue" (*nīla*) is stated in a way that encompasses all [shades];

"blue-colored" (*nīlavaṇṇa*) is stated by way of color; "blue-appearing" (*nīlanidassana*) is stated by way of appearance, meaning they are seen as being entirely blue, with no visible gaps and no unmixed colors.
"Blue-shining" (*nīlanibhāsa*), however, is stated by way of radiance; it means they possess a blue radiance.
The meaning is "endowed with blue radiance. By this, he shows their extreme purity;
for it is precisely by way of pure color that these four bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*) are described. Furthermore, regarding the method of preparing the kasiṇa here, it is said:
"One who takes up the blue kasiṇa takes up the sign (*nimitta*) in something blue—whether in a flower, a cloth, or a colored mineral," and so forth.
The preliminary work (*parikamma*) and the method for attaining absorption (*appanā-vidhāna*) have all been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

However, it should be understood that these eight meditative attainments of the bases of mastery (*abhibhāyatana-jjhāna*) are both part of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), supports for the round, supports for insight (*vipassanā*), pleasant dwellings in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*), supports for the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and supports for cessation (*nirodha*);
yet they are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*) and not supramundane (*lokuttara*).

435. Regarding the phrase "one possessing form sees forms": here, "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the fine-material jhāna (*rūpajjhāna*) produced by way of the blue kasiṇa and so forth among the internal [objects] such as head-hairs;

one who has this is "possessing form" (*rūpī*). "He sees forms externally" means that he also sees external forms, such as the blue kasiṇa and so forth, with the eye of jhāna. By this, [it is shown] regarding the kasiṇas which have both internal and external objects.
The four fine-material-sphere jhānas have been shown for a person who has produced jhāna internally.
"Perceiving the formless internally" means not perceiving form internally; the meaning is that one has not produced fine-material-sphere jhāna with respect to one's own head hair and so forth.
By this, the fine-material-sphere jhānas of a person who has performed the preliminary work externally and produced jhāna externally are shown.
"Intent upon the beautiful alone": by this, the jhānas based on the well-purified color-kasinas, such as blue and so forth, are shown.

Although there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) toward "the beautiful" within the actual absorption (*appanā*), nevertheless, one who dwells having made the pure, beautiful kasina the object of focus comes to be described as "intent upon the beautiful. Therefore...
Thus was the teaching given. However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, it is asked: "How is it that one is intent upon the beautiful? This is liberation:
here, a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... [and so on] ...because loving-kindness has been developed, beings become free from repulsiveness.
With a mind imbued with compassion... [and so on] ...with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy... [and so on] ...with a mind imbued with equanimity..."
“He dwells having pervaded one quarter with his mind... [and so on] ...because equanimity has been developed, beings become non-repulsive.
Thus he is resolved upon what is beautiful; this is called liberation.
Regarding the phrases “entirely transcending perceptions of form,” and so forth, everything that ought to be said has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
443. Regarding the phrase "he develops the earth-kasina" (*pathavikasiṇa*): here, it is called a *kasina* in the sense of being "all-encompassing.

Earth itself as the *kasina* is the "earth-*kasina*" (*pathavikasiṇa*). This term is a designation for the preparatory earth, for the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*), for the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*), and also for the jhāna that has arisen taking that sign as its object.
However, in this context, it refers to that which has the earth-*kasina* as its object.
It is *jhāna* that is intended here, for it is this that he develops. This same method applies to the water-kasina and the others as well.

However, by one who develops these kasinas, having purified his virtue and being established in perfectly pure virtue, after cutting off whatever obstacle exists among the ten obstacles, [he should approach] a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) who bestows the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Having approached, each should take up whatever is suitable for them according to their own temperament;

then, abandoning a monastery that is unsuitable for the development of the kasiṇas and dwelling in one that is suitable, they should sever minor impediments and develop [the meditation subjects] without neglecting any part of the method of cultivation.
This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, is in the *Visuddhimagga*.
...was stated. For although the consciousness kasiṇa was not explicitly mentioned there, in terms of its actual meaning, it is the consciousness that occurs in the space kasiṇa.
Moreover, this is stated by way of the object, not by way of the attainment itself.
For when one develops this base of infinite consciousness by making "infinite consciousness" the object, one is said to be developing the consciousness kasiṇa. These too—
The ten kasinas are both bases for the round of existence, bases for the path, and bases for insight;

they are also for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life, bases for the higher knowledges (abhiññā), and bases for cessation (nirodha). However, they are exclusively mundane and not supramundane. 453.
"He develops the perception of foulness": the perception of foulness refers to [the meditation] upon the ten objects, beginning with the bloated corpse (uddhumātaka).

The meaning is that he develops, intensifies, and increases the perception accompanied by the first jhāna that has arisen; he causes what has not yet arisen to arise, and he preserves what has already arisen.
Furthermore, the entire method for developing the ten kinds of foulness (asubha) has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"He develops the perception of death" refers to conventional death (*sammuti-maraṇa*), momentary death (*khaṇika-maraṇa*), and death as total cutting off (*samuccheda-maraṇa*).
The meaning is that one develops the perception arising by taking the threefold death as its object; one produces it when unarisen and guards it when arisen.
Alternatively, the very mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) defined by the characteristics stated above is here called the "perception of death" (maraṇasaññā);
the meaning is that one develops, produces, and increases that. The method for its development has already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.

"He develops the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment" means that he develops, produces, and increases the perception arising in one who contemplates the nine kinds of repulsiveness, such as the repulsiveness of the act of going [to eat], with respect to physical nutriment consisting of the various types of what is eaten, drunk, and so forth.
The method for developing this is also explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. "The perception of non-delight in the entire world..."
"He develops" means he develops the perception of non-delight and the perception of weariness toward the entire world of the three realms.

"He develops the perception of impermanence" means he develops the perception that arises regarding the five aggregates as "impermanent," which discerns the rise, fall, and changeability of the five aggregates of clinging. "He develops the perception of suffering in what is impermanent" means...
He develops the perception arising as "suffering," which apprehends the characteristic of suffering defined as oppression within the five aggregates that are impermanent.

He develops the perception arising as "non-self" regarding what is suffering: he develops the perception arising as "non-self," which apprehends the characteristic of non-self defined as the mode of lack of mastery within the five aggregates that are suffering in the sense of being oppressed.
He develops the perception of abandoning: the fivefold abandoning is the object.

He develops the perception that arises having made [dispassion] its object. "He develops the perception of dispassion" means he develops the perception that arises having made the fivefold dispassion itself its object.
"He develops the perception of cessation" means he develops the perception that arises having made the cessation of formations its object;
some also say it is the perception that arises having made Nibbāna its object.
And here, by means of these three perceptions— the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of suffering in what is impermanent—

powerful insight (balavavipassanā) is described. Furthermore, by means of the ten perceptions beginning with "he develops the perception of impermanence," the very commencement of insight is described.
473. The recollections of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) and so forth have already had their meaning explained. 483.
"Accompanied by the first jhāna" (*paṭhamajjhānasahagata*) means gone together with, or occurring along with, the first jhāna; the sense is that it is associated with the first jhāna.
"He develops the faculty of faith" (*saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti*) means he develops the faculty of faith having made it accompanied by the first jhāna.
"Brūheti" means "increases. This method applies everywhere.
The commentary on the *Apara-accharā-saṅghāta-vagga*. 19.
Commentary on the *Kāyagatāsati-vagga*.
563. Regarding the phrase "pervaded by mind," there are two kinds of pervasion: pervasion by water and pervasion by the divine eye.
Therein, having attained the water-kasina, the pervasion by water is called "pervasion by water.
Even when the great ocean is thus pervaded, all rivers flowing into the sea are included within it. However, by increasing the light, [one sees] with the divine eye...

The vision of the entire ocean is called the pervasion of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). Even when the great ocean is thus pervaded, all the small rivers flowing into the great ocean are indeed included within it.
"Included within that" means they have entered into the interior of that bhikkhu’s meditation. Regarding the term *vijjābhāgiyā*:
here, they are called "partaking of true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiyā*) because they partake of true knowledge by way of association; they belong to the portion of true knowledge.

They are "pertaining to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*) because they operate within the sphere of true knowledge (*vijjā*). In this context, there are eight types of true knowledge: insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*), and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
According to the former sense, the mental states associated with these are also "pertaining to true knowledge.

According to the latter sense, any one among them is "true knowledge," while the rest are "pertaining to true knowledge. Thus, both true knowledge itself and the mental states associated with true knowledge are included.
They should be understood as pertaining to true knowledge (*vijjā*). 564.
"For the sake of great urgency" means for the purpose of a great sense of spiritual urgency. The same method applies to the following two phrases as well.
And here, "great urgency" refers to insight (*vipassanā*); "great goal" refers to the four paths; and "great security from bondage" (*mahāyogakkhema*)...
The four fruits of asceticism are called the "great goal. Alternatively, the path together with insight is called "great urgency";
the four fruits of asceticism are called the "great benefit"; and Nibbāna is called the "great security from bondage.

"For the sake of mindfulness and clear comprehension" means for the purpose of both mindfulness and knowledge. "For the attainment of knowledge and vision" means for the sake of the knowledge of the divine eye. "For dwelling in happiness in this very life" means...
"For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very present life" means for the sake of abiding in happiness within this very current existence.

"For the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation" means for the purpose of reviewing the fruit of true knowledge (*vijjā*) and liberation (*vimutti*). Here, "true knowledge" refers to the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*), and "liberation" refers to the remaining factors associated with it.
Their "fruit" is the fruit of Arhatship (*arahatta-phala*); thus, the meaning is "for the realization of that."
571. "The body, too, becomes tranquil" means that both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the physical body born of karma (*karajakāya*) become tranquil;

it becomes one whose agitation has subsided. "Applied thought and sustained thought, too"—these factors are said to be "tranquilized" by the second jhāna, but here it is stated with reference to their coarse subsiding.
"Entirely" means completely; the sense is that all [factors] without remainder. "Conducive to true knowledge" (*vijjābhāgiya*) means belonging to the portion of true knowledge.
These have already been shown below by way of analysis. 574.
"Ignorance is abandoned" means that the root of the round—the dense darkness, the great gloom of unknowing—is abandoned in eight instances.
"Knowledge arises" means that the knowledge of the path of Arahantship arises. "The conceit 'I am' is abandoned" means [the thought] "I am"...
The ninefold conceit is abandoned. "Latent tendencies" refers to the seven latent tendencies. "Fetters" refers to the ten fetters. 575.

"For the differentiation of wisdom" means for the purpose of reaching the differentiation of wisdom. "For final nibbāna through non-clinging" means for the purpose of realizing final nibbāna without conditions. 576.
"There is penetration of the manifold elements" means there is penetration of the characteristics of the eighteen elements. "Penetration of the diverse elements."

"It occurs" means that there is penetration of the characteristics through the diversity of those very eighteen elements. "The analytical knowledge of the various elements occurs" expresses the knowledge of the classification of elements.
Knowledge of the differentiation of elements is the wisdom that knows: "When this particular element is predominant, such-and-such a state arises.
Furthermore, this knowledge of the classification of elements does not belong to everyone; it belongs to the Buddhas alone.
It is not exhaustive. That was not taught in its entirety by the Perfectly Enlightened One. Why? Because there would be no purpose in teaching it. 584.
Regarding the sixteen phrases beginning with "for the attainment of wisdom," they are found in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
"Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma. These, monks, are the four things that, when developed..."
“...when cultivated, they lead to the acquisition of wisdom …pe… they lead to penetrative wisdom.
Having thus established the matrix, these [qualities] are explained in detail. For it has been said:
“They lead to the acquisition of wisdom. What is the acquisition of wisdom? It is the four knowledges of the paths and the four…”

The acquisition, attainment, reaching, mastery, realization, and fulfillment of the knowledges of the fruits, the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the seventy-three knowledges, and the seventy-seven knowledges—
which lead to the acquisition of wisdom— this is the acquisition of wisdom.
“They lead to the increase of wisdom. What is the increase of wisdom? The wisdom of the seven trainees (*sekha*) and of the virtuous worldling (*puthujjanakalyāṇaka*) increases;
the wisdom of the *arahant* is already increased and further increased. That they lead to the increase of wisdom—this is the increase of wisdom.
“They lead to the expansion of wisdom. What is the expansion of wisdom? [The wisdom] of the seven trainees and of the virtuous worldling... [increases].
And wisdom reaches abundance; the wisdom of an Arahant has reached abundance; they conduce to the abundance of wisdom—this is the abundance of wisdom.
They conduce to great wisdom. What is great wisdom? It is called "great wisdom" because it grasps great meanings, great phenomena...
[and so on] ...great linguistic expressions, great inspired insights, and the great aggregate of virtue.
The great aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; the great [distinctions between] the possible and the impossible;
the great dwellings and attainments; the great noble truths; the great foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, and bases of psychic power;
the great faculties, the great powers, the great factors of enlightenment, the great noble path, and the great...
Because it grasps the fruits of recluseship, the great direct knowledges, and the great ultimate goal—Nibbāna—it is "great wisdom" (*mahāpaññā*);
because they lead to the state of great wisdom, this is "great wisdom.
Because they lead to the state of broad wisdom: "What is broad wisdom? Wisdom that operates extensively across various aggregates (*khandha*) is broad wisdom."
Vast wisdom. Vast regarding the various elements; vast regarding the various sense bases; vast regarding the various modes of dependent origination;
vast regarding the various forms of emptiness and non-apprehension; vast regarding the various meanings, phenomena, definitions, and inspired eloquences;
vast regarding the various aggregates of virtue, and the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Vast...
Wisdom that operates regarding various places and non-places, various individual meditative abidings and attainments, various noble truths, various foundations of mindfulness,
right efforts, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment,
various noble paths, various fruits of recluseship, and various direct knowledges— this is called "wide wisdom" (*puthupaññā*). Wide.
“Broad wisdom” (*puthupaññā*) is so called because knowledge proceeds toward Nibbāna, the ultimate truth, having transcended those phenomena that are common to various people.
They lead to the state of broad wisdom; thus, this is “broad wisdom. They lead to the state of vast wisdom (*vipulapaññā*). “What is vast wisdom?
It is vast wisdom because it grasps a vast range of meanings... [and so on]...”
It is "vast wisdom" (*vipulapaññā*) because it grasps the vast ultimate truth, *nibbāna*. It is called "vast wisdom" because these [qualities] lead to the state of vast wisdom.
They lead to the state of profound wisdom (*gambhīrapaññā*). "What is profound wisdom? Knowledge that operates regarding the profound aggregates is profound wisdom.
The detailed explanation is similar to that of "wide wisdom" (*puthupaññā*). Regarding the profound ultimate truth, *nibbāna*...
Knowledge proceeds; thus it is profound wisdom (*gambhīrapaññā*). Because they lead to the state of profound wisdom, this is profound wisdom.
Because they lead to the state of peerless wisdom (*asāmantapaññā*), [it is said]: "What is peerless wisdom?

It is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) that has been attained, realized, and touched by the wisdom of a person through the discernment of meaning. Through the discernment of phenomena, language, and eloquence..."
The analytical knowledge of perspicuity has been attained, realized, and touched by his wisdom;
no one else is able to surpass him regarding meaning, phenomena, language, and perspicuity, and he cannot be surpassed by others—
thus he is one of peerless wisdom.
The wisdom of a virtuous worldling is far, very far, and extremely far from the wisdom of one who has entered the eighth stage; it is neither near nor proximate.
Compared to the virtuous worldling, one who has entered the eighth stage possesses incomparable wisdom.

The wisdom of one who has entered the eighth stage is far [from the wisdom] of a stream-enterer... [and so on] ...compared to one who has entered the eighth stage, the stream-enterer possesses incomparable wisdom. [The wisdom] of the stream-enterer...
The wisdom of a once-returner is far, very far, and extremely far from the wisdom of a non-returner;

it is not near, nor is it close. The wisdom of a non-returner is far, very far, and extremely far from the wisdom of an arahant; it is not near, nor is it close. The wisdom of an arahant is far, very far, and extremely far from the wisdom of a paccekabuddha;
it is not near, nor is it close. Compared to an arahant, a paccekabuddha possesses incomparable wisdom. And compared to a paccekabuddha, [the world] including the devas...
In this world, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is supreme, possessing peerless wisdom.

He is skilled in the analysis of wisdom and possesses penetrating knowledge... [as above] ...Having repeatedly formulated their questions, they approach the Tathāgata and ask them—questions that are profound and concealed—and those questions are explained and answered by him.
These have been pointed out by the Blessed One as causes, and when applied by the Blessed One, they succeed.
Then the Blessed One outshines others therein, namely, by means of wisdom; thus he is the foremost among those of peerless wisdom.
Because they lead to peerless wisdom, this is called "peerless wisdom" (*asāmantapaññā*).
“They lead to vast wisdom. What is vast wisdom? It is called vast wisdom because it overcomes lust; it is called vast wisdom because it has overcome [lust].

It is called vast wisdom because it overcomes hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, disparagement, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, aggression, conceit, arrogance, pride, negligence, and heedlessness.
It is "vast wisdom" (*bhūripaññā*) because it overcomes all defilements, all misconducts, all volitional formations, and all kamma leading to existence;
it is "vast wisdom" because it is one who has overcome [them]. It is "vast wisdom" because it is the wisdom that crushes lust, which is an enemy;
[it crushes] hatred, delusion... pe... all kamma leading to existence is an enemy, and it is the wisdom that crushes that enemy. Vast.
It is called "earth" (*pathavī*); one who is endowed with wisdom that is as vast, extensive, and abundant as that earth is "one of abundant wisdom" (*bhūripañño*).

Furthermore, this is a designation for wisdom itself—namely, "abundant," "intellect," and "guide"—and because these qualities lead to the state of being one of abundant wisdom, it is called "abundant wisdom.
It leads to an abundance of wisdom. "What is the abundance of wisdom? Here, someone holds wisdom in high esteem."
One who is characterized by wisdom, intent on wisdom, devoted to wisdom, whose banner is wisdom, whose emblem is wisdom, for whom wisdom is the dominant factor; one who abounds in investigation,
abounds in scrutiny, abounds in looking down, abounds in looking around, whose nature is to look all about,

who dwells in clarity, who is characterized by that, who values that, who abounds in that, who is inclined toward that, who tends toward that, who leans toward that, who is devoted to that, and for whom that is the dominant factor.

Just as one who values the group is called "one who is devoted to the group," and one who values robes, a bowl, or lodgings is called "one who is devoted to lodgings," so too here someone values wisdom and is characterized by wisdom... [and so on] ...having that as his dominant influence;
these things lead to an abundance of wisdom—this is the abundance of wisdom.
“They conduce to quick wisdom. What is quick wisdom? Quick wisdom is that by which one very quickly fulfills the precepts.

Quick wisdom is that by which one very quickly fulfills restraint of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the aggregate of virtue, and the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Swift wisdom is that which swiftly penetrates what is possible and what is impossible; it fulfills the meditative abidings and attainments; it penetrates the Noble Truths;

it develops the foundations of mindfulness; and it develops the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path—it is swift wisdom.
It is swift wisdom because it swiftly realizes the fruits of recluseship.

“Swift wisdom” (sīghapaññā) means that one penetrates the direct knowledges (abhiññā) very swiftly; it is swift wisdom because one realizes the ultimate goal, Nibbāna, very swiftly; those things which lead to the state of swift wisdom are called “swift wisdom.

“Quick wisdom” (lahupaññā) means that one fulfills the moral precepts (sīla) very quickly... [as above] ...those things which lead to the state of quick wisdom are called “quick wisdom. What is quick wisdom? It is quick wisdom because one fulfills the moral precepts very quickly... [as above] ...those things which lead to the state of quick wisdom are called “quick wisdom.”
“They lead to laughter-wisdom. What is laughter-wisdom?

Here, someone who is full of knowledge, full of contentment, full of laughter, and full of gladness fulfills the precepts; this is laughter-wisdom... [and so on] ...he realizes the ultimate goal, Nibbāna;
this is laughter-wisdom. Thus, they lead to laughter-wisdom—this is laughter-wisdom.
“They conduce to fleetness of wisdom. What is fleetness of wisdom? Whatever form—past, future, or present;
whatever feeling; whatever perception; whatever formations; whatever consciousness—past, future, or present;
internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near.

Or, the wisdom that swiftly impels [the mind] toward all consciousness as impermanent is "impelling wisdom" (*javanapaññā*); the wisdom that swiftly impels it toward [consciousness] as suffering and non-self is "impelling wisdom.
The eye... [and so on] ...aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, is swiftly impelled as impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
this is "impelling wisdom. Form, whether past, future, or present, is impermanent in the sense of destruction.

Having weighed, scrutinized, discerned, and made manifest that "suffering" is in the sense of being fearful, and "non-self" is in the sense of being coreless, one swiftly speeds toward the cessation of form, which is Nibbāna;
thus it is "swift wisdom. …pe… one swiftly speeds toward the cessation of aging-and-death, which is Nibbāna;
thus it is "swift wisdom. Form …pe… aging-and-death, whether past, future, or present, is subject to destruction.

Having weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that [all things] are subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation, one swiftly speeds toward Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death;
thus it is "swift wisdom" (*javanapaññā*). Because they lead to the state of swift wisdom, this is called swift wisdom.
Because they lead to the state of sharp wisdom: "What is sharp wisdom? It is sharp wisdom because it quickly cuts off the defilements."

She does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, eradicates, and brings to non-existence any arisen thought of sensual desire, thought of ill will, or thought of cruelty, nor any evil unwholesome states as they arise; thus she is one of keen wisdom.
She does not tolerate, abandons, dispels, [and eradicates] any arisen lust, hatred, or delusion... [and so on] ...nor any kamma leading to existence.
It brings about their disappearance and leads them to non-existence; thus it is "sharp wisdom" (*tikkhapaññā*).

On a single seat, the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), and the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) are attained, realized, and touched through wisdom;
thus it is "sharp wisdom. Because they lead to the state of sharp wisdom, this is called "sharp wisdom."
“They conduce to penetrative wisdom. What is penetrative wisdom?
Here, someone is full of agitation, full of terror, full of distaste, full of dissatisfaction, and full of disenchantment toward all conditioned phenomena;
he does not delight in them, but turns his face away from all conditioned phenomena. He penetrates the mass of greed that has never before been pierced and never before been shattered.
"It pierces" means penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*). It pierces and shatters the mass of hatred, the mass of delusion, anger, resentment...
[and so on] ...all kamma leading to existence that has never before been pierced and never before shattered;
thus it is "penetrative wisdom. That which leads to the state of penetrative wisdom—this is penetrative wisdom.
The meaning here should be understood according to the very same method stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

For the only difference is that there the plural is used, whereas here the singular is used; the rest is exactly the same. Moreover, these sixteen types of great wisdom are explained as being a mixture of both mundane and supramundane.
Commentary on the Chapter on Mindfulness Directed to the Body. 20. Commentary on the Chapter on the Deathless (Amatavagga), Verses 600–611.
"They do not partake of the deathless, monks" means they do not partake of Nibbāna, which is free from death.
The meaning is as follows. But surely Nibbāna is supramundane (*lokuttara*), whereas mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is mundane (*lokiya*);

how then, while enjoying that [mindfulness], do they enjoy the Deathless (*amata*)? Because it is to be attained by developing that [mindfulness]. For one who develops mindfulness directed to the body attains the Deathless, while one who does not develop it does not attain it.
Therefore it was said thus. By this same method, the meaning is to be understood in all instances.
And here, "neglected" (*viraddha*) means not attained; "undertaken" (*āraddha*) means fulfilled. "They were negligent" (*pamādiṃsu*) means they are heedless.
"Forgotten" (*pamuṭṭha*) means lost from memory, forgotten, or ruined. "Cultivated" (*āsevita*) means practiced from the beginning.
"Developed" (*bhāvita*) means increased. "Made much of" (*bahulīkata*) means done again and again. "Not fully understood" (*anabhiññāta*) means not known through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
"Unknown": "Not fully understood" means not fully understood by way of the full understanding of the known (*ñātapariññā*). "Unrealized" means not made manifest before one's eyes.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout. This concludes the commentary on the Chapter on the Deathless (*Amatavagga*).
The commentary on the First Chapter, consisting of one thousand discourses, from the Manorathapūraṇī,
the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is completed.
